title: The Moral Benefits of Capitalism
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that broadly shared economic growth under capitalism can reduce poverty while encouraging opportunity, tolerance, social mobility, and moral progress.
searchSummary: Examines whether capitalism can produce moral benefits rather than being inherently anti-Christian. Drawing on Benjamin Friedman's work, Ehrman argues that broadly shared economic growth can improve health, opportunity, tolerance, social mobility, hope, and altruism, while stagnation and concentrated gains foster resentment and exclusion. Because Jesus never addressed modern economic systems, the relevant question is how his values might guide conduct within capitalism and whether inherited religious wisdom can still inform modern economic life.

title: Is Capitalism Anti-Christian?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reconsiders whether capitalism is anti-Christian by applying Jesus' moral teachings to human behavior rather than condemning modern economic systems themselves.
searchSummary: Reconsiders Ehrman's youthful conviction that capitalism was morally corrupt and incompatible with Jesus' teaching. He regrets judging his business-minded father through an uninformed zero-sum view and now distinguishes an economic system from the behavior of people within it, noting that capitalism can both exploit and reduce poverty. Since capitalism did not exist in Jesus' world, Ehrman proposes evaluating modern conduct by Jesus' values rather than declaring any political or economic structure inherently Christian or anti-Christian.

title: September 2026 Gold Q&A
author: jennao
description: Announces the September 2026 member Q&A and provides instructions for submitting questions and participating in the live Zoom session.

title: Martyrs, Forgers, and Textual Scholars:  Intriguing Questions From Readers
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers reader questions about miraculous martyrdom stories, the disputed authorship of the Pastoral Epistles, and the future of textual criticism.
searchSummary: Answers reader questions about martyr stories, the use of secretaries to defend Pauline authorship, and the future of textual criticism. Martyr narratives attribute extraordinary composure to faith, though their literary portrayals need not report historical experience accurately. No ancient parallel supports a secretary independently composing lengthy first-person letters such as the Pastorals for Paul, while future textual scholarship may illuminate manuscripts and scribal practices without greatly changing the reconstructed New Testament text.

title: Flipping a Coin. Cephas and Peter: One Person or Two?
author: BDEhrman
description: Questions whether Peter and Cephas were different people, emphasizing the improbability that two early Christians shared the same rare nickname.

title: Other Suggestions That Peter and Cephas Were Two Different People
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Paul may distinguish Cephas from Peter by portraying Cephas as a convert who received a resurrection appearance.

title: Did Paul Know that Peter and Cephas were Two Different People?
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Paul's distinct references to Peter and Cephas in Galatians suggest they were different people rather than two names for one apostle.

title: Paying Your Religious Dues:  The Studied Indifference of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Interprets Matthew's temple-tax story as showing Jesus' indifference to earthly institutions because God's coming kingdom remained his central concern.
searchSummary: Examines Matthew's story of Jesus paying the temple tax through a coin found in a fish. Although the miracle is probably legendary, Jesus' willingness to pay rather than give needless offense may preserve his relative indifference to political and economic systems when they did not conflict with God's will. Matthew may have used the episode after 70 CE to encourage Jewish believers to tolerate Rome's humiliating replacement tax while focusing on conduct suited to God's approaching kingdom.

title: Were Peter and Cephas the Same Person?
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys early Christian evidence that some writers regarded Peter and Cephas as different people. These traditions challenge their customary identification despite John 1:42.

title: Problems of Suffering and Why Gospels Started Being Written: Questions from Readers
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers reader questions about suffering and God, evaluating miracle claims historically, and the emergence of written Gospels after Paul's death.
searchSummary: Answers questions about whether extreme suffering undermines belief in an all-loving, all-powerful God, whether miracle stories were intended symbolically, and why Gospel writing expanded after Paul's lifetime. Ehrman argues that widespread gratuitous suffering challenges a God who both governs and loves the world, historical methods cannot make miracles the most probable explanation, and symbolic authorial intent requires evidence. He attributes the Gospel-writing surge after 70 partly to disappearing eyewitnesses and competing traditions about Jesus.

title: What Did Jesus’s Violent Action in the Temple Actually Mean?
author: BDEhrman
description: Interprets Jesus' Temple disruption as an apocalyptic symbol of its coming destruction rather than an attack on Judaism or social reform.
searchSummary: Interprets Jesus's disruption of commerce in the Jerusalem temple as an enacted parable of its coming destruction rather than an attack on Judaism or a program of reform. The money changers and animal sellers enabled sacrifices required by Jewish law, making simple opposition to their presence inadequate. Following E. P. Sanders, Bart argues that Jesus symbolically announced God's imminent judgment, when the present religious and political order would be overthrown through divine intervention.

title: Blog Dinner in NYC, September 1.  Interested?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a September 1 dinner in New York City for blog members and provides attendance details.

title: Prophetic Condemnations of Jews Within Judaism Before Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Places Jesus' Temple protest within Jewish prophetic condemnations of sacrifice without justice, distinguishing it from later Christian anti-Judaism.

title: Gist and Exaggeration: Jesus and the Cleansing of the Temple
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that the Gospels exaggerate Jesus' Temple action but preserve a smaller historical protest that attracted the authorities' attention.

title: Render Unto Caesar: Jesus’s Indifference to Human Governments and Economies
author: BDEhrman
description: Interprets 'Render unto Caesar' as reflecting Jesus' apocalyptic indifference to Roman government and economics while affirming that human lives belong to God.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus' instruction to render Caesar's things to Caesar reflects indifference to human governments rather than support for a political system. Because Jesus expected God soon to overthrow every corrupt earthly authority and establish the kingdom through the Son of Man, neither rebellion nor reform was his priority. Caesar could receive the coin bearing his image, while people, made in God's image, owed their whole lives to God and should focus on serving him.

title: Was Jesus’s Crucifixion One Big Mistake?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines two Gnostic accounts in which Christ escaped crucifixion: Basilides's identity-switch story involving Simon of Cyrene and the Coptic Apocalypse of Peter's claim that only Jesus's physical form suffered.

title: The Triumphal Entry and Jesus’s Mistaken Identity
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Jesus expected to rule God's coming kingdom but was crucified when authorities mistook his apocalyptic claim for political insurrection.
searchSummary: Explains Jesus's entry into Jerusalem and execution through his apocalyptic understanding of messiahship. Jesus expected God to overthrow evil, establish an earthly kingdom, and install him as its king, while his disciples would share rule over Israel. Although Jesus neither organized rebellion nor sought political reform, Jerusalem's leaders and Pilate interpreted his royal claim as insurrection. Bart concludes that Rome executed a pacifist apocalyptic revolutionary because authorities misunderstood the mechanism of his expected kingdom.

title: The Implausibility of the Triumphal Entry
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Roman authorities would have suppressed the Gospels' public messianic triumphal entry, although Jesus probably entered Jerusalem before his arrest.
searchSummary: Argues that the Gospel accounts of Jesus' triumphal entry cannot be historical as narrated, because Roman authorities would have immediately suppressed crowds publicly acclaiming a new Jewish king during Passover. The evangelists use royal prophecies and messianic titles to portray Jesus entering Jerusalem to inaugurate God's kingdom. Jesus probably did enter the city, but the public spectacle conflicts with what is known about Roman security and his later arrest.

title: Understanding Jesus:  A Swedish Podcast Interview
author: jennao
description: Announces a Swedish podcast interview about Love Thy Stranger in which Bart discusses the book's principal arguments and supporting evidence.
searchSummary: Introduces a Swedish podcast interview about the principal arguments of Ehrman's Love Thy Stranger and the evidence he uses to support them. The conversation forms one episode of a multipart series and offers an extended exchange that Ehrman found especially interesting. Although the host welcomes listeners in Swedish, the interview changes to English after roughly ninety seconds, making the shared recording accessible to the blog's English-speaking audience.

title: Religion, Politics, and Resistance in Jesus’ Day
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how inseparable religion and politics shaped Jesus' opposition to Roman and Jewish authorities and his expectation that God would replace their rule.
searchSummary: Distinguishes Jesus's condemnation of existing authorities from a program to reform or replace them through human action. In the ancient world, political and religious power were inseparable: Roman government rested on state cults, while Jerusalem's priestly leadership administered both temple and civic life. Bart argues that Jesus opposed both systems because his apocalyptic worldview anticipated their imminent destruction by God and the establishment of a wholly new order, not because he advocated institutional change.

title: Thoughts on Jesus and Activism.  What Do You Think?
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Jesus opposed unjust authorities but focused on repentance and care for sufferers rather than reform because God's kingdom was imminent.
searchSummary: Explores the tension between Jesus' condemnation of the existing order and his lack of a program for political reform or revolution. Jesus expected God, not human activists, to destroy corrupt governments and establish a perfect kingdom, while followers repented, aided sufferers, and lived according to God's will. Taxes, rulers, and institutions were temporary concerns; resisting evil mattered, but trying to repair a system destined for divine replacement did not occupy Jesus' apocalyptic mission.

title: Jesus the Pacifist
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Jesus rejected armed resistance to Rome and treats the disciple's sword at his arrest as a distorted historical memory.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus was a pacifist rather than an armed revolutionary, despite the Gospel story of a disciple wielding a sword at his arrest. Jesus' numerous teachings on love, peace, and nonviolence fit his apocalyptic expectation that God would overthrow Rome without human assistance, while the disciples' failure to be arrested makes an actual armed defense implausible. The garden episode may have developed to illustrate the saying that those who live by the sword die by it.

title: The Indifference of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Jesus' apocalyptic indifference to ordinary social, economic, and political concerns with Stoic detachment, arguing that the expected arrival of God's kingdom made earthly attachments expendable.
searchSummary: Compares Jesus' attitude toward worldly concerns with Stoic indifference while emphasizing their different foundations. Stoics sought inner well-being by detaching from uncontrollable externals, whereas Jesus demanded sacrifice of possessions, family, security, status, and even life for God's approaching earthly kingdom. Because divine intervention would soon replace the present political, economic, and social order with paradise, Jesus treated modern concerns about personal happiness and preferred systems as temporary matters that could not compare with gaining the kingdom.

title: The Sadness of Beginning to Doubt
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts how biblical contradictions and questions about Jesus' divinity, especially sayings found only in John, began Bart's painful movement from evangelical Christianity.
searchSummary: Recounts the painful beginnings of Ehrman's doubts about Jesus' divinity while studying at Princeton Seminary. Recognizing biblical contradictions and the absence of explicit divine claims outside John weakened convictions central to his evangelical faith, leading him to question whether Jesus actually made John's exclusive claims. A conversation with his former pastor Evan Goranson shows the emotional cost of admitting that historical evidence could overturn beliefs cherished by people he loved.

title: Was Moses Called God?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Exodus and Philo of Alexandria could portray Moses as functioning as God, becoming divine, or attaining immortality, providing a Jewish precedent for calling an exalted human divine.
searchSummary: Explains Jewish traditions in which Moses could function as God, become divine, or even appear as a preexistent heavenly being. Exodus calls Moses God to Aaron, while Philo describes him as God's uniquely perfect prophet, heir, king, and divinely transformed immortal whose contemplation joins him closely to the Creator. These traditions provide a Jewish precedent for granting a human divine status without identifying him as God Almighty.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: The King of Israel Was Called … God?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Psalms and Isaiah portray Israel's human king as a divine figure without equating him with God Almighty.
searchSummary: Shows that biblical writers could call Israel's human king God without equating him with God Almighty. Psalms 110 and 45 place the king beside God and directly address him as God, while Isaiah 9 gives a Davidic ruler titles including Mighty God and Everlasting Father. Such royal language reflects graded divinity and divine adoption, providing an ancient Jewish framework for later claims that Jesus possessed God's status, authority, and power.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: Jewish Precedents for Jesus Becoming God
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys Jewish and biblical precedents for figures other than the one God being called divine, setting up an explanation for early claims about Jesus' divine status.
searchSummary: Explains how ancient Jewish monotheists could regard the king of Israel as both God's son and, in a qualified sense, divine. Biblical traditions call angels and Israel God's sons, while 2 Samuel 7, Psalms 89 and 2 portray the Davidic king as specially chosen, adopted, or begotten by God. This uniquely close relationship prepared the conceptual ground for calling an exalted human God without identifying him as the one Almighty God.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: How Can Monotheists Think a Human Could Become God?
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses early Jewish texts about righteous humans becoming angels to explain how Jewish monotheists could imagine a human being exalted to divine status.
searchSummary: Demonstrates that ancient Jewish monotheism allowed righteous humans to be transformed into angelic beings. Second Baruch expects the righteous to surpass angels, 2 Enoch portrays Enoch receiving heavenly clothing and becoming indistinguishable from an angel, and other traditions exalt Moses above celestial beings. These examples show that Jesus' Jewish followers could understand a mortal as becoming divine without abandoning belief in one supreme God.

title: August 2026 Gold Q&A Announcement
author: jennao
description: Announces the August 2026 Gold and Platinum member Q&A session and provides details for submitting questions and joining the live Zoom event.

title: Personal Faith, Textual Problems, and the Miracles of Jesus: More Readers’ Questions
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers reader questions about faith and biblical criticism, a difficult textual variant in 2 Peter, and how miracle stories about Jesus may have developed.
searchSummary: Answers questions about sustaining Christian faith amid biblical problems, the disputed ending of 2 Peter 3:10, and the origin of Jesus' miracle stories. Ehrman separates faith from biblical inerrancy, explains why the strongly attested reading found remains unresolved despite the preference for harder readings, and argues that miracle traditions developed as sincere rumor rather than deliberate fraud after followers came to regard the risen Jesus as God's Son and evidence of the approaching kingdom.

title: How the Year 1517 Revolutionized Biblical Studies
author: BDEhrman
description: Traces how Luther's 95 Theses and appeal to scriptural authority helped create conditions for historical-critical study of canon, authorship, and biblical discrepancies.
searchSummary: Explains how Luther's 1517 protest against indulgences and later doctrine of Scripture alone helped create conditions for historical-critical biblical study. Treating the text rather than church authority as decisive encouraged original-language analysis, literal interpretation in historical context, comparison of authors, recognition of contradictions, and investigation of authorship and canon formation. Luther did not anticipate modern criticism, but his willingness to question some New Testament books and reject harmonization weakened inherited interpretive controls.

title: Two Years that Transformed the World of Biblical Studies.
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Erasmus's first published Greek New Testament helped launch modern biblical scholarship and raised the textual questions that led to New Testament textual criticism.
searchSummary: Explains how Erasmus's 1516 Greek New Testament helped initiate modern textual criticism. Printing the original language encouraged historical interpretation, but Erasmus's rushed edition relied on a few late manuscripts and even translated missing Revelation verses back from Latin, exposing uncertainty about the original wording. Later scholars collected variant readings until John Mill documented thirty thousand differences, forcing Protestant readers who privileged Scripture's exact words to develop methods for reconstructing the text from competing manuscripts.

title: The Martyrdom of Polycarp (Another Book of the Apostolic Fathers): In a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces The Martyrdom of Polycarp as the earliest surviving Christian account of a martyr's trial and death outside the New Testament.
searchSummary: Examines the Martyrdom of Polycarp as the earliest surviving Christian martyr narrative outside the New Testament and as an argument for a particular approach to martyrdom. Its parallels with Jesus, miracles, and legendary details portray Polycarp's death as divinely approved, while the failed volunteer Quintus warns Christians not to seek execution. The account also reflects emerging beliefs about relics, martyr anniversaries, eternal reward, Jewish responsibility, and cosmic conflict, although its date and eyewitness claims remain disputed.

title: 2 Clement (one of the “Apostolic Fathers”) in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces 2 Clement as the earliest surviving Christian homily outside the New Testament and explains its significance.
searchSummary: Explains 2 Clement as the earliest surviving Christian homily outside the New Testament rather than a second letter by Clement of Rome. The sermon interprets Scripture for its congregation, cites both familiar and otherwise unknown sayings of Jesus, and urges repentance, self-control, charity, and preparation for judgment in response to salvation. Its use of oral traditions and developing scriptural authorities, congregational setting, theology, and presbyteral leadership suggest an anonymous mid-second-century Christian community.

title: Christian Justifications for Lying
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether early Christian forgers could justify deception as a noble lie, contrasting that view with Augustine's rejection of all lying.
searchSummary: Examines whether lying can be morally justified and applies the question to Christian forgery. Ancient thinkers defended noble lies that protected or benefited others, while Augustine rejected deception under every circumstance. Ehrman considers modern and ancient examples, including authors who concealed their identities to promote what they regarded as truth. He concludes that most religious forgeries did not protect anyone from serious harm and violated the Golden Rule by deceiving readers whom the authors themselves would not want to deceive.

title: Ancient Christians Who Wanted to Lie
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores why ancient Christian authors might have considered lying acceptable when promoting what they regarded as religious truth.
searchSummary: Explores how ancient thinkers, including Christians, evaluated lies told for beneficial ends. Aristotle emphasized truthfulness, while Plato, Socrates, Clement, and Origen allowed medicinal or protective deception; Scripture itself portrays lies that save lives or advance divine purposes. Augustine alone insisted that lying was never permissible. Ehrman asks whether Christian forgers similarly believed that conveying religious truth justified false authorship, while acknowledging that their motives cannot be recovered and that exposed readers would probably have condemned them as liars.

title: Evangelicals Who Lie to Promote the(ir) Truth….
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the First-Century Mark controversy to argue that some evangelical advocates defend their views by repeating or promoting false claims.
searchSummary: Revisits evangelical manuscript collector Scott Carroll's false claim that Ehrman dates Mark to about 200 CE and regards it as the last Gospel. Ehrman has consistently dated Mark to around 70 and considered it the first Gospel written. He argues that Carroll used the rumored first-century fragment to portray mainstream scholarship dishonestly, even though the fragment was later dated to the late second or early third century and contains only a few partial verses.

title: Free Course on … Hell!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a free online course on Jesus, the Bible, and the development of Christian ideas about hell and eternal punishment.
searchSummary: Announces a course examining where the Christian belief in hell as eternal conscious torment originated. Ehrman argues that neither the Bible nor Jesus teaches that disembodied souls divide between heavenly paradise and endless punishment, and that misleading translations have encouraged that reading. The lectures trace how second-century Christianity replaced Jewish expectations of bodily resurrection and an earthly kingdom with non-Jewish ideas of immortal souls experiencing permanent blessing or despair, concluding that Jesus' teaching offers no reason to fear eternal torment.

title: Exonerating Pilate to Implicate the Jews
author: BDEhrman
description: Traces how Christian accounts increasingly exonerated Pilate while shifting blame for Jesus' death onto Jews and Jewish leaders.

title: Jesus the Forager
author: BDEhrman
description: Tests whether Gospel passages support the idea that Jesus' group sometimes survived by foraging during the ministry.

title: Foraging in the World of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why foraging may fit the economic world of Jesus, Galilee, and the largely agrarian Roman Empire.

title: Pro-Roman Jews in First-Century Palestine? Guest Post by Christopher Stanley
author: jennao
description: Introduces Christopher Stanley's argument that some Jews in first-century Palestine may have opposed revolt and sympathized with Rome.
searchSummary: Examines Jews in first-century Palestine who opposed the revolt of 66-73 CE or actively supported Rome. Drawing on Josephus, Christopher Stanley identifies elites, priests, merchants, soldiers, city councils, suppliers, and refugees whose interests or loyalties aligned with Roman rule rather than rebellion. His historical novel uses this neglected evidence to imagine the divided loyalties of a Galilean Jewish trader caught between ancestral attachment, Roman stability, and revolutionary pressure.

title: Did Jesus Have Wealthy Donors?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether wealthy donors supported Jesus' group, especially in light of Luke's reference to women who provided for the ministry.

title: How Did Jesus and His Disciples Get Enough to Eat?
author: BDEhrman
description: Raises the historical question of how Jesus and the Twelve ate while living as itinerant preachers without ordinary income.

title: The Execution of Pontius Pilate for Killing Jesus (!)
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents and contextualizes the apocryphal Handing Over of Pilate, where Pilate is punished by Tiberius but repents and turns to Christ.
searchSummary: Explains the Handing Over of Pilate, a fictional sequel to Pilate's report in which Emperor Tiberius condemns the governor for crucifying Jesus. Pilate destroys pagan idols by invoking Christ, blames Jewish leaders, repents, and converts before his execution; a heavenly voice blesses him, and an angel receives his severed head. The story exalts Jesus, transfers responsibility away from Pilate, and helps explain why some Eastern churches eventually honored Pilate as a saint.

title: July 2026 Gold Q&A Announcement
author: jennao
description: Announces the July 2026 Gold and Platinum member Q&A session and provides the meeting details for participants.

title: A Blog Dinner In Central London July 15.  Wanna Come?
author: BDEhrman
description: Invites blog members to a July 15 dinner in central London and explains the logistics for attending.

title: Did Pontius Pilate Write a Letter Explaining Why He Crucified Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces and translates the apocryphal Report of Pilate, a letter portraying Jesus' trial, death, and resurrection from Pilate's perspective.
searchSummary: Examines the Report of Pontius Pilate, a late fictional letter to Emperor Tiberius recounting Jesus' miracles, crucifixion, resurrection, and the supernatural events surrounding them. The narrative portrays Pilate as reluctant and largely innocent while assigning responsibility to Jesus' Jewish opponents, some of whom receive immediate divine punishment. Although the surviving work may date to the fourth or fifth century, references by Tertullian show that Christians imagined some form of Pilate correspondence much earlier.

title: Jesus and the Gospel of John: Some Readers’ Good Questions
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers reader questions about the Gospel of John, including its presentation of Jesus, authorship, and historical reliability.
searchSummary: Answers two questions about the Gospel of John: whether John son of Zebedee could have produced it through a secretary, and whether its divine claims preserve Jesus' own words. Ancient secretaries normally recorded dictation rather than composing polished works for illiterate clients, leaving no evidence for the proposed authorship model. Because explicit declarations of divinity appear only in John and not the Synoptics or other early sources, they are unlikely to be historical.

title: How Do You Publish a Book for a General Audience?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the practical difficulties scholars face when trying to publish trade books for general readers.
searchSummary: Explains why first-time authors face a publishing Catch-22 when seeking a professional trade publisher. Publishers and reputable literary agents prefer writers with proven sales, yet unknown authors often need an agent before a publisher will even examine a proposal. Ehrman contrasts this barrier with his own entry through established scholarly publishing and advises that an exceptionally strong prospectus, sample chapter, and credible agent offer the narrowest conventional route for newcomers.

title: The Realities of Publishing a Scholarly Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how scholarly publishing depends on academic credentials, specialized training, and the expectations of academic publishers.
searchSummary: Explains why academic presses rarely consider scholarly books from authors without advanced credentials in the relevant field. Ehrman details the years of languages, seminars, examinations, original research, dissertation writing, and oral defenses required for a doctorate in early Christianity. He argues that this training equips scholars to produce genuinely new knowledge and that academic publishers use credentials and peer review to protect scholarship, even though anyone remains free to publish ideas elsewhere.

title: Memory of My Past: My First Girlfriend and Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts a high-school memory of becoming born again and trying to convert a Jewish former girlfriend.
searchSummary: Recalls Ehrman's first attempt as a newly born-again sixteen-year-old to convert his Jewish former girlfriend. Having learned that salvation required personally accepting Jesus, he could not answer her simple question about why someone who already had God needed Jesus and offered an embarrassingly weak response. The encounter exposes how little he understood his new faith and helped spur the intense biblical and theological study that soon took him to Moody Bible Institute.

title: Did Paul Have an Exalted View of Himself?
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Paul understood himself as specially appointed to bring Gentiles into God's people without adopting Jewish law.
searchSummary: Explains that Paul viewed his apostolic mission as a divine calling to bring gentiles into God's people without requiring them to become Jews. Paul interpreted his vision of the risen Jesus through prophetic passages in Isaiah and Zechariah about the nations worshiping Israel's God. His experience changed his understanding of Jesus and Jewish law while preserving his conviction that he remained a faithful Jew.

title: The Most Likely Capitalist Parable of Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Interprets the Parable of the Talents and Pounds as apocalyptic teaching rather than an endorsement of capitalist investing.
searchSummary: Rejects a capitalist reading of the Parable of the Talents by interpreting it within Matthew's apocalyptic discourse. The absent master represents Jesus, the entrusted wealth represents his message, and the servants must spread that message while awaiting his delayed return and judgment rather than pursue material profit. Luke makes the delay explicit, and both Gospels oppose accumulating possessions; the parable's assumption of an unexpectedly long absence also suggests that later Christians placed it on Jesus' lips.

title: The Parable of the Sower as Advice for Capitalists
author: BDEhrman
description: Rejects capitalist readings of the Parable of the Sower by reading it in Mark's context as a warning against wealth.
searchSummary: Rejects interpreting Mark's parable of the sower as capitalist advice about investing for maximum returns. Mark says Jesus used parables to prevent outsiders from understanding, then explains the soils as different responses to God's message: some reject it, some abandon it under pressure, some let wealth and worldly concerns choke it, and some bear abundant fruit. The parable predates capitalism but challenges modern attempts to make Jesus endorse comfort, possessions, and financial accumulation.

title: The Capitalist Parables of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques attempts to make Jesus into a capitalist, socialist, or Marxist by stressing how interpreters often remake Jesus in their own image.
searchSummary: Examines how interpreters project modern economic commitments onto Jesus by developing possible capitalist readings of the Sower and the Talents. The Sower can resemble diversified investment or careful market selection, while the Talents appears to praise bold management that doubles entrusted capital. These plausible analogies illustrate how easily parables can become support for contemporary capitalism, but the post leaves open whether either reading reflects Jesus' meaning or the Gospel writers' literary contexts for resolution in the following discussion.

title: Why Not Believe in a God Who is *Not* Active in the World?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why belief in a noninterventionist God does not resolve the problem of suffering that led to atheism.
searchSummary: Considers why rejecting an active, all-loving and all-powerful God should lead to atheism rather than belief in an uninvolved deity. Ehrman grants that deism is conceivable but argues that belief in any divine being requires positive reasons, while extreme suffering counts against traditional theism and no observable intervention supports an inactive God. He suggests deism often functions as an emotionally reassuring fallback after theodicy weakens theism, not as a conclusion supported by independent evidence.

title: How To Figure Out If a Miracle Happened…  Questions from Readers
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers reader questions about historical evaluation of miracle claims, Paul's report of 500 resurrection witnesses, and the causes of Roman persecution at Lyon.
searchSummary: Answers three reader questions illustrating how historians evaluate difficult claims. Even if miracles are possible, ordinary explanations for testimony remain more probable, so history cannot establish supernatural causation; Paul's unique report of five hundred resurrection witnesses is therefore more likely an unchecked rumor than proof. A separate response attributes the Lyon persecution to Christians' refusal of public cult and accusations of godlessness, cannibalism, and incest, rather than to a rival economic system.

title: More Criticisms of the Criticisms of the Gospel of John (by John! Spong)
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues engaging John Shelby Spong's interpretation of the Gospel of John, especially Spong's claims about John's Christology and symbolism.
searchSummary: Challenges John Shelby Spong's claim that the Fourth Gospel discourages literal readings and instead expresses mystical human transformation. John's misunderstandings, extravagant miracles, and incarnation theology are meant to be taken seriously within the narrative: Jesus is God become human, whose incarnation enables believers to become God's children. Spong's nonliteral interpretation serves a modern pastoral effort to preserve Christian spirituality, whereas historical interpretation must explain what John's author intended in the ancient text.

title: Controversies About the Gospel of John: The Views of John Spong
author: BDEhrman
description: Engages John Shelby Spong's skeptical reading of John and compares Spong's public presentation of scholarship with critical views of the Gospel's historicity.
searchSummary: Evaluates John Shelby Spong's skeptical claims about the Fourth Gospel's authorship, Jesus traditions, signs, and characters. The Gospel was not written by John son of Zebedee, and its signs do not preserve historical events; its Jesus chiefly reveals his heavenly identity and performs signs that validate those claims. Yet unhistorical characters such as Nicodemus or the Samaritan woman need not have been knowingly invented or presented as fiction, so historicity and authorial intention must remain distinct.

title: Radical Skeptic (about the Bible) and Episcopal Bishop: John Spong
author: BDEhrman
description: Remembers John Shelby Spong as an Episcopal bishop who brought critical biblical scholarship to broad Christian audiences.
searchSummary: Profiles Episcopal bishop John Shelby Spong as a public advocate for historically critical Christianity. Spong rejected biblical literalism, the physical resurrection, virgin birth, and traditional doctrines while remaining a Christian leader who urged believers to integrate modern knowledge with faith. Ehrman notes that Spong was not a professional biblical scholar and did not advance academic research, but values his courage in communicating scholarship to churches and challenging fundamentalism's claim to define authentic Christianity.

title: Questions on Proving the Resurrection and Sundry Other Things
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers reader questions about proving the resurrection, eyewitness claims, composite Pauline letters, miracles, and John the Baptist.
searchSummary: Answers varied questions about resurrection, transmitted testimony, composite Pauline letters, thermodynamics, and John the Baptizer. It argues that resurrection is a matter of faith that historians can neither prove nor disprove, while a claim to use eyewitness writing requires investigation because every link may misunderstand, distort, or invent. It also explains why 2 Corinthians and possibly Philippians were deliberately compiled, and why supernatural agency is a theological presupposition rather than a historical conclusion.

title: These Are Weird Parables.  Do They Make Sense?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces two puzzling Lukan parables about wealth, the Rich Fool and the Dishonest Steward, and asks how they fit together.
searchSummary: Introduces two puzzling parables found only in Luke: the rich fool who builds larger barns and the dishonest steward who reduces his master's debts. The post explains why their apparent lessons about wealth and planning for the future seem difficult to reconcile. It invites readers to consider why Jesus condemns the prudent landowner yet praises the dishonest steward before offering a solution in a later post.

title: Did the Doctrine of Predestination Lead to Capitalism?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Max Weber's argument that Protestant predestination, especially in Calvinist thought, helped shape the modern capitalist drive for disciplined profit.

title: Predestination!  What do you think?
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys biblical passages and theological problems connected with predestination, grace, divine sovereignty, free will, Augustine, Calvin, and double predestination.

title: Doesn’t Goodness Point to the Existence of God?  And Gospel Perplexities.  Good Readers’ Questions
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to reader questions about goodness and suffering, Luke's presentation of Jesus' divine sonship, and how anonymous gospels circulated.
searchSummary: Responds to questions about whether beauty and goodness support God's existence, Luke's inconsistent timing of Jesus' divine titles, the disciples' commitment, and anonymous Gospel circulation. Ehrman values goodness without considering it evidence requiring God, while extreme human suffering challenges loving providence. He explains Luke's layered Christology, notes Jesus' ministry may have lasted months rather than three years, and argues followers can sacrifice for a compelling message while an author's identity disappears as texts circulate beyond their first audience.

title: Did the Glories of Martyrdom Lead to Christian Conversions?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether stories of Christian martyrs' endurance under torture helped persuade outsiders to convert.

title: June 2026 Gold Q&A Announcement
author: jennao
description: Announces the June 2026 Gold and Platinum member Q&A, including the format, question deadline, live participation instructions, and planned focus on Paul's letters.

title: The Fear of Hell as an Incentive to Convert
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Christian preaching about hell could make conversion seem urgent, especially when paired with stories of divine power and miracles.

title: Was Augustine Telling the Truth About Miracles He’d Seen?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Augustine's reports of miracles as evidence for how miracle claims functioned in Christian arguments for conversion.

title: Biographical Accounts of Early Christian Miracles (Based on Eyewitnesses!)
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses later Christian biographies of Gregory the Wonderworker and Martin of Tours as miracle-centered stories of conversion and religious power.

title: And the Miracles Just Keep on Comin’
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys legendary miracle stories outside the New Testament, including traditions about Edessa, Thaddaeus, John, and Peter.

title: How Could Christian Miracles Convert the Empire if Miracles Don’t Happen?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how miracle stories could promote conversion even if the miracles themselves did not happen.
searchSummary: Explains how reports of miracles could drive Christian conversion even if the miracles themselves never occurred. Early sources consistently attribute conversions to extraordinary signs, while most people who believe miracles in any era know them through testimony rather than direct experience. Repeated stories, told with conviction and eventually written in narratives such as Acts, could persuade some listeners that Christian claims were divinely validated. The historical effect therefore depends on belief in the reports, not on proving supernatural events.

title: Why Christian Miracles Converted the Empire
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that early Christian conversion accounts most often explain Christian success by appealing to miracles.
searchSummary: Argues that perceived miracles were the principal attraction drawing pagans to Christianity. Ancient worshippers sought divine benefits such as healing and protection, and Christian missionaries claimed their God demonstrated superior power through signs. Acts repeatedly links spectacular deeds by Peter, Paul, and other believers with mass conversions, establishing a narrative pattern continued in later Christian literature. Ehrman does not affirm that the miracles occurred; his historical point is that outsiders believed the reports and converted because they signaled divine power.

title: Superior Health Care as an Explanation for the Spread of Christianity?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates the modern claim that Christianity spread because Christian communities provided better health care during epidemics.
searchSummary: Evaluates Rodney Stark's proposal that superior Christian nursing during epidemics accelerated the religion's growth. Christian sources praise believers' care and disparage pagans, but their apologetic bias requires scrutiny, and close contact with the sick also infected and killed many caregivers. Dionysius of Alexandria explicitly describes Christians dying after nursing and burying victims. With no outsider evidence that better health care attracted converts, Ehrman rejects survival through nursing as a sufficient explanation and turns instead to conversion accounts emphasizing miracles.

title: A Modern “Common Sense” About What Made Christianity Attractive to Converts
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines the claim that Christianity attracted converts because Christian communities offered unusually strong social support.
searchSummary: Questions the popular claim that Christianity spread because outsiders were attracted to its close community, mutual support, and charitable care. Churches did offer family-like material benefits that could retain members, but surviving Christian accounts never identify those benefits as the reason people converted. Outsiders were excluded from worship and often knew little about church life, while hostile rumors could make it repellent. Ehrman distinguishes reasons for remaining in a community from reasons for joining and seeks another explanation for conversion.

title: What an Ancient Enemy of Christianity Said About Why It Was Successful
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Celsus's critique of Christianity to show how one ancient pagan opponent understood Christian success.
searchSummary: Uses the pagan critic Celsus to examine who joined Christianity and whether sophisticated argument drove conversion. Celsus mockingly portrays missionaries persuading slaves, laborers, children, and women, while Paul, Origen, and Lactantius likewise acknowledge that most believers were lower-class and uneducated. Limited evidence also suggests women may have outnumbered men in some churches, although precise conclusions are uncertain. Because educated converts remained exceptional until the second century, Ehrman concludes that elite writings and intellectual debates were not Christianity's engine of growth.

title: How Did Christianity Succeed?  An Older View That Many People Still Have
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques an older scholarly explanation for Christianity's success and contrasts it with conversion, exclusivity, and mission.
searchSummary: Surveys the older scholarly explanation that Christianity triumphed because pagan religion had decayed and could no longer satisfy spiritual needs. Edward Gibbon combined providence and Christianity's supposed superiority with five historical causes: Christian zeal, belief in immortality, miracles, strict morality, and effective organization. Later scholars repeated versions of this argument, often assuming Christianity was morally and religiously superior. Ehrman presents the model as foundational but outdated, preparing to reassess its assumptions with newer scholarship and evidence.

title: Do You Know The Golden Ass?   (Is a Mystery Religion like Christianity?)
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Apuleius's The Golden Ass as evidence for ancient mystery religion and Greco-Roman religious experience.
searchSummary: Apuleius's The Golden Ass follows Lucius from his transformation into a donkey to his rescue and initiation by the goddess Isis. The story illuminates an ancient mystery religion with themes resembling Christianity, including salvation, new life, devoted service, and hope after death. Its nonexclusive worship and Lucius's later initiation into Osiris's mysteries also show important differences from early Christian commitment.

title: Christianity:  A Weirdly Exclusivist Religion
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Christian exclusivity made the movement unusual in the Roman world and helped reshape religious allegiance.
searchSummary: Explains how Christianity's combination of evangelism and exclusive worship enabled it to displace pagan religions. Pagans could add new cults without abandoning old gods, but Christian conversion required rejecting every competing deity, making religious choice an identity-defining commitment. Exclusivity without mission would have remained marginal, while mission without exclusivity would merely add another cult. Spread through personal networks therefore produced a one-way demographic effect: every convert enlarged Christianity while removing a worshipper from paganism, progressively shrinking the traditional religious world.

title: Some Important Readers’ Questions on Some Gospel Head-Scratchers
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to reader questions about Luke's Christology, Gospel tensions, and how New Testament writers handle Jesus' identity.
searchSummary: Answers three questions about Gospel interpretation: Luke's apparently inconsistent portrayals of when Jesus became God's Son, why disciples might have followed Jesus without historically verifiable miracles, and how anonymous Gospels could circulate and be reused. Luke emphasizes Jesus's innocence and combines different Christological traditions; Jesus's ministry may have lasted only months; and original audiences may have known anonymous authors whose identities disappeared as copies traveled. Matthew and Luke used Mark as adaptable material, not inviolable authority.

title: How Early Christians Made Converts.  (Tent revivals?)
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines how early Christians made converts without modern-style rallies, mass campaigns, or organized door-to-door evangelism.
searchSummary: Argues that Christianity spread through social networks rather than organized missions, mass rallies, or door-to-door evangelism. After Paul, surviving sources name almost no missionaries during the first four centuries, and their stories are often legendary. Converts instead spoke with relatives, friends, neighbors, coworkers, and acquaintances, creating chains of persuasion that expanded incrementally across families and communities. Because Christianity was both missionary and exclusive, each new believer also abandoned pagan worship, allowing slow person-to-person growth to erode traditional religions over generations.

title: Converting the World:  Why Has Christianity Always Been “Missionary”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores why Christianity became a missionary religion and why that feature mattered for its spread in the Roman world.
searchSummary: Explains why Christianity developed an evangelistic mission unmatched by pagan cults and ancient Judaism. Pagan worshippers could add gods without recruiting others, while Jews welcomed converts but rarely sought them; Christianity's concern for outsiders was therefore a novelty. Ehrman connects it to the Christian message that judgment was imminent, salvation came only through Christ, and love required warning others. Urging conversion became a way to rescue neighbors and enemies from destruction or punishment, giving mission a theological and moral imperative.

title: Blog Dinner in Waynesville NC, May 19.  Wanna Come?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a blog dinner in Waynesville, North Carolina, with attendance details for interested members.

title: Jesus and Capitalism:  My Next Book (A Big Change)
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a planned book on Jesus, capitalism, socialism, and related economic questions from a New Testament perspective.

title: Want To Be Involved in More In-Depth Discussion of Key Issues?  A Blog Opportunity
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Blog Stewards seminar and provides a study guide to Romans 1-3, focusing on Paul's argument, theology, and purpose in writing.

title: A Common But Lousy Argument That We KNOW What the NT Originally Said: Anniversary Post #14
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques the argument that abundant New Testament manuscripts prove secure access to the original text.
searchSummary: Challenges the popular claim that the New Testament's thousands of surviving manuscripts guarantee knowledge of its original wording. Other classical texts remain disputed despite scholarly confidence, and manuscript quantity cannot compensate for the scarcity of copies close to the first century; roughly 94 percent of Greek New Testament manuscripts date after the ninth century. The evidence may often approximate what authors wrote, but superior attestation alone cannot establish certainty.

title: Sailing Cruise to Caribbean Islands in January.  Want to Come with Me?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a January 2027 Caribbean sailing cruise and describes the trip format, ship, and lecture component.

title: The Morality of War
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the morality of war while explaining why the blog normally avoids direct political commentary.

title: May 2026 Gold Q&A Announcement: We’re Trying Something New!
author: jennao
description: Announces a May 2026 Gold and Platinum member Q&A with a revised format that includes live participant questions.

title: Nile Cruise: Cancellation
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the cancellation or postponement of the planned Nile cruise because of conditions in the Middle East.

title: Was Jesus the Incarnation of an Angel?  Anniversary Post #13
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the argument that Paul understood Christ's pre-existent state in angelic terms.
searchSummary: Revisits Ehrman's argument that Paul understood Christ as God's chief angel before his human birth. The Greek construction in Galatians 4:14 identifies Jesus with an angel rather than presenting two ascending comparisons. This reading makes Paul’s other claims cohere: Christ was a preexistent divine mediator who became human and was then exalted above his former status to equality with God. The Philippians Christ poem supplies the larger narrative for this angelic incarnation and exaltation.

title: An Amazing Fragment of a Lost Gospel: Anniversary Post #12
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses a fragmentary lost gospel, possibly related to the Gospel of Peter, featuring a conversation between Jesus and Peter.

title: Active Pastors Who Have Lost Their Faith: Anniversary Post #11
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses pastors who remain in ministry after losing belief and why leaving the pulpit can be difficult.
searchSummary: Explains the emotional, social, vocational, and financial crisis faced by clergy who lose supernatural belief while continuing to minister. Ehrman recalls serving as an interim pastor as his own faith weakened and describes why leaving can threaten family relationships, identity, livelihood, and the people depending on a pastor. He highlights the Clergy Project, which confidentially supports former and current religious professionals through community, counseling, career assistance, and grants, and urges compassion across believing and nonbelieving communities.

title: The Seven Sleepers of Ephesus: Platinum Post by Douglas Wadeson, MD
author: jennao
description: Presents the legend of the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus, including its Christian setting and later appearance in the Qur'an.
searchSummary: Retells the late antique legend of seven Christian youths who sleep through persecution and awaken after the empire becomes Christian. Christian and Qur'anic versions use their extraordinary sleep as evidence that God can restore the dead bodily, although the story varies in duration, location, and detail. Douglas Wadeson treats it as a likely doctrinal legend and asks what its invention and later acceptance reveal about early Christians' willingness to create stories that conveyed religious truth.

title: A Letter Written by Jesus!?  Anniversary Post #10
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses ancient traditions claiming that Jesus corresponded with King Abgar of Edessa.

title: Anniversary Post #9:  Misquoting Misquoting Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Misquoting Jesus has often been misunderstood, especially by critics concerned about its implications for faith.

title: May 2026 Platinum Webinar Announcement
author: jennao
description: Announces a Platinum member webinar on the Gospel of Thomas with date, time, access details, and replay information.

title: Different Words, VERY Different Theologies, and Understanding Which Words They Were. Readers’ Questions
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to reader questions about resurrection language, textual wording, and theological meaning in New Testament interpretation.
searchSummary: Answers related questions about how precise terminology and uncertain wording affect New Testament interpretation. It distinguishes near-death experiences, temporary restorations to mortal life, and resurrection to immortality; separates forgiveness from atonement; and argues that Acts 20:28 does not clearly give Luke an atonement doctrine. Textual critics can identify the likely wording in most passages, although certainty without originals is impossible and disputed variants do not overturn major Christian doctrines.

title: Bad Bible Jokes.  (And do you have any?)
author: BDEhrman
description: Collects Bible jokes prompted by Genesis and other biblical allusions, while inviting readers to add more.

title: Anniversary Post #8:  When Is a Contradiction Not a Contradiction?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains what counts as a contradiction in Gospel comparison and why definitions matter in debates about biblical discrepancies.
searchSummary: Defines a contradiction as two statements that cannot both be literally true at the same time, while acknowledging that judgments of plausibility and sensible reading affect disputed cases. Ehrman distinguishes genuine contradictions from omissions, such as Mark and John not mentioning Jesus' virgin birth, and from historical-development arguments that do not meet strict logical criteria. The post establishes terminology for a Gospel debate without equating inerrancy or inspiration with freedom from contradiction.

title: Does God Care What We Wear? A Platinum Post by Douglas Wadeson, MD
author: jennao
description: Examines religious clothing rules in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, asking whether dress regulations have scriptural grounding.
searchSummary: Compares clothing rules in the Torah, New Testament, and Quran, including laws about mixed fabrics, gendered dress, modesty, and distinctive religious garments. The guest author questions whether such regulations consistently reflect divine priorities and notes how selectively believers apply them. The post concludes that modesty can be reasonable while arguing that moral responsibility cannot be reduced to prescribed clothing alone.

title: Celebrating our 14th Anniversary!  Check Out the Unusual Q&A!
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the recording of a fourteenth-anniversary Q&A built around playful historical hypotheticals.

title: Anniversary Post #7:  Doing a Graduate Degree in Early Christian Studies
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why pursuing a PhD in New Testament or early Christianity is far more demanding than many prospective students expect.
searchSummary: Explains why earning a PhD in New Testament or early Christianity requires years of intensive, specialized training. Students complete seminars, learn modern and ancient research languages, pass extensive written and oral examinations, propose original research, write a book-length dissertation, and defend it before a faculty committee. Graduate teaching also expands professors' knowledge through students' projects, while the rigor of the program produces genuine expertise; Ehrman recommends the path only to people unable to imagine pursuing another life.

title: Anniversary Post #6  Is Mark’s Seemingly Simple Gospel Unsophisticated?
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Mark's Gospel is more literarily sophisticated than its simple style may first suggest.
searchSummary: Argues that Mark is a sophisticated literary artist rather than a simple recorder of Jesus' life. The Gospel links Jesus' baptism and crucifixion through repeated images of the Spirit, something being ripped open, a voice, and recognition of God's Son. At the baptism God privately identifies Jesus after the heavens split; at his death the Temple curtain splits and a Roman centurion finally recognizes him. This structure reveals a suffering Son whose death opens access to God.

title: Anniversary Post #5: Why I Was Reluctant to Write The Triumph of Christianity
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why writing The Triumph of Christianity seemed unusually difficult because of the scope of the historical question.
searchSummary: Explains why writing The Triumph of Christianity required a broad research project. Ehrman wanted an account of how a marginal Jesus movement displaced Roman religions and transformed the empire, but the subject demanded mastery of pagan practice, Christian distinctiveness, missionary methods, growth rates, persecution, apologetics, Constantine's conversion, anti-pagan policy, and Western consequences. Earlier seminars and years of reading supplied a foundation, yet integrating specialist scholarship into one coherent popular narrative remained daunting enough that he postponed the project for years.

title: Anniversary Post #4: Why Gospels Matter Even Where They Are Not Historical
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that the Gospels can matter even when particular stories are not historically accurate, because memory also shapes meaning.
searchSummary: Argues that the Gospels retain profound value even when their accounts are historically inaccurate. As memories shaped by early Christian communities, their differences and distortions reveal how people understood Jesus and can carry literary, ethical, and religious meaning apart from factual precision. Historical investigation remains important, but the remembered Jesus transformed Christianity, the Roman world, and later civilization far more than a scholarly reconstruction did. Studying memory therefore illuminates both Jesus and the communities whose recollections continue to shape lives.

title: Anniversary Post #3:  My Response to an Ill-Tempered Richard Carrier
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to Richard Carrier's criticism of the claim that first-century pagan sources do not mention Pontius Pilate.
searchSummary: Defends Ehrman's discussion of Pontius Pilate against Richard Carrier's claim that he overlooked key evidence. Ehrman had explicitly acknowledged the Caesarea inscription and the accounts of Philo and Josephus while arguing that no contemporary Roman literary source mentions Pilate, making Jesus' absence from such sources unsurprising. Carrier's attack on a compressed article without considering the fuller book illustrates how context can be ignored and why Ehrman declines exchanges with scholars he considers uncivil.

title: Anniversary Post #2: Why Were the Gospels Written Anonymously?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the New Testament Gospels circulated anonymously and why that differs from some other ancient writings.

title: Anniversary Post #1:  Defending Misquoting Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Defends Misquoting Jesus against criticisms that the book exaggerated or distorted the problem of textual variation.
searchSummary: Defends Misquoting Jesus against evangelical critics who argue that textual variants are insignificant because they threaten no cardinal Christian doctrine. Ehrman distinguishes changes to doctrine from changes that affect the meaning, theology, or interpretation of important passages and books, citing disputed readings about the adulterous woman, resurrection appearances, Jesus' agony, atonement, and divinity. Variants can therefore matter greatly even when theologians can support their doctrines from other passages.

title: Celebrating The Blog’s 14th Anniversary!  Do You Have a Favorite Post?
author: BDEhrman
description: Marks the blog's fourteenth anniversary by inviting readers to nominate favorite posts for republication.
searchSummary: Celebrates the blog's fourteenth anniversary with statistics on its output, reader engagement, and charitable impact. Since 2012 it had published about 4,300 posts, generated more than 165,000 comments, and raised nearly $3.5 million while directing membership fees entirely to charity. Bart announces a retrospective series featuring one April post from each year and invites readers to nominate favorite posts for a second fourteen-entry collection, explaining why their selections mattered.

title: The Distinctively Jewish Roots of Jesus’ Ethics
author: BDEhrman
description: Shows how Jesus' ethical teachings stand within Jewish scripture and Jewish moral teaching rather than apart from them.
searchSummary: Shows that Jesus' ethics arose within Jewish Scripture and teaching rather than appearing without precedent. Prophetic concern for the poor, Hillel's negative Golden Rule, and close parallels with Jesus son of Sirach illuminate Jesus' commands about generosity, humility, wealth, repentance, and judgment, while leaving room for distinctive emphases. These teachings transformed Western moral thought because Christianity spread through the Roman world and rooted its ethics specifically in Jesus, not because compassion and charity were absent from earlier Judaism.

title: Understanding the Gospels, Jesus, and the Spread of Christianity: Great Readers’ Questions
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to reader questions about Jewish proselytizing, Christian word-of-mouth conversion, and Jesus' Son of Man sayings.
searchSummary: Answers three questions about Christian origins and Jesus. Ancient Judaism did not conduct a broad missionary campaign comparable to Christianity, whose growth depended on stories transmitted orally across languages and cultures for decades, producing both continuity and substantial change. The historical Jesus' apocalyptic Son of Man was not God but a lesser heavenly agent, possibly angelic, empowered to execute God's judgment. Together the answers distinguish Jewish and Christian expansion, explain oral tradition's instability, and clarify Jesus' expectation of divine intervention.

title: Rethinking Faith Podcast Interview About Love Thy Stranger
author: jennao
description: Discusses a Rethinking Faith podcast interview about Love Thy Stranger and the book's argument about Jesus' ethical legacy.
searchSummary: Shares one of Ehrman's podcast interviews promoting Love Thy Stranger: How the Teachings of Jesus Transformed the Moral Conscience of the West. He distinguishes this Rethinking Faith conversation from the many interviews surrounding the book's release because its engaged interviewer understood the book's argument particularly well. The brief post does not restate that argument or its evidence, instead directing readers to the recorded exchange as the substantive discussion.

title: Early Christian Reactions to “Heresies” in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes early Christian reactions to heresy and the role those disputes played in defining orthodox belief.
searchSummary: Explains how competing early Christian groups defined one another as orthodox or heretical while claiming apostolic authority for sharply different beliefs about God, Jesus, creation, Judaism, and salvation. Eusebius portrayed orthodoxy as original and heresies as later corruptions, whereas Walter Bauer argued that forms later condemned often appeared early or initially dominated particular regions. Modern evidence supports extensive diversity, followed by the victorious proto-orthodox movement establishing hierarchy, creeds, canon, and a history that legitimized its success.

title: The First Attempts to Wipe Out Christianity
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why early persecutions were limited before the mid-third century and how later threats to Christianity became more serious.

title: When Emperors Became More Involved in Christian Persecutions
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how imperial involvement made Christian persecution more organized and dangerous in the Roman world.
searchSummary: Roman persecution of Christians became more systematic only when emperors intervened directly. Marcus Aurelius may have been connected with the violence at Lyons, while Decius required empire-wide sacrifice primarily to restore divine favor rather than specifically to attack Christians. Christianity was not broadly outlawed throughout the empire until the early fourth century, when Diocletian and his colleagues launched the Great Persecution.

title: You’re Invited: The Blog Turns 14
author: BDEhrman
description: Invites readers to a fourteenth-anniversary blog event.
searchSummary: Invites members to celebrate the blog's fourteenth anniversary through an informal live Zoom cocktail hour. Rather than a lecture or conventional question session, Bart proposes playful historical and biblical hypotheticals, offers his own answers, and encourages attendees to participate by video, chat, or submitted questions. The announcement supplies the event date and access details while marking fourteen years, thousands of posts, and more than $3 million raised for charity.

title: Early Persecutions of Christians, in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes early persecutions of Christians before empire-wide suppression became a sustained threat.
searchSummary: Corrects the idea that Christianity was illegal from the beginning or that Roman emperors continuously persecuted believers across the empire. Early hostility usually arose locally because Jewish communities rejected a crucified messiah, pagan neighbors blamed Christians' refusal to worship the gods for disasters, and outsiders suspected their private meetings. Nero targeted Roman Christians as arsonists, while Pliny under Trajan executed only those who refused sacrifice; empire-wide persecution did not begin until Decius in 249 CE.

title: The Rise of Christian Anti-Judaism, in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes the rise of Christian anti-Judaism and the debate over whether followers of Jesus should keep Jewish law.
searchSummary: Traces Christian anti-Judaism to disputes over the claim that the crucified Jesus was Israel's messiah and that faith in him, rather than Jewish birth or law observance, defined God's people. Christians appropriated Jewish Scripture as prophecy and as evidence of their religion's antiquity, even while rejecting many of its commands and denying Jewish interpretations. By the second century, hostile rhetoric accused Jews of deicide; after Constantine, Christian political power transformed such claims into discrimination, destruction, and violence.

title: April 2026 Gold Q&A: Get Your Questions In!
author: jennao
description: Announces the April 2026 Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: Early Christian Views of Judaism, In a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys early Christian views of Judaism, especially whether following Jesus required keeping Jewish customs and laws.
searchSummary: Surveys the spectrum of early Christian positions on Judaism and Jewish law. Jewish Christian groups such as the Ebionites required Jesus's followers to join Israel's covenant through circumcision and observance, while Marcion separated Jesus and his loving God from the creator, law, and Scriptures of the Jews. Most Christians occupied intermediate positions: Paul exempted gentiles from the law, Hebrews treated Judaism as a divinely given foreshadowing, and Matthew presented Jesus as fulfilling and observing it.

title: Readers’ Questions on the Accuracy of the Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to reader questions about Gospel accuracy, historical reliability, and how contradictions affect interpretation.
searchSummary: Addresses whether Gospel legends could arise quickly and whether Luke's prologue guarantees eyewitness research and historical accuracy. False stories can emerge through invention, misunderstanding, rumor, or ordinary memory distortion, so later legends justify critically examining earlier traditions. Greek vocabulary in Luke 1 suggests predecessors composed narratives based on earlier eyewitness reports, while Luke claims careful acquaintance and orderly writing but never says he personally interviewed witnesses; a conventional historiographic preface asserts reliability without proving it.

title: The Good Done By Christianity to Our World
author: BDEhrman
description: Considers Christianity's moral legacy by weighing harms done in Christian history against ethical ideals shaped by Jesus' teachings.

title: The Dark Side of Christianity: How I (Partially) End My New Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Previews the conclusion of Love Thy Stranger by discussing Christianity's darker legacy alongside its influence on Western moral conscience.

title: Advance Preview–How I Begin My New Book: Love Thy Stranger
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the opening of Love Thy Stranger and explains how the book frames Jesus' teachings about moral obligation to strangers.

title: The Letter to Diognetus: An Unknown Gem among the Apostolic Fathers (in a Nutshell)
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Letter to Diognetus as an early Christian apology and a notable work among the Apostolic Fathers.
searchSummary: Introduces the Epistle to Diognetus as an anonymous second-century Christian apology defending Christianity against pagan and Jewish practices while praising believers' moral life and divine salvation through God's Son. Its final two chapters likely come from a separate Christian homily, and neither the author nor the addressee can be identified securely. The work survives through copies of a single manuscript discovered in a Constantinople fish shop and later destroyed during Strasbourg's bombardment in 1870.

title: Why in Particular I’d Love to Get my Grubby Paws on Paul’s Lost Letters
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why lost letters of Paul would be especially valuable for understanding Paul's thought and influence.

title: Paul’s Lost Letters
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses the lost letters of Paul and why additional Pauline writings would matter for early Christian history.

title: While We’re Talking About the Reliability of Eyewitnesses…
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses research on eyewitness memory to question simple appeals to eyewitness reliability.
searchSummary: Surveys empirical evidence that eyewitness status does not guarantee an accurate report. Students observing a staged confrontation misreported 26 to 80 percent of its details, DNA later overturned many convictions based solely on witnesses, and respondents vividly remembered nonexistent footage of an Amsterdam plane crash. Because inference, hearsay, and imagination can become false memory, even eyewitness accounts of Jesus' dramatic miracles would require independent evaluation rather than automatic acceptance.

title: Eyewitness Accounts of Miracles
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines eyewitness miracle reports in another religious tradition as a test case for claims about resurrection testimony.
searchSummary: Uses miracle traditions about the Baal Shem Tov to test whether alleged eyewitness transmission establishes supernatural events. A source written fifty-four years after his death claims truthful informants and reports healings, exorcisms, weather control, heavenly journeys, and resurrection, yet outsiders readily recognize the stories as legendary. Gospel miracle accounts deserve the same historical scrutiny: eyewitness claims make them neither necessarily reliable nor necessarily unreliable, and each tradition must be evaluated rather than accepted selectively because it supports Christianity.

title: Christ’s legalism, his divine and human nature, stories of his father Joseph — and other questions.
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to reader questions about Jesus' relation to law, Christ's divine and human nature, and traditions about Joseph.
searchSummary: Answers several reader questions, beginning with whether Jesus was legalistic in his approach to Torah. It argues that Jesus upheld Jewish law but prioritized its greater principles, especially love of neighbor and care for people, when commandments appeared to conflict. The post also addresses traditions about Joseph, developments in Pauline and Johannine Christianity, Christ's divine and human natures, and abbreviated sacred names in manuscripts.

title: A Legal Case for Jesus’s Resurrection
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses a hypothetical murder case to test whether legal reasoning can establish Jesus' resurrection historically.

title: A New Proof of the Resurrection.  What Do YOU Think?
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses a debate with Jonathan Sheffield over a proposed proof of Jesus' resurrection.
searchSummary: Presents Jonathan Sheffield's argument that Roman officials and ancient writers would have investigated early Christian resurrection claims and exposed them if they were fraudulent. Because Pilate, Tiberius, Josephus, Tacitus, Suetonius, and Plutarch left no such refutation, Sheffield infers that they accepted the resurrection. Ehrman contrasts this argument with the limitations and contradictions of Christian sources and his broader view that resurrection is a matter of faith, not the most probable conclusion available to historical inquiry.

title: Does God Care What We Eat? – Platinum Post by Doug Wadeson
author: jennao
description: Presents a Platinum member post about biblical and religious food rules.
searchSummary: Compares food restrictions in the Torah, Quran, and early Christian writings, asking whether religious diets reflect divine commands, health concerns, or ancient cultural assumptions. The guest author examines kosher animals, Jesus' teaching in Mark, Paul's approach to gentile converts, and continuing disputes in Acts and Revelation. The post concludes that moral impurity arises from human conduct and intention rather than from particular foods.

title: How Important Actually Was Paul (When Alive and After)?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Paul's importance during life, later Christian memory of Paul, and the reliability of traditions about Paul.

title: Does Papias Say Matthew and Mark Wrote OUR Matthew and Mark?
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Papias's comments about Matthew and Mark do not clearly refer to the canonical Gospels now known by those names.
searchSummary: Argues that Papias does not provide reliable evidence that the apostles Matthew and Mark wrote the canonical Gospels bearing their names. Papias describes Matthew as a Hebrew collection of sayings, unlike the Greek narrative that used Mark and Q, and claims Mark omitted nothing learned from Peter despite its extreme brevity. He may have known different works or repeated inaccurate traditions; either way, the canonical Gospels apparently circulated anonymously until Irenaeus named their authors around 180 CE.

title: Do the Synoptics Present an Early Character of the Jesus Movement?  –Platinum Post by Ryan Fleming
author: jennao
description: Presents a Platinum member argument that some core Synoptic Gospel material may predate Paul's letters.
searchSummary: Presents Ryan Fleming's argument that core Synoptic traditions may predate Paul's letters despite later post-70 additions. He compares baptism, Jewish law, Christology, James, resurrection appearances, gentile mission, eschatology, and the Lord's Supper, treating the Synoptics as preserving a more primitive Jewish Jesus movement than Paul's theology. The proposal challenges standard Gospel dating by suggesting early source texts behind Matthew, Mark, and Luke, rather than claiming the completed canonical Gospels themselves necessarily preceded Paul.

title: Is Papias Generally Trustworthy?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates Papias's reliability as evidence for traditional claims about the authorship of Matthew and Mark.
searchSummary: Challenges appeals to Papias as trustworthy evidence for the authorship of Matthew and Mark. Papias reports extravagant traditions about Jesus producing impossibly abundant crops and Judas becoming grotesquely swollen before dying, neither of which is historically credible.
