Because his information came through several layers of oral transmission and proves unreliable where it can be evaluated, scholars cannot selectively trust his preferred authorship claims while dismissing his other stories merely because they conflict with prior beliefs.

title: Does Papias Provide Us Direct Access to the Teachings of the Apostles?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Papias provides direct access to apostolic teaching or later traditions about Gospel authorship.
searchSummary: Argues that Papias does not provide direct access to Jesus' apostles despite claims about consulting reliable oral informants. His own description places several links between them: apostles told elders, companions heard the elders, and Papias questioned those companions; modern readers receive the report through Eusebius. Because eyewitnesses, earwitnesses, and repeated transmission can all introduce error, this fourth- or fifth-hand chain cannot by itself authenticate Papias's later claims that Matthew and Mark wrote Gospels.

title: Papias in a Nutshell.  An Important Figure Among the Apostolic Fathers
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Papias as a controversial Apostolic Father whose fragments became important for debates about Gospel authorship.
searchSummary: Introduces Papias, an early second-century bishop whose lost five-volume Expositions survives only in quotations by later church writers. Its fragments preserve traditions about Mark and Matthew, Jesus's sayings and millennial kingdom, Judas's death, the adulterous woman, and later miracles, while showing Papias's preference for living oral testimony over books. Claims that he knew the apostle John are uncertain, and Eusebius valued his apostolic connections but disparaged his literal expectation of Christ's earthly thousand-year reign.

title: Announcing the “Sponsor a Stranger” Campaign
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the Sponsor a Stranger campaign connected with Love Thy Stranger and the blog's charitable work.

title: Free Live Debate on the Resurrection (March 2)
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a free live debate on the historical evidence for Jesus' resurrection.
searchSummary: Announces a free live debate between Bart Ehrman and Jonathan Sheffield on whether Jesus rose from the dead. The event is framed around historical evidence, including early testimony, purported eyewitnesses, the empty tomb, and the origins of Christian resurrection belief. The post supplies the March 2 broadcast time and viewing link and invites readers to watch and discuss the arguments. It does not itself assess the evidence or reveal either participant's complete case.

title: The Earliest Christian Apologist:  Quadratus in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Quadratus as the earliest surviving Christian apologist and explains the significance of Christian apology.
searchSummary: Introduces Quadratus as the earliest surviving Christian apologist, known only through Eusebius and one brief quotation from a defense reportedly addressed to Emperor Hadrian around 125 CE. Quadratus argued that Jesus's miracles had enduring, publicly observable effects because some people he healed or raised remained alive into the apologist's own time. The claim may have aimed to distinguish Jesus from other miracle workers, but its credibility depends partly on whether such witnesses could realistically have survived that long.

title: What Are the Chances?  The Logic of “Intelligent Design”
author: BDEhrman
description: Considers the logic of intelligent design arguments about the origin of life from a nonexpert perspective.
searchSummary: Argues that life's highly improbable emergence does not logically require intelligent design because improbability is not impossibility. Ehrman contrasts statistical prediction with historical events that actually occurred, using the enormous number of stars and galaxies, personal coincidences, and the incalculable odds of any individual's existence to show that extraordinarily unlikely outcomes happen constantly. Unless an event violates mathematics or physical law, chance remains a sufficient possibility even when its probability seems almost unimaginable.

title: Interesting Questions from Readers (Including on the Consistency of Mark and the Reality of Suffering)
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to reader questions about Mark's consistency, scribal changes, suffering, and studying the New Testament without Greek.
searchSummary: Answers questions about Jesus' anguish in Mark, a disputed resurrection reading in 1 Corinthians, Ehrman's loss of faith, and evaluating scholarship without Greek. Mark portrays suffering serving salvation even when Jesus cannot understand it, while textual evidence favors Paul's claim that not all will die before transformation. Ehrman separates his agnosticism from personal tragedy and fundamentalism, and advises nonspecialists to compare respected experts, examine arguments, and consider whether theological commitments constrain a scholar's conclusions.

title: Who Wrote the Shepherd of Hermas, and When?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains what can be known about the authorship and date of the Shepherd of Hermas.
searchSummary: Investigates who wrote the Shepherd of Hermas and when this popular early Christian apocalypse was composed. Conflicting ancient claims identify Hermas with Paul's acquaintance, a Roman church official, or the brother of Bishop Pius, but these traditions served different arguments about the book's authority. Its theology, church organization, and lack of New Testament quotations instead support a cautious early-second-century date, perhaps between 110 and 140 CE.

title: What’s Actually *in* the Shepherd of Hermas?
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes the contents of the Shepherd of Hermas, including its revelations, angelic messages, and moral instruction.
searchSummary: Surveys the Shepherd of Hermas, an early Christian apocalypse built around five visions, twelve commandments, and ten parables delivered to a Roman Christian named Hermas. Its imagery includes an elderly woman representing the church, a tower built from believers, and a monster symbolizing persecution. The book chiefly urges moral reform and teaches that Christians receive one final opportunity to repent after baptism before judgment arrives.

title: Blog Dinner in Charlottesville, VA on March 21.  You Interested?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a blog dinner in Charlottesville, Virginia, with attendance details for interested members.

title: A Sign From God?  Mormon Missionaries and Me
author: BDEhrman
description: Tells a story about Mormon missionaries and a supposed divine sign from the author's evangelical youth.

title: If It Wasn’t “For Your Sins” Why Did Jesus Die (according to Luke)?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Luke's view of Jesus' death when Luke does not present it as an atoning sacrifice for sins.
searchSummary: Argues that Luke treats Jesus' death as the rejection of an innocent prophet rather than an atoning sacrifice for sin. Drawing especially on the missionary speeches in Acts, the post explains that the crucifixion awakens guilt and leads people to repent and receive God's free forgiveness. It contrasts Luke with Mark and Paul, who portray Jesus' death as a payment or sacrifice made on behalf of others.

title: March 2026 Gold Q&A Announcement
author: jennao
description: Announces the March 2026 Gold Q&A and invites Gold and Platinum members to submit questions.

title: Has Luke Gotten Rid of the Idea That Jesus Died for Your Sins?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Luke removed or softened the idea that Jesus' death was for sins.
searchSummary: Argues that Luke deliberately removed Mark's indications that Jesus' death was an atoning sacrifice. Luke omits the ransom saying and places the tearing of the Temple curtain before Jesus dies, turning it into a sign of judgment rather than restored access to God. Because this theology also appears throughout Acts, the post concludes that the disputed Last Supper words about Jesus' body and blood were probably added by scribes.

title: The Controversy Over Jesus’ Last Supper in Luke (Did He Speak of Dying “For you”?)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the textual problem in Luke 22:19-20 and its importance for whether Luke portrays Jesus' death as for others.
searchSummary: Examines whether Luke originally described Jesus' Last Supper bread and wine as his body and blood given for others. One early Greek witness and some Latin manuscripts lack the relevant clauses, and Ehrman finds accidental omission implausible. Deliberate deletion also fails to harmonize Luke's cup-bread sequence with other accounts, whereas addition would make the passage resemble 1 Corinthians, Matthew, and Mark and supply familiar sacrificial symbolism, giving scribes clear reasons to expand it.

title: Should You Say It Like You Mean It?  Those Inoffensive Critical Scholars…
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on why critical scholars often state controversial conclusions in muted or inoffensive ways.
searchSummary: Reflects on why critical scholars often use cautious technical language that obscures controversial conclusions. Luke's lack of a theology of the cross means that Luke does not present Jesus as dying for sins, just as calling a falsely attributed ancient work pseudepigraphal can avoid calling it a forgery. The post argues that scholars should communicate such conclusions clearly and honestly while avoiding unnecessary offense.

title: Yet More: A Christian Forger Who Warns Against Reading Forgeries!
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses the irony of a forged Christian text warning readers against forged writings.
searchSummary: Examines the irony of the Apostolic Constitutions, a forgery in the apostles' names that warns Christians against forged apostolic and apocryphal books. Its author condemns rival pseudepigrapha as poisonous because they teach views he considers false while presenting his own doctrine as authentically apostolic. The warnings also divert suspicion from his deception. The strategy succeeded: later church authorities accepted portions as apostolic and blamed objectionable material elsewhere in the work on subsequent heretical interpolation rather than recognizing its false authorship.

title: And an Ancient Christian Deceived Deceiver (i.e. Forger)
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines an early Christian example of a forger warning against deception while using deception.
searchSummary: Identifies the Apostolic Constitutions as a forgery assembled from earlier church orders and falsely presented as the work of Jesus' apostles. First-person claims by Peter, Paul, James, and others establish an apostolic authority supposedly extending directly to Christ and God, despite occasional chronological and narrative mistakes. Ehrman highlights the central irony that this deceptive author condemns people who speak lies while grounding his own ecclesiastical instructions in a fabricated identity, setting up the further case of a deceiver being deceived.

title: Should You “Give It All Away”?  The Views of Wealth in the Shepherd of Hermas
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Jesus' radical teaching on wealth with the softer approach to charitable giving in the Shepherd of Hermas.
searchSummary: Examines the Shepherd of Hermas's teaching about wealth, poverty, and charitable giving. Its parable of the elm and vine presents rich and poor Christians as mutually dependent: the wealthy supply material aid, while the poor repay them through spiritually effective prayers. Rather than demanding that believers surrender everything, the text allows the rich to retain wealth if they use it generously, a position critics view as making the poor instruments of wealthy Christians' salvation.

title: An Ancient Apocalypse Among the Apostolic Fathers: The Shepherd of Hermas
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Shepherd of Hermas as an early Christian apocalypse among the Apostolic Fathers.
searchSummary: Introduces the Shepherd of Hermas as a Roman Christian apocalypse whose revelations are conveyed through an elderly woman and an angelic shepherd. Its five visions, twelve mandates, and ten similitudes address repentance, moral conduct, persecution, and the church, symbolized by a tower assembled from stones representing believers. The book offers baptized Christians one further chance to repent and urges them to reform before the church is completed and divine judgment arrives.

title: A Great Story of a Deceived Deceiver
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts an ancient story about a forger deceived by another forgery, used to introduce literary deception.
searchSummary: Recounts ancient stories about Heraclides Ponticus, an accomplished philosopher repeatedly associated with fraud, plagiarism, and forgery. After deceptive schemes involving his funeral and a fabricated oracle, Heraclides accepted a play forged under Sophocles' name by his former student Dionysius and cited it as authentic. Hidden acrostics eventually exposed the trick and mocked his literary competence, although modern scholars debate the anecdote's historicity. Ehrman uses the tale to introduce the recurring irony of deceivers who themselves become victims of literary deceit.

title: The Second Coming (Yeats)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Yeats's The Second Coming depends on Christian imagery and religious literacy.
searchSummary: Uses W. B. Yeats's “The Second Coming” to show why knowledge of Christian tradition matters for understanding modern culture even apart from religious belief. Written after the First World War shattered nineteenth-century confidence in science, progress, and peace, the poem repurposes apocalyptic imagery to depict modern disorder rather than predict a literal Antichrist. Ehrman invites readers to ponder its enduring vision of collapsing social order and the threatening new age symbolized by the beast approaching Bethlehem.

title: About Work Habits and Productivity…
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses work habits, productivity, and the author's earlier approach to getting large amounts of writing done.
searchSummary: Explains the work habits behind Ehrman's high research and writing output while acknowledging that his approach can be excessive. He attributes his productivity to intense concentration, disciplined resistance to distractions, scheduled breaks, adequate sleep, and careful allocation of time rather than simply working longer hours. Writing and analytical problems command his deepest focus, while structured routines help him complete necessary tasks efficiently and preserve time for the projects he most wants to pursue.

title: Why I Wrote Love Thy Stranger and Significant Benefits that Can Come Your Way
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Love Thy Stranger was written and describes benefits connected with pre-ordering the book.

title: Greek Island Trip: Cancellation
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the cancellation of a planned Greek Islands lecture cruise.

title: From Eternal Torment to Styles of Greek to the Dating of Ignatius: Interesting Readers’ Questions
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to reader questions about eternal torment, Paul's gospel, Greek style, and the dating of Ignatius.

title: The Most Egregious Copying Mistake by a New Testament Scribe
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains a major scribal mistake in Luke's genealogy of Jesus and how accidental copying errors could enter New Testament manuscripts.
searchSummary: Explains common accidental copying errors in New Testament manuscripts, including omitted lines caused by a scribe's eye jumping between similar endings. The post then examines manuscript 109, whose copyist read Luke's two-column genealogy across the columns instead of down them. The resulting sequence makes Phares the ancestor of humanity and places God in the middle of the genealogy as the son of Aram.

title: Just How Careless Could an Ancient Christian Scribe Be?
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the Muratorian Canon to show how careless copying could produce badly transmitted Christian texts.

title: Interested in Q?  Did It Exist?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the debate over whether Q existed and announces an event featuring scholars on both sides of the question.

title: The Muratorian Canon (The first “list” of Christian canonical books)
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Muratorian Canon as the earliest surviving list of Christian canonical books and summarizes its contents and textual problems.
searchSummary: Examines the Muratorian Canon, probably a late-second-century Roman list preserved in a poor eighth-century Latin manuscript. It accepts most eventual New Testament books, rejects writings considered forged or heretical, excludes several later canonical epistles, and includes Wisdom of Solomon plus a disputed Apocalypse of Peter. Its treatment of the Shepherd of Hermas shows that perceived apostolic antiquity, acceptable teaching, and suitability for church reading shaped early judgments while the canon remained unsettled.

title: When Did Paul and the Gospels Become Canonical Scripture?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Justin Martyr, Marcion, and Irenaeus show different stages in the movement toward a New Testament canon.
searchSummary: Traces the movement from Justin Martyr's loose use of unnamed apostolic memoirs to Irenaeus's insistence on exactly four named Gospels about thirty years later. The intervening growth of Marcion's eleven-book canon and other rival movements likely encouraged proto-orthodox Christians to define their authorities more sharply. Irenaeus also reclaimed Paul from Marcionites and Gnostics, extensively using his letters and accepting the Pastoral Epistles, whose church offices and attacks on false knowledge supported proto-orthodox concerns.

title: The Death of Joseph the Carpenter, as Told By Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a translated excerpt from the History of Joseph the Carpenter in which Jesus narrates Joseph's illness, life, and death.
searchSummary: Presents an excerpt from the History of Joseph the Carpenter in which Jesus narrates the final illness of his earthly father. At age 111, Joseph confesses his sins, recalls Mary's miraculous pregnancy and an episode from Jesus' infancy, recognizes Jesus as divine savior, and fears the approach of death. Jesus and Mary remain beside him while the account uses Joseph's deathbed lament to explore repentance, mortality, and confidence in Jesus' power to save.

title: Here’s an Apocryphal Gospel You Probably Don’t Know!  The History of Joseph the Carpenter.
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the History of Joseph the Carpenter as a little-known apocryphal Gospel that fills gaps in traditions about Joseph.
searchSummary: Introduces the History of Joseph the Carpenter, a Coptic and Arabic work probably composed in Byzantine Egypt during the late sixth or early seventh century. Narrated by Jesus, it makes Joseph an elderly widower with children, thereby explaining Jesus' brothers, and describes Joseph's guardianship of Mary, death, heavenly deliverance, preserved body, and feast day. The work combines infancy-gospel traditions with Jewish testament literature and later stories about Mary's death and assumption.

title: Why Was the Canon Still Up For Grabs in the Second Century?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why second-century Christians valued authoritative writings without yet having a closed New Testament canon.
searchSummary: Shows that proto-orthodox Christians still held sharply different views of written authority in the mid-second century. Polycarp extensively echoes future New Testament books, the Shepherd of Hermas scarcely cites earlier texts, and 2 Clement quotes sayings of Jesus that include traditions outside the canonical Gospels. These contrasting practices, along with continuing disagreement over works such as Barnabas, Revelation, and the Apocalypse of Peter, demonstrate that neither a closed canon nor its eventual contents had yet been established.

title: Authors, Authorities, and Who Gets To Write the Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines how early Christian groups tied scriptural authority to apostolic authorship and claims about reliable access to Jesus.
searchSummary: Explains how early Christian groups grounded textual authority in an author's supposed connection to Jesus and the apostles. Proto-orthodox Christians attributed anonymous Gospels to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, treated common names such as James and John as famous apostolic figures, and accepted several writings that critical scholars regard as pseudonymous. Few New Testament books were actually written by Jesus' disciples, but all could be called apostolic once the emerging church defined them as preserving apostolic teaching.

title: How and When Did Christians Decide What Should Be in the New Testament Canon?
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes the criteria church fathers used when deciding which writings belonged in the New Testament canon.
searchSummary: Outlines four criteria used in forming the New Testament canon: antiquity, apostolic association, widespread church use, and orthodox teaching. Marcion's mid-second-century collection of Luke and ten Pauline letters may have prompted proto-orthodox leaders to promote four Gospels and a broader apostolic collection, but agreement developed slowly. Athanasius first named the present twenty-seven books in 367, and debate over Revelation, Hebrews, disputed epistles, Hermas, Barnabas, and other works continued beyond his declaration.

title: Why Did Early Christians Want a New Canon of Scripture?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why early Christians, already using Jewish Scripture, came to want a distinct collection of authoritative Christian writings.
searchSummary: Explains why Christians developed a distinct collection of authoritative writings alongside Jewish Scripture. Jesus' teachings and Paul's letters were already treated as Scripture by some early Christians, while competing groups attributed Gospels, letters, acts, and apocalypses to apostles in support of conflicting beliefs. The struggle between emerging orthodoxy and rival Christianities made written authority crucial: the victorious proto-orthodox movement accepted books supporting its theology and excluded those associated with alternative views.

title: Important Questions About Matthew and Paul
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to reader questions about Jeremiah in Matthew, translation issues, and Paul's language about Jesus and crucifixion.
searchSummary: Answers four questions involving Matthew and Paul. It explains “den of robbers” as financial violence, finds a plausible literary echo between Matthew's temptation and crucifixion scenes, and clarifies that Papias says Matthew composed or compiled sayings in Hebrew. It also rejects treating 1 Thessalonians 2:14-16 as an interpolation: Paul's reference to divine wrath need not describe Jerusalem's destruction, and the disputed term is better translated “Judeans” within a comparison of local persecution.

title: My Last Lecture at UNC – The Most Significant Discovery in the History of Biblical Studies
author: jennao
description: Shares the recording of a final UNC retirement lecture on a major discovery in biblical studies.

title: Christ and the Gods:  Check It Out!
author: jennao
description: Shares a documentary and full interview related to Christ and the Gods.
searchSummary: Presents both the complete Christ and the Gods documentary and Ehrman's full standalone interview recorded for it. He explains that documentaries typically divide expert interviews into brief excerpts, leaving most of each contributor's discussion outside the finished film. Providing both versions lets viewers compare the selected comments used in the larger production with the uninterrupted interview, preserving the fuller context and content that the documentary's edited narrative could not include.

title: February 2026 Gold Q&A Announcement
author: jennao
description: Announces the February 2026 Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: Christian Churches Steadfastly Refusing To Help Those in Need….
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses a viral test of churches' responses to need to reflect on Jesus' teaching about helping strangers.

title: The New Testament in a Nutshell: The 50 Word Summaries of Each Book (All of them!)
author: BDEhrman
description: Collects fifty-word summaries of every New Testament book from the New Testament in a Nutshell series.
searchSummary: Collects fifty-word summaries designed to distinguish the central purpose and emphasis of every New Testament book. The overview moves from the four Gospels and Acts through Paul's life, undisputed letters, disputed and pastoral epistles, Hebrews, the Catholic epistles, and Revelation, identifying each work's characteristic narrative, theology, ethical concern, audience, or controversy. It provides a compact reference for explaining how books differ rather than treating the New Testament as a single undifferentiated message.

title: When Did We Get Chapters and Verses? A Quick Answer
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains when chapter and verse divisions entered biblical manuscripts and printed Bibles.

title: Weren’t Jewish Scribes Fully Accurate to the Letter?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how the Masoretic Text was standardized and why Jewish scribal transmission was more complex than claims of perfect copying suggest.

title: Do We Know if Our Copies of the Hebrew Bible (Old Testament) Are Accurate?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the textual history of the Hebrew Bible and the difficulties of knowing the exact words of its earliest authors.

title: Q1 Platinum Webinar Announcement
author: jennao
description: Announces a Platinum webinar on the birth of the Trinity with lecture and Q&A details.

title: The Formation of the Hebrew Bible: The Common Scholarly View Today
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the common scholarly view that the Hebrew Bible canon formed gradually, with Torah, Prophets, and Writings becoming fixed at different times.
searchSummary: Presents the common modern reconstruction of Hebrew Bible formation as a gradual process rather than a single official decision. The Torah was widely authoritative by the fifth century BCE, the Prophets by the second century BCE, and the Writings remained less settled until around the first century CE. Evidence from Ezra, Sirach, the New Testament, and Dead Sea Scrolls supports this sequence, while language, perceived antiquity, and broad communal use probably influenced inclusion in the final twenty-four-book Jewish canon.

title: When Was the Hebrew Bible Canonized?  The Traditional View
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes the traditional scholarly view that the Hebrew Bible canon developed in stages from Torah to Prophets to Writings.
searchSummary: Reviews the older theory that the Hebrew Bible became canonical in three fixed stages: Torah by 400 BCE, Prophets by 200 BCE, and Writings at a Council of Jamnia around 90 CE. Scholars still accept gradual formation in that general sequence, but now regard the process as less orderly. Although Jewish leaders gathered after Jerusalem's destruction to reshape religious life around Scripture, evidence does not support the claim that Jamnia officially fixed and closed the canon.

title: Charts Showing the Organization of the English Old Testament and the Hebrew Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Provides charts comparing the organization of the Hebrew Bible and English Old Testament, including differences among Christian Old Testament canons.
searchSummary: Compares the organization of the Hebrew Bible with Christian Old Testaments. The Jewish Tanakh arranges twenty-four books as Torah, Prophets, and Writings, while Protestant English Bibles divide the same contents into thirty-nine historical, poetic, and prophetic books. Roman Catholic and Orthodox canons also incorporate deuterocanonical works absent from the Jewish and Protestant collections, and Greek and Slavonic Orthodox traditions contain additional differences. The charts clarify that biblical contents and arrangement vary among religious communities.

title: Getting the Hebrew Bible:  A Primer (What is the Old Testament…)
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the contents, organization, and formation of the Hebrew Bible as background for studying the biblical canon.
searchSummary: Introduces the contents and organization of the Hebrew Bible as background for studying canon formation. English Christian Old Testaments arrange thirty-nine books as historical, poetic, and prophetic works, whereas the Hebrew Tanakh counts the same material as twenty-four books divided into Torah, Nevi'im, and Kethuvim. The different order and counting reflect distinct organizational traditions, while the Torah remains the first and most authoritative section in the Jewish arrangement.

title: Rarely Asked Questions About Why THESE Letters of Paul Are in the Canon
author: BDEhrman
description: Frames new research questions about why these letters of Paul, including disputed Pauline letters, became part of the New Testament canon.
searchSummary: Raises neglected questions about why these particular Pauline letters survived and entered the canon. Paul likely wrote hundreds of letters during a thirty-year mission, and surviving works such as Philippians and 2 Corinthians may combine multiple letters, yet only seven authentic letters remain alongside later pseudonymous works and Hebrews. Ehrman asks how this small collection formed, whether early Gospel writers knew other Pauline letters, and why these writings rather than Paul's many lost communications became authoritative.

title: The Year in Review: 2025!
author: BDEhrman
description: Reviews the blog's 2025 activity, fundraising, membership, and charitable work.
searchSummary: Reviews the blog's scholarly, charitable, and organizational accomplishments during 2025. It published 303 posts, generated nearly 5,000 comments, introduced the Blog Steward membership tier, exceeded its Food Bank appeal goal, and distributed $480,500 to charities, bringing four-year giving above $2 million. Bart also highlights the New Testament in a Nutshell series, migration to a stable new platform, expanded member activities, and the staff, volunteers, and readers responsible for the year's progress.

title: From A (to Z of the New Testament) to B(eyond Deconstruction): Guest Post by James F. McGrath
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents James McGrath's discussion of how New Testament scholarship can help readers reexamine or reconstruct faith.
searchSummary: Argues that biblical scholarship can support constructive reconstruction after inherited beliefs collapse. James McGrath rejects inerrancy as an idolatrous attempt to obtain certainty, since readers inevitably reinterpret biblical errors rather than accept every text literally. Using Job, he contrasts friends who defend a rigid theology with Job's honest appeal to experience, concluding that critical study can foster humility, mystery, and positive convictions instead of merely defining oneself against a former faith.

title: Alphabet Soup of the New Testament: Guest Post by James F. McGrath
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents James McGrath's explanation of writing a lay introduction to New Testament scholarship that goes beyond basic facts.
searchSummary: Explains James McGrath's inductive approach to introducing New Testament scholarship through puzzles that require scholarly methods. Rather than presenting conclusions book by book, he begins with textual contradictions, cultural misunderstandings, and familiar passages, then shows how source, redaction, historical, literary, and linguistic analysis address them. This structure helps readers understand why scholars reach conclusions, avoids circular reasoning, and makes academic methods useful and approachable without pretending that experts always agree.

title: The A-Z of the New Testament: Guest Post by James McGrath
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces James McGrath's guest series on The A to Z of the New Testament and public communication of biblical scholarship.
searchSummary: Introduces James McGrath's effort to make essential New Testament scholarship accessible beyond classrooms and seminaries. Churches often omit authorship, pseudepigraphy, and the Synoptic Problem because ministers fear disruption, sermons prioritize practical inspiration, and Sunday-school teachers lack training. The A to Z of the New Testament therefore begins with engaging textual puzzles and introduces scholarly methods organically, offering readers who may not complete a textbook an inviting way to confront the Bible's historical and cultural complexity.

title: January 2026 Gold Q&A Announcement
author: jennao
description: Announces the January 2026 Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: My Interview about Christmas with Nicholas Kristof (New York Times)
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses a New York Times interview about Christmas, Love Thy Stranger, and public misunderstandings of the Bible and early Christianity.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's New York Times interview with Nicholas Kristof about Christmas and the forthcoming Love Thy Stranger. Ehrman explains his frustration with short interviews because scholarly claims appear without the evidence and qualifications needed to defend them, inviting criticism from readers relying on familiar but poorly examined assumptions about Jesus, the Bible, and early Christianity. He presents the blog as a place for fuller scholarly explanation and directs readers to the interview, titled What Would Surprise Jesus About Christmas 2025?

title: Pubs and Churches on Christmas Eve
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on Christmas Eve churchgoing in England, religious decline, and the continuing value of Christian worship traditions.
searchSummary: Reflects on the tension Ehrman felt attending an Anglican Christmas Eve service while nearby pubs overflowed with celebration. He could not accept the service's claim that divine incarnation had overcome darkness, given the world's immense suffering, yet he resonated with its ideals of gratitude, sacrifice, generosity, and concern for others more than with thoughtless pleasure. His preferred world joins genuine enjoyment with lives shaped by humane Christian values, whether people hold those commitments as believers, agnostics, or atheists.

title: Reflecting on the Christmas Tree and Faith
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on Christmas trees, memory, faith, and the emotional pull of holiday traditions.
searchSummary: Uses memories of Christmas trees to reflect on Ehrman's former Christian faith and the meaning it retains after belief has ended. Trees once brought peace, light, generosity, family tradition, and contemplation, while faith similarly illuminated one season of his life before drying out and passing away. Although he regards the Christmas story as metaphor rather than history, he believes its themes of love, giving, and light in darkness can continue shaping conduct after both decorations and doctrine are gone.

title: Comics from My Office Door
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares favorite comics removed from a longtime office door after moving out of the office.

title: Light Cast on the Formation of the Christian Canon in Polycarp’s Short Letter
author: BDEhrman
description: Shows how Polycarp's letter draws heavily on earlier Christian writings and helps illuminate the formation of Christian Scripture.
searchSummary: Uses Polycarp's short letter to show how earlier Christian writings were becoming authoritative in the early second century. Its moral exhortations weave together more than a hundred quotations and allusions, mostly from texts later included in the New Testament, including Paul, the Pastorals, Hebrews, Synoptic traditions, Acts, and 1 Peter. Polycarp's reliance on these sources, church hierarchy, doctrinal boundaries, and opposition to docetism anticipates concerns that later shaped proto-orthodox Christianity and its canon.

title: The Letter of Polycarp to the Philippians (Another Apostolic Father) in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Polycarp's letter to the Philippians, its connection with Ignatius, and its place among the Apostolic Fathers.
searchSummary: Explains Polycarp's letter to the Philippians as both a cover note accompanying collected letters of Ignatius and advice for a church facing leadership problems. Its uncertain chronology may indicate one early letter or two writings later combined, because one section seeks news of Ignatius while another appears to know of his martyrdom. Polycarp condemns docetic teachers denying Christ's flesh and bodily resurrection but recommends repentance and restoration for the elder Valens and his wife after financial misconduct.

title: A Bizarre Scandal Involving the Dead Sea Scrolls
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts a legal scandal connected with the Dead Sea Scrolls and a lecture on their significance for Jesus and early Christianity.

title: Was Jesus a Member of the Dead Sea Scroll Community (the Essenes)?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Jesus was not simply a member of the Dead Sea Scrolls community while the Scrolls still illuminate Jewish apocalyptic views.
searchSummary: Asks whether Jesus belonged to the Essene community associated with the Dead Sea Scrolls. Although both criticized Jerusalem's leadership and expected an imminent apocalyptic intervention, Jesus showed no concern for the Essenes' Zadokite priesthood, calendar, separation, or strict ritual purity. His association with sinners and social outcasts directly opposed their withdrawal from impurity, making shared apocalyptic expectations valuable historical context but not evidence that Jesus was an Essene.

title: Why Do the Dead Sea Scrolls Matter for Understanding Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how the Dead Sea Scrolls matter for understanding Jesus by illuminating the Jewish world from which Christianity emerged.
searchSummary: Explains why the Dead Sea Scrolls matter for understanding Jesus even though they contain nothing about him or his followers. Their biblical manuscripts, community rules, hymns, commentaries, and prophecies illuminate a Jewish sect living near Jesus' time and place, especially its strongly apocalyptic worldview. Because Jesus was also a Jewish apocalyptic prophet, the scrolls clarify his historical environment while remaining evidence for Essene beliefs rather than direct evidence about Christianity.

title: What Are the Dead Sea Scrolls?  The Basics
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Dead Sea Scrolls, their discovery, contents, and connection with the Essenes at Qumran.
searchSummary: Introduces the discovery, contents, and historical importance of the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Essene community commonly associated with them. The collection includes early Hebrew Bible manuscripts, commentaries, hymns, prophecies, and community regulations that reveal rigorous purity practices, communal organization, and imminent apocalyptic expectations. These Jewish texts preserve manuscripts nearly a millennium older than previously known copies and illuminate the religious world of Jesus without placing him inside the Essene sect.

title: My Birdbrain View of Agnosticism
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on human cognitive limits and uses bird intelligence as an analogy for agnosticism about ultimate reality.
searchSummary: Explains Ehrman's agnosticism through the analogy of birds unable to comprehend the humans who feed them. If intelligences vastly beyond humanity exist, people may be no more capable of recognizing or describing them than birds are of understanding human minds and lives. This does not support the biblical God or promise benevolent supervision; it instead grounds epistemological humility, because humans cannot know whether material reality is all that exists or what any superior beings might be like.

title: If It Is All Matter, Why Should It Matter?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on materialism, consciousness, and why meaning can still matter if everything is material.
searchSummary: Argues that a wholly material and ultimately transient universe does not make human life meaningless. Ehrman accepts that bodies, brains, personalities, and the cosmos consist of matter and energy and will eventually disappear, yet meaning exists in present experience rather than requiring eternal purpose. Family, friendship, learning, work, food, exercise, nature, and countless other attachments genuinely matter to him, so mortality directs attention toward what deserves time and effort rather than logically nullifying value.

title: Some Key Passages from the Gospels:  Questions from Readers
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to Gospel questions about John's incarnation theology, virgin birth traditions, and related passages.
searchSummary: Answers questions about Johannine incarnation, signs, Gospel dating, and apocalyptic expectation. John may have understood the preexistent Son to enter the world through an ordinary biological birth, a view later harmonized with Luke's virgin birth tradition; written reports of Jesus' signs enable later readers to believe without seeing them. Repeated fulfilled predictions support post-event Gospel composition, while Mark still expected God's kingdom to arrive powerfully and Luke reframed that expectation as already becoming present.

title: A Heart-Rending Story and Stunning Condemnation: The Prophet Hosea
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Hosea's message of divine love, betrayal, judgment, and Israel's unfaithfulness.

title: Ignatius: Eager to be Eaten by the Wild Beasts
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Ignatius's eager embrace of martyrdom and the belief that suffering could imitate Christ's passion.
searchSummary: Explains why Ignatius of Antioch eagerly sought martyrdom while being taken to Rome for execution around 110 CE. In his letter to Roman Christians, Ignatius asks them not to intervene and imagines wild beasts consuming his body so that he can imitate Christ and reach God. His insistence on bodily suffering also opposes docetic Christians who denied Christ's genuine humanity, making his anticipated death both personal devotion and a theological claim.

title: December 2025 Gold Q&A Announcement
author: jennao
description: Announces the December 2025 Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: A Glimpse of Proto-orthodox Views in the Letters of Ignatius
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Ignatius's letters to show features of proto-orthodox Christianity, including church unity, authority, and opposition to rival teachings.
searchSummary: Uses Ignatius of Antioch's seven authentic letters to illustrate major proto-orthodox concerns in the early second century. Ignatius demands unity, rejects teachings that compromise Jesus' full humanity and divinity, and makes obedience to a single bishop essential for valid worship and church order. These instructions reveal both the diversity of early Christianity and an emerging strategy for consolidating authority around one leader presented as God's earthly representative.

title: Uh, Duh.  What I SHOULD Have Said.  (Bethlehem)
author: BDEhrman
description: Revisits the Bethlehem birth narratives by explaining a missed argument against reconciling Matthew and Luke on Joseph and Mary's hometown.
searchSummary: Compares Matthew's and Luke's incompatible explanations for how Jesus was born in Bethlehem but raised in Nazareth. Ehrman details Luke's historically problematic census and immediate return to Nazareth, against Matthew's Bethlehem residence, flight to Egypt, and later relocation north. He rejects Jimmy Akin's two-home migrant-worker harmonization because it lacks ancient evidence and conflicts with Luke's lodging problem, arguing that reconciliation and historical probability pursue different goals.

title: Letters by A Christian About to Be Martyred: Ignatius of Antioch in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the letters of Ignatius of Antioch as early proto-orthodox Christian writings composed on the way to martyrdom.
searchSummary: Introduces Ignatius of Antioch and the seven letters he wrote while Roman guards transported him toward execution around 110 CE. Churches in Asia Minor sent delegations to support him, prompting letters to five congregations, Rome, and Polycarp that repeatedly address his beliefs, authority, and anticipated martyrdom. Although Ignatius enthusiastically desired death by wild beasts, his arrest and the internal conflict he left in Antioch remain obscure, making him both historically important and psychologically controversial.

title: Did Jesus Teach in Greek?
author: jennao
description: Argues that Jesus almost certainly taught in Aramaic rather than Greek, despite arguments to the contrary.
searchSummary: Argues that Greek wordplay in Matthew and the Gospels' Greek composition do not show that Jesus taught in Greek. The recorded wording comes from authors writing decades later for Greek-speaking audiences, while linguistic, educational, and demographic evidence indicates that rural Galileans normally spoke Aramaic and lacked advanced Greek schooling. Ehrman uses the case to warn that theological commitments can make weak evidence appear compelling when researchers begin with a desired conclusion instead of historical plausibility.

title: Why I Don’t Like Public Debates
author: jennao
description: Reflects on public debates and why fixed commitments often make them poor settings for changing minds.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman finds public debates frustrating despite believing they may help a few open-minded listeners. Participants whose identities depend on a conclusion often claim objectivity while defending beliefs held since childhood, and audiences usually seek confirmation rather than evaluation. Ehrman acknowledges that changing his own views does not make him right; arguments still require evidence. He urges debaters and listeners to follow the difficult path of genuine inquiry, remaining willing to discover that deeply important convictions are mistaken.

title: A Gold Nugget Often Overlooked: The Book of Zechariah
author: jennao
description: Introduces Zechariah as an under-read prophetic book and explains its division into First and Second Zechariah.

title: Errors That Are Not Mistakes in the Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Clarifies differences among error, mistake, falsehood, deceit, and lie for interpreting biblical contradictions.
searchSummary: Distinguishes error, mistake, falsehood, lie, and deceit to clarify debates about biblical accuracy. A mistake is an unintended error, a lie is an intentional falsehood meant to deceive, and an erroneous report need not be either; therefore a disciple could report a mistaken resurrection experience without lying. Likewise, Matthew intentionally reversing Mark's report of Jesus' instruction about carrying a staff may not be a mistake or deceit, but remains factually erroneous.

title: Some Good Questions On John and the Appearance of Jesus in the World
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to questions about John's incarnation theology, Paul's phrase "born of a woman," and the study of the historical Jesus.
searchSummary: Responds to questions about Paul's 'born of a woman,' scholarly expertise, independent Gospel traditions, and John's Christology. Paul uses family language to explain how Christ's human birth enables believers' adoption as God's children. Even if Gospel writers knew earlier accounts, distinct traditions can still attest recurring subjects independently, while experts deserve consideration rather than unquestioning trust. John presents the New Testament's highest Christology, but its varied claims about Jesus do not yet equal fourth-century orthodox formulations.

title: Lies, Contradictions, Mistakes, and the Meaning of Words.  What Do You Think?
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses resurrection claims and Gospel differences to probe what counts as lying, error, contradiction, or intentional change.
searchSummary: Introduces a language problem behind arguments about resurrection testimony and Gospel discrepancies. Ehrman challenges the false choice that disciples either saw the risen Jesus or lied, and Mike Licona's claim that Matthew's intentional reversal of Mark's staff instruction is not an error. By asking readers to distinguish error, mistake, falsehood, deceit, and lie, the post prepares the argument that sincere reports can be false and deliberate literary changes can still convey erroneous information.

title: The Striking Prayers of the Didache
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines the Didache's versions of the Lord's Prayer and Eucharistic prayers in relation to early Christian worship.

title: Help Feed Families in Need (With a Particularly Enticing Incentive!): Ehrman Blog Annual Appeal
author: jennao
description: Launches the annual blog appeal for the Food Bank of Central and Eastern North Carolina, with an incentive tied to The New Testament in a Nutshell.
searchSummary: Launches the 2025 annual appeal for the Food Bank of Central and Eastern North Carolina with a $20,000 fundraising goal and Bart's dollar-for-dollar match. Donors of at least $50 receive an advance digital edition of The New Testament in a Nutshell, which organizes and edits the blog series on all twenty-seven New Testament books. The post explains the Food Bank's mission, donation-identification procedure, January delivery, and goal of sending $40,000 to fight hunger.
secondaryKeywords: Food Bank of Central and Eastern North Carolina

title: Intriguing Instructions for How To Run the Church:  More on the Didache
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the Didache's instructions on baptism, fasting, Eucharist, itinerant prophets, and apocalyptic expectation.

title: The Didache: An Important Early Christian Document in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Didache as an early Christian document about ethics, church order, rituals, and the coming end.
searchSummary: Introduces the Didache as an early Christian compilation combining the Two Ways ethical teaching, rules for rituals and itinerant leaders, and an apocalyptic discourse. Its first section contrasts the ways of life and death through commands drawn from Jesus traditions and moral instruction resembling James, emphasizing love, generosity, humility, truthful conduct, and avoidance of violence, sexual wrongdoing, magic, greed, and oppression. The document illuminates Christian ethics, worship, fasting, authority, and community organization around 100 CE.

title: Are You Interested in a More Interactive Approach on the Blog? Reflections on the First Blog Stewards Seminar
author: jennao
description: Describes a Blog Stewards seminar on the Gospel of John's Prologue as an example of more interactive blog programming.

title: How Do You Date a Book Such as Barnabas?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how scholars date ancient writings, using the Letter of Barnabas as the main example.

title: Why Was the Letter of Barnabas Attributed to Barnabas (Part 2)
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that the attribution of the Letter of Barnabas may be connected with Marcion and disputes over the Old Testament.

title: November 2025 Gold Q&A Announcement
author: jennao
description: Announces the November 2025 Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: Why Would Anyone Claim Barnabas Wrote “The Epistle of Barnabas”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores why the anonymous Letter of Barnabas came to be attributed to Barnabas, the companion of Paul.

title: The Epistle of Barnabas in a Nutshell (Part 2)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how the Letter of Barnabas interprets Jewish dietary laws, circumcision, and Scripture figuratively rather than literally.
searchSummary: Explains how the Epistle of Barnabas converts Jewish dietary laws and circumcision into figurative Christian teachings rather than literal commands. Prohibited animals symbolize unethical behavior, while Abraham's 318 servants become, through Greek numerical interpretation, a prediction of Jesus and the cross. The work ends with opposing moral ways of light and darkness and concludes that Jews never understood their Scriptures or covenant; Christians alone inherit God's promises by accepting Christ and living uprightly.

title: The Epistle of Barnabas in a Nutshell (Part 1)
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Letter of Barnabas as an early Christian anti-Jewish writing that claims the Old Testament as a Christian book.
searchSummary: Introduces the Epistle of Barnabas as an anonymous Christian treatise, probably written around 130 CE rather than by Paul's companion. Using allegorical interpretation, it claims Jews broke God's covenant at Sinai and were deceived into reading their Scriptures and laws literally. Sabbath observance, for example, allegedly predicts a future thousand-year divine rest rather than weekly cessation from work. The argument makes the Old Testament exclusively Christian and represents a forceful early attack on Judaism.

title: Christ-killers; the date of Luke; and the literacy of Matthew: Questions and Responses
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to questions about anti-Judaism in 1 Thessalonians, the planned canon book, Luke's date, and whether Matthew could have written his Gospel.
searchSummary: Answers three historical questions involving early Christianity and the New Testament. Ehrman argues that Paul blamed Judeans rather than Jews generally for Jesus' death, explains that his canon book will investigate debates over individual books rather than repeat lists, and rejects dating Acts from its silence about Paul's death. He also argues that Matthew was unlikely to be literate and that the anonymous Gospel was composed in Greek, drawing extensively from Mark rather than a Hebrew work by the apostle.

title: How the Heavenly Lights and the Resurrection of the Phoenix Reveal God’s Will
author: BDEhrman
description: Shows how 1 Clement uses cosmic order and the phoenix to argue for restoring proper church leadership in Corinth.
searchSummary: Shows how 1 Clement appeals to nature and resurrection traditions to defend orderly leadership in the Corinthian church. The harmonious movements of the heavens, seasons, seas, and winds demonstrate that God's creation follows an appointed order, so the Corinthians should restore the presbyters they displaced. The letter also cites the legendary phoenix's recurring rebirth as evidence that resurrection is credible and that those disrupting divine and ecclesiastical order will face judgment.

title: June 2026 Cruise Details – Norway & Svalbard
author: BDEhrman
description: Provides details for a June 2026 Norway and Svalbard cruise with lectures on the choice of the Gospels.

title: Was 1 Clement Written BEFORE Some of the New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses the date of 1 Clement and whether it may be earlier than some New Testament writings.
searchSummary: Assesses when 1 Clement was written and whether it may predate some New Testament books. Although the traditional date of about 95-96 CE was once tied to an alleged persecution under Domitian, that evidence is weak; other internal clues still favor the late first century. References to the apostolic generation, surviving appointed leaders, and a church without a single bishop make an early date plausible, while details about Corinth and succession argue against composition before 70.

title: Did “Pope” Clement Write 1 Clement?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why 1 Clement was attributed to Clement of Rome and evaluates early traditions about that attribution.
searchSummary: Investigates whether Clement of Rome wrote the work traditionally called 1 Clement. The letter presents itself as a message from the Roman church to Corinth and never names Clement, while later traditions variously identify him as Paul's associate, a Roman bishop, or an official handling foreign correspondence. Because Rome probably still contained multiple house churches without a single ruling bishop, Clement remains a possible author or representative, but calling him a pope is anachronistic and the attribution cannot be proved.

title: 1 Clement in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces 1 Clement as a Roman church letter urging Corinthian rivals to restore displaced church leaders.
searchSummary: Explains 1 Clement as a late first-century letter from Rome intervening after rivals removed established presbyters from leadership in Corinth. Rather than addressing the coup immediately, the author uses Jewish Scripture, Greco-Roman harmony rhetoric, nature, resurrection imagery, and examples of jealousy and obedience to argue that God requires order and unity. The dissenters should relinquish power, restore the displaced leaders, reject ambition, and reestablish peace, although the letter itself never names Clement as its author.

title: You’re Invited to Bart’s Final Lecture December 7th!
author: jennao
description: Announces a final UNC public lecture marking Bart Ehrman's retirement from university teaching.

title: Was Jesus Poor? Platinum post by Douglas Wadeson, MD
author: jennao
description: Examines whether Jesus was poor by considering Gospel traditions, Nazareth, Joseph's trade, and signs of economic status.

title: A New Thread!  The Apostolic Fathers: In a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a new In a Nutshell series on the Apostolic Fathers and explains why these non-canonical writings matter.
searchSummary: Introduces the Apostolic Fathers as a modern, unofficial collection of diverse proto-orthodox writings from roughly the late first through second centuries. Although traditionally associated with companions of Jesus's apostles, most or all lack such direct connections, and some were once treated as Scripture in important manuscripts or churches. The collection includes letters, sermons, church instruction, apology, apocalypse, martyr narrative, and fragments that illuminate Christian belief, ethics, authority, ritual, interpretation, and developing orthodoxy beyond the New Testament.

title: For Further Reading:  Jude and Revelation
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends further reading on Jude and Revelation, including introductory works, commentaries, and online resources.
searchSummary: Recommends accessible and advanced resources for studying Jude, Revelation, and early apocalypticism. Ehrman organizes the bibliography into general studies, detailed commentaries, and reliable online courses, briefly identifying each work's argument, perspective, or intended audience. Selections cover authorship, historical context, literary genre, theology, violence, gender imagery, and modern end-time interpretation, with Ehrman and Hugo Mendez's textbook offered as an initial overview before readers pursue specialized scholarship.

title: The Revelation of John at a Glance, with Questions for Reflection
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Revelation as an ancient apocalypse and offers reflection questions about its message and interpretation.
searchSummary: Summarizes Revelation as a Christian prophet's symbolic vision of God's catastrophic defeat of evil and creation of a renewed world. Written by a John other than the son of Zebedee, it belongs to the ancient apocalypse genre and was intended to sustain Christians through suffering. Earlier material may reflect Nero's reign, while the final form likely dates to Domitian. Reflection questions ask readers to assess modern predictions, symbolic and literal passages, and Revelation's relationship to other ancient writings.

title: Blog Dinner in Chapel Hill!!  Come Celebrate My Retirement with Me!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Chapel Hill blog dinner connected with a UNC retirement lecture.

title: Three Common Misunderstandings of the Book of Revelation
author: BDEhrman
description: Challenges three common misunderstandings of Revelation involving symbolic language, eternal torment, and warnings about altering the book.
searchSummary: Corrects three misunderstandings about Revelation. Its symbols primarily express mysterious heavenly realities rather than conceal sedition from Roman officials; the lake of fire symbolizes the permanent annihilation of sinners, death, and Hades rather than eternal human torment; and the closing curse targets scribes who alter the text, not readers who question its prophecy. Ironically, surviving manuscripts contain many variants despite that warning, sometimes making the author's original wording difficult or impossible to recover.

title: Having Some Fun with 666!
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses modern interpretations of 666 and invites humorous examples of identifying the number with contemporary figures.
searchSummary: Uses humorous attempts to identify 666 with modern politicians, media organizations, institutions, mathematics, buildings, Roman numerals, and even Barney to expose the flexibility of arbitrary number games. Ehrman recalls recurring claims that disliked public figures must be the Beast and invites readers across political and religious positions to invent playful examples without abuse. The collected calculations demonstrate how easily ingenuity can manufacture contemporary meanings, underscoring why such identifications reveal more about interpreters than Revelation's historical message.

title: Questions on Jesus as God, the Belief in the Resurrection, Secretaries in Early Christianity, and the KJV!
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to questions about Jesus as God, resurrection belief, early Christian secretaries, and the King James Version.

title: 1 and 2 Peter and Jude “At a Glance,” and Questions for Reflection
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes 1 Peter, 2 Peter, and Jude at a glance with reflection questions about authorship, persecution, and false teaching.
searchSummary: Summarizes the central issues in 1 Peter, 2 Peter, and Jude and supplies questions for reflection. First Peter, probably written pseudonymously, encourages persecuted Christians in Asia Minor to remain faithful; 2 Peter combats unnamed teachers and explains the delayed end; Jude warns against allegedly immoral intruders. The accompanying questions invite readers to assess authorship arguments, Pauline influence, persecution, apostolic eyewitness claims, delayed eschatology, and the rhetoric used against rival Christians.

title: Hebrews and James:  “At a Glance” and “Questions for Reflection”
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Hebrews and James at a glance with reflection questions about authorship, audience, Judaism, and faith.

title: Lecturing on a Cruise up the Coast of Norway to Svalbard.  Wanna Go With Me?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a June 2026 lecture cruise along the Norwegian coast to Svalbard.

title: Understanding the Book of Revelation as an Apocalypse
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Revelation as an apocalypse by showing how its visions, angels, and symbolism fit an ancient literary genre.
searchSummary: Shows how Revelation follows the conventions of ancient apocalypses: a prophet receives angel-mediated heavenly visions, symbols encode earthly realities, catastrophes repeat for effect rather than form a linear timeline, and tragedy culminates in divine triumph. John's exalted Christ symbolizes kingship, judgment, power, and presence among seven churches. The book promises that God will soon end persecution and vindicate faithful sufferers, while warning Christians not to abandon their commitments before judgment and the eternal kingdom arrive.

title: Personal Annoucement: My Retirement from the University
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces Bart Ehrman's retirement from UNC and reflects on the shift from university teaching to books, the blog, and other work.
searchSummary: Announces Ehrman's retirement from UNC after more than four decades of university teaching, including thirty-seven years at Chapel Hill. Although he will miss direct engagement with students, he welcomes leaving grading, meetings, administration, and academic politics behind. Retirement will give him more time for books, the blog, online courses, lectures, family, friends, travel, reading, cooking, and other pursuits, making the decision feel like an exciting transition rather than an end to teaching or scholarship.

title: Revelation is an Apocalypse.  What Is An Apocalypse?
author: BDEhrman
description: Defines ancient apocalypses and explains how apocalyptic worldview helps readers understand Revelation.
searchSummary: Defines apocalypticism as a dualistic worldview expecting God's imminent defeat of evil and apocalypse as the literary genre that expresses it. Ancient apocalypses use first-person heavenly visions, angelic interpreters, symbolic historical sketches, pseudonymous prophets, escalating repetitions, and movement from suffering to vindication. Written during crises, they do not primarily chart a precise future timeline. They reveal heaven's interpretation of present oppression and motivate endangered communities to remain faithful because God controls history and will soon reward them.

title: The Book of Revelation: When and Why?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Revelation's likely historical setting under Nero and Domitian and its critique of Rome during Christian suffering.
searchSummary: Dates Revelation's final form to about 95 CE under Domitian while recognizing material reflecting Nero's reign. Its symbols address first-century Christians facing Roman opposition, not events millennia later: Babylon is Rome, the seven hills identify its capital, and 666 encodes Caesar Nero in Hebrew letters. John promises that God will overthrow Rome, its emperor, and the evil they embody. Followers of Christ must endure present suffering because divine judgment, vindication, and a renewed creation are near.

title: Q4 2025 Platinum Webinar Announcement
author: jennao
description: Announces a Platinum webinar on the delay of the Parousia in early Christianity.

title: The Book of Revelation:  Who Wrote It?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Revelation's author was a Christian prophet named John rather than John the son of Zebedee, and how the book came to be accepted as apostolic scripture.
searchSummary: Argues that Revelation was written by a Christian prophet named John, not John son of Zebedee or the author of the Fourth Gospel. Ancient critics such as Dionysius distinguished their Greek style, clarity, tone, and self-presentation. Revelation entered the canon gradually because orthodox theologians found it useful for affirming Christ's equality with God and Augustine spiritualized its millennium, after which apostolic authorship was inferred. Doubts nevertheless persisted through Martin Luther, who assigned it secondary status.

title: Why Most People Who Read Revelation Are Wrong About It
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Revelation is not a prediction of the modern end times but a book rooted in its ancient context.
searchSummary: Rejects modern claims that Revelation secretly predicts events in the reader's own era. Authors address their original audiences, whereas prophecy interpreters repeatedly move failed end-time deadlines and force ancient symbols into contemporary technology. Hal Lindsey's identification of Revelation's locusts as attack helicopters ignores the text's statement that they torture without killing, the opposite of military weapons. Historical interpretation begins with everything the passage says and its first-century setting rather than assembling selected details into a predetermined picture.

title: The Book of Revelation in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Revelation as a symbolic apocalypse about divine judgment, catastrophe, and the creation of a new world.
searchSummary: Narrates Revelation's progression from Christ's messages to seven Asian churches through escalating seals, trumpets, bowls, beasts, and divine judgments. The slaughtered Lamb opens history's scroll; Babylon falls; Christ defeats the Beast; Satan is imprisoned, released, and destroyed; the dead face judgment; and death itself enters the lake of fire. God then creates a new heaven, earth, and Jerusalem without pain or death. John presents these symbolic catastrophes and final restoration as events that will occur soon.

title: Four More Intriguing Topics on the Historical Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes four conference lectures on the historical Jesus from the New Insights Into the New Testament conference.

title: Four Intriguing Topics in the Study of the Historical Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes four conference lectures on historical Jesus research, including lost sources, Pilate, miracles, and Barabbas.

title: Problems with the Gospels: A Primer for the Study of the Historical Jesus (Part 2)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how historians assess the canonical Gospels as valuable but limited sources for reconstructing Jesus' life.
searchSummary: Explains both the historical value and limitations of the canonical Gospels. They preserve early, layered traditions with Palestinian and Aramaic roots, yet anonymous non-witnesses wrote them decades later in Greek after oral transmission, shaping accounts for theological purposes and producing discrepancies. Because older authenticity criteria can conflict or reflect scholars' assumptions, newer approaches use memory studies and recurring patterns across sources to reconstruct broad features of Jesus more securely than isolated sayings or narrative details.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: A Primer for the Study of the Historical Jesus:  Our Non-Gospel Sources
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces non-Gospel sources and critical issues scholars consider when studying the historical Jesus.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: Jude, The Denigration of Angels, and the Followers of Paul
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Jude attacks extreme post-Pauline claims about grace, morality, and angelic beings.

title: Seventy Years on This Planet and One Fundraiser: You’re Invited
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a seventieth-birthday fundraiser and live lecture on major archaeological and scholarly discoveries.
searchSummary: Turns Bart's seventieth birthday into a fundraiser for the blog's charities through a live online lecture on major archaeological and scholarly developments during his fifty-year career. Suggested donations correspond to his age or the blog's fourteen years, with identifying payment instructions and registration details. Every registrant receives access to the live event or recording, and all proceeds support charities addressing growing needs rather than funding a personal birthday celebration.

title: Does Jude Attack Pauline Christians?
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Jude was forged to oppose an extreme form of post-Pauline Christianity that severed grace from moral conduct.
searchSummary: Argues that the forged letter of Jude attacks a late first-century form of Pauline Christianity rather than generic immorality alone. Jude accuses intruders of turning divine grace into licentiousness, denying Christ, and living lawlessly, charges likely exaggerated by hostile polemic. Ehrman connects the dispute not directly to Paul's teaching about works of Jewish law but to Ephesians' broader claim that salvation comes through grace rather than good deeds, which Jude portrays opponents as extending into active antinomianism.

title: October 2025 Gold Q&A Announcement
author: jennao
description: Announces the October 2025 Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: Unpacking 1 Enoch, the Apocryphal Writing Quoted by Jude
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the Book of the Watchers section of 1 Enoch and its apocalyptic vision of judgment.

title: 1 Enoch:  The Scripture Quoted by Jude
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces 1 Enoch as the apocryphal Jewish text quoted by Jude and as an early source on postmortem existence.

title: Jude as Pseudepigraphic (i.e., forged)
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents reasons scholars regard Jude as pseudepigraphic, including its late setting, language, and appeal to earlier apostolic authority.
searchSummary: Argues that the Letter of Jude was probably written pseudonymously rather than by Jesus' brother. Its late-first-century setting, treatment of the apostolic age as past, and sophisticated Greek rhetoric point to a highly educated author. The writer also appears conversant with Hebrew Scripture and Aramaic Enoch traditions. Ehrman considers those abilities implausible for Jude, an Aramaic-speaking laborer from rural Nazareth whose family was remembered as poor, working-class peasants.

title: Book of Jude:  Who Wrote it?  When? And Why? (part 1)
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the authorship problem in Jude and the case that the letter was written in the name of Jesus' brother.

title: Heaven, the Hedonic Treadmill, and Homer (Simpson)  Platinum Post by Douglas Wadeson MD
author: jennao
description: Uses a guest post to question whether endless heavenly pleasure would remain satisfying over eternity.
searchSummary: Questions whether endless heavenly bliss would remain satisfying once people adapted to it through the psychological "hedonic treadmill." Douglas Wadeson contrasts popular heavenly imagery with Jesus' expectation of God's renewed earthly kingdom, then considers pleasure, work, worship, relationships, memory, and the fate of loved ones in hell. Examples from Revelation, the Quran, The Twilight Zone, and The Simpsons expose unresolved paradoxes, suggesting that perpetual pleasure or punishment might change identity, lose emotional force, or become intolerably monotonous.

title: The Letter of Jude in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Jude as a warning against false teachers who turn grace into license and face divine judgment.
searchSummary: Explains Jude as a warning against intruding teachers whom the author accuses of denying Christ, promoting immoral behavior, and dividing the community. Although their actual doctrines remain unclear beneath extensive invective, Jude presents past rebels as examples of the severe judgment awaiting them. The letter invokes Israel, Cain, Korah, Sodom and Gomorrah, and traditions from 1 Enoch and other apocrypha as authoritative evidence, while its claimed identity as Jude, brother of James, raises authorship questions.

title: Cleopatra, Virgin Births, and Professional Scribes: More about antiquity…
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to reader questions about the Paraclete in John, virgin birth claims, and professional scribes in antiquity.
searchSummary: Answers three questions about language and writing in antiquity. Ehrman rejects a false etymology that makes Paraclete mean excessive praise, explains that Isaiah 7:14 describes an already-pregnant young woman rather than explicitly a virgin, and distinguishes professional documentary scribes from authors of sustained literary works. He argues that ancient evidence does not support imagining secretaries composing complex New Testament books for illiterate disciples.

title: Questions on Forgeries, Historical Errors, and Alterations of Texts!
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to questions about forged Pauline letters, historical errors in the Passion narratives, and textual alterations.
searchSummary: Answers questions about why forged Pauline letters gained acceptance, whether later manuscripts reliably preserve church fathers, and which Passion traditions may be historical. Ancient authors and their associates could rarely track privately circulating forgeries, while familiar scriptural quotations were especially vulnerable to scribal harmonization. Historical criticism evaluates every claim separately, allowing scholars to accept broad events surrounding Jesus' death while rejecting particular episodes unsupported by the evidence.

title: A New Way to Support the Blog: Become a Blog Steward
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Blog Steward program as a way to support the blog's operating costs while membership fees continue going to charity.
searchSummary: Introduces Blog Stewards, a $1,000 annual membership tier designed to cover the blog's operating expenses while preserving its practice of sending ordinary membership fees entirely to charity. Stewards receive Platinum benefits, quarterly small-group seminars with assigned readings, monthly behind-the-scenes newsletters, and periodic impact reports. Bart explains that the program formalizes support previously supplied by a few donors and invites members able to contribute more to sustain the platform, staff, and scholarship.

title: Some Reflections on Our (My) Finitude and the Fear of Death
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on mortality, finitude, and finding meaning if death is the end of personal existence.

title: The DeuteroPauline Epistles “At a Glance,” With Questions for Reflection
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes 2 Thessalonians, Ephesians, and Colossians as disputed Pauline letters and offers reflection questions about their theology and authorship.
searchSummary: Summarizes the three Deutero-Pauline letters and the principal reasons scholars debate their authorship. Second Thessalonians differs from Paul on when the end will come, Colossians uses distinctive language and treats believers' resurrection as already accomplished, and Ephesians differs in style and theology while addressing Jewish-Gentile unity. Reflection questions invite readers to test arguments on both sides and consider how a forged apostolic letter could have entered the New Testament canon.

title: 1, 2, and 3 John: For Further Reading
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends further reading on the Johannine epistles, including accessible studies, commentaries, and online resources.

title: 2 John and 3 John in a Single Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes 2 John and 3 John as short letters from the elder about false teaching, hospitality, and community conflict.
searchSummary: Explains 2 and 3 John as brief letters from an unnamed elder addressing conflicts within connected house churches. Second John warns a community not to welcome teachers who deny that Christ came in the flesh, while 3 John supports Gaius against Diotrephes over hospitality, authority, and rival Christian travelers. Their relationship to 1 John, common authorship, historical setting, and possible chain of literary imitation remain debated, but both defend one Christology against competing believers.

title: The Weird Textual Variant of 1 John 4:3:  False Teachers Who “Loose” Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains textual variants in 1 John 4:3 and their connection to separationist Christology and proto-orthodox concerns.

title: Was Jesus Christ Two Beings, One Human (Jesus) and One Divine (Christ)?
author: BDEhrman
