description: Introduces the looses-Jesus variant in 1 John 4:3 and the separationist view that divided Jesus from the divine Christ.

title: 1 John: Who Wrote It, When, and Why?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines the authorship, date, and purpose of 1 John in relation to the Gospel of John and the Johannine community.
searchSummary: Examines the authorship and date of 1 John through its relationship to the Gospel of John. Shared language and themes reveal a literary connection, but differences in style and eschatology make common authorship unlikely: 1 John expects imminent judgment, whereas the Gospel emphasizes eternal life already possessed. The letter was probably written around 100-120 CE by a later author influenced by the Gospel, although a newer theory interprets it as an anonymous forgery imitating Johannine authority.

title: 1 John in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces 1 John as an unusual New Testament letter focused on right belief, love within the community, and opposition to false teachers.
searchSummary: Explains 1 John as an open letter or tract responding to Christians who left its community and denied that Christ came in genuine flesh. The author labels them antichrists, argues that denying Jesus's humanity undermines his atoning death, and rejects their apparent claim to be without sin. Drawing language and imagery from John's Gospel, the work identifies confession, obedience, and especially mutual love as marks of those who truly know God and possess eternal life.

title: My First Scholarly Encounter with the Canon of the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on early scholarly work with Bruce Metzger and renewed interest in how the New Testament canon formed.
searchSummary: Recounts Ehrman's first scholarly study of canon formation in Bruce Metzger's graduate seminar and its connection to his work on Didymus the Blind. Didymus treated 1 Clement, the Shepherd of Hermas, and Barnabas as Scripture even after his Alexandrian contemporary Athanasius listed only the present twenty-seven New Testament books. That evidence showed that Athanasius's 367 letter did not close debate, launched Ehrman's first academic publication, and established his lasting interest in the canon.

title: Why Wasn’t Peter’s Apocalypse Included in the New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the Apocalypse of Peter nearly entered the New Testament canon and why its universal salvation theme may have counted against it.
searchSummary: Argues that the Apocalypse of Peter probably lost canonical acceptance because its earliest recoverable form taught universal salvation. The work was treated as Scripture by some Christians from the second through fourth centuries, but surviving Greek and Ethiopic versions reveal later editorial changes. In the older ending, the apostles' pleas move Christ to release, baptize, and save everyone in hell. As most church leaders condemned that doctrine, the book failed the requirement that canonical writings teach accepted orthodoxy.

title: My Next Book: Creating the Bible — How We Got the Canon of the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a planned book on how the twenty-seven New Testament books came to be accepted as Christian Scripture.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's planned study of how twenty-seven particular writings became the New Testament while other Gospels, letters, and apocalypses were excluded. Discoveries such as the Gospel of Peter and Nag Hammadi library revealed competing early Christian groups with their own apostolic books, challenging assumptions that the outcome was inevitable. The project will explain why individual works won or lost acceptance, why consensus took centuries, and how authorship, theology, usage, and church conflict shaped the collection.

title: Paul’s Letters to the Philippians and to Philemon, “At a Glance” and with Questions for Reflection
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Philippians and Philemon at a glance with reflection questions about Paul's imprisonment, gratitude, and slavery.

title: Scheduled Blog Maintenance – Monday Sept. 8th
author: jennao
description: Announces scheduled blog maintenance for the launch of a new behind-the-scenes platform.

title: Questions: Did Paul state that Jesus was put in a tomb? Is Jesus like Pagan gods? Is the hope for a messiah like the belief in Santa?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to questions about Jesus' burial, pagan analogies to resurrection and exaltation, Revelation's authorship, and Jewish messianic expectations.
searchSummary: Answers four reader questions about early Christianity and Jewish expectations. Bart explains that Paul's word for Jesus' burial does not specify a tomb or exclude other places for remains; distinguishes Jewish resurrection from pagan divine revival and compares Jesus's exaltation with humans made divine; argues Revelation's John probably used his real name; and describes biblical and later Jewish messiahs as human rulers expected to deliver Israel rather than mythical figures.

title: 1 Thessalonians at a Glance, and Questions for Reflection
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes 1 Thessalonians as Paul's earliest surviving letter and offers reflection questions about mission, conversion, and the expected end.

title: Paul’s Letter to the Galatians “At a Glance” and Questions for Reflection
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Galatians as Paul's angry response to missionaries requiring Gentile circumcision and Jewish Law observance.
searchSummary: Provides an overview of Galatians as Paul's forceful response to missionaries who required gentile believers to adopt circumcision and other practices of Jewish law. Paul defends the divine origin of his gospel and insists that justification comes through faith in Christ rather than Torah observance. The post also explores the tension between freedom from the law and Paul's claim that love of neighbor fulfills it.

title: The Birth of Christianity (My Other Class): Check Out the Writing Assignments!
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes writing assignments for a course on early Christian history and literature after the New Testament.
searchSummary: Explains how weekly position papers prepare students for discussion in a course on Christianity from the post-New Testament period through the fourth century. The assignments ask students to analyze ancient texts, take defensible positions, and consider issues such as conversion, martyrdom, Gnosticism, women, Judaism, miracles, and hell. Ehrman argues that writing before class encourages careful reading, independent thought, and more productive conversation without requiring students to find a single correct answer.

title: The Bible and Suffering:  My NEW Course at UNC This Term
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a UNC course on biblical explanations for suffering, violence, free will, and divine responsibility.
searchSummary: Presents the syllabus for Ehrman's undergraduate course on biblical explanations of suffering within Jewish and Christian traditions. The course examines punishment, testing, human evil, redemptive suffering, free will, demonic powers, apocalyptic judgment, and claims that suffering is senseless. Its readings and assignments are designed to compare the Bible's diverse responses, evaluate religious claims critically, develop students' own views, and strengthen oral and written communication without promoting a particular belief.

title: So Did Secretaries Write the Apostles’ Letters for Them?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether ancient secretaries could have composed apostolic letters for illiterate figures such as Peter or John.
searchSummary: Evaluates whether ancient secretaries commonly coauthored or independently composed substantial letters for people who could not write. Evidence for such practices is nearly absent: secretaries reliably took dictation, elites sometimes permitted minor editing, and illiterate clients hired scribes for brief formulaic documents. The few Ciceronian examples of writing in another's name were exceptional and acknowledged as deceptive. Ehrman concludes that secretaries cannot plausibly explain sophisticated Christian works attributed to illiterate apostles.

title: Couldn’t 1 and 2 Peter Have Been Written By Peter’s Secretaries?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores ancient secretarial practices to assess whether secretaries could explain the polished Greek of letters attributed to Peter.
searchSummary: Examines the common proposal that secretaries transformed Peter's ideas into the polished Greek of 1 and 2 Peter. Ancient evidence strongly supports secretaries taking exact dictation, but offers only sparse examples of minor stylistic editing for wealthy Roman elites and none of wholesale rewriting of complex theological treatises for poor laborers. Since style is not the only reason scholars question these letters, Ehrman argues that invoking an otherwise unattested secretary does not rescue Petrine authorship.

title: For Further Reading on James, 1 Peter, and 2 Peter
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends further reading on James, 1 Peter, and 2 Peter, including accessible studies, commentaries, and online resources.
searchSummary: Recommends accessible scholarship for studying James, 1 Peter, 2 Peter, Jude, and early Christian persecution. Ehrman briefly annotates introductory studies, sociological treatments, works on martyrdom and Roman perceptions of Christians, and major scholarly commentaries, explaining the audience or value of each. He also points readers to his New Testament textbook and a reliable online lecture course. The list is designed to help non-specialists pursue historical setting, theology, authorship, suffering, and close textual interpretation.

title: 2 Peter: Who Wrote It, When, and Why?
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents the case that 2 Peter is pseudonymous and explains why the book's authenticity was disputed in early Christianity.

title: 2 Peter in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes 2 Peter as a warning against false teachers, immoral lifestyles, and denial of coming judgment.
searchSummary: Explains 2 Peter as a purported apostolic warning against Christian teachers accused of immoral conduct, distorting Paul's letters, and denying the approaching judgment. The author invokes Peter's presence at Jesus's transfiguration and treats Paul's writings alongside Scripture to establish authority, although the opponents' precise beliefs remain unclear. Because God's sense of time differs from humanity's and delay permits repentance, Christ's return remains imminent; the present world will be destroyed by fire and replaced by a righteous creation.

title: September 2025 Gold Q&A
author: jennao
description: Announces the September 2025 Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: Platinum Repost: The Death and Afterlife of Jesus: A Historical Reconstruction Part II – Guest Post by Platinum Member Mark Reichert
author: jennao
description: Presents the second part of a Platinum member's historical reconstruction of events after Jesus' crucifixion.
searchSummary: Presents guest author Mark Reichert's speculative reconstruction that Jesus survived crucifixion temporarily rather than rising in a glorified body. Reichert proposes that Joseph of Arimathea obtained the body through a centurion, concealed signs of life, removed Jesus from the tomb, and arranged later appearances before Jesus died from his injuries. He acknowledges lacking proof but argues that premature declaration of death is more plausible than resurrection and ascension.

title: Jesus, Essenes, Bible Translations, and 2 Thessalonians: Readers’ Questions and Answers
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to questions about Jesus and the Essenes, Bible translations, and the authorship of 2 Thessalonians.

title: Why An Author Claiming to Be Peter Wanted to Sound Like Paul
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that the author of 1 Peter may have used Pauline-sounding language to reconcile Petrine authority with Pauline Christianity.
searchSummary: Explains why a pseudonymous author might write in Peter's name while making him sound like Paul. First Peter principally encourages Christians facing local social hostility, but its Pauline voice also presents Peter and Paul as united leaders. Ehrman compares Acts, which similarly harmonizes the apostles amid persecution, and argues that solidarity at the top models the unified front suffering communities require. The forgery therefore joins pastoral encouragement with an implicit claim of apostolic agreement.

title: Is 1 Peter More Like 1 Paul?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why 1 Peter sounds Pauline while still advancing a distinct argument under Peter's name.
searchSummary: Argues that 1 Peter deliberately sounds Pauline even though its author has a distinct agenda. Its letter structure, vocabulary, scriptural quotations, theology, ethics, associates, and closing formula repeatedly echo both authentic and later Pauline writings. Differences from Paul do not erase the imitation; an author using Pauline language would naturally adapt it to his own message. Ehrman concludes that the writer claims Peter's authority while actualizing Pauline traditions, raising the question of why Peter is made to speak like Paul.

title: Why Does the Author of 1 Peter Sound Like Paul Instead of Peter?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the problem that 1 Peter claims Petrine authority while sounding unlike traditions associated with Peter.
searchSummary: Shows that little in 1 Peter reflects what is otherwise known about the historical Peter. The letter addresses Gentile converts in Paul's mission territory, lacks Peter's association with Jewish law, names Pauline coworkers, and uses Pauline greetings and themes. Even its claim to witness Christ's sufferings does not uniquely evoke Peter, who fled and denied Jesus. Ehrman concludes that without Peter's name readers would not attribute the work to him; its content sounds far more like Paul.

title: Did The Apostle Peter Write 1 Peter?
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses evidence about literacy in Roman Palestine to question whether Peter could have composed 1 Peter in literary Greek.
searchSummary: Uses literacy studies and archaeology to argue that the historical Peter could not have composed 1 Peter. Only a small urban elite in Roman Palestine could read, fewer could write, and literary Greek required extensive specialized education. Peter was an Aramaic-speaking fisherman from impoverished, largely illiterate Capernaum, while the letter displays polished Greek rhetoric and mastery of the Septuagint. Neither adult schooling nor a secretary provides a historically supported explanation, making pseudonymous authorship more probable.

title: 1 Peter: Who Wrote It, When, and Why?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines the authorship, date, and purpose of 1 Peter, especially its concern with Christians facing persecution.
searchSummary: Introduces the authorship, date, and purpose of 1 Peter. The letter addresses Christians facing hostility and urges exemplary conduct modeled on Christ's unjust suffering. Although it claims to come from Peter in Rome, its use of Babylon as a code for Rome likely reflects the post-70 destruction of Jerusalem, after Peter's traditional death. More decisively, its educated Greek composition conflicts with the low literacy of an Aramaic-speaking Galilean fisherman, prompting doubts about authenticity.

title: The Death and Afterlife of Jesus: A Historical Reconstruction Part I – by Mark Reichert (Platinum Member Winner)
author: admin
description: Presents a Platinum member's reconstruction of Jesus' crucifixion, burial, and resurrection traditions.
searchSummary: Begins guest author Mark Reichert's historical reconstruction of Jesus's death and reported appearances. After reviewing Gospel relationships and accepting crucifixion under Pilate as probable, Reichert questions Pilate's release of the body, John's spear wound, and standard resurrection claims. He argues that some crucifixion victims could be removed alive and suggests that an empty tomb and post-crucifixion appearances might reflect Jesus's survival, a theory developed in the second installment.

title: 1 Peter in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes 1 Peter as a letter to persecuted Gentile Christians urging faithful suffering in imitation of Christ.
searchSummary: Explains 1 Peter as a circular letter encouraging gentile Christians in Asia Minor who face local hostility after abandoning their former social and religious lives. The author strengthens group identity by portraying believers as God's family, temple, priesthood, and chosen people, while urging honorable conduct, submission, and gentle defense to silence suspicion. Their suffering should imitate Christ rather than result from wrongdoing, and steadfast believers will receive salvation when God's imminent judgment ends their temporary exile.

title: Am I?  AI?  What do you think?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on artificial intelligence, consciousness, free will, and whether human thought is fundamentally different from machine processing.
searchSummary: Questions whether human consciousness is fundamentally different from the artificial intelligence produced by machines. Ehrman rejects a nonmaterial soul because personality, memory, emotion, choice, and identity depend entirely on a molecular brain that can be altered by physical damage, yet he cannot explain how those molecules generate consciousness or free will. Since machines are also material configurations and repeatedly exceed predicted limits, he leaves open whether they might eventually become conscious and what that possibility means for humanity.

title: Q3 2025 Platinum Webinar – September 9th
author: jennao
description: Announces a Platinum webinar on biblical explanations for suffering.

title: Why Would Someone Forge the Letter of James?
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that James may have been forged to oppose a form of Pauline Christianity that separated faith from works.

title: Why James Did Not Write James
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the book of James does not reflect the known concerns of James of Jerusalem.

title: Could James, the Brother of Jesus, Even Write?
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses literacy, Greek style, and James's Galilean background to question whether Jesus' brother could have written the letter of James.
searchSummary: Argues that James, Jesus' brother, was unlikely to have written the Letter of James. The work's sophisticated Greek grammar, rhetoric, moral discourse, and use of the Septuagint require advanced Hellenistic education unavailable to a laborer from rural Nazareth. Learning conversational Greek later would not produce literary composition. Ehrman also notes that early sources portray James as deeply concerned with Jewish observance, whereas the letter lacks the distinctive cultural and ritual commitments expected from Jerusalem's Jewish-Christian leader.

title: James: Who, When, and Why?  Does It Claim to be by THAT James (the brother of Jesus)?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether the letter of James claims to be written by James, the brother of Jesus.

title: The Book of James in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes James as a collection of ethical instruction insisting that living faith must be shown through works.
searchSummary: Explains James as a collection of ethical exhortations drawing on Jewish wisdom and traditions resembling Jesus's teachings, especially the Sermon on the Mount. Its recurring concerns include disciplined speech, dangers of wealth, patience in suffering, care for the poor, prayer, healing, confession, and restoration within the community. Against claims that belief alone justifies, the author insists that genuine faith necessarily appears in conduct: a person is justified by works because faith without works is dead.

title: 1 and 2 Corinthians “At a Glance,” and Questions for Reflection
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes 1 and 2 Corinthians at a glance with reflection questions about Paul's responses to conflict in Corinth.

title: Some Readers’ Questions and Some Responses
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to reader questions about 2 Thessalonians, textual variants, Revelation, Eusebius, and Papias.
searchSummary: Answers questions about 2 Thessalonians, John 16:15, and the authorship of Revelation. Ehrman regards secretarial explanations for 2 Thessalonians as possible but unsupported, argues that John 16:15 was accidentally omitted when a scribe skipped between identical line endings, and finds no evidence identifying Revelation's John with John the Elder. Eusebius proposed that identification centuries later to separate Revelation from the stylistically different Fourth Gospel, leaving the author's actual identity unknown.

title: Will Everyone be Saved? (Everyone??)
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys the Christian idea of universal salvation and New Testament passages, especially in Paul, that may support it.

title: Can You “Lose Your Salvation”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Hebrews teaches that salvation can be lost and contrasts that with once-saved-always-saved theology.

title: Does the Book of Hebrews Indicate Jesus Ever Came To Earth?  A Response to Richard Carrier.
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to Richard Carrier's claim that Hebrews presents Jesus as a heavenly rather than earthly figure.
searchSummary: Rejects Richard Carrier's claim that Hebrews portrays Jesus as an angelic being crucified in the heavens rather than a person who lived on earth. Hebrews says God brought Jesus into the inhabited world, that he shared human flesh and blood, taught people who heard him, faced temptation, prayed with tears, descended from Judah, and endured a cross. Ehrman argues that authors normally need not specify that a crucifixion occurred on earth because that location is already assumed.

title: August 2025 Gold Q&A
author: jennao
description: Announces the August 2025 Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: The Letter to the Hebrews: For Further Reading
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends further reading on Hebrews and the relationship between Jews and Christians in early Christianity.

title: The Book of Hebrews:  Who Wrote It, When, and Why?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Hebrews as an anonymous sermon-like work and considers its authorship, date, audience, and purpose.

title: The Letter to the Hebrews: In a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Hebrews as the first General Epistle in the series and summarizes its major topics and setting.
searchSummary: Explains Hebrews as an anonymous exhortation to persecuted Christians not to abandon their faith for Judaism. Using the Jewish Scriptures, the author argues that Christ surpasses prophets, angels, Moses, Joshua, priests, covenant, tabernacle, and repeated sacrifices, fulfilling what the former system only foreshadowed. The old covenant was divinely given but provisional and obsolete; Jesus's heavenly priesthood and single sacrifice bring complete salvation, while apostasy rejects God's fulfillment and exposes former believers to coming judgment.

title: A Hiatus in My Responses
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a temporary pause in comment responses during a meditation retreat while scheduled posts continue.

title: The Death of Peter
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys early traditions and legends about Peter's martyrdom, including the later upside-down crucifixion story.

title: The Death of Paul
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys early references and later legends about Paul's martyrdom.

title: Some Readers’ Questions and Responses
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to questions about Jesus and the Essenes, John the Baptist, Bible translation, and 2 Thessalonians.

title: Unusual Fundraiser:  Want to Read the Pre-Published Manuscript of my New Book?
author: admin
description: Announces a fundraiser offering donors access to a pre-publication manuscript of a new book on altruism.
searchSummary: Invites donors of $1,000 to read and comment on a prepublication draft of The Origins of Altruism before Bart submits it to his publisher. Because the trade book is intended for general readers, he seeks feedback beyond scholarly colleagues and offers acknowledgment in the published volume. The fundraiser gives participants early access, helps improve the manuscript, and directs the contribution to blog-supported charities, while noting that the eventual commercial edition will remain available at an ordinary price.

title: Explaining the Triumph of Christianity
author: admin
description: Explains the cultural significance of Christianity's rise and its transformation of the Roman world and Western history.
searchSummary: Frames Christianity's triumph as a contingent transformation that reshaped Western culture, ethics, institutions, and concern for marginalized people. Christian ideals of equal worth, love, and service challenged Rome's ethic of dominance, even when believers failed to practice them. Ehrman asks how a few Galilean followers became millions and argues that Constantine accelerated but did not cause the outcome. His historical account avoids celebrating or condemning the victory, because Christianity's gains also entailed the loss and suppression of other religious cultures.

title: Time Zone widget
author: Diane
description: Displays a time-zone widget for blog scheduling.

title: Paul’s Letter to the Romans “At a Glance,” and Questions for Reflection
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Romans at a glance with reflection questions about Paul's gospel, mission, and relationship to Jewish Law.
searchSummary: Introduces Romans as Paul's explanation of his gospel before seeking support from Roman Christians for a mission to Spain. The letter addresses how Jews and gentiles are made right with God, the role of Jewish law, and Israel's place in salvation history. It presents both judicial and participationist models of salvation while asking how Paul's law-free gospel relates to Christian moral conduct.

title: The Transformation of Paul’s Teaching:  The Apocalypse of Paul
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the Apocalypse of Paul's vision of heavenly bliss and hellish punishment in the afterlife.

title: Fundamentalist Apologists, Christian and Mythicist
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares mythicist arguments about Jesus' nonexistence with conservative Christian apologetic reasoning.
searchSummary: Compares mythicist advocacy with conservative Christian apologetics despite their opposite conclusions about Jesus. Both approaches can begin with strong commitments, present specialized evidence readers cannot independently evaluate, multiply arguments faster than critics can answer them, and dismiss disagreement as ignorance or bias. Ehrman contrasts these persuasive strategies with the historical evidence accepted by specialists across religious and nonreligious perspectives, which he plans to present while also addressing leading mythicist objections to Jesus' existence.

title: Did Jesus Exist?  Why I Don’t Enjoy Reading the Mythicists
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why mythicist arguments about Jesus' nonexistence are difficult and frustrating to engage.
searchSummary: Explains why responding comprehensively to mythicist arguments is frustrating and unusually time-consuming. Detailed claims about sources such as Epiphanius, Josephus, Tacitus, and early Christian writings may require pages of historical context to expose problems contained in a single paragraph, while book-length rebuttals invite still longer replies. Ehrman nevertheless argues that claims Jesus never existed should be evaluated seriously and prepares to present the evidence and answer questions for a public course despite the diminishing returns of exhaustive debate.

title: July 2025 Gold Q&A
author: jennao
description: Announces the July 2025 Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: Submit Your Platinum Post Vote!
author: jennao
description: Invites Platinum members to vote on which guest post should be shared with the wider blog.

title: Paul’s Vision of Heaven and Hell
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Apocalypse of Paul as a non-canonical account of Paul's journey through heaven and hell.
searchSummary: Introduces the Apocalypse of Paul, a late-third-century account that expands Paul's brief reference to visiting the third heaven into a guided tour of heavenly rewards and hellish punishments. Drawing partly on the Apocalypse of Peter, the work uses Paul's authority to address later Christians rather than preserve historical memory and eventually influenced medieval afterlife traditions and Dante. Its moral emphasis makes conduct after conversion decisive: even professing Christians face damnation when they fail to live ascetically and righteously.

title: Chastity Within Marriage?  Paul Taught THAT?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how the Acts of Paul and Thecla makes sexual chastity, even within marriage, central to its gospel message.

title: Paul and His Most Famous Woman Disciple
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Acts of Paul and Thecla and the legendary story of Paul's most famous female disciple.

title: Should We Keep “Slaves” in the New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses the problem of translating the Greek term for enslaved people in the New Testament.
searchSummary: Examines whether the Greek word doulos should be translated as slave, servant, bond-servant, or enslaved person. Ancient slavery differed from American racial slavery, yet doulos still identified someone legally owned by another, making servant misleading despite modern connotations. Ehrman recounts debates within the NRSV committees and argues that translations should preserve the Bible's morally troubling historical realities rather than soften them through less accurate terminology.

title: Paul’s Letter to Philemon: For Further Reading
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends further reading on Philemon and the wider context of Paul's undisputed letters.

title: Reader Survey Webinar Registration
author: jennao
description: Invites survey participants to a webinar on lessons from more than 4,000 blog posts.

title: Philemon and the Morality of Slavery
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Philemon to discuss Paul's posture toward slavery, social justice, and apostolic authority.

title: The Letter to Philemon in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Philemon as Paul's appeal for Onesimus to be received by Philemon without punishment.
searchSummary: Explains Philemon as Paul's personal appeal concerning Onesimus, a slave who apparently fled after wronging his master, sought Paul as a mediator, and converted while Paul was imprisoned. Paul asks his convert Philemon to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother without punishment and offers to cover any debt while reminding Philemon of his own obligation. The letter does not clearly request manumission, but Paul may be seeking Onesimus's return to serve him in mission.

title: The Evolution of Jewish Monotheism–Platinum Post By Daniel Kohanski
author: jennao
description: Presents a Platinum member post on how Israelite and Jewish monotheism developed over time.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: Another Puzzling Figure in the Hebrew Bible: Woman Wisdom?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores whether Woman Wisdom in Proverbs reflects a modified idea of a divine female companion to Yahweh.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: Who Was the Suffering Servant of Isaiah 53?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the Suffering Servant passages in Second Isaiah and why they have been especially important for Christian interpretation.
searchSummary: Argues that Isaiah 53 originally describes Israel rather than a future suffering messiah. Second Isaiah addresses Judeans after Jerusalem's destruction and portrays the servant's suffering as past, with vindication still to come; nearby passages explicitly identify the servant as Israel. Although Christians later applied the text to Jesus, the passage never calls its subject the messiah and speaks first to the experience and hoped-for restoration of exiled Israelites.

title: One of the Stranger Stories of Scripture
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the Genesis story of the sons of God, the daughters of humans, and the Nephilim.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: How We Know the World Was Created in 4004 BCE…
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains James Ussher's biblical chronology and the calculation that creation occurred in 4004 BCE.

title: Understanding the Hebrew Bible: The “Old” Testament in Modern Scholarship
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a revised Bible textbook and Hebrew Bible course, then explains the Documentary Hypothesis and modern views of Pentateuchal sources.
searchSummary: Introduces resources for studying the Hebrew Bible and explains the modern scholarly view that the Pentateuch developed from multiple sources rather than being written by Moses. Ehrman recommends introductory books, describes the J, E, D, and P sources associated with the Documentary Hypothesis, and notes the contradictions, divine names, and differing concerns used to identify them. He also explains that recent scholarship generally makes the Pentateuch's composition later and more complex than Wellhausen proposed.

title: Acts of the Jewish Christians: Rethinking Their Role in the First Jewish-Roman War – Platinum Post by Rizwan Ahmed
author: jennao
description: Presents a Platinum member argument reconsidering whether Jewish Christians may have participated in the First Jewish-Roman War.
searchSummary: Proposes that some Jewish followers of Jesus may have participated in the First Jewish-Roman War rather than all fleeing Jerusalem for Pella. Rizwan Ahmed combines Josephus's account of devastated Galilee and Judea, the execution of James, Torah-observant tensions, messianic expectations, and the political influence of Jerusalem's Jesus movement to challenge the later flight tradition. Although explicit evidence of Christian participation is lacking, the movement's Jewish setting makes complete neutrality and disappearance historically questionable.

title: My Least Favorite Passage of the Pastorals:  Those Silent and Submissive Women….
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques the Pastoral Epistles' command for women to be silent and submissive in church.

title: The Pastoral Epistles. For Further Reading
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends further reading on the Pastoral Epistles, especially authorship, institutionalization, and Pauline forgery.
searchSummary: Provides an annotated guide to scholarship on the Pastoral Epistles and related disputed Pauline writings. Recommended studies address later developments in Pauline theology, the social institutionalization of Pauline churches, constructions of Paul's legacy, and the ancient practice of writing under another person's name. Commentaries on First Timothy, Second Timothy, and Titus supply detailed treatment of authorship, date, historical setting, themes, and disputed passages, while an online course offers a broader New Testament introduction.

title: More Evidence That the Pastoral Epistles Were Written After the Days of Paul
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that the Pastorals reflect later proto-orthodox concerns with clergy, creed, and canon.
searchSummary: Argues that the Pastoral Epistles reflect proto-orthodox Christianity after Paul's lifetime rather than the apostle's own historical setting. Their treatment of faith as an authoritative body of teaching, appeal to Christian sayings as Scripture, established clergy, social respectability, opposition to ascetic and Gnosticizing teachers, and restrictions on women fit a later institutional church. A follower wrote in Paul's name to authorize responses to problems facing churches a generation or two after his death.

title: The Later (post-Pauline) Context of the Pastoral Epistles
author: BDEhrman
description: Places the Pastoral Epistles in a later context of early Christian diversity and emerging proto-orthodoxy.
searchSummary: Uses the Pastoral Epistles' church organization and opposition to false teaching to place them after Paul's lifetime within developing proto-orthodox Christianity. Paul's congregations were largely charismatic communities without a single local ruler, but later churches established bishops, presbyters, and deacons to control doctrine and practice. The Pastorals instruct authorized representatives to appoint qualified leaders and transmit approved teaching. This emerging hierarchy anticipates the clergy, creed, and canon that helped proto-orthodox Christianity defeat competing forms.

title: Who Wrote the Pastoral Epistles?  When?  And Why?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the authorship question for the Pastoral Epistles and the case that they were not written by Paul.
searchSummary: Explains why most scholars attribute First Timothy, Second Timothy, and Titus to one later author rather than Paul. Their vocabulary includes unusually many words characteristic of second-century Christians, familiar Pauline terms carry changed meanings, and their false teachers and organized church structures fit a post-Pauline proto-orthodox setting. These cumulative differences suggest that an unknown Christian invoked Paul's identity to defend established teaching and administration against competing forms of Christianity.

title: The Pastoral Epistles of 2 Timothy and Titus in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes 2 Timothy and Titus as Pastoral letters concerned with church leadership, false teaching, and moral conduct.
searchSummary: Compares 2 Timothy and Titus as Pastoral Epistles presenting Paul's instructions to appointed church leaders. Second Timothy depicts an imprisoned Paul awaiting death, asking Timothy to visit, preserve moral character, and suppress teachers who claim resurrection has occurred; Titus directs its recipient to appoint elders in Crete, reject speculative Jewish-Christian teaching, and instruct social groups in proper conduct. Both use apostolic authority to promote disciplined leadership, orthodox instruction, and orderly communities, though each presupposes a different setting.

title: The Pastoral Epistle of 1 Timothy in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Pastoral Epistles and summarizes 1 Timothy's concerns about false teachers and church organization.
searchSummary: Introduces 1 Timothy and the Pastoral Epistles as writings attributed to Paul that direct Timothy and Titus to control false teaching and organize churches. First Timothy instructs Timothy in Ephesus to appoint respectable male bishops and deacons, regulate prayer, women, widows, wealth, and community conduct, and silence opponents. Their myths, genealogies, law teaching, asceticism, and claimed knowledge may anticipate Gnosticism, while stronger hierarchy provides a unified response to doctrinal and social disorder.

title: In the Weeds with the Author of 2 Thessalonians
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a detailed argument that 2 Thessalonians imitates 1 Thessalonians rather than coming from Paul.
searchSummary: Argues that Second Thessalonians imitates First Thessalonians rather than coming from the same author. Its opening, closing, unusual phrases, sequence of themes, double thanksgivings, eschatological section, ethical instruction, and warning against idleness closely reproduce features of the earlier letter that Paul does not repeat this way elsewhere. The extensive borrowing makes sense as a later writer's effort to sound Pauline, especially when the independently composed portions differ from Paul's style and theology.

title: 2 Thessalonians, The Modern State of Israel,  World War III, and the Return of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how some evangelical interpretations of 2 Thessalonians and rebuilt-Temple prophecy affect modern apocalyptic expectations.

title: 2 Thessalonians: For Further Reading
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends further reading on 2 Thessalonians and the broader Deutero-Pauline letters.
searchSummary: Provides an annotated reading guide to Second Thessalonians and the wider Deutero-Pauline corpus. Recommended books examine later developments in Pauline theology, institutionalization within Pauline churches, constructions of Paul's legacy, and ancient Christian forgery, while two detailed commentaries defend Pauline authorship from different perspectives. The list encourages readers to compare competing arguments about authorship, date, historical setting, and eschatology rather than relying only on one critical conclusion.

title: Time to Vote: Help Choose the Next Platinum Post!
author: jennao
description: Invites Platinum members to vote on guest posts after a backlog of submissions.

title: 2 Thessalonians:  Who Wrote It, When, and Why?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether 2 Thessalonians was written by Paul or by a later author imitating Paul's style.
searchSummary: Argues that Second Thessalonians was written after Paul's death to restrain Christians expecting Jesus' immediate return. Unlike First Thessalonians, where the end arrives suddenly without warning, the disputed letter requires rebellion and the man of lawlessness to appear first; its claim that Paul always authenticated letters by hand also conflicts with his actual practice. A later follower used Paul's authority to promote patient work, endurance, and a revised apocalyptic timetable.

title: 2 Thessalonians in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes 2 Thessalonians as a Pauline-sounding letter about persecution, judgment, and the timing of Jesus' return.
searchSummary: Explains 2 Thessalonians as a Pauline-sounding letter to persecuted Christians who believe the Day of the Lord has arrived or is immediately at hand. The author insists that a satanically empowered lawless figure must first claim divinity before Christ returns to destroy him, and tells members who stopped working to support themselves. Similarities to 1 Thessalonians may reflect imitation, while the letter's different timetable and self-authenticating signature raise doubts that Paul wrote it.

title: Interesting Questions from Readers (5/27/2025)
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to reader questions about women's head coverings in 1 Corinthians, missing lines in P46, and minor agreements among the Synoptic Gospels.

title: 1 Thessalonians and the Coming Rapture
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why 1 Thessalonians 4 does not teach the modern evangelical doctrine of the rapture.

title: 1 Thessalonians.  For Further Reading
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends further reading on 1 Thessalonians and the broader study of Paul's undisputed letters.

title: 1 Thessalonians: Who, When, and Why
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines the authorship, date, and purpose of 1 Thessalonians, including the roles of Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy.

title: 1 Thessalonians in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces 1 Thessalonians as Paul's earliest surviving letter and the earliest Christian writing now known.
searchSummary: Explains 1 Thessalonians as Paul's earliest surviving letter and the oldest extant Christian writing, addressed to pagan converts facing local persecution. Paul rejoices that they remained faithful, urges sexual holiness, and comforts those worried that believers who died before Jesus's imminent return had lost salvation. The dead will rise first to meet Christ, followed by the living, including Paul; this scene expresses participation in the returning king's arrival rather than a later dispensational rapture.

title: June 2025 Gold Q&A
author: jennao
description: Announces the June 2025 Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: Interesting Questions from Readers
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to reader questions about Acts' reliability, Paul, translation issues, and other biblical topics.
searchSummary: Answers questions about Paul's travels, inclusive language, and the time between Jesus' death and resurrection. Ehrman cautions against combining Acts with Paul's letters into one reliable itinerary, explains why Greek masculine plurals may require English phrases such as brothers and sisters, and doubts that Jews automatically counted every partial day as a full day. He suggests on the third day preceded the less chronologically precise phrase three days.

title: Colossians: For Further Reading
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends further reading on Colossians and the broader Deutero-Pauline letters.
searchSummary: Provides an annotated guide to scholarship on Colossians and other disputed Pauline letters. The recommended books examine later Pauline theology, constructions of Paul's legacy, ancient forgery, and the social institutionalization reflected in Ephesians, Colossians, and the Pastorals. Specialized commentaries treat Colossians alongside closely related Ephesians and introduce the major questions of authorship, date, historical setting, theology, and interpretation, while an online course supplies broader context.

title: The Book of Acts “At a Glance” and Controversial Questions
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Acts at a glance with study questions about Luke's second volume and its major topics.
searchSummary: Provides an at-a-glance introduction to Acts and questions for studying its authorship, date, historical value, and theological aims. It traces the movement from Jerusalem to a worldwide Gentile mission, emphasizing the Spirit's guidance, apostolic harmony, repentance, forgiveness, and freedom from Jewish law for Gentile converts. The study questions invite readers to compare Peter and Paul, examine Paul's evangelistic work, and identify the book's principal messages.

title: Did Paul Write That Letter?  Getting Into the Weeds…
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a detailed scholarly argument that Colossians was written in Paul's name by someone else.
searchSummary: Presents the cumulative scholarly case that Colossians was written by someone falsely claiming to be Paul. Statistical comparisons show major differences in conjunctions, infinitives, relative clauses, and sentence construction from the undisputed letters. Its theology also treats believers as already resurrected, describes redemption as forgiveness, elevates Christ differently, and embraces stable household ethics rather than Paul's imminent expectation. Together these consistent stylistic and substantive departures indicate a later author adapting Pauline themes while seeking Paul's authority.

title: The Letter to the Colossians: Who, When, and Why?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines the authorship, date, and purpose of Colossians and the reasons many scholars doubt Pauline authorship.

title: The Letter to the Colossians, in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Colossians as a letter warning against false teachers while presenting Christ as supreme over every power.
searchSummary: Explains Colossians as a prison letter, probably written in Paul's name, opposing teachers who combine Jewish observance, ascetic practice, visions, and angel worship. The author declares Christ the image of God in whom divine fullness dwells and through whom all powers were created and subdued; believers already share his heavenly status and need neither law nor mystical intermediaries. Their exalted identity nevertheless requires moral conduct and ordered relationships among spouses, children, parents, slaves, and masters.

title: Some Interesting Questions of the Week
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to reader questions about Old Testament authorship, Pauline letters, and other biblical issues.

title: How Athens Made Me Rethink….
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on how Athens prompted fresh thinking about Christianity's rise among lower-status people in the cultured Greco-Roman world.
searchSummary: Reflects on the contrast between Paul's unsuccessful preaching at Athens and Christianity's eventual conquest of the Greco-Roman world. Standing on the Areopagus between the Agora and Acropolis, Ehrman realized that a low-status preacher's message ultimately displaced the civilization whose philosophers mocked him. That improbable victory inspired The Triumph of Christianity. He regards it with sadness as well as wonder, because Christian dominance accompanied the neglect or destruction of pagan achievements in art, architecture, literature, and philosophy that cannot be recovered.

title: Some Intriguing Questions about Paul’s Letters
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to questions about Paul's relationship with the Jerusalem apostles, Galatians, and resurrection traditions.

title: Is the “Christ Poem” of Philippians Really a Poem?  When Did Jesus Really Become “Equal” With God?
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses the structure and Christology of the Philippians Christ poem, including Christ's equality with God.
searchSummary: Clarifies the Greek structure and theology of the Philippians Christ poem. Although English word order obscures its balanced lines, the Greek can still be arranged in poetic stanzas. The passage portrays Christ as a preexistent divine being who was not initially God's equal, became human, and was then exalted so that Isaiah's language of universal worship of Yahweh applies to Jesus. It therefore combines incarnation with a subsequent elevation to equality with God.

title: The Death and Afterlife of Jesus: A Historical Reconstruction Part II – Guest Post by Platinum Member Mark Reichert
author: jennao
description: Presents the second part of a Platinum member's historical reconstruction of events after Jesus' crucifixion.
searchSummary: Presents guest author Mark Reichert's speculative reconstruction that Jesus survived crucifixion temporarily rather than rising in a glorified body. Reichert proposes that Joseph of Arimathea obtained the body through a centurion, concealed signs of life, removed Jesus from the tomb, and arranged later appearances before Jesus died from his injuries. He acknowledges lacking proof but argues that premature declaration of death is more plausible than resurrection and ascension.

title: The Most Widely Discussed Passage of Philippians
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Philippians Christ poem as a key passage for Paul's incarnation Christology.
searchSummary: Introduces Philippians 2:6-11 as a highly structured composition Paul probably quotes rather than creates. Its unusual vocabulary, balanced form, and second half's imperfect fit with Paul's appeal to selfless service point to a preexisting poem. It describes a divine Christ relinquishing heavenly privilege, becoming human, dying, and then receiving universal lordship. Because the poem predates Philippians, it shows that incarnation Christology arose before Paul's surviving letters, within decades of Jesus' death.

title: Luke and John “At a Glance” and Controversial Questions
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Luke and John at a glance with study questions about their distinctive portraits of Jesus and salvation.
searchSummary: Presents textbook-style summaries and discussion questions for the Gospels of Luke and John. Luke is described through its date, sources, prophetic portrait of Jesus, movement of salvation from Jews to Gentiles, and continuation in Acts. John is distinguished by its later date, disputed traditional authorship, unique narratives, divine portrait of Jesus, and signs. Study questions invite comparison, redaction analysis, and evaluation of historical claims.

title: Philippians: For Further Reading
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends further reading on Philippians and the broader study of Paul's undisputed letters.

title: The Death and Afterlife of Jesus: A Historical Reconstruction Part I – Guest Post by Platinum Member Mark Reichert
author: jennao
description: Presents a Platinum member's reconstruction of Jesus' crucifixion, burial, and resurrection traditions.
searchSummary: Begins guest author Mark Reichert's historical reconstruction of Jesus's death and reported appearances. After reviewing Gospel relationships and accepting crucifixion under Pilate as probable, Reichert questions Pilate's release of the body, John's spear wound, and standard resurrection claims. He argues that some crucifixion victims could be removed alive and suggests that an empty tomb and post-crucifixion appearances might reflect Jesus's survival, a theory developed in the second installment.

title: Philippians: Who Wrote It, When, and Why?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Philippians as an authentic Pauline letter and considers whether it combines more than one letter.

title: Philippians in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Philippians as a prison letter about joy, support, self-giving, and warnings against circumcision teachers.
searchSummary: Explains Philippians as Paul's prison letter thanking the church for material support while urging joy, unity, and concern for others despite suffering. The Christ poem presents Jesus relinquishing divine status to serve and die before God exalts him, making self-giving the community's model; Paul also discusses Epaphroditus, Timothy, and possible death. He warns against teachers demanding gentile circumcision, contrasts law-based and faith-based righteousness, and asks Euodia and Syntyche to reconcile.

title: May 2025 Gold Q&A
author: jennao
description: Announces the May 2025 Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: Matthew and Mark “At a Glance” with Controversial Questions
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Matthew and Mark at a glance with study questions about sources, redaction, and each Gospel's emphases.
searchSummary: Provides concise scholarly profiles and discussion questions for Matthew and Mark. Matthew is presented as an anonymous Greek Gospel from about 80–85 CE that used Mark, Q, and M to portray Jesus as Jewish Messiah, new Moses, and authoritative interpreter of the Law, while criticizing Jewish leaders. Mark, written around 70 CE, portrays the misunderstood Son of God who must suffer, die, and be vindicated. Questions invite debate about antisemitism, Christology, historicity, and each Gospel's distinctive portrait.

title: Ephesians:  For Further Reading
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends further reading on Ephesians and the broader Deutero-Pauline letters.
searchSummary: Provides an annotated guide to scholarship on Ephesians and the wider Deutero-Pauline collection. The recommended studies compare later Pauline theology with the undisputed letters, examine how Pauline churches became institutionalized, trace constructions of Paul's legacy, and explain ancient literary forgery. Commentaries treating Ephesians together with closely related Colossians offer detailed analysis of authorship, date, historical context, theology, and disputed passages, supplemented by an online New Testament course.

title: Some Important Questions From Blog Readers
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to reader questions about the collection of Paul's letters, 2 Peter, and related early Christian texts.

title: Does a Different “Writing Style” Show (convincingly?) That Ephesians is a “Forgery”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why differences in writing style remain important for assessing whether Paul wrote Ephesians.
searchSummary: Evaluates the claim that stylistic differences in disputed Pauline letters result from coauthors rather than forgery. Although several letters name associates alongside Paul, proponents provide no ancient evidence showing that coauthorship produced long works with substantially different language, style, and content. Surviving coauthored letters do not reveal how composition was divided or support equal authorial roles. Ehrman argues that undocumented committee composition is therefore less probable than literary forgery, a practice abundantly attested throughout antiquity.

title: Can We Trust You When You Say “Most Scholars” Think Something?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how claims about what most scholars think are based on professional familiarity rather than formal surveys.
searchSummary: Defines a critical scholar as one who weighs evidence and leaves conclusions open rather than requiring them to confirm inerrancy or church tradition. Ehrman does not dismiss evangelical scholarship, but argues that institutional and theological environments can reinforce predetermined answers. His claims about majority critical views reflect what research scholars teach across non-evangelical colleges and major doctoral programs, not a formal poll or every scholar, and consensus itself remains a report of expert judgment rather than proof.

title: Ephesians: Who Wrote the Letter, When, and Why?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines the case that Ephesians was written in Paul's name by a later author.
searchSummary: Argues that Ephesians was written by a later follower of Paul, probably near the end of the first century. Its unusually long and complex sentences differ sharply from Paul's style, while its claims that believers are already raised and enthroned with Christ, its altered meaning of works, and its portrayal of Paul's former life conflict with undisputed letters. The author used Paul's authority to promote unity between Jewish and Gentile Christians and their reconciliation with God.

title: Ephesians in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Ephesians as a circular letter about unity, salvation, ethical life, and Christ's cosmic role.
searchSummary: Explains Ephesians as a circular letter, probably written by a later follower in Paul's name, reminding gentile Christians that Christ saved them rather than their good deeds. Christ's death removes the law as a barrier between Jews and gentiles, reconciles both groups to God, and reveals their shared heavenly identity. The letter urges believers to embody this unity through ethical conduct, church life, household relationships, and resistance to spiritual evil, while its wording and theology raise authorship questions.

title: Christ’s Preexistence in Galatians (Was Jesus an Angel?)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Galatians 4:14 shaped an argument that Paul understood Christ as a preexistent angelic being.
searchSummary: Explains why Galatians 4:14 led Ehrman to understand Paul's Christology as angelic incarnation. Paul's Greek comparison identifies Jesus Christ as an angel of God, possibly the chief angel, rather than placing Christ above a separate angelic category. This reading presents Christ as a preexistent divine being and manifestation of God who became human. Combined with Philippians 2, it yields a coherent account of Christ descending into human life and later being exalted to equality with God.

title: How Do We Know the Chronology of Paul’s Life and Letters?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why reconstructing the chronology of Paul's life and letters is difficult and evidence-dependent.

title: Key Questions about Paul
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to questions about Paul's relationship with Jerusalem apostles, Jewish Law, and resurrection traditions.
searchSummary: Addresses three historical questions about Paul: his conflict with Peter and the Jerusalem apostles, belief in Jesus' empty tomb, and competing accounts of his conversion. The central discussion explains that gentiles were accepted without becoming Jews, yet mixed communities still disputed kosher practice and shared meals. Paul demanded full fellowship, while Peter's withdrawal at Antioch suggests that the disagreement remained serious and unresolved.

title: Is Paul One of Matthew’s Enemies?
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Matthew and Paul on whether followers of Jesus should keep the Jewish Law.
searchSummary: Compares Matthew's teaching about Jewish law with Paul's rejection of requiring gentile believers to observe it. Both connect salvation with Jesus' death and resurrection, but Matthew's Jesus insists that every command remains valid and that followers must practice and teach the Law, whereas Paul curses those who demand Torah observance from gentiles. The conflict appears substantial, raising—but not resolving—whether Matthew knew Paul's views, wrote against them decades later, or regarded Paul as an enemy.

title: Galatians: For Further Reading
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends further reading on Galatians and the broader study of Paul's undisputed letters.

title: Galatians:  Who, When, and Why?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Galatians as an authentic Pauline letter written against missionaries requiring Gentile law observance.
searchSummary: Explains why Galatians is accepted as an authentic letter by Paul and examines its likely date, audience, and occasion. After Paul founded gentile churches, rival missionaries argued that followers of the Jewish messiah must adopt Torah observance and circumcision. Paul answered that his gospel came directly from Christ and that requiring the law for salvation undermined Christ, even though Christian freedom still required ethical conduct.

title: Galatians in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Galatians as Paul's urgent argument that Gentiles are made right with God by faith in Christ, not Torah observance.
searchSummary: Explains Galatians as Paul's angry defense of his law-free gospel against missionaries urging his gentile converts to adopt circumcision and Jewish observance. Paul recounts his revelation of Christ and dealings with the Jerusalem apostles, then argues from Abraham that justification comes through faith rather than works of the law. The law could identify wrongdoing but not overcome sin; believers instead receive the Spirit, whose transforming power produces loving conduct without requiring gentiles to become Jews.

title: Proof that Luke Used Matthew?  And Interpolations in Luke about the Virgin Birth.
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to questions about whether Luke used Matthew and whether Luke's virgin birth material includes interpolations.
searchSummary: Answers two questions about Luke's sources and textual development. A five-word agreement between Matthew and Luke is treated as relevant but insufficient proof that Luke copied Matthew because scribal harmonization, different copies of Mark, or oral tradition could explain it. The post also considers whether Luke originally lacked the infancy narrative and whether the phrase as was supposed entered the genealogy later, concluding that the possibility is plausible but not required.

title: Interpolations and Textual Variants in the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Distinguishes interpolations from ordinary textual variants using examples from 2 Corinthians and other New Testament passages.
searchSummary: Distinguishes textual variants from proposed interpolations using passages in 1 and 2 Corinthians. Variants are changes made after a text entered circulation and are evidenced by competing manuscript readings; interpolations are hypothetical additions made before the common ancestor of all surviving copies and therefore appear in every manuscript. Ehrman argues that translation brackets should mark manuscript-supported textual corruptions, such as Mark's longer ending, rather than passages scholars suspect were inserted before the recoverable manuscript tradition began.

title: Taking 2 Corinthians to Pieces….
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the argument that 2 Corinthians may be composed from multiple Pauline letters spliced together.

title: 2 Corinthians: For Further Reading
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends further reading on 2 Corinthians and the broader study of Paul and the Pauline letters.

title: 2 Corinthians: Who Wrote It, When, and Why?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines 2 Corinthians as an undisputed Pauline letter complicated by evidence of multiple letter fragments.

title: 2 Corinthians in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes 2 Corinthians as Paul's reflection on a strained relationship with Corinth and challenges to apostolic authority.
searchSummary: Explains 2 Corinthians as portions of multiple letters tracing Paul's damaged and restored relationship with his Corinthian converts. Chapters 10–13 attack rival “super-apostles,” defend Paul's authority through his weakness and suffering, and threaten a painful visit; chapters 1–9 celebrate reconciliation, reflect on ministry through hardship, and promote a collection for Jerusalem. Their sharply different tones and references to visits and correspondence suggest the earlier hostile letter was placed after the later conciliatory one.

title: Platinum Webinar: April 29th
author: jennao
description: Announces a Platinum webinar on Marcion and Marcion's followers.

title: Questions on Jesus’ Eschatology, Mark’s Accuracy, and Why Genre Matters
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to questions about Jesus' eschatology, Mark's accuracy, and the importance of genre for interpretation.
searchSummary: Answers questions about several methods and historical judgments in New Testament study. Ehrman rejects realized eschatology as an apologetic reinterpretation of Jesus' failed expectation, finds a female author of Luke possible but highly improbable given ancient literacy patterns, and explains why Mark preserves only a small and uncertain portion of Jesus' life. He distinguishes genre criticism, which interprets a work through conventions such as ancient biography, from redaction criticism of editorial changes and form criticism of oral units.

title: One of the Most Misunderstood Verses of Paul:  Flesh and Blood Will Not Inherit the Kingdom
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Paul's view that resurrection involves a transformed body rather than a disembodied afterlife.
searchSummary: Explains Paul's statement that “flesh and blood” cannot inherit God's kingdom without turning his resurrection hope into a bodiless afterlife. In 1 Corinthians 15, mortal bodies are related to their resurrected forms as seeds are to mature plants: continuous yet radically transformed into imperishable, spirit-composed bodies. Both the dead and those still living at Christ's return receive this change. Paul later allows an interim presence with Christ before the final bodily resurrection.

title: 1 Corinthians: For Further Reading
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends further reading on 1 Corinthians and the broader study of Paul and the Pauline letters.

title: Do We Have the Lord’s Supper All Wrong?  Platinum Post by Douglas Wadeson MD
author: jennao
description: Examines whether the Lord's Supper was invented by Paul or inherited from earlier disciples.

title: 1 Corinthians:  Who, When, and Why?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines 1 Corinthians as an undisputed Pauline letter and explains its date, purpose, and Corinthian setting.

title: Help Shape the Future of the Blog!
author: jennao
description: Asks members to complete a reader survey connected with the blog's next development phase.

title: 1 Corinthians in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes 1 Corinthians as Paul's response to ethical, communal, worship, and resurrection problems in Corinth.
searchSummary: Surveys the many disputes Paul addresses in 1 Corinthians, including factions, lawsuits, sexual conduct, marriage, idol meat, women's head coverings, the Lord's Supper, spiritual gifts, worship, and resurrection. Paul repeatedly argues that believers form one body whose members must use freedom and gifts in loving service rather than self-exaltation. He rejects claims that resurrection is already complete, insisting that believers will receive transformed bodies in the future and that bodily life therefore matters morally now.

title: Two Fundamental Questions: How Do You Date a Manuscript and How Do you Know the Meaning of a Word?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to questions about manuscript dating through palaeography and how scholars determine word meanings.

title: April 2025 Gold Q&A
author: jennao
description: Announces the April 2025 Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: Guest Post by Dr. Paul Fredriksen Part III: The Conversions of “Christianity”
author: jennao
description: Presents Paula Fredriksen's discussion of early Christian conversion, Eusebius, and the development of Christianity over five centuries.
searchSummary: Paula Fredriksen challenges Eusebius's triumphal account of a unified Christianity emerging from Judaism, defeating heresy, surviving persecution, and finding peace under Constantine. She uses textual criticism, rhetoric, inscriptions, archaeology, and ancient beliefs about divine agency to reconstruct a more diverse history. Jewish-Christian interaction continued, orthodoxy gained force through imperial power, and post-Constantinian Christians often persecuted other Christians more systematically than pagan Rome had.

title: Guest Post by Dr. Paula Fredriksen Part II: The Politics of Piety
author: jennao
description: Presents Paula Fredriksen's discussion of Roman piety, ancient religion, and the political setting of Christian persecution.
searchSummary: Paula Fredriksen explains that ancient religion functioned as inherited civic and family custom rather than as a private set of beliefs. Worship sustained communities and the empire's relationship with its gods, shaping measures such as Decius's universal sacrifice order. Constantine and Theodosius eventually replaced this pluralistic arrangement with imperial support for Nicene Christianity, helping create a more modern conception of religion.

title: Guest Post by Dr. Paula Fredriksen Part I: Ancient Christianities: Multiplicity, Messy Origins, and “Monotheism”
author: jennao
description: Introduces Paula Fredriksen's Ancient Christianities and its argument for messy, diverse origins rather than a single uniform Christianity.
searchSummary: Paula Fredriksen argues that Christianity was diverse from its beginnings and only later came to be imagined as a single, uniform movement. She places Jesus and Paul firmly within Judaism, challenges the description of Paul as law-free, and explains that ancient Jews could acknowledge other divine beings while worshiping Israel's God alone. Christianity emerged as a separate religion only in retrospect.

title: Paul and Women Apostles
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Romans 16 points to women leaders and apostles in Paul's churches.
searchSummary: Argues that Paul recognized women as important church leaders by examining Junia in Romans 16:7. Paul calls Junia and Andronicus prominent among the apostles, yet some English translations changed the common feminine name Junia into the unattested masculine Junias because translators assumed an apostle had to be male. Ehrman contrasts this evidence with misogynistic passages that probably were not written by Paul or were later inserted into his letters.

title: The Earliest Understanding of Christ?  The Hint in Paul’s Letter to the Romans
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Romans 1:3-4 to argue that an early Christology understood Jesus as exalted to divine sonship after resurrection.

title: Paul’s Letter to the Romans: For Further Reading
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends further reading on Romans and the broader scholarly study of Paul.

title: Unusually Important for the Letter to the Romans: Paul’s Models of Salvation
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Paul's judicial and participationist models of salvation in Romans.

title: The Letter to the Romans: Who, When, and Why?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Romans as an authentic Pauline letter written to secure support for a western mission.

title: Will I See Fido in Heaven?  Webinar on the Afterlife of Animals with Me and Barbara Ambros
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a webinar comparing Christian and Buddhist views of animals in the afterlife.
searchSummary: Announces a comparative webinar asking whether animals possess souls, enter heaven, experience salvation, or return through reincarnation. Ehrman and Buddhist scholar Barbara Ambros examine how Christianity and Buddhism understand pets and other animals after death, highlighting differences between heavenly afterlife and rebirth traditions. The event also supports graduate research and teaching through UNC's Robert Miller Graduate Student Excellence Fund, with registration open to the public and all suggested donations directed to student conference and professional-development expenses.

title: A Major Milestone on the Blog! $3 Million Donated to Charity!!
author: jennao
description: Celebrates the blog passing three million dollars in charitable donations and recounts the blog's fundraising origins.
searchSummary: Celebrates the blog surpassing $3 million distributed to charities since its 2012 launch. Bart recounts expecting to raise only $20,000 in three years, contrasts that estimate with the previous year's $580,000, and describes the twin missions of public scholarship and helping people in need. He credits membership fees, donors, Jen Olmos, volunteers, and sustained publication, emphasizing that all membership revenue goes to charity and encouraging readers to help expand the community.

title: New Course Announcement: The Other Doubting Thomases
author: jennao
description: Announces a course on resurrection narratives and the disciples' doubt in the Gospels and Acts.
searchSummary: Announces a two-lecture course examining why several New Testament resurrection narratives say that some of Jesus' disciples doubted even when the risen Jesus appeared before them. Ehrman asks what these recurring doubt traditions mean, where they originated, and whether they may preserve a historical memory that some apostles never accepted the resurrection. The course treats the familiar story of Doubting Thomas as only one part of a broader and rarely examined problem in the Gospels and Acts.

title: Interested in Visiting the Greek Islands with Me?  Spots Still Available!
author: BDEhrman
description: Invites readers to join a Greek Islands trip and previews the itinerary.

title: Paul’s Letter to the Romans in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Pauline letters sequence and summarizes Romans as Paul's explanation of sin, salvation, and faith.
searchSummary: Explains Romans as Paul's presentation of his gospel to a church he did not found, seeking support for a planned western mission and correcting misunderstandings about his teaching. All people are enslaved to sin, and both Jews and gentiles receive justification and liberation through faith in Christ's death and resurrection rather than works of law. God has not rejected Israel, all Israel will ultimately be saved, and grace enables ethical obedience rather than lawless behavior.

title: Paul’s Life and Letters:  For Further Reading
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends further reading on Paul's life, letters, and significance.

title: The Life of Paul in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Paul's life as a persecutor turned missionary after a vision of the resurrected Jesus.
searchSummary: Reconstructs Paul's life primarily from his undisputed letters, distinguishing their firsthand evidence from potentially conflicting claims in Acts and later legend. A zealous Greek-speaking Jew and Pharisee, Paul persecuted Jesus's followers until a vision convinced him that God had raised Jesus and that his death brought salvation apart from Jewish law observance. He then established gentile churches across the eastern Mediterranean, supported himself through manual work, endured opposition, and probably died as a martyr, though details remain uncertain.

title: The Significance and Letters of Paul, in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Paul's significance and the seven undisputed letters as central evidence for early Christianity.
searchSummary: Explains why Paul became Christianity's most influential figure after Jesus through his prominence in the New Testament, development of theology about Jesus's death and resurrection, and mission to gentiles. Understanding him requires separating seven undisputed letters from later writings in his name and treating Acts cautiously when it conflicts with Paul's testimony. Because his letters answer particular community problems rather than systematically presenting his thought, readers must reconstruct their missing situations before interpreting his arguments and silences.

title: Personal Update:  My Book on the Ethics of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces completion of a manuscript on Jesus' ethics and explains the revised title and focus.

title: Dating Manuscripts and Understanding Mark: Readers’ Questions
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to questions about Mark's historical value, manuscript dating, and the messianic secret.
searchSummary: Answers questions about Mark's historical value, manuscript dating, and messianic secrecy. Mark preserves only a tiny and imperfect portion of Jesus' life but is the earliest primary Gospel source and should be compared with others. Palaeography dates manuscripts through changing handwriting styles, while carbon dating estimates when writing material originated. Jesus probably disclosed messianic claims privately, and Mark's secrecy motif may explain why such claims were not widely known during his ministry.

title: The Gospel of Mark: Are You Interested in a More Extended Discussion?
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes an extended lecture course on the Gospel of Mark and its major topics.
searchSummary: Outlines an eight-lecture course examining Mark's literary, historical, and textual problems. Topics include the crucified Messiah, widespread failure to understand Jesus, apocalyptic teaching, Jewish law, discipleship through suffering, the passion narrative, the abrupt ending at 16:8, significant scribal variants, and anonymous authorship. Reflection questions invite readers to evaluate Mark's Christology, historical credibility, literary irony, relationship to Judaism, manuscript evidence, and the tradition connecting the Gospel with Peter's companion John Mark.

title: Join Me on a Cruise from Athens to Venice This Summer!
author: jennao
description: Invites readers to consider a summer cruise from Athens to Venice.

title: March 2025 Gold Q&A
author: jennao
description: Announces the March 2025 Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: Webinar Announcement: The Afterlife of Animals with Barbara Ambros
author: jennao
description: Announces a webinar on animal afterlife beliefs in Buddhism and Christianity.

title: Did Jesus BECOME the Son of God?  The Christology of Acts
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains exaltation Christology in Acts and contrasts it with incarnation Christology.

title: The Acts of the Apostles:  For Further Reading
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends further reading on Acts and the broader study of Luke's two-volume work.
searchSummary: Offers an annotated guide to further reading on Acts and Luke-Acts for readers who want to pursue its history, literature, theology, and social setting.
