Ehrman recommends accessible introductions, major commentaries, online courses, and specialized studies, noting the focus and value of individual works. The post functions as a curated bibliography rather than advancing a single argument about Acts, and it distinguishes resources suitable for general readers from more technical scholarship.

title: The Acts of the Apostles:  Who Wrote It, When, and Why?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Acts as the second volume of Luke and argues against identifying its author as Paul's traveling companion.
searchSummary: Examines who wrote Acts, when it was composed, and what purposes shaped its account of early Christianity. Differences between Acts and Paul's letters make the traditional identification of the author as Paul's companion unlikely, while arguments for a date around 120 based on Josephus remain inconclusive; Ehrman favors the 80s. Acts portrays a Spirit-directed mission, harmonizes Paul with Jerusalem's apostles, legitimizes Gentile inclusion without Jewish law, and stresses repentance and resurrection over atoning death.

title: The Book of Acts in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Acts as Luke's account of Christianity's Spirit-driven spread from Jerusalem to Rome.
searchSummary: Introduces Acts as Luke's companion volume narrating Christianity's Spirit-directed expansion from Jerusalem to Rome and from Jews to gentiles. Peter dominates its opening, Paul its later chapters, while miracles, preaching, persecution, and divine guidance advance the mission and portray apostolic agreement. Acts presents repentance rather than atonement in its preaching, has Peter authorize a law-free gentile mission before Paul, and depicts unusually harmonious communities, raising historical questions when its account differs from Paul's own letters.

title: More Interesting Questions from Blog Readers
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to questions about atonement in Matthew and John, Jesus' Son of Man sayings, and translating 'Sabbaths' in the resurrection narratives.
searchSummary: Answers questions about Gospel atonement theology, Jesus' Son of Man sayings, and the resurrection's day. Ehrman sees Matthew largely following Mark's ransom theology and John combining salvation through revelation with salvation through Jesus' death. He argues that Jesus originally distinguished himself from Daniel's future Son of Man, and uses Mark's sequence of burial before Sabbath and discovery afterward to explain why the tomb is found Sunday.

title: The Gospel of Matthew.  Are You Interested in a More Extended Discussion?
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes an extended lecture course on Matthew and its major interpretive issues.
searchSummary: Outlines an eight-lecture course examining Matthew through literary, historical, redactional, and sociohistorical questions. The lectures treat its genealogy, fulfillment citations, birth narrative, Sermon on the Mount, Jewish law, tensions between Jewish and anti-Jewish themes, anonymous authorship, and later influence. Throughout, comparison with Mark reveals Matthew's distinctive portrait of Jesus as Jewish Messiah and new Moses, while attention to audience, Papias, textual changes, and reception history shows how the Gospel arose and shaped Christianity.

title: The God Hypothesis. What Do You Think?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on why God's existence cannot be proved or disproved empirically.

title: All Four Gospels in One Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares all four Gospels in one nutshell summary while noting differences in miracles and atonement.
searchSummary: Compares Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John as the earliest narrative accounts of Jesus while emphasizing each Gospel's distinctive portrait. All present his teachings, miracles, rejection, Roman crucifixion, and resurrection as part of God's saving plan, but they differ in theology and detail. Matthew stresses Scripture and law, Mark the misunderstood suffering messiah, Luke the rejected prophet and divine man, and John the preexistent divine Word who became human and grants eternal life.

title: John Versus the Synoptics:  How Does Jesus Raise the Dead?
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares how John and the Synoptic Gospels portray Jesus raising the dead.
searchSummary: Compares the raising of Jairus' daughter in Mark with the raising of Lazarus in John to expose different Gospel portraits of Jesus. Mark's private miracle follows an unintended delay, whereas John's Jesus deliberately waits for Lazarus to die and raises him publicly so observers will believe in his divine mission. Unlike the Synoptics, where Jesus resists using signs to prove his identity and proclaims God's kingdom, John joins spectacular signs with teachings about Jesus' heavenly identity.
topics: Signs in the Gospel of John

title: The Gospel of John:  For Your Further Reading
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends further reading on the Gospel of John, including studies, commentaries, and online resources.
searchSummary: Provides an annotated guide to further study of the Gospel of John for general readers and advanced students. Recommended books address Johannine theology, symbolism, literary design, social history, characters, relations with the Synoptic Gospels, and the Gospel's treatment of Jews. The guide also identifies accessible and more specialized commentaries for passage-level interpretation, along with Hugo Mendez's online New Testament course, while cautioning readers to evaluate unscreened internet resources carefully.

title: The Gospel of John:  Who Wrote It, When, and Why?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines the Gospel of John's anonymity, traditional attribution, and the beloved disciple tradition.
searchSummary: Examines who wrote the Gospel of John, when it appeared, and why it was composed. The anonymous author was not John son of Zebedee, an illiterate Aramaic-speaking fisherman, and the text distinguishes its author from the Beloved Disciple, who may be an idealized literary figure or source of community tradition. Probably written around 90-95 CE, perhaps later, the Gospel presents Jesus as the preexistent divine revealer whose believers receive salvation amid a hostile world.

title: The Gospel of John in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes John as a Gospel where Jesus is a preexistent divine being who reveals God and grants eternal life.
searchSummary: Surveys the Gospel of John's distinctive portrait of Jesus as the preexistent divine Word who becomes human to grant eternal life to believers. Unlike the Synoptics, John omits parables, exorcisms, repentance, and Jesus' proclamation of God's coming kingdom, replacing them with extended claims about his heavenly identity. Its spectacular 'signs' publicly validate those claims, while belief brings life in the present and rejection brings condemnation, culminating in the resurrection as confirmation of Jesus' divinity.
topics: Signs in the Gospel of John

title: Some Intriguing Questions from Readers 2/2025
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to reader questions about the difference between historical reconstruction and the inaccessible real past.
searchSummary: Answers three unrelated questions about historical reconstruction, Nazi antisemitism, and possible literary dependence between Paul and John. Historical figures are scholarly reconstructions rather than direct access to past people, though critical methods remain the best guide available. Nazi persecution classified Jews racially, not principally by religion. Paul and John share beliefs about Jesus and salvation, but their different understandings of faith, resurrection, and eternal life offer no compelling evidence that John borrowed from Paul.

title: Did Jesus Have a Near-Death Experience? – Platinum Post by Douglas Wadeson MD
author: jennao
description: Presents a Platinum member post questioning whether Jesus' death can be compared to modern near-death experiences.

title: For Further Reading on the Synoptic Problem and Its Possible Solutions
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends further reading on the Synoptic Problem and proposed solutions.

title: Other Sources for Matthew and Luke:  M and L!  And Who CARES?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the proposed M and L sources for material unique to Matthew and Luke.
searchSummary: Explains the proposed M and L sources for material unique to Matthew and Luke within the four-source solution to the Synoptic Problem. These labels may represent written documents, oral traditions, multiple sources, or some combination, but they account for familiar stories absent from Mark and Q. The post emphasizes that identifying an evangelist's sources allows redaction criticism to reveal how Matthew and Luke reshaped inherited traditions to express their distinctive concerns.

title: Q1 Platinum Webinar: The Mystery of the Beloved Disciple
author: jennao
description: Announces a Platinum webinar on the mystery of the beloved disciple.

title: Evidence for Q: The Sequence of the Sayings
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues for Q by showing how Matthew and Luke place shared sayings in different narrative contexts.

title: An Argument for Q:  The Hypothetical Source That Seems to Have Existed
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why many scholars posit Q rather than thinking Matthew copied Luke or Luke copied Matthew.

title: The Q Source Used by Matthew and Luke
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Q as a hypothetical sayings source used by Matthew and Luke alongside Mark.

title: Materialism, Personal Identity, and Resurrection: Part 2 – Platinum Post by Dennis J. Folds, Ph.D.
author: jennao
description: Presents a Platinum member post connecting bodily resurrection and personal identity with modern materialism.
searchSummary: Explores how bodily resurrection and personal identity might be imagined within modern materialist accounts of consciousness. Dennis Folds proposes two broad models: God could reconstitute a person's biological procession so conscious life resumes, or permanently preserve that completed life like a recording in a timeless reality. Paul offers only the image of a seed becoming a transformed body. Folds remains uncertain but finds hope in the possibility that continued existence depends entirely on God's creative remembrance.

title: Was Mark Really Written First?  The Arguments for “Markan Priority”
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the arguments for Markan priority in the Synoptic Problem.
searchSummary: Explains why most scholars conclude that Mark was the written source independently used by Matthew and Luke. Patterns of verbal agreement show each later Gospel alternately retaining or changing Mark, while Matthew and Luke rarely agree substantially against him; their shared non-Markan material appears in different narrative locations. Mark's rougher Greek, difficult statements, greater detail within shared episodes, and coherent narrative order are easier to explain as material later writers revised than as changes Mark introduced into smoother, longer accounts.

title: Gospel Problems:  Does Matthew Ever “Correct” Mark?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Matthew's apparent corrections of Mark support the view that Matthew used Mark as a source.
searchSummary: Uses Matthew's version of the rich man's question to illustrate why scholars think Matthew copied and sometimes corrected Mark. Mark has the man call Jesus “good,” prompting a response that only God is good and potentially implying that Jesus is neither good nor divine. Matthew moves “good” from Jesus to the deed required for eternal life, producing a more awkward exchange but removing the theological problem. This editorial direction makes better sense from Mark to Matthew than the reverse.

title: Materialism, Personal Identity, and Resurrection: Part 1 – Platinum Post by Dennis J. Folds, Ph.D.
author: jennao
description: Presents a Platinum member post on personal identity and what resurrection of the body would mean.
searchSummary: Examines what identifies the particular person who would be raised when a human body and personality continually change throughout life. Dennis Folds describes personal identity as a biological procession rather than a fixed physical snapshot, then contrasts the Jewish view that the person is an embodied unity with the Greek idea of an immortal soul temporarily inhabiting a body. Christianity combined these frameworks, creating tensions that modern biology, psychology, and cosmology make even harder to resolve.

title: Why Assume the Synoptic Gospels Were COPYING One Another (and Other Sources)?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why close verbal agreement among Matthew, Mark, and Luke points to copying or shared written sources.
searchSummary: Demonstrates that extensive word-for-word agreement among Matthew, Mark, and Luke requires literary copying or shared written sources rather than independent memory of the same events. A classroom eyewitness exercise shows that independent accounts never reproduce long identical wording, especially decades later. Mark's shorter Gospel is not a condensation of Matthew because its shared stories are often longer; the standard four-source model therefore has Matthew and Luke use Mark, Q, and their respective special sources M and L.

title: The Synoptic Problem:  Matthew, Mark, and Luke.  Who’s Zoomin Who?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Synoptic Problem: why Matthew, Mark, and Luke are so similar yet different.
searchSummary: Introduces the Synoptic Problem by asking how Matthew, Mark, and Luke can share stories, sequence, and exact wording while also differing in content and detail. Such verbatim parallels indicate common written sources, and the dominant four-source hypothesis proposes that Matthew and Luke independently used Mark, a shared sayings source called Q, and separate bodies of material labeled M and L. The foundational issue is Markan priority, whose supporting evidence the following posts examine.

title: Bart Ehrman and Kevin Grant – The Apocalypse: Literal or Metaphor?
author: jennao
description: Shares an interview with Kevin Grant about whether Jesus' apocalyptic teaching should be taken literally.
searchSummary: Introduces a recorded conversation between Ehrman and blog member Kevin Grant about Jesus' apocalyptic teaching. Their discussion asks whether Jesus literally expected a coming apocalypse, how readers should understand his severe predictions, and whether those statements permit metaphorical interpretation. The post supplies the video rather than a written answer and briefly identifies Grant as the author of What the Hell Is Hell?, leaving the interview itself to develop their competing or complementary approaches.

title: Is the Gospel of Luke Anti-Jewish?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Luke's portrayal of Jewish rejection of prophets and Jesus should be considered anti-Jewish.
searchSummary: Argues that Luke contains a strong anti-Jewish element by portraying Jews who reject Jesus as heirs to a pattern of rejecting God's prophets. The post locates this portrayal in conflicts between Luke's Christian community and Jews who did not accept Jesus as Messiah. Drawing on a lasting insight from F. C. Baur, it explains how an author's later beliefs and social circumstances shape narratives about earlier events.

title: The Gospel of Luke: For Further Reading
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends further reading on Luke, including studies, commentaries, and online resources.
searchSummary: Provides an annotated guide to further study of the Gospel of Luke for interested general readers. Recommended introductory works address Luke-Acts, redaction criticism, social context, literary methods, and the Gospels generally, with guidance about their intended level. The post also identifies passage-by-passage commentaries, specialized studies of the birth and Passion narratives, a feminist commentary, and a reliable online course on the Synoptic Gospels.

title: Gold Q&A for February!
author: jennao
description: Announces the February 2025 Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: The Gospel of Luke: Who Wrote It?  When?  And Why?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines the authorship, date, and purpose of Luke, including doubts about identifying the author as Paul's companion.
searchSummary: Examines who wrote Luke, when it was composed, and why. The anonymous author was probably not Paul's companion Luke, despite the traditional argument from Acts' first-person passages and Colossians, but was likely an educated Gentile Christian writing around 80-85 CE. The post argues that Luke reshaped Mark to present God's delayed plan: the gospel must reach Gentiles, believers must care for people in need, and repentance must be preached before the end.

title: The Gospel of Luke in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Luke as a Gospel portraying Jesus as a divine man, rejected prophet, and bringer of salvation to Gentiles.
searchSummary: Surveys Luke's distinctive portrait of Jesus as both a Greco-Roman divine man and the final Jewish prophet rejected by his own people. Luke emphasizes God's plan to extend salvation to Gentiles, Jesus' concern for the poor and marginalized, and a calm prophetic death followed by resurrection. The post also explains that Jesus' death prompts repentance and free forgiveness rather than functioning as an atoning sacrifice.

title: Mark’s Messianic Secret
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Mark's messianic secret and why Jesus' identity remains hidden until suffering and death are understood.
searchSummary: Explains William Wrede's theory that Mark's messianic secret is a theological invention rather than a historical feature of Jesus' ministry. Early believers first regarded Jesus as God's Son after the resurrection, while Mark's community believed he already held that identity during life. Commands to conceal healings, teachings, Peter's confession, and the Transfiguration reconcile those positions by claiming Jesus kept his identity hidden until afterward. The motif shows that Mark reshaped history to communicate theology.

title: The Gospel of Mark:  For Further Reading
author: jennao
description: Recommends further reading on Mark, including studies, commentaries, and online resources.
searchSummary: Provides an annotated guide to further study of Mark for general readers and advanced students. Recommended books address the Gospel's message, literary design, Christology, Synoptic relationships, and messianic secret; detailed commentaries supply introductions and passage-by-passage interpretation. Online courses cover Mark and the Synoptic Gospels through lectures, questions, and community study. The selections distinguish accessible starting points from demanding scholarship and caution readers to evaluate less controlled online material carefully.

title: The Gospel of Mark: Who, When, and Why
author: jennao
description: Examines the authorship, date, and purpose of Mark and the later tradition connecting it with Peter.
searchSummary: Reconstructs Mark as an anonymous Greek Gospel written around 70–75 CE after Jerusalem's destruction, not by the Aramaic-speaking John Mark or from Peter's testimony. Papias's earlier tradition is uncertain, while Irenaeus first clearly names the surviving book around 180 CE. The author may have preserved circulating traditions, but his principal purpose was theological: to defend a crucified and risen Messiah whose suffering fulfilled Scripture even though family, leaders, disciples, and nearly everyone else failed to understand him.

title: The Gospel of Mark in a Nutshell
author: jennao
description: Summarizes Mark as the earliest surviving Gospel explaining how a crucified Jesus could be the messiah.
searchSummary: Summarizes Mark's portrayal of Jesus as the authoritative, miracle-working Son of God and unexpected Messiah who saves through suffering and death. Jesus announces God's approaching kingdom, conceals his identity, teaches outsiders obscurely, and remains misunderstood by family, leaders, and disciples. Only at the crucifixion does a gentile centurion recognize him, while the torn Temple curtain signals access to God. The women then flee the empty tomb silently, leaving the disciples unaware but the reader informed.

title: The Flukes of Life: How I Almost Never Became a Professor
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the unlikely path from graduate school to a university teaching career.
searchSummary: Recounts how Ehrman nearly failed to obtain an academic position after training at theological institutions and specializing in Greek manuscripts and Didymus the Blind. A chance phone call led him to replace a Rutgers professor on emergency leave, teaching New Testament introduction and Paul's writings. That temporary appointment continued for several years, gave him essential experience in a secular university, and ultimately helped make possible the permanent teaching career he later established at UNC.

title: Was (the author of) Matthew Really a Jew?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores whether the author of Matthew was Jewish and how the Gospel relates to Judaism.
searchSummary: Considers whether Matthew's misunderstanding of Hebrew poetic parallelism proves that the evangelist was a gentile. In retelling Zechariah's description of one donkey in two synonymous lines, Matthew treats the lines literally as two animals and depicts Jesus riding both into Jerusalem. John Meier argued that a Jew familiar with Hebrew poetry would not make this error. Other Jewish interpreters, however, also separated parallel lines in this way, so the amusing episode cannot establish Matthew's ethnic or religious identity.

title: The Gospel of Matthew: For Further Reading
author: jennao
description: Recommends further reading on Matthew, including studies, commentaries, and online resources.
searchSummary: Offers an annotated guide for studying Matthew beyond a brief overview. Introductory books cover Jesus as new Moses, the infancy narratives, Sermon on the Mount, Matthean community, feminist interpretation, and critical methods; commentaries provide passage-by-passage analysis and reception history. Online recommendations include extended courses on Matthew and the Synoptic Gospels. The guide distinguishes accessible starting points from advanced resources and advises readers to evaluate unscreened internet material carefully.

title: The Gospel of Matthew:  Who, When, and Why?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Matthew's anonymous authorship, later attribution, sources, date, and purpose.
searchSummary: Reconstructs Matthew's authorship, date, sources, and purpose. The anonymous author was not the Aramaic-speaking tax collector but an educated Greek-speaking Christian, probably Jewish, who used Mark, Q, and oral traditions outside Palestine around 80–85 CE. He expanded and revised Mark to present Jesus as the Jewish Messiah, new Moses, and authoritative interpreter of enduring Jewish law. Israel's leaders reject Jesus, allowing the message of salvation to move outward to the gentile world.

title: The Gospel of Matthew in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Matthew as a Gospel about Jesus as Jewish messiah, interpreter of the Law, miracle worker, and rejected savior.
searchSummary: Summarizes Matthew's distinctive portrait of Jesus as the Jewish Messiah who fulfills Scripture, embodies a new Moses, interprets the Law, and demands lives of sacrificial love. Its genealogy, infancy narrative, five discourses, miracles, judgment teachings, death, and resurrection unfold God's plan despite tensions within the account. Jewish leaders reject Jesus, but care for people in need determines entry into the kingdom, and the risen Messiah commissions disciples to carry his teachings and salvation to all nations.

title: Rambling Meditations on What It Means to Exist….  What Do You Think?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on consciousness, the self, the brain, and what it means to exist.
searchSummary: Meditates on how a person can think, remember, choose, and possess a will when the brain consists entirely of nonliving atoms and molecules. Ehrman locates identity in the physical brain rather than an enduring soul, noting that injury or surgery can change the self and death ends the person even as constituent atoms continue. He finds this mortality sad rather than frightening but remains puzzled by how unconscious cells and matter collectively produce life, consciousness, and apparently voluntary decisions.

title: The New Testament Gospels in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the New Testament Gospels as early narratives of Jesus' life, death, and resurrection that also make theological claims.
searchSummary: Introduces the four New Testament Gospels as ancient biographies and proclamations of faith that narrate Jesus's ministry, teaching, miracles, death, and resurrection. Their shared traditions and structure, especially among Matthew, Mark, and Luke, suggest common sources, while differences and contradictions reveal each author's theological aims and limit straightforward historical use. Readers should therefore study each Gospel both literarily, for its distinctive portrayal of Jesus, and historically, by evaluating authorship, date, context, sources, and embellishment.

title: What Is The New Testament?  Can You Actually Say?
author: BDEhrman
description: Defines the New Testament as a collection of twenty-seven writings that came to be regarded as Christian Scripture.
searchSummary: Defines the New Testament as twenty-seven writings believed to convey apostolic authority and the Christian new covenant established through Jesus. Its Gospels, Acts, epistles, and Revelation address Jesus' life, Christianity's spread, community belief and behavior, and the end of the age. Although most are early Christian works, many are anonymous or pseudonymous rather than written by their traditional apostolic authors. The collection developed gradually and reached broad consensus only around the fourth and fifth centuries.

title: Seats Still Available!  Blog Dinner in Tampa this Friday (January 17)
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces available seats for a Tampa blog dinner.

title: Do You Understand the Entire New Testament? Announcing My New Blog Thread
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a new blog thread designed to summarize every New Testament book in one-sentence form and broader context.

title: Other Critical Approaches to the New Testament (by Prof. Shaily Patel)
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Shaily Patel's overview of ideological criticism and other nontraditional approaches to New Testament study.
searchSummary: Surveys ideological methods that complement traditional historical study of the New Testament. Postcolonial criticism examines empire and interpreters' political locations; feminist and queer approaches expose gender and sexual norms and recover marginalized voices; liberation theology reads from the standpoint of oppressed communities and joins interpretation to action; minority criticism analyzes race, ethnicity, and the Bible's use in oppression. Each approach asks how ancient texts and modern scholarship reflect power, identity, exclusion, and readers' social positions.

title: Getting the Bible Digitally (by Jeffrey Siker)
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Jeffrey Siker's excursus on digital Bibles and how technology affects reading and interpretation.

title: Was Mark the First Gospel?  Evidence for “Markan Priority”
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains evidence for Markan priority, including patterns of agreement among the Synoptic Gospels.
searchSummary: Explains three lines of evidence for Markan priority: patterns of wording, narrative sequence, and the character of editorial changes. Matthew and Luke usually agree with Mark in alternating combinations but rarely together against him, and they place shared non-Markan sayings differently while preserving Mark's order. Their versions also smooth Mark's awkward Greek and difficult ideas, while Mark's shared stories are usually fuller despite his Gospel's shorter total length, making later abbreviation by Mark implausible.

title: Blog Dinner in Tampa Fl.  Friday January 17.  You Interested?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Tampa blog dinner for local or traveling blog members.

title: Did Christians Invent the Idea of “Atonement” / “Vicarious Suffering”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains that vicarious suffering and atonement were not Christian inventions but had earlier cultural precedents.

title: Was There No Room in the “Inn” or in the “Guestroom”?  And Doesn’t Caesar Augustus Himself Describe His Census?  More Questions from Readers
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to questions about translating Luke's birth narrative and claims about Augustus's census.
searchSummary: Answers reader questions about Luke's infancy narrative and historical context. The Greek kataluma may mean an inn or guestroom, while tekton describes an ordinary manual worker rather than a symbolic divine architect. Augustus' census of Roman citizens in 8 BCE does not match Luke's universal registration under Quirinius or require travel to ancestral homes. The post also recommends reference works for studying early Christian writings and their historical sources.

title: Was Jesus from “Israel”?  Did Jesus “Pre-exist”?  Answers to Readers Questions
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to questions about what to call Jesus' homeland and whether Jesus was thought to preexist.
searchSummary: Answers three reader questions about historical and theological language. Ehrman explains why calling Jesus an Israelite, Palestinian, Judean, or Galilean each presents historical complications; argues that even sacrificial acts can contain self-interested motives; and clarifies John's Prologue. In John 1, the preexistent Logos is not yet the human Jesus: the Word becomes Jesus only when it becomes flesh in verse 14, so saying that “Jesus” personally preexisted is less precise than saying the Logos did.

title: Finding Value in Writings You Don’t “Believe” (In response to my Newsweek article on Christmas)
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on finding value in biblical narratives even when their historical claims are not accepted.

title: 2024: Ehrman Blog Year in Review
author: jennao
description: Reviews the blog's 2024 fundraising, staffing, platform plans, and educational mission.
searchSummary: Reviews a record-setting 2024 in which the blog published more than 300 posts, received about 16,000 comments, and donated approximately $588,000 to charity, bringing lifetime giving near $3 million. Bart also announces CEO Jen Olmos's leadership and DesignHammer's work on a new platform while reaffirming the blog's scholarly and charitable missions. He thanks departing staff and volunteers, identifies the principal supported organizations, and describes membership revenue as separate from operating expenses.

title: Did Jesus Come to Bring Peace?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Luke's birth narrative presents Jesus as bringing peace and fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy.

title: A Matching Grant for our End of the Year Giving 2024:  Consider the Blog and Its Mission!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a year-end matching grant for blog charity donations.
searchSummary: Announces a $5,000 matching challenge for the final days of the 2024 annual appeal benefiting Urban Ministries of Durham. Bart connects the request to rising homelessness and shelters turning away local families, stressing that additional funds can reduce suffering even if money alone cannot solve the problem. Donors of any amount can attend or receive a recording of his lecture on Jesus and giving, with the post providing donation-identification, registration, and confirmation instructions.

title: Being Consistently Critical (In the Good Sense)
author: admin
description: Explains critical scholarship as the consistent use of judgment to evaluate historical claims.
searchSummary: Explains that critical history means evaluating evidence rather than reflexively attacking it. Every source, including the Gospel of John, Josephus, Tacitus, and the Talmud, must be tested for bias, plausibility, consistency, and agreement with independently assessed evidence. A student's reluctance to question sayings attributed to Jesus illustrates selective criticism: accepting a claim because a favored text contains it bypasses the historical task. Consistent inquiry applies the same standards even when conclusions challenge personal commitments.

title: January 2025 Gold Q&A
author: jennao
description: Announces the January 2025 Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: Approaching the New Testament Historically
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the difference between reading the New Testament theologically and studying it historically.
searchSummary: Distinguishes a historical reading of the Bible from a confessional or theological one. Historians reconstruct publicly accessible human events from evidence that investigators of any religious outlook can examine, so they can describe beliefs and probable events but cannot determine which theology is true or whether God caused them. Believing historians may make faith claims in another capacity, while historical study remains limited to explaining what biblical authors said, how their writings arose, and what probably happened.

title: Twelve Days of Christmas Day 12: My Article on Christmas in Newsweek: Part 2
author: jennao
description: Reposts the second part of a Newsweek article on Christmas traditions and apocryphal infancy stories.

title: Twelve Days of Christmas Day 11: My Article on Christmas in Newsweek Part 1
author: jennao
description: Reposts the first part of a Newsweek article on the Gospel of Jesus' Wife, the Proto-Gospel of James, and non-canonical traditions about Jesus' birth.

title: Twelve Days of Christmas Day 10: What Can We Know About Jesus’ Birth?
author: jennao
description: Explains the limits of what can be known historically about Jesus' birth.

title: Twelve Days of Christmas Day 9: A Key Contradiction in the Birth Narratives of Jesus
author: jennao
description: Explains a major contradiction between Matthew and Luke concerning Egypt, Nazareth, and the movements of Jesus' family.
searchSummary: Compares Matthew's and Luke's incompatible accounts of Jesus' birth. Matthew assumes that the family lives in Bethlehem, receives the Magi there, flees to Egypt for an extended period, and relocates to Nazareth only after Herod dies. Luke instead places their home in Nazareth, brings them temporarily to Bethlehem for a census, and returns them home after purification rites about a month later. The different itineraries cannot both describe what the family did after Jesus was born.

title: Twelve Days of Christmas Day 8: Why Was Jesus Born of a Virgin in Matthew and Luke?
author: jennao
description: Explains why Matthew and Luke use virgin birth stories to make theological claims about Jesus.
searchSummary: Explains that Matthew and Luke use the virgin birth for different theological purposes. Matthew reads the Greek Isaiah 7:14 as predicting a virgin and makes Jesus' birth one of several events fulfilling Scripture, although the Hebrew passage concerns a young woman and an immediate political sign. Luke connects conception by the Holy Spirit directly with Jesus being God's Son. Later Christian interpretation combines these distinct claims with John's incarnation theology, obscuring what each Gospel independently emphasizes.

title: Twelve Days of Christmas Day 7: The Birth of Jesus in Luke
author: jennao
description: Explains Luke's birth narrative and how it differs from Matthew's account.

title: Twelve Days of Christmas Day 6: Why Does Matthew Have the Story of the “Wise Men”?
author: jennao
description: Explains why Matthew alone includes the Magi and how the story fits Matthew's distinctive emphases.
searchSummary: Explains why Matthew includes the legendary story of the Magi. Pagan astrologers recognize and worship the newborn Jewish Messiah, while Herod, priests, and Scripture experts know where prophecy locates him but either ignore or try to kill him. This irony introduces Matthew's larger pattern: Jesus fulfills Jewish Scripture yet is rejected by his people's powerful leaders, whose knowledge is not matched by faithful conduct, while gentiles accept him. The infancy story thus anticipates the Gospel's subsequent conflict and worldwide mission.

title: Twelve Days of Christmas Day 5: Matthew’s Version of the Birth of Jesus
author: jennao
description: Summarizes Matthew's version of Jesus' birth, including genealogy, Joseph, and distinctive infancy traditions.
searchSummary: Reconstructs Matthew's distinctive birth narrative without importing details from Luke. Joseph and Mary already live in a Bethlehem house, where Jesus is born, receives the Magi months later, and escapes Herod's massacre through a flight to Egypt. After Herod dies, fear of Archelaus prevents the family from returning home to Judea, so they relocate to Nazareth. The setting, extended timeline, and planned return all show that Matthew assumes Bethlehem—not Nazareth—was their original hometown.

title: Twelve Days of Christmas Day 4: O Little Town of Nazareth?
author: jennao
description: Argues that Matthew and Luke's efforts to place Jesus' birth in Bethlehem point to Nazareth as Jesus' actual hometown.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus was probably born in Nazareth rather than Bethlehem. Matthew and Luke both know him as a Nazarene but independently construct implausible, contradictory journeys to place his birth in Bethlehem and fulfill Micah 5:2. Matthew starts the family in Bethlehem, sends it to Egypt, and later relocates it north; Luke starts in Nazareth, invokes an otherwise unknown empire-wide ancestral census, and returns the family after six weeks. Their incompatible explanations suggest that neither Bethlehem story is historical.

title: Twelve Days of Christmas Day 3: A Different Account of Joseph and Mary!
author: jennao
description: Introduces the Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew as a later infancy Gospel expanding traditions about Mary, Joseph, and Jesus.
searchSummary: Explains how the seventh-century Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew reworked and expanded the earlier Proto-Gospel of James, becoming highly influential in medieval Christianity. Its account places Mary in the Temple, committed to lifelong virginity, until a miraculous dove emerging from Joseph's branch identifies the elderly widower as her divinely chosen guardian. Mary receives the purple thread for the Temple curtain, while an angel confirms the other virgins' mocking title for her, Queen of Virgins.

title: Twelve Days of Christmas Day 2: The Myth of the First Christmas
author: jennao
description: Explains why the familiar Christmas story is a conflation of Matthew and Luke with significant historical problems.

title: A Cruise This Summer: From Athens to Venice.  Interested?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a summer cruise from Athens to Venice with lectures and itinerary details.

title: Twelve Days of Christmas Day 1: From a Historical View
author: jennao
description: Reposts an earlier Christmas-season reflection on reading Jesus' birth stories historically.

title: The Hobby Lobby, the Museum of the Bible, and Incredible Academic Fraud
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines allegations of manuscript fraud involving Hobby Lobby, the Museum of the Bible, and New Testament fragments.
searchSummary: Recounts the scandal involving Hobby Lobby, the Museum of the Bible, Oxford papyrologist Dirk Obbink, and manuscripts from the Egypt Exploration Society's Oxyrhynchus collection. The fragment promoted as a first-century copy of Mark proved to be a tiny late-second- or early-third-century scrap, while Obbink allegedly sold manuscripts he did not own and assigned implausibly early dates. Ehrman highlights the financial, academic, and religious motives that enabled the deception.

title: The Low-Down on That First-Century Gospel of Mark
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the controversy over the alleged first-century fragment of Mark and how the claim unraveled.
searchSummary: Recounts how a fragment promoted as a first-century copy of Mark proved to be a small second- or third-century Oxyrhynchus papyrus. Dirk Obbink allegedly sold it and other Egypt Exploration Society texts he did not own to Hobby Lobby for the Museum of the Bible, based partly on claims of extraordinary antiquity. Investigation by scholars and institutional records identified thirteen unlawfully removed manuscripts, which the museum agreed to return, exposing failures of provenance, disclosure, and acquisition oversight.

title: Final Reflections on Mummy Masks and Manuscripts
author: BDEhrman
description: Concludes a series on mummy masks, manuscript fragments, and media claims about the earliest Gospel manuscript.
searchSummary: Presents Candida Moss and Joel Baden's assessment of the unpublished fragment advertised as a pre-90 CE copy of Mark recovered from mummy cartonnage. They identify unresolved questions about its text, date, ownership, provenance, testing, and scholarly examination. The article also challenges the destruction of Egyptian funerary artifacts, especially when less destructive recovery methods exist, and argues that unsupported claims cannot be evaluated until the papyrus and its documentation are made public.

title: A True Expert Speaks About Mummy Masks and Papyri
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents an expert papyrologist's critique of claims about mummy masks and newly discovered New Testament papyri.
searchSummary: Shares papyrologist Roberta Mazza's critique of claims that early Christian manuscripts were being recovered from Egyptian mummy cartonnage. She explains that published cartonnage papyri are generally too early to contain Christian texts, that specialists have less destructive recovery methods, and that proper provenance and documentation are essential. She also warns that sensational publicity can inflate the antiquities market and provide cover for illicit papyri while the alleged first-century Mark remains unavailable for scrutiny.

title: Annual Appeal 2024: Behind the Mission Pt. 1
author: jennao
description: Announces the 2024 annual appeal supporting Urban Ministries of Durham and the blog's charitable mission.
searchSummary: Supports the blog's first annual appeal for Urban Ministries of Durham by explaining its longstanding partnership and presenting an interview with executive director Sheldon Mitchell. The blog community had already given the organization more than $1 million, including $110,000 during 2024, for food, shelter, and pathways toward stability. Donors of any amount receive access to Bart's January lecture on Jesus and the culture of giving, while the interview describes UMD's mission, community impact, and reliance on contributors.

title: Can We Defend Destroying Mummy Masks?
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Craig Evans's defense of using mummy masks to recover papyrus fragments and the ethical questions involved.
searchSummary: Presents Craig Evans's defense of dismantling damaged or low-quality mummy cartonnage to recover ancient writings. Evans argues that owners and specialists select only pieces judged less valuable than the texts they may contain and compares the process to destructive choices made during archaeological excavation. Ehrman's later note adds that project leader Dirk Obbink was found to have sold manuscripts he did not own, complicating the assurances about expertise, ownership, and responsible stewardship offered in the defense.

title: Destroying Mummy Masks
author: BDEhrman
description: Questions the destruction of mummy masks in the pursuit of possible New Testament manuscript discoveries.
searchSummary: Revisits the 2015 controversy over reports that a first-century fragment of Mark had been recovered by dismantling an Egyptian mummy mask. Ehrman notes that the manuscript's extent, date, provenance, ownership, and scholarly verification remained undisclosed while Christian apologists publicized the discovery. He emphasizes the ethical cost of destroying ancient Egyptian artifacts in hopes of finding Christian texts and asks whether religious priorities and the antiquities market were driving the work.

title: Readers’ Questions and My Responses (11/2024)
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to reader questions about Psalm 110, messiahship, and crucifixion traditions in the Gospels.
searchSummary: Answers reader questions about Mark's use of Psalm 110, Jesus' predictions of his death, and whether his baptism led him to believe he was the messiah. Mark portrays Jesus as both David's descendant and exalted Lord, while the passion predictions and baptismal signs likely reflect later Christian storytelling rather than Jesus' own foreknowledge. The literary parallels between baptism and crucifixion reveal Mark's theology but do not establish the events historically.

title: Special Webinar Announcement: Ehrman Blog Annual Appeal
author: jennao
description: Announces an annual appeal webinar supporting Urban Ministries of Durham.
searchSummary: Launches the blog's first annual appeal with a goal of raising $50,000 for Urban Ministries of Durham by the end of 2024. All proceeds support food, shelter, and stability services, and every donor can attend or receive a recording of Bart's lecture on how Jesus transformed charitable culture. The announcement explains donation-identification and webinar registration procedures and promises further stories throughout December showing the organization's work and the practical effect of reader support.

title: Jewish Disagreements About the Afterlife: Pharisees and Sadducees
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Pharisaic and Sadducean views of resurrection and afterlife in first-century Judaism.
searchSummary: Compares Pharisaic and Sadducean views of death and resurrection using later sources, especially a disputed scene in Acts. Pharisees and Essenes appear to have expected God to raise the dead for judgment, rewarding the faithful and punishing opponents, while Sadducees rejected resurrection and perhaps any conscious afterlife. Although Acts likely invents Paul's courtroom maneuver and incorrectly places Pharisees in the Sanhedrin, the episode reflects genuine Jewish disagreement about the end of life.

title: Jewish Sects at the Time of Jesus: The Essenes and the Fourth Philosophy
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Essenes and the Fourth Philosophy as Jewish groups known from Josephus and relevant to Jesus' world.
searchSummary: Surveys two Jewish movements described by Josephus: the Essenes and his unnamed Fourth Philosophy. The Essenes associated with Qumran pursued rigorous law observance, communal property, ritual purity, and an imminent apocalyptic victory under priestly and royal messiahs. The Fourth Philosophy instead united groups such as Sicarii and later Zealots around resistance to foreign rule, including assassination, revolt, and violent defense of Israel's divinely granted land.

title: Jewish Sects in the time of Jesus:  Pharisees and Sadducees
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the emergence of Pharisees and Sadducees within late Second Temple Judaism.
searchSummary: Explains how the Pharisees and Sadducees emerged as influential Jewish groups during the Hasmonean period and differed over Torah interpretation. Pharisees developed oral traditions intended to help people obey written law in daily life, while Sadducees emphasized the written Torah, priesthood, and Temple worship. Their contrasting social positions and beliefs about resurrection, angels, and authority shaped Jewish life around the time of Jesus.

title: Judaism 200 Years Before Jesus:  The Maccabean Revolt
author: BDEhrman
description: Sketches Judean history before Jesus, with special attention to the Maccabean revolt and its aftermath.
searchSummary: Traces Judea from Persian rule through Hellenization, Seleucid control, the Maccabean revolt, and Roman conquest to explain the Judaism inherited by Jesus. Antiochus IV's interference with Jewish worship and identity provoked a priestly rebellion that reclaimed and rededicated the Temple, established Hasmonean sovereignty, and replaced the traditional Zadokite high priesthood. These political and religious upheavals shaped later Jewish divisions, apocalyptic expectations, and the historical setting of early Christianity.

title: How to be Content with Life Even When It’s Rotten: The Stoic View
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the Stoic pursuit of contentment through indifference to circumstances outside one's control.

title: How Not To Be Bothered When Bad Things Happen:  The Stoics
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Stoic views of reason, divine order, and freedom from distress amid suffering.

title: Does this World Make Any Sense?  The Ancient Stoics
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Stoicism as a major Greco-Roman moral philosophy and asks how it relates to altruism.

title: Platinum Webinar for December: Topic TBD
author: jennao
description: Announces a Platinum webinar and provides scheduling information for members.

title: Intriguing Questions and Attempted Answers!
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to reader questions about worship language for Jesus in Paul and other New Testament issues.

title: December 2024 Gold Q&A – Get Your Questions Answered!
author: jennao
description: Announces the December 2024 Gold Q&A and invites questions from members.

title: Isn’t It Good Enough to Help Family, Friends, and Community?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Aristotle's view that virtue is rooted in community life and concern for the common good.
searchSummary: Aristotle understood human flourishing as possible only within the polis, where people cultivated virtue through relationships with family, friends, and social equals. His ethics therefore encouraged concern for a bounded community but did not impose responsibility for strangers, enemies, or the poor outside it. This limited altruism provides a contrast with Jesus' command to extend active care beyond customary social connections.

title: How Can We Be Happy?  An Age-Old Question.
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Aristotle to introduce happiness as the larger setting for ancient ethics and altruism.
searchSummary: Aristotle treated happiness not as a passing feeling but as eudaimonia, the deep flourishing that makes an entire life go well. Because humans are political beings, this fulfillment depends on living in a stable community and developing excellence of character through virtuous action. His account establishes the philosophical framework for comparing Greco-Roman ethics with later Christian ideas about altruism and care for others.

title: New Interview on Agnosticism
author: jennao
description: Shares a radio interview on agnosticism with Mindy Todd, Stephen Prothero, and Nell Fields.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's appearance on Mindy Todd's program The Point for a conversation about agnosticism. The discussion also includes religion scholar Stephen Prothero and Reverend Nell Fields of Waquoit Congregational Church, giving the program perspectives from scholarship, ministry, and Ehrman's own position. The brief post does not summarize their definitions, agreements, or disagreements; it directs readers curious about what each participant says to the complete recorded conversation.

title: What Do You Really Want in Life?  And How is that Related to Altruism?
author: BDEhrman
description: Begins explaining why the origins of altruism require comparing Jesus' teachings with ancient pagan religion and ethics.
searchSummary: Ancient Greek and Roman religion generally concerned worship practices, while philosophy and social convention supplied ethical guidance. Aristotle began ethical reflection by asking what final good people seek, identifying it as happiness or eudaimonia rather than pleasure, wealth, or honor alone. This distinction sets up a comparison between ancient ideals of personal flourishing and Jesus' stronger emphasis on serving other people.

title: Brief Reflections on Time and the Meaning of Life.  What Do You Think?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on time, anxiety, and learning to approach daily life with less pressure.
searchSummary: Reframes Ehrman's anxiety about insufficient time as a problem of attitude rather than an actual shortage. Inspired by Paul Loomans's Time Surfing and ancient moral philosophy, he recognizes that everyone fills the same daily hours and that stress comes from demanding more tasks and resisting interruption. He reduces his desired way of life to being happy, healthy, and helpful, emphasizing choices whose benefits endure into the future rather than pleasures that satisfy only the immediate moment.

title: How Do We Explain Human Moral Codes: So Similar Yet So Different?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a book chapter on why moral codes are both widely shared and culturally varied.

title: How I Begin My Book on Jesus, Ethics, and Altruism
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the opening of a book on Jesus' ethics and the rise of moral obligation toward strangers.

title: Another Reason for Thinking Jesus Called Himself the Messiah
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Jesus' expectation of future rule supports a messianic self-understanding.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus probably regarded himself as the future messianic king because his crucifixion is consistently tied to the charge that he claimed to be King of the Jews. Early Christians did not normally use that title, making its appearance at his trial unlikely to be their invention. Pilate needed no interest in apocalyptic nuance: any claim to kingship challenged Roman sovereignty and was sufficient grounds for crucifixion.

title: Blog Fundraiser: The Origins of Altruism Pre-Publication Manuscript Sneak Peek
author: jennao
description: Announces a fundraiser offering donors early access to a draft of The Origins of Altruism.
searchSummary: Offers advance access to Bart's manuscript The Origins of Altruism as a tiered fundraiser for the blog's charities. A $1,000 donor can read and comment on the draft, receive acknowledgment and a signed copy; higher tiers add an author webinar or sponsorship of a future Donor Impact Lecture with input on its topic and beneficiary. Bart presents the arrangement as benefiting readers, his revision process, and charitable organizations, with all donations going to charity rather than overhead.

title: Could Moses Have Been Thutmose, the Overseer of Borderlands? Platinum Post by Serene
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum member proposal identifying Moses with an Egyptian official named Thutmose.

title: Why Should We Think Jesus Called Himself the Messiah?
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Jesus likely understood messiahship apocalyptically rather than as military revolt or later Christian doctrine.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus privately understood himself as the messianic king of God's coming earthly kingdom. His promise that the twelve disciples would rule Israel is likely historical because later Christians would not invent a saying that included Judas; a kingdom with twelve subordinate rulers still requires one king. After believing Jesus was raised, his followers transformed this expectation by identifying him with the heavenly Son of Man who would return to rule.

title: Albert Schweitzer and the Apocalyptic Jesus
author: admin
description: Uses Albert Schweitzer and Jewish apocalypticism to frame Jesus' messianic self-understanding.
searchSummary: Explains how Albert Schweitzer established the modern scholarly case that Jesus was an apocalyptic prophet who expected God's kingdom within his generation and viewed himself as its messiah. Bart points to Jewish apocalypticism in the Dead Sea Scrolls and to end-time teachings across Mark, Q, M, and L. Because these emphases weaken in Luke, disappear in John, and face rejection in Thomas, he argues that later Christians modified Jesus's message after the expected end failed to arrive.

title: Jerusalem Through the Ages!  Interested in an Expert Discussion?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a departmental panel on Jodi Magness's book about Jerusalem's history.

title: An Imagined Dialogue for the Dispute Between Paul & Barnabas in Acts Part 4 by Angus Nisbet
author: Diane
description: Presents the final installment of Angus Nisbet's imagined reconstruction of the dispute between Paul and Barnabas.
searchSummary: Concludes a guest author's imaginative dialogue in which Barnabas challenges Paul's authority, conduct, and opposition to Jewish Christian leaders. Drawing on Pauline letters, Acts, and later traditions, the reconstruction portrays conflict over Torah, gentile inclusion, apostolic legitimacy, and Paul's relationships with Peter and James. Its suggestions about hostility toward Paul and his eventual death are presented as speculative possibilities rather than established historical conclusions.

title: What Would an Apocalyptic Jew (Jesus!) Mean By Calling Himself Messiah?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how an apocalyptic Jewish framework shapes the claim that Jesus understood himself as messiah.
searchSummary: Defines the Jewish apocalyptic worldview that frames Jesus's proclamation and his understanding of messiahship. Bart organizes it around cosmic dualism, pessimism about improving the present age, God's coming vindication through judgment and resurrection, and the imminence of that intervention. The earliest Jesus traditions fit this framework: the Son of Man would soon destroy evil, establish God's kingdom, and judge those who refused to repent, while Jesus called Israel to trust God and love one another in preparation.

title: Can We Know What Jesus Said About Himself?
author: BDEhrman
description: Addresses whether the Gospels can preserve reliable evidence about what Jesus said regarding messiahship.
searchSummary: Explains why historians cannot accept every Gospel saying as something the historical Jesus actually said about himself. Claims in John and predictions of Jesus' death may reflect later Christian beliefs, especially when they express exactly what post-resurrection communities wanted Jesus to have known. Historical reconstruction therefore compares independent sources and weighs authorial interests before using sayings to decide whether Jesus considered himself the messiah.

title: Take My New Testament Pop Quiz!
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a New Testament pop quiz formerly used on the first day of class.
searchSummary: Reproduces the introductory New Testament quiz Ehrman used on the first day of his large undergraduate course. The questions test basic knowledge of the canon, original language, dates, Gospels, major figures, authorship traditions, and chronology. Ehrman used the exercise to break the ice, teach several facts while reviewing the answers, and demonstrate that even students with substantial exposure to the Bible often lacked elementary historical knowledge about the New Testament.

title: November Gold Q&A:  Ask Your Questions!
author: jennao
description: Announces the November 2024 Gold Q&A and explains how members can submit questions.

title: An Imagined Dialogue for the Dispute Between Paul & Barnabas in Acts Part 3 by Angus Nisbet
author: Diane
description: Continues Angus Nisbet's imagined reconstruction of the dispute between Paul and Barnabas, including John Mark and the Essenes.
searchSummary: Continues a speculative guest reconstruction of the break between Paul and Barnabas by imagining John Mark as an observer aligned with Jerusalem's Jewish Christians. The dialogue uses Acts, Paul's letters, and later traditions to explore disagreements about circumcision, dietary law, apostolic authority, faith, and good works. It proposes possible motives and connections, including an Essene background, while acknowledging that the narrative goes beyond surviving historical evidence.

title: Island Hopping with History: Join Our Greek Odyssey this May!
author: jennao
description: Announces a Greek Islands lecture trip and summarizes the itinerary.

title: Would the Resurrection Make Anyone Believe Jesus Was the Messiah?
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that belief in resurrection alone would not have led Jesus' followers to call Jesus the messiah.
searchSummary: Argues that belief in Jesus' resurrection could not by itself have caused his followers to call him the messiah, because no Jewish expectation connected messiahship with dying and rising. The title Christ became central immediately after Jesus' death, indicating that followers already applied it during his lifetime. Resurrection belief therefore confirmed and transformed an existing conviction rather than creating the identification of Jesus as messiah from nothing.

title: An Imagined Dialogue for the Dispute Between Paul & Barnabas in Acts Part 2 by Angus Nisbet
author: Diane
description: Continues Angus Nisbet's imagined reconstruction of Paul and Barnabas's dispute using Acts and non-canonical traditions.
searchSummary: Reconstructs an imagined dispute in which Paul accuses John Mark and Jerusalem missionaries of corrupting the gospel by requiring gentile circumcision and Torah observance. Using language from Galatians, Romans, Corinthians, Acts, and later anti-Pauline traditions, Barnabas answers that Paul misrepresented Peter, James, and Jewish believers. The dialogue explores early Christian conflict over authority and law while remaining a creative hypothesis rather than a historical transcript.

title: A Particular Problem with a Crucified Messiah
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why a crucified messiah created a major obstacle for Jewish acceptance of Christian claims.
searchSummary: Explains why a crucified messiah appeared not merely weak but cursed according to Deuteronomy's statement about anyone hanged on a tree. Before his conversion, Paul likely regarded Christian claims about Jesus as blasphemous for precisely this reason. After believing Jesus was raised, Paul reinterpreted the curse: Christ had borne it undeservedly for others, turning an apparent proof against messiahship into the basis of salvation.

title: Paul and the Crucified Messiah in 1 Corinthians
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses 1 Corinthians to show how Paul addressed the scandal of a crucified messiah.
searchSummary: Uses 1 Corinthians to explain why most Jews found Christian claims about a crucified messiah implausible. Paul says Jews sought divine signs, while the Christians offered Christ crucified, a message that appeared weak, foolish, and fundamentally contrary to expectations of a powerful deliverer. His language identifies crucifixion as the central stumbling block, supporting the historical conclusion that Jesus' manner of death hindered Jewish acceptance of Christian preaching.

title: Why Would A Christian Author Lie About Who He Was?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why some ancient Christian authors wrote in the names of famous figures and why such works were considered deceptive.
searchSummary: Asks how authors who valued truth could justify falsely writing as Paul, Peter, or another authority. Ephesians praises truth while, in Ehrman's view, deceiving readers about its Pauline authorship. Ancient moral traditions supplied two answers: Augustine prohibited every lie, but many pagans, Jews, and Christians accepted deception that achieved a greater good, as illustrated by Plato and biblical stories. Christian forgers may therefore have considered false identity permissible when it gave beneficial teaching greater authority, despite others condemning the act.

title: Blog Etiquette in These Troubling Times!
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on maintaining respectful blog discussion during polarized times.

title: An Imagined Dialogue for the Dispute Between Paul & Barnabas in Acts Part I by Angus Nisbet
author: Diane
description: Introduces Angus Nisbet's imagined dialogue about Paul, Barnabas, Jewish Christian conflict, and Acts.
searchSummary: Introduces a four-part imagined dialogue about why Paul and Barnabas separated over John Mark in Acts. The guest author proposes that the disagreement may have involved deeper disputes over Jewish law, gentile salvation, apostolic authority, and competing forms of early Christianity. By combining Paul's letters, Acts, and later noncanonical traditions, the series offers a deliberately speculative reconstruction intended to illuminate tensions that the surviving sources only partially reveal.

title: Forged Books, Anonymous Books, and The Use of Secretaries as Authors in the NT
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains distinctions among forged, anonymous, and secretary-assisted writings in discussions of New Testament authorship.
searchSummary: Distinguishes anonymous writings, later false attributions, homonymous authors, correctly named works, and forgeries whose authors deliberately claim another identity. Ehrman then rejects the secretary hypothesis used to explain disputed Pauline letters. Ancient secretaries normally took dictation, occasionally corrected grammar, or composed short documents for illiterate clients; evidence does not show them independently writing substantial theological works under another person's name. Such an act would itself have been considered forgery, making pseudonymous authorship better supported than secretarial composition.

title: Unexpected Social Agendas in the New Testament.  Who Woulda Thought?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines New Testament ethical problems involving slavery and family values.

title: Jesus as God in the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses textbook sidebars to discuss early Christian claims about Jesus' divinity and exaltation.
searchSummary: Summarizes two New Testament textbook discussions about how Jesus came to be regarded as divine. Pagan and Jewish traditions treated mortals taken into heaven as gods, making resurrection and exaltation a plausible basis for the earliest Christian claim; Paul also depicts Christ as preexistent, involved in creation, and perhaps calls him “God over all” in Romans 9:5. The translation of that verse remains disputed, but Paul's Christology clearly extends beyond an ordinary human sonship.

title: Oral Traditions and the Dates of Our Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how oral tradition affects dating and interpreting the Gospels, especially Mark, Q, John, and Papias.

title: Why CAN’T the Hard Problems Have Simple Answers?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on why the Bible gives multiple, sometimes conflicting, answers to hard questions about suffering.
searchSummary: Argues that the Bible offers multiple, sometimes contradictory answers to suffering rather than one timeless solution to every modern question. Selective readers often enforce favored biblical rules while ignoring adjacent commands, so responsible interpretation requires examining and evaluating each author's claims. Ehrman's goal is neither conversion nor deconversion, but thoughtful engagement with suffering as lived reality, avoiding simplistic, abstract theodicies by comparing biblical responses in their ancient contexts and considering their value for modern reflection.

title: October 2024 Gold Q&A Replay
author: jennao
description: Announces the replay of the October 2024 Gold Q&A and the next scheduled session.

title: Suffering. Is It Really Worth Talking About? Doesn’t the Bible Give the Right Answer?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces God's Problem by explaining why biblical responses to suffering deserve serious historical and theological attention.

title: Doesn’t “Free Will” Explain Suffering?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether free will adequately explains suffering in a world governed by a loving, all-powerful God.

title: New Course by Bart Ehrman: The Genius of the Acts of the Apostles
author: jennao
description: Announces an online course on Acts as theological storytelling about the rise of Christianity.
searchSummary: Announces a course on Acts that examines the book as both an account of early Christianity and a work of theological storytelling. The lectures address Luke and Acts as a unified narrative, Acts' portrayal of Paul compared with his letters, its reports of miracles and divine intervention, its authorship, and the growth of the Christian movement. The course asks how history, theology, and literary strategy combine in Acts rather than treating it as a simple factual record.

title: The Problem of Suffering? So What’s the Problem?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why suffering becomes a special intellectual problem in monotheistic belief.
searchSummary: Defines the classical problem of suffering as the apparent incompatibility of an all-powerful God, an all-loving God, and the reality of suffering. Proposed solutions limit divine power or love, deny suffering, attribute pain to punishment, invoke an afterlife, or add explanations such as free will, yet each faces difficulties when righteous people suffer and the wicked prosper. The Ethiopian famine illustrates why theodicy is not merely a logical puzzle but a confrontation with catastrophic, unequal human pain.

title: How Can We Imagine That God is Active in Our World? (A genuine, not rhetorical, question)
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on divine action, miracles, and the problem of suffering after leaving Christian faith.
searchSummary: Reflects on divine absence through a Christmas Eve prayer asking God to enter the world's darkness again. Biblical narratives portray God intervening to rescue, heal, and feed people, yet children still die from hunger, unsafe water, disease, violence, and other preventable misery on an immense scale. Ehrman explains that teaching biblical responses to suffering revealed their diversity: punishment, demonic opposition, testing, mystery, and resignation offered conflicting explanations rather than a single satisfying answer.

title: Hurricanes, Suffering, And My Loss of Faith
author: BDEhrman
description: Connects Hurricane Helene, biblical views of disaster, and the problem of suffering that contributed to loss of faith.
searchSummary: Recounts how the problem of suffering, rather than biblical contradictions, ultimately led Ehrman from committed Christianity to agnosticism. His education and ministry weakened fundamentalist views of an inerrant Bible without ending his faith, but years of confronting extreme global misery made an actively loving and all-powerful Judeo-Christian God increasingly impossible for him to reconcile with reality. The post introduces God’s Problem and connects its enduring questions to a fundraiser for Hurricane Helene victims.

title: And Yet Other Apocrypha: 2 Maccabees and Others, Including Psalm 151!
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys 2 Maccabees, Psalm 151, and other Old Testament apocryphal writings accepted in some Christian traditions.

title: October Gold Q&A – Get Your Questions Answered!
author: jennao
description: Announces the October Gold Q&A and explains how members can submit questions.

title: Still More Books of the Apocrypha:  Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, and Baruch
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, and Baruch as Old Testament apocryphal writings.

title: Some More of the OT Apocrypha: the Letter of Jeremiah, Additions to Daniel, and 1 Maccabees
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes the Letter of Jeremiah, additions to Daniel, and 1 Maccabees among the Old Testament Apocrypha.

title: Platinum Webinar for October:  “The Literacy of Jesus: Could the Christian Savior Read and Write?”
author: jennao
description: Shares a Platinum webinar recording on whether Jesus could read and write.
searchSummary: Provides the recording of an October 2024 Platinum webinar on whether Jesus could read and write. The lecture explains why Jesus' literacy is historically uncertain, places him within the low literacy rates and educational conditions of ancient Palestine, and assesses what biblical texts do and do not say about his abilities. The event offers a focused treatment of the difference between reading, writing, and literary composition rather than assuming that Jesus' role as a teacher proves formal education.

title: Some of the Old Testament Apocrypha: Tobit, Judith, and Additions to Esther
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Tobit, Judith, and additions to Esther as Old Testament apocryphal writings.

title: Introducing the Old Testament Apocrypha
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains what the Old Testament Apocrypha are and how they differ from early Christian apocrypha.

title: Was the Apocalypse of Peter Originally Considered Part of the New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the Apocalypse of Peter was known and sometimes accepted, but ultimately excluded from the New Testament canon.
searchSummary: Traces the Apocalypse of Peter's substantial but declining canonical status. The Muratorian list, Clement of Alexandria, Methodius, later church use, and a canon list in Codex Claramontanus show that many Christians treated it as inspired Scripture from the second through fifth centuries. Ehrman argues that it was eventually excluded because its earliest version taught universal salvation, a doctrine increasingly condemned by church leaders; later scribes removed that ending only after the work had fallen from favor.

title: The First Ancient Christian List of the Books (allegedly) of the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Muratorian Fragment as an early list of Christian writings and its significance for the canon.
searchSummary: Examines the Muratorian Fragment as the earliest surviving Christian canon list and a late-second-century witness to four named Gospels. It includes twenty-two eventual New Testament books while accepting Wisdom of Solomon and the Apocalypse of Peter and excluding several later canonical epistles. Ehrman proposes that an influential Roman edition first grouped the four anonymous Gospels under the names Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, shaping both this list and Irenaeus's contemporary four-Gospel canon.

title: Was the New Testament Canon Really Closed in 367 CE?
author: BDEhrman
description: Challenges the common claim that Athanasius's 367 letter closed the New Testament canon.
searchSummary: Rejects the common claim that Athanasius closed the New Testament canon in 367 when he listed the present twenty-seven books. Didymus the Blind, a contemporary Christian authority in the same city of Alexandria, continued quoting the Shepherd of Hermas, 1 Clement, and other works as Scripture. Early manuscripts likewise included Hermas, Barnabas, and Clement within New Testament collections. This evidence shows that Athanasius represented one influential position rather than an immediate, universal settlement.

title: Special Webinar Announcement: Hurricane Helene Fundraiser
author: jennao
description: Announces a Hurricane Helene fundraiser tied to a lecture on biblical views of disaster.
searchSummary: Organizes an emergency fundraiser after Hurricane Helene devastated western North Carolina. Donors of any amount support the Community Foundation of Western North Carolina's Emergency and Disaster Response Fund and receive access to Bart's webinar on biblical explanations for disasters, live or recorded. Jen Olmos reports that Bart was temporarily stranded but safe, describes the region's extensive damage, and provides donation-identification, registration, and confirmation steps for the relief event.

title: Finding All the Earliest Christian Texts in One Place
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the rationale for an anthology of the New Testament and other earliest Christian writings.

title: Why Were Some of the Earliest Christian Books Left OUT of the NT?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how early Christian writings circulated and why some eventually became Scripture while others did not.
searchSummary: Explains how circulating Christian writings linked distant congregations and gradually acquired authority as traditions about Jesus and the apostles. Diverse communities promoted conflicting books and beliefs, prompting proto-orthodox leaders to favor works considered ancient, apostolic, orthodox, and widely used. Agreement remained incomplete for centuries: churches differed over Gospels, Paul, Revelation, Hermas, Barnabas, and other writings. Athanasius's twenty-seven-book list in 367 emerged from these prolonged struggles rather than ending them immediately.

title: ALL the Christian Writings of the First Hundred Years
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces an anthology that places the New Testament alongside other surviving Christian writings from the first century of Christianity.

title: Some Interesting Random Questions
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to questions about 1 Clement and Scripture, the sinner's prayer, the Woman Caught in Adultery, and translating Greek compound verbs.
searchSummary: Answers four unrelated questions about early Christianity and biblical language. Ehrman explains that 1 Clement was an anonymous Roman church letter citing the Old Testament, not a papal declaration of inerrancy; identifies the sinner's prayer as modern evangelical practice; discusses the mixed Greek-Latin name Pericope Adulterae; and shows how context makes related Greek verbs mean either lifting the ark or carrying flood victims away.

title: Platinum Webinar: Could Jesus Read and Write?
author: jennao
description: Announces a Platinum webinar on whether Jesus could read and write.
searchSummary: Announces an October 2024 Platinum webinar examining whether Jesus could read and write. Ehrman frames the subject as a genuine scholarly debate rather than a settled inference from Gospel portrayals, promising to review the historical evidence, recent research, and competing interpretations. The session includes a lecture, questions, and discussion designed to distinguish what can be established about literacy in ancient Palestine from later assumptions about the education expected of a religious teacher.

title: A PROOF of the Resurrection of Jesus.  What Do YOU Think?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates an apologetic argument that Christianity's growth proves the resurrection of Jesus.

title: More About My Book “Did Jesus Exist”
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on responses from mythicists to Did Jesus Exist? and critiques weak knowledge of New Testament scholarship.
searchSummary: Explains the purpose and intended audience of Did Jesus Exist amid hostile reactions from some mythicists. Ehrman notes that many confident skeptics lack basic knowledge of New Testament texts and scholarship, whereas trained specialists across religious positions overwhelmingly conclude that Jesus was historical. The book therefore addresses genuine seekers rather than committed conspiracy theorists, presenting evidence without a Christian agenda and arguing that a historical Jesus existed even if he differed substantially from later devotional portrayals.

title: My Book “Did Jesus Exist” (an answer to the mythicists)
author: BDEhrman
