description: Introduces Did Jesus Exist? as a response to mythicist claims that Jesus was invented.
searchSummary: Introduces Did Jesus Exist as a response to the growing mythicist claim that Jesus was wholly invented. Ehrman describes discovering a vocal literature largely outside professional New Testament scholarship and distinguishes its varying levels of knowledge and argument. Although expert agreement alone is not proof, trained historians possess relevant linguistic and historical methods. The book therefore takes stronger mythicist arguments seriously while setting out evidence for the near-universal scholarly conclusion that Jesus was a historical person.

title: Paul and the Anachronistic Origins of Early Christianity – Part 2 by Dr. Robyn Faith Walsh
author: Diane
description: Presents Robyn Faith Walsh's argument that Paul's letters may have shaped Gospel writers and later accounts of Christian origins.
searchSummary: Presents Robyn Faith Walsh's argument that Paul's earlier letters may have served as direct literary sources for Gospel traditions rather than merely sharing a pre-Pauline oral tradition. Parallels concerning divorce, missionary support, the Last Supper, and Jesus's sayings are usually attributed to community memory, even when Paul says he received information through revelation from the risen Lord. Privileging the later Gospels as access to a pre-Pauline historical Jesus can therefore impose an anachronistic model of Christian origins.

title: Paul and the Anachronistic Origins of Early Christianity – Part 1 by Dr. Robyn Faith Walsh
author: Diane
description: Presents Robyn Faith Walsh's challenge to treating the Gospels rather than Paul as the starting point for Christian origins.
searchSummary: Challenges conventional reconstructions that place the Gospel narratives at the beginning of Christian history. Robyn Faith Walsh argues that ancient biographies pursued literary characterization rather than modern factual documentation, while canonical arrangements encouraged scholars to invent neat gospel timelines, communities, and oral chains. Because Paul's letters are the earliest secure evidence for the Jesus movement and describe practices later attributed to Jesus, she proposes testing whether the Gospel writers drew from Pauline material instead of assuming direct transmission from Jesus.

title: Gold Q&A:  Ask Your Questions!
author: admin
description: Announces the September Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: Can We Get Rid of Our Presuppositions?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how presuppositions affect historical judgments about miracle claims in the Gospels.

title: Jesus, the Law, and a New Covenant (Lecture)
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a lecture on Jesus, Jewish Law, and the idea of a new covenant.
searchSummary: Introduces a recorded keynote lecture on Jesus, Jewish law, and the idea of a new covenant. The lecture was delivered at a symposium honoring Hebrew Bible scholar George Mendenhall, where specialists examined law and covenant in the ancient Near East, the Hebrew Bible, and Second Temple Judaism. The post highlights the lecture's unexpected popularity and provides the video rather than a written transcript of its argument.

title: Why Don’t Pastors Teach What They Know about the Bible?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why pastors often do not teach congregations what critical scholarship says about the Bible.
searchSummary: Asks why pastors rarely share the historical-critical knowledge they acquired in seminary, including contradictions, pseudonymous books, textual changes, noncanonical writings, and uncertainty about biblical history. A church attendee's frustration after Ehrman's historical-Jesus lectures illustrates the gap between scholarly education and congregational teaching. Ehrman rejects both automatic resistance and eager rejection of faith, urging thoughtful engagement while questioning whether pastors withhold information from paternalism, fear of controversy, institutional pressure, or job concerns.

title: New Insights Into Paul!  Conference this Weekend!  Wanna Come??
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a conference on Paul and Paul's letters for non-specialist audiences.

title: Major Contradictions (and Other Problems) in the Old Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys contradictions and other critical problems in the Old Testament.
searchSummary: Surveys contradictions and moral problems in the Hebrew Bible, including conflicting creation sequences, Noah's animals, God's revealed name, repeated destruction of Egyptian livestock, divinely commanded massacres, and vengeance against children. Ehrman argues that historical criticism lets each biblical author speak from a distinct cultural and theological setting rather than forcing agreement. Inspiration need not imply infallibility, and questioning biblical portrayals of God is different from questioning God himself.

title: Critical Problems With the Bible, in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how critical study can unsettle inerrantist views of Scripture by exposing biblical contradictions.
searchSummary: Explains how recognizing discrepancies can make the Gospels more intelligible than harmonizing them into an invented composite account. Examples include incompatible placements of the Temple cleansing, differing predictions and reports of Peter's denials, conflicting figures at Jesus' tomb, and internal discontinuities in John's signs and farewell discourse. Ehrman attributes some internal problems to authors combining divergent sources and argues that proposed reconciliations often describe events unlike any canonical Gospel's own narrative.

title: What Seminarians Learn About the Bible (Often to Their Surprise)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how seminarians encounter the historical-critical method and its difference from devotional Bible reading.
searchSummary: Contrasts devotional reading, which asks how Scripture guides belief and life, with historical criticism, which investigates authorship, sources, contexts, contradictions, textual transmission, and original meaning. Seminarians often arrive expecting pious instruction but encounter evidence that traditional attributions and historical narratives are unreliable or legendary. Some accept these conclusions and others resist, but sustained analysis makes harmonizing every discrepancy increasingly difficult and can unsettle assumptions about biblical inerrancy and absolute historical accuracy.

title: Jesus Interrupted:  My Most Thorough Explanation of Critical Scholarship on the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Jesus Interrupted as an accessible overview of critical scholarship on the New Testament.
searchSummary: Introduces Jesus Interrupted as an effort to communicate mainstream critical scholarship that universities and seminaries teach but churches and the public rarely hear. The book addresses contradictions, forgery, the historical Jesus, canon formation, and doctrines later readers mistakenly assume appear in the New Testament. Ehrman explains that first-year seminarians often expect devotional application but instead meet rigorous historical study, while many lack even basic biblical knowledge needed to understand the scholarly questions.

title: How Many of Those Early Christians Could Read?
author: BDEhrman
description: Estimates early Christian literacy and considers how many believers could read or write around 100 CE.
searchSummary: Estimates that around 100 CE an average Christian congregation of seventy may have included only four adult male readers, perhaps about four hundred literate Christians worldwide. This creates a striking tension because Christianity relied heavily on authoritative texts in a society where most believers could not read. Literate church leaders controlled access to Scripture and its interpretation, giving literacy social and religious power that may have discouraged efforts to spread reading skills more broadly.

title: Special Gold Members Event:  A Live AMA (Ask Me Anything)
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Gold-only live Q&A event to make up for a missed monthly session.

title: The Quest for the Historical Paul: Sorting Through Our Sources (Part 2) by Dr. James Tabor
author: Diane
description: Presents James Tabor's second post on sources for reconstructing Paul's life and letters.

title: The Quest for the Historical Paul: Sorting Through Our Sources (Part 1). Guest Post by James Tabor
author: Diane
description: Presents James Tabor's first post on the difficulty of reconstructing the historical Paul from surviving sources.

title: The Next Ten Commandments Platinum Guest post by Douglas Wadeson MD
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a Platinum guest post on biblical commandments beyond the Decalogue.
searchSummary: Examines the laws immediately following the Ten Commandments in Exodus, including rules governing slavery, violence, injury, pregnancy, and livestock. The guest author questions whether these provisions reflect timeless divine wisdom or the priorities of an ancient society, while noting occasional principles that might inform modern justice. The post challenges selective appeals to biblical law by asking readers to consider the full legal collection, not merely the Decalogue.

title: How Strikingly Few Early Churches Were There?  How Amazingly Many Christian Letters?
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Keith Hopkins's work to estimate early Christian communities and the volume of Christian letters.
searchSummary: Explores what sparse evidence about early churches and lost correspondence implies for Christian diversity. Before dedicated buildings, multiple house churches could coexist within one city with leaders, membership rules, beliefs, and practices. Even conservative estimates imply that thousands of letters circulated between communities before 150 CE, yet only about fifty survive. Conversely, many towns may have had no church at all. The documentary loss makes it impossible to determine how isolated congregations related, communicated, or developed common forms of Christianity.

title: Were Christians Statistically Insignificant in the First 200 years?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether early Christians were numerically insignificant before Constantine.
searchSummary: Uses projected growth rates to argue that Christians remained statistically insignificant through the first two centuries. Even steady forty-percent growth per decade would leave them one-hundredth of one percent of the empire in 100 CE and roughly one-third of one percent in 200. Contemporary rulers could therefore ignore them except as local nuisances, despite Christian perceptions of expansion and persecution. Imperial campaigns emerged in the third century only after cumulative person-to-person conversion produced numbers large enough to attract state concern.

title: Exaggerating the Numbers of Early Christians
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why ancient sources often exaggerate or fail to provide reliable numbers for early Christians.
searchSummary: Shows why Christian claims about membership cannot be used as reliable population statistics. Acts reports thousands of Jerusalem converts within weeks, while Paul and Tertullian describe the gospel or Christians as filling the world; these figures conflict with populations, pagan testimony, archaeological evidence, and missionary narratives. Such rhetoric expressed confidence and identity rather than measured totals. Because neither churches nor officials kept conversion records, historians must estimate Christian growth indirectly instead of treating canonical or apologetic exaggerations as demographic facts.

title: New Insights into the New Testament 2024:  A Conference you DON’T Want to Miss!!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a conference on Paul and Paul's letters for lay readers.

title: If You’re Counting Christians, Who Counts as a Christian?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores the difficulty of defining who counts as Christian when estimating early Christian growth.
searchSummary: Explains why counting Christians requires deciding whom the label includes. Early believers held different views about God, Christ, creation, and practice, and some continued Jewish or pagan worship while revering Jesus. Sparse records, produced mainly by an educated elite, cannot reveal most people's commitments or how communities defined membership. Because no theological boundary can be applied consistently, Ehrman adopts a broad working definition that counts anyone who considered themselves a worshipper of the Christian God while acknowledging the resulting uncertainty.

title: How Many Christians Were There in 100 CE? 150? 250? 300?
author: BDEhrman
description: Estimates the number of Christians at various points in the first three centuries using growth-rate calculations.
searchSummary: Constructs approximate Christian population totals by varying growth rates across four centuries rather than assuming one constant rate. Ehrman proposes rapid expansion from roughly twenty believers in 30 CE to about 1,000–1,500 by 60, slower growth to 7,000–10,000 by 100, roughly three million by 300, and around thirty million by 400. These are educated ranges, not measurements, but they accommodate early missionary momentum, later cumulative growth, Constantine's influence, and the shrinking pool of non-Christians available for conversion.

title: How Many Early Christians Were There and When?  Crunchin’ the Numbers
author: BDEhrman
description: Calculates early Christian growth rates and problems in moving from small beginnings to later expansion.
searchSummary: Revises Rodney Stark's constant forty-percent-per-decade model because it produces too few Christians in Paul's lifetime and too many by 400 CE. Paul's letters independently attest numerous established communities with dozens of members only twenty-five years after Jesus, requiring unusually rapid initial growth. Later rates had to decline as the movement became large. Ehrman treats births, deaths, nursing, and martyrdom as demographically minor and anchors a flexible model between about twenty believers in 30 CE and thirty million in 400.

title: How Fast Did Early Christianity Grow?  Doing the Math
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how growth-rate math can be used to estimate the spread of early Christianity.
searchSummary: Introduces Rodney Stark's calculation that Christianity could grow from 1,000 adherents in 40 CE to six million in 300 through a plausible forty-percent increase per decade. Exponential growth makes small annual gains produce enormous later totals without mass conversions, much like Mormon expansion. Ehrman accepts the mathematical insight but identifies endpoint problems: that rate cannot explain growth from roughly twenty original believers to Paul's many churches, and if continued after 300 it would exceed the empire's entire population by 400.

title: Major Change on the Blog!  Announcing our New CEO: Jen Olmos
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces Jen Olmos as the blog's new CEO and reviews the blog's growth and charitable mission.

title: The Conversion of the Emperor Constantine
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Constantine's conversion and why it became a transformative event in Christian and Roman history.
searchSummary: Constantine's conversion in 312 transformed Christianity's relationship with Roman power without immediately making it the state religion or single-handedly ensuring its success. He moved from additive polytheistic worship to exclusive devotion to the Christian God, a kind of religious choice unusual outside Judaism and Christianity. Imperial recognition, privileges, funding, and elite support then strengthened a movement that the government had recently tried to suppress.

title: Heartache and Loss:  When a Religion is Destroyed
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the cultural and emotional losses caused by Christianity's displacement of traditional Roman religions.
searchSummary: Examines the human and cultural losses concealed by Christianity's triumph through the destruction of Palmyra's temple of Allat. Under Theodosius I, anti-pagan laws and regional Christian zeal encouraged temple closures, mutilation of divine statues, and destruction meant to demonstrate pagan gods' powerlessness. Archaeology places the temple's deliberate ruin in this campaign. Ehrman acknowledges Christianity's enduring cultural contributions but emphasizes that its victory assaulted living religions, sacred objects, and communities whose grief matched the victors' celebration.

title: Was Christianity Bound to Take Over the Ancient World?
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Christianity's dominance in the Roman Empire was not historically inevitable.
searchSummary: Rejects the assumption that Christianity was destined to dominate the Roman world. A movement of roughly twenty Galilean believers became tens of millions over several centuries, requiring historical explanation rather than an appeal to providence or a claim that Constantine caused everything. Constantine accelerated conversion, but Ehrman argues Christianity might have succeeded without him and did not eliminate paganism. The book treats the outcome neutrally as a victory for Christians that also inflicted profound losses on adherents of displaced religions.

title: Losing Your Religion: Today and in Antiquity
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses modern loss of faith to imagine the experience of ancient people whose religions were displaced by Christianity.
searchSummary: Connects the pain of modern religious doubt with the ancient displacement of traditional religions by Christianity. Matthew Arnold's “Dover Beach” once mirrored Ehrman's own distress as education weakened his evangelical certainty, but he now approaches such loss historically and empathizes with people forced to abandon inherited faiths. Christianity's expansion transformed the Roman world more completely than modern skepticism transformed Christianity, leaving ancient pagan worshippers to face a similarly agonizing collapse of religious certainty and culture.

title: Did Jesus Have Secret Disciples Among the Elite?
author: BDEhrman
description: Questions whether members of Jerusalem's elite could plausibly have been secret followers of Jesus.

title: A (Modern-Discovered) Gospel That Shows Jesus Was Married With Children?
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques a modern claim that a newly discovered Gospel showed Jesus married to Mary Magdalene and had children.
searchSummary: Rejects the claim that the ancient story Joseph and Aseneth is a lost Gospel showing that Jesus married Mary Magdalene and had children. The text is a well-known Jewish pseudepigraphal romance explaining how the patriarch Joseph could marry the Egyptian Aseneth by portraying her conversion to his God. Reading Joseph and Aseneth as coded names for Jesus and Mary lacks evidence, and the surviving Syriac manuscript contributes nothing historical about Jesus' marital status.

title: Jesus’ Followers in History and Legend
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how history and legend shape later accounts of Peter, Paul, and Mary Magdalene.

title: My Book on Peter, Paul, and Mary Magdalene
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Peter, Paul, and Mary Magdalene as a study of major followers of Jesus in history and legend.

title: My Edition of the Apostolic Fathers
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Loeb Classical Library edition of the Apostolic Fathers and its scholarly purpose.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's two-volume Loeb Classical Library edition of the Apostolic Fathers and reproduces part of its scholarly general introduction. The excerpt explains how a diverse group of early noncanonical writings gradually came to be collected under that label, despite uncertain apostolic connections and varying ancient circulation. It traces manuscript evidence and changing scholarly interest from antiquity through the Renaissance and Reformation, showing why these texts illuminate Christianity immediately after the New Testament period.

title: The Reliability of Eyewitnesses and Abraham Lincoln’s Watch
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the story of Abraham Lincoln's watch to reflect on memory, testimony, and eyewitness reliability.
searchSummary: Uses Abraham Lincoln's pocket watch to show how a direct participant's memory can change over decades. Watchmaker Jonathan Dillon later quoted a message he claimed to have inscribed during the Fort Sumter attack, but opening the watch revealed substantially different wording without his remembered references to slavery or the president. Since the Gospels were written after a comparable interval by non-witnesses relying on repeated oral reports, eyewitness memory cannot guarantee their precise accuracy.

title: How I Almost Published “Lost in Transmission”
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts how Misquoting Jesus received its title instead of the originally preferred Lost in Transmission.
searchSummary: Explains how publishers choose marketable trade-book titles and recounts why Misquoting Jesus replaced Ehrman's preferred title, Lost in Transmission. Editors propose and test titles with colleagues and marketing departments, while authors may object or see titles changed across markets. Although Ehrman thought the published title misrepresented the book's broader discussion of scribal alterations, its success demonstrated the publisher's judgment; an editor later commemorated his rejected choice on a special bound copy.

title: July 2024 Platinum webinar video
author: Diane
description: Shares the July 2024 Platinum webinar video.

title: Misquoting Jesus and My Fall From Fundamentalism
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how textual variants and the absence of original manuscripts shaped a move away from biblical inerrancy.
searchSummary: Explains how studying New Testament manuscripts undermined Ehrman's belief that the Bible was verbally inspired and inerrant. If God preserved neither the originals nor certainty about all their words, he concluded that Scripture was a collection of human writings whose authors held differing perspectives rather than one perfectly consistent divine message. That shift made textual criticism essential for recovering what those authors likely wrote and evaluating their distinct claims.

title: How Scholarship Changed My Life
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes how study of New Testament manuscripts and scribal mistakes changed a planned evangelical scholarly path.
searchSummary: Describes how studying Greek, manuscripts, and Mark transformed Ehrman's evangelical belief in biblical inerrancy. At Wheaton and Princeton, access to original languages raised questions about translations and error-filled copies. A paper defending Mark's incorrect reference to Abiathar prompted a professor to suggest that Mark simply made a mistake, opening consideration of other contradictions and textual variants. The experience redirected a quest to defend inspiration toward historical scholarship willing to revise beliefs in light of evidence.

title: Why I Wrote Misquoting Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Misquoting Jesus brought textual criticism to a general audience despite scholarly doubts about public interest.
searchSummary: Traces Ehrman's path from a conventional Episcopal upbringing through a born-again conversion and rigorous Bible study at Moody Bible Institute. Moody taught that Scripture was verbally inspired and without error, yet also acknowledged that the originals are lost and surviving copies contain accidental and intentional changes. The tension made recovering the original wording a compelling theological problem and led Ehrman toward Greek, ancient languages, and New Testament textual criticism.

title: Interested in Textual Criticism?  Probably My Most Useful (Edited) Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces an edited academic volume on New Testament textual criticism and its major scholarly essays.

title: Women and Gender: Early Christianity in a Patriarchal World
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys women's roles, suppression, and alternative expressions of faith in early Christianity.

title: August Gold Q&A–Get Your Qs In!
author: Diane
description: Announces the August Gold Q&A and invites member questions.

title: Competing Interpretations of Scripture in the Early Church
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Ptolemy and Irenaeus as examples of competing early Christian interpretations of Scripture.

title: Ancient Ways of Interpreting Scripture
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces early Christian methods of interpreting Scripture and the debates those methods produced.

title: Does Paul Have Contradictory Views of the Law, Love, and Salvation?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Paul's teaching on love creates tension with Paul's law-free message of salvation.
searchSummary: Examines Paul's apparent contradiction between teaching that Gentiles are justified apart from Jewish law and insisting that love fulfills the entire law. Galatians and Romans reject law observance as the basis of salvation yet ground Christian ethics in loving one's neighbor, while Paul also imposes standards beyond love. Ehrman considers distinctions between cultic and ethical commandments but leaves unresolved exactly how Paul's law-free gospel can require fulfillment of the law.

title: Salvation, Love, and the Jewish Law in Paul.  Are His Views Internally Coherent?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the problem of how Paul's views of salvation, love, and Jewish Law fit together.
searchSummary: Examines how Paul's teaching about salvation apart from Jewish law relates to his emphasis on Christian love. It reconstructs Paul's reasoning from his vision of the risen Jesus: Christ's death must be God's universal means of salvation, so gentiles need not adopt circumcision, kosher practice, or other Torah requirements. The post argues that Paul likely expected Jews to remain observant while fiercely rejecting law observance as a condition for gentile salvation.

title: Did the Roman Government Become More “Moral” Once it Became Christian?
author: BDEhrman
description: Considers whether Christian emperors made Roman government more ethically responsive to social problems.
searchSummary: Christian emperors sometimes addressed suffering through measures against infanticide, child sale, hunger, and poverty, but Christianization did not consistently make Roman government more humane. Laws against beggars grew harsher, slavery and violent entertainment changed little, and judicial punishments became more severe and torturous. The evidence therefore presents a mixed moral legacy rather than a simple story of either Christian improvement or Christian corruption.

title: More Major Issues Confronting the Early Christians.
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues an overview of debates that shaped early Christian thought, interpretation, and practice.
searchSummary: Surveys major issues addressed by Ehrman's anthology After the New Testament through primary texts from second- and third-century Christianity. The selections illuminate competing methods of interpreting Scripture, preaching, increasingly powerful church government, baptism and eucharist, women's authority, religiously grounded ethics, and developing doctrine. These subjects show that early Christianity involved social organization, ritual, and moral practice as well as theology. Ehrman urges readers to encounter the ancient sources directly and provides further scholarship for broader historical study.

title: Major Issues in the Earliest Christian Centuries (In my Book After the New Testament)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the thematic structure of After the New Testament and the major issues it presents from early Christian history.

title: My Most Helpful Book?   After the New Testament: A Reader in Early Christianity
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces After the New Testament as an anthology of important Christian writings from the second and third centuries.
searchSummary: Introduces After the New Testament as an anthology designed to make the diverse primary literature of second- and third-century Christianity accessible. Archaeological and manuscript discoveries reveal disputes over gods, Christ, Scripture, women, martyrdom, worship, ethics, and authority that Eusebius's later narrative of original unity obscures. Because Eusebius wrote from the victorious orthodox perspective, his history must be supplemented. The collection presents substantial texts from proto-orthodox and alternative groups, organized by the issues they address rather than by later theology.

title: Not a Game-Changer?  Why I’d Still Be Thrilled to Have a First-Century Gospel Fragment
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why a genuine first-century Gospel fragment would be exciting even if not a major textual breakthrough.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman would still welcome a genuine first-century fragment of Mark even though it would probably not overturn existing scholarship. A small early scrap would provide valuable physical evidence that Mark circulated and was copied in the first century, likely confirming current reconstructions of the text and its transmission. Its importance would lie in adding an unusually early piece to a fragmentary manuscript record, not in proving Gospel reliability or transforming knowledge of Jesus.

title: How Would a First-Century Fragment of the Gospels Actually Change What We Know/Think?
author: BDEhrman
description: Considers whether a first-century Gospel fragment would change conclusions about Mark or the New Testament text.
searchSummary: Asks what a rumored first-century fragment of Mark could actually contribute if scholars already claim confidence in the Gospel's original text. A small fragment matching or differing from reconstructed Mark would largely confirm possibilities scholars already accept, not prove that the entire text was preserved accurately. A fragment containing an early title or evidence for Mark's disputed ending, however, could significantly change knowledge of the Gospel's attribution or transmission.

title: Would It Matter if We DID Have a First-Century Manuscript of Mark?
author: BDEhrman
description: Questions whether an unpublished first-century fragment of Mark would matter without expert verification and public access.
searchSummary: Tests several possibilities for what a genuine first-century fragment of Mark might contain. Whether its wording closely matched later manuscripts, showed a few variants, or differed substantially, a small fragment would largely confirm what scholars already expect about early copying. Only a lengthy, unmistakable copy radically different from the known Gospel could significantly alter the picture. Ehrman argues that apologetic excitement instead exaggerates what such a scrap could establish about eyewitnesses, accuracy, or Jesus.

title: More on the Initial Debacle on First-Century Mark (in relation to the Dead Sea Scrolls)
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts the early controversy over Dan Wallace's claim about a first-century Mark fragment and its comparison to the Dead Sea Scrolls.
searchSummary: Challenges Dan Wallace's comparison of the rumored first-century Mark fragment with the Dead Sea Scrolls. The Scrolls supplied an extensive new Jewish library and biblical manuscripts roughly a thousand years earlier than previously known copies, whereas the Mark item was described as a tiny scrap of an already familiar text. Ehrman also criticizes the secrecy surrounding its dating and provenance, arguing that even an authentic first-century fragment would probably confirm rather than revolutionize existing textual scholarship.

title: The Parables!  Have You Signed up for the Course?  (This weekend!)
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a course on Jesus' parables taught by Amy-Jill Levine.
searchSummary: Introduces Amy-Jill Levine's course on interpreting Jesus' parables within their first-century Jewish setting. Rather than reducing them to comfortable lessons about forgiveness, charity, or persistence, the course examines their provocations concerning economics, ethics, insiders and outsiders, enslaved people, women, and unequal power. Recovering what Jesus' original audiences might have heard also exposes later antisemitic readings and distinguishes the parables themselves from the theological meanings imposed on them by Gospel authors and subsequent Christians.

title: The Debacle Over the First-Century Copy of Mark
author: BDEhrman
description: Reintroduces the long-running controversy over the alleged first-century copy of Mark.
searchSummary: Reconstructs how Dan Wallace announced an alleged first-century copy of Mark during a 2012 debate without disclosing the fragment, its provenance, its extent, the dating evidence, or the expert involved. Ehrman places the claim within New Testament textual criticism, where surviving copies contain hundreds of thousands of variants and the earliest known Mark manuscript was then dated around 200. He objects to using unverifiable evidence as a debate tactic while withholding the information scholars would need to assess it.

title: What If Another Christianity Had Won?
author: BDEhrman
description: Imagines how world history might have differed if another form of early Christianity had become dominant.
searchSummary: Explores what Christianity and Western history might have looked like if a form other than proto-orthodoxy had won early contests for dominance. Different victors could have produced other doctrines about God and Christ, different Testaments or canonical books, and a radically altered relationship between Christianity and the Roman Empire. Ehrman outlines Lost Christianities: forged and rediscovered texts, Ebionite, Marcionite, Gnostic, and proto-orthodox movements, their literary conflicts, and the gains and losses created by proto-orthodox victory.

title: More Lost Christianities
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys non-canonical Gospels and other writings used by early Christian groups outside the emerging canon.
searchSummary: Examines the many Gospels, acts, letters, and apocalypses once revered by Christian groups but excluded from the New Testament. The proto-orthodox victors selected writings that supported their theology, hierarchy, creed, and practices, marginalized rival texts, and portrayed their own position as the original majority faith. Modern discoveries and critical study recover some of the suppressed diversity, allowing historians to reassess orthodox accounts of early conflict and understand what Christianity both gained and lost through canon formation.

title: Lost Christianities
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Lost Christianities and the diversity of early Christian groups and beliefs.
searchSummary: Introduces Lost Christianities by arguing that Christian belief and practice in the second and third centuries were more radically diverse than modern denominations. Self-identified Christians disagreed over how many gods existed, who created the world, whether Jewish Scripture was inspired, whether Jesus was human or divine, and whether his death brought salvation. No settled New Testament yet governed these debates; competing groups used different Gospels, Acts, letters, and apocalypses, many attributed to apostles and later suppressed or forgotten.

title: More Lost Scriptures
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses writings left out of the New Testament and the later process of canon formation.
searchSummary: Introduces Lost Scriptures as an accessible anthology of forty-two early Christian writings that were sometimes treated as sacred but excluded from the New Testament. Debate continued for centuries after Athanasius listed the present canon in 367, and rejected works survive as complete texts, fragments, quotations, or modern rediscoveries. Organized as Gospels, acts, epistles, apocalypses, and ancient canon lists, the collection shows the variety of Christian authorities while avoiding misleading labels such as pseudepigrapha or apocrypha as strict categories.

title: A Remembrance of John Shelby Spong–Platinum Post By Ray Zubler
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum remembrance of John Shelby Spong and Spong's role in popularizing critical biblical scholarship.

title: ANOTHER Blog Dinner!  Thursday, July 18, Wimbledon.  Interested?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a second Wimbledon blog dinner for members.

title: Lost Scriptures
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Lost Scriptures as an anthology of non-canonical early Christian writings.
searchSummary: Explains that the New Testament emerged from centuries of conflict among diverse Christian groups rather than appearing as a complete collection after Jesus' death. Competing communities produced apostolic Gospels, acts, letters, and apocalypses supporting different gods, Christologies, views of salvation, and relationships to Judaism. The proto-orthodox movement eventually prevailed, promoted its books as authentic Scripture, suppressed rival texts, and rewrote the controversy as though its beliefs had always represented Christianity from Jesus and the apostles onward.

title: June Gold Q&A Video
author: Diane
description: Shares the June Gold Q&A video.

title: My First Trade Book:  Jesus, Apocalyptic Prophet
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Jesus: Apocalyptic Prophet as a trade book presenting Jesus within Jewish apocalypticism.
searchSummary: Introduces Bart's first trade book, Jesus: Apocalyptic Prophet of the New Millennium, through its preface and explanation of its purpose. Bart presents the scholarly view of Jesus as a first-century Jewish apocalypticist who expected God's imminent intervention and the arrival of the Kingdom. He also explains his commitment to showing general readers the historical evidence and methods behind that interpretation rather than simply asking them to accept scholarly conclusions.

title: How Can We Possibly Know a Scribe’s Intentions?  My Most Important Theoretical Reflection
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how intentionality can be used as a functional category when evaluating scribal changes.

title: Free Lecture on Paul’s Life and Letters, Thursday (July 11)
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a free lecture on Paul's life and letters connected with an upcoming conference.

title: The Evolution of Jewish Monotheism–Platinum Post By Daniel Kohanski
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum member post on the development of Jewish monotheism.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: Are Scribes of Texts Actually Authors?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether scribes who altered texts should be understood as authors rather than copyists.

title: The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture, 2nd edition
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the aims and later reflections behind The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture.
searchSummary: Explains how The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture challenged textual criticism's narrow pursuit of a single original New Testament text. Ehrman argues that scribal variants also preserve evidence about early Christian social history, theological conflict, anti-Judaism, and the settings in which copyists worked. The book helped redirect the field toward asking what variants reveal about scribes and communities, while later scholarship also questioned what an original text could mean.

title: July Gold Q&A: Your Turn
author: Diane
description: Announces the July Gold Q&A and invites member questions.

title: Does God Have Chromosomes? Guest Post by Douglas Wadeson, MD
author: Diane
description: Presents a physician's questions about the biology implied by the virgin birth.

title: Did People Have Time for Jesus? – Guest Post from Platinum Member Doug Wadeson, MD.
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum guest argument that rural Galileans could plausibly have gathered to hear Jesus.

title: Platinum Webinar July 6
author: Diane
description: Announces a Platinum webinar on how historians can discuss New Testament miracles.

title: Finishing and Publishing My Dissertation
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes finishing and publishing a dissertation on Didymus the Blind's Gospel quotations under Bruce Metzger.
searchSummary: Describes how Bruce Metzger's deliberately hands-off supervision suited Ehrman's independent approach to completing his dissertation on Didymus the Blind's Gospel quotations. After the defense, Ehrman published its methodological chapter as an article and the remaining study as his first scholarly book. He then encouraged Gordon Fee to establish a series devoted to church fathers' New Testament texts, contributed its inaugural volume, later coauthored another, and eventually became the series editor before a former student succeeded him.

title: How I View the Bible as Both a Critical Scholar and a Christian: Guest Post by Judy Siker
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Judy Siker's reflection on combining critical biblical scholarship with Christian faith.
searchSummary: Explains how Judy Siker combines critical biblical scholarship with Christian faith by treating questions and ambiguity as spiritually productive rather than threatening. Historical study exposes inconsistencies, uncertain authorship, and cultural distance, but these findings challenge only models requiring factual inerrancy or universal answers. Siker understands Scripture as an imperfect collection of human reflections on encounters with transcendent reality, whose unresolved struggles and limited language deepen her curiosity, humility, and participation in the Christian tradition.

title: Is It Possible To Continue Believing?  Guest Post by New Testament Scholar Judy Siker
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Judy Siker's account of how critical New Testament study can coexist with Christian belief.
searchSummary: Recounts Judy Siker's path from a moderate Protestant upbringing through critical New Testament study to careers as a scholar and ordained minister. College courses answered questions about Genesis and other texts without threatening her belief, unlike classmates whose conservative assumptions made scholarship feel deceptive or destructive. Advanced study of contradictions and historical problems remained compatible with faith because curiosity, church participation, and belief in God were never dependent on biblical inerrancy or freedom from difficult questions.

title: The Reason for Detailed Work on Textual Criticism
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why detailed work on Didymus the Blind's Gospel quotations matters for textual criticism.

title: May Gold Q&A Video
author: admin
description: Shares the May Gold Q&A video.

title: My First Book!  A Dissertation on Textual Criticism of the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a published dissertation on textual criticism and the Gospel quotations of Didymus the Blind.
searchSummary: Recounts how Ehrman's first book grew from his Princeton dissertation under Bruce Metzger on reconstructing New Testament quotations in Didymus the Blind. Gordon Fee's work showed that patristic citations can locate forms of the text in particular times and places, but memory, paraphrase, and inconsistent quotation make that evidence difficult to recover. Newly discovered Didymus commentaries from Toura gave Ehrman unexplored material for developing a rigorous textual study.

title: The Arch-Heretic of Them All? Simon of Samaria — Guest Post From Dr. David Litwa
author: Diane
description: Presents David Litwa's discussion of Simon of Samaria and the construction of early Christian heresy.

title: NEW COURSE!  “The Parables of Jesus” with Amy-Jill Levine
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a remote course on the parables of Jesus taught by Amy-Jill Levine.
searchSummary: Announces Amy-Jill Levine's course on hearing Jesus' parables as provocative Jewish stories in their original historical and cultural setting. Its four lectures examine how first audiences and Gospel writers understood the stories, how antisemitic interpretations developed, and what the parables imply about economics, ethics, social outsiders, slavery, and women's roles. The course aims to replace familiar simplified lessons with historically grounded readings that recover the parables' humor, moral challenge, and capacity to unsettle their audiences.

title: Does Altruism Even Exist?  Some Personal Reflections Based on a Crazy Anecdote
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses a personal anecdote to question whether pure altruism exists.
searchSummary: Uses Ehrman's rescue of a woman and child from a brakeless car to ask whether apparently heroic action can ever be purely altruistic. Although his intervention plainly benefited strangers, possible motives included pleasing God, becoming a virtuous person, receiving approval, or avoiding future guilt; the distorted newspaper account also illustrates unreliable reporting. The episode introduces a broader ethical distinction among beneficial actions, personal motivations, and perceived obligations, preparing an inquiry into how Jesus reshaped Western moral conscience.

title: The New Book I’m Writing About Altruism:  Putting It In a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes the argument of a book project on Jesus' teachings and the rise of altruism.
searchSummary: Presents the proposed argument of Bart's book on altruism: modern Western concern for suffering strangers developed largely from Jesus's teachings, inherited from Jewish ethics and spread through Christianity. Greek and Roman moral obligations generally centered on family, friends, citizens, and social equals rather than unknown outsiders. Although Christians often modified or failed to practice Jesus's demands, their emphasis on the poor and marginalized eventually inspired charities, hospitals, orphanages, poorhouses, elder care, and public assistance.

title: Can You Disprove the Existence of God?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on whether God's existence can be disproved and how such questions arise in conversation.

title: Toe-to-Toe with Evangelical New Testament Scholar Peter Williams:  Can We Trust the Gospels?
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a televised debate with Peter Williams over whether the Gospels can be trusted.
searchSummary: Introduces a televised debate with evangelical textual scholar Peter Williams over whether the Gospels are completely trustworthy. Ehrman respects Williams's expertise but argues that his defense largely answers objections critics do not make while failing to confront the historical reasons scholars question Gospel reliability. The post directs readers to evaluate the exchange themselves. Its central concern is the gap between reassuring arguments that satisfy committed believers and arguments that actually address contradictions, sources, authorship, and historical accuracy.

title: An Early Christian Advocate of Licentious Living?  Carpocrates — Guest Post by Dr. David Litwa
author: Diane
description: Presents David Litwa's discussion of Carpocrates and the reputation of libertine early Christian groups.

title: June Gold Q&A: Whaddya Wanna Know?
author: Diane
description: Announces the June Gold Q&A and invites member questions.

title: Platinums! Time to Upvote a Platinum Post!
author: Diane
description: Invites Platinum members to vote on which guest post should be shared with the full blog.

title: A Debate with Peter Williams on Textual Variants
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a debate with Peter Williams on textual variants and the reliability of the New Testament text.
searchSummary: Presents a recorded debate between Bart Ehrman and evangelical textual scholar Peter J. Williams about New Testament manuscript variation and the arguments in Misquoting Jesus. Williams defends the New Testament's reliability and considers Ehrman's assessment too pessimistic, while both participants bring specialist knowledge of the manuscripts to their disagreement. The post offers the exchange as an alternative perspective at the conclusion of a series asking whether textual variants matter, inviting readers to evaluate the competing positions.

title: Why Textual Variants Matter Even for Those Who Do NOT Think the Bible is Infallible
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why textual variants matter even apart from claims about biblical infallibility.
searchSummary: Argues that textual variants matter even without a belief in biblical infallibility because readers need to know what each biblical author actually wrote. Treating the New Testament as a single harmonized message obscures the distinct perspectives of Mark, Matthew, Luke, John, Paul, and James. Variants affecting resurrection appearances, Jesus' emotions, atonement, divine sonship, ascension, and other issues can therefore substantially alter an individual author's theology, despite most manuscript differences being insignificant.

title: Why Bible-Believing Christians Care About Textual Variants
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why textual variants matter for readers who believe God gave the exact words of Scripture.
searchSummary: Explains why manuscript variants pose a particular challenge for Christians who believe God inspired the Bible's exact words. Ehrman initially saw textual criticism as a sacred effort to recover those words from fallible copies, but later questioned why a God who miraculously inspired a text would not preserve it accurately. The loss of the originals and proliferation of uncertainty led him away from mechanical inerrancy toward a less literal understanding of Scripture, though not directly to agnosticism.

title: If Textual Variants Don’t Change Any Key Doctrines — Then Who Cares?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to the claim that textual variants are unimportant because no central Christian doctrine is overturned.
searchSummary: Argues that textual variants can matter even when none overturns a fundamental Christian doctrine. Most manuscript differences are trivial, and doctrines normally rest on many interpreted passages rather than one disputed reading, but doctrinal impact is an impoverished measure of significance. Variants can alter stories, an author's theology, Jesus' words and deeds, Christian practices, and relationships among New Testament writings, all of which remain historically and religiously important.

title: A Bizarre “Gnostic” Religion:  The Naassenes – Guest Post by Dr. David Litwa
author: Diane
description: Presents David Litwa's introduction to the Naassenes and their unusual mixture of Christian and Greco-Roman religious traditions.
searchSummary: David Litwa describes the Naassenes as an early Christian group that combined biblical interpretation with Greek mythology, philosophy, astrology, and mystery traditions. Their complex teaching included a hidden spiritual meaning in many scriptures, ascetic practices, unusual views of sexuality, and possible associations with snakes. The group demonstrates how cosmopolitan and nonexclusive some forms of ancient Christianity could be before orthodox boundaries hardened.

title: Serious Hypothetical (And Realistically Possible) Problems With Copies of Paul’s Letters
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores practical problems that arise after Paul's letters were copied, circulated, and possibly edited.
searchSummary: Uses a hypothetical copying history for Philippians to show why surviving manuscripts cannot guarantee Paul's exact wording. Early copies could contain different errors, and a poor copy circulated through Thessalonica and Rome might become the ancestor of most later witnesses after better local copies disappeared. Because the earliest fragment survives about 150 years after Paul, neither manuscript quantity nor genealogical reconstruction can prove word-for-word identity with the letter sent to Philippi.

title: Even More Snarly Problems If Paul Dictated His Letters
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how dictation, correction, and recopying complicate the idea of an original Pauline letter.
searchSummary: Extends the problem of defining an original Pauline letter by considering dictation, correction, and authorial intention. Paul might change his mind, misspeak, be misunderstood, or fail to catch an error before a secretary produced a clean copy, leaving several plausible candidates for the original wording. Since Philippians may combine two letters and the surviving copies are much later and textually varied, deciding which readings are original first requires defining what original means.

title: If Paul Dictated His Letters, How Can We Know What He Said?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines how Paul's use of a secretary complicates claims about the original text of Philippians.
searchSummary: Explains how Paul's practice of dictating letters complicates the idea of an original text. A secretary could mishear or miswrite Paul's words; Paul might correct the draft; and the secretary could introduce new errors while preparing the clean copy that was sent and later reproduced. The original could therefore mean Paul's intention, his spoken words, the secretary's first notation, Paul's corrections, or the dispatched copy, and those forms need not agree.

title: Is There Even Such a Thing as the “Original” Text of Philippians?
author: Diane
description: Questions what an original text means when Philippians may combine multiple letters and later copying.
searchSummary: Examines whether Philippians has a definable original if the canonical letter combines two earlier Pauline letters. Calling the edited compilation original would attribute it partly to an unknown editor who may have omitted or altered material, while calling the two separate letters original points to forms that no longer survive independently. The composite nature of the text therefore complicates both authorship and the textual critic's goal of recovering what Paul produced.

title: Is Paul’s Letter to the Philippians Actually Two Letters Cut and Spliced Together?
author: Diane
description: Presents the argument that Philippians may be two Pauline letters spliced into one.

title: Did Paul Have a Brain Disorder?  (And did it help him?!)  Platinum post by Douglas Wadeson MD
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a Platinum member's medical hypothesis about Paul and the experiences that shaped Christian mission.

title: Do We Have the Original Text of Philippians?
author: admin
description: Introduces a series on whether the original text of Philippians can be identified.
searchSummary: Answers reader questions about whether surviving Philippians represents Paul's original letter. Philippians is authentically Pauline, but it may combine two letters, a copy is never the physical original, and the earliest surviving witness dates roughly 150 years after Paul. Scholars probably reconstruct much of the wording accurately, yet without an original for comparison they cannot measure how close that reconstruction is or know with certainty what has been lost or altered.

title: John the Baptist: The Most Influential Religious Innovator in History by James McGrath (Part 3)
author: Diane
description: Presents James McGrath's final argument for John the Baptist's overlooked influence on later religious history.

title: REMINDER:  My Webinar — When Does Life Begin?  The Status of the Unborn in the Biblical Tradition
author: BDEhrman
description: Reminds readers about a webinar on the status of the unborn in biblical tradition.

title: John the Baptist: The Most Influential Religious Innovator in History by James McGrath (Part 2)
author: Diane
description: Continues James McGrath's case that John the Baptist was a major religious innovator.

title: John the Baptist: The Most Influential Religious Innovator in History by James McGrath (Part 1)
author: Diane
description: Introduces James McGrath's series arguing for the historical and religious significance of John the Baptist.

title: Is Paul’s Second Letter to the Corinthians Actually FIVE Letters?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores the scholarly proposal that 2 Corinthians may be composed from five Pauline letters.

title: Is Paul’s Second Letter to the Corinthians Actually TWO Letters?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why many scholars think 2 Corinthians may combine two originally separate Pauline letters.

title: Three Early Christian Writings Spliced Together Into One: The Didache
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the Didache to illustrate how early Christian writings could be compiled from multiple sources.

title: An Important Early Christian Writing
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Didache as an early Christian writing relevant to questions about originals and later additions.

title: The Silencing of Women: 1 Cor. 14:34-35 as an Interpolation
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 may be a later interpolation rather than Paul's own instruction.
searchSummary: Argues that 1 Corinthians 14:34-35, which commands women to remain silent in church, was inserted after Paul's lifetime. Its language closely resembles the non-Pauline Pastoral Epistles, contradicts Paul's recognition of women ministers, prophets, and apostles, and interrupts a discussion of prophecy. Manuscripts place the verses in different locations, suggesting an original marginal note entered the text. Ehrman concludes that Paul permitted women's public participation despite retaining some assumptions of male authority.

title: Knowing Paul’s Views of Women…
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses questions about women in 1 Corinthians to introduce the problem of original text and later interpolation.

title: When Does Life Begin?  The Status of the Unborn in the Biblical Tradition.
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a course on biblical traditions about when life begins and the status of the unborn.

title: A Major Argument That We Can Be Sure We Have the Original Text
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the tenacity of the tradition argument for confidence in reconstructing the New Testament text.
searchSummary: Challenges the argument that the manuscript tradition's tenacity ensures the New Testament's original readings survive. Early readings often reappear in medieval manuscripts because later trained scribes preserved inherited variants, but that practice reveals nothing about less careful first- and second-century copyists who introduced most changes. Since the original and the earliest generations of copies are lost, no surviving evidence can show that every early variant, including the original reading, continued into extant manuscripts.

title: Dubious Arguments That We CAN Get to the “Original Text”
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques arguments that surviving manuscripts allow certainty about the original New Testament text.
searchSummary: Evaluates two arguments offered for confidence in the New Testament's original text: its unusually abundant manuscript evidence and the tradition's preservation of early variants. Numerous mostly late copies do not establish what missing originals said, and other classical texts are even less certain; religious copyists also had ideological reasons to alter Scripture. The persistence of readings from papyri into later manuscripts is important, but does not by itself prove that every original reading survived.

title: Don’t the MOST Manuscripts Show What An Author Wrote?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the majority reading among manuscripts is not automatically the original reading.
searchSummary: Explains why the reading found in most New Testament manuscripts is not automatically original. More than 94 percent of Greek witnesses are medieval and often form one related textual family, while a small number of substantially earlier manuscripts frequently agree against them. Historical preference for the King James Version encouraged defenses of the majority text, but modern textual scholars generally regard early evidence as more probative than raw manuscript totals or theological claims about preservation.

title: April Gold Q&A Video
author: Diane
description: Shares the April Gold Q&A video.

title: Even If We Can Imagine an “Original” Text, How Could We Know if We Had It?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why having many manuscripts still does not prove recovery of the original New Testament text.
searchSummary: Argues that even a definable original New Testament text may be unrecoverable if all surviving manuscripts descend from an altered first copy. An early copyist could introduce errors, additions, or omissions that every later witness inherited, leaving no comparison capable of exposing them. This uncertainty matters especially to evangelicals who locate divine inspiration in the authors' exact Greek words; without originals or several nearly contemporary copies, confidence remains probable rather than demonstrable.

title: Is There an Original Text Even of One of MY Books??
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the publication process of a modern book to complicate the idea of an original text.
searchSummary: Uses the many drafts and editorial stages of Jesus Before the Gospels to question what counts as a book's original text. An author's outline, first draft, revisions, submitted manuscript, copyedited version, and publication are all distinct forms, while ancient works such as Romans add dictation and secretarial correction to the problem. Ehrman tentatively favors the first circulated form, although it is not literally the earliest form and earlier versions may be inaccessible.

title: May Gold Q&A: Keep Those (Metaphorical) Cards & Letters Coming!
author: Diane
description: Announces the May Gold Q&A and invites member questions.

title: How Can We Even IMAGINE an “Original” Text of the Gospels?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why defining the original text of the Gospels is harder than it first appears.
searchSummary: Explains why the "original" text of a Gospel is difficult to define, using John as the central example. An author might revise drafts, issue later editions, incorporate earlier sources, or dictate to a secretary, leaving several plausible stages that could be called original. Because surviving manuscripts may descend only from a later form, textual critics increasingly reconstruct the "initial text" behind existing copies, even though that recoverable ancestor may differ from the author's earliest or published wording.

title: Two KINDS of Originals.  How Do We Know We Have Either?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains two problems with original texts: recovering New Testament wording and identifying the composite literary form of books such as Isaiah.
searchSummary: Distinguishes confidence about wording from questions about a book's compositional form. Historical knowledge is rarely absolute: manuscript agreement can make many New Testament readings virtually certain, while conflicting witnesses leave others doubtful or unknowable. Biblical books may also combine writings from different periods, as Isaiah's shifts from eighth-century judgment to exilic consolation and postexilic exhortation indicate, so an editor's final compilation differs from the earlier texts that produced it.

title: A High-level Intellectual with an Infuriating “Solution” to Why There is Suffering
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a debate with Richard Swinburne on suffering and the adequacy of theistic explanations.
searchSummary: Introduces a rebroadcast of Ehrman's 2009 radio debate with Oxford philosopher Richard Swinburne about whether the world's suffering is compatible with Christian theism. Ehrman recalls becoming genuinely angry because Swinburne's explanations seemed intellectually remote from the misery being discussed and deficient in empathy for people enduring terrible pain. Moderated by Justin Brierley for Unbelievable, the recording presents sharply contrasting approaches to the problem rather than a written reconstruction of their arguments.

title: Did Paul Favor Gender Equality?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Paul's letters support or resist gender equality in early Christian communities.

title: Women in the World of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Places Jesus' interactions with women against wider ancient views of women and social status.

title: Reminder!  WHY PROPHECY FAILS!  Fundraiser for Sudan With James Tabor
author: BDEhrman
description: Reminds readers about a Sudan fundraiser featuring James Tabor on failed prophecy and apocalyptic expectation.
searchSummary: Reminds readers about a fundraising interview with James Tabor on why biblical prophecy repeatedly produces failed modern predictions. Drawing on Tabor's work with the Branch Davidians and both scholars' study of apocalypticism, the event examines how interpreters use ancient texts to forecast contemporary events. Admission donations support Doctors Without Borders amid the underreported humanitarian catastrophe in Sudan, with reduced or free access available for readers unable to pay and instructions supplied for identifying donations.

title: Jesus and Women
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines traditions about women in Jesus' ministry as possible background for women's prominence in early Christianity.

title: Was Paul a Misogynist?
author: admin
description: Reopens whether Paul's views justify calling Paul a misogynist.

title: Does My Work on the Historical Jesus Confirm the Quran?
author: Diane
description: Responds to claims about Islam, the Gospels' Greek language, and majority critical scholarship.
searchSummary: Answers questions about Islam, the Gospels' original language, and critical scholarship. Ehrman rejects claims that his historical work confirms Islamic teaching, especially because he regards Jesus' crucifixion as certain. He argues that linguistic features and extensive verbatim agreements show the Synoptic Gospels were composed in Greek rather than independently translated from Aramaic, and defines critical scholars as historians whose religious commitments do not determine their conclusions.

title: Fundamentalist Christians Are Not the Only Ones to Make Dumb Arguments…
author: Diane
description: Critiques weak apologetic arguments about the Quran while distinguishing them from serious study of Islam.
searchSummary: Rejects the claim that accurate preservation proves a sacred text's divine origin, truth, or superiority. Careful Jewish and Muslim copying practices can explain stable transmission without a miracle, while the New Testament's numerous variants undermine comparable Christian preservation claims and cannot guarantee that an original reading survives. Even a perfectly unchanged Qur'an would show only faithful reproduction, just as identical printed copies of secular books do not establish that their contents are true.

title: Am I Converting to Islam?
author: admin
description: Uses a false rumor about Bart converting to Islam to explain how oral traditions can change even while eyewitnesses are available.

title: Wanna come to the live recording of the Gold Q&A?  Saturday May 27
author: BDEhrman
description: Invites Gold and Platinum members to watch a live recording of the Gold Q&A.

title: More Hard Issues on the Qur’an Fragments
author: Diane
description: Offers final reflections on early Quran fragments from Birmingham and the limits of discussing material outside one's expertise.
searchSummary: Explains why the Birmingham Quran fragments matter as written evidence for evaluating claims of exact transmission. Ehrman distinguishes religious confidence in continuous oral memorization from what historians can verify, since unrecorded recitations from earlier centuries cannot be compared directly. He does not deny that the Quran may have been preserved accurately; he argues that historians need early manuscripts to test that claim and notes scholarly cautions about the fragments' interpretation.

title: Responses to my Post on the Discovery of an Ancient Manuscript of the Quran
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts responses to reader comments about the Birmingham Quran fragments and their significance.
searchSummary: Examines questions and scholarly cautions raised by the Birmingham Quran fragments. Accurate copying would not establish that the Quran's accounts of Jesus are historically correct, while radiocarbon testing dates the parchment rather than the ink. Ehrman also presents concerns about script, possible parchment reuse, the Sanaa manuscript, and claims announced through the press. He concludes that paleographic, codicological, and imaging studies are needed before the fragment's date and significance become established.

title: An Astounding Quran Manuscript Discovery
author: Diane
description: Reposts a discussion of the Birmingham Quran manuscript discovery and why it drew public attention.
searchSummary: Explains the significance of Quran pages whose parchment was radiocarbon dated to Muhammad's lifetime or shortly afterward. If their wording closely matches later copies, they may show unusually stable transmission and invite comparison with the many variants in Christian manuscripts. Ehrman emphasizes, however, that accurate preservation does not prove a text's historical or religious claims. The fragments are important evidence for textual history, not proof that the Quran or any other well-attested book is true.

title: Fundraiser for Sudan With James Tabor
author: Diane
description: Announces a Sudan fundraiser featuring James Tabor on failed prophecy and David Koresh's apocalyptic worldview.
searchSummary: Announces a fundraising conversation with James Tabor about why modern biblical prophecy repeatedly fails. Tabor's research on Waco and the Branch Davidians supplies a case study for examining how Christian prophets derive confident but mistaken forecasts from ancient texts. Attendance donations go to Doctors Without Borders' humanitarian work in Sudan, with flexible access for those unable to afford the suggested amount and practical instructions for making an identifiable donation and receiving the Zoom link.

title: Major Ways to Compare and Contrast the Quran With the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Outlines a course comparing historical problems in the New Testament and the Quran.
searchSummary: Outlines a comparative course applying historical methods to the New Testament and Quran. Paired lectures examine textual preservation, contradictions and legendary narratives, reconstruction of the historical Jesus and Muhammad, and scriptural connections to intolerance and violence. Each tradition is evaluated beyond apologetic or polemical assumptions, asking what manuscripts, sources, and academic scholarship can establish. The closing discussion considers whether committed Christians and Muslims can investigate their scriptures critically while maintaining religious belief.

title: The Bible and the Quran: Their Historical Problems.  A New Course!!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a course comparing historical, textual, and literary problems in the Bible and the Quran.

title: “Lovemaking” in the Song of Songs – Platinum Post From Dan Kohanski
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum guest study of translation issues in the Song of Songs.
searchSummary: Guest contributor Dan Kohanski argues that dodim in the Song of Songs should be translated lovemaking rather than love. Uses in Proverbs and Ezekiel explicitly concern sexual intercourse, while the Song transforms the term's raw physical sense into mutual erotic affection. Because the lovers meet secretly and appear unmarried, Kohanski concludes that the poem celebrates a sexual love affair and that a more explicit English rendering best communicates its meaning.

title: What’s It Like in Sheol?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines what 1 Samuel 28 suggests about Sheol and the dead in the Hebrew Bible.

title: We Need An Experienced Fundraiser!
author: Diane
description: Seeks a volunteer fundraiser to help expand the blog's charitable work.
searchSummary: Seeks an experienced nonprofit fundraiser to volunteer with the blog. After raising more than $2 million for Urban Ministries of Durham, the regional Food Bank, Durham Literacy Center, CARE, and Doctors Without Borders, the organization wants to develop better methods for increasing its charitable contributions. The brief announcement describes the blog's combined mission of sharing serious scholarship with general readers and helping people in need, then directs qualified supporters to contact the team by email.

title: What About People Who Come Back From the Dead in the Hebrew Bible?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Hebrew Bible stories in which dead people are revived or contacted.

title: More on Sheol: Was it an Actual Place?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Sheol in the Hebrew Bible should not be equated with later ideas of hell.

title: Could Moses be Thutmose, the Overseer of the Borderlands? – Platinum Post from Serene
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum guest proposal identifying Moses with the Egyptian official Thutmose.

title: What Is Sheol in the Hebrew Bible?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Sheol and the Hebrew Bible's varied views of death and afterlife.

title: Other “Unknown” Sayings of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Collects sayings attributed to Jesus outside the surviving canonical Gospels.
searchSummary: Collects sayings attributed to Jesus that survive outside the extant Gospels in Papias, Barnabas, 2 Clement, Justin, the Preaching of Peter, Clement of Alexandria, and Origen. They envision extravagant abundance in the coming kingdom, endurance through suffering, judgment according to conduct, love of enemies, apostolic mission, and additional ethical commands. These “agrapha” preserve otherwise unknown forms of Jesus traditions, though their appearance in later Christian authors does not by itself establish that Jesus actually spoke them.

title: April Gold Q&A: Ask Away!
author: Diane
description: Announces the April Gold Q&A and invites member questions.

title: Did People Have Time for Jesus? – a Platinum Post from Doug Wadeson, MD.
author: Diane
description: Presents Doug Wadeson's argument that Galilean crowds could have had time to hear Jesus.

title: Ever Hear of an Agraphon?  An “Unwritten” Saying of Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces agrapha as sayings attributed to Jesus outside the canonical Gospels.
searchSummary: Defines agrapha as sayings attributed to the historical Jesus that survive outside extant canonical or noncanonical Gospels. Sources include nongospel writings, manuscript variants, and church-father quotations from lost Gospels, while post-resurrection sayings and recognizable Gospel quotations are excluded. Ehrman presents several scribal additions containing otherwise unknown sayings and explains that agrapha illuminate not only potentially authentic teachings but also how Jesus traditions circulated and developed orally and textually in early Christianity.

title: Is the Paul of Acts at Odds with the Paul of His Own Letters?
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Paul's speeches in Acts with his letters, especially their different understandings of Jesus' death and salvation.

title: Is the Message of Paul in Acts the Same as the Message of Paul According to Paul?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the problem of whether Acts accurately represents Paul's preaching.

title: My Favorite Fragment of a Lost Gospel.  Is It the Gospel of Peter??
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether a favorite Oxyrhynchus Gospel fragment may belong to the Gospel of Peter.

title: What We Knew about the Gospel of Peter Before We Had the Gospel of Peter
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Eusebius helped identify the discovered fragment as the Gospel of Peter.

title: An Unusually Large “Fragment” of a Lost Gospel:  The Gospel of Peter
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the surviving fragment of the Gospel of Peter as background for a discussion of lost Gospels.

title: Is That a Portion of a Famous Lost Gospel?
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses a mysterious Gospel harmony fragment and whether it could come from the Diatessaron.
searchSummary: Examines a small Greek Gospel-harmony fragment discovered at Dura Europos that combines details from all four canonical Passion narratives. The fragment may come from Tatian's second-century Diatessaron, a single continuous account used widely in Syriac Christianity before separate Gospel translations replaced it, but the identification remains uncertain because other harmonies also circulated. Reconstructing Tatian's lost work depends largely on later commentaries and translations rather than a surviving copy of the original composition.

title: Was Jesus Opposed to Women and Childbirth?  The Lost Gospel of the Egyptians
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents sayings from the Gospel of the Egyptians about women, childbirth, and death.
searchSummary: Reconstructs the lost Gospel of the Egyptians from six quotations preserved by Clement of Alexandria. In dialogues with Salome, Jesus appears to oppose childbirth, sexual difference, and perhaps procreation itself, ideas Clement allegorically reinterprets while rejecting their literal ascetic implications. The work was probably composed in second-century Egypt, but its form is uncertain, and it should not be confused with the unrelated Coptic Gospel of the Egyptians discovered at Nag Hammadi.

title: A Really Scathing Review of My Book on Suffering
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a sharply critical review of God's Problem and reflects on criticism of the book.
searchSummary: Reprints Will Willimon's sharply critical review of God’s Problem, which portrays Ehrman's treatment of suffering as autobiographical, reductionist, morally self-assured, and unable to appreciate biblical ambiguity or theological complexity. Willimon argues that the book dismisses sophisticated theodicies without engaging them, reduces Job and other texts, and ends with a banal call to alleviate suffering. Ehrman supplies the hostile review without rebuttal, inviting readers to assess an opposing response he now finds more humorous than outrageous.

title: Making the Gospels Say What You WANT Them To Say
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to Robert Barron's critique of How Jesus Became God and the use of the Gospels in Christology.
searchSummary: Rejects Robert Barron's attempt to read Johannine incarnation Christology into the Synoptic Gospels through alleged scriptural symbolism. Fear on the road, entry from the east, and authority to pronounce forgiveness do not establish that Mark's Jesus is the preexistent God; the last instead reflects authority granted by God. Ehrman argues that Mark presents Jesus as a human exalted or adopted into divinity, whereas John presents a divine being who becomes human.

title: Dealing With Reviews of My Books By People Who (Apparently) Haven’t Read Them
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on book reviews that criticize arguments without accurately representing them.
searchSummary: Responds to Robert Barron's review of How Jesus Became God by arguing that it attacks positions the book does not take.
