Ehrman neither labels the disciples' visions hallucinations nor decides whether Jesus truly was resurrected or divine, and his reconstruction bears no resemblance to Hugh Schonfield's Passover Plot. He welcomes serious historical criticism but objects to ridicule and theological reassurance that substitute misrepresentation for engagement with his evidence and stated conclusions.

title: March 2024 Platinum webinar
author: Diane
description: Shares the March 2024 Platinum webinar.

title: Public Lecture at Wake Forest University: April 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Wake Forest lecture on Armageddon and modern effects of end-times belief.

title: Among Paul’s Enemies….
author: BDEhrman
description: Imagines what could be learned from writings by Paul's Christian opponents, especially in Galatia.
searchSummary: Reconstructs the dispute behind Galatians by asking how Paul's Christian opponents might have defended their demand that gentile believers adopt Jewish law. They likely argued that following the Jewish messiah required joining God's covenant people through circumcision, Sabbath, and kosher practice. Paul responded that salvation came through faith in Christ alone, yet the post stresses that only his side survived and that his opponents' lost writings would clarify the conflict.

title: Reminder!  Platinum Webinar This Evening (Tuesday, March 26)!  Did Jesus Really Mean It?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reminds Platinum members about a webinar on the difficult ethics of Jesus in the Gospels.

title: What Did Paul’s Christian Enemies Write About Him?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why letters from Paul's Christian opponents would illuminate conflicts within early Christianity.
searchSummary: Argues that Paul inherited Christianity rather than inventing it and was one voice within a diverse movement. He received traditions about Jesus' saving death and resurrection from earlier believers, while most of his surviving congregational letters reveal Christian opponents advancing rival gospels. Their writings have disappeared, and the later New Testament's heavy emphasis on Paul exaggerates his original centrality. Acts and later church fathers made him Christianity's hero even while muting or misunderstanding distinctive features of his teaching.

title: A Self-Evaluation of My Self-Debate:  Is the Book of Acts Historically Reliable?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reviews the strengths and weaknesses of a classroom self-debate on the historical reliability of Acts.
searchSummary: Distinguishes two questions often blurred in assessing Acts: whether its author followed respectable ancient historiography and whether the narrated events actually occurred as described. An author could meet contemporary literary standards while remaining factually inaccurate, so knowledge of first-century customs or favorable comparison with ancient historians does not establish reliability. Ehrman concludes that arguments about historical context are valuable for understanding how Acts works, but the modern reliability question requires independent evidence about its specific claims.

title: Is the Book of Acts Reliable?  The Affirmative REBUTTAL of the Negative Case
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents the affirmative rebuttal defending the historical reliability of Acts.
searchSummary: Presents the affirmative rebuttal in Ehrman's classroom debate over the historical reliability of Acts. The case argues that Luke should be judged by ancient standards, broadly agrees with Paul's itinerary and preaching, adapts messages to different audiences, and accurately knows first-century places and institutions confirmed by archaeology. Apparent discrepancies are treated as minor details or contextual differences. This is a deliberately constructed debate position rather than Ehrman's stated conclusion, designed to model the strongest defense of Acts.

title: Is the Book of Acts Historically Reliable?  The Negative REBUTTAL of the Affirmative Case
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents the negative rebuttal against arguments for the historical reliability of Acts.
searchSummary: Rebuts arguments that Acts is reliable because its author sought accuracy, used eyewitnesses, and traveled with Paul. Luke's preface never claims personal consultation with witnesses, while the abruptly appearing “we” passages may derive from a source or a literary device rather than autobiography. Most importantly, Acts conflicts with Paul's letters about his movements, companions, preaching, and theology, so even hypothetical eyewitness participation would not establish the narrative's accuracy.

title: The Book of Acts is NOT RELIABLE!  The Negative Case
author: BDEhrman
description: Lays out the negative case that Acts is not historically reliable.
searchSummary: Presents the negative case that Acts is not historically reliable. Ehrman points to internal contradictions in accounts of Jesus' ascension and Paul's conversion, then compares Acts with Paul's letters on travel, Jerusalem contacts, and pagan idolatry. Knowledge of first-century institutions cannot establish that narrated events occurred. Because Acts repeatedly conflicts with itself and with Paul's firsthand testimony, the argument concludes that Luke prioritizes an effective theological story over consistent historical reconstruction, even when some settings and details are accurate.

title: March Gold Q&A Video
author: Diane
description: Shares the March Gold Q&A video.

title: ANOTHER March Platinum Webinar!  Did Jesus Really Mean It?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a replacement Platinum webinar on the difficult ethics of Jesus in the Gospels.

title: Announcing a FREE Course!  “Did Peter Hate Paul?”
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a free course on whether Peter and Paul were in conflict.

title: Arguments for “Historical Accuracy” That Are All Smoke and Mirrors.
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques common arguments for Acts' historical accuracy based on correct names, places, and official titles.
searchSummary: Explains why archaeological confirmation of places, titles, and customs in Acts does not establish the truth of its stories. A writer may accurately know the Areopagus, Thessalonian officials, or a temple at Lystra while inventing events set there, just as a false modern story can use real buildings and people. Such evidence shows that Luke knew the first-century Roman world; it does not verify what allegedly happened. Historical reliability requires testing narratives, not merely confirming their settings.

title: The Book of Acts IS HISTORICAL!  The Affirmative Argument
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents the affirmative case for the historical reliability of Acts in a classroom self-debate.
searchSummary: Presents the strongest affirmative case that Acts is historically reliable without endorsing it. Luke's preface declares an orderly investigation grounded in eyewitness tradition, the “we” passages appear to identify the author as Paul's traveling companion, and Acts sometimes agrees with Paul's letters. Archaeological confirmation of places and titles, including Athenian meeting sites, Thessalonian politarchs, and a temple of Zeus outside Lystra, is offered as evidence that the writer knew the settings and events he described.

title: Who Cares if the Book of Acts is Historical??
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Acts' historical reliability matters for reconstructing early Christianity's first decades.
searchSummary: Explains why Acts' historical reliability matters for reconstructing Christianity's first three decades, since it is the only surviving narrative of that period. Acts selectively follows Peter and Paul while presenting a Spirit-directed, miracle-filled, harmonious movement that advances from Jerusalem to the Gentile world and remains compatible with Judaism. Because these literary and theological themes may shape its portrayal, readers must ask whether the events and unity it describes reflect what actually happened.

title: Important Literary Features of the Book of Acts
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces literary features of Acts that matter before judging its historical reliability.
searchSummary: Examines Acts' deliberate literary parallels, both between Jesus in Luke and the apostles in Acts and between Peter and Paul within Acts. The characters receive the Spirit, preach, heal, face opposition, experience deliverance, and advance the Gentile mission in closely corresponding ways. These patterns display Luke's artistry and support his claim that God continues Jesus' work through the apostles, while also raising questions about how literary and theological design has shaped the historical narrative.

title: What is the Book of Acts About?
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Acts as Luke's account of the disciples and Christianity's spread after Jesus' resurrection.
searchSummary: Introduces Acts as the second volume of Luke's account, beginning with Jesus' resurrection and ascension and following the church's expansion from Jerusalem to Rome. The narrative features Pentecost, the Spirit's power, apostolic miracles, Jewish opposition, Gentile inclusion, Paul's conversion, missionary journeys, trials, and arrival in Rome. Because Acts is the earliest surviving account of Christianity's birth and spread, its literary aims and historical accuracy are central questions for reconstructing the movement's beginnings.

title: Gold Q&A:  Ask Your Questions!
author: jennao
description: Announces the March Gold Q&A and invites member questions.

title: Is There Any Point Doing a Public Debate?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the value and limits of public debates.
searchSummary: Questions whether public debates promote understanding when participants and audiences usually arrive committed to a side. Ehrman describes frustration with complicated but weak arguments that sound authoritative to non-specialists, then explains his classroom exercise of debating both sides of whether Acts is historically accurate. Although he judges the negative case stronger, most students favored the affirmative. The result motivates a series examining both positions, the skill of arguing opposing views, and the uncertain educational value of debate itself.

title: Did Paul Exchange Letters with the Greatest Roman Philosopher of His Day??
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the forged correspondence between Paul and Seneca and its long reception history.
searchSummary: Examines fourteen fourth-century letters forged as correspondence between Paul and the Roman philosopher Seneca. The brief exchanges praise Paul's moral and intellectual stature, claim that Emperor Nero admired his writings, and portray Seneca defending Christians after Rome's fire and condemning Nero's cruelty. Although historically fabricated, the collection answered why elite contemporaries never mentioned Christianity and persuaded later Christians that the era's greatest philosopher knew, respected, and perhaps accepted Paul's message.

title: Paul’s Letter to the … Laodiceans?  Long Thought to be Part of the New Testament!
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the forged Letter to the Laodiceans and why some churches treated it as Pauline Scripture.
searchSummary: Investigates why the otherwise banal forged Letter to the Laodiceans was written and later circulated within many Latin New Testaments. The text strings together phrases from Galatians and especially Philippians, perhaps responding to traditions about a Marcionite Laodicean letter inspired by Colossians 4:16. Ehrman proposes that a proto-orthodox author created a deliberately Pauline-sounding "real" letter whose existence would discredit the rival forgery, explaining both its derivative content and its remarkable canonical success.

title: Platinum Webinar for March:  Ethics Without God??
author: Diane
description: Announces a Platinum webinar on whether ethics require belief in God.

title: Paul’s *THIRD* Letter to the Corinthians?  A Very Interesting Forgery
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Third Corinthians as an orthodox forgery responding to other Pauline forgeries.
searchSummary: Explains Third Corinthians, a second-century orthodox forgery preserved within the Acts of Paul and designed to refute teachings resembling Marcion's. A fabricated Corinthian letter reports denials of the creator, Christ's flesh, the prophets, and bodily resurrection; Paul's invented response affirms each against the heretics. Ironically, the forger equates flesh with the resurrected body, contradicting Paul's own technical use of flesh for sinful human nature while claiming apostolic authority.

title: The Two Gods of Marcion and the Forgeries in the Name of Paul
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Marcion's two-God theology and its connection to Pauline forgeries.
searchSummary: Explains Marcion's two-god theology and its relationship to his distinctive Christian canon. Rejecting the Jewish creator as different from Jesus' loving God, Marcion accepted no Old Testament, used an edited Luke and ten Pauline letters, and removed passages he believed had been corrupted by Judaizing scribes. The Muratorian Canon also reports Marcionite forgeries addressed to Alexandria and Laodicea, now lost, which likely presented his teachings about the gods, Christ's apparent humanity, and salvation even more directly.

title: The Heretic Marcion and Forgeries of Pauline Letters
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces non-canonical Pauline forgeries connected with Marcion and later disputes over Paul.
searchSummary: Introduces non-canonical letters forged in Paul's name by first explaining Marcion, a second-century Christian who regarded Paul as the supreme apostle. Marcion sharply separated Jewish law from Christ's gospel, concluding that the just creator of the Old Testament differed from the loving God who sent Jesus for salvation. His competing Christian system and devotion to Paul created a setting in which supporters and orthodox opponents produced rival Pauline writings to authorize their theological claims.

title: Facts Hidden Among the Legends of the Apostle Paul?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores how scholars separate fact from legend in sources about Paul.
searchSummary: Uses parallel stories about Paul in canonical Acts and later apocryphal writings to expose the difficulty of separating history from legend. Miraculous punishments, resuscitations, persecution escapes, and a talking baptized lion employ similar narrative patterns even when some appear inside the New Testament. Canonical location alone therefore cannot establish factuality. Ehrman argues that sources surrounding Paul mix historical records, legendary development, and combinations of both, requiring critical reconstruction rather than automatic acceptance of one collection and dismissal of another.

title: Our Controversial Sources About the Controversial Paul
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys the sources for Paul's life, including authentic letters, Acts, and later legends.

title: How Much Fact, How Much Fiction? The Life of Peter
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines legendary stories about Peter and the difficulty of separating history from fiction.

title: Archaeology in the Time of Jesus!  New Course March 2-3!!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a course on archaeology in the time of Jesus taught by Jodi Magness.

title: The Disciple Peter in History and Legend
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Peter as a figure known through both historical evidence and later Christian legend.

title: Jesus and Mary Magdalene Seen Kissing??
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines claims about Jesus and Mary Magdalene kissing in the Gospel of Philip and modern popular culture.

title: When Did Mary Magdalene Become a Prostitute?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Mary Magdalene came to be identified as a prostitute despite the New Testament evidence.

title: Was Mary Magdalene a Prostitute?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the New Testament does not portray Mary Magdalene as a prostitute.

title: Some Random Reflections on Our Significance
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on human significance in light of time, space, mortality, and ancient texts.
searchSummary: Reflects on human significance within an unimaginably old and vast universe. A bear encounter and the constellation Ursa Major become metaphors for people's desire to make themselves appear important despite their brief, tiny existence, a tendency that can produce vanity and danger. Ehrman nevertheless argues that lives and actions matter here and now through how people treat and help one another, so mortality should encourage present enjoyment and service rather than despair or endless self-magnification.

title: February Gold Q&A Video
author: Diane
description: Shares the February Gold Q&A video.

title: Changing the Past in Light of the Present
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how oral cultures reshape past events in light of present needs.

title: Still Spots Open:  Blog Dinner in Wichita KS, this Thursday Feb. 22
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces remaining spots for a Wichita blog dinner.

title: Proof That Historical Narratives (not just myths) Constantly Change in Oral Cultures
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses anthropological evidence to show that historical traditions change in oral cultures.
searchSummary: Uses anthropological research on historical narratives to show that oral traditions change at every stage of transmission, not only when conveying myths or poetry. An observer interprets selectively, each later informant adds personal and cultural biases, and only what one teller recalls becomes available to the next. Because every recitation can create a variant, frequently repeated early Christian stories about Jesus were especially exposed to alteration before reaching Gospel writers or their written sources.

title: When is “The Same” Memory/Tradition/Story Not Actually “The Same”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Shows how oral performers can call different versions of a tradition the same despite major variation.
searchSummary: Shows that oral cultures may regard different performances as the same tradition. Milman Parry, Albert Lord, and Jack Goody recorded epic songs and ritual myths whose length, wording, and content varied enormously between performers and even between performances by one person, while communities insisted they were unchanged. These traditions are not exact analogues for Gospel prose, but they warn against assuming oral societies preserve fixed wording. Early Jesus stories could retain a broad gist while undergoing alteration, addition, and omission.

title: How Do We Know About Oral Cultures?  By Starting Where You’d Never Suspect!
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the study of oral cultures through Milman Parry and Albert Lord's work on epic singers.
searchSummary: Explains how Milman Parry and Albert Lord's study of Yugoslav epic singers transformed understanding of oral tradition. Performers did not preserve fixed wording; they recomposed songs for each audience and occasion while regarding versions with the same basic story as identical. Without written records, oral cultures could not compare performances or define an original text as literary cultures do. This research cautions that early Christian storytellers could sincerely transmit the same Jesus tradition while continually altering its language and details.

title: Do People in Oral Cultures Have Better Memories?
author: BDEhrman
description: Questions the assumption that oral cultures preserve traditions more accurately than literate cultures.
searchSummary: Rejects the assumption that people in oral cultures possess biologically stronger memories or preserve traditions unchanged because writing is unavailable. Anthropologists find that they forget as much as literate people, but forgotten material cannot be recovered from a record, and each new version displaces earlier ones. Literacy reduces the need to memorize while enabling comparison and correction. These findings matter for Jesus traditions circulated orally for decades: stories could be altered, expanded, or invented before the Gospels recorded them.

title: Were Matthew and Luke Plagiarists?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Matthew and Luke's use of Mark counts as plagiarism in ancient terms.
searchSummary: Examines whether Matthew and Luke's unacknowledged, often verbatim use of Mark and Q should be called plagiarism. Ancient writers such as Vitruvius, Polybius, and Pliny strongly condemned appropriating another author's work. Yet the charge is complicated because the Synoptic Gospels are anonymous and their authors do not claim borrowed material under their own names. Other anonymous and forged Christian works reveal similarly difficult boundaries among literary borrowing, plagiarism, and pseudonymous authorship.

author: BDEhrman

author: BDEhrman

title: Plagiarism!  Was It Condemned in the Ancient World?  (Is Matthew Guilty of It?)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores ancient views of plagiarism and whether Matthew's use of Mark would have counted as theft.

title: Gospel Thrillers Part III by Andrew Jacobs
author: Diane
description: Presents Andrew Jacobs's discussion of how Gospel thrillers resemble real controversies over discovered Gospels.

title: Gospel Thrillers Part II by Andrew Jacobs
author: Diane
description: Presents Andrew Jacobs's account of the plots and cultural fears inside Gospel thrillers.
searchSummary: Examines modern Gospel thrillers that imagine the discovery or suppression of alternative accounts of Jesus. These novels often combine Middle Eastern settings, Dead Sea Scrolls, secret Gnostic groups, institutional conspiracies, and documents that challenge familiar beliefs about Jesus, gender, Judaism, or Christian origins. Their plots reveal modern cultural anxieties about the Bible's vulnerability and church authority, even when the stories ultimately restore conventional assumptions after temporarily destabilizing the accepted account.

title: January Gold Q&A Video
author: Diane
description: Shares the January Gold Q&A video.

title: Gospel Thrillers Part I by Andrew Jacobs
author: Diane
description: Introduces Andrew Jacobs's study of Gospel thrillers as fiction about conspiracies and vulnerable biblical texts.
searchSummary: Introduces Andrew Jacobs's Gospel Thrillers and explains the fictional genre he traces from The Q Document onward. These novels imagine newly discovered early Christian writings whose contents threaten accepted beliefs and attract political or religious conspiracies. Jacobs argues that such stories reflect American fears and hopes about a Bible made vulnerable by textual discoveries, scholarly revision, translation, and the possibility that suppressed evidence could overturn familiar accounts of Christianity.

title: How Do Scholars Make the Apocalyptic Jesus Non-Apocalyptic?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains strategies scholars use to argue against an apocalyptic interpretation of Jesus.
searchSummary: Evaluates two scholarly strategies for reconstructing a non-apocalyptic Jesus despite the apocalyptic portrait in the earliest surviving sources. One posits a hypothetical original edition of Q without later end-time additions; another dates fragmentary or later-attested noncanonical Gospels earlier than Mark, Q, M, and L. Bart regards both as speculative special pleading and emphasizes the clearer chronological pattern: early sources consistently preserve apocalyptic teaching, while later sources mute, replace, or reject it after the end did not occur.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: A Less-Expected Argument that Jesus Preached the End of All Things
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that John the Baptist and early Christian apocalyptic expectation support an apocalyptic Jesus.
searchSummary: Presents a continuity argument that Jesus must have been an apocalypticist because both the beginning and aftermath of his ministry were apocalyptic. Jesus voluntarily joined John the Baptist, who proclaimed imminent judgment, and the earliest communities formed after Jesus's death expected his return as cosmic judge at the end of the age. Since Jesus's ministry connects these two well-attested movements, Bart concludes that its central orientation must also have anticipated God's imminent intervention and kingdom.

title: How the Gospels Transformed the Apocalyptic Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how later Gospel traditions increasingly softened or transformed Jesus' apocalyptic message.
searchSummary: Traces how later Gospel writers softened or replaced Jesus's predictions of an imminent apocalyptic kingdom. Luke edits Mark so that Jesus no longer promises the kingdom's powerful arrival within his hearers' lifetimes, John offers eternal life in the present through faith, and Thomas rejects a future earthly kingdom altogether. Bart argues that this chronological movement away from end-time expectation is evidence that the earlier, strongly apocalyptic traditions more accurately preserve Jesus's message before Christians adapted it to the kingdom's delay.

title: The Jesus Seminar and the Non-Apocalyptic Jesus. Hey, Why Not?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Jesus Seminar and its non-apocalyptic portrait of Jesus.
searchSummary: Introduces the Jesus Seminar and explains Bart's agreement with its critical methods but disagreement with its non-apocalyptic reconstruction of Jesus. The earliest independent sources, including Mark, Q, M, and L, repeatedly attribute imminent judgment, the Son of Man's arrival, and an earthly kingdom to Jesus, whereas John and Thomas do not. Bart argues that this chronological pattern favors an apocalyptic historical Jesus whose message was gradually muted as the predicted end failed to occur.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: Blog Dinner, Waynesville NC, Feb 7.  Anyone Interested?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Waynesville blog dinner for members.

title: In Support of Religious Studies at a Major University
author: BDEhrman
description: Defends the value of Religious Studies as a university discipline.
searchSummary: Argues that religious studies is indispensable to universities because religion profoundly shapes international conflict, domestic policy, social debates, and cultural life. Understanding those forces requires nonsectarian expertise across traditions and methods rather than assumptions drawn from media or confessional training. Defending UNC Greensboro's threatened department, Ehrman emphasizes the field's interdisciplinary reach and contends that informed voters, leaders, and communities need university-based study of religion to navigate antisemitism, Islamophobia, political disputes, and conflicts rooted in competing religious commitments.

title: How to Sugarcoat Scripture but Seem Sophisticated.  Final Guest Post by Jill Hicks-Keeton
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Jill Hicks-Keeton's critique of sophisticated efforts to make troubling biblical passages appear benign.

title: We Need a Blog Volunteer!  Do You Have Experience With Non-profit Taxes?
author: Diane
description: Seeks a volunteer with nonprofit tax experience for the blog.

title: How To Make the New Testament Non-Patriarchal.  Good Luck with *That* One.  Guest post by Jill Hicks-Keeton
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Jill Hicks-Keeton's critique of attempts to make Paul's writings appear non-patriarchal.

title: Making the Bible Benevolent: Guest Post by Jill Hicks-Keeton
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Jill Hicks-Keeton's argument that evangelical readers often make difficult biblical texts appear benevolent.

title: Atonement Doctrine – A Platinum Post by Manuel Fiadeiro
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum member reflection on atonement doctrine and models of salvation.

title: Paul, the Apostate: a Platinum Post by Manuel Fiadeiro
author: admin
description: Presents a Platinum member's controversial claims about Paul, apostasy, and Christian separation from Judaism.

title: How’s the Christian World Doin’ These Days with the Ethics of Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Sketches a book project on Jesus' ethics, altruism, charity, and forgiveness.
searchSummary: Assesses how modern Christians measure against Jesus' teachings on love, charity, and forgiveness. Racism, hostility toward outsiders, prosperity preaching, revenge, and selective moral politics contradict those teachings, yet hospitals, shelters, food banks, disaster relief, and personal sacrifice also reflect their enduring influence. Ehrman, though no longer Christian, praises people who care for the needy, strangers, foreigners, and marginalized groups, arguing that faithfully practicing these ethics can improve society and transform Christians and non-Christians alike.

title: When Is Forgiveness not Forgiveness?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a discussion of forgiveness in Greek, Roman, and early Christian ethical thought.
searchSummary: Greek and Roman practices usually granted forgiveness when an offender offered an excuse, repayment, or some other satisfaction. Jesus instead required repentance but did not demand a penalty, making restored relationship the central point. Later Christians increasingly explained reconciliation through atonement and penance, developments that Ehrman distinguishes from forgiveness in its strict sense because they require a debt to be paid.

title: Thoughts on Cosmology, a Platinum Post From Charles Hawkins
author: admin
description: Presents a Platinum guest reflection on ancient and modern cosmology in relation to biblical texts.
searchSummary: Contrasts the Bible's ancient three-story cosmos with successive scientific models from Copernicus and Newton to modern astronomy and billions of galaxies. Biblical expectations that heavenly beings descend through clouds made sense when God was located above a firmament, but no longer fit contemporary knowledge of the universe. Charles Hawkins concludes that literal Second Coming and rapture scenarios preserve an obsolete cosmology and cannot readily be reconciled with modern evidence about Earth's place in space.

title: Love in Action: Christian Views of Charitable Giving
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how early Christian love took practical form in charitable giving.

title: Is Christian Love Different from Love?
author: BDEhrman
description: Clarifies Christian love as agape and distinguishes it from common modern readings of 1 Corinthians 13.

title: Reminder:  My Course on the Gospel of Matthew.  This Weekend!
author: BDEhrman
description: Reminds readers about an online course on the Gospel of Matthew.

title: The Fate of Jesus’ Ethics after His Death
author: BDEhrman
description: Sketches how Jesus' apocalyptic ethics were carried forward and modified after Jesus' death.
searchSummary: Explains how Jesus' followers preserved but modified his radical apocalyptic ethics as the expected end failed to arrive. One-time abandonment of possessions became sustainable generosity, and aid increasingly focused on fellow Christians as a new family, while love, charity, and forgiveness adapted to Greco-Roman social realities. As Christianity spread, these revised principles expanded concern for suffering strangers and helped shape Western conscience, private charity, and public policy beyond the narrower patterns of ancient beneficence and kinship.

title: The Origins of Altruism: My Next Book as It Stands Now
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the evolving focus of a book project on altruism, love, forgiveness, and Christian ethics.

title: I’m Going to the Greek Islands.  Interested in Joining Me?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Greek Islands lecture trip.

title: Our Commitment to Charity
author: BDEhrman
description: Connects the blog's charitable mission with Jesus' teachings and the Christian history of charity.
searchSummary: Reaffirms that the blog began primarily to raise money for charity while making scholarship accessible to nonspecialists. Bart connects that mission with Jesus's influence on Western commitments to helping strangers, explains that all membership fees and donations go to charity without overhead deductions, and reports lifetime giving above $2 million. He profiles Doctors Without Borders, CARE, Urban Ministries of Durham, the regional Food Bank, and Durham Literacy Center and explains how donors may designate contributions.

title: How Jesus “Fills” Scripture “Full” in Matthew
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Matthew's second mode of fulfillment, where events in Scripture foreshadow Jesus.
searchSummary: Explains Matthew's typological sense of fulfillment, in which earlier biblical events acquire their fullest meaning in Jesus rather than merely predict him. Israel's exodus, passage through water, wilderness testing, and reception of law reappear in Jesus' escape from a tyrant, return from Egypt, baptism, forty-day temptation, and Sermon on the Mount. Matthew thereby presents Jesus as a new Moses who completes rather than abolishes the earlier Law, authoritatively interpreting it for followers who must continue to observe it.

title: What Does It Actually Mean to “Fulfill” Scripture?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains different meanings of fulfill in Matthew's use of Scripture.
searchSummary: Examines Matthew's fulfillment citations and the sometimes literalistic interpretations behind them. Most present Jesus as fulfilling prophetic predictions, but the claim that he would be called a Nazorean may depend on Hebrew wordplay connecting Nazareth with Isaiah's “branch.” Matthew likewise misreads poetic parallelism as two animals and has Jesus enter Jerusalem on both a donkey and its colt. Such readings reflect ancient interpretive practices and do not by themselves prove that Matthew was a gentile.

title: Is Matthew Duplicitous in His Reading of Scripture?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Matthew's scriptural interpretation is deceptive or consistent with ancient Jewish interpretive practices.
searchSummary: Defends Matthew's use of Hosea's exodus verse for Jesus as an ancient interpretive practice rather than simple duplicity. Jewish and Christian readers often sought allegorical, numerical, prophetic, or hidden meanings beyond an author's historical reference. The Dead Sea Scrolls' pesher commentaries similarly apply Habakkuk's ancient words to Romans, Jerusalem factions, and the Qumran community centuries later. Matthew reads Scripture through a comparable assumption that God embedded meanings about Jesus unknown to the original prophets.

title: Putting Final Polish on a Bible Translation.  Ouch.
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the difficulty of checking consistency across a major Bible translation.
searchSummary: Describes Ehrman's painstaking work checking the completed NRSV for consistency across biblical books and translation subcommittees. He compared repeated Hebrew and Greek terms, reviewed every passage for adherence to inclusive-language policies, and identified inconsistent stylistic choices using primitive 1980s computer tools. The work also required enforcing fine grammatical rules, including the committee's distinction between restrictive that and nonrestrictive which, before the translation could be finalized.

title: My (Backstage) Work for the New Revised Standard Version Translation
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts backstage research work for the NRSV translation committee.
searchSummary: Recounts Ehrman's transition from poorly paid adjunct work to a full-time research position supporting the NRSV's final editorial committee. Because separate subcommittees had revised different biblical books with varying methods, vocabulary, style, and inclusive-language practices, a three-person group reviewed the entire translation for consistency. Ehrman served as its research assistant while the group standardized uneven passages and sometimes reversed decisions that translators had debated for years.

title: How Do We Fit in the Universe?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on Psalm 8 and humanity's place in the universe.
searchSummary: Uses Psalm 8 to contrast an ancient biblical universe with modern knowledge of trillions of galaxies. The psalmist already wondered why God would attend to small human beings beneath a comparatively simple heaven, while today's scale magnifies that question beyond comprehension. Ehrman observes that believers may respond with gratitude for divine concern and unbelievers with disbelief that humanity occupies God's attention, yet both perspectives can share awe before the universe's staggering magnitude.

title: How to Botch a Bible Translation (because of inclusive language)
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques an inclusive-language decision in the NRSV that affects the meaning of a New Testament quotation.
searchSummary: Identifies a serious consequence of applying inclusive language mechanically in the NRSV. Rendering Psalm 8 with plural references to humanity works in its original context, but Hebrews quotes the Psalm specifically about the singular Christ who was temporarily lower than angels and then exalted. By retaining plural, inclusive wording in Hebrews, the translation obscures the author's Christological argument even though its policy is appropriate in the Psalm itself.

title: A Sensible Approach to Inclusive Language in Bible Translation?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the NRSV committee's policy for inclusive language in Bible translation.
searchSummary: Explains the NRSV committee's three-part inclusive-language policy: general human references became inclusive, explicitly gendered passages remained gendered, and masculine language for God was retained. Ehrman illustrates difficult judgments involving legal codes, addresses to male audiences, and generic words for humanity. He supports the policy's accuracy while showing how phrases such as fishers of men resist translations that are simultaneously inclusive, precise, familiar, and elegant.

title: Should Bible Translations Be Gender-Neutral?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the problem of gender-neutral language in modern Bible translation.
searchSummary: Examines why gender-inclusive Bible translation is both ethically important and linguistically difficult. Ehrman argues that masculine-default language reflects and reinforces male social dominance, yet translators must preserve literary quality and the Bible's genuinely patriarchal assumptions rather than modernize them away. Generic masculine nouns, singular pronouns, references to God, and passages addressed specifically to men create competing demands of accuracy, inclusivity, grammar, tradition, and readability.

title: 2023 In Review
author: Diane
description: Reviews the blog's 2023 activity, charitable giving, and plans for the future.

title: Problems with Translating a Single Greek WORD
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses one Greek word to show how difficult and consequential Bible translation decisions can be.
searchSummary: Explains why even a single Greek word may lack an exact English equivalent. Words for love and slavery carry nuances and cultural associations that do not map neatly across languages, forcing translators to choose between literal consistency and idiomatic clarity. Ehrman describes the NRSV committee's varied translation philosophies and endorses its governing principle of being as literal as possible and as free as necessary.

title: December Gold Q&A Video
author: Diane
description: Shares the December Gold Q&A video.

title: How Do You Translate the Bible? My Work for the New Revised Standard Version Committee
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces work with the NRSV committee and broader issues in Bible translation.
searchSummary: Introduces the NRSV revision process and Ehrman's early role as a graduate-student scribe for its Old Testament subcommittees. New manuscript discoveries, changes in English, inclusive-language concerns, and advances in scholarship required revising the RSV word by word through committee votes. Ehrman also explains how rare Hebrew vocabulary made expertise in related Semitic languages essential for inferring meanings that the limited surviving Hebrew corpus cannot establish by itself.

title: Nazareth in the Time of Jesus: the Archaeological Record
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes archaeological evidence that Nazareth existed in Jesus' time.

title: A Blog Challenge Grant, A Worthy Cause for Your End-of-the-Year Giving
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a matching challenge grant for end-of-year blog donations.

title: The Gift of Christmas (2023)
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on Christmas gift-giving and the story's emphasis on giving to others.

title: The Myth That Nazareth Was a Myth
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques mythicist arguments that Nazareth did not exist in Jesus' day.
searchSummary: Rejects mythicist attempts to explain Nazareth as an invented hometown for an invented Jesus. G. A. Wells offers no evidence that Mark confused “Nazarene” with a Jewish sect, while multiple independent Gospel traditions associate Jesus with Nazareth. René Salm infers nonexistence from later expensive tombs and an unexcavated proposed village site, but those facts cannot establish that an earlier poor settlement was absent. Ehrman concludes that archaeology and historical reasoning support Nazareth's existence in Jesus' lifetime.

title: Did Nazareth Even Exist?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the mythicist claim that Nazareth was invented and explains why the issue matters.
searchSummary: Introduces and critiques the mythicist claim that Nazareth did not exist when Jesus lived. Ehrman first notes that even a nonexistent hometown would not prove Jesus himself was invented, then examines Frank Zindler's theory that Christians derived Nazareth from a Hebrew term meaning “branch.” Mark explicitly locates Jesus there, every manuscript preserves the verse, multiple independent sources connect Jesus with the village, and Zindler supplies neither textual evidence nor a plausible historical mechanism for the alleged invention.

title: Interpreting a Text to Make It Seem Orthodox: Luke and Its View of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how interpreting Luke alongside other texts could make its Christology appear more orthodox.

title: Hark, the Herald Angels What Now?  Guest Post by Esther J. Hamori
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Esther Hamori's discussion of Gabriel and troubling angelic figures in biblical tradition.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: Biblical Monsters and Their Violent God!  Guest Post by Esther Hamori
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Esther Hamori's book on biblical monsters, violent divine beings, and difficult portraits of God.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: How Did Early Christians Make Unorthodox Texts Seem Orthodox?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how canon placement could make a potentially unorthodox text seem orthodox.
searchSummary: Shows how proto-orthodox Christians could make potentially unorthodox texts support orthodox Christology. Placing four Gospels in one canon encouraged readers to combine Mark's baptism, Luke's birth, and John's preexistence into a doctrine found fully in none alone. Apocryphal narratives such as the Protevangelium of James further guided interpretation by portraying Jesus' birth as miraculous and the infant as divine, countering adoptionist readings that understood him as a human later chosen by God.

title: December 2023 Platinum webinar
author: Diane
description: Shares the December 2023 Platinum webinar.

title: Why Would an Editor ADD the Virgin Birth to Luke?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores why an editor might add the virgin birth to Luke to reinforce orthodox Christology.
searchSummary: Explores how Luke's text could have been expanded and altered to discourage an adoptionist reading of Jesus. Adding the infancy narrative would make Jesus God's son from conception rather than baptism, while scribes changed the baptismal declaration from today I have begotten you to the wording familiar from Mark. Related changes at the transfiguration and elsewhere show how textual transmission could make Luke more compatible with developing orthodox Christology.

title: No Virgin Birth? Was Jesus ADOPTED by God to be His Son?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Luke originally portrayed Jesus as adopted as God's son at baptism.
searchSummary: Argues that an early form of Luke may have lacked the infancy narrative and portrayed Jesus as appointed God's Son at baptism. Marcion may have inherited rather than removed a version without chapters 1-2, while early Christian quotations support the baptismal wording today I have begotten you. Luke's transfiguration, genealogy, Acts, and Nazareth sermon reinforce an adoptionist reading in which the Spirit empowers a previously human Jesus for his ministry.

title: Did Luke’s Gospel Originally Contain a Virgin Birth?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Luke originally contained the birth narratives and virgin birth.
searchSummary: Introduces a historical investigation of whether Luke's earliest form supported an adoptionist understanding of Jesus. The post argues that scholars must consider noncanonical texts, manuscript variants, and earlier editions rather than only the final canonical text. It outlines evidence that Luke's infancy narrative may be a secondary addition, including the apparent beginning at Luke 3, the later chapters' silence about Jesus' birth, the genealogy's placement, and summaries in Acts.

title: When Modern Christians Came to Think “The End is Near”
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how modern Christian expectations about Israel and the end times developed.

title: American Support of Israel: A (Widely) Unknown Part of the History
author: BDEhrman
description: Traces apocalyptic roots of some modern Christian support for the modern state of Israel.

title: Bart’s Going Viral–And You Can Help!
author: Diane

title: Are You Willing To Donate Blog Memberships to Those Who Can’t Afford It?
author: admin
description: Invites donations to fund blog memberships for readers unable to afford them.
searchSummary: Invites readers to fund annual blog memberships for people who want access but cannot afford the fee. Donors contribute in roughly $30 increments, notify the team by email, and make a tax-deductible payment through the blog; memberships are then offered through public and social-media announcements as quickly as funds arrive. Bart describes the program as a recurring holiday tradition that expands access to scholarship while continuing the community's broader support for the blog and its charities.

title: Jesus in Illuminated Manuscripts and Legends: Video Post
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a Getty Museum lecture on Jesus legends in medieval Gospel illumination.
searchSummary: Presents Ehrman's Getty Museum lecture on medieval illuminated Gospel manuscripts and the legends represented in their artwork. He argues that these manuscripts matter not only for preserving texts but also because their images tell stories, including episodes absent from the canonical Gospels. Medieval artists drew on noncanonical traditions about Jesus and sometimes treated those apocryphal accounts as Gospel truth comparable to Scripture, making visual evidence important for understanding how medieval Christians received both canonical and extrabiblical narratives.

title: So: Did Anyone Think of Jesus as a Miracle-Worker Before His Crucifixion?
author: BDEhrman
description: Weighs whether Jesus was seen as a miracle worker during Jesus' own lifetime or only later.
searchSummary: Considers whether stories of Jesus as a miracle worker circulated during his lifetime or arose after followers believed he had been raised and exalted. Early Christians interpreted healings, exorcisms, nature miracles, and raisings as tangible signs that God's kingdom would soon defeat disease, demons, chaos, and death. Although the evidence cannot settle the question, Bart inclines toward seeing many miracle traditions as later memories created to validate Jesus's apocalyptic proclamation and divine authority.

title: Platinum Webinar for December:  “O Little Town of Nazareth?  Where Was Jesus Actually Born?”
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Platinum webinar on whether Jesus was born in Nazareth rather than Bethlehem.

title: What’s the *Point* of Jesus’ Miracles?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how miracle stories about Jesus make theological claims about identity and divine power.
searchSummary: Explains how Gospel miracle stories validate changing claims about Jesus and God's kingdom rather than serving as neutral reports. John uses signs to prove Jesus's identity, Luke presents the kingdom as already present in his ministry, and earlier Synoptic traditions treat healings and exorcisms as previews of its imminent arrival. Bart concludes that the earliest interpretation integrates Jesus's powerful deeds with his apocalyptic message: the miracles demonstrate in advance what God's coming rule will accomplish.

title: Volunteer Needed!!  Interested in Recording Audio Versions of the Blog Posts?
author: Diane
description: Seeks a volunteer to record audio versions of blog posts.

title: Was Jesus Considered a Miracle Worker During His *Lifetime*?

title: Gold Q&A!!  Ask Your Questions!
author: BDEhrman

title: Were Jesus’ Miracles in the Original Texts of the Gospels?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to whether miracle stories appear in the earliest surviving Gospel manuscripts.
searchSummary: Argues that miracle stories belonged to the Gospels before the earliest surviving substantial manuscripts around 200 CE. Independent Greek witnesses, second-century translations, later manuscript lines, and quotations by geographically separated church fathers contain the same accounts, leaving no trace of an earlier non-miraculous Gospel form. This textual conclusion does not establish that Jesus performed miracles; it establishes that Luke and the other evangelists originally reported them.

title: I’m Lecturing on a Cruise this Summer.  Interested in coming?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a summer lecture cruise from Amsterdam to Lisbon.

title: The Miracles of the Emperor Vespasian. A Platinum Post by Ryan Fleming
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum guest post comparing Vespasian's miracle stories with Gospel miracle traditions.

title: Is There Any Sarcasm in the New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how sarcasm can be identified in New Testament writings despite the limits of ancient texts.
searchSummary: Identifies likely sarcasm in Jesus and Paul despite the absence of vocal tone and facial cues in written texts. Jesus' image of criticizing a speck while carrying a log mocks hypocritical judgment; Paul ridicules Corinthians who imagine themselves already reigning and tells circumcision advocates in Galatia to castrate themselves. Context is decisive, because literal readings would reverse Paul's broader arguments about present suffering, future glorification, and Gentile freedom from Jewish law.

title: Was Joseph the Actual Father of Jesus?  Announcing a Special Online Christmas Course
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Christmas course arguing that some New Testament sources may imply Joseph was Jesus' actual father.
searchSummary: Introduces a two-lecture course arguing that several New Testament sources assume or imply that Joseph was Jesus' biological father rather than affirming a virgin birth. Ehrman points to Paul, Mark, John, passages within Matthew and Luke, Jesus' genealogies, later scribal changes, and subsequent Jewish and pagan traditions. The course considers why the virgin birth appears explicitly in only two New Testament passages and how belief in it nevertheless became central to Christian thought.

title: Do You Want to Take the Final Exam for My Course: “Birth of Christianity”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the final exam questions for a course on Christianity from the post-New Testament period to Constantine.
searchSummary: Presents the final-exam format and possible essay questions for Ehrman's undergraduate course on Christianity from the post-New Testament period through Constantine. Students must identify important people, texts, and concepts, then construct evidence-based essays with clear theses. The questions assess pagan and Christian religions, anti-Judaism, persecution, conversion, Constantine, noncanonical texts, women, competing Christian groups, Christology, the Trinity, and formation of the New Testament canon.

title: An Intriguing and Unusual Demonstration of Early Christian Differences…
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Destro and Pesce's work on Jesus traditions, oral transmission, and Gospel writing.
searchSummary: Presents Adriana Destro and Mauro Pesce's theory that Gospel geography preserves evidence of Christian diversity from the movement's beginnings. Mark, Matthew's special material, Luke's special material, and John emphasize different regions for Jesus' activity and resurrection appearances. Followers remaining in those locations could have preserved and developed distinct memories and interpretations before their traditions entered the Gospels. The model suggests scattered Palestinian groups, not one unified Jerusalem church, formed differing understandings of Jesus immediately after his death.

title: How Paul’s Own Writings Show the Earliest Church Was Split Over “Orthodoxy” and “Heresy”
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Paul's letters to show that divisions later called orthodoxy and heresy already appear in early Christianity.

title: How the Canon Itself Tames the Diversity of the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how placing diverse writings in one canon can make them appear more unified than they are.
searchSummary: Argues that binding diverse New Testament writings into one canon encourages readers to assume theological unity and overlook real disagreements. Paul and James differ over faith and works, while Matthew and Paul differ over Jewish law; Luther recognized such tensions and placed four disputed books at the end of his translation. Because Christians often regard all twenty-seven books as the consistent speech of one divine author, canonical context smooths differences and masks the wider diversity of earliest Christianity.

title: But Your Own Teacher Bruce Metzger Didn’t Think That!
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to objections based on differences between Bart Ehrman's views and Bruce Metzger's Christian commitments.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman's disagreements with his mentor Bruce Metzger do not imply defective scholarship or disrespect. Appeals to a teacher's authority cannot resolve historical or theological problems, and Metzger welcomed independent judgment despite their close relationship. Metzger believed scholars could recover about 99 percent of the New Testament text, whereas Ehrman sees that confidence as partly faith-based because substantial witnesses appear long after the originals and cannot reveal changes made during the earliest copying period.

title: Wasn’t Early Christianity Basically Unified?  Why Fret About Occasional Diversity?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether early Christianity was unified despite evidence of regional and theological diversity.
searchSummary: Defends Walter Bauer's broad claim that early Christianity comprised many competing forms rather than one dominant orthodoxy with marginal heresies. Newly found biblical manuscripts cannot identify their users because proto-orthodox, Marcionite, and Gnostic Christians shared many eventual New Testament books. By contrast, newly recovered noncanonical works are overwhelmingly associated with views later condemned, including the Nag Hammadi texts and the Gospels of Mary and Judas. Their Egyptian preservation does not confine their origins or circulation to Egypt.

title: The Revolutionary Understanding of Orthodoxy and Heresy: An Evaluation of Bauer’s Views
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates Walter Bauer's challenge to the traditional account of orthodoxy and heresy.

title: Does God Have Chromosomes? Platinum Post by Douglas Wadeson, MD
author: Diane
description: Presents a physician's questions about the biology implied by the virgin birth.
searchSummary: Uses modern genetics to probe the doctrine that Jesus was conceived without a human father yet remained fully human and fully divine. A human body requires paired chromosomes, raising the question of where Jesus' paternal genetic material originated and whether created DNA would make God a biological father or a creator. The guest author compares possible answers with Arian, adoptionist, and docetic Christologies, arguing that contemporary theology must address biological knowledge absent from ancient birth narratives.

title: What’s the Best Way to Read a Non-Fiction Book?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains a practical approach to reading nonfiction for research and scholarly work.
searchSummary: Explains that the best way to read nonfiction depends on the reader's knowledge, purpose, and need for detail. Ehrman reads unfamiliar or especially important books completely, highlights them, and takes extensive notes, but skims introductions, conclusions, and selected chapters when he already knows the evidence or needs only a specific argument. Reviews, research assistants, and targeted chapter reading can identify relevance, allowing scholars to spend close attention where a book contributes genuinely new information.

author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a course on scribal changes and why readers may never know the original text at every point.
searchSummary: Announces a course on how and why scribes changed New Testament texts and why the authors' wording can remain uncertain. The course addresses interpretively important variants, the difficulty of defining and recovering an original text, scribal motivations, and the methods scholars use to choose among readings. It also promises close examination of previously undiscussed cases whose evidence makes confident decisions especially difficult, extending themes associated with Misquoting Jesus.

author: BDEhrman

author: BDEhrman

title: Aren’t You Inconsistent in Your View of the Historicity of the Gospels?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to the charge that using contradictions differently in Nag Hammadi and Gospel accounts is inconsistent.
searchSummary: Clarifies that contradictions establish limits on details without automatically disproving an event's basic gist. When two accounts conflict, at least one is wrong at that point, but one account or a shared core may still be historical. Deciding whether Jesus had a last meal, an empty tomb was discovered, or the Nag Hammadi books were found in a jar requires additional evidence about plausibility and context. Contradictions raise questions; they do not by themselves demonstrate total fabrication.

author: BDEhrman

searchSummary: Reminds readers about Joseph Lam's public lecture on creation accounts elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible and their relationship to creation traditions from the ancient world. The event also supports graduate students in religious studies by raising funds for dissertation research travel and conference participation. The post explains why those activities matter for academic training and future teaching careers while providing registration, donation, and video information for the lecture.

title: Our Most Important Discovery of Ancient Christian Writings:  The Nag Hammadi Library
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Nag Hammadi Library as the most important discovery of ancient Christian writings.

title: Another Mythicist View of Jesus’ Brothers
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to mythicist attempts to explain away references to Jesus' brother James.
searchSummary: Rejects Robert Price's proposal that James was called Jesus' brother only because he spiritually resembled or understood a heavenly Christ. The apocryphal traditions Price cites portray James and Thomas as actual relatives, with the Acts of Thomas making Thomas Jesus' physical identical twin despite their disagreement. A nineteenth-century Chinese leader's symbolic claim to be Jesus' younger brother cannot explain first-century Palestinian usage. Ehrman concludes that these comparisons reinforce rather than dissolve the evidence that Paul knew Jesus' biological brother.

title: New Policy on Platinum Guest Posts
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a new policy limiting Platinum guest post submissions.

title: What the Jesus “Mythicists” Say About the Brothers of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how mythicists deal with Paul's reference to James as the Lord's brother.
searchSummary: Argues that Paul's acquaintance with James, “the brother of the Lord,” provides strong evidence that Jesus existed. Paul distinguishes Jesus' brothers from other believers and from Cephas, while Greek has a separate word for cousin; independent sources also identify James as Jesus' sibling. Mythicist proposals for an otherwise unattested Jerusalem missionary group called “brothers of the Lord” lack supporting evidence and fail to explain why James, but not fellow leader and missionary Cephas, receives the designation.

title: Were Jesus’ Brothers His … Brothers?  The Proto-Gospel of James
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how the Proto-Gospel of James reimagines Jesus' brothers and Mary's family.

title: Misquoting Jesus Podcast: Special One-Year Anniversary Edition
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a live Q&A for the first anniversary of the Misquoting Jesus podcast.
searchSummary: Announces the first anniversary edition of Ehrman's weekly Misquoting Jesus podcast, normally structured as co-host Megan Lewis interviewing him about topics also discussed on the blog. For the anniversary, the program changes to a live question-and-answer format using questions submitted and then asked by listeners, with Lewis serving as moderator. The post explains how to watch live or later on YouTube and podcast services while highlighting Lewis's expertise in ancient history, Assyriology, and classics.

title: When a Gospel Meets the Twilight Zone: As Time Stands Still in the Proto-Gospel of James
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines the Proto-Gospel of James scene where time stops at Jesus' birth.

title: The Gospel Before the Gospel: The Proto-Gospel of James
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Proto-Gospel of James and its focus on Mary's origins and status.

title: But If It Didn’t Really Happen, Who Cares?
author: BDEhrman
description: Clarifies that interpreting Mark's leper story is a literary question, not just a reconstruction of what happened.
searchSummary: Distinguishes literary interpretation of Mark's leper story from historical investigation of what Jesus actually did. A story can communicate meaning even when the narrated event did not occur, just as literature about fictional or historical figures remains worth studying. Mark's portrayal of Jesus therefore deserves analysis on its own terms, while historians may separately use Gospel sources critically to reconstruct Jesus' life. These different questions require different methods applied to the same text.

title: Is Christ *Merely* the “Adopted” Son of God?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why adoptionist Christology could still be a high view of Jesus' divine status.
searchSummary: Argues that adoption as God's son represented an extraordinarily high status in the Roman world, not an inferior or merely symbolic relationship. Elite adoptees such as Augustus inherited their father's property, standing, authority, and power precisely because they were deliberately chosen as worthy successors. Early Christians who said God adopted Jesus at his resurrection therefore claimed that Jesus inherited divine privileges, could defeat death, forgive sins, judge the world, and rule with God's authority.

title: If Luke Didn’t Originally Have a Birth Story — Then What?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores the implications if Luke originally began with John the Baptist and Jesus' baptism.
searchSummary: Explores how Luke could be read if its first edition lacked the infancy narrative and began with John the Baptist and Jesus' baptism. Marcion may have inherited such a version rather than excising its opening chapters. The early baptismal reading today I have begotten you would then support an adoptionist interpretation in which God selected and empowered Jesus as his Son, although the post stops short of claiming that Luke himself was an adoptionist.

title: Did Luke Originally Have the Birth Narrative (chapters 1-2)?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Luke's birth narrative may have been added after an earlier edition of the Gospel.
searchSummary: Argues that Luke's birth narrative may have been added in a second edition of the Gospel. The genealogy fits more naturally after Jesus' baptism if the work originally moved from its preface directly to chapter 3. Other evidence includes chapter 3's formal opening, the later narrative's silence about the infancy traditions, and summaries in Acts that begin Jesus' story with John the Baptist rather than his birth.

title: Early Gospels in Circulation: An Even Messier Scenario
author: BDEhrman
description: Proposes a messier model of early Gospel circulation with multiple written and oral sources.
searchSummary: Proposes that early Gospel transmission was far more fluid than a fixed set of four canonical books. Authors and copyists may have revised multiple written accounts using oral traditions and now-lost sources, while Matthew, Luke, and later Gospels could have known versions unlike those preserved today. Similar stories therefore do not automatically prove direct literary dependence on an extant Gospel, complicating the Synoptic Problem and source claims about John or Papyrus Egerton 2.

title: Reading the Bible in a Secular Age: Guest Post by Prof. Julius-Kei Kato
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Julius-Kei Kato's book on reading the New Testament as spiritual ancestry in a secular age.
searchSummary: Julius-Kei Kato introduces Reading the Bible in a Secular Age, which treats the New Testament as a textual village inhabited by the West's spiritual ancestors. He outlines a hermeneutical journey through Mark, Matthew, Luke, John, Paul, and Jesus, intended to help religious and nonreligious readers understand their spiritual inheritance. The book then brings readers back to the secular present to embrace, question, and construct meaning from that inherited tradition.

title: The Creation Stories in the Hebrew Bible (outside of Genesis!).   A Lecture You May Be Interested In
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a lecture on creation stories in the Hebrew Bible beyond Genesis.
searchSummary: Announces Joseph Lam's public lecture on biblical creation stories beyond Genesis and their connections with other ancient Near Eastern accounts. The event serves as a fundraiser for graduate students in religious studies, particularly for dissertation research travel and presenting scholarship at professional conferences. Ehrman explains the academic value of those opportunities and invites readers interested in the Hebrew Bible, ancient creation traditions, and graduate education to attend or support the program.

title: Proposed Solutions For the Four Metaphysical Puzzles Related to Jesus From an Islamic Perspective From Omar Robb
author: Diane
description: Offers an Islamic interpretation of Jesus' crucifixion, mission, ascension and return, and miraculous birth.

title: The Messy World of the Early Christian Gospels.  Who Is Copying What?
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Papyrus Egerton 2 to question simple models of how early Gospels copied one another.
searchSummary: Questions simple models in which later Christian Gospels drew only from the four canonical accounts. Using Papyrus Egerton 2, the post proposes a crowded early literary environment containing many lost Gospels that authors freely combined, revised, and expanded before Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John became uniquely authoritative. If Egerton directly used Mark and John, its alterations could illuminate early textual forms and show these works were treated as adaptable reports; similarities might also derive from unknown shared sources.

title: Why Would Jesus Get Angry at this Poor Leper?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores why Mark might portray Jesus as angry when healing a leper.
searchSummary: Argues that Mark portrays Jesus as angry when people question his willingness, authority, or ability to heal. Proposed explanations involving the leper's future disobedience, Jewish law, Satan, or general suffering do not fit the passage as closely. Parallel scenes show Jesus rebuking doubt, opposing resistance to Sabbath healing, and becoming indignant when disciples prevent children from receiving his touch. Jesus heals the leper because he resents the implication that he might be unwilling to help.

title: Did Jesus Think He Was Going to Atone for the Sins of the World? A Platinum Post by Manuel Fiadeiro
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum member's argument about whether Jesus expected to atone for sins.

title: Why Is Jesus So Angry?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains anger as a recurring Markan motif connected with Jesus' healing power.
searchSummary: Examines a recurring pattern in Mark: Jesus becomes angry or indignant in settings involving healing and the transmission of divine power. He rebukes doubt about his ability to exorcise a boy, objects when disciples block children from his touch, and condemns opponents who resist Sabbath healing. These scenes suggest that Mark's Jesus reacts sharply when people question or obstruct his power and desire to heal, providing context for his anger before cleansing the leper in Mark 1:41.

title: Jesus and Another Leper: Getting Angry at the Poor Fellow?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the textual variant in Mark 1:41 where Jesus is either angry or compassionate.
searchSummary: Argues that Mark 1:41 originally said Jesus became angry before healing a leper, although most manuscripts say he felt compassion. Scribes were more likely to soften an offensive reference to anger than to create it, and Matthew and Luke consistently omit Mark's anger while preserving references to compassion. Their omission suggests their early copies contained the difficult reading. The post establishes the textual case before asking why Mark portrays Jesus as angry in this scene.

title: Was Jesus Conceived out of Wedlock by Mary and a Jewish Relative, Pantera?  Part III Guest Post by James Tabor
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents James Tabor's concluding argument about Pantera and traditions concerning Jesus' biological father.

title: September 2023 Gold Q&A (video)
author: Diane

title: (Part 2) A Discussion on the Issue of Suffering and the Moral in Job’s Story. A Platinum Post From Omar Robb
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum member's second discussion of suffering and the moral of Job.
searchSummary: Presents Omar Robb's argument that suffering cannot logically disprove God because divine purposes and properties cannot be inferred straightforwardly from human moral expectations. Robb attributes most suffering to stable natural laws, accumulated human decisions, and social unfairness, while allowing rare divine support within nature. Recasting Job's heavenly scenes as literary fabrication, he interprets the earthly story as encouragement to endure hardship through faith or another sustaining commitment, while acknowledging that resilience does not guarantee recovery.

title: Was the Father of Jesus … Pantera?  Part II Guest Post by James Tabor
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues James Tabor's discussion of Pantera, mamzer status, and traditions about Jesus' father.

title: Who Was Jesus’ Biological Father? Part I. Guest Post by James Tabor
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces James Tabor's series on Joseph, Pantera, and questions about Jesus' biological father.

title: Did Luke Read Galatians? Platinum Post by Guillermo Mondon
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum member's argument that Acts may depend on Galatians.
searchSummary: Presents Guillermo Mondon's guest proposal that Acts was composed in the second century by an author who knew and reworked Galatians. Mondon argues that Acts reshapes Paul's conversion, the Antioch dispute, and relations with Peter and James to harmonize leaders whose disagreements remain visible in Paul's letters. His reconstruction treats Acts' three conversion narratives as deliberate reinterpretations of Paul's compressed account. Ehrman publishes the hypothesis for discussion while making clear that he does not accept it.

title: The Gospel according to Mel (Gibson)
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses The Passion of the Christ in a course on how films portray Jesus differently.

title: Is It Better to Follow Christ or to Live a Contented Life? Paul vs. Epicurus
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Paul's moral vision with Epicurus and ancient philosophical ideas of contentment.

title: One of our Earliest Gospels from Outside the New Testament: The Egerton Papyrus.
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Papyrus Egerton 2 as an early non-canonical Gospel fragment.

title: Time to Vote!
author: Diane
description: Invites Platinum members to vote on which guest post should appear on the full blog.

title: (Part I) A Discussion on Spirit, Death, Afterlife, Consciousness, and Free Will. A Platinum Post From Omar Robb
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum member's reflections on spirit, death, afterlife, consciousness, and free will.

title: That’s in the New Testament, Right?  An Interesting Non-Canonical Story.
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Papyrus Egerton 2 through a non-canonical Jesus story that resembles Gospel traditions.

title: About Those Ebionites and Their Peculiar Gospel
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains what can and cannot be known about the Gospel of the Ebionites from Epiphanius's quotations.
searchSummary: Examines fragmentary quotations from the Gospel of the Ebionites to ask how its Jewish-Christian setting shaped its portrayal of Jesus. Epiphanius associates the text with poorly understood groups that may have practiced Torah observance, vegetarianism, and voluntary poverty, yet its Jesus rejects eating the Passover lamb and calls for sacrifices to end. Ehrman considers whether these sayings reflect concern about pagan-sacrificed meat or belief that Jesus rendered Temple sacrifice unnecessary, while stressing that the surviving evidence permits only tentative reconstruction.

title: Paul, the Apostate: a Platinum Post by Manuel Fiadeiro
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum member's retelling of Paul's conversion and mission.

title: Locusts or Pancakes?  The Dietary Preferences of John the Baptist.
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how the Gospel of the Ebionites changes John the Baptist's diet from locusts to pancakes.

title: Contradictions?  What Contradictions?  Harmonizing the Gospels.
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the Gospel of the Ebionites to discuss harmonizing Gospel contradictions.
searchSummary: Criticizes harmonizing Gospel discrepancies by combining separate accounts into a new composite story. Proposals that Jesus cleansed the Temple twice or Peter denied him six times can preserve literal compatibility, but they create events that no canonical Gospel narrates. Ehrman argues that this method sacrifices each author's integrity and distinctive interpretation of Jesus, treating an anthology as one continuous work instead of reading Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John on their own terms.

title: A Conference on the Gospels for Non-Scholars!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a conference on the Gospels for non-specialist audiences.
searchSummary: Previews a public conference presenting ten scholarly lectures on the Gospels for nonspecialists. Topics include Jesus' family, symbolism in John, failed apocalyptic prophecy, Jerusalem archaeology, scriptural allusions, Gospel authorship and literacy, burial traditions, the woman caught in adultery, Jesus and women, and a textual variant in Mark. The program demonstrates how historical, literary, archaeological, and textual methods generate new insights into Gospel narratives and their transmission.

title: The Pauline Style and a Discussion About Paul’s Motivation. A Platinum Post From Omar Robb
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum member's reflections on Pauline style and Paul's broader motivations.

title: The Apocryphal Gospels By and For Jewish Christians
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Jewish-Christian Gospels known only through quotations by church fathers.

title: Want to Study the Early Christian Apocrypha?
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a doctoral seminar syllabus for studying early Christian apocrypha.
searchSummary: Presents the syllabus for Ehrman's doctoral seminar on early Christian apocrypha. Students translate Greek, analyze noncanonical Gospels, Acts, epistles, and apocalypses, evaluate textual and historical problems, review scholarship, give research presentations, and produce a substantial term paper. The course also examines forgery and the formation of the New Testament canon through texts including the Gospel of Thomas, Gospel of Peter, infancy Gospels, apocryphal Acts, and Apocalypse of Peter.

title: Jesus, Sun Myung Moon, and Me: a Platinum Post from William Poe
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum member's personal reflection on Christianity, spiritual seeking, and Sun Myung Moon.
searchSummary: Compares William Poe's experience as a disciple of Sun Myung Moon with patterns in early Christianity. Charismatic authority, claims of messianic status, opposition, persecution, communal belonging, and worldwide mission helped both movements inspire sacrifice and reinterpret failure, while Poe's eventual divorce, acknowledgment of being gay, and anthropological study led him from the Unification Church to agnostic atheism. His personal experience suggests that modern new religions can illuminate what discipleship and conversion may have felt like in ancient Christianity.

title: A Hugely Memorable Moment: When I Saw Codex Sinaiticus
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts a memorable visit to see pages of Codex Sinaiticus at Saint Catherine's Monastery.

title: September Gold Q&A–Get Those Questions in!
author: Diane
description: Announces the September Gold Q&A and invites member questions.

title: My Trip to Saint Catherine’s Monastery on Mount Sinai: Discovery Site of Codex Sinaiticus
author: BDEhrman
description: Provides background for a visit to Saint Catherine's Monastery and the history of Codex Sinaiticus.

title: The Discovery of Codex Sinaiticus: One of the Most Important Manuscripts of the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Codex Sinaiticus as the oldest complete New Testament manuscript and recounts its discovery.
