title: Mark 13:30–a New Argument for an Old Hypothesis. A Platinum Post From Omar Robb
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum member's argument about Mark 13:30 and the destruction of the Temple.
searchSummary: Proposes that Mark 13:30 originally referred only to Jerusalem's destruction within Jesus' generation, not also to the Son of Man's return. Oral transmission allegedly combined separate sayings about war, false messiahs, and the end, moving the generational prediction beside material whose timing no one knows. Eusebius's account of Christians fleeing Jerusalem and parallels with Daniel support the reconstruction, although the argument acknowledges uncertain dating, late evidence, and alternative origins for the prophecy.

title: Does Archaeological Evidence Show that Jesus Was Buried on the Day He Died?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to archaeological arguments about whether Jesus received same-day burial after crucifixion.
searchSummary: Evaluates whether the buried remains of the crucified man Yehohanan support Jesus's same-day tomb burial. Bart argues that one unusually placed, possibly aristocratic victim cannot establish a general practice, especially because neither Yehohanan's crime nor the time his body remained exposed is known. Disputed broken bones also cannot prove removal before sunset. He concludes that the find does not overcome Roman practice toward Jesus as an alleged enemy of the state.

title: Josephus’ One Statement About the Burial of Crucified Victims in Judea
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates Josephus's brief statement about Jewish burial of crucified victims in Judea.
searchSummary: Examines Josephus's statement that Jews buried even crucified offenders before sunset, the strongest textual argument for Jesus's burial. Bart questions whether Josephus exaggerates Jewish piety, refers to Roman crucifixions, describes a longstanding or universal custom, or includes political enemies. Because mass crucifixions clearly went unburied and Jesus was executed as a rival king, he concludes that any occasional accommodation for ordinary criminals would not establish a decent same-day burial for Jesus.

title: Thoughts on Cosmology, a Platinum Post From Charles Hawkins
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum guest reflection on ancient and modern cosmology in relation to biblical texts.
searchSummary: Contrasts the Bible's ancient three-story cosmos with successive scientific models from Copernicus and Newton to modern astronomy and billions of galaxies. Biblical expectations that heavenly beings descend through clouds made sense when God was located above a firmament, but no longer fit contemporary knowledge of the universe. Charles Hawkins concludes that literal Second Coming and rapture scenarios preserve an obsolete cosmology and cannot readily be reconciled with modern evidence about Earth's place in space.

title: Bogus Arguments for Disbelief
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques illogical arguments used against Christian belief.
searchSummary: Identifies three logically invalid arguments sometimes used against Christianity. A flawed Bible would undermine inerrancy, not every form of Christian faith; Jesus' absence from surviving first-century pagan sources is unsurprising for a minor Palestinian figure and does not establish nonexistence; and doubts about immediate burial would challenge Gospel resurrection narratives, not logically disprove every possible resurrection scenario. Ehrman urges believers and nonbelievers alike to distinguish historical findings from conclusions those findings cannot support.

title: How Relevant is Josephus for Knowing What Happened to the Body of Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Josephus provides useful evidence for Jesus' burial after crucifixion.
searchSummary: Evaluates passages from Josephus used to argue that Romans permitted Jewish burial of crucified bodies. One quotation concerns later procurators, not Pilate, while another summarizes Mosaic ideals rather than describing actual first-century practice; nearby commands that disobedient children be executed reveal the difference. Josephus therefore shows that Jews valued burial, not that Roman authorities honored that preference for condemned insurgents. Historical use of a source requires its date, argument, genre, and immediate context rather than isolated quotations.

title: Did Jews Always Bury Their Dead on the Day of their Death?  Was Jesus Buried Then?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates claims that Jewish burial customs make same-day burial of Jesus historically likely.
searchSummary: Challenges the argument that Roman respect for Jewish customs required Jesus's burial before sunset. Bart shows that Josephus's comments concern Roman accommodation of Jewish laws against idolatrous images and Jews' obligation to bury people they themselves executed. Because Romans crucified Jesus for political sedition, Jewish burial law did not bind his executioners. Roman authorities could respect selected customs while still leaving alleged enemies of the state exposed as a warning.

title: August 2023 Gold Q&A (video)
author: Diane
description: Shares the August 2023 Gold Q&A video.

title: Premarital Sex in The Song of Songs: A Platinum Post by Dan Kohanski
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum member's reading of sexuality in the Song of Songs.

title: The Evidence of Josephus for the Burial of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Josephus as a potentially important source in debates over Jesus' burial.
searchSummary: Introduces Josephus as the principal first-century Jewish source for evaluating claims about the burial of crucified people. Bart recounts Josephus's aristocratic background, military role in the Jewish revolt, surrender to Rome, relationship with Vespasian, and later historical writings. He emphasizes Josephus's political purposes while recognizing his exceptional value, then frames the question of whether passages about Jewish burial customs apply to Jesus, whom Rome executed as an enemy of the state.

title: Why Do Some (Many?) Scholars Not Treat the Bible Like Other Ancient Sources?
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that biblical texts should be treated with the same critical standards as other ancient sources.
searchSummary: Argues that the Bible and every other ancient source must receive the same critical scrutiny. Numerous late New Testament manuscripts do not guarantee exact knowledge of the originals, just as sparse classical manuscripts leave uncertainty about Plato, Cicero, and others; classicists openly investigate these problems. Historians must likewise test authorship, contradictions, bias, textual transmission, and factual claims in Josephus, Tacitus, Eusebius, and scripture. No statement becomes reliable merely because a respected or favored ancient author makes it.

title: How To Be a Consistently Critical Historian, In the Good Sense
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why historians must use all ancient sources critically and consistently.
searchSummary: Explains why historians must handle every ancient source cautiously and by consistent standards. A student's reliance on John's divine sayings of Jesus illustrates the temptation to exempt a valued text from the criteria used elsewhere. Historians instead assess each claim against source bias, internal coherence, external evidence, and historically grounded probabilities, whether the source is scripture, Josephus, Tacitus, or the Talmud. Selectively trusting supportive documents and criticizing inconvenient ones produces prejudice rather than historical reconstruction.

title: Polling Test Post (Ben)
author: FreedomBen
description: Publishes a test post for polling functionality.

title: Did Jesus Believe the End Would Come Within his Lifetime? Maybe Not!  Platinum Post by Rizwan Ahmed
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum member's challenge to the view that Jesus expected the end within Jesus' generation.
searchSummary: Challenges the claim that Jesus predicted the world's end within his lifetime while retaining his identity as an apocalyptic prophet. The explicit sayings are confined to Mark, lack independent attestation, and may project early Christian expectations back onto Jesus. Paul's earlier letters connect an imminent end to Jesus' resurrection rather than his teachings. The evidence therefore permits, but does not establish, that Jesus expected his generation to witness the end, affecting how his ethical teaching and prophetic accuracy are understood.

title: Corpses Left on Roman Crosses?  Penalties for Removing them Early?  A Humorous Story (?!) from Antiquity
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Petronius's Satyricon to illustrate Roman assumptions about bodies left on crosses.

title: Does Jesus Call Himself God in His Trial Before the Sanhedrin and the High Priest Caiaphas?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Jesus' Sanhedrin trial in Mark does not straightforwardly show a historical claim to be God.
searchSummary: Argues that Mark's Sanhedrin trial does not provide historical evidence that Jesus claimed to be God. The nighttime festival proceeding lacks witnesses and contains a blasphemy charge that does not fit claims to be Messiah, Son of God, or Daniel's Son of Man. Within Mark's theology, however, Jesus is both the Son of Man and a divine figure, allowing the high priest to interpret his answer as blasphemous. The scene reflects Mark's later Christology rather than a recoverable historical exchange.

title: Was “King of the Jews” Really the Charge Against Jesus, Leading to his Crucifixion?
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that the charge King of the Jews best explains Jesus' crucifixion by Rome.

title: Pontius Pilate, Intransigent Governor, Crucifier of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Pontius Pilate as a harsh governor in response to claims that Pilate respected Jewish sensitivities.
searchSummary: Argues that historical evidence contradicts the claim that Pilate learned to respect Jewish customs and therefore would have permitted Jesus's burial. Bart cites Pilate's use of Temple funds for an aqueduct and his violent suppression of the resulting protest, together with Philo's denunciation of his cruelty and corruption. These accounts portray an intransigent governor unlikely to suspend Roman treatment of crucified enemies merely because leaving a body exposed offended Jewish sensitivities.

title: Did Pilate Allow Jesus to be Buried Because He Had “Learned his Lesson”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares competing portraits of Pilate and their implications for Jesus' burial.
searchSummary: Rejects the claim that Pilate's early dispute over Roman standards taught him to respect Jewish customs and therefore permit Jesus's burial. Josephus says Pilate knowingly introduced imperial images at night, refused six days of protests, and threatened mass execution before demonstrators accepted death rather than submission. Bart argues that Pilate withdrew to avoid the political consequences of killing Judea's leaders, not from sensitivity, and continued acting brutally afterward.

title: Gold Q&A for August!
author: admin
description: Announces the August Gold Q&A and invites member questions.

title: How Accurate Are Orally-Transmitted Reports? A Platinum Post From Imran M. Usmani
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum member's challenge to Bart Ehrman's views on oral tradition using Islamic hadith scholarship.
searchSummary: Argues in a guest post that Islamic Hadith scholarship offers a model for evaluating oral reports about Jesus. Bukhari assessed chains of transmission, transmitter character and memory, and multiple independent attestations, finding changed wording and details but often a stable central idea. The author speculates that Mark may likewise have investigated competing reports carefully and preserved their essence, although he acknowledges no direct evidence for Mark's methods and weaknesses in Bukhari's reliance on transmitters rather than content.

title: Was Pilate Sensitive to Jews and their Customs (such that he would allow decent burials for crucified victims)?
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques the argument that Pilate would have allowed decent burial out of sensitivity to Jewish customs.
searchSummary: Evaluates whether Philo's account of golden shields shows that Pilate respected Jewish customs enough to permit crucified bodies to be buried. Bart emphasizes that Pilate stubbornly rejected Jewish appeals and removed the shields only after Emperor Tiberius intervened, while Philo portrays him as corrupt, cruel, and violently inhumane. The episode therefore undermines rather than supports a consistently accommodating Pilate, though Bart frames his burial conclusion as a probability judgment rather than certainty.

title: Why Critical Scholarship on the Gospels Helps *Believers* in the Bible!
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how critical Gospel scholarship can be theologically useful for believers.
searchSummary: Argues that recognizing Gospel discrepancies can enrich interpretation by preserving each author's distinctive theological message. Mark portrays Jesus dying in despair and abandonment, while Luke presents him calm, forgiving, and confident in God; combining their sayings into one harmonized account erases both portraits. Critical comparison therefore does not diminish the Gospels but allows believers and nonbelievers to hear each narrative's literary and theological claims instead of replacing them with a reader-created composite Gospel.

title: We Have Crucifixion Nails!  Isn’t that Evidence for Jesus’ Burial?
author: BDEhrman
description: Assesses whether crucifixion nails provide evidence that Jesus was buried after crucifixion.
searchSummary: Rejects alleged crucifixion nails from Judean tombs as evidence that executed victims received decent burials. Bart notes that nails found near ossuaries, including Caiaphas's, were not attached to crucified skeletons and could serve as talismans or tools for inscribing bone boxes before being discarded as impure. Forensic archaeologist Joe Zias identifies only Yehohanan's nailed ankle as relevant physical evidence, leaving the other nails unable to establish any burial practice.

title: Serious Discount on my Book!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a discount on Armageddon at Barnes & Noble.

title: A Proposition That Ramesses-the-Sixth (Ramesses VI) Was the Pharaoh of the Exodus by Omar Robb
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum member's historical proposal identifying Ramesses VI as the Pharaoh of the Exodus.

title: Is Critical Biblical Scholarship Valid?  What the New Testament Itself Indicates!
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that the New Testament itself supports reading the Gospels critically rather than as precise historical records.
searchSummary: Argues that Matthew and Luke themselves treated Mark critically rather than as an inviolable historical record. They reorder, add, omit, and alter Mark's stories, sometimes changing major theological meanings, while Luke explicitly says earlier accounts prompted his more orderly effort to establish the truth. Modern scholars likewise can value a Gospel while questioning its accuracy and revisions; treating canonical texts as exempt from questions applied to noncanonical Gospels is a theological choice, not a historical method.

title: Hey, Stop Trashing the Gospels!
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why questioning the historical accuracy of Gospel burial accounts is not the same as trashing the Gospels.

title: Creating the Qu’ran:  Where Did the Scripture of Islam Really Come From? Guest post by Stephen Shoemaker
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Stephen Shoemaker's argument about the formation and transmission of the Quran.
searchSummary: Presents Stephen Shoemaker's historical-critical argument that the Qur'an reached its canonical form under Caliph Abd al-Malik around the turn of the eighth century rather than under Uthman. Islamic and near-contemporary non-Islamic sources, along with the later state's administrative capacity, support a prolonged formation from oral and written traditions. Shoemaker argues that material rooted in Muhammad was modified and supplemented across diverse conquered regions before imperial standardization suppressed competing versions and established the surviving text.

title: Were Roman Leaders Told to Provide Decent Burials for Crucified Victims?  (Really?)
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques the claim that Roman authorities were instructed to grant decent burial to crucified victims.
searchSummary: Examines a Roman legal ruling cited to show that executed criminals could be released for burial. Although the Digest preserves an earlier rule allowing relatives to request bodies, it explicitly notes that permission could be denied for high treason and does not specifically establish burial for crucified people. Because Rome executed Jesus as a rival king and political threat, Bart argues that the cited law supports nonburial as part of crucifixion's punishment and deterrent.

title: Did Romans Show Clemency to Crucified Criminals?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Roman clemency toward prisoners applies to crucified enemies of the state.
searchSummary: Challenges claims that Roman clemency makes Jesus's prompt burial historically probable. The cited examples concern prisoners or offenders in other places and periods, not people crucified for treason; even Albinus released petty offenders for bribes while executing those deemed worthy of death. Bart argues that isolated mercy toward lesser criminals cannot establish a practice of releasing crucified enemies of the state, whose prolonged exposure served Roman punishment, humiliation, and deterrence.

title: Want to Watch Our Tár Movie Review With Maestra Gisele Ben-Dor?
author: Diane
description: Offers a recorded movie-club discussion of Tár with conductor Gisele Ben-Dor in exchange for a donation.

title: Time to Vote for Your Favorite Platinum Post
author: Diane
description: Invites Platinum members to vote on a guest post.

title: Preparing for that “Final Trip” (outta here).  What Do You Think?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on mortality, memory, remorse, and preparing for the end of life.
searchSummary: Uses Julian Barnes's The Sense of an Ending to reflect on memory, history, mortality, and preparing for death. The novel's observation that historical certainty emerges from imperfect memory and inadequate documentation applies both to personal recollection and Ehrman's reconstruction of antiquity, while its image of cremation makes his own extinction tangible. Rather than producing despair, awareness that everyone dies and is eventually forgotten relativizes daily concerns, deepens gratitude for existence, and strengthens his desire to help others value life.

title: My Interview With Glenn Siepert
author: Diane
description: Shares an interview with Glenn Siepert about Armageddon and end-times interpretation.
searchSummary: Introduces Glenn Siepert's interview with Ehrman about Armageddon: What the Bible Really Says About the End. Recorded for Siepert's What If Project, the conversation features questions Ehrman considered especially strong and moves into subjects he found unusually interesting. The post does not identify those specific questions or summarize Ehrman's responses, instead presenting the recording itself and briefly noting Siepert's new book about grief, broken dreams, damaged relationships, resilience, and finding courage to continue.

title: Jesus the Half-Nabataean Prince, a Platinum Post by Serene
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum member's proposal about Jesus' ancestry and Nabataean connections.

title: Alleged “Proof” That Crucified Jews Were Allowed Decent Burials
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Craig Evans's counterarguments about Roman crucifixion practices and Pilate in the debate over Jesus' burial.
searchSummary: Analyzes Philo's account of crucified prisoners released for burial near an emperor's birthday, rejecting it as proof of a general Roman practice applicable to Jesus. The rare Alexandrian concession honored a Roman holiday, involved bodies already hanging before the festival, and delivered them to relatives, not unrelated petitioners. Bart concludes that none of these circumstances fits Jesus's execution for treason in Jerusalem during Passover or supports burial on the day of crucifixion.

title: New Insights into the New Testament:  An Event You DON’T Want to Miss!
author: Diane
description: Announces a two-day conference on the canonical Gospels for non-specialist audiences.

title: A Proposition That the First Greek Converts to Jesus Were a Few Ascetic Pythagorean Philosophers. A Platinum Post From Omar Robb
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum member's proposal that early Greek converts to Jesus included ascetic Pythagorean philosophers.
searchSummary: Proposes, without documentary evidence, that a few ascetic Pythagorean philosophers became early Jewish followers of Jesus and helped Christianity enter the Greek world. Their philosophical training, preaching ability, moral framework, spirituality, and open brotherhood supposedly enabled rapid expansion, while Jerusalem's destruction freed Greek churches from Jewish authority and made Paul's anti-law arguments useful. The guest author presents this as a speculative model for the poorly documented years 33–50 CE, whose value depends on explanatory reach rather than demonstrated historical support.

title: Does It Even Matter If Jesus Was Given a Proper Burial?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Jesus' burial matters for historical arguments about the empty tomb.
searchSummary: Explains why Bart considers Jesus's burial historically important but irrelevant to his personal agnosticism or the possibility of resurrection. A proper tomb would not demonstrate that God raised Jesus, while delayed burial or a common grave would not make divine resurrection impossible, though it would challenge the third-day and empty-tomb traditions. He therefore presents his disagreement with Craig Evans as a historical probability dispute rather than an argument driven by theological stakes.

title: More Reasons for Thinking Jesus was Not Given a Decent Burial
author: BDEhrman
description: Gives additional reasons for doubting the tradition that Joseph of Arimathea gave Jesus a decent burial.
searchSummary: Offers two additional reasons for doubting Jesus received a recognizable tomb burial: ancient authorities commonly denied executed criminals honorable burial, and surviving accounts portray Pilate as violent and indifferent to Jewish sensitivities. Bart cites Greek and Roman examples of common graves or nonburial, then compares increasingly sympathetic Gospel portrayals of Pilate with harsher descriptions in Luke, Josephus, and Philo. He concludes that normal policy and Pilate's character make prompt burial historically unlikely.

title: Did Romans Allow Decent Burials for Crucified Criminals?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Roman crucifixion practices make same-day burial of Jesus historically unlikely.
searchSummary: Argues that standard Roman crucifixion practice included leaving corpses exposed to decay and scavengers as part of public humiliation and deterrence. Literary references consistently describe crucified bodies feeding birds or animals, while Philo's exceptional holiday clemency involved earlier executions, connected families, and an emperor's birthday rather than Passover. Bart concludes that Jesus might conceivably have been an exception, but the historical evidence favors exposure and later disposal over a known tomb.

title: Literary Problems with the Gospel Accounts of Jesus’ Burial
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines literary problems in the Gospel accounts of Jesus' burial by Joseph of Arimathea.
searchSummary: Identifies literary reasons to doubt Mark's account that Joseph of Arimathea buried Jesus. Joseph belongs to the council that Mark says unanimously condemned Jesus, while Paul never names him and Acts preserves a different tradition in which Jewish leaders collectively place Jesus in a tomb. Bart suggests that an initially vague burial tradition may have acquired a named benefactor as stories developed, partly because a known tomb was narratively necessary for proclaiming it empty.

title: Reminder:  Why I’m Not a Christian — tomorrow!
author: Diane
description: Reminds readers about a free course on leaving Christian faith and finding meaning without God.
searchSummary: Announces a free four-lecture course in which Ehrman explains why he left Christianity. The course combines his personal faith journey with scholarly development, doubts about God's existence, fears and difficulties surrounding deconversion, and ways nonbelievers find meaning and purpose without God. A lengthy question period allows further discussion. The post supplies attendance and later-access information rather than presenting the course's arguments, emphasizing that the autobiography serves to illustrate one path out of belief.

title: Back to Whether Jesus Was Really Given a Decent Burial
author: BDEhrman
description: Reintroduces a detailed thread defending the view that Jesus probably was not given a decent burial.
searchSummary: Introduces Bart's extended defense of his minority view that Jesus probably did not receive a same-day tomb burial from Joseph of Arimathea. He explains that the series revisits his argument in How Jesus Became God and responds to Craig Evans's learned evangelical defense of the Gospel tradition. Bart regards Evans's essay as the strongest available opposing case but proposes to examine whether its literary, historical, and archaeological evidence actually supports its conclusions.

title: Is the USA the Antichrist of the Book of Revelation?  Slavic Views of the Apocalypse.  Guest Post by Mikhail Abakumov
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Mikhail Abakumov's discussion of Slavic apocalyptic views identifying the United States with Revelation's Antichrist.
searchSummary: Mikhail Abakumov examines how interpreters project current enemies onto Revelation. American fundamentalists identified the Soviet Union or Russia as Antichrist, while some Slavic Christians cast the United States in that role and map the Ukraine war, China, COVID controls, and economic power onto biblical prophecy. Such readings are subjective because Revelation addressed first-century audiences rather than encoding modern technology or geopolitics. Abakumov instead treats Antichrist as recurring people and systems opposing God, making the struggle ethically relevant in every generation.

title: Male Superiority in Antiquity
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains ancient Greek and Roman arguments for male superiority and their cultural legacy.

title: More on Love:  Why Were Greek Men Especially Attracted to Prepubescent Boys?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores why classical Athenian culture idealized pederastic relationships between men and adolescent boys.

title: An Important Difference in John–a Platinum Post by Ryan Fleming
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum member's comparison of John's chronology and narrative differences with the Synoptic Gospels.
searchSummary: Catalogs differences between John and the Synoptic Gospels in chronology, vocabulary, Christology, crucifixion, resurrection appearances, and expectations of Jesus' return. John omits potentially embarrassing traditions, portrays Jesus carrying his own cross, places followers near the crucifixion, introduces the spear wound and Thomas's inspection of Jesus' wounds, and lacks promises of an imminent return. The guest author interprets these alterations as evidence of John's later composition and creative reshaping rather than reliable historical reporting.

title: The Narrow Road to … Hell?  Guest Post by Glenn Siepert
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Glenn Siepert's reflection on Matthew's narrow road saying in relation to grief and moving forward.
searchSummary: Reinterprets Jesus' narrow and wide roads in Matthew as contrasting difficult love, peace, and forgiveness with easier hatred, violence, and bitterness rather than separating strict Christians from people destined for hell. Glenn Siepert connects the teaching to communities facing loss and revenge, arguing that destructive impulses fill the broad road while grace is less commonly chosen. He clarifies that forgiveness need not mean unsafe reconciliation, especially when abuse or continuing harm makes renewed relationship dangerous.

title: Radiocarbon Dating of the Qur’an.  Has It Solved the Problem?  Guest Post by Stephen Shoemaker
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Stephen Shoemaker's caution about using radiocarbon dating to settle the origins of the Quran.

title: Questions about Dating the Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to reader questions about how scholars date the canonical and non-canonical Gospels.
searchSummary: Explains how scholars distinguish the date of a surviving manuscript from the earlier date when its text was composed. Manuscripts are usually dated paleographically, while compositions are bounded by historical references, dependence on earlier works, quotation by later authors, theology, context, and anachronisms; fragments normally imply a fuller familiar work without proving its exact extent. Luke-Acts is placed after Mark but likely before early second-century citations, and silence by earlier writers does not establish a late date.

title: Why Discrepancies and Contradictions *Enrich* Our Understanding of the Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Gospel discrepancies can clarify each author's distinctive theological portrait of Jesus.
searchSummary: Argues that Gospel discrepancies preserve each evangelist's distinctive message rather than creating problems to be harmonized. Mark portrays an abandoned, suffering Jesus whose death opens access to God and models trust when suffering seems meaningless. Luke presents a calm, confident Jesus who knows God remains present and models forgiveness and concern for others. Combining the accounts erases their contrasting theological interpretations of suffering and God's involvement in it.

title: Our Inner Herod.  Guest Post by Glenn Siepert
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Glenn Siepert's reflection on Herod in Matthew and its use for personal reflection.
searchSummary: Uses Matthew's story of Herod and the Magi to reflect on grief, lost power, and recovery after personal disaster. Herod's fear of losing his position becomes a warning that preoccupation with what has been destroyed can separate people from their inner wisdom and prevent them from recognizing new possibilities. The post encourages readers facing collapsed relationships or other losses to remain alert to ways the divine may still be present without promising that pain will quickly disappear.

title: The Life of Brian and Jesus:  Was Jesus Really Buried on the Day of the Crucifixion?
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Life of Brian to argue that parody can illuminate historical questions about Jesus' burial.
searchSummary: Uses parody in Life of Brian to illuminate Roman crucifixion and challenge the Gospel account of Jesus' immediate decent burial. Ancient sources show that victims normally remained exposed as part of Roman humiliation; Philo's narrow birthday exception, Jewish burial law, and Pilate's brutal record do not make Jesus a likely exception. The film's indifference to Jewish sensitivities caricatures a genuine imperial reality. Ehrman argues that perceptive parody can generate historical questions and expose assumptions that conventional scholarship overlooks.

title: Announcing a NEW (Free!) Course:  Why I Am Not A Christian
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a free autobiographical course on leaving Christianity and finding meaning afterward.
searchSummary: Announces Ehrman's free autobiographical course explaining how biblical scholarship transformed his Christianity and eventually led him from evangelical faith to agnosticism. Four lectures trace his rejection of inerrancy, loss of belief in God, emotional and social struggles during deconversion, fear of hell, and discovery of meaning and ethical purpose without faith. Rather than seeking conversions or deconversions, the course encourages thoughtful, honest examination of belief and shows why leaving Christianity ultimately produced a happier, more meaningful life for him.

title: Vespasian Miracles. A Platinum Post by Ryan Fleming
author: Diane
description: Presents a Platinum member's discussion of miracle stories attributed to the emperor Vespasian.

title: More on the Life of Brian and the Historical Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Life of Brian to reflect on eyewitness testimony and misunderstandings in historical memory.
searchSummary: Uses Life of Brian's misheard Sermon on the Mount to question claims that eyewitnesses guaranteed Gospel accuracy. The Gospels neither claim eyewitness authorship nor preserve events that witnesses could readily report, and eyewitness presence would not ensure reliability. Psychological and legal research shows that perception, storage, and recall are vulnerable to distortion, suggestion, and confident false memory, even shortly after dramatic events. Traditions written decades after Jesus therefore require historical evaluation regardless of whether an eyewitness once stood behind them.

title: Blog Dinner in London, Tuesday July 25.  Interested?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a London blog dinner for members.

title: The Life of Brian and the Historical Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a conference paper on Life of Brian and the historical Jesus.
searchSummary: Uses The Life of Brian's parody of Jerusalem street preachers to illuminate the historical setting of Jesus's apocalyptic message. Bart recalls initially finding the scene offensive because it made Jesus resemble other prophets of doom, then explains why further study changed his view. Sayings from John the Baptist, Jesus son of Ananias, the Dead Sea Scrolls, and Jesus of Nazareth share an expectation that God would soon end the present order, judge evil, and require repentance.

title: What Is (Sexually) “Unnatural”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Questions what people mean by calling sexual acts or identities unnatural.

title: How the Bible Can Help Those in Pain — Even Non-Believers.  Guest Post by Glenn Siepert
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Glenn Siepert's book on using biblical stories to think through grief and loss.
searchSummary: Explains the personal and interpretive background of Glenn Siepert's book Emerging From the Rubble. After leaving fundamentalism and losing his father, Siepert reads thirty stories from Matthew as responses to a Jewish Christian community grieving Jerusalem's destroyed Temple, then asks how those stories might help modern readers face death, divorce, illness, and shattered dreams. The Bible remains meaningful not as an inerrant guidebook but as an enduring collection of human narratives that can reveal possibilities within loss.

title: June 2023 Gold Q&A (video)
author: Diane
description: Shares the June 2023 Gold Q&A video.

title: The (Lost) Greater Questions of Mary (Rated R) (X?)
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses the lost Greater Questions of Mary and the difficulty of knowing whether it existed.
searchSummary: Examines the alleged Greater Questions of Mary, known only from a hostile quotation by the fourth-century heresy-hunter Epiphanius. He associates the text with the Phibionites and describes Jesus performing a sexual ritual before Mary Magdalene to illustrate a Gnostic rejection of procreation, which was thought to imprison divine sparks in new bodies. Because Epiphanius is the sole and unreliable witness, scholars must consider whether the Gospel or even its quoted episode ever existed.

title: The Lost Gospel of Basilides
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the lost Gospel of Basilides and the problem of knowing lost Gnostic texts through hostile witnesses.
searchSummary: Explains the possible lost Gospel of Basilides, known only through hostile reports about this early Gnostic teacher. According to Irenaeus, Basilides taught that Jesus exchanged appearances with Simon of Cyrene, causing the Romans to crucify Simon while the invulnerable Christ stood nearby laughing. Similar scenes in other Gnostic writings deny that divine Christ could truly suffer, but it remains uncertain whether Basilides' account came from an actual Gospel or from an oral tradition.

title: The Road from the “Duo of Philo” to the “Trinity of Nicaea”–Guest Post by Omar Robb
author: Diane
description: Presents Omar Robb's guest post tracing ideas from Philo to the Nicene doctrine of the Trinity.
searchSummary: Omar Abur-Robb proposes that Greek metaphysics shaped Christian movement from Philo's distinction between God and the Logos toward Nicene Trinitarian doctrine. He traces this through Justin's Father, Son, and Spirit, Arius's subordinate created Son, and Alexander's coeternal Son equal with the Father. He argues that institutional stability and Constantine's desire for unity favored Alexander at Nicaea, though several links in the reconstruction are explicitly presented as assumptions.

title: Did Paul Get Along with the Other Apostles?
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Paul's letters with Acts to ask whether Paul was in harmony or conflict with the Jerusalem apostles.

title: After Paul Converted…  Does the Book of Acts Contradict Paul Himself?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines differences between Acts and Paul's own account of what happened after Paul's conversion.
searchSummary: Compares Paul's account of events after his conversion with the narrative in Acts. Paul insists that he consulted no one, avoided Jerusalem, and met only Cephas and James three years later; Acts has him confer with Ananias and promptly join all the Jerusalem disciples. Ehrman concludes that Acts preserves a broadly historical outline but reshapes details to portray apostolic unity, making Paul's sworn firsthand testimony more credible for reconstructing his own movements.

title: Was Paul Authorized to Persecute Christians?
author: BDEhrman
description: Questions Acts' claim that Jerusalem authorities authorized Paul's persecution of Christians and uses it to assess Acts' reliability on Paul.

title: Was Abraham “Just Plain Nuts?” A Platinum Post by Douglas Wadeson MD
author: Diane
description: Uses Abraham and Isaac to raise the ethical problem of Abraham's conduct in Genesis and whether Scripture presents Abraham as commendable.

title: Can the Qur’an and Early Islam Be Studied Critically (Like the NT and Early Christianity?)  Guest Post by Stephen Shoemaker
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Stephen Shoemaker's argument for studying the Qur'an and early Islam with historical-critical methods used for the Bible and early Christianity.
searchSummary: Explains why historical-critical study of the Qur'an and early Islam remains less developed than comparable biblical scholarship. Stephen Shoemaker argues that many researchers still accept traditional claims that the Qur'an preserves Muhammad's exact words, fixed soon after his death and arranged according to a reliable chronology. Those assumptions prevent source, form, and redaction criticism despite questions about Mecca's setting and the text's sophisticated Jewish and Christian knowledge, leaving its formation history insufficiently investigated.

title: Did the Curtain in the Temple Really Rip in Half at Jesus’ Crucifixion?
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the torn temple curtain at Jesus' death as a test case for memory, Gospel tradition, and historical plausibility.
searchSummary: Argues that the temple curtain probably did not tear when Jesus died, since the Synoptic accounts conflict and no independent source mentions such a remarkable event. In Mark, the story symbolically expresses Jesus' death as an atoning sacrifice that opens direct access to God beyond temple priests and rituals. Whether invented deliberately or produced through sincere imagination and retelling, the episode became a shared Christian memory. Its historical weakness does not erase what it reveals about Mark's theology and community.

title: Was Jesus an Ascetic Street Preacher or a Man With a Plan? A Platinum Post From Omar Robb
author: Diane
description: Presents a speculative guest reconstruction of Jesus' mission in relation to John the Baptist and Zechariah.

title: Did The Twelve Become Only Three? Platinum post by Douglas Wadeson MD
author: admin
description: Considers whether most of the Twelve may have left the Jesus movement after Jesus' death rather than continuing as Acts assumes.

title: Help Wanted: Join Bart Ehrman Professional Services as a Writer/Editor!
author: Chrishuntley
description: Announces a writer and editor opening for Bart Ehrman Professional Services and its biblical-studies content work.

title: Did Pilate Really Release A Dangerous Criminal, Barabbas, at Jesus’ Trial?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates the Barabbas release story in Jesus' trial before Pilate as a possible distorted Gospel memory.
searchSummary: Argues that Pilate's release of Barabbas is a distorted memory rather than historical custom. No external evidence shows Roman governors freeing condemned prisoners at Passover, and the ruthless Pilate would not release an insurrectionist who killed in resistance to Rome. The story instead shifts responsibility for Jesus' death toward the Jewish crowd and contrasts two “sons of the father”: the violent Barabbas and the self-sacrificing Jesus. Manuscripts naming the prisoner Jesus Barabbas make this Christian theological contrast even sharper.

title: Were Jesus Followers Really Armed and Dangerous in the Garden of Gethsemane?
author: BDEhrman
description: Questions whether the Gospel arrest stories preserve a real armed confrontation involving Jesus' followers.
searchSummary: Questions whether Jesus' followers carried swords and fought during his arrest. If they had attacked the party, Roman authorities would likely have detained them with a leader suspected of rebellion; traditions portray Jesus as teaching nonviolence. The episode may have developed to provide a narrative setting for the saying that those who live by the sword die by it. As Christian memory, it reassured Roman audiences that Jesus and his followers rejected armed resistance despite his execution for insurrection.

title: The Slippery Slope of Extreme DIAKRISIS (Discernment). A Platinum Post by Barry Haney
author: Diane
description: Uses a fictional interreligious conversation around 200 CE to explore discernment and religious boundaries among pagans, Jews, and Christians.
searchSummary: A fictional conversation set in Antioch around 200 CE brings a pagan, a Jew, and a Christian together to debate truth, covenant, and exclusive religious claims. Each speaker defends a different way of discerning divine reality while confronting the dangers of dismissing other traditions too quickly. The exchange ends with disagreement but mutual respect, presenting humility and continued dialogue as alternatives to extreme religious judgment.

title: Did Jesus Really Cleanse the Temple?
author: BDEhrman
description: Assesses the historicity of Jesus' temple disruption and how memory may have shaped the Gospel accounts.
searchSummary: Concludes that Jesus probably caused a disturbance in Jerusalem's temple, perhaps symbolically anticipating its destruction, but that Gospel details are exaggerated. John relocates the event and adds a whip, while Mark implausibly depicts one man shutting down the vast complex without immediate arrest. The expanded memory served later Christian theology by portraying Jesus as superseding temple sacrifice and external ritual. It presents true worship as prayer, inward devotion, and access to God through Jesus rather than the Jewish cult.

title: Away from life for a while
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a temporary meditation retreat and explains that blog comments will be delayed.

title: Did the Triumphal Entry Really Happen?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates the triumphal entry as a remembered or reshaped Gospel tradition about Jesus entering Jerusalem as messiah.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus entered Jerusalem for Passover but probably did not receive the Gospels' messianic acclamation. Roman troops monitoring the volatile festival would have arrested anyone welcomed as the Davidic king who would displace their rule. Matthew's awkward two-animal ride further shows tradition reshaped by literal interpretation of Hebrew poetry. The triumphal entry became a distorted Christian memory portraying Jewish crowds as fickle: celebrating Jesus as Messiah, then rejecting him when he did not become the political ruler they expected.

title: June Gold Q&A
author: Diane
description: Announces the June Gold Q&A and invites Gold and Platinum members to submit questions.

title: The Bart Ehrman Movie Club Presents: Life of Brian
author: Diane
description: Introduces a movie-club discussion of Life of Brian in relation to Gospel portrayals, historical Jesus study, and Jesus films.

title: Jesus’ Trial Before Pilate: Some of the Distorted Memories of the Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Gospel memories of Jesus' trial before Pilate, especially John's distinctive portrayal and possible distortions.
searchSummary: Uses Gospel differences in Jesus' trial before Pilate to identify historically distorted memories. John intensifies Jewish responsibility, depicts implausible private conversations and repeated negotiations, and makes Jesus' Passover symbolism central, while later Gospels increasingly absolve Pilate. Roman authorities, not "the Jews," executed Jesus, and the trial scenes reflect later Christian conflict with non-Christian Jews. These narratives remain historically valuable because their distortions reveal how later communities reshaped Jesus' death to address their own controversies and theology.

title: Jesus’ Trial Before Pilate: What Can We Actually Know?
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Jesus' trial before Pilate to show how historians test Gospel memories against historical probability.
searchSummary: Introduces two ways to identify distorted Gospel memories: compare incompatible accounts and assess historically implausible details. Jesus' appearance before Pilate and execution as “King of the Jews” form a plausible historical gist, but later Gospels increasingly absolve Pilate and blame Jewish leaders and crowds. Matthew adds Pilate's handwashing, Luke repeatedly declares Jesus innocent, and John places the proceeding before rather than after the Passover meal. These changes reveal historical distortion and the later communities' growing anti-Jewish interpretation of Jesus' death.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: The Radical Teachings of Jesus–And Why No One Follows Them
author: BDEhrman
description: Outlines a proposed book on the radical ethical demands of Jesus and why later Christians often do not follow them.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus radicalized Jewish concern for the needy by extending love to everyone, including outsiders and enemies, and demanding complete self-sacrifice rather than limited generosity. His reason was apocalyptic: God would soon judge humanity, annihilate opponents, and admit those living entirely for others into the kingdom. Because that imminent end never arrived, followers quickly softened “give everything” into sustainable charity, producing influential Christian ethics that changed the world but no longer represented Jesus' full demand.

title: The Events Leading up to the Death of Jesus: What Can We Know and Not Know?
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes what can and cannot be known about events leading to Jesus' death using the concept of gist memory.
searchSummary: Identifies a broadly reliable historical outline of Jesus' final week while separating it from disputed Gospel details. Jesus traveled to Jerusalem for Passover, disrupted the temple, preached God's coming kingdom, was betrayed and arrested, appeared before Pilate as a suspected king, and was crucified with two others. Independent sources and Roman practices support this gist. Questions about the triumphal entry, armed disciples, Barabbas, Pilate's innocence, and the torn temple curtain require separate analysis because those remembered particulars may be distorted.

title: If We Can Know the “Gist” of What Jesus Said and Did … What’s the Gist?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why distorted memories can still preserve the basic gist of Jesus' words and deeds.
searchSummary: Explains that memory often preserves gist while losing or reconstructing details, but asks how broadly “gist” must be defined. John Dean confidently misremembered the substance of recorded Watergate conversations, combining typical encounters and an inflated sense of his role. Such errors arose after nine months despite intelligence and strong memory. Gospel reports written decades after Jesus through chains of storytellers therefore cannot be assumed to preserve exact speeches, settings, or narrower topics simply because their general subject is historical.

title: Were Jesus’ Most Amazing Deeds the Ones Most Likely to be Remembered?
author: BDEhrman
description: Questions whether spectacular events in Jesus traditions would necessarily be remembered more accurately.
searchSummary: Shows that vivid memories of extraordinary events are not necessarily accurate. “Flashbulb memory” research found that people confidently misremembered where and how they learned of the Challenger explosion, often rejecting records created the next day when those contradicted later recollection. Suggestion can also implant events that never occurred, and manufactured memories feel factual. Consequently, spectacular deeds attributed to Jesus would not be preserved reliably; an eyewitness's vivid confidence years later cannot establish that a miracle or saying happened as remembered.

title: Vote for Your Favorite Platinum Post
author: admin
description: Invites Platinum members to vote on recent guest posts.

title: Eyewitness Testimony: The Importance of Actual Expertise
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques New Testament scholarship that appeals to eyewitness testimony without engaging expertise on memory and eyewitness reliability.
searchSummary: Criticizes New Testament arguments about eyewitnesses that ignore specialized psychological and legal research. Experiments since 1902 show eyewitness reports can contain extensive errors, while DNA exonerations reveal convictions often rested on mistaken identification. In another study, most respondents remembered television footage of a plane crash that was never filmed and supplied imagined details. Dramatic imagery, inference, and hearsay can create confident false memories. Even eyewitness testimony about Jesus' miracles would therefore require critical evaluation rather than automatic trust.

title: Eyewitnesses and Guaranteed Accuracy
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses research on false memory to challenge the assumption that eyewitness testimony guarantees accurate Jesus traditions.
searchSummary: Uses traditions about the eighteenth-century Baal Shem Tov to show that alleged eyewitness origins do not guarantee historical accuracy. Accounts written fifty-four years after his death claim reliable informants yet describe healings, exorcisms, weather control, heavenly journeys, and raising the dead, while his disciples reshape his teachings differently. Devotees accepted these stories, but outsiders recognize legendary development. Gospel accounts of Jesus must likewise be assessed individually: eyewitness involvement would make them neither necessarily reliable nor necessarily false.

title: “You Have Heard His Blasphemy!” But Did They? A Platinum post by Daniel Kohanski
author: Diane
description: Offers a guest argument about whether Mark's trial scene supports the charge of blasphemy against Jesus.
searchSummary: Proposes that Mark's high priest never presents a legally coherent Jewish charge of blasphemy against Jesus. Torah defines blasphemy as cursing God's name, while Jesus' reported words do not qualify; Roman audiences could instead associate blasphemy with sacrilege, imperial dignity, or false witness. Mark allegedly invents the nighttime trial to portray Jewish leaders manufacturing a baseless accusation while concealing the Roman political offense that led to crucifixion. Only the next morning's consultation and transfer to Pilate may preserve history.

title: Being Realistic about How Stories about Jesus Spread before the Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how stories about Jesus spread through early Christian missionaries who were not eyewitnesses.
searchSummary: Reconstructs how stories about Jesus circulated through converts as Christianity spread before the Gospels. Missionaries persuaded people who then retold the traditions to family, neighbors, coworkers, worshippers, baptismal candidates, and new communities far from Palestine. Most transmitters were neither eyewitnesses nor speakers of Jesus' language, and stories served evangelism, instruction, worship, encouragement, and practical guidance. Ehrman argues that repeated oral transmission across such settings inevitably altered and sometimes created material, raising questions about whether Gospel traditions retain authorized eyewitness memories.

title: Who Was Spreading the Stories about Jesus Before the Gospels?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines who carried Jesus traditions before the Gospels, emphasizing the role of non-eyewitness missionaries and storytellers.
searchSummary: Explains that most early churches and missionaries known from the New Testament were not founded by eyewitnesses to Jesus. Missionaries such as Paul, Apollos, Epaphras, and unnamed evangelists nevertheless had to tell potential converts who Jesus was, what he taught, why he died, and what followed. These non-witnesses therefore spread the traditions widely, and even Peter's confrontation with Paul shows that eyewitness status did not confer unquestioned authority over how Jesus' significance was interpreted.

title: The 3rd Rail – A Critique of Jesus. Platinum Post by Steve Clark
author: Diane
description: Presents a guest critique of Jesus' teachings and moral legacy prompted by Bertrand Russell's critique of Christianity.

title: Jesus, Eyewitnesses, and Stories Floating Around….
author: BDEhrman
description: Challenges the claim that eyewitnesses carefully guarded Jesus traditions during the decades before the Gospels.
searchSummary: Argues that stories about Jesus spread rapidly through non-witnesses even during his lifetime and increasingly after his death. With roughly 97 percent of Palestinian Jews unable to write, traditions circulated mainly by speech; a modern experiment showed thirty-three witnesses' emotional experience reaching 881 people within three days through successive retellings. Eyewitnesses could not monitor every conversation or correction, so decades of oral circulation across expanding communities created abundant opportunities for change and invention.

title: May Gold Q&A Video
author: Diane
description: Shares the May Gold Q&A video in two parts.

title: More on Secret Mark as a Forgery (by Morton Smith?)
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues the case that Morton Smith may have forged the Secret Gospel of Mark letter attributed to Clement.

title: Did Morton Smith Forge the Secret Gospel of Mark?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces reasons for suspecting that Morton Smith forged the letter describing the Secret Gospel of Mark.

title: Blog Dinner in London on Monday June 12.  Interested?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a London blog dinner for members.

title: Was Jesus a Simplistic Person or an Extraordinary One? A Platinum Post by Omar Abur-Robb
author: Diane
description: Presents a guest reflection asking whether Jesus should be understood as an ordinary figure or an extraordinary founder of a movement.
searchSummary: Argues that Christianity's rapid movement from a Palestinian group into the Greco-Roman world suggests Jesus was an extraordinary teacher with charisma, leadership, storytelling ability, and determination. A fictional comparison with Chinese converts transforming Mormonism illustrates how improbable such cultural expansion appears. The guest author acknowledges limited evidence and scholarly disagreement but rejects the argument that sparse contemporary records disprove Jesus' exceptional qualities, since ancient documentation is incomplete and other influential figures such as Socrates also lack extensive surviving records.

title: Are *Groups* of Story Tellers (Think: Ancient Followers of Jesus) More Likely to Preserve Traditions Accurately than Individuals?
author: BDEhrman
description: Questions whether group storytelling contexts make oral traditions about Jesus historically reliable.
searchSummary: Argues that group storytelling does not protect traditions from distortion and may make collective memory less accurate. Dominant speakers can introduce misinformation that social pressure turns into persistent shared recollection. Theodore Weeden compared Kenneth Bailey's supposedly stable Middle Eastern oral stories with earlier written versions and found major changes in wording, events, and content, including a story identified as folklore. Modern group performance therefore cannot establish that early Christian communities controlled Jesus traditions or preserved them accurately over decades.

title: Back in the Saddle Again…
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a return from travel and plans to catch up on comments and member content.

title: Do Modern Mideastern Story Tellers Show How the Ancient Traditions of Jesus Were Circulated?
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques the use of modern Middle Eastern storytelling practices as evidence for accurate Gospel tradition.
searchSummary: Challenges Kenneth Bailey's proposal that communal storytelling preserved Jesus traditions because eyewitnesses corrected inaccurate retellings. Such supervision might operate within a village describing local events, but eyewitnesses were not stationed throughout Palestine or the Greek-speaking churches where stories circulated. Corinth illustrates the problem: Paul, Apollos, converts, and later believers repeatedly told Jesus stories without any known witness present, so informal correction could reflect shared versions rather than historically verified details.

title: Did Jesus Believe The End Would Come Within His Lifetime? Platinum Post by Rizwan Ahmed
author: Diane
description: Presents a guest argument about whether Jesus expected the end to come within Jesus' own generation.
searchSummary: Questions whether Jesus taught that the end would occur within his generation while accepting that he was an apocalyptic prophet. A guest writer argues that the explicit sayings all derive from Mark, lack independent attestation, and may project early Christian expectations based on Jesus' resurrection back onto Jesus himself. The post concludes that evidence for a lifetime deadline is weak and that distinguishing imminent judgment from an explicitly generational prediction changes how Jesus' ethical teaching and prophetic accuracy are evaluated.

title: Do Modern Mideastern Customs of Story Telling Show that the Gospels Are Accurate?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates claims that modern Middle Eastern storytelling customs support the historical accuracy of Gospel traditions.

title: More Problems with Thinking Jesus’ Followers Memorized the Stories about Him
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains problems with the theory that Jesus' disciples memorized sayings and stories with rabbinic precision.
searchSummary: Rejects the theory that Jesus' disciples memorized and transmitted his words and deeds verbatim. Mark says Jairus approached Jesus before his daughter died, while Matthew says she was already dead; treating these as two separate resurrections only protects the theory from contrary evidence. More broadly, the Gospels contain extensive differences and were written decades later by educated Greek-speaking Christians, not Jesus' Aramaic-speaking peasant disciples. Stories circulated among distant believers with no eyewitness contact, making universal memorization implausible.

title: My New Online Course on Paul and Jesus!
author: Diane
description: Announces an online course comparing Paul and Jesus.

title: Didn’t the Disciples Memorize Jesus’ Teachings and Accounts of His Life?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the idea that disciples may have memorized Jesus traditions and explains why that solution is historically problematic.
searchSummary: Examines Birger Gerhardsson's claim that Jesus trained his disciples to memorize teachings verbatim as later rabbis did. The proposal makes oral Gospel tradition appear controlled, but it projects practices from the Mishnah and Talmud, written centuries later, into Jesus' lifetime before rabbinic Judaism had developed. The Gospels never show Jesus drilling disciples, transmitting an oral law, or requiring exact repetition. With little first-century evidence, later rabbinic pedagogy cannot demonstrate that Jesus traditions were memorized or preserved word for word.

title: Was Jesus Literate or Illiterate? A Platinum Post by Omar Abur-Robb
author: Diane
description: Presents a guest discussion of whether Jesus was likely literate in light of Galilean poverty and literacy rates.
searchSummary: A Platinum guest post challenges the default assumption that Jesus was an illiterate Galilean peasant. Omar Abur-Robb points to Nazareth's proximity to larger communities, Gospel portrayals of Jesus reading, teaching, debating, and citing Scripture, and later Jewish traditions crediting him with learned arguments. The post proposes that Jesus may have come from a financially stable family able to support education, while acknowledging that the evidence is probabilistic and can be interpreted in competing ways.

title: Stories of Jesus Passed on By Word of Mouth.  When Scholars First Took Oral Traditions Seriously.
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how form critics began treating Gospel stories as oral traditions shaped before being written.
searchSummary: Explains how form critics recognized the Gospels as collections of oral stories rather than eyewitness records. They classified recurring forms such as healings and controversies and examined each form's “situation in life,” arguing that communities reshaped Jesus traditions to address worship, conflict, evangelism, and other present needs. Although later scholars reject some of their skepticism, the central insight remains: anonymous authors decades removed from Jesus inherited oral memories whose forms reveal both possible history and community interpretation.

title: Does Mark Present the Bare-Bones Facts about Jesus’ Life?
author: BDEhrman
description: Challenges the older scholarly view that Mark preserves a bare-bones factual account of Jesus' life.
searchSummary: Explains why Mark cannot be treated as a bare record of Jesus' life despite being the earliest and tersest Gospel. William Wrede showed that commands to conceal Jesus' messianic identity form a theological explanation for why he was not recognized as Messiah during his ministry. Later form critics argued that Mark created the narrative framework around independent stories inherited through oral tradition. The Gospel therefore combines theology, editorial arrangement, and circulating memories rather than providing an unembellished historical biography.

title: Was Levi of Alphaeus the “the Beloved Disciple”? Platinum Post by Gregory Hartzler-Miller, MATS
author: Diane
description: Presents a guest redaction-critical proposal about Levi of Alphaeus, the beloved disciple, and the Gospel of Peter.
searchSummary: Presents a speculative redaction-critical argument that Levi son of Alphaeus may underlie John's unnamed Beloved Disciple. The proposal links Matthew's replacement or obscuring of Markan characters, John's "other disciple" and three Marys at the cross, and the Gospel of Peter's fragmentary ending, where Levi accompanies Peter after the resurrection. By reading these details as deliberate literary echoes, the guest author suggests that later Gospel writers transformed and concealed Levi's identity, while acknowledging that the theory departs from scholarly consensus.

title: How Can We Get Behind “False Memories” of Jesus to the Historical Facts?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how scholars tried to get behind false memories of Jesus by privileging Mark's Gospel.
searchSummary: Traces how scholars came to regard Gospel traditions as distorted memories shaped during oral transmission before the evangelists wrote. Contradictions among canonical accounts show that some stories were altered or invented, leading form critics to investigate traditions behind the texts. Nineteenth-century solutions first privileged Mark as the earliest, least embellished, and supposedly most historical Gospel, supported by Markan priority and the reconstruction of Q. The post leaves that solution open for subsequent examination rather than endorsing Mark as straightforward history.

title: Did Early Christians “Invent” Memories of Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces false social memories as a way to think about invented or reshaped memories of Jesus.
searchSummary: Surveys theories about how early Christians developed memories of Jesus. Reimarus accused the disciples of inventing resurrection claims, form critics argued communities reshaped or created stories for their needs, and Gerhardsson proposed controlled memorization of Jesus' teachings. The post favors an oral process: converts across the Roman world told and retold Jesus traditions during evangelism, instruction, worship, baptism, and encouragement for decades before the Gospels. These circulated stories became each community's memory of Jesus and could change without deliberate fabrication.

title: Jesus’ Resurrection: A Challenging Hypothetical.  Guest Post by Ryan Fleming
author: admin
description: Presents a guest hypothetical designed to test arguments about whether Jesus was raised from the dead.

title: The Father and the Son. A Platinum Post by Omar Abur-Robb
author: Diane
description: Presents a guest exploration of when Christians began calling God Father and how that language relates to later Trinitarian thought.

title: How Can We “Remember” Someone (say, Jesus) We Never Knew?
author: BDEhrman
description: Clarifies why memory can include inherited social recollections rather than only firsthand personal experience.
searchSummary: Defends using “memory” for knowledge beyond experienced events. Psychologists distinguish episodic memory of experiences from semantic memory of learned facts, and either can be false. Sociologists also study collective memory, in which social groups construct recollections of shared people and events. Christians therefore can remember Jesus without having met him, just as communities remember political leaders or wars. Gospel traditions may be true or false semantic and collective memories shaped by the identities and circumstances of the groups preserving them.

title: In What Sense is a Made-Up Story about Jesus a False *Memory*??
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how invented or reshaped Gospel stories can still function as false memories of Jesus within a community.
searchSummary: Explains why an invented Gospel story still becomes a false memory once communities accept and transmit it as Jesus' past. Luke's historically implausible census journey to Bethlehem may have been inherited or created by Luke; either way, millions remembered Jesus' birth through that narrative. The post distinguishes reliable gist memories of Jesus' final week from questionable details and episodes. Determining who first fabricated a tradition is less important to memory analysis than examining how it entered circulation and became recollection.

title: Dr. Bart D. Ehrman, Apostle to the Atheists. A Platinum Post by Robert Droney
author: Diane
description: Presents a guest objection to the label Christian atheist and its implications for faith, unbelief, and conversion.

title: Blog Announcement:  Comments!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a temporary pause in comment responses during travel while scheduled blog posts continue.

title: Creation Stories of the Ancient World (Part 2): An Ancient Egyptian Account
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Genesis with an ancient Egyptian creation account to ask how Israelite creation traditions fit their ancient context.

title: May Gold Q&A:  Submit your questions!
author: Diane
description: Announces the May Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: Does Understanding “Memory” Have Any Bearing on the Study of the Historical Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why memory studies matter for evaluating Gospel traditions about the historical Jesus.
searchSummary: Connects psychological, sociological, and oral-memory research with historical Jesus study. Memory reconstructs scattered traces rather than replaying a stored recording, so gaps can produce faulty or false recollections. Early Christians remembered legendary events, while collective-memory analysis asks both whether shared traditions are accurate and what versions reveal about the communities preserving them. Studying oral transmission then addresses how such memories changed before writing. These approaches supplement historical criticism by explaining both distortion and the social meaning of remembered Jesus traditions.

title: Was Matthew Attacking Paul?
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Matthew's Gospel appears to resist a major element of Paul's message about Jewish Law.
searchSummary: Argues that Matthew's teaching about Jewish law conflicts sharply with Paul's insistence that gentile believers must not adopt Torah observance. Both connect salvation with Jesus' death and resurrection, but Matthew presents Jesus declaring that every command remains valid and that followers must practice and teach the Law. The post cannot determine whether Matthew knew Paul or his writings, yet concludes that Matthew opposes a major Pauline position that had probably circulated more broadly among Christians.

title: The Road From the “Duo of Philo” to the “Trinity of Nicaea” A Platinum Post by Omar Abur-Robb
author: Diane
description: Presents a guest proposal connecting Philo's thought with the later development of Nicene Trinitarian doctrine.
searchSummary: Omar Abur-Robb proposes that Greek metaphysics shaped Christian movement from Philo's distinction between God and the Logos toward Nicene Trinitarian doctrine. He traces this through Justin's Father, Son, and Spirit, Arius's subordinate created Son, and Alexander's coeternal Son equal with the Father. He argues that institutional stability and Constantine's desire for unity favored Alexander at Nicaea, though several links in the reconstruction are explicitly presented as assumptions.

title: Remembering Columbus, Remembering Christ
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses collective memory of Columbus to illustrate how societies can remember famous figures, including Jesus, in distorted ways.
searchSummary: Uses changing portrayals of Christopher Columbus to illustrate how collective memory reflects present values. Earlier Americans celebrated a discoverer and civilizer, while later accounts emphasize colonization, enslavement, violence, and Indigenous destruction. The issue is choosing one portrait but recognizing why communities remember selectively. Early Christians likewise transmitted Jesus stories orally for forty to sixty-five years through uncertain chains of eyewitnesses and storytellers. Those memories can help reconstruct Jesus while revealing the interests of the communities that reshaped them.

title: How Do We “Remember”  Lincoln?
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Abraham Lincoln to explain collective memory and its relevance for later Christian memories of Jesus.
searchSummary: Uses Abraham Lincoln's changing reputation to explain collective memory. Although celebrated as a civil-rights champion, Lincoln expressed views opposing racial equality, and his image rose and shifted after death as national needs changed, especially during the modern civil-rights movement. Communities reconstruct the past by selecting morally useful features for present concerns without fabricating everything. The same process can shape Christian memories of Jesus: traditions may preserve history while emphasizing, omitting, or distorting elements that serve a community's identity and values.

title: When I Got Seriously Interested in Memory (at least insofar as I remember)
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the personal and scholarly experiences that led to sustained work on memory and Jesus traditions.
searchSummary: Describes experiences that led Ehrman to study memory. His uneven episodic recall, including forgetting an earlier visit to Crete, raised questions about why different memory systems succeed or fail. Professionally, he wanted to understand eyewitness recollection and decades of oral Jesus tradition. Rather than begin with New Testament scholarship, he studied cognitive psychology and legal research directly, including false and repressed memories and DNA exonerations that exposed mistaken eyewitness testimony, before evaluating biblical scholars' use of that evidence.

title: Did The Twelve Become Only Three? Platinum post by Douglas Wadeson MD
author: Diane
description: Considers whether most of the Twelve may have left the Jesus movement after Jesus' death rather than continuing as Acts assumes.

title: My Forgotten Book on Memory
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on Jesus Before the Gospels as an underappreciated book about memory, eyewitnesses, and Gospel traditions.
searchSummary: Reintroduces Jesus Before the Gospels as a study of memory's implications for Gospel history. Memory reconstructs distributed traces rather than replaying a mental recording, allowing gaps, substitutions, and false recollections. The book combines cognitive psychology, eyewitness research, sociology of collective memory, and anthropology of oral cultures. These fields help assess whether Jesus traditions preserve events accurately and explain why Christian groups remembered him differently. Mnemohistory studies what those memories reveal about the communities that created and shared them.

title: And Here’s My Final Exam on The Birth of Christianity
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a final exam from a course on Christian developments after the New Testament through Constantine.
searchSummary: Reproduces the final examination for Ehrman's course on Christianity between the New Testament and Constantine. Short identifications test knowledge of early groups, writers, persecutions, doctrines, practices, and noncanonical texts. Two essays require students to assess the evidence for Constantine's conversion and explain one early Christian work in detail, showing how the course combines historical developments with close study of writings such as the Gospel of Thomas, Gospel of Mary, and Coptic Apocalypse of Peter.

title: Was Jesus a False Prophet?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a podcast episode asking whether Jesus should be understood as a failed apocalyptic prophet.
searchSummary: Introduces a podcast discussion of whether Jesus was a false prophet because he predicted God's kingdom within his generation and the expected end did not occur. The episode considers what apocalyptic prophecy meant in its ancient setting, how Jesus resembled and differed from contemporary prophets, whether he anticipated crucifixion, and how Gospel writers and later Christians handled the failed timetable. It also asks whether a demonstrably mistaken prediction makes Christian faith unreasonable or requires a different understanding of Jesus.

title: Wanna Take My Final Exam In New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a final exam from an Introduction to the New Testament course.
searchSummary: Presents an undergraduate New Testament final that combines concise identifications with evidence-based essays. The terms assess biblical, historical, literary, and textual-critical knowledge, while the essays ask students to evaluate a Gospel's historical accuracy, argue whether Jesus was an apocalyptic prophet, compare early Christian views of Judaism, or reconstruct problems addressed in one of Paul's undisputed letters. Ehrman explains how advance essay choices allow preparation while the examination still requires broad command of the course.

title: Good Friday or Easter?  CNN OpEd
author: Diane
description: Summarizes a CNN op-ed contrasting Christian focus on Easter glory with the suffering emphasized on Good Friday.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's Easter CNN essay contrasting Christians' attraction to resurrection glory with the demanding suffering represented by Good Friday. The Gospels portray Jesus embracing death and teaching followers to serve others despite the cost, while Revelation culminates with a conquering Christ and saints ruling a golden city with force. Ehrman argues that church attendance and popular preference reveal a desire for triumph over sacrifice, mirroring the New Testament canon's movement from the suffering Jesus to visions of domination.

title: Is 2 Thessalonians a Forgery?  From 132 CE?  Platinum Guest Post by Omar Robb
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest argument that 2 Thessalonians may be a forgery connected with the Bar Kokhba revolt.
searchSummary: Proposes that a Thessalonian Christian forged Second Thessalonians during the Bar Kokhba revolt around 132 CE. The guest author suggests that some Jewish Christians may have identified the victorious rebel leader as the returning Messiah, prompting a priest to invoke Paul and insist that Jesus could return only after the man of lawlessness appeared. The scenario is speculative, but it attempts to connect the letter's apocalyptic warning with a specific crisis before its mid-second-century attestation.

title: “Death is nothing to us.”  What Do YOU Think?
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Epicurus to invite reflection on whether death should be feared.
searchSummary: Explains Epicurus's argument that death should not be feared because it can never be experienced by the person who dies. Humans and their souls consist of atoms that disperse at death, while the uninvolved gods neither punish nor reward them; meaningful pleasure therefore lies in friendship, thought, simple enjoyment, health, and freedom from bodily and mental pain rather than reckless indulgence. Accepting mortality removes needless religious anxiety and helps people enjoy the limited life they actually possess.

title: My Best Best-Selling Fluke
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on why Misquoting Jesus unexpectedly became a bestselling book about New Testament manuscripts.
