searchSummary: Recounts the unlikely chain of media events that turned Misquoting Jesus, a book about Greek New Testament manuscripts, into Ehrman's best-selling trade book. A scheduling mistake placed him on both national radio programs, prompting a Washington Post profile that led to a Daily Show interview with Jon Stewart. That exposure sent the book to number one on Amazon and number five on the New York Times list, launching his trade-book career through timing and publicity rather than a repeatable formula.

title: A Scandalous Discovery of a Scandalous Gospel?
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts Morton Smith's reported discovery of the letter describing the Secret Gospel of Mark.
searchSummary: Describes Morton Smith's account of finding a purported letter of Clement of Alexandria that quotes a Secret Gospel of Mark. Clement says Mark produced a spiritual edition in Alexandria, later altered by the Carpocratians, and preserves a story of Jesus raising and privately teaching a lightly clothed young man. The passage resembles Lazarus and the rich young man while suggesting homoerotic overtones, although Clement rejects the explicit phrase "naked man with naked man" as a Carpocratian corruption.

searchSummary: Introduces Michael Shermer's podcast conversation with Ehrman about Armageddon: What the Bible Really Says About the End. Ehrman notes their parallel biographies: both converted to evangelical Christianity as teenagers, attended conservative Christian colleges, and later left the faith. Shermer's work on the history of science, religious skepticism, and Skeptic Magazine frames their discussion, which Ehrman describes as unusually interesting and shares with permission rather than summarizing its particular arguments in the post.

searchSummary: James Tabor explains how David Koresh interpreted Revelation's seven seals during the Waco siege. Koresh saw himself as the second messianic Lamb who could unlock Scripture and feared the deaths after the federal raid placed his community within the fifth seal's martyrdom sequence. Apocalyptic interpretation joined fixed text, inspired interpreter, and changing context; aggressive government tactics unintentionally confirmed Koresh's Babylon narrative, while discrepancies in timing and location left an opening that informed negotiation might have used peacefully.

title: The Discovery of a Lifetime: A Secret Gospel of Mark?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Secret Gospel of Mark controversy as either a major manuscript discovery or a modern forgery.
searchSummary: Recounts Morton Smith's claimed 1958 discovery of a previously unknown letter attributed to Clement of Alexandria at Mar Saba monastery. While cataloguing its neglected library, Smith found an eighteenth-century handwritten copy on blank pages in an old printed volume of Ignatius. Because no personal correspondence from Clement was otherwise known, the find promised a lost early Christian document. The post sets up the letter's quotation of a potentially scandalous Secret Gospel of Mark without yet assessing authenticity.

author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a lecture on the history of the rapture and the modern Left Behind expectation.
searchSummary: Announces a lecture tracing the history and consequences of belief in the rapture. Ehrman recalls expecting an imminent rapture, tribulation, Antichrist, and destruction of the world during his evangelical years, then argues that this end-time scenario is not actually taught in the Bible. The lecture explains where the doctrine originated, why millions of Christians continue to expect it, and what social and personal harm can follow from believing that the end is near.

title: How Does An Author Write a Bestseller?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why bestsellers usually result from publishing circumstances and readership response rather than authorial planning.
searchSummary: Explains why literary quality and conventional advertising alone rarely make a trade book a New York Times bestseller. Major publishers can improve a book's chances, but sales are driven chiefly by media attention, influential interviews, podcasts, and recommendations that expose the work to large audiences. Ehrman describes publicity for Armageddon while emphasizing how unusual bestseller success remains among hundreds of daily releases; authors should do their best without expecting any particular book to break through.

title: Biblical Prophecy and the Coming Destruction of the Dome of the Rock
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how some evangelical readings of prophecy connect Israel, the Dome of the Rock, and end-times expectations.
searchSummary: Explains how evangelical end-time interpretation shapes support for Israeli control of Jerusalem. Revelation's sealed remnant of Israel is understood as Jews converted to Jesus, while 2 Thessalonians requires a lawless Antichrist to occupy a rebuilt temple before Christ returns. Because the Dome of the Rock stands on the Temple Mount, believers conclude it must be removed and Israel must control the site. These expectations have influenced evangelical political mobilization and Israeli efforts to secure American Christian support.

title: The Coming Apocalypse and U.S. Foreign Policy on Israel

title: The Apocalypse and the Situation in Ukraine: Interview with a Ukrainian Christian Scholar
author: BDEhrman

searchSummary: Introduces Ukrainian scholar Mikhail Abakumov's interview with Ehrman about Armageddon after Russia's invasion forced Abakumov from Donetsk to Poland. The conversation includes Abakumov's account of how Ukrainian Christians understand the book's apocalyptic subject differently from Americans, alongside his theological studies and refugee assistance. Ehrman found the exchange compelling enough to interview Abakumov in return for Misquoting Jesus, while this post shares the earlier program hosted and published by Abakumov.

title: REVELATION, A Novel.  Excerpts from Blog Guest Poster Gary McCarragher
author: Diane
description: Shares excerpts from Gary McCarragher's novel Revelation, centered on a New Testament scholar with a fundamentalist past.
searchSummary: Presents the opening chapters of Gary McCarragher's novel Revelation, centered on New Testament scholar Bart Trask and his conservative Christian family. Trask returns home to announce a general-audience book about Jesus and seek permission to conduct public lectures in a nearby church. His plan provokes conflict with his brother over faith, evidence, family loyalty, and whether historical scholarship about Jesus necessarily threatens evangelical belief.

title: Of COURSE the Rapture is in the New Testament — There for all to see!  Right?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why many Christians think the rapture is taught in the New Testament and where the idea comes from.

title: Is The Rapture in the New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether the rapture is found in the New Testament or is a later apocalyptic interpretation.
searchSummary: Introduces the claim that the popular rapture doctrine is absent from Revelation and emerged only with John Nelson Darby in the 1830s. Fundamentalist interpretation nevertheless convinced many readers that Revelation predicts an imminent twenty-first-century evacuation of believers. First Thessalonians describes dead and living Christians rising to meet Jesus as he descends, but Paul addresses concern that deceased believers might miss God's approaching kingdom. Ehrman prepares to explain why this passage does not teach the later pre-tribulation rapture system.

title: Was the Roman Soldier Pantera Jesus’ Father? His Cousin? Platinum Guest Post by Omar Abur-Robb
author: admin
description: Presents a guest discussion of James Tabor's claims about Pantera and traditions concerning Jesus' father.

title: Armageddon Has Arrived!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the publication of Armageddon and reflects on a long-standing interest in Revelation.
searchSummary: Introduces Armageddon and Ehrman's revised interpretation of Revelation. He rejects both evangelical claims that it predicts imminent modern events and liberal portrayals of it as a comforting metaphor of hope. Revelation instead celebrates God's wrath, catastrophic violence, vengeance, and domination, saving obedient followers while destroying nearly everyone else, without mentioning divine love. The book compares this agenda with Jesus' teachings on love, nonretaliation, poverty, and service and traces harmful psychological, political, military, and environmental consequences of modern apocalyptic belief.

title: Why Would an Atheist Be Obsessed with Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why an atheist scholar remains fascinated by the disparity between the historical Jesus and the divine Christ whose worship transformed Western civilization.
searchSummary: Explains why Jesus remains central to Ehrman's work after his departure from Christianity. Beyond Jesus' historical influence, Ehrman is fascinated by the gap between an apocalyptic Jewish preacher who did not claim divinity and the divine Christ proclaimed after his death. That proclamation enabled Gentile conversion, Christianity's expansion, Constantine's adoption of the faith, and its formative influence on Western civilization, making the process by which Jesus became God historically decisive.

title: You Have No Right To Question Why You Suffer. What???
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines God's response to Job and whether it offers a satisfying answer to undeserved suffering.
searchSummary: Interprets God's whirlwind speeches as a refusal to explain Job's innocent suffering rather than a satisfying answer to it. God overwhelms Job with divine power, demands submission, and treats the desire for rational justification as presumptuous, even though Job has committed no wrongdoing. Ehrman rejects readings based on hidden guilt, cosmic perspective, or divine distraction and asks whether omnipotence makes cruelty just, since an unaccountable God who may torment innocents appears to place might above moral right.

title: Creation Stories of the Ancient World (Part 1): On Enuma Elish and Genesis 1  Guest Post by Joseph Lam
author: BDEhrman

title: Does God Punish Those Who Do *Right*?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores Job's dispute with friends who wrongly insist that suffering proves moral guilt.
searchSummary: Traces Job's defense against friends who insist his suffering proves secret sin. Job knows he is innocent, depicts God as a violent attacker, observes that wicked people prosper without later judgment, and refuses to confess offenses he did not commit. Although divine power would prevent a fair hearing, Job demands an audience and preserves his integrity; Elihu then repeats the punishment theory before God appears, setting up the poem's confrontation between innocent suffering and unanswerable authority.

author: BDEhrman

searchSummary: Promotes prepublication orders for Armageddon while reproducing its substantive preface. Ehrman rejects futuristic readings that map Revelation onto modern events and liberal readings that reduce it to hope for sufferers. He argues that the book centers divine wrath, mass violence, obedient servitude, and domination rather than love, sharply contrasting with Jesus' teaching on service and nonretaliation. Modern apocalyptic interpretation has also encouraged trauma, political violence, foreign-policy distortions, environmental fatalism, and inaction during real global crises.

title: Is the God of Job Worthy of Worship?
author: BDEhrman
description: Questions whether the God portrayed in Job's folktale is morally worthy of worship.
searchSummary: Critiques the prose tale's explanation that innocent suffering tests whether devotion to God is genuine. God authorizes Job's undeserved losses, illness, and children's deaths to answer the Satan's challenge, and later replacement children cannot undo those murders or make individuals interchangeable. Although interpreting hardship as a test may provide endurance, Ehrman argues that a deity who tortures innocents to prove loyalty may inspire fear but is not morally worthy of praise or worship.

author: BDEhrman

title: The Voice at Jesus’ Baptism–An Intriguing Version in the Gospel of the Ebionites
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the Gospel of the Ebionites to compare different versions of the heavenly voice at Jesus' baptism.
searchSummary: Examines how the fragmentary Gospel of the Ebionites reconciles conflicting versions of the heavenly voice at Jesus' baptism. Matthew, Mark, and an early form of Luke give different wording, while the noncanonical Gospel has the voice speak three times and deliver each version. Ehrman presents this ingenious but implausible solution as possible evidence that the work harmonized canonical traditions, while explaining the uncertainty surrounding the three reconstructed Jewish-Christian Gospels.

title: Is the Gospel of Mark in Papias Our Gospel of Mark?
author: BDEhrman
description: Questions whether Papias was referring to the canonical Mark and Matthew when discussing Gospel origins.
searchSummary: Argues that Papias does not clearly identify the canonical Gospels of Matthew and Mark or provide reliable evidence for their traditional authorship. His Matthew is a Hebrew sayings collection unlike the surviving Greek narrative, while his claims about Mark as Peter's complete and accurate interpreter do not fit the canonical Gospel. Papias also preserves fantastic stories about Judas and miraculous abundance, showing that his guarantees of carefully remembered truth cannot justify selectively trusting his authorship traditions.

title: Who Wrote the Gospels?  Our Earliest (Apparent) Reference
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Papias as an early source often used in arguments about Gospel authorship.
searchSummary: Introduces Papias as the earliest apparent source connecting Gospels with Matthew and Mark while explaining why his testimony is uncertain. Writing around 120–130 CE, Papias reports traditions received through several intermediaries: Mark accurately recorded Peter's preaching without order, and Matthew composed sayings in Hebrew. Because no surviving fragment quotes either Gospel and Papias's descriptions do not clearly fit the canonical books, the evidence cannot establish that those books already carried their familiar names.

title: Did Mark Write Mark?  What the Apostolic Fathers Say
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Apostolic Fathers evidence for the claim that Mark wrote the Gospel of Mark.
searchSummary: Introduces the difficulty of using Papias to prove that John Mark wrote the second Gospel. The canonical Gospels are anonymous, and earlier Apostolic Fathers quote or combine Gospel traditions without naming Matthew, Mark, Luke, or John or invoking eyewitness authorship. Examples from 1 Clement, the Didache, Ignatius, and Polycarp show this consistent silence. Papias is the possible exception, but his fragmentary testimony requires careful evaluation before it can establish the authorship of Mark or Matthew.

title: Seeing the Problem of Suffering as a PROBLEM
author: BDEhrman
description: Frames the problem of suffering as a conflict among claims about God's power, God's love, and human pain.
searchSummary: Develops theodicy as the unresolved tension among divine power, divine love, and actual suffering, especially the suffering of righteous people. Biblical punishment and later afterlife explanations address some cases but not others, while Epicurus framed the dilemma long before the Enlightenment. The Ethiopian famine forced Ehrman's students beyond detached theorizing, and he evaluates free will and Leibniz's best-possible-world defense alongside Voltaire's critique that senseless misery makes such optimism implausible.

title: Is Suffering a “Problem” for Believers?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why suffering becomes a serious problem for believers in an all-powerful and loving God.
searchSummary: Explains how teaching biblical views of suffering first made theodicy a serious problem for Ehrman while he was still a Christian pastor. Biblical authors offer divergent explanations, including punishment, hostile cosmic powers, testing, unknowable mystery, and resignation, rather than one consistent answer. The classical conflict among an all-powerful God, an all-loving God, and real suffering leads some thinkers to limit divine power or love, deny suffering, or seek additional explanations for why the innocent suffer.

title: Wait, Was Jesus Married?  Guest Post by Kyle Smith
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines how Gospel accounts of Martha and Mary were conflated in later interpretation and used to portray Mary as Christ's devoted bride.

title: How Does Something “Mean”
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses an everyday misunderstanding to introduce how meaning depends on context, inference, and interpretation.
searchSummary: Argues that words and actions acquire meaning from their literary, cultural, and historical contexts. Taking a neighbor's newspaper, burning incense, or raising a finger can signify opposite things under different circumstances; biblical discussions of same-sex relations likewise arose within assumptions unlike modern ones. Applying ancient statements directly today without contextual translation enables selective use of scripture for present agendas. Responsible interpretation first asks what a text or action meant in its own world before considering contemporary relevance.

title: How Theologians and Historians Approach the Same Bible Differently.  Guest Post by Daniel Kohanski
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest explanation of how historians and theologians ask different questions of the same biblical texts.
searchSummary: Contrasts theological and historical approaches to biblical claims. Theology begins with Scripture's divine truth and reasons from that premise, while history withholds assumptions, prefers natural explanations, and treats conclusions as probable and revisable. Joshua stopping the sun illustrates the difference: historians examine the story as a claim shaped by Assyrian religious symbolism rather than evidence of a cosmic miracle. Once theology asserts historical fact, Kohanski argues, its claims become subject to ordinary historical scrutiny.

title: Do You Want to Discuss the Movie Tár with World-Renowned Conductor Gisele Ben-Dor?  Blog Fundraiser for Earthquake Victims in Turkey/Syria
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a fundraiser for earthquake victims in Turkey and Syria built around a discussion of the film Tár.
searchSummary: Organizes a discussion of the film Tár with internationally renowned conductor Gisele Ben-Dor to raise emergency funds after the earthquake in Turkey and Syria. Participants can watch the film beforehand, hear Ben-Dor assess its portrayal of conducting and abusive power, and join a live question session hosted by Bart. Suggested donations support Doctors Without Borders, while larger gifts qualify for signed advance books or a private conversation and all readers may donate without attending.

author: BDEhrman

title: An Intriguing Anti-Jewish Variant:  Did Jesus Pray “Father forgive them”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines the textual variant in Luke where Jesus prays for forgiveness from the cross and its anti-Jewish implications.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus' prayer for his executioners in Luke 23:34 was original to the Gospel but removed by some early Christian scribes. Its themes of prayer, forgiveness, ignorance, and Jesus' composure fit Luke, while its wording does not resemble a scribal harmonization with Stephen's prayer in Acts. Growing anti-Jewish polemic supplied a motive for omission because Christians understood Jesus as forgiving Jewish leaders whom they believed God had punished.

title: Anti-Jewish Alterations of the New Testament Writings?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how some scribes altered New Testament texts in ways that intensified anti-Jewish readings.

title: New Testament Manuscripts That Reveal Later Theological Controversies
author: BDEhrman
description: Shows how New Testament manuscripts can reveal later theological disputes as well as earlier textual forms.

title: My New Online Course on the Gospel of Mark!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces an online course on the Gospel of Mark.
searchSummary: Introduces a course designed to correct the view that Mark is merely a short, unsophisticated version of Matthew and Luke. Its lectures examine Mark's paradoxical suffering Messiah, universal failure to understand Jesus, possible claims to divinity, historical reliability, sources, and intentional scribal changes. The course asks how Mark's distinctive literary and theological portrait shapes Jesus' life and death, distinguishing the evangelist's message from a simple chronological record while offering lectures, questions, and further readings.

title: New Testament Manuscripts as Windows into Early Christian History
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses manuscript changes to show how the New Testament text can illuminate early Christian history.
searchSummary: Argues that New Testament manuscripts illuminate early Christian social history as well as the wording of lost originals. Scribal changes can reveal the theological and social pressures surrounding heresy, anti-Judaism, and women's authority, while manuscript dates, origins, and physical features inform studies of magic, mission, literacy, and the use of texts. Ehrman therefore treats later readings not merely as errors to discard but as evidence of what particular Christian communities read, interpreted, and contested.

title: February Gold Q&A:  Go for the Gold!
author: BDEhrman

title: Was the Roman Soldier Pantera Jesus’ Father? His Cousin? Platinum Guest Post by Omar Abur-Robb
author: BDEhrman

title: Finally: The Martyrdom of Polycarp as a Clever Christian Forgery
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that the Martyrdom of Polycarp is a clever Christian forgery advancing theological claims through false authorship.
searchSummary: Concludes that the Martyrdom of Polycarp is a later forgery written as eyewitness testimony. Its developed veneration of relics fits the third century better than Polycarp's lifetime, while an implausible colophon invents a chain through Irenaeus and a miraculous rediscovery by Pionius to explain the text's late appearance. The author used alleged firsthand authority to validate a legendary narrative promoting proper martyrdom, opposing Jews and voluntary martyrdom, and affirming God's support for orthodox martyrs.

title: January 2023 Gold Q&A (Video)
author: Diane
description: Shares the January 2023 Gold Q&A video.

title: Evidence of Forgery.  More Reasons the Martyrdom of Polycarp Was Not Written by Someone There
author: BDEhrman
description: Gives additional reasons for doubting that the Martyrdom of Polycarp was written by an eyewitness.
searchSummary: Identifies historical and literary evidence that the Martyrdom of Polycarp was not written by a witness. Its unsuitable stadium, unrealistic trial, incompatible official dates, miraculous details, and close imitation of Jesus' passion indicate later legend rather than observation. The text also condemns voluntary martyrdom while presenting developed concepts of martyr identity that otherwise appear later, suggesting an author who projected later controversies backward and invoked eyewitness authority precisely to make the constructed account believable.

title: Do Eyewitnesses Prove Miracles?  Can They Be Faked?  The Martyrdom of Polycarp
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the Martyrdom of Polycarp to ask whether eyewitness claims can establish miracles or be fabricated.
searchSummary: Argues that the Martyrdom of Polycarp's eyewitness claims undermine rather than support its authenticity. The narrator invokes firsthand hearing, sight, or smell precisely for its least credible miracles: silent torture victims, a heavenly voice, flames arching around Polycarp, and a perfumed body that does not burn. This selective self-insertion functions as a literary guarantee meant to overcome reasonable doubt, suggesting a later author deliberately assumed eyewitness identity to authenticate miraculous claims.

title: Recreational Drugs in the New Testament?  Platinum Guest Post by Douglas Wadeson
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest discussion of possible psychoactive drug use in New Testament contexts, especially around John the Baptist.

title: Can We Take the Martyrdom of Polycarp at Face Value?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why scholars have questioned whether the Martyrdom of Polycarp is an authentic eyewitness account.
searchSummary: Reviews scholarly debate over whether the Martyrdom of Polycarp preserves an eyewitness account. Miracles, Gospel parallels, relic veneration, and apparently later terminology led some scholars to date it centuries after Polycarp, while another influential theory preserved a historical core by assigning problematic material to several redactors. Subsequent scholarship challenged that layered solution and treated the text more coherently, leaving unresolved historical problems that require evaluating the claimed witness rather than accepting a bare factual core by default.

title: Is the Martyrdom of Polycarp an Authentic Account?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether the Martyrdom of Polycarp is authentic or a later forged account.
searchSummary: Introduces the case that the Martyrdom of Polycarp is a later forgery rather than a contemporary eyewitness letter. The work names an alleged writer and carrier, supplies a miraculous chain of manuscript recovery, and presents Polycarp's death through apologetic, anti-Jewish, and anti-voluntary-martyr polemics. Its repeated parallels with Jesus' passion and claims of divine assistance show a crafted defense of Christianity, making the narrator's asserted presence a historical question to prove rather than a date to assume.

title: Was Moses High on Mt. Sinai?  Part 1   Platinum Post by Douglas Wadeson MD
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest proposal about psychoactive drug use in Hebrew Bible traditions surrounding Moses and Sinai.

title: More about the First Christian Martyr Text
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues an introduction to the Martyrdom of Polycarp and explains later reconsideration of its date and eyewitness claims.
searchSummary: Presents the earlier scholarly consensus that the Martyrdom of Polycarp was substantially unified and written soon after the event, while acknowledging major uncertainty about its integrity and date. Incompatible official dates, possible later chapters, miraculous additions, Gospel parallels, anti-Montanist themes, and differing manuscript endings complicate an eyewitness attribution. Ehrman notes that he later abandoned this widely held position, making the post a record of the traditional case rather than his final judgment.

author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Martyrdom of Polycarp as the earliest full Christian narrative devoted to martyrdom.

title: Vote on Your Favorite Platinum Post!
author: admin
description: Invites Platinum members to vote on recent guest posts.

title: A Spectacular Martyrdom and an Intriguing Textual Change
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces textual variants in the Martyrdom of Polycarp and other Apostolic Fathers writings.
searchSummary: Evaluates whether a dove originally emerged from Polycarp's body when he was martyred. Although Eusebius omits the bird, every surviving manuscript includes it, and the surrounding narrative already contains spectacular miracles. Ehrman suggests a scribe may have removed the dove because the account parallels Jesus' passion and could support a Gnostic separation of the divine Christ from the human Jesus. He retains the dove, showing how textual decisions directly determine what translators present.

title: The New Testament Ain’t the Only Text with Important Scribal Changes!
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains that scribal changes affect ancient Christian writings beyond the New Testament.
searchSummary: Explains how scribal changes affect the Apostolic Fathers just as they affect New Testament writings. Since the original manuscripts are lost and surviving copies disagree, editors must reconstruct earlier wording from separate and sometimes fragile textual traditions. A striking example in Ignatius's Letter to the Magnesians contrasts whether God's Word came from silence; the unusual Armenian reading may preserve the original because later scribes had a theological reason to alter language that sounded Gnostic.

title: Are the Gospels Anti-Jewish?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether the Gospels are anti-Jewish and distinguishes that ancient issue from modern anti-Semitism.
searchSummary: Distinguishes ancient Christian anti-Judaism, based on religion and customs, from modern racial anti-Semitism while tracing increasing Jewish blame in Gospel passion narratives. Across Mark, Luke, Matthew, and John, Pilate becomes progressively more reluctant or innocent as Jewish leaders and crowds assume greater responsibility for Jesus's execution. Later apocryphal traditions intensify this trajectory until Pilate can become a Christian saint, helping create theological hostility that produced discrimination and violence once Christians gained political power.

title: What’s So Hard about Translating Ancient Texts?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains practical difficulties in translating ancient texts, especially for the Apostolic Fathers.
searchSummary: Explains the many scholarly tasks required to publish a bilingual edition of ancient texts. An editor must reconstruct the original-language text, select meaningful manuscript variants for the apparatus, establish translation principles, render every passage carefully, and introduce each work and the collection. Ehrman recounts undertaking these demanding responsibilities for the Loeb Apostolic Fathers and later the Apocryphal Gospels, emphasizing how translation projects differ from writing conventional scholarly books.

title: Watching Notes for Jesus of Montreal!  (My Favorite Jesus Movie!)
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares viewing notes for a movie-club discussion of Jesus of Montreal.

title: What About Translations of Other Ancient Christian Writings?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why ancient Christian writings outside the Bible also require careful translation from original languages.
searchSummary: Explains why translating ancient Christian texts is necessarily an act of interpretation and introduces Ehrman's Loeb Apostolic Fathers project. The Loeb series places Greek or Latin beside English with a concise textual apparatus, while the Apostolic Fathers preserve the earliest proto-orthodox writings outside the New Testament. Replacing Kirsopp Lake's outdated edition required Ehrman to confront practical decisions that readers of translations or even scholars using original languages may not recognize.

title: Do All Modern Translators of the New Testament Translate the Same Greek Text?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains which Greek text modern New Testament translators use and why manuscripts matter for translation.
searchSummary: Explains that most modern New Testament translators use the same reconstructed Greek text produced by the United Bible Societies committee and shared with the Nestle-Aland edition. The UBS edition emphasizes major variants and confidence ratings for translators, while Nestle-Aland provides scholars a much fuller textual apparatus. Neither is inerrant: disputed readings remain, and translators sometimes choose alternatives to the printed text when manuscript evidence supports another judgment.

title: Armageddon!  My New Book on the Revelation of John.
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces Armageddon and summarizes its argument about Revelation's violence, influence, and interpretation.
searchSummary: Announces Armageddon and summarizes its challenge to two dominant readings of Revelation. The book addressed first-century Christians rather than predicting modern events, yet it is not simply a metaphor of hope: its language emphasizes God's wrath, vengeance, torment, and destruction of everyone outside his obedient followers. Ehrman traces the personal and social harm caused by futuristic readings and argues that John's violent form of Christianity conflicts with Jesus' teachings, inviting readers to ask whether Revelation is consistent with his gospel.

title: Do Public Debates Do Anyone Any Good?  What Do You Think?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on whether public debates clarify controversial issues or mostly reinforce existing views.
searchSummary: Uses dramatizations of the 1968 William Buckley-Gore Vidal television debates to ask whether public debates change minds or mainly entertain and intensify existing loyalties. Their exchanges attracted viewers and produced memorable conflict, yet did not resolve political divisions or determine electoral outcomes. Ehrman extends the question to presidential, policy, and religious debates, where audiences often judge rhetorical performance or seek confirmation. He invites readers to consider what winning means and whether expert debates produce practical intellectual benefit.

title: Paul and the Gospels: Platinum Guest Post by Ryan Fleming
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest proposal about the relationship between Paul's message and the Gospel traditions about Jesus.

title: Famous Passages that Are Not Original: How Do Modern Translators Deal with Them?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how modern translators handle famous New Testament passages that were probably added by later scribes.
searchSummary: Examines how the NRSV presents three famous passages scholars consider later additions: the Trinitarian formula in 1 John, the woman taken in adultery, and Mark's additional endings. The first appears only in a footnote, while the others remain in double brackets with notes. Ehrman argues that these conventions are too subtle and should tell ordinary readers directly that scribes added the passages rather than expecting them to decode editorial symbols.

title: Problems with the King James Version: What Were the Translators Translating?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how the King James Version depended on Greek texts based on late and limited manuscript evidence.
searchSummary: Explains why the King James New Testament contains passages absent from earlier manuscripts. Its translators relied on the Textus Receptus, derived largely from Erasmus's few late Greek witnesses, including a form of 1 John 5:7-8 apparently supplied from Latin to preserve an explicit Trinitarian statement. Later manuscript discoveries showed that this verse, the woman taken in adultery, and Mark's longer ending were scribal additions despite their familiarity and literary power.

title: Can We Trust the Bible?  The First Published (as opposed to Printed) Greek New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Traces the first published Greek New Testament and its importance for later Bible translation.
searchSummary: Recounts how Erasmus produced the first published Greek New Testament before the already printed Complutensian Polyglot appeared. Working quickly from a few late manuscripts, he back-translated missing Revelation verses from Latin, creating readings unattested in Greek witnesses. Nevertheless, his editions became the foundation for Western printed texts for three centuries, while later publishers largely reproduced them and Stephanus introduced manuscript notes and the verse divisions still used today.

title: My All-Time Favorite Jesus Movie.  Wanna Discuss It With Me?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a movie-club discussion of Jesus of Montreal.

title: What Is a Viable Christian Theology?  Platinum Guest Post by Joel Scheller
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest reflection on what could make Christian theology viable for modern sophisticated believers.
searchSummary: Proposes revising the Wesleyan Quadrilateral so modern Christian theology gives reason greater authority than Scripture, tradition, and communal experience. Joel Scheller argues that historical and textual scholarship exposes human elements, contradictions, and transmission problems in the Bible that Wesley could not evaluate, making unchanged scriptural priority inadequate. He further suggests adding conscience alongside reason as a fifth foundational element, allowing rational analysis and moral intuition to correct one another before shaping biblical interpretation, inherited doctrine, and Christian practice.

title: Can We Trust the Bible?  The First Printed Greek New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the first printed Greek New Testament and why printed editions matter for Bible translation.
searchSummary: Traces the first printed Greek New Testament to the Complutensian Polyglot organized by Cardinal Ximenes de Cisneros. Printing enabled standardized, inexpensive Bibles, but Western scholars initially privileged the Latin Vulgate and often lacked Greek. The multilingual project finished its New Testament in 1514 but was distributed only in 1522; the exact Greek manuscripts used remain uncertain, and a later report claimed the library sold ancient parchments for making fireworks.

title: What New Testament Do New Testament Translators Translate?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains that New Testament translators work from reconstructed Greek texts rather than a single manuscript.
searchSummary: Explains that New Testament translators work from an eclectic critical Greek text rather than any single manuscript. Textual scholars compare variant readings across many witnesses and choose the wording most likely written by each author, producing a reconstructed text no surviving manuscript exactly matches. Modern translators generally rely on the identical Greek text printed in the UBS and Nestle-Aland editions, whose differing apparatuses document the manuscript evidence behind disputed choices.

title: A FREEBIE for Gold and Platinum Members Only
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a free webinar for Gold and Platinum members after technical problems with Q&A postings.

title: Infamous Typos in the King James Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys famous typographical errors and revisions in editions of the King James Bible.

title: The King James Bible: Some Intriguing Word Choices
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines distinctive word choices in the King James Bible and how translation decisions shape meaning.
searchSummary: Explains why the King James Version, despite its immense literary importance, is unsuitable as a modern study Bible. Its underlying Greek manuscripts were late and flawed, while four centuries of language change have left many words, animal names, phrases, and sentences obscure or misleading. Ehrman supplies humorous and confusing examples to show that readers may either fail to understand the wording or confidently assign meanings the translators never intended.

title: Did Jesus Believe in Hell?  My Interview With Kevin Grant
author: Diane
description: Shares an interview with Kevin Grant about whether Jesus believed in hell.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's interview with Kevin Grant about Grant's book Did Jesus Believe in Hell? Their discussion presents shared historical and biblical reasons for rejecting the idea that Jesus taught eternal conscious torment. Grant addresses readers who may distrust Ehrman's books but remain open to a religiously sympathetic argument grounded in Scripture. The interview aims to reassure believers that they need not fear everlasting punishment while exploring the biblical language and later theological developments that produced conventional Christian teachings about hell.

title: If the King James Was Good Enough for Paul, It’s Good Enough for Me
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the King James Bible to introduce problems involved in producing modern Bible translations.
searchSummary: Introduces three reasons the King James Version can mislead modern Bible students: inferior underlying Greek manuscripts, occasional theological bias, and four centuries of English-language change. Ehrman focuses on familiar words whose seventeenth-century meanings differ sharply from current usage, including conversation, admiration, meat, prevent, quick, wealth, and careful. Such wording can produce coherent but incorrect interpretations even though the translation remains a landmark of English literature.

title: Just Follow That Star!
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why following the Bethlehem star in Matthew creates practical and astronomical problems.

title: Christmas Reflections 2022 (from ten years on)
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers a Christmas reflection on incarnation, human suffering, and the meaning of the season.
searchSummary: Reflects on Ehrman's enduring attraction to Christian ethics despite no longer believing the incarnation or divine intervention. A Christmas Eve service once intensified his anger at God's apparent silence amid suffering, but years later its ideals of humility, generosity, care for the marginalized, and self-sacrifice resonated more deeply than secular consumerism and self-interest. He wishes visible nonreligious communities cultivated these values as effectively as humble churches and finds the Christmas story morally meaningful as myth rather than historical reality.

title: O Little Town of Nazareth?
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Matthew and Luke on Bethlehem, Nazareth, and the theological aims of the birth narratives.
searchSummary: Compares Matthew and Luke's irreconcilable explanations for Jesus' birth in Bethlehem despite his known association with Nazareth. Matthew begins the family in Bethlehem and moves them after Herod's death, while Luke brings them from Nazareth for an implausible Roman census and quickly returns them home. The post concludes that both narratives were created to connect Jesus with Micah's Bethlehem prophecy and that Jesus was probably born in Nazareth.

title: Want to Watch/Discuss a Jesus Movie with Me?  The Blog Movie Club!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a blog movie-club discussion of Jesus of Montreal.

title: Instead of “From Nazareth” was Jesus a “Nazarite”??
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Jesus was called a Nazarite rather than being identified with the village of Nazareth.

title: Did Jesus Actually Come from Nazareth?
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Jesus most likely came from Nazareth despite the birth stories placing Jesus' birth in Bethlehem.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: Are You Willing To Give a Holiday Gift Membership To Someone Who Needs It??

title: Did Jesus Appear to 500 People After His Resurrection?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Paul's claim that more than five hundred people saw the risen Jesus at one time.

title: Did Christ Save *Everyone* When He Descended to Hades?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores the Harrowing of Hell and whether Christ's descent to Hades implied salvation for everyone there.
searchSummary: Examines whom Christ allegedly saved when he descended to Hades and whether his victory extended to every soul. Early theologians variously limited salvation to Israel's patriarchs and prophets, expanded it to righteous Jews and Gentiles, or claimed universal liberation while elsewhere preserving judgment and punishment. Ehrman shows how apparently absolute statements by Paul, Origen, and Cyril were qualified, while other Christians offered salvation to everyone who accepted Christ's preaching after death and opponents rejected any postmortem second chance.

title: Did Jesus Descend to Hell After He Died?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the tradition that Jesus descended to hell between death and resurrection.
searchSummary: Traces the origins and competing meanings of Christ's descent to Hades between his death and resurrection. Although the earliest creeds and Gospel narratives are silent, Acts, Ephesians, and especially 1 Peter encouraged speculation that Jesus preached salvation to the dead, rescued Israel's righteous, or defeated death and demonic powers. Writers from the Gospel of Peter through Justin, Marcion, Origen, Melito, and later theologians disagreed over his audience and purpose, producing the doctrine later called the Harrowing of Hell.

title: What Would the Apostle Paul Think of The Trinity?  Platinum Guest Post by Joel Scheller
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest argument about how Paul's Christology would compare with later Trinitarian doctrine.

title: The Mind-Body Problem As My Personal Dilemma.  What Do YOU Think?

title: December Gold Q&A
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the December Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: A Truly Great New Testament Scholar:  E. P. Sanders in Memoriam
author: BDEhrman
description: Remembers E. P. Sanders as a major New Testament scholar whose work reshaped the study of Jesus, Judaism, and Paul.

title: What about Forgeries IN the New Testament?  Is it Possible?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the possibility that some writings inside the New Testament may be forgeries.
searchSummary: Argues that Pauline forgeries circulated during the New Testament period and that some canonical books may themselves be forged. Second Thessalonians warns against a false Pauline letter yet is widely judged pseudonymous, illustrating how forgers condemned rival forgeries to appear authentic. Ancient Christians also disputed Revelation, Jude, 2 Peter, the Pastorals, and Hebrews on authorship grounds. Ehrman concludes that forgery was recognized and condemned within early Christianity even while deceptive writings entered circulation and, in some cases, the canon.

title: Forgeries in the Names of the Apostles: Some of the Most Interesting
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys early Christian writings falsely attributed to apostles across Gospels, Acts, letters, and apocalypses.
searchSummary: Surveys forged Christian Gospels, Acts, epistles, and apocalypses attributed to apostles. Examples include the Gospel of Peter's spectacular resurrection, the Acts of Paul and Thecla's sexual renunciation, correspondence between Paul and Seneca, and Peter's tour of heaven and hell. Ancient Christians disagreed over whether such writings were genuinely apostolic and scriptural or fabricated, and more than one hundred early works were accused of forgery. Ehrman then asks whether the practice also occurred during the first-century New Testament period.

title: Writing Forgeries to Show the Truth
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why early Christians sometimes used forged writings to promote what they regarded as religious truth.
searchSummary: Explains why conflicting Christian groups forged writings in apostolic names to authorize their versions of religious truth. Most apostles were probably illiterate, yet Gospels, letters, and apocalypses appeared under their identities because unknown authors lacked influence. Ancient critics regarded this pseudonymous practice as deliberate deception, even when authors believed their teachings justified it. Ehrman distinguishes later false attribution of anonymous books from works making false authorial claims and introduces the scholarly conclusion that both phenomena affect the New Testament.

title: Are You Interested in an End-of-the-Year Donation Opportunity?  Blog Challenge Grants!!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces end-of-year challenge grants for the blog's charitable giving.
searchSummary: Announces two year-end challenge grants totaling $25,000 and asks readers to raise the matching amount by December 31. Meeting the challenge would generate $50,000 and move the blog closer to distributing half a million dollars to charity during 2022, far above its previous annual record. Bart welcomes gifts of every size, lists the five supported charities, explains how to designate a beneficiary, and emphasizes that all contributions go directly to charitable work without overhead deductions.

title: Is It A Sin To Be Transgender? Platinum guest post by Douglas Wadeson MD
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest discussion of transgender identity, biblical interpretation, and moral judgment.

title: Can Christianity Be Seen as “Objective” Truth?  Modern and Ancient Views.
author: BDEhrman
description: Contrasts modern evangelical concern for objective truth with ancient ways of understanding Christian claims.
searchSummary: Ancient pagan religion emphasized performing prayers, sacrifices, and other inherited rites correctly rather than affirming creeds or possessing exclusive religious truth. Christianity made correct belief and a single path to salvation central, creating disputes over authority, apostolic succession, accepted writings, orthodoxy, and heresy. This historical contrast complicates modern claims that objective doctrinal truth has always defined religion in the same way.

title: The Other Virgin Births in Antiquity
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a lecture on other virgin birth stories in antiquity.
searchSummary: Challenges mythicist claims that Jesus was copied from numerous pagan saviors sharing his virgin birth, crucifixion, miracles, and resurrection. Works by Kersey Graves, Timothy Freke, and Peter Gandy list supposed parallels involving Osiris, Mithras, and other figures without citing ancient evidence, instead repeating assertions from modern writers. Ehrman distinguishes different Christian doctrines about Mary's virginity and argues that genuine ancient extraordinary-birth traditions are historically interesting but do not support the sweeping claimed parallels.

title: Our Platinum Webinar:  The Infancy Gospels!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Platinum webinar on apocryphal Infancy Gospels connected with Christmas traditions.

title: Is Judaism Legalistic?  Misunderstanding the Law of Moses
author: BDEhrman
description: Challenges the stereotype that Judaism is legalistic by explaining the role of the Law of Moses.
searchSummary: Challenges the Christian stereotype that Judaism treated Torah as an impossible legal system through which people earned salvation. In traditional Jewish understanding, God had already delivered and chosen Israel; keeping the law was a grateful response to that saving relationship. The post explains that detailed legal codes are not inherently absurd or unmanageable and presents Torah as divine guidance for worship, community, and Israel's identity as a holy people.

title: Is The Exodus a Myth?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces historical questions about the Exodus, Moses, and the foundations of Judaism.

title: Are There Contradictions in the Pentateuch?
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses contradictions in the Pentateuch to introduce source-critical problems in the first five biblical books.
searchSummary: Uses contradictions in the Pentateuch to explain why scholars view it as a composite work rather than a book written entirely by Moses. Conflicting creation and flood accounts, repeatedly destroyed Egyptian livestock, and disagreement over when God's name Yahweh became known indicate sources with different traditions. Ehrman outlines the Documentary Hypothesis, which identifies several sources written centuries apart and later edited together, while noting that modern scholarship recognizes additional complexity.

title: Other Virgin Births In Antiquity!  A New Online Lecture, with Q&A
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a lecture on virgin birth traditions outside the New Testament.

title: Do We Have the Original Hebrew Bible (Old Testament)?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces evidence from the Dead Sea Scrolls and Septuagint for the textual history of the Hebrew Bible.

title: So Which Text is Original??  My View of 1 Thessalonians 2:7
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains a textual problem in 1 Thessalonians 2:7 and argues for the original reading.
searchSummary: Concludes that Paul probably wrote "gentle" rather than "infants" in 1 Thessalonians 2:7 despite stronger early manuscript support for "infants." Correctors preferred "gentle," but their activity occurs centuries after Paul; his other uses of "infants" are negative, an infant-nurse is contextually awkward, and contemporary philosophical writings use a gentle nurse for a guiding authority. The case illustrates how textual critics balance manuscript evidence, scribal behavior, authorial usage, context, and historical parallels.

title: Do We KNOW What Paul Wrote?  If You Think So, Answer This….
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Paul's letters to show why scholars cannot always know exactly what a New Testament author wrote.
searchSummary: Explores the unresolved variant between "gentle" and "infants" in 1 Thessalonians 2:7. "Infants" is common in Paul's letters but always negative, while "gentle" is otherwise absent yet fits the image of a nurse; conversely, scribes might simplify the difficult mixed metaphor, and Paul sometimes uses mixed metaphors elsewhere. Because linguistic habits, context, and scribal probability point in competing directions, trained scholars cannot claim certain knowledge of Paul's word.

title: November Gold Q&A
author: FreedomBen
description: Apologizes for a missed Gold Q&A posting and provides member updates.

title: December Platinum Webinar!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a December Platinum webinar.

title: How Changing a Single Letter of a Single Word Can Change the Meaning of a Passage
author: BDEhrman
description: Shows how a one-letter textual variant in 1 Thessalonians can change the meaning of Paul's statement.

title: A Challenge Grant to the Blog!  Can You Help Match It?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a holiday challenge grant for blog fundraising.
searchSummary: Announces an anonymous $20,000 holiday challenge grant and asks Platinum members to provide the matching funds. Donations of any size will support the blog's charities in disaster relief and ongoing efforts against hunger, with every penny directed outward rather than retained for operations. The post explains how contributors should notify the team by email and use the blog's PayPal or Stripe options, while thanking members regardless of whether they can make an additional gift.

title: What Is Paul’s First Surviving Letter All About?  1 Thessalonians
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the purpose of 1 Thessalonians while setting up further discussion of Pauline textual variants.

title: How To Leave the Faith and Not Destroy the Family:  Thanksgiving Reflection 2022
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on leaving faith without destroying family relationships in a Thanksgiving tribute to a deceased mother.
searchSummary: Honors Ehrman's mother for preserving their loving relationship after his departure from the Christian faith caused her profound pain. Their arguments over biblical error, salvation, politics, and social issues proved irreconcilable, but they stopped debating, emphasized shared life, and continued supporting one another without surrendering conviction. Against contemporary polarization and demonization, Ehrman presents her example as evidence that people can oppose beliefs, seek common values, encourage one another's best qualities, and practice love without rejecting the person.

title: Religion and the Wrecking Ball of Truth
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Forged to explore evangelical concern for truth and the problem of religious deceit.
searchSummary: Explains how evangelicalism's commitment to objective truth and apologetic proof helped lead Ehrman away from fundamentalist Christianity. Intensive study showed him that New Testament manuscripts preserve numerous variants, the Bible contains irreconcilable contradictions, and inspired words were not perfectly transmitted. He resisted these conclusions because he valued divine truth, but eventually regarded Scripture as thoroughly human. The same demand to follow evidence that once supported his apologetics became a force dismantling inerrancy and broader claims about biblical authority.

title: Me and the “Truth”: A Bit of Autobiography
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects autobiographically on truth, faith, and the opening argument of Forged.
searchSummary: Uses a teenage lie about smoking and drinking to introduce Ehrman's changing commitment to truth. At Moody Bible Institute he embraced absolute Christian truth and believed Scripture gave direct access to it, yet that same determination to follow verifiable evidence eventually led him away from fundamentalism. The irony is that evangelical insistence on objective truth can cause believers to test their religion, discover that its claims appear wrong, and retain their devotion to truth outside the faith that cultivated it.

title: Why Would Scribes Mess with Mark’s Very First Verse?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether scribes altered Mark's opening verse for theological reasons involving Jesus as Son of God.
searchSummary: Argues that scribes probably added "Son of God" to Mark 1:1 intentionally rather than losing it accidentally. An identical omission at the opening of unrelated manuscripts is unlikely, while no theological motive explains deliberate removal. Mark's baptism and crucifixion could support Gnostic Christians who separated the human Jesus from a temporarily indwelling divine Christ. Adding the title before the baptism let proto-orthodox copyists insist that Jesus Christ was already, and always had been, God's Son.

title: Do We Know How Mark Began His Gospel?  Another Scribal Change
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses a variant in Mark 1:1 to show why the Gospel's original opening is textually uncertain.
searchSummary: Explains why the presence of "Son of God" in Mark 1:1 could reflect an accidental copying error, while withholding the preferred conclusion. Because sacred names were abbreviated and ancient writing lacked spaces, the phrase occupied only four Greek letters beside another identical letter. A scribe returning to the exemplar could skip from one matching letter to the next and omit the entire title. The variant matters to Mark's presentation of Jesus even though the Gospel calls him God's Son elsewhere.

title: Did God Mock Jesus on the Cross?  A Scribal Change?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines a scribal change that may have softened a troubling line about Jesus on the cross.
searchSummary: Concludes that Mark originally has Jesus ask why God has "forsaken" him, not "mocked" him, despite a striking minority reading. The Aramaic wording, Matthew's use of Mark, and nearly all manuscripts support "forsaken," whereas "mocked" fits the surrounding taunts. A scribe may have changed the wording to prevent Gnostic Christians from reading the cry as the divine Christ abandoning the human Jesus at death. The alteration neutralizes that interpretation while preserving Mark's scene of humiliation.

title: An Error in Mark?  Did Scribes Change It?
author: BDEhrman
description: Shows how scribes may have changed Mark's mistaken attribution to Isaiah.
searchSummary: Uses Mark's opening scriptural quotation to show how textual critics identify an intentional scribal correction. Mark attributes combined language from Exodus, Malachi, and Isaiah to "Isaiah the prophet," while later manuscripts replace that phrase with the more accurate "in the prophets." The difficult wording appears in the earliest witnesses and better explains why a copyist would intervene. Establishing the oldest recoverable text comes before deciding whether Mark made an actual error or simply named the quotation's principal source.

title: How Can “Group Hallucinations” Possibly Happen?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how group visions or hallucinations are discussed in historical arguments about Jesus' resurrection appearances.

title: Intriguing Scribal Errors Made by Accident
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces accidental scribal errors and why some manuscript differences matter more than others.

title: Why Paul Was Persecuted (Or Claimed He Was).  Guest Post by Daniel Kohanski
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest argument about why Paul claimed persecution and what that reveals about early Christianity.
searchSummary: Daniel Kohanski argues that Paul's exclusive mission to gentiles disrupted the religious arrangements that protected both Roman civic piety and Jewish communal privileges. Urging converts to abandon traditional gods could threaten the pax deorum, while admitting uncircumcised gentiles created conflict within Jewish communities. Roman beatings and synagogue discipline may therefore reflect social and legal efforts to contain Paul's activities rather than a simple policy of persecuting Christianity.

title: How Did Scribes Change Their Manuscripts?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains different kinds of manuscript evidence for scribal changes in the New Testament.
searchSummary: Explains that most New Testament manuscript differences are trivial but some affect an author's theology, including views of Jesus' divinity, atonement, and the Trinity. Determining the earliest wording requires understanding how scribes changed texts, traditionally divided into accidental and intentional alterations. Ehrman cautions that apparent mistakes may reflect attempted corrections and seemingly purposeful changes may be accidental, making scribal intention difficult to prove and requiring a more careful method for identifying theologically motivated corruption.

title: Do Church Fathers Show What the Authors of the NT Actually Wrote?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces patristic quotations as evidence for reconstructing the wording of the New Testament.

title: Was Paul Thinking about Committing Suicide?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Paul's words in Philippians imply thoughts about death, martyrdom, or suicide.

title: What Are Ancient “Versions” of  the New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains ancient versions as translations that help scholars reconstruct the New Testament text.
searchSummary: Explains how ancient translations into Latin, Syriac, Coptic, and other languages help textual critics reconstruct the New Testament. Versions can preserve readings from Greek manuscripts older than most surviving copies, especially additions or omissions, but grammatical differences often conceal articles, word order, or tense. Scholars must date each version, identify its source language, reconstruct its earliest form from later copies, and cautiously translate it back into Greek for comparison.

title: What Charities does the Blog Support?
author: admin
description: Summarizes the charities supported by the blog and the scale of its fundraising.
searchSummary: Explains where the blog's $1.8 million in charitable distributions had gone after ten and a half years. Membership fees, direct donations, book clubs, and fundraisers support Doctors Without Borders, CARE, Urban Ministries of Durham, the Food Bank of Central and Eastern North Carolina, and Durham Literacy Center; separate fundraising covers overhead. Bart describes each organization's medical, poverty-relief, housing, food, or literacy work and reiterates that neither he nor blog operations receive money from ordinary revenue.

title: Trying to Make Scholarship Interesting
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on how scholars can make specialized research interesting and accessible to non-specialist readers.
searchSummary: Explains how Ehrman learned that even important material must be made interesting for its intended audience. Teaching teenagers as a Moody student showed him that enthusiasm, relevance, stories, and clear communication matter as much as information. That lesson later persuaded him to write a New Testament textbook after technical scholarly monographs, opening the way to trade books and public lectures; each form requires distinct skills, but all depend on understanding the audience rather than assuming a subject sells itself.

title: New Testament Manuscripts:  Good News and Bad News
author: admin
description: Explains how New Testament manuscripts help reconstruct the text while also creating serious complications.

title: On a couple of personal notes…
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares personal updates about a new podcast and other matters outside the blog's regular scholarly posts.

title: Is it Possible Jesus Didn’t Teach the Golden Rule?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether the Golden Rule goes back to Jesus or was placed on Jesus' lips by later followers.
searchSummary: Evaluates whether Jesus historically taught the Golden Rule despite its widespread use before him and its survival in only one shared Gospel source, Q. Ehrman rejects the objection that it promotes egoistic reciprocity, distinguishing its proactive command to imagine another's needs from judicial retaliation for past harm. Because the rule coheres with Jesus' repeated demands to love neighbors, aid strangers, and identify with people in need, he concludes that it encapsulates Jesus' ethics and probably originated with him.

title: The Greek Manuscripts of the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Greek manuscripts as central witnesses for reconstructing the wording of the New Testament.

title: The Strange World of Textual Criticism
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces textual criticism as the field that asks what New Testament authors wrote without having their originals.
searchSummary: Defines textual criticism as the disciplined reconstruction of an author's wording from copies that differ, not general interpretation or literary analysis. Because scribes introduce accidental and intentional changes, editors must compare witnesses and sometimes choose among an author's own revisions even when an autograph survives. The method applies to every transmitted work, uses rigorous criteria rather than guesswork, and usually recovers a close approximation while leaving some important readings genuinely uncertain.

title: Did Jesus Give the Sermon on the Mount?
author: BDEhrman
description: Questions whether Jesus delivered the Sermon on the Mount as Matthew presents it.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus probably did not deliver the Sermon on the Mount as the single, lengthy discourse recorded by Matthew. Matthew wrote decades later in another language, and Luke distributes much of the shared material differently, including a shorter Sermon on the Plain with important changes. Many individual sayings may go back to Jesus, but Matthew likely assembled them into a programmatic sermon presenting Jesus as a new Moses whose followers must fulfill Jewish law.

title: Can’t We Just Get Rid of Some of the Books of the Bible?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to a reader question about whether books such as Hebrews and Revelation should remain in the New Testament canon.
searchSummary: Explains why books admitted to the canon under mistaken apostolic attributions are unlikely ever to be removed. Ancient leaders favored writings considered early, widespread, orthodox, and apostolic, often judging authorship by acceptable content rather than modern linguistic analysis. Scholarship now disputes traditional authorship for Hebrews, Revelation, and numerous epistles, but the canon rests on longstanding religious authority rather than historical conclusions. Scholars can reassess who wrote its books, yet no recognized process exists to revise the collection.

title: Armageddon in Biden and the Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Connects modern political language about Armageddon with biblical and popular interpretations of Revelation.
searchSummary: Explains Armageddon's biblical origin and political afterlife in response to President Biden's warning about nuclear war. Revelation expected Christ soon to destroy first-century Rome, but later interpreters repeatedly reassigned its battle to their own future. Nuclear technology intensified these expectations, influencing leaders such as Ronald Reagan and encouraging fatalism about war, climate change, hunger, and environmental damage. Ehrman warns that treating global destruction as divinely foreordained can discourage prevention precisely when political choices could produce a real catastrophe.

title: Little Known Aspects of The Golden Rule as Found in the Sermon on the Mount
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains lesser-known features of the Golden Rule within Matthew's Sermon on the Mount.
searchSummary: Explains the Golden Rule's role within Matthew's Sermon on the Mount before considering whether Jesus historically said it. Matthew makes the rule a summary of “the Law and the Prophets” and places it within the first of five major discourses, reinforcing his portrayal of Jesus as a new Moses who authoritatively interprets God's law. The wording differs from Luke and ultimately derives from an Aramaic tradition translated into Greek, but the post postpones its historical evaluation.

title: What Does It Mean to Be an Active Research Scholar?  Editing Scholarly Journals (And Why Is Peer-Review Important?)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains scholarly journal editing, peer review, and the less visible labor of academic research.

title: Why Do Historians Treat Jesus Differently from Every Other Historical Figure?
author: BDEhrman
description: Questions whether historians should treat Jesus differently from other ancient figures when assessing what was said and done.
searchSummary: Proposes explaining historical Jesus research through ordinary historical reasoning rather than specialized labels such as multiple attestation or dissimilarity. Historians gather early independent sources, compare agreements and contradictions, test plausibility and context, identify possible legends and anachronisms, and favor evidence unlikely to have been invented. These procedures resemble evaluating witnesses in court and apply to every past figure. Removing technical labels makes clear that Jesus is not receiving custom rules, even though his surviving sources are late, interested, and problematic.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: More Interesting Topics in New Testament Studies.  Other Writing Assignments for my Undergrads
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares additional undergraduate writing assignments on major topics in New Testament study.
searchSummary: Presents the second half of weekly writing and debate assignments for an introductory New Testament course. Students interpret difficult sayings in the Gospel of Thomas, assess whether Jesus taught eternal torment, compare the religions of Jesus and Paul, debate Paul's views of women and New Testament passages concerning same-sex relations, and answer a sweeping critique of the New Testament. The assignments require close reading, independent research, opposing arguments, and defensible positions rather than memorized conclusions.

title: October Gold Q&A
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the October Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: Suffering, Evil, and the Range Effect  Platinum Guest Post by Dennis J. Folds, Ph.D.
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest reflection on suffering, evil, and the range effect in evaluating pain and loss.
searchSummary: Proposes that suffering and perceived evil inevitably arise from conscious creatures judging extremes relative to their experienced range. Physical and emotional pain promote survival, moral condemnation protects communities, and even a redesigned world without current horrors would produce new standards for intolerable suffering. Rejecting the traditional just, loving God, Dennis Folds nevertheless infers a creative force driving life, intelligence, and values, advocating Christian humanism and scientific progress to reduce suffering rather than divine intervention.

title: Vote on your favorite Platinum Post: The Next Round!
author: admin
description: Invites Platinum members to vote on recent guest posts.

title: Interesting Topics in New Testament.  My Weekly Writing Assignments for Undergrads
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares undergraduate writing assignments designed to introduce students to New Testament interpretation.
searchSummary: Presents the first half of weekly position-paper assignments for an introductory New Testament course. Students compare Jesus with Greco-Roman divine figures, analyze Mark's portrayal of Jesus, compare resurrection accounts, conduct redaction criticism on Luke, contrast Nicodemus with the Samaritan woman in John, and assess the Gospel of Peter's literary relationships. The exercises teach careful citation, comparison, historical reading, source analysis, and interpretation of each Gospel's distinctive emphases.

title: Publishing in Academic Journals
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how academic journals function within professional scholarship and publication.

title: My New Podcast.   Help!  I Need Questions.
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a new Misquoting Jesus podcast and asks readers to suggest questions.
searchSummary: Announces Ehrman's weekly Misquoting Jesus podcast, hosted by ancient historian Megan Lewis, and asks readers to submit concise questions for its opening episodes. The show will use interviews, listener questions, commentary, trivia, and occasional guest scholars to explain New Testament and early Christian scholarship to general audiences. Initial subjects include Ehrman's journey, textual criticism, canon, forgery, Gospels, women, historical reliability, and apocalypticism, with the podcast operating separately from the blog's narrated-post audio program.

title: I’ll Be In Denver November 17.  Interested in a Blog Dinner?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Denver blog dinner during the Society of Biblical Literature meeting.

title: Getting the PhD in New Testament Studies
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the training and qualifications involved in earning a PhD in New Testament studies.
searchSummary: Reconstructs Ehrman's training as a New Testament scholar, from undergraduate Greek through an MDiv and PhD with Bruce Metzger. His preparation combined biblical exegesis, modern and ancient research languages, seminars, comprehensive examinations, and a dissertation using Didymus the Blind's Gospel quotations to locate textual forms in fourth-century Alexandria. He stresses that professional expertise requires sustained mastery and original scholarship, while warning that scarce humanities jobs make doctoral study sensible only for people deeply committed to the intellectual work itself.

title: How Serendipity Changed My Life: The Apostolic Fathers
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on how work on the Apostolic Fathers unexpectedly shaped an academic career.
searchSummary: Recounts how a chance taxi conversation led Ehrman to produce a new Loeb Classical Library edition of the Apostolic Fathers. His seminar had exposed the limitations of Lake's dated text and translation, and the stranger sharing his taxi happened to work with the Loeb series. After Ehrman raised the issue with the editor at a conference, she invited him to undertake the revision, turning an unplanned encounter into his first major translation project and another decisive act of professional serendipity.

title: What’s It Like to Teach PhD Seminars?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains what teaching PhD seminars involves at a research university.
searchSummary: Explains the structure, rigor, and purpose of Ehrman's doctoral seminars in New Testament and early Christianity. Students enter with ancient and modern research languages, read manuscripts and scholarship, translate texts, discuss specialized problems, and write publishable research papers. Seminar subjects include textual criticism, forgery, Apostolic Fathers, apocrypha, anti-Judaism, orthodoxy and heresy, and foundational New Testament methods, all intended to train the next generation of research scholars and university teachers.

title: Did the Israelites Practice Human Sacrifice?  Platinum Guest Post by Joel Scheller
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest argument about human sacrifice in Israelite tradition and moral problems in Scripture.

title: The Birth of the Trinity – Platinum Webinar September 2022
author: FreedomBen
description: Shares the September 2022 Platinum webinar on the birth of the Trinity.

title: When Did Jesus Die?  Dating Jesus’ Death by the Earthquake
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines a proposed earthquake-based date for Jesus' death and the limits of that evidence.
searchSummary: Rejects an attempt to date Jesus' death to April 3, 33 CE by matching geological evidence with Matthew's crucifixion earthquake. Matthew alone reports the quake alongside darkness, a torn Temple curtain, opened graves, resurrected corpses, and a centurion's confession. These elements function as theological symbols showing cosmic upheaval, access to God, coming resurrection, and gentile recognition of Jesus. Treating the earthquake as a literal historical datum therefore misreads and misuses Matthew's narrative.

title: Would I Be Personally Upset if the Mythicists Were Right (That Jesus Never Existed)?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to whether mythicist conclusions about Jesus' nonexistence would be personally troubling.
searchSummary: Explains that Ehrman has no personal or professional need for Jesus to have existed and would change his conclusion if the evidence required it. He contrasts historical inquiry with Christian apologetics and mythicist arguments that appear to confirm commitments held before investigation. His own research changed his understanding of Jesus from a divine miracle worker to a mistaken apocalyptic prophet. Because evidence rather than personal preference should govern historical conclusions, he accepts the strong scholarly case for Jesus' existence.

title: A Major Forgery in the Hebrew Bible?  Guest Post by Platinum Member Dennis Folds
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest argument that a major Hebrew Bible text may involve forgery.
searchSummary: Presents Dennis Folds's argument that the law discovered during Josiah's reign was a forged core of Deuteronomy that centralized worship and priestly power in Jerusalem. Folds links Jeremiah's charge against lying scribes and his emphasis on exclusive worship and social justice to opposition against sacrificial requirements, tithes, and centralized authority. Although the identification cannot be proved, the essay argues that this document transformed Israelite religion by establishing Moses as lawgiver and a written covenant administered by religious elites.

title: What Serious Research Projects Can Undergraduates Do in Early Christianity?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains serious research projects undergraduates can pursue in early Christian studies.
searchSummary: Explains how undergraduate honors theses introduce capable students to sustained original research in early Christianity. Using projects on Passover imagery and atonement and on apologetic themes in Luke-Acts, Ehrman shows that successful topics must be narrow enough to manage yet significant and complex enough to reward investigation.
