These yearlong projects require scholarly reading, substantial writing, and an oral defense, helping students discover both the demands of research and whether advanced academic work genuinely suits their interests and abilities.

title: What’s It Like to Teach at a Research University?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains teaching responsibilities at a research university and how they differ across institutions.
searchSummary: Describes how teaching at a research university balances lighter course loads with demanding expectations for original scholarship. Ehrman contrasts his large historical introduction to the New Testament, supported by graduate-led discussion sections, with smaller undergraduate electives and doctoral seminars. He explains why a secular classroom studies authorship, historical reliability, contradictions, and cultural context without promoting belief or disbelief, and why introducing undergraduates to research-based ways of thinking remains one of his most rewarding responsibilities.

title: Is Christianity Responsible for Gender Equality and Consent?
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses a debate over whether Christianity is responsible for modern ideas of gender equality and consent.
searchSummary: Introduces a discussion with evangelical Christian Glen Scrivener over whether Christianity produced modern commitments to equality, compassion, consent, and improved treatment of women. Ehrman disputes the claim that these social values result from Christianity's beneficent influence and becomes especially forceful when interpretations of the Bible affect people's lives. The exchange appears on Justin Brierley's Unbelievable program, which regularly pairs evangelical and non-evangelical perspectives. The post directs readers to hear both sides rather than supplying the complete arguments.

title: How Useful Are Our Earliest New Testament Manuscripts?
author: BDEhrman
description: Assesses how useful the earliest New Testament manuscripts are for reconstructing the original text.
searchSummary: Explains why the earliest New Testament manuscripts are simultaneously the most valuable and most troublesome witnesses. Most copies are medieval, while early papyri are fragmentary and follow generations of lost exemplars; their copyists were generally less skilled and their texts differ markedly from later manuscripts and from one another. They stand closer to the originals but preserve many early alterations, making chronological proximity essential without making any early witness automatically reliable.

title: The Problem: Not Enough Killing!  Platinum Guest Post by Douglas Wadeson
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest challenge to troubling biblical violence by focusing on claims that not enough killing occurred.

title: What is it Like to Supervise PhD Dissertations?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains what supervising PhD dissertations involves within professional academic life.
searchSummary: Describes supervising doctoral dissertations as an honor that demands extensive reading while continually expanding a professor's expertise. Ehrman illustrates the breadth through projects on Jewish women's inscriptions, New Testament manuscripts, martyrdom, Matthew's source text, Josephus, Paul's Gentile mission, resurrection visions, and Syriac traditions about women. Because advanced students become specialists in their own subjects, committee members must learn unfamiliar evidence and methods well enough to evaluate original book-length arguments, making dissertation guidance intellectually enriching but exceptionally time-consuming.

title: What Do Professional Scholars Actually Do?  Part 1: Introduction
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a series on what professional scholars at research universities do.
searchSummary: Introduces a series explaining what senior faculty members at research universities actually do. Ehrman proposes using his own career as a representative example, covering dissertation supervision, writing and editing, undergraduate and graduate teaching, student theses, languages, professional reading, academic training, and conferences. Rather than defend expert authority directly, the series aims to make the varied obligations behind a research appointment visible to readers who may know university professors primarily through their classroom teaching.

title: Understanding the Gospels: Suggested Readings!
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends readings for studying the New Testament Gospels.
searchSummary: Provides an annotated reading guide for studying the canonical Gospels at introductory and advanced levels. Recommended works cover Gospel genre, individual narratives, infancy and passion accounts, the Synoptic Problem and Q, oral tradition and memory, literacy, textual criticism, canon formation, early Christian diversity, and historical approaches to the New Testament. The annotations identify each book's subject, accessibility, and scholarly depth, allowing readers to choose broad introductions, specialized monographs, or technical reference collections.

title: Big Questions for Studying the New Testament Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces major questions for studying Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John historically.
searchSummary: Organizes major questions for historically and literarily studying Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. The prompts ask readers to evaluate authorship, dating, sources, reliability, miracles, myth, discrepancies, eyewitness testimony, oral memory, textual variants, canon formation, and the value or limits of critical scholarship. Rather than supplying conclusions, the exercise helps readers articulate how historical problems affect interpretation, distinguish differences from contradictions, and consider what individual Gospel emphases reveal about Jesus and early Christianity.

title: Final Lectures in My Course “The Unknown Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John”
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes final lectures from a course on the canonical Gospels.
searchSummary: Summarizes the final three lectures of a course on the canonical Gospels. Ehrman shows how differences among the Gospels reveal each author's literary and theological aims, explains how scribal copying introduced both minor and consequential textual changes, and traces why Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John became authoritative. The lectures connect Gospel comparison, textual criticism, anonymity, apostolic attribution, and canon formation to the historical study of what these writings originally said and meant.

title: Why Paul Was Persecuted (Or Claimed He Was).  Platinum Guest Post by Daniel Kohanski
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest argument about why Paul claimed persecution and what that reveals about early Christianity.
searchSummary: Daniel Kohanski argues that Paul's exclusive mission to gentiles disrupted the religious arrangements that protected both Roman civic piety and Jewish communal privileges. Urging converts to abandon traditional gods could threaten the pax deorum, while admitting uncircumcised gentiles created conflict within Jewish communities. Roman beatings and synagogue discipline may therefore reflect social and legal efforts to contain Paul's activities rather than a simple policy of persecuting Christianity.

title: More on My New Course: The Unknown Gospels:  Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes additional lectures from a course on the canonical Gospels.
searchSummary: Summarizes three course lectures on critical Gospel study. One traces Strauss's concept of historically nonfactual but religiously meaningful myth through Judas's death and Barabbas; another explains how anonymous, non-eyewitness Gospels grew from changeable oral memories; the third examines Mark, Q, M, L, and possible Johannine sources. Comparing how writers revise traditions reveals both historical contradictions and distinctive theology, so differences should be studied rather than harmonized into a single account.

title: My New Course: The Unknown Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John)
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces an online course on the canonical Gospels and what scholars know about them.
searchSummary: Introduces an accessible course on how historical scholars study Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Its opening lectures survey their shared narratives and distinctive accounts, explain the rise of historical Gospel scholarship, and frame questions about authorship, date, sources, contradictions, reliability, and scribal transmission. Ehrman argues that recognizing historical problems does not diminish the Gospels; instead, their differences help readers understand each text as a separate ancient work with its own portrayal of Jesus.

title: Our Next Platinum Webinar!  Tuesday September 27
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Platinum webinar on the birth and meaning of the doctrine of the Trinity.

title: September Gold Q&A
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the September Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: Did King David Actually Exist?
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses research for a Hebrew Bible course to ask what historians can know about King David.

title: Why I Want to Write a Book on Christian Love
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains a planned book project on Christian love, wealth, and social obligation in the Roman world.

title: Is It Even Possible to Follow Jesus’ Teaching to “Love Your Neighbor as Yourself”
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Jesus' command to love one's neighbor can realistically be practiced.
searchSummary: Explains how Jesus' command to love one's neighbor as oneself changed Christian moral ideals even though Christians rarely practiced its demand for complete self-sacrifice. Church teachers linked imitation of Christ's death with giving surplus resources to anyone in need, not merely family, friends, or social equals. Although empire, slavery, inequality, and church wealth persisted, this ethic encouraged poverty relief, hospitals, orphanages, charitable institutions, and governmental assistance, making service and material aid to strangers enduring features of Western moral consciousness.

title: Jesus’ Teachings on Love and Salvation
author: BDEhrman
description: Connects Jesus' teaching on love with questions about salvation and ancient ethics.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus made active love rather than ritual observance or religious identity the requirement for entering God's coming kingdom. Loving God and neighbor meant feeding, clothing, housing, forgiving, and refusing retaliation against anyone in need, including Samaritans, enemies, and pagans; the sheep and goats receive judgment according to such conduct. These demands were intentionally impractical because Jesus expected the end soon: followers had to sacrifice wealth and security now to champion the poor and receive salvation under God's rule.

title: Who Was The Last Non-Christian Emperor of Rome?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Julian as the last non-Christian emperor and places that question after Constantine's conversion.
searchSummary: Julian, the last pagan Roman emperor, tried to reverse Christianity's growing privilege without creating new martyrs. He restored temples and sacrifices, reduced benefits for Christian clergy, barred Christian teachers from teaching the pagan classics, and promoted pagan charitable institutions. His brief reign reveals both the continuing strength of traditional religion and how profoundly Christianity had already changed the empire's understanding of religious identity.

title: A Funny Story about the Rapture
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses a funny story to introduce modern rapture belief and its history.

title: Is There Anything “Religious” about “Ethics”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Contrasts Greco-Roman ethics centered on status, reciprocity, and benefaction with Jewish and Jesus traditions connecting ethics to religion and love of neighbor.
searchSummary: Greek and Roman religion usually focused on cultic practice, while ethics arose from philosophy, social rank, reciprocity, and civic benefaction. Judaism more closely joined worship with moral obligation, and Jesus expanded concern for one's neighbor while placing that demand within his apocalyptic proclamation of God's kingdom. The comparison shows both the Jewish roots and the distinctive reach of early Christian teachings about love and service.

title: Love.  How I’ve Shifted the Focus of My Book on Charity.
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains a shift from a book on charity and wealth toward a broader study of Christian love.
searchSummary: Ehrman explains why his planned book on Christian charity broadened into a study of love as a transformative ethical practice. Greco-Roman moral thought commonly sought personal flourishing and directed assistance toward family, friends, and social equals, while accepting hierarchy and domination. Emerging Christian rhetoric instead made sacrificial concern for the well-being of all others a central moral obligation rooted in Jesus' Jewish tradition.

title: Why Even Conservative Christians Should Accept Evolution: Blog Anniversary Guest Post by Michael Shermer (part  2)
author: Diane
description: Presents Michael Shermer's argument that conservative Christians can accept evolution.

title: Do You Need the Holy Spirit to Interpret the Bible?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to the claim that only guidance from the Holy Spirit makes correct biblical interpretation possible.
searchSummary: Rejects the claim that interpreters need the Holy Spirit to understand Scripture. Devout Christians who all claim spiritual guidance reach contradictory conclusions on major doctrines and passages, while agnostic scholars can reach the same readings as believers, providing no observable evidence that the Spirit determines interpretation. Because the Bible uses human languages, grammar, and historical settings, Ehrman argues that responsible understanding depends on knowledge, diligence, honest inquiry, and dialogue rather than possession of a particular religious experience.

title: I’m Thinking about Starting a Podcast.   Your Opinion?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks readers for feedback on starting a new podcast separate from the blog's audio posts.
searchSummary: Invites readers to evaluate Ehrman's proposal for a weekly audio and video podcast about New Testament and early Christian scholarship. He outlines a host-led interview format with listener questions, multipart topics, occasional guest scholars, limited advertising, and possible live episodes, all designed to reach audiences who prefer podcasts to books or blogs. The post especially solicits advice about choosing an engaging interviewer whose perspective and chemistry would support clear explanations of scholarly conclusions and Ehrman's own positions.

title: Did the Apostles Use Secretaries to Write their Books?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether illiterate apostles could have used secretaries to produce writings attributed to them.
searchSummary: Concludes a series on whether ancient secretaries could explain books attributed to illiterate apostles. Secretaries demonstrably took dictation and occasionally made minor corrections for wealthy elites, but evidence that they coauthored complex works or independently composed them in another's name is nearly nonexistent. The rare Ciceronian cases involved brief communications and acknowledged deceit. Ehrman therefore regards the secretary hypothesis for Petrine or disputed Pauline letters as wishful thinking when abundant evidence for pseudonymous writing already exists.

title: Why Christians and Conservatives Should Accept Evolution: Blog Anniversary Guest Post by Michael Shermer (part 1)
author: Diane
description: Presents Michael Shermer's argument that Christians and conservatives should accept evolution.

title: Vote on your favorite Platinum Post: The Next Round!
author: BDEhrman
description: Invites Platinum members to vote on recent guest posts.

title: Did Ancient Writers Use Secretaries?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how ancient writers used secretaries and what that means for claims about apostolic authorship.
searchSummary: Surveys ancient evidence for the first two proposed roles of secretaries: recording dictation and editing an author's style. Exact dictation is well attested, while stylistic intervention appears only rarely among wealthy, educated Roman elites employing highly trained assistants. Nothing supports secretaries comprehensively rewriting long theological treatises for lower-class figures such as Peter. Ehrman also stresses that disputed Christian letters differ from authentic works in content as well as style, limiting what secretarial editing could explain.

title: How Many People Were Literate in Antiquity?
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses ancient literacy rates to assess whether apostles such as Peter could plausibly have written books.
searchSummary: Explains how rare literacy and literary composition were in antiquity, especially Roman Palestine. Perhaps ten percent could read in the most favorable settings, roughly three percent in Palestine, and far fewer could write coherent works or compose elegant prose in a second language. Education required years, money, and leisure concentrated among urban elites. These findings make it historically implausible that Peter, an Aramaic-speaking fisherman from rural Galilee, authored a sophisticated Greek letter such as 1 Peter.

title: Studying the New Testament in Graduate School
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on graduate training in New Testament studies and the demands placed on PhD students.
searchSummary: Argues that traditional New Testament doctoral programs often provide extraordinary depth but insufficient breadth. Intensive language study and verse-by-verse exegesis develop transferable research skills, yet can leave students underprepared in other Christian writings, Judaism, Greco-Roman religions, philosophy, and the wider ancient world. Ehrman favors UNC's model, which situates New Testament texts within ancient Mediterranean religions and combines broad historical formation with dissertation specialization, producing scholars and teachers better able to understand early Christianity within its interconnected cultural environment.

title: Did the Romans Stage Jesus’ Crucifixion?  Platinum Guest Post by Ryan Fleming
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest theory that the Romans staged Jesus' crucifixion as part of a larger plan.

title: Did Jesus Believe in Armed Resistance to the Romans?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Jesus supported armed resistance against Rome or was executed as an insurrectionist.

title: The Canon of the New Testament:  Why It Matters
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the New Testament canon matters for how readers interpret diverse early Christian writings.
searchSummary: Explains how treating twenty-seven distinct writings as one canonical book can obscure their authors' differing historical perspectives. Readers often harmonize Matthew with Paul, Mark with Luke, Luke with John, and Paul with James, even where their teachings diverge. Recovering how the canon formed allows each writing to be read on its own terms and reveals the diversity of early Christianity rather than assuming that every New Testament author delivers one consistent theological message.

title: Did Jesus Collaborate with the Romans to Produce His Movement?  Platinum Guest Post by Ryan Fleming
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest theory that Jesus' movement emerged through collaboration with Roman authorities.

title: Are You Interested in Volunteering for the Blog??
author: BDEhrman
description: Seeks volunteers to help with the blog's operations and future growth.

title: How Evangelical Apologists Are Changing Their Arguments: Anniversary Guest Post: Kurt Jaros
author: Diane
description: Presents an evangelical apologist's account of how apologetic arguments are changing.
searchSummary: Argues that contemporary evangelical apologetics engages difficult objections more openly and academically than older fundamentalist defenses. Kurt Jaros credits Plantinga's free-will defense with answering the logical contradiction between God and evil while leaving evidential suffering questions, surveys scholarship complicating alleged conflict between science and religion, and treats Gospel differences through ancient literary license rather than forced harmonization. Moving the Temple cleansing illustrates how narrative adaptation can preserve meaning without requiring rigid chronological reporting.

title: When Did We Get the Final Canon of the New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the long process by which Christians came to a final New Testament canon.
searchSummary: Explains that the New Testament canon was not established at Nicaea, by an emperor, or through an early binding vote. Instead, broad agreement emerged by about the fifth century through repeated reading, citation, and copying, while other valued works remained outside Scripture. Canon formation narrowed acceptable Christian belief and practice, yet placing diverse writings together also encouraged readers to harmonize authors whose theological, ethical, and practical positions were not always consistent.

title: How Did They Decide Which Books to Include in the New Testament Canon?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains criteria early Christians used when deciding which books belonged in the New Testament canon.
searchSummary: Describes how emerging orthodox Christians evaluated books for the New Testament according to apostolic origin, widespread church use, and theological acceptability. The four Gospels and many Pauline writings gained early authority, while books such as 2 Peter, Revelation, the Apocalypse of Peter, and the Shepherd of Hermas remained disputed. Athanasius listed the present twenty-seven books in 367, but regional Christian traditions continued to preserve different canons rather than immediately accepting one universal decision.

title: Did the Romans Help Create the Jesus’ Movement?  Platinum Guest Post by Ryan Fleming
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest theory that Roman authorities helped create or promote the Jesus movement.
searchSummary: Proposes a speculative theory that Roman authorities helped create the Jesus movement to weaken Jewish resistance and promote submission, taxation, and acceptance of gentiles. The guest author interprets Christian use of the Roman term “good news,” divine-son language, miraculous motifs, and Gospel parallels with imperial figures as signs of Roman influence, then suggests Jesus' miracles and survival of crucifixion were staged. This first installment outlines proposed cultural parallels but does not provide direct evidence of Roman collaboration or clandestine control.

title: Problems in the Gospels–How do YOU Talk to Believers About Them?  What Do You Think?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks readers how to discuss Gospel problems with believers in a constructive way.
searchSummary: Invites readers to consider how best to discuss Gospel contradictions and historical problems with Christians committed to biblical inerrancy. A questioner finds that leading with disputed authorship, source theories, discrepancies, and Mark's original ending sounds needlessly negative and provokes defensiveness. The post offers possible starting points—historically probable teachings of Jesus or the methods of critical historians—but deliberately leaves the practical answer open for readers to supply from their own experience.

title: Writings of the Apostles in the Canon of the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why writings attributed to apostles became central to the formation of the New Testament canon.
searchSummary: Explains why apostolic authority became central to forming a Christian canon amid disputes over belief and practice. Christians increasingly treated Jesus' sayings and apostolic writings as Scripture, but numerous authentic, anonymous, and falsely attributed works competed for authority. Later readers ascribed anonymous Gospels to apostolic figures and evaluated writings claiming names such as Paul, Peter, James, and Thomas, since authors invoked apostles to secure influence for their positions in early Christian conflicts.

title: I’m Doing a Speaking Event in Waynesville Next Week!
author: Diane
description: Announces a speaking event in Waynesville, North Carolina.

title: The Birth of (the Messiah?) John the Baptist? Anniversary Guest Post by James F. McGrath
author: Diane
description: Presents James McGrath's guest argument about John the Baptist, messiahship, and birth traditions.
searchSummary: Proposes that infancy traditions about John the Baptist may lie behind portions of Luke, the Proto-Gospel of James, and later Mandaean literature. The guest author identifies passages in which John appears as a royal or messianic child and suggests that material now referring to Jesus may have been adapted from a coherent John-centered source. The reconstruction remains hypothetical but highlights John's unusually prominent place at the beginnings of early Christian narratives.

title: Why Did Christians Even Need a Canon of Scripture?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why early Christians came to need a canon of authoritative Scripture.
searchSummary: Explains why Christians developed a new canon despite inheriting Jewish Scripture. The Hebrew Bible supplied authoritative guidance, but the expanding movement faced questions about gentile observance, Christ's nature, salvation, resurrection, sin, ethics, and worship that its inherited texts did not directly resolve. Competing Christian communities offered sharply different answers, creating a need for recognized written authorities that could define acceptable belief and practice as the religion spread beyond Jesus' earliest Jewish followers.

title: Reminder:  Ask Me Anything!  Tomorrow! (Wed. Aug. 17).
author: BDEhrman
description: Reminds readers about an Ask Bart Anything fundraiser.
searchSummary: Reminds readers about a voluntary-donation Ask Bart Anything event benefiting people affected by the war in Ukraine. Proceeds are divided between Doctors Without Borders and CARE, and Bart matches the total up to $5,000; readers unable to donate remain welcome. The largest contributor above the stated threshold receives a private Zoom conversation. The post repeats the event schedule and explains how to request access by email and contribute through the blog's payment options.

title: Is That One a Difference or a Contradiction?
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Gospel resurrection stories to explain the difference between a mere difference and a contradiction.
searchSummary: Distinguishes reconcilable differences from contradictions through resurrection narratives. Matthew's Galilean appearances conflict with Luke's same-day Jerusalem appearance and command to remain there, whereas differing lists of women at the tomb could technically be partial reports of a larger group. Ehrman considers that numerical reconciliation strained but not logically impossible, illustrating that historical reading requires both formal compatibility and judgments about how people ordinarily communicate rather than automatic skepticism or harmonization.

title: The Difference Between Differences and Contradictions
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Gospel differences become contradictions when they cannot be reconciled.
searchSummary: Defines contradictions as differences that cannot reasonably be reconciled and tests the distinction against Gospel passion narratives. Mark and John place Jesus' death on different days, Luke and Mark time the torn Temple curtain differently, and Mark's silent women conflict with Matthew's successful message to the disciples. Ehrman rejects interpretations that insert unstated delays or events, arguing that extraordinary explanations readers would never use elsewhere should not override what each narrative plainly says.

title: Critical Scholarship from a Sophisticated Faith Perspective. Blog Anniversary Guest Post by Judy Yates Siker
author: Diane
description: Presents Judy Yates Siker's account of doing critical scholarship from a sophisticated faith perspective.
searchSummary: Explains how Judy Siker's critical study of biblical diversity and imperfection enriches rather than negates her Christian faith. She treats Scripture as a human tapestry whose knots, uneven threads, and contrasting perspectives become clearer when viewed from multiple angles, requiring tolerance for ambiguity and willingness to live with questions. Academic analysis and civil conversation can expose complexity without destroying sacred meaning, while also encouraging ethical responsibility and generosity in the present.

title: An Equally Strange View of the Crucifixion
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the Coptic Apocalypse of Peter's unusual separation between Jesus' suffering body and the divine Christ.

title: August Gold Q&A
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the August Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: The OTHER Apocalypse of Peter (Stranger still…)
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Coptic Apocalypse of Peter as a Gnostic text distinct from the better-known Apocalypse of Peter.

title: Ask Me Anything!  Mark Your Calendar.
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces an Ask Bart Anything fundraiser for the blog.
searchSummary: Announces a live Ask Bart Anything fundraiser in which participants may ask questions on any subject. Voluntary donations support Doctors Without Borders and CARE's work for people suffering in Ukraine, with Bart matching contributions up to $5,000 and welcoming readers who cannot pay. The highest qualifying donor receives a private Zoom conversation. The post provides the event time, email procedure for obtaining a link, and instructions for donating through PayPal or Stripe.

title: You Don’t Think Peter Wrote 1 and 2 Peter?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why 1 Peter and 2 Peter are unlikely to have been written by Peter.
searchSummary: Argues that the historical Peter probably did not write 1 or 2 Peter, either personally or through a secretary. Acts calls Peter unlettered, while 1 Peter is sophisticated Greek composed with detailed knowledge of the Septuagint; later mastery of those skills is historically implausible. Silvanus is identified as the letter carrier, not its composer, and no ancient parallel supports an unnamed writer creating a complex letter under another person's name as an accepted practice. Pseudonymous authorship better fits the evidence.

title: A Major Forgery in the Hebrew Bible?  Platinum Guest Post by Dennis Folds
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest argument that a major Hebrew Bible text may involve forgery.
searchSummary: Publishes Dennis Folds's thesis that Josiah's discovered law book was a Deuteronomic forgery opposed by Jeremiah. The proposed document conveniently mandated worship in a divinely chosen central location, sacrifices, tithes, and priestly authority, while earlier narratives and prophets show little awareness of a written Mosaic law. Jeremiah instead stresses loyalty to YHWH and justice for vulnerable people. Folds argues that the alleged discovery consolidated Jerusalem's religious establishment and shaped later Jewish and Christian assumptions about Scripture and authorized interpreters.

title: Why Do Some Smart People Just Not Think?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on theodicy after being asked to exchange views with a conservative Christian theologian.
searchSummary: Argues that historical criticism of the Bible cannot by itself disprove God's existence, because contingent events involving Jesus, Moses, Scripture, or Christianity do not determine whether a divine reality exists. Such findings may challenge particular religious claims, but not divinity in every conceivable form. Ehrman's agnosticism instead arises from his inability to reconcile massive human suffering with the traditional Jewish and Christian God who is all-powerful, loving, active, prayer-answering, and committed to human welfare.

title: Reading Genesis—Are You Lost in Translation? Anniversary Guest Post by James Tabor
author: Diane
description: Presents James Tabor's guest discussion of translation problems in Genesis.
searchSummary: Guest contributor James Tabor argues that Genesis 1:1 describes conditions when God began creating rather than creation from nothing. Presenting his Transparent English Bible, he favors a highly literal method that preserves Hebrew grammar, repeated sounds, idioms, repetition, and unfamiliar imagery that smoother translations obscure. His examples show how conventional English renderings can communicate general meaning while concealing the original text's distinctive structure, vocabulary, and theological implications.

title: A Writing of Peter that *Barely* Got Into the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why 2 Peter barely made it into the New Testament canon despite doubts about Petrine authorship.
searchSummary: Explains how 2 Peter entered the New Testament despite centuries of doubt about its authorship and authority. Early Christians rarely cited it, and some leaders explicitly rejected it as forged, but its affirmation of apostolic unity, praise of Paul's letters as Scripture, and rejection of universal salvation made it useful to later orthodox Christians. By presenting its author as an eyewitness and companion to Paul, the letter eventually gained canonical acceptance while other Petrine writings were excluded.

title: A Letter from Peter to James … Against Paul!
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a letter from Peter to James that opposes Paul and illustrates writings excluded from the canon.
searchSummary: Introduces a forged letter attributed to Peter and addressed to James that attacks Paul as an enemy of the Mosaic law. The work reflects later Jewish Christian claims that Peter and James upheld Torah while Paul corrupted Jesus' message by creating a law-free gentile faith. Because orthodox Christianity honored Paul and portrayed apostolic agreement, this anti-Pauline text had little chance of entering the New Testament canon despite its claimed authority.

title: Why Do I “Trash” the Gospels??
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to accusations that critical study of the Gospels amounts to trashing them.
searchSummary: Defends critical Gospel study as identifying what the texts are rather than attacking them for failing to be inerrant history. Scholars evaluate which traditions are historical, explain how nonhistorical elements arose, and interpret each story's literary and theological meaning using evidence and disciplined criteria. Even an event judged historical may contain legendary details, such as the heavenly voice at Jesus' baptism; recognizing this complexity respects the authors' purposes better than falsely treating every narrative feature as factual reporting.

title: Anyone in/around Asheville NC in August?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a possible blog dinner near Asheville, North Carolina.

title: Reminder about My Gospels Course This Weekend
author: BDEhrman
description: Reminds readers about an online course on the four canonical Gospels.

title: Another Book by “Peter” That Could Have Become Scripture
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the Gospel of Peter was once considered by some Christians as possible Scripture.
searchSummary: Uses the Gospel of Peter to illustrate how apostolic attribution and theological acceptability worked together in canon formation. Justin Martyr may have known the text, and Serapion initially allowed a church to use it because it claimed Peter's authority. After reading passages that could support a docetic view of Jesus, however, Serapion concluded that Peter could not have written it and prohibited it, demonstrating how later orthodoxy shaped judgments about both doctrine and authorship.

title: Does God Create People to Roast in Hell?  Anniversary Guest Post by Jason Staples
author: Diane
description: Presents Jason Staples's guest discussion of election, judgment, and whether God creates people for hell.

title: A Book That Nearly Became Scripture: The Apocalypse of Peter
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the Apocalypse of Peter to illustrate a book that nearly became part of Christian Scripture.
searchSummary: Explains why the once-popular Apocalypse of Peter ultimately failed to enter the New Testament. Some early Christians treated its guided tour of heaven and hell as Scripture, but textual evidence indicates that its earliest form ended with all sinners receiving salvation after punishment. Later editors removed this universalist conclusion, yet church leaders who considered universal salvation heretical rejected the book. Its changing reception illustrates theological orthodoxy as a decisive criterion in canon formation.

title: And Then My NEXT Book Project: How Did We Get the Canon of the NT?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a planned book project on how Christians formed the New Testament canon.
searchSummary: Introduces a planned trade book on why these twenty-seven writings, rather than other early Christian Gospels, letters, and apocalypses, became the New Testament. Discoveries such as the Gospel of Peter and Nag Hammadi writings exposed the breadth of early Christian literature and renewed questions about selection. The process lasted centuries: communities used competing Scriptures, disputed several eventual New Testament books, and reached broad agreement only after Athanasius first listed the familiar collection in 367.

title: Is It Even Possible to Follow Jesus’ Teaching?  What Do You Think?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Jesus' demanding teaching on wealth and voluntary poverty can be followed.
searchSummary: Asks whether anyone genuinely follows Jesus' command to love one's neighbor as oneself. Jesus expanded “neighbor” beyond fellow Israelites to strangers and enemies, requiring people to provide others the food, shelter, clothing, and care they secure for themselves. Early church fathers reasoned that retaining any surplus while another person lacks necessities violates that equality; Ehrman finds the logic difficult to refute and invites readers to consider whether authentic obedience would require living near subsistence so others can survive.

title: Specious Arguments for the Truth of the Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques weak arguments that use manuscript evidence to prove the truth of the Bible.
searchSummary: Rejects the claim that abundant New Testament manuscripts prove either the books' historical reliability or certain recovery of their wording. Copy totals measure popularity and preservation, not truth, and hundreds of witnesses descended from a corrupted exemplar may be inferior to a few early, accurate copies. All ancient writings require both textual reconstruction and critical evaluation of their claims; Christian medieval scribes preserved Scripture more often because they valued it, not because its accuracy was miraculously guaranteed.

title: Doing Critical Scholarship as a Committed Christian:  Anniversary Guest Post by Jeffrey Siker
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Jeffrey Siker's account of doing critical biblical scholarship as a committed Christian.
searchSummary: Argues that church commitment and critical scholarship can correct and strengthen one another. Jeffrey Siker values early Christian diversity beyond canonical boundaries while recognizing that the canon became an important source of later Christian identity. Scholars must attend to historical context, ideological assumptions, and changing language, while churches must engage research rather than project ancient texts directly onto modern controversies. Public scholarship adds another partner by connecting academic knowledge with contemporary readers and ethical service.

title: Did Christians Invent Hospitals?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the role of early Christianity in the institutional development of charitable care and hospitals.

title: Were Early Christians Really Charitable?  Or Was It All Talk?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether early Christian teaching about charity produced actual charitable practice.

title: Did Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John Write Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John?  Free video.
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a free video on whether Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John wrote the Gospels bearing their names.
searchSummary: Shares Ehrman's free lecture asking whether the canonical Gospels were actually written by Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. The fifty-minute presentation and question period examine when those titles appeared, why the authors do not identify themselves, what evidence supports the traditional attributions, and how historians could determine authorship. It belongs to a separate online-course series explaining how historical scholars understand the Bible and invites viewers who missed the original event to watch and submit further questions.

title: Announcing a New Live Course on the Gospels!  Interested?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces an online course on Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.

title: Our Platinum Webinar!  Tuesday July 19.
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Platinum webinar on Peter and Paul as dueling apostles.

title: How Could Jesus Be BOTH Divine and Human at Once?  An Intriguing Ancient View
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores an ancient Christian attempt to explain how Christ could be both divine and human.
searchSummary: Explains Origen's speculative solution to how Christ could be both fully divine and genuinely human. Origen believed all souls preexisted, fell from contemplation of God's Word to varying degrees, and became demons, humans, or angels. One soul alone remained perfectly united with the Word, becoming divine like iron heated in fire. That soul became the human Jesus while remaining inseparably joined to God's Son. Later theologians rejected the broader preexistence theory despite its sophisticated incarnation model.

title: Christians Who Reversed Jesus’ Teachings:  Wealth is GOOD!
author: BDEhrman
description: Shows how some later Christians treated wealth as spiritually useful despite Jesus' harder teachings.
searchSummary: Shows how Clement of Alexandria transformed Jesus' demand that a rich man sell everything into a defense of Christian wealth. Clement interprets divestment spiritually: believers may retain possessions if they abandon attachment, know God, and support the poor. Charity becomes an investment that purchases heavenly reward, allowing wealth to serve salvation rather than obstruct it; this influential reading reverses Jesus' literal demand while reassuring prosperous Christians that their resources can make them useful to others and acceptable to God.

title: “Redemptive Gifts”: Can Giving to Charity Save Your Soul?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how charitable giving came to be seen by some Christians as spiritually redemptive.

title: Rescheduled (and RE-scheduled!) Platinum Webinar July 19
author: Diane
description: Announces a rescheduled Platinum webinar.

title: July Gold Q&A
author: Diane
description: Announces the July Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: Softening Jesus’ Message on Giving up (Literally) Everything
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how later Christian teaching softened Jesus' demand that disciples give up everything.
searchSummary: Traces how Christians softened Jesus' demand for complete voluntary poverty into a sustainable obligation to give generously. Luke's Zacchaeus, 1 Timothy, Paul's collection for Jerusalem, and the Shepherd of Hermas allow believers to retain property while sharing it, making charity accessible across social classes. This adaptation also creates a reciprocal theology: the rich materially support the poor, whose spiritually effective prayers benefit their patrons, thereby turning wealth from an obstacle into a means of unity, merit, and salvation.

title: Early Christianity and War.  Guest Post by Dan Kohanski
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest discussion of early Christianity, war, and developing Christian attitudes toward violence.

title: Did Jesus Insist on Voluntary Poverty?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Jesus required voluntary poverty from followers in light of the coming Kingdom of God.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus required disciples to embrace voluntary poverty, not merely practice moderate generosity. The rich man must sell everything, the Twelve abandon possessions, homes, livelihoods, and families, and other sayings condemn earthly treasure while blessing the literally poor and hungry. Promised replacement families refer to hospitality from a new community rather than material enrichment; followers trust God for survival and gain treasure in the coming kingdom, while the severe consequences for dependents left behind remain unaddressed.

title: Mike Licona’s Response to My Post on Contradictions
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares Mike Licona's response to arguments about Gospel contradictions.
searchSummary: Presents Mike Licona's defense against an apparent contradiction in Jesus' missionary instructions. Mark says the disciples may take a staff, while Matthew and Luke explicitly forbid one; Licona argues that Matthew simplifies Mark while preserving the passage's overall point about traveling without provisions. Ehrman withholds his own response and asks readers to evaluate whether attention to the shared gist legitimately resolves opposite instructions or merely dismisses a factual difference as pedantic.

title: Does Luke Have Contradictory Views of the Atonement?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Luke contains contradictory views about atonement in the Gospel and Acts.
searchSummary: Examines whether Acts 20:28 contradicts Luke's consistent rejection of atonement by saying God obtained the church through Jesus' blood. Read within Luke-Acts, the verse concerns God's ownership of the church and the guilt produced by shedding an innocent prophet's blood, not a sacrifice that pays for sin. Jesus' death moves hearers to repentance and forgiveness, so the passage does not import Paul's theology of vicarious atonement into Luke.

title: If Jesus’ Death Was Not an Atonement: Why Did He Die??
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Luke's account of Jesus' death if Luke does not present it as an atonement for sins.
searchSummary: Explains why Jesus had to die in Luke even though Luke does not portray the crucifixion as an atoning sacrifice. The speeches in Acts present Jesus as God's innocent prophet and Messiah, rejected and killed by people who did not recognize him. Awareness of that guilt leads hearers to repent, after which God freely forgives them. The post contrasts this model with Mark and Paul, where Jesus' death pays the debt of others.

title: Does Luke Get Rid of the Atonement?
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Luke may have removed or minimized atonement language found in other Gospel traditions.
searchSummary: Argues that Luke removed the atonement theology found in his source, Mark. Luke omits Mark's saying that Jesus gives his life as a ransom and moves the Temple curtain's tearing to before Jesus' death, making it signify judgment rather than restored access to God. This pattern supports the shorter Last Supper text and the conclusion that scribes added words about Jesus' body and blood being given for others.

title: How Do You Decide What an Author Actually Wrote?  The Last Supper
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the Last Supper in Luke to show how scholars decide what an author wrote.

title: What Did Jesus Say at the Last Supper?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Luke's Last Supper wording and its importance for Luke's view of atonement.
searchSummary: Introduces the textual problem in Luke's account of the Last Supper. Some early manuscripts lack the statements that Jesus' body is given and his blood poured out for others, producing a shorter and less familiar account without explicit atonement theology. The post explains that scholars must compare manuscript evidence, Luke's vocabulary and theology, and likely scribal motives to decide whether these words were omitted from or added to the Gospel.

title: Which James in Galatians?  Platinum Guest Post by Gregory Hartzler-Miller
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest discussion of which James Paul refers to in Galatians.
searchSummary: Proposes that Mark distinguishes two women named Mary and two leaders named James, challenging the usual identification of Jesus' brother with the Jerusalem pillar. Linguistic clues in Mark's burial narrative allegedly separate James the Less, Jesus' brother, from James son of Alphaeus, whose mother visits the tomb. This reconstruction assigns Paul's supportive pillar James and the restrictive "some from James" to different men. The eight theses depart from scholarly consensus and call for rereading Galatians and Luke-Acts accordingly.

title: What’s the Point?  Hey, *IS* There a Point?  The Book of Ecclesiastes
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Ecclesiastes as a biblical book that questions easy answers about the point of life.

title: Digging Deep into Afterlife Journeys
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a detailed interview about scholarly research on early Christian journeys to heaven and hell.
searchSummary: Introduces an unusually technical Christian Humanist Podcast interview about Ehrman's academic book Journeys to Heaven and Hell. The interviewer, an English professor with a Christian perspective, read the book closely and questioned Ehrman for an hour about both its specialized scholarly problems and their wider significance. Ehrman emphasizes that few interviews investigate one of his research monographs so deeply, presenting the recording as a serious exploration rather than a general promotional conversation about a trade book.

title: Blog Dinner.  London.  Tuesday, July 12.  Interested?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a London blog dinner.

title: A Skeptical View of Life … From the Bible!
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Ecclesiastes to show a skeptical voice within the Bible itself.

title: Yeah, Those Are Contradictions.  My Response to Firth.
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to Matthew Firth's attempt to reconcile Gospel contradictions.
searchSummary: Responds to Matthew Firth's attempts to reconcile four Gospel contradictions through Greek grammar, narrative abbreviation, hypothetical family relationships, and inserted chronology. Ehrman argues that Matthew makes Jairus's daughter already dead, Matthew and Luke give Joseph different fathers, their infancy itineraries cannot fit together, and Luke leaves no time for Matthew's Galilean resurrection appearance. Literary motives may explain altered stories, but they do not eliminate the resulting factual conflicts.

title: There Are No Contradictions in the Gospels!  The Response by Matthew Firth
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Matthew Firth's response arguing that alleged Gospel contradictions can be reconciled.
searchSummary: Presents Matthew Firth's proposed reconciliations for four apparent Gospel contradictions. He appeals to Greek nuance, Matthew's narrative abbreviation, and Jairus's distress to align accounts of his daughter; Levirate marriage to reconcile Joseph's genealogies; unstated years to accommodate Matthew's infancy story; and a temporal gap in Luke for Matthew's Galilean resurrection appearance. Firth concludes that none is necessarily contradictory, while the post invites readers to assess his reasoning.

title: Onan the Barbarian: How an obscure Bible character affected reproductive rights.  Platinum Guest post by Douglas Wadeson MD
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest discussion of Onan, reproductive ethics, and later interpretations of biblical law.

title: Gospel Contradictions: My Debate with Rev. Matthew Firth
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a blog debate with Matthew Firth over contradictions in the Gospels and Acts.
searchSummary: Argues for four contradictions between Gospel accounts: whether Jairus's daughter was dying or already dead, whether Jacob or Heli fathered Joseph, whether Jesus' family fled to Egypt or returned directly to Nazareth, and whether disciples went to Galilee or remained in Jerusalem after the resurrection. Ehrman presents each narrative's sequence and wording, asking readers to compare the passages rather than assume harmony, as the opening case in his debate with Matthew Firth.

title: Gold members Q&A for June
author: Diane
description: Announces the June Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: Check Out this Play in NYC!!
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a play and support project centered on clergy who have lost faith while remaining in ministry.
searchSummary: Introduces The Unbelieving, a documentary-style New York play built from interviews with clergy who no longer believe in God but remain in ministry. Their training, income, families, identities, and communities make disclosure potentially devastating, forcing a choice between secrecy and major personal loss. Ehrman connects the production to Daniel Dennett and Linda LaScola's research, Caught in the Pulpit, and the confidential Clergy Project, which supports religious professionals navigating unbelief, transition, and life after ministry.

title: The Invention of Charity:  My Prospectus for the Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a prospectus for a planned book on Christianity and the invention of charity.
searchSummary: Shows Ehrman drafting a prospectus for The Invention of Charity and explains how a trade-book proposal moves through an agent and publisher toward a possible contract. The proposed book contrasts Greco-Roman uses of wealth with Jewish and Christian obligations toward people in need. Its central argument is that Christianity universalized and institutionalized inherited Jewish concern for the poor, helping produce charitable expectations and institutions that profoundly changed Western society despite Christianity's damaging historical legacies.

title: An Interesting Interview on Journeys to Heaven and Hell
author: Diane
description: Shares an interview on journeys to heaven and hell in early Christian traditions.
searchSummary: Introduces a podcast interview about Journeys to Heaven and Hell, Ehrman's scholarly study of ancient narratives in which living visitors tour the realms of the dead. He notes that academic books rarely receive attention, but guided journeys through heavenly rewards and hellish punishments interest audiences beyond specialists in early Christianity. Interviewer Mike Delgado uses his knowledge of the subject to draw out the book's engaging material, making its historical texts and larger questions about afterlife traditions accessible to general listeners.

title: My book: Literary Forgery and Counterforgery in Early Christianity!
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on a scholarly book about literary forgery and counterforgery in early Christianity.
searchSummary: Introduces Forgery and Counterforgery as a study of literary deceit in early Christian polemics. Ehrman notes that very few surviving first-century Christian works correctly name their authors, while later centuries produced writings falsely attributed to apostles, Jesus, and church fathers. The book situates canonical and noncanonical forgeries within wider Greco-Roman and Jewish practices, examining motives, techniques, detection, and attitudes toward deception. Its special focus is how rival Christians invoked prestigious identities to win disputes over authority, doctrine, ritual, and organization.

title: Are Christian Apologists Just Being Dishonest?  What Do YOU Think?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Christian apologists are being dishonest or are shaped by prior commitments.
searchSummary: Asks whether Christian apologists sincerely believe strained defenses of Gospel inerrancy. The example contrasts Mark's instruction to take a staff with Matthew's prohibition; Mike Licona accepts that Matthew deliberately reversed Mark yet denies that the false report is an error because ancient biographers altered sources. Ehrman considers that reasoning untenable but judges that apologists generally believe their arguments rather than knowingly deceive, then invites readers to assess their honesty.

title: Blog Dinner in London?  Interested?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a London blog dinner.

title: Why Not Just Believe in a *Different* Kind of God?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why a different understanding of God did not resolve the problem of suffering.
searchSummary: Considers deism as an alternative after suffering undermines belief in an all-powerful, loving, active God. Ancient polytheism and henotheism could explain hostile divine forces, while deism removes responsibility by positing a creator who starts the universe but never intervenes. Ehrman finds no argument disproving such a deity, yet also no positive evidence, explanatory necessity, emotional attraction, or practical consequence supporting it; an uninvolved God appears to him like functionally atheistic residue from abandoned theism.

title: Time Again: Vote on your favorite Platinum Post
author: BDEhrman
description: Invites Platinum members to vote on recent guest posts.

title: Another Historical Scholar’s Understanding of the Resurrection
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts another historical scholar's view of the resurrection while reflecting on How Jesus Became God.

title: Interested in Joining Me on a Tour To Tuscany?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a lecture tour to Tuscany.

title: And Did Paul Write 2 Thessalonians?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why many scholars think Paul did not write 2 Thessalonians.
searchSummary: Argues that Second Thessalonians is a later Pauline forgery because its timetable for Jesus' return contradicts First Thessalonians. Paul expects the end suddenly and within his generation, whereas the disputed letter requires rebellion and an Antichrist figure to appear first. Its insistence that Paul's handwritten greeting authenticates every letter does not match his actual practice and reads instead like a forger's effort to distinguish his work from another letter circulating under Paul's name.

title: Controversial Me….
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on being regarded as controversial in public discussions of the Bible.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman considers his reputation for controversy misleading. His popular claims about Jesus, manuscripts, authorship, and early Christianity generally reflect mainstream critical scholarship learned in Christian academic settings, but his public visibility and effort to make unfamiliar research engaging cause ordinary conclusions to sound provocative. Critics now perceive unchanged textbook language as insensitive because his persona has shifted, yet he refuses to make scholarship dull or inaccessible merely to avoid offense and seeks understanding rather than shock.

title: Did Paul Write “Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why many scholars think Ephesians was written in Paul's name by someone else.
searchSummary: Explains why most critical scholars conclude that Paul did not write Ephesians despite its Pauline themes. The letter's long, complex sentences and unusual vocabulary differ from Paul's normal style, while its claims that believers are already saved, raised, and seated with Christ conflict with his expectation of a future resurrection. A later Christian apparently wrote in Paul's name to address Jewish-Gentile relations and promote unity within churches shaped by Paul's legacy.

title: An Even More Unusual Story of What Happens to the Rich…
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares the Rich Man and Lazarus with an Egyptian tale about reversed fortunes after death.
searchSummary: Compares Luke's Rich Man and Lazarus with an Egyptian tale in which afterlife judgment reverses the fortunes of an honored rich man and a neglected poor man. Luke may condemn the rich man's failure to aid Lazarus, or wealth itself, since the Gospel elsewhere blesses the poor and demands divestment. The resurrection allusion shows that Jesus did not tell this parable in its present form, although its negative judgment on wealth may still preserve a position Jesus taught elsewhere.

title: Lazarus and the Rich Man: What To Do with Wealth
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the parable of Lazarus and the Rich Man to discuss wealth, judgment, and the afterlife.
searchSummary: Interprets the Rich Man and Lazarus as a parable about wealth rather than a map of heaven and hell. Its emphasis falls on the rich man's luxury and Lazarus's destitution, their reversed fortunes after death, and the sufficiency of Moses and the prophets to warn the living. Because the story never describes either man's character, it leaves open whether wealth itself condemns the rich man or whether his decisive failure was allowing a known neighbor to starve outside his gate.

title: Free Webinar on June 12!  Did Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John Actually Write Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a free webinar on the authorship of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.

title: How Do You Get a Book Published??
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains practical steps and realities involved in getting a trade book published.
searchSummary: Explains the difficult path by which an unknown writer may secure publication of a first trade book. Established scholars may be invited by publishers or submit a detailed prospectus, after which a contract governs length, deadlines, rights, royalties, and an advance against future earnings. New authors usually need a literary agent to reach publishers, but agents also favor proven writers; therefore a completed, exceptional manuscript, persuasive proposal, and agent willing to take the risk are often essential.

title: You Mean Everyone (Except the Truly Destitute) Needs to Give? But How Much?
author: Diane
description: Asks how much Christians should give if generosity toward the poor is required.

title: A Christian NDE and the Problem with Being Filthy Rich
author: Diane
description: Uses the Acts of Thomas to connect near-death experience traditions with warnings about wealth.
searchSummary: Explains how the Acts of Thomas connects charity, wealth, and eternal reward through a near-death journey. Thomas gives King Gundaphorus's construction funds to the poor, thereby building him a magnificent palace in heaven that the king's deceased brother briefly sees. The vision converts both men to generous Christian patrons. Ehrman argues that the story treats wealth as dangerous to salvation but permits continued affluence paired with charity, favoring sustained generosity over the stricter demand to surrender every possession.

title: Who Buried Moses?  Platinum Guest Post by Lou Suarez
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest discussion of who buried Moses and the translation problems in Deuteronomy.
searchSummary: Guest contributor Lou Suarez examines the ambiguous Hebrew statement about Moses' burial in Deuteronomy 34:6. Translations variously say God buried him, someone buried him, he was buried, or even that Moses buried himself, with each choice drawing on grammar, context, parallels, and later Jewish traditions. Suarez concludes that the linguistic evidence does not settle the subject and that theological or literary preferences often determine how translators resolve the ambiguity.

title: Thomas’s Trip to India and the Problem of Wealth
author: Diane
description: Introduces the Acts of Thomas as an apocryphal story linking Thomas's mission to India with wealth ethics.

title: Apologies to Gold/Platinum Members!
author: BDEhrman
description: Apologizes to Gold and Platinum members for a delayed Q&A recording.

title: A Lively Interview on my New Book “Journeys”
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares an interview about Journeys to Heaven and Hell and early Christian tours of the afterlife.
searchSummary: Introduces Mitch Jeserich's accessible Letters and Politics interview about Ehrman's scholarly book Journeys to Heaven and Hell: Tours of the Afterlife in the Early Christian Tradition. Although the book addresses academics and begins at a technical level, parts of its analysis, including material about wealth, can reach general readers. Ehrman praises Jeserich's knowledge of early Christianity and the ancient world and his carefully targeted questions, making this rare interview about an academic monograph enjoyable rather than burdensome.

title: Concerns for the Poor in the Jewish Tradition
author: BDEhrman
description: Shows how Jewish concern for the poor shaped the Christian emphasis on almsgiving and charity.

title: What the Earliest *Christians* Thought About Wealth
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains early Christian views of wealth after comparing them with Greek and Roman moral philosophy.
searchSummary: Early Christian teaching made wealth and care for the poor central ethical concerns, drawing on Jewish scripture and Jesus rather than elite Greco-Roman benefaction. Some Christians urged complete divestment, while others allowed wealth if its owners generously supported the destitute without expecting social repayment. Promised treasure in heaven supplied a religious incentive for almsgiving and helped foster institutions for vulnerable people, though it did not produce structural economic reform.

title: Shouldn’t the Upper Classes Help the … Upper Classes?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how ancient benefaction often served upper-class status rather than direct aid to the poor.
searchSummary: Ancient euergetism required or encouraged wealthy people to fund civic buildings, entertainments, and assistance for members of their own social class. Voluntary gifts usually carried expectations of reciprocity and rarely targeted the destitute, whom writers such as Seneca could deem unworthy or beyond useful help. Even public distributions benefited limited groups and often served political order more than sustained relief of poverty.

title: Does Wealth Make You More … Virtuous?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines ancient arguments about whether wealth helps or harms virtue.
searchSummary: Greco-Roman philosophers often criticized wealth because it could corrupt the wealthy person's character, not because inequality harmed the poor. Seneca argued that riches could support virtue when held without attachment and used generously, yet generosity normally benefited social peers, reputation, or civic stability. Ancient elite giving therefore centered largely on the giver's moral standing and happiness rather than systematic concern for impoverished people.

title: The Critique of the “Very Reverend Robert Barron”
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to Robert Barron's critique of How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Reprints Ehrman's response to Robert Barron's critique of How Jesus Became God and argues that Barron misrepresents its historical claims. The book does not call resurrection appearances invented hallucinations, claim unprecedented discoveries, or resemble Hugh Schonfield's Passover Plot; it deliberately leaves theological judgments to readers. Ehrman welcomes evidence-based criticism but rejects attacks that replace engagement with caricature and defend prior religious commitments by inaccurately portraying the scholarship under review.

title: The Problem with “Time Management”
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on time management, productivity, and the deeper problem of how time is used.
searchSummary: Challenges conventional time management by arguing that greater efficiency can prevent people from enjoying the present. Ehrman's lifelong drive to finish one accomplishment and reach the next created stress and postponed happiness, while Paul Loomans's Time Surfing and Oliver Burkeman's Four Thousand Weeks encouraged intuition, reduced busyness, and acceptance of life's limited duration. The Mexican fisherman parable illustrates the absurdity of sacrificing present contentment to acquire success that supposedly permits the same contentment only after retirement.

title: Early Christianity and War.  Platinum Guest Post by Daniel Kohanski
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest discussion of early Christianity, war, and developing Christian attitudes toward violence.

title: Fabulously Rich But Not Attached to the Lucre (?)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Cynic criticism of wealth and detachment from possessions in the Greco-Roman world.
searchSummary: Ancient philosophers disagreed over whether happiness required abandoning wealth or merely becoming detached from it. Cynic thinkers embraced poverty so possessions could not control or distress them, while the more common view allowed affluence if its owner lived virtuously and without craving more. The debate, preserved in Xenophon's Symposium, focused on the well-being and character of elites rather than the injustice suffered by the poor.

title: The Ancient Argument for Getting Rid of All Your Wealth
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces ancient debates over wealth among pagan and Christian authors.

title: Did Christians Invent Charity?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a proposed book on how Christianity transformed ideas and practices of charity.

title: Reflections on Teaching at UNC-Chapel Hill
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on teaching at UNC-Chapel Hill and the experience of undergraduate instruction.
searchSummary: Reflects on teaching within UNC's research-oriented religious studies department and its cooperative graduate program with Duke. Ehrman describes strong faculty and students, large undergraduate lecture courses paired with graduate-led discussion sections, and small doctoral seminars centered on original languages and scholarship. He explains how this structure gives undergraduates access to expert lectures and personal discussion while allowing doctoral students to receive specialized training in New Testament, early Christianity, and related ancient texts.

title: My Next Three Books!
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains three possible book projects under consideration for a general audience.
searchSummary: Presents three possible trade-book projects and asks readers which Ehrman should pursue first. One would reconstruct Pontius Pilate in history, the Gospels, and later Christian legend; another would explain how Christian teaching transformed ancient attitudes toward charity and poverty; the third would trace why particular writings entered the New Testament canon while others did not. Ehrman outlines the evidence, historical stakes, and public interest behind each idea before choosing his next project.

title: May Q&A
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the May Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: Demons and Christians in Antiquity: Guest Post by Travis Proctor
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Travis Proctor's guest discussion of demons and early Christian culture.

title: I’m Puzzled about Time.  Is there a “Present”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on time, the present moment, and puzzles raised by Augustine and modern thought.
searchSummary: Questions whether a definable present moment exists between the past and future. Any interval identified as “now” can be divided indefinitely, with each portion becoming past before it can be recognized, even though the inaccessible past and unrealized future seem to leave the present as the only actuality. Ehrman connects this paradox to historical knowledge, Augustine, Collingwood, and Zeno, concluding that a historian needs the present to understand the past while struggling to explain what the present could be.

title: My Debate With Roman Catholic Apologist Jimmy Akin
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a debate with Roman Catholic apologist Jimmy Akin.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's first debate with a Roman Catholic apologist, Jimmy Akin, on the historical reliability of the New Testament Gospels. Although Gospel reliability is often associated with Protestant evangelical apologetics, Akin defends it from a Catholic perspective. Ehrman describes their substantial disagreement and his decision to adopt a less combative tone because the exchange remained cordial. He provides the debate video and asks readers to compare the competing arguments rather than declaring a rhetorical winner.

title: Do My Research Assistants Do My Work for Me?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the role research assistants play in scholarly work and what work remains the scholar's own.
searchSummary: Explains how Ehrman uses research assistants without delegating his scholarly judgments or authorship. Graduate students summarize literature to help him decide what to read closely, gaining paid experience with serious research, but he personally examines every source he ultimately uses. Rejecting accusations surrounding Did Jesus Exist?, he states that assistants worked instead on checking his technical study of early Christian forgery, while he read and evaluated the mythicist literature himself because the argument required direct responsibility for the evidence.

title: Does the Bible Condemn Homosexuality?  Recording of The Blog Webinar
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a webinar recording on whether the Bible condemns homosexuality.

title: The Plausibility of the Fourth Gospel: The Sayings of Jesus. Guest Post by Dennis Folds
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest argument that John's sayings of Jesus may be historically plausible compared with the Synoptics.
searchSummary: Advances a guest author's controversial case that John may preserve Jesus' self-understanding more accurately than Mark. John's Jesus repeatedly claims heavenly origin and divine sonship, teachings that could have made contemporaries regard him as dangerously insane and prompted his execution. The argument proposes that followers reinterpreted these sayings after believing Jesus was raised, helping generate Johannine and Pauline faith. If John preserves such claims, the guest author concludes, Jesus was either divine as claimed or profoundly deluded.

title: What’s Eternal Life Like?  Ask Paul…
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Paul's view that eternal life involves a transformed body rather than a bodiless heaven.
searchSummary: Explains Paul's vision of eternal life as existence in a transformed body rather than as a permanently disembodied soul. In 1 Corinthians 15, the mortal body resembles a seed that becomes a different yet continuous form: an imperishable, powerful, spirit-composed body unable to suffer or die. “Flesh and blood” means humanity in its present corruptible condition, not embodiment itself. At Christ's return, the dead are raised and the living changed, while Paul later considers an interim presence with Christ.

title: Eternal Life is in the BODY?  Really?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Paul expected bodily resurrection rather than the soul's departure to heaven or hell.
searchSummary: Reconstructs Paul's argument in 1 Corinthians 15 that Jesus' bodily resurrection guarantees a future bodily resurrection for his followers. Christ is the first fruits of the coming harvest; if believers will not be raised, neither was Christ, and Christian salvation collapses. Paul answers objections rooted partly in Greek preference for an immortal soul by distinguishing resurrection from simple corpse revival. God transforms the perishable human body into a new, glorious form continuous with what died.

title: Understanding the Future Resurrection of the Dead…
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Paul's teaching on the future resurrection of the dead and common misunderstandings of it.
searchSummary: Introduces 1 Corinthians 15 as Paul's defense of a future bodily resurrection for believers, not an attempt to prove Jesus rose. Some Corinthians denied that the dead would be raised, perhaps because their Greek-influenced outlook favored an immortal soul freed from the body or because they regarded resurrection as already spiritually realized. Paul treats that denial as a threat to his gospel: Jesus was bodily raised, and his followers likewise will receive transformed, immortal, spiritual bodies at history's climax.

title: Why Romans Crucified People and Who Was Crucifixion Reserved For?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Roman crucifixion practices and the social classes of people normally subjected to crucifixion.

title: What Is the Didache & When Was the Didache Written
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Didache, its date, and its relevance for early Christian writings and the Synoptic Problem.

title: Was The Messiah Supposed to Be Born of a Virgin?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Isaiah, the Septuagint, and Matthew shaped the claim that the messiah would be born of a virgin.
searchSummary: Explains why Matthew connects Jesus' virgin birth with Isaiah 7:14 and distinguishes two kinds of scriptural fulfillment in the Gospel. Some citations appear to predict Jesus, while others give earlier events a fuller meaning through him. Isaiah's Hebrew text concerns a pregnant young woman and an immediate political crisis, not a virgin-born future Messiah; Matthew relied on a Greek translation using a term that came to mean virgin and applied the passage to Jesus within a theology of divine planning.

title: Does Isaiah 53 Predict Jesus’ Death and Resurrection?  Most-Commented Blog Posts: #1
author: Diane
description: Discusses whether Isaiah 53 predicts Jesus' death and resurrection.
searchSummary: Argues that Isaiah 53 does not originally predict Jesus' death and resurrection or describe a future messiah. The servant's suffering is narrated as past, the word messiah never appears, and Second Isaiah explicitly identifies God's servant as Israel amid the Babylonian exile. Christians later read the passage messianically because they already believed the crucified Jesus was the messiah and sought scriptural explanations for his suffering and anticipated vindication.

title: Why Paul Persecuted the Christians
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Paul may have persecuted Christians before joining the Jesus movement.
searchSummary: Explains why Paul likely persecuted the earliest Christians: their proclamation of a crucified Jesus as God's messiah contradicted Jewish expectations of a powerful royal, priestly, or heavenly deliverer. Jesus had been defeated and executed rather than triumphing over Israel's enemies. After his followers believed he was raised, they reinterpreted suffering passages such as Isaiah 53 around him, but Paul initially regarded that message as dangerous blasphemy against God and Scripture.

title: Pilate Released Barabbas.  Really??
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates the Gospel claim that Pilate released Barabbas instead of Jesus.
