title: What We KNOW about Jesus.  Platinum guest post by Dan Kohanski
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest discussion of what historians can know about Jesus.

title: Blog Platinum Webinar!  For You Platinums Only!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Platinum webinar on a Christmas-related topic.

title: Did Paul Know What Jesus Taught?  More Reflections
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines what Paul clearly knew about Jesus' teachings.
searchSummary: Examines Paul's references to a “word” or “command of the Lord” whose source is uncertain. His teaching about believers meeting the returning Jesus could preserve an otherwise lost saying attributed to the historical Jesus or a prophecy delivered in a Christian congregation; the evidence cannot decide. Other references that closely match surviving Gospel sayings more probably reflect traditions about Jesus, demonstrating that Paul regarded Jesus as a historical teacher even though he quotes him surprisingly infrequently.

title: Are You Willing To Donate Blog Memberships to Those Who Can’t Afford It?
author: Diane
description: Invites donations for blog memberships for readers who cannot afford them.
searchSummary: Invites members to sponsor holiday blog memberships for readers who cannot afford access. Donations in roughly $30 increments fund one or more annual subscriptions, which the team advertises publicly and distributes as requests arrive throughout the season and year. Contributors notify the blog by email and pay through the site's donation options. Bart emphasizes that the tax-deductible tradition broadens access, responds to frequent requests, and allows current members to share the educational community with others.

title: An Article about Religious Studies by One of My Undergraduate Students
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares an undergraduate student's article on the academic study of religion.
searchSummary: Presents an undergraduate's explanation of why religious studies complements her work on war, peace, and conflict. She describes the field as nonconfessional study of religion as a historical and cultural phenomenon, capable of challenging inherited beliefs without proving or disproving faith. Learning about competing early Christian traditions initially unsettles her Christianity, but ultimately helps her see religions as human structures of stories and rituals that sustain hope, meaning, and faith while revealing societies' deepest fears and aspirations.

title: What Paul Says about Jesus’ Teachings
author: BDEhrman
description: Lists and evaluates what Paul says about Jesus' teachings.
searchSummary: Identifies several places where Paul invokes teachings he attributes to Jesus. Words from the Last Supper closely parallel Luke, his prohibition of divorce resembles Mark, and his command that missionaries receive support matches a saying preserved in Matthew and Luke. These correspondences make prophetic revelations from the heavenly Christ less likely than traditions Paul believed came from the historical Jesus, providing evidence that Paul knew Jesus had taught while highlighting how little of that teaching appears in his letters.

title: What Paul Knows about Jesus’ Death, and What Led Up to It
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains what Paul knew about Jesus' death and the events leading to it.

title: My Final Exam This Semester!  The Birth of Christianity.
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares final exam questions from a Birth of Christianity course.
searchSummary: Outlines the final examination for Ehrman's course on the rise of Christianity through the early fourth century. Students identify important texts, people, practices, and concepts, then write thesis-driven essays based on course readings and lectures. The possible questions cover Christianity's relationship to Roman religion and Judaism, persecution, apologetics, conversion, Constantine, noncanonical writings, women, competing Christian groups, and the differences between early fourth-century orthodoxy and the teachings of the historical Jesus.

title: Did Paul Know Much about the Historical Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks how much Paul knew about the historical Jesus.

title: A Thanksgiving Reflection, 2021
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers a Thanksgiving reflection on gratitude, family, friends, and the holiday season.
searchSummary: Explores Ehrman's simultaneous gratitude for a fortunate life and guilt about others whose lives contain relentless suffering. He left Christianity because an active, loving, powerful God seemed incompatible with natural disaster, disease, starvation, and human misery, yet he still considers undirected gratitude essential to reflective life. Rather than resolving the emotional tension, he uses it to cultivate appreciation and motivate generosity toward family, friends, and strangers, treating compassionate action as the healthiest response to unequal fortune.

title: Why Do Fundamentalists Support the State of Israel?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why fundamentalist support for Israel is tied to apocalyptic expectation.

title: A Rare Opportunity!  Want to Read My Book on Revelation (before it’s published)?
author: BDEhrman
description: Invites readers to donate for the chance to read a draft of a book on Revelation.
searchSummary: Offers donors advance access to Bart's draft book on Revelation in exchange for a $1,000 charitable contribution. The manuscript challenges predictions that Revelation describes the modern future and examines its theology, violence, and compatibility with Jesus's teachings. Bart seeks comments from informed general readers alongside scholarly reviewers, promises acknowledgment to participants, and presents the arrangement as simultaneous manuscript review and fundraising, with all proceeds directed to blog-supported charities rather than retained by him.

title: Why Cynics Thought Being Poor Was Ironically Better
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why ancient Cynics could regard poverty as better than wealth.

title: A Humorous Take on Wealth From a Great Satire of Antiquity
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses ancient satire to illustrate Cynic criticism of wealth and possessions.

title: Must Jesus Divide Families? Part 2 of 2.   Platinum  Guest post by Douglas Wadeson
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues a guest discussion of Jesus' sayings about dividing families and the demands of discipleship.
searchSummary: A guest writer argues that Jesus acknowledged the family conflict discipleship could cause rather than desiring division for its own sake. Marriage, children, love, and fidelity remain valuable, but allegiance to Jesus and God's kingdom takes priority when relatives reject a believer's commitments. Modern religious shunning illustrates the harm of enforcing conformity; the proposed alternative is respectful listening, empathy, and tolerance, applying Jesus' command to love even enemies across disagreements without requiring anyone to surrender sincerely held convictions.

title: Should You Give Up All Your Possessions to Be Happy?  The Ancient Cynic View
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the ancient Cynic argument that happiness requires giving up possessions that can be lost.

title: Announcement: Did the Christmas Story Really Happen? Upcoming All-Day Event! (VIDEO)
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces an all-day webinar on whether the Christmas stories happened.
searchSummary: Announces a four-lecture webinar examining the historical and legendary dimensions of Jesus' birth. The program asks why only Matthew and Luke narrate a virgin birth, how their accounts differ or contradict one another, whether their scriptural and chronological claims withstand scrutiny, and where familiar Christmas details originated. It also considers later infancy legends and what, if anything, historians can know about Jesus' parents, birthplace, and early life.

title: Jesus the First-Century Tea Partier
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques Bill O'Reilly's portrait of Jesus as a first-century political conservative.

title: Really Riled By O’Reilly
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues a critical response to Bill O'Reilly's Killing Jesus.

title: Killing Jesus Is Killing Me……
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques historical claims about Pilate and Jesus in Bill O'Reilly's Killing Jesus.

title: Bill O’Reilly, Expert on the Historical Jesus!
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a critical evaluation of Bill O'Reilly's Killing Jesus as a work on the historical Jesus.

title: God’s Mercy and Justice: The Opening of a Chapter in Journeys to Heaven and Hell
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses early Christian afterlife traditions to ask whether God is more just or more merciful.
searchSummary: Examines whether divine justice or mercy ultimately governs the punishments portrayed in Christian journeys to the afterlife. Ehrman contrasts the majority tradition of eternal damnation with universalist readings in which God's love eventually restores every sinner. He argues that the earliest Apocalypse of Peter promised Christ would release the damned, but a later scribe removed or altered that passage. The change reversed the work's theology and may have been intended to make the apocalypse more acceptable as Christian Scripture.

title: Gold Q&A for November!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the November Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: Time Magazine Cover Story on Lost Christianities.  Kind Of….
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts a Time magazine anecdote connected with Lost Christianities.

title: Webinar of Interest?   Dune and Islam!  How To Understand the Movie.
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a webinar on Dune and Islam by Carl Ernst.

title: The Massive Diversity of Early Christianity. My Book: Lost Christianities
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Lost Christianities and its argument about the diversity of early Christian groups and writings.
searchSummary: Introduces Lost Christianities through the extraordinary range of beliefs held by second- and third-century followers of Jesus. Christians disagreed over the number and character of gods, creation, Jewish Scripture, Jesus' humanity and divinity, his death, and salvation. These communities lacked a universally recognized New Testament and appealed to competing apostolic writings, many later condemned as forged. Proto-orthodox victory caused alternative forms and their texts to be repressed, destroyed, or forgotten, leaving modern readers with a misleading impression of early unity.

title: How I’ve Changed My Approach To Writing
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on changes in writing habits while beginning a trade book on Revelation.
searchSummary: Explains how Ehrman changed from drafting trade books at extreme speed to using a less stressful writing schedule. After years of research and detailed outlining, he once produced a chapter a day and completed first drafts in roughly two weeks because writing caused more anxiety than research or revision. While drafting his Revelation book, he deliberately reduced daily output, accepted slower progress, and prioritized enjoyment, relationships, and sustainable productivity over constant accomplishment.

title: Those Darn Demons!  Guest Post by Douglas Wadeson
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest discussion of Jesus' healings and exorcisms in relation to demons.

title: Why I Prefer the NRSV
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the NRSV remains a preferred Bible translation despite specific disagreements with it.

title: Do I Hold a Grudge against Bruce Metzger?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to whether there was resentment toward Bruce Metzger after leaving Christian faith.

title: What Do YOU Think?  Does Biblical Scholarship Change, Damage, or Destroy the Claims of Faith?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks readers whether critical biblical scholarship changes, damages, or destroys claims of faith.
searchSummary: Invites readers to consider how critical biblical scholarship should affect Christian faith. Discoveries of contradictions, historical errors, anachronisms, and conflicts with modern knowledge lead some people to separate scholarship from faith, others to revise their beliefs, and still others to abandon belief entirely. Ehrman asks whether any response is necessary or self-evident and notes that family and community ties can make theological change especially difficult.

title: Announcement:  Did Jesus Call Himself God?  LIVE Webinar on Nov. 7th, 2021 (VIDEO)
author: Chrishuntley
description: Announces a live webinar on whether Jesus called himself God.

title: Change the Context, Change the Meaning:  The Apocalypse!
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Revelation must be read within the genre and context of ancient apocalypses.
searchSummary: Explains why genre and context control meaning. Ronald Reagan's joking announcement about bombing Russia would have meant something radically different in a formal presidential address, just as a fictional virus report differs from front-page news. Literary genres create shared expectations between authors and readers even when conventions are modified. Because Revelation belongs to the ancient apocalypse genre and arose in a particular historical setting, ignoring either context produces interpretations the author and original audience would not have recognized.

title: A Solution to a Major Anomaly in the Study of Paul: Guest Post by Richard Fellows
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest proposal about Paul, Timothy, Jerusalem, and confusion over Jewish Law in Galatia.
searchSummary: Presents Richard Fellows's proposal that Titus and Timothy were the same associate of Paul, with Titus functioning as a Roman praenomen adopted by Timothy. Fellows connects Paul's letters and Acts through travel patterns, Corinthian relationships, naming practices, circumcision, and the Jerusalem meeting, arguing that Galatians 2 and Acts 16 describe the same episode. If correct, the theory would affect judgments about Acts' reliability, Paul's position on circumcision, apostolic agreement, and the forged status of the Pastoral Epistles.

title: How Yahweh of the Israelites Became God of All: Guest Post by Dan Kohanski
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest account of how Israel's God came to be understood as God of all.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: Why Would Later Scribes Be Interested In Having Jesus “Sweat Blood”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why later scribes may have added Luke's bloody sweat passage to emphasize Jesus' suffering.
searchSummary: Explains why a second-century scribe may have added Luke's account of Jesus receiving angelic support and sweating like blood. Justin, Irenaeus, and Hippolytus used the passage to prove that Jesus possessed a genuinely human body capable of anguish and suffering. Ehrman places the addition within conflicts over adoptionist, docetic, separationist, and proto-orthodox Christologies, arguing that it strengthened an anti-docetic understanding of Christ as fully human rather than merely appearing to suffer.

title: How I Opened My Book on Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the opening of Jesus: Apocalyptic Prophet of the New Millennium.
searchSummary: Presents the preface to Bart's book Jesus: Apocalyptic Prophet of the New Millennium and its case for an evidence-based popular history of Jesus. The book explains the broad scholarly view that Jesus expected God soon to overthrow evil, abolish existing institutions, and establish an earthly kingdom within his generation. Bart argues that readers deserve not merely a reconstruction but the sources, historical methods, and reasoning behind it, allowing them to evaluate or reject the route to his conclusions.

title: A New Three-Week Book Club!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a three-week blog book club focused on historical Jesus books.

title: Must Jesus Divide Families? Platinum Guest Post by Douglas Wadeson
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest discussion of Jesus' sayings about family division and discipleship.
searchSummary: Examines Gospel sayings in which Jesus replaces kinship with a family, predicts household division, and demands allegiance above parents, spouses, children, and life itself. A guest writer connects this posture with Jesus' and Paul's expectation that the age would end soon, making marriage and family continuity temporary concerns. Later Pauline forgeries emphasize household management and children after the expected end failed to arrive, while the post leaves open whether Jesus sought division or merely warned disciples about its likely cost.

title: Starting My New Trade Book on Revelation
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on starting a new trade book on Revelation and changing approaches to writing.
searchSummary: Reflects on beginning a trade book about Revelation and learning to write for readers outside the academy. Ehrman argues that authors must identify their audience because scholarly monographs, textbooks, and general-interest books require different levels, assumptions, and tones. Although trade writing can damage a scholar's reputation or tenure prospects, he learned to address adult nonspecialists while continuing original research and ultimately values a career combining scholarship, university teaching, and accessible public communication.

title: Was Jesus in Agony Before His Arrest?  The Unexpected Answer in Luke.
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Luke originally portrayed Jesus in agony before arrest.

title: Knowing What Jesus Said and Did
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces historical methods for knowing what Jesus said and did.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: Bruce Metzger and My Loss of Faith
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on Bruce Metzger's faith and whether Metzger influenced a later loss of faith.
searchSummary: Explains that Ehrman does not know how his devout mentor Bruce Metzger regarded his loss of faith because they never discussed personal belief. Their relationship centered on New Testament manuscripts, early Christianity, and scholarship rather than pastoral guidance, a boundary common among academic colleagues with differing religious commitments. Metzger remained a committed Christian and praised Misquoting Jesus, but Ehrman cannot infer his private reaction. Shared research interests made personal theology unnecessary to their productive and respectful professional relationship.

title: Second October Gold Q & A
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a second October Gold Q&A.

title: An Unexpected Argument Against Jesus’ “Sweating Blood”
author: BDEhrman
description: Gives an argument against the originality of Luke's bloody sweat passage.
searchSummary: Argues from literary structure that Luke 22:43-44, where an angel strengthens Jesus and his sweat becomes like blood, was not original. Without those verses, Jesus' prayer forms a chiasm centered on prayer: Jesus prays and calmly faces arrest, while the sleeping disciples fail their trial. Adding the agony verses destroys that structure and contradicts Luke's consistent removal of Jesus' distress from Mark's Passion narrative.

title: Jesus in the Face of Death?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Luke's portrayal of Jesus before death differs if the bloody sweat passage is not original.
searchSummary: Uses redaction criticism to compare Jesus' prayer before arrest in Mark and Luke. Luke omits Mark's descriptions of deep distress, reduces Jesus' repeated plea to one conditional prayer, and portrays him as calm and controlled. The disputed verses about an angel and sweat like blood reintroduce precisely the agony Luke otherwise removes. The post therefore concludes that a later scribe, not Luke, probably added those verses.

title: Vote for a Platinum Guest Post to Go to the World at Large!
author: BDEhrman
description: Invites Platinum members to vote on recent guest posts.

title: Did Jesus Sweat Blood?  Another Problem with the NRSV
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the bloody sweat passage to illustrate a textual disagreement with the NRSV.
searchSummary: Argues that Luke 22:43-44, where an angel strengthens Jesus and his sweat resembles blood, was added by later scribes. The verses are absent from important early manuscripts, conflict with Luke's otherwise composed portrayal of Jesus' passion, and disrupt the passage's literary structure. Ehrman criticizes the NRSV for retaining them in double brackets, which most readers will not understand, instead of placing a familiar but nonoriginal passage in a footnote.

title: Can We Reconstruct the New Testament from the Writings of the Early Church Fathers?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates apologetic claims that church fathers' quotations could reconstruct the New Testament.

title: Who Knew?  Our Oldest Commentary on the Book of Revelation
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the oldest known commentary on the book of Revelation.
searchSummary: Examines Victorinus of Pettau's third-century Revelation commentary, recovered in original form after Jerome removed its earthly millennium. Victorinus combined future expectation with historical interpretation: Babylon was Rome, 666 identified Nero, Nero would return, and Revelation's disaster cycles retold the same events rather than forming a linear chronology. Other symbols became the Gospels, biblical books, patriarchs, and apostles. His varied readings show that supposedly obvious modern interpretations arose through centuries of changing historical and cultural assumptions rather than timeless common sense.

title: Another Problem with the NRSV: Knowing What To Translate
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why translators must decide what Greek text to translate before translating Luke.
searchSummary: Explains that Bible translators must first determine which Greek wording to translate because the New Testament survives in differing manuscripts rather than original copies. The NRSV includes the longer form of Luke's Last Supper, where Jesus' body and blood are given for others. The post argues that scribes created this familiar wording and that the shorter text is original, because the addition inserts atonement theology otherwise absent from Luke-Acts.

title: John Shelby Spong: In Memoriam
author: BDEhrman
description: Remembers John Shelby Spong as a major public voice for critical biblical scholarship and liberal Christianity.

title: My Relationship with Bruce Metzger: More on the Personal Side
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on Bruce Metzger's personality and a personal mentor-student relationship.

title: What Do Translators Translate?  It’s Not So Obvious…
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Bible translators first have to decide which wording of the text is original.
searchSummary: Explains why reconstructing the Greek text precedes translating the New Testament into English. Using Luke's Last Supper as an example, the post challenges the NRSV's decision to print words about Jesus' body and blood being given for others. It argues that the shorter manuscript form is original and that later scribes expanded it to resemble other accounts, thereby introducing an atonement doctrine foreign to Luke's Gospel and Acts.

title: What Do YOU Think?  The Experience of Death.
author: BDEhrman
description: Invites readers to share views on the experience of death.

title: A More Serious (Specific) Problem with the NRSV Translation
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains a specific NRSV translation problem and how it affects interpretation.
searchSummary: Identifies an inclusive-language mistranslation in the NRSV's rendering of Hebrews 2:6-7. Psalm 8 appropriately speaks of humanity generally, but Hebrews interprets its singular man and son of man specifically as Christ. Reusing plural phrases such as human beings and mortals obscures the New Testament author's Christological argument and makes the surrounding passage difficult to understand, showing that a sound inclusive-language policy can still produce inaccurate results when applied without context.

title: What Do I Think of the New Revised Standard Version?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates the New Revised Standard Version after earlier posts on its production and problems.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman considers the NRSV the best available Bible translation while still disputing some of its choices. He argues that John 3:22 should say Jesus entered the land of Judea, not the Judean countryside, even though Jerusalem is already in Judea. The smoother NRSV wording hides a geographical inconsistency that reveals how the Gospel's author combined sources and left literary transitions between them.

title: Two Gold Q&A’s for October!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces two October Gold Q&A sessions after a missed September installment.

title: Behind the Scenes of the New Revised Standard Version
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares behind-the-scenes stories from work on the NRSV translation committee.
searchSummary: Recounts two stories from the NRSV revision process: the committee's search for a name and a fundamentalist protest against the earlier RSV. Ehrman jokes that the new version might have been called RSVP, then describes preserving the ashes of an RSV publicly burned with a blowtorch over controversial scholarly changes. The episode illustrates how strongly readers can react when a translation alters familiar language or challenges inherited doctrine.

title: More of My Work for the NRSV Bible Translation Committee
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues reminiscences of work as a secretary for the NRSV translation committee.
searchSummary: Describes Ehrman's expanded role as the NRSV committee's full-time administrative and research assistant after completing his doctorate. He computerized years of decisions, checked repeated words and passages for consistency, reviewed inclusive-language implementation, flagged problems in accuracy and English style, and prepared the finished translation for its publishers. Coordinating the work of multiple subcommittees required months of detailed comparison before the NRSV appeared in 1989.

title: Why these Caricatures of the Old Testament God? Guest post by Amy-Jill Levine
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Amy-Jill Levine's critique of Christian caricatures of the God of the Old Testament.

title: Did Paul Want to Please the Jerusalem Apostles?  Guest post by Richard Fellows
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest argument about whether Paul wanted to please the Jerusalem apostles.

title: Why and When Did We Get This Canon of the New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why and when Christians came to have the present New Testament canon.
searchSummary: Corrects the claim that Nicaea or Constantine decided the New Testament canon and describes a gradual, contested process lasting centuries. Early Christian communities recognized different writings as Scripture, including works eventually excluded, while the victorious proto-orthodox tradition shaped the final collection. Athanasius first listed the familiar twenty-seven books in 367, but disagreement continued. Church leaders favored works considered ancient, apostolic, widely used, and consistent with the theology they regarded as orthodox.

title: Christian Stereotypes of “the God of the Old Testament.”  Marcion is Alive and Well and Well and What To Do About It.  Guest Post by Marc Zvi Brettler
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Marc Zvi Brettler's critique of Christian stereotypes about the God of the Old Testament.

title: How Becoming an Agnostic Affected My Personal Life
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on how becoming agnostic affected family, friendships, and personal relationships.
searchSummary: Describes how Ehrman's movement from evangelicalism to liberal Christianity strained relationships more sharply than his later agnosticism. Graduate study convinced him that biblical contradictions and historical problems undermined views he had previously promoted to family, friends, and church communities, producing arguments, lost friendships, and years of family tension. He eventually stopped discussing religion with relatives and formed new friendships. His present advice prioritizes loving relationships and shared life over trying to force close companions into agreement about religious beliefs.

title: Jewish Indifference to Jesus and the Problems It Caused: Platinum Guest Post by Dan Kohanski
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest discussion of Jewish indifference to Jesus and its impact on early Christian argument.

title: Was Peter Crucified Upside Down?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines traditions about Peter's martyrdom and the claim that Peter was crucified upside down.

title: An Impromptu FREEBIE.   A Zoom Lecture Tomorrow Morning!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a free Zoom lecture for readers.

title: Then Who WAS the First Bishop of Rome (if not Peter)?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains who may have been the first bishop of Rome if Peter was not.
searchSummary: The earliest evidence indicates that Rome did not have a single bishop during Peter's lifetime or for decades afterward. Paul, Ignatius, 1 Clement, and the Shepherd of Hermas instead point to congregations governed by groups of presbyters or multiple leaders. A citywide episcopal office emerged only as scattered house churches became more unified around the middle of the second century, making later claims about Peter, Linus, or Clement historically anachronistic.

title: Was Peter the First Pope?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates the claim that Peter was the first pope.
searchSummary: Peter was important to churches in Jerusalem, Antioch, Corinth, Alexandria, and Rome, but the evidence does not support calling him Rome's founder or first bishop. Paul's letter shows a Roman congregation already existed before either apostle arrived, and Peter is absent from its greetings. Later claims that Peter and Paul founded the church served Rome's growing authority, while its actual founders were probably anonymous travelers who brought the faith to the capital.

title: Working as a Secretary for the New Revised Standard Version
author: BDEhrman
description: Recalls work as a secretary for the New Revised Standard Version under Bruce Metzger.
searchSummary: Recounts Ehrman's graduate work recording decisions for the committee revising the RSV into the NRSV. Expert subcommittees evaluated proposed changes verse by verse using Hebrew, Greek, related languages, ancient translations, manuscript discoveries, and modern scholarship, then settled each choice by majority vote. Ehrman explains why collaborative voting reduces individual translators' idiosyncrasies while acknowledging that attendance and narrow vote margins can determine the wording ultimately printed.

title: Jesus’ View of Salvation: Who Can Have Eternal Life?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Jesus' view of salvation and who can receive eternal life.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus made salvation depend on conduct rather than gender, ethnicity, nationality, or religious identity. Luke's narrow door warns that some Jews will be excluded while outsiders enter, and the Good Samaritan shows an impure religious outsider fulfilling God's law better than Temple officials who protect ritual purity. Loving God means materially caring for any neighbor in need; those who do so receive eternal life, while supposedly chosen or observant people who neglect others fail the law's central demand.

title: Jesus and the Coming Destruction: Who, Why, and How?
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Jesus' apocalyptic teaching on destruction with Revelation's judgment language.
searchSummary: Contrasts Jesus's coming judgment with later Christian salvation claims through the parable of the sheep and goats. Bart argues that the saying likely reflects Jesus because entry into God's kingdom depends on helping people in need, not faith in Jesus's death and resurrection. He interprets the wicked's eternal punishment as irreversible death rather than everlasting conscious torment: the fire remains, but those condemned are annihilated, while the compassionate inherit eternal life in the earthly kingdom.

title: On the Flipside: The Glorious Salvation of Saints in the Teachings of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Jesus' teaching on the salvation of the righteous in the coming kingdom.
searchSummary: Describes Jesus' promised salvation as embodied resurrection into God's eternal kingdom rather than ordinary life resumed after death. The redeemed join a joyful banquet with Israel's patriarchs and become like angels, no longer marrying or subject to death, suffering, or evil. In answering the Sadducees, Jesus appeals to God's present-tense identification as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to argue that the dead remain destined for resurrection and a transformed, immortal existence under divine blessing.

title: The Horrible Fate of Sinners: Jesus’ Teaching on Gehenna
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Jesus' teaching on Gehenna and the fate of sinners.
searchSummary: Explains that Jesus' warnings about Gehenna concern permanent destruction rather than eternal conscious torment in hell. Gehenna was a desecrated valley outside Jerusalem associated with child sacrifice, prophetic slaughter, unburied corpses, worms, and fire; it was not an ancient burning garbage dump. Drawing on Isaiah and earlier Jewish judgment traditions, Jesus portrays God as able to annihilate both body and life-force there, preventing resurrection and leaving sinners permanently dead, dishonored, and excluded from God's coming kingdom.

title: Reminder:  My Public Lecture on the Book of Revelation — This Saturday!
author: BDEhrman
description: Reminds readers about a public lecture on Revelation.

title: Jesus’s Apocalyptic View of Destruction
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Jesus' apocalyptic view of destruction in comparison with Revelation.
searchSummary: Sets out the apocalyptic worldview needed to compare Jesus's expectation of divine destruction with Revelation's. Jewish apocalypticists divided reality between good and evil, viewed the present age pessimistically, expected God to vindicate the righteous through resurrection and judgment, and believed this intervention was imminent. Bart places Jesus within this framework: the Son of Man would soon defeat evil and establish God's kingdom, while Israel had to repent, trust God, and practice love before judgment arrived.

title: Bruce Metzger and My Strange Dissertation Defense
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts a strange dissertation defense involving Bruce Metzger and Didymus the Blind.
searchSummary: Recounts Ehrman's unexpectedly easy dissertation defense after extensive preparation for rigorous questioning about his highly technical textual research. While teaching three new Rutgers courses and raising a family, he had completed the dissertation through intensive weekend work and expected Princeton's full New Testament faculty to probe its statistical method and conclusions. Instead, Bruce Metzger asked only about other ancient people named Didymus or known for blindness, and the remaining faculty lacked enough specialized knowledge to challenge the study deeply.

title: Weird (But Common) Ways To Read the Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques common ways religious readers handle the Bible without reading it carefully.
searchSummary: Critiques two common approaches that prevent readers from understanding biblical books in their historical and literary contexts. The "Ouija Board" approach treats random verses as personal divine messages, while the "Jigsaw Puzzle" approach combines passages from unrelated authors and periods into a single theological or prophetic scheme. Ehrman argues that each biblical writing should instead be read as a complete book, with attention to its author, setting, structure, recurring ideas, and purpose.

title: MORE Assignments on the Birth of Christianity
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares additional writing assignments from a Birth of Christianity course.
searchSummary: Presents the later position-paper assignments for a course on the rise of Christianity. Students analyze Perpetua's martyrdom and visions, anti-Judaism in Barnabas, two contrasting Apocalypses of Peter, the Gospel of Mary's myth and gender conflicts, early canon lists, and the Acts of Thecla. A final exercise asks them to respond to a forceful critique of Christianity's historical effects, requiring close textual interpretation, ethical evaluation, and historically informed argument.

title: Student Papers for “The Birth of Christianity”
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains weekly position-paper assignments for a Birth of Christianity course.
searchSummary: Presents the opening position-paper assignments for Ehrman's course on early Christianity after the New Testament. Students identify their own questions, compare Luke's Jesus with Greco-Roman divine figures, reconstruct pagan, Jewish, and Christian arguments, assess miracle stories as explanations for conversion, and interpret the Martyrdom of Polycarp. The assignments prepare students for discussion by requiring them to read primary sources closely, evaluate historical plausibility, and explain each author's purposes.

title: Was Paul Really at Odds with Peter and James?  Guest Post by Richard Fellows
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest argument about whether Paul was at odds with Peter and James.

title: Pop Quiz on Early Christianity
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a pop quiz used on the first day of an early Christianity course.
searchSummary: Reproduces an ungraded first-day quiz for a course on Christianity from the post-New Testament period through Constantine. Questions test chronology, Christian population, early claims about Jesus' divinity, paganism, Christianity's relationship to Judaism, Gnosticism, noncanonical Gospels, the papacy, heresy and orthodoxy, the Trinity, and the Roman establishment of Christianity. Ehrman uses the exercise to introduce basic course material while acknowledging that students begin with little knowledge of this period.

title: My Syllabus for “The Birth of Christianity”
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the syllabus for a Birth of Christianity course.
searchSummary: Presents the syllabus for a historical course on Christianity from immediately after the New Testament through its establishment in the Roman Empire. The class examines expansion, persecution, anti-Judaism, diverse Christian groups, apocryphal writings, canon formation, church offices, women, ritual, asceticism, Christology, and the Trinity. Primary-source readings, position papers, quizzes, and a final exam are designed to replace modern myths with historically grounded knowledge without assuming or promoting any religious commitment.

title: Platinum apologies: the LINK for the webinar
author: BDEhrman
description: Provides a missing link for a Platinum webinar.

title: Recording of our Platinum Webinar: History of Biblical Scholarship
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the recording of a Platinum webinar on the history of biblical scholarship.

title: Does God Really Care How He Is Worshiped?  The Book of Hosea.
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Hosea to examine divine wrath, worship, and prophetic criticism.

title: Bruce Metzger and Me: Reminiscences on my Dissertation
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on Bruce Metzger, Didymus the Blind, and the writing of a dissertation.
searchSummary: Explains why Bruce Metzger's restrained dissertation supervision worked well for Ehrman's independent temperament. Metzger read chapters, answered questions, and corrected language without directing every argument, then remained involved after retirement while David Adams became the official adviser. Ehrman turned the methodological chapter into an article and the remainder into his first book, proposed that Gordon Fee launch a series for studies of church fathers' biblical texts, and later contributed to and edited that continuing scholarly enterprise.

title: On Giving.   Platinum Guest Post by Judith Coyle
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest reflection on giving and the blog's charitable purpose.
searchSummary: Reflects on giving as a transformative human act and encourages blog members to remember the charitable purpose behind their participation. Judith Coyle misses the humorous membership prompts that once regularly highlighted the blog's mission and suggests readers inspire one another toward continued generosity. Quoting Kent Nerburn, she presents giving not as subtraction or grand display but as everyday sharing that creates connection, joy, compassion, and a community of people attentive to others' needs.

title: Reminder:  Fund Raiser for Afghanistan on Sunday
author: BDEhrman
description: Reminds readers about a fundraiser for Afghanistan.
searchSummary: Reminds readers about an Afghanistan relief fundraiser benefiting Doctors Without Borders. Bart's webinar surveys the unfamiliar assumptions and practices of Roman polytheistic religion encountered by the earliest Christian missionaries, followed by live questions. Attendance is open even without payment, while voluntary donations of any size go entirely to medical relief and the largest donor can receive a private conversation. The post repeats the event schedule, access procedure, donation instructions, and educational focus.

title: Sin and Divine Punishment As a Dominant Theme of Scripture
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains sin and divine punishment as a pervasive theme in Scripture.

title: Israel’s Conquest of the Promised Land: Did Any of That Happen?
author: BDEhrman
description: Questions the historicity and moral meaning of Israel's conquest of the promised land.

title: Destroy More Others!  The Israelites’ Conquest of the City Ai
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the conquest of Ai to discuss biblical violence against outsiders.

title: Fund Raiser for Afghanistan:  This Sunday!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a fundraiser for Afghanistan relief through Doctors Without Borders.
searchSummary: Announces an Afghanistan relief fundraiser supporting Doctors Without Borders as the organization remains active amid escalating crisis. Bart will present a webinar on religion in the Roman world and the pagan environment encountered by early Christian missionaries, followed by questions. Everyone may attend regardless of ability to pay, all voluntary donations go directly to relief, and the highest donor may receive a private conversation. The post supplies timing, email access, and payment instructions.

title: God’s Destruction of the “Other”: Joshua and the Battle of Jericho
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Jericho to examine biblical depictions of God's destruction of outsiders.

title: What Do YOU Think?   A Matter of Life and Death
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a reader-response feature on life, death, and personal opinion.
searchSummary: Invites readers to consider personal identity and death in light of the body's constant cellular replacement. If nearly every cell changes over a decade, Ehrman asks in what sense someone remains the same person, how consciousness emerges from parts that possess no awareness, and why complete bodily death should be feared when previous cells disappear without regret. The post deliberately offers questions rather than conclusions, inaugurating a feature where readers can discuss difficult issues without receiving Ehrman's own reply.

title: When / If you have a blog problem!
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how readers should report technical problems with the blog.

author: BDEhrman
description: Invites Platinum members to vote on a guest post for the full blog.

description: Presents a physician's guest reflection on Jesus' healing miracles.

author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Paul thought faith in Christ would bring salvation.

title: It’s Coming Soon
author: BDEhrman
description: Apologizes for a delay in producing the Gold Q&A recording.

title: The Essence of Religious Literacy: A Christian Perspective. Guest Post by Fredrick Ackun
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest reflection on religious literacy from a Christian perspective.

title: Is This a God You Want to Worship?  Some Horrors of Scripture.
author: BDEhrman

title: A Blog Event!  Want to Join a three-week Blog Book Club??
author: BDEhrman

searchSummary: Launches a three-session online book club as a charitable fundraiser. Participants discuss Misquoting Jesus, then Timothy Paul Jones's critical response Misquoting Truth, and finally join Bart for questions about both books. Moderators, summaries, breakout options, and flexible attendance support broad participation; a suggested donation goes entirely to blog-supported charities, but inability to pay does not exclude anyone. The post explains registration, donation, meeting format, reading assignments, and the September schedule.

title: Why God Had to Destroy the Outsiders…
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why some Hebrew Bible writers thought outsiders had to be destroyed to protect Israel's purity.

title: Platinum Webinar for August!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces an August Platinum webinar.

title: God is Holy and You Better Worship Him!
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains divine holiness, worship, and wrath in the Hebrew Bible.
searchSummary: Explains holiness in the Torah as being set apart for God through worship, communal ethics, and practices distinguishing Israel from other nations. Sabbath observance, festivals, sacrifices, kosher food, endogamy, and exclusive worship all maintained that identity. The post argues that biblical divine wrath often responds not only to conventional wrongdoing but also to idolatry, assimilation, and violations of ritual purity that threatened Israel's covenantal distinctiveness.

title: Jesus the Healer, Repossessed?  Platinum guest post by Douglas Wadeson MD
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a physician's guest reflection on Jesus as healer and exorcist.

title: Finally: Cephas and Peter.  What Do I Really Think?
author: BDEhrman
description: Concludes a series on whether Cephas and Peter were the same person.

title: Gold Q&A for August!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the August Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: The God of Wrath According to the Prophet Amos
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the prophet Amos's portrayal of divine wrath and coming judgment.

title: The God of Wrath in Both Old and New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that divine wrath appears in both the Old Testament and the New Testament.

title: For Blog Members in the U.K.!   Special Zoom Event.
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a special Zoom event for blog members in the United Kingdom.

title: My New View of the Book of Revelation
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a changed interpretation of Revelation and why the book should be read carefully.
searchSummary: Explains Ehrman's emerging rejection of Revelation after decades of teaching it as hope for oppressed believers. Close Greek reading and scholarship led him to see a ruthless deity who tortures and destroys everyone who does not worship Jesus, exceeding even Joshua's violence. He plans to contrast John's vengeance and domination with Jesus' own message and argue that Revelation dangerously corrupts the gospel despite its author's Christian identity. Addressing readers who revere or reject the book without reading it remains difficult.

title: The Naivety of the Nativity: Platinum Guest Post by Joel Scheller
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest critique of the Gospel birth narratives and their historical problems.
searchSummary: Presents a guest comparison arguing that the popular Christmas story improperly combines incompatible details from Matthew, Luke, and later traditions. Matthew and Luke disagree about the family's home, chronology, rulers, travel, visitors, and movements after Jesus' birth, while neither mentions a stable or livestock. The post urges Christians to read the separate sources critically rather than force their discrepancies into a single harmonized and supposedly factual narrative.

title: Cephas and Peter: Final Arguments, Summary, and Implications
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes final arguments and implications for distinguishing Cephas from Peter.

title: More Hints that Cephas Was Not Peter
author: BDEhrman
description: Gives further evidence for the possibility that Cephas and Peter were not the same person.

title: More On Bruce Metzger and Me: How I Got Interested in my Dissertation Topic
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts how Bruce Metzger helped shape a dissertation topic on Didymus the Blind and textual criticism.
searchSummary: Recounts how Gordon Fee's work on church-father quotations led Ehrman to his dissertation topic under Bruce Metzger. Patristic citations can date and locate forms of the New Testament text, but quotation from memory, adaptation, and paraphrase make reconstruction methodologically difficult. Metzger proposed the newly discovered commentaries of Didymus the Blind, and editor Ludwig Koenen supplied an unpublished handwritten commentary, giving Ehrman untouched evidence for a rigorous study of Didymus's New Testament text.

title: Some Evidence that Cephas and Peter WERE Two Different People
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents evidence that some early Christians distinguished Cephas from Peter.

title: Congratulations Fredrick Ackun!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces Fredrick Ackun as the winning Platinum guest post author.

title: Jesus Healing the Paralyzed.  How Do We Explain the Stories?  Platinum Guest Post by Douglas Wadeson, MD
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a physician's guest discussion of Jesus healing paralytics and how such stories might be explained.

title: Were Cephas and Peter Two Different People?  A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reopens an older thread on whether Cephas and Peter were two different early Christian figures.

title: Bruce Metzger and the “Favor” He Did Me On My PhD Exams
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts a favor Bruce Metzger provided during PhD examinations.
searchSummary: Describes the structure and pressure of doctoral comprehensive examinations through Ehrman's experience with Bruce Metzger. After seminars and months of multilingual reading, students wrote several closed-book essays during long examinations and then defended their answers orally before faculty. Expecting Metzger's familiar questions, Ehrman instead received a customized canon question based on his bibliography, misattributed a scholar's position, feared he had failed, and discovered during the oral examination that the error had escaped notice.

title: Understanding the Apocalypse as an “Apocalypse”
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Revelation must be understood as an ancient apocalypse rather than a modern prediction manual.
searchSummary: Applies the apocalypse genre to Revelation. John's angel-mediated vision uses interpretable ancient symbols, escalating disaster cycles that repeat rather than form a chronological sequence, and a triumphal movement from present suffering to God's renewed kingdom. Repeated assurances of imminence address persecuted first-century churches. The book both comforts the faithful with promised vindication and warns wavering Christians of severe judgment, urging them to endure because God controls history, will soon destroy their enemies, and will reward those who remain loyal.

title: Returning to the Whore of Babylon
author: BDEhrman
description: Places the Whore of Babylon in Revelation within the book's first-century historical context.
searchSummary: Identifies Revelation's Whore of Babylon through the book's own first-century clues rather than modern speculation. The woman sits on a satanic beast whose seven heads are seven hills and is explicitly the city ruling earthly kings: Rome, traditionally built on seven hills. Called Babylon because Rome, like ancient Babylon, destroyed Jerusalem and its temple, she embodies imperial luxury, economic exploitation, and persecution of Christians. The symbol targets John's Roman world, not a modern nation, religion, or future woman.

title: Nazis and the Meaning of the Word “Jew”: Guest Post by Jason Staples
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Jason Staples's guest discussion of the word Jew and its misuse in Nazi ideology.
searchSummary: Challenges the assumption that ancient sources used Israelite and Jew as interchangeable labels. Jason Staples argues that Jews were understood as descendants of Judah and therefore one subset of the larger twelve-tribe Israel, which could also include Samaritans and dispersed northern Israelites. Recognizing this distinction clarifies Second Temple hopes for restoring all Israel and exposes how a theory shaped by Nazi-era usage persisted in scholarship despite weak ancient evidence.

title: Platinum Members Only!  Vote for your Favorite Platinum Guest Post
author: BDEhrman
description: Invites Platinum members to vote on recent guest posts.

title: Is Revelation Describing Warfare in the Twenty-first Century??
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Revelation should be read in its Roman imperial setting rather than as twenty-first-century warfare.
searchSummary: Rejects Hal Lindsey's interpretation of Revelation's locusts as modern attack helicopters. Although rotors, pilots, armor, and weapons can be made to resemble selected details, the creatures explicitly torture people for five months without killing anyone or harming vegetation, behavior incompatible with machines designed for destruction. Such futuristic readings make history culminate in the interpreter's era and ignore inconvenient wording. Reading Revelation as first-century symbolic literature better respects the text and its claim about God's sovereignty over evil.

title: Problems with Comments on Revelation!
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains technical problems affecting comments on James Tabor's Revelation posts.

title: An Interview about Heaven and Hell: American Freethought Podcast
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares an American Freethought Podcast interview about Heaven and Hell.
searchSummary: Introduces John C. Snider's American Freethought Podcast interview with Ehrman about his book on heaven and hell. The conversation considers whether the Bible clearly teaches that human beings possess eternal souls and whether heaven and hell should be understood as literal realities. By framing these as central questions rather than supplying conclusions in the introductory post, Ehrman directs readers to the recorded interview for his historical account of how biblical and later Christian afterlife beliefs relate.

title: Jesus the Healer: Those Darn Demons.     Platinum guest post by Douglas Wadeson MD
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a physician's guest discussion of demons and Jesus' healing stories.

title: Interested in Hearing Three of My Lectures?  Jesus according to the Early Christians
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers recordings of three lectures on how early Christians understood Jesus.
searchSummary: Makes three recorded lectures available on less familiar early Christian portrayals of Jesus. The lectures compare Jesus with other ancient divine men, examine later legends about his supernatural childhood, and trace beliefs about his descent to Hades between death and resurrection. Together they show how Greco-Roman comparisons and influential noncanonical stories expanded Christian understandings of Jesus beyond the narratives preserved in the New Testament Gospels.

title: The Historical Background to the Book of Revelation
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the historical background needed to interpret Revelation in context.
searchSummary: Places Revelation within its first-century authorship, date, and social setting. Its prophet John was neither the Gospel's author nor Jesus' disciple; his Semitic-influenced Greek, theology, and references to apostles distinguish him. Material may date from Nero's 60s persecution, while the completed book likely comes from about 95 CE under Domitian. John addressed Asian churches facing persecution, martyrdom, poverty, false teachers, and fading commitment, promising that God would soon destroy the oppressive Roman government and end their suffering.

title: Comments on Blog Comments!
author: BDEhrman
description: Clarifies blog comment policies and procedures for members.

title: Prophecies and Saints in the Book of Daniel.  Platinum Guest Post by Daniel Kohanski
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest discussion of Daniel, prophecy, resurrection, and the saints.
searchSummary: Argues that Daniel popularized two literary techniques later visible in Christian writing: absolute prophecy and the idealization, or “saintization,” of religious heroes. Daniel presents past events as inevitable predictions to validate its still-future promise that Antiochus will fall and the faithful dead will awaken to eternal life. It also depicts Daniel as faultlessly wise and faithful. Daniel Kohanski traces comparable idealization in Jubilees, Hellenistic philosophy, Luke's portrayal of Jesus, and later Islamic views of prophets.

title: Understanding Revelation: A Sine Qua Non (Overlooked by most readers)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains an overlooked requirement for understanding Revelation on its own terms.
searchSummary: Describes literary conventions needed to interpret ancient apocalypses. Pseudonymous authors borrowed revered identities to authorize heavenly knowledge and could "predict" events already past, as Daniel does. Bizarre visions communicate through symbols, while recurring disasters create a spiral rather than a literal timeline. Their movement from suffering to divine triumph motivates endangered communities to remain loyal. Revelation is an unusual nonpseudonymous example, but its purpose likewise concerns hope and perseverance, not a precise schedule of modern future events.

title: Metzger, the Squirrel, and Me (…and Jesus).
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues a Bruce Metzger anecdote about a squirrel and its connection to Jesus scholarship.

title: My Mentor Bruce Metzger and the Infamous Squirrel
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces memories of Bruce Metzger through a locally famous squirrel story.
searchSummary: Recounts the Princeton Seminary story in which Bruce Metzger responds to a squirrel's fatal fall by announcing that he knows the Greek word for squirrel. Ehrman explains how variations changed the language, companion, and dialogue as the anecdote circulated, revealing both Metzger's learning and the instability of oral retelling. A colleague's observation that Metzger would simply supply the word rather than boast about knowing it convinces Ehrman that the familiar version was altered, leaving its origin for a later post.

title: Gold Q&A for July 2021!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the July 2021 Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: How I Take Notes When Doing Research for a Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how research notes are taken while preparing a book on Revelation.
searchSummary: Explains Ehrman's system for recording and organizing the extensive research behind a trade book. He builds a bibliography, reads and evaluates each source himself, creates notes of varying depth, and stores files by author and topic in searchable folders containing scholarship, primary texts, ideas, outlines, and chapters. Graduate assistants may compile references or summaries, but their work helps him prioritize rather than replace his reading; reviewing all notes then guides the book's structure and argument.

title: Apocalypse (the genre) and Apocalypticism (the worldview)
author: BDEhrman
description: Distinguishes apocalypse as a literary genre from apocalypticism as a worldview.
searchSummary: Distinguishes apocalypticism, a worldview dividing reality into good and evil ages awaiting imminent divine judgment, from apocalypse, the literary genre expressing that worldview. Revelation belongs among Jewish and Christian works such as Daniel, Enoch, Baruch, Hermas, and Peter rather than standing alone. These first-person, angel-mediated visions use heavenly journeys and symbolic historical sketches to interpret earthly suffering. They protest oppressive powers and assure faithful readers that God will soon defeat evil, vindicate them, and replace present misery with bliss.

title: The Book of Revelation and the END.   Starting at the Beginning.
author: BDEhrman
description: Begins a new thread on Revelation and its meaning for general readers.
searchSummary: Surveys Revelation's contents from John's vision of the exalted Christ and messages to seven Asian churches through the escalating seals, trumpets, and bowls of divine wrath. The Lamb defeats Babylon, the Beast, and their allies; Satan is imprisoned, released, and finally condemned after the resurrection and judgment. The book ends with a new heaven, new earth, and New Jerusalem where suffering, evil, and death disappear. This narrative overview prepares for later discussion of how Revelation should be interpreted.

title: Memories of Bruce Metzger: When I First Realized I Couldn’t Write
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts how Bruce Metzger helped reveal weaknesses in early scholarly writing.
searchSummary: Recounts how Bruce Metzger's severe critique of Ehrman's dissertation proposal exposed weaknesses in his writing and prompted lasting improvement. Because the historically focused textual project faced skepticism in a theological institution, Metzger examined its style and substance line by line to ensure approval. Although devastated, Ehrman recognized the care and insight behind the criticism, revised the proposal, and concluded that effective writing is a learned discipline developed through demanding feedback rather than an innate gift.

title: My Mentor Bruce Metzger
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Bruce Metzger as a mentor and major New Testament textual scholar.

title: Was Jesus Like One of the Pagan Fertility Gods?
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques the claim that stories of Jesus' death and resurrection were modeled on pagan fertility gods.

title: Blog Dinner in London?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a London blog dinner.

title: Other Gods Who Died and Rose from the Dead?
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues a Q&A with Ben Witherington on dying-and-rising gods and Jesus' resurrection.
searchSummary: Rejects two mythicist explanations for Christianity's origins. Careful study of ancient sources undermined the once-popular category of pagan gods who both died and bodily rose, since cited deities generally either disappear without dying or die without returning. G. A. Wells's revised theory likewise fails because Paul's recent, crucified Jesus cannot plausibly derive from an obscure person living a century earlier plus Jewish Wisdom speculation. Earliest Christians identified Jesus chiefly as the crucified Messiah, not Wisdom.

title: Some Intriguing Questions about Jesus’ Predictions and Mental Health
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about Jesus' predictions, apocalyptic expectation, and mental health.
searchSummary: Addresses why Christianity survived Jesus's unfulfilled prediction of an imminent kingdom and whether that prediction indicates mental illness. John Gager's cognitive-dissonance model suggests that disappointed believers reinterpreted the delay, intensified missionary activity, and gained reassurance from converts rather than abandoning their faith. Bart does not fully endorse the theory, but rejects diagnosing Jesus as insane because apocalyptic expectations were common in his historical setting and seeing himself as the future messiah did not amount to claiming present divinity.

title: An Unusual Interview with an Ex-Muslim, Informed, Atheist
author: FreedomBen
description: Shares an interview with an ex-Muslim atheist about religion and early Christianity.
searchSummary: Introduces Hanny Seylim's Critical Faculty interview with Ehrman about his scholarly work. Seylim, a former Muslim raised between Egypt and Ireland who now lives in Melbourne, interviews critical thinkers across subjects from physics to the New Testament and brings substantial knowledge of early Christianity to the conversation. Ehrman characterizes the resulting exchange as unusually strong, but the brief post does not enumerate its specific questions or conclusions, leaving the recording as the substantive content.

title: Fiction and Fact, Legend and History.  Is it Either / Or?
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses how fiction, fact, legend, and history relate in the study of Jesus traditions.
searchSummary: Distinguishes literary shaping from wholesale invention in assessing Gospel traditions and Jesus' existence. Matthew can model Jesus on Moses, and stories about Jesus can resemble accounts of other divine men, without making either the events or the person entirely fictional. Historical figures such as Alexander, Vespasian, and Apollonius also attracted miraculous legends. Moreover, ancient parallels are neither complete nor interchangeable: Jesus' virginal conception and bodily resurrection differ significantly from commonly cited pagan birth and afterlife stories.

title: Texts and Towns that Allegedly Didn’t Exist (So Did Jesus?)
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to mythicist claims about lost texts, Nazareth, and the existence of Jesus.
searchSummary: Explains why alleged interpolations and claims about Nazareth require evidence rather than convenience. Passages preserved in every manuscript could theoretically be later additions, but compelling literary or historical grounds are necessary; simply removing references that contradict mythicism is circular. The existence of Jesus also would not depend on the accuracy of his reported hometown. In any case, farms, a house, coins, and other archaeological evidence establish that the small settlement of Nazareth existed during the relevant period.

title: How Do We Know If Jesus Did Something?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains historical criteria for deciding whether Jesus probably did or said something.
searchSummary: Explains how historians evaluate Jesus traditions and why the evidence extends far beyond Mark. Paul describes a Jewish Jesus with relatives, disciples, teachings, a final meal, and a crucifixion, while independent sources behind Matthew, Luke, John, Thomas, and Peter preserve additional early traditions. Multiple attestation and dissimilarity can positively support historicity, whereas contextual implausibility can exclude claims. Failure to satisfy a positive criterion creates uncertainty, not proof that a tradition or person was invented.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: Some Key Evidence for Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes key evidence used in arguments for the historical existence of Jesus.
searchSummary: Presents multiple independent sources, Paul's personal contacts, and the crucified Messiah as key evidence for Jesus' existence. Paul knew Peter and Jesus' brother James, while Mark, Q, M, L, John, and other traditions independently portray a Galilean Jewish teacher. Jewish expectations did not anticipate a Messiah defeated by execution, so followers trying to invent a persuasive savior would not naturally choose crucifixion. Their proclamation is best explained by a real Jesus whom they considered Messiah despite knowing he was crucified.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: Why My Book on Revelation Has Been Different To Write
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on why writing a trade book on Revelation has differed from earlier book projects.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman's planned trade book on Revelation developed more slowly and less predictably than his earlier books. His usual method moves from a clear thesis through two years of exhaustive reading, detailed notes, and increasingly granular outlines before a rapid first draft. Pandemic pressures delayed the project, but uncertainty also gave him unusual freedom to reconsider its argument and structure, making the extended exploratory period potentially valuable rather than merely a failure to meet his normal schedule.

title: The Reconstruction of Q: Platinum Guest Post by Steve Sutter
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest discussion of reconstructing Q as a source behind Matthew and Luke.

title: What About Other References to Jesus Outside the New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys references to Jesus outside the New Testament.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: Evidence for Jesus Outside the New Testament: Part 2 of My Exchange with Ben Witherington
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues an exchange with Ben Witherington on evidence for Jesus outside the New Testament.
searchSummary: Rejects arguments from silence that treat the absence of contemporary public records as evidence that Jesus never existed. Almost all ancient people left no surviving documentary trace, and historians routinely use interested sources critically rather than discarding them for bias. Paul's early letters provide especially strong evidence because he knew Jesus' teachings, his closest disciple Peter, and his brother James within years of the reported death. These facts cannot be explained plausibly by simply declaring every Christian source unusable.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: Why I Wrote my book Did Jesus Exist?  Interview with Evangelical Scholar Ben Witherington
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Did Jesus Exist? was written in response to mythicist claims.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman prioritized Did Jesus Exist and approached the question as a historian. Growing public mythicism lacked a book-length response from a specialist in New Testament and early Christian history, and establishing existence logically preceded a planned study of how Jesus became regarded as God. Ehrman distinguishes historical inquiry from exegesis, textual criticism, theology, and miracle claims, while suggesting that some mythicist advocacy is driven by opposition to religion rather than disinterested assessment of evidence.

title: How Then Do Most Ancient Manuscripts Get Discovered?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how ancient manuscripts are usually discovered and why major finds are rare.
searchSummary: Explains how ancient manuscripts have been found and why systematic searches are uncommon today. Nineteenth-century scholars examined uncatalogued libraries and monasteries, while Grenfell and Hunt excavated Oxyrhynchus's rubbish mounds and recovered thousands of papyri, including unknown sayings of Jesus. Although uncatalogued manuscripts still surface, many spectacular discoveries, including Nag Hammadi and the Dead Sea Scrolls, occurred by chance. Ehrman remains unsure why archaeologists have not more often tried to replicate targeted rubbish-dump excavations.

title: The Issue of “Tenure” for Professors
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains tenure for professors in light of a controversy at UNC-Chapel Hill.
searchSummary: Defends academic tenure as protection for independent research and teaching rather than a personal guarantee against accountability. Professors undergo years of evaluation in research, teaching, and service, but once tenured can present evidence-based conclusions that offend political, religious, or public opinion without fear of dismissal. Using the Nikole Hannah-Jones controversy and biblical scholarship as examples, Ehrman argues that universities cannot generate new knowledge if trustees, legislators, donors, or voters can enforce acceptable conclusions by controlling faculty employment.

title: Gold Q&A for June!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the June Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: What Kind of Ancient Christian Books Might Be Discovered?
author: BDEhrman
description: Considers what startling ancient Christian books might still be discovered.
searchSummary: Evaluates the chances that lost early Christian works such as Q or an unknown Pauline letter will be discovered. Finds usually consist either of new manuscripts of known books or wholly unexpected texts, while documents merely hypothesized by scholars almost never appear; named works such as the Gospels of Peter and Judas are rare exceptions. The Letter to Diognetus illustrates both serendipity and fragility: its sole known manuscript was found in a fish shop, published, and later destroyed.

title: Final Live Lecture on Jesus as The Christians Saw Him:  SATURDAY!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the final live lecture in a series on how early Christians understood Jesus.

title: The Trinity!  A Final Summation
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes the development of the Trinity from early Christian views of God, Christ, and the Spirit.

title: The Coming of the Holy Spirit in John:  A Key to the Trinity
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses John's Farewell Discourse to connect the Holy Spirit with later Trinitarian theology.
searchSummary: Explains how John's Farewell Discourse contributed to later Trinitarian doctrine through its portrayal of the Paraclete. After Jesus departs, the Father sends this "Spirit of Truth" to teach, remind, testify, judge, and speak with Jesus' authority. "Paraclete" means one called alongside and conveys guidance and support better than any single English equivalent. Father, Son, and Spirit remain distinct yet act in complete unity and delegated authority, providing later Christians with conceptual material for the Trinity.

title: Confusing Messages about Jesus and the Father:  John 14
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains confusing statements in John 14 about Jesus' relationship to the Father.
searchSummary: Examines John 14's seemingly conflicting claims about Jesus and the Father. Seeing Jesus reveals the Father because the Father authorizes his words and works, yet Jesus also says the Father sent him and "is greater than" him. John therefore presents profound unity without the full equality later required by orthodox Trinitarian theology. The chapter illustrates how New Testament writings can support competing theological conclusions and introduces the Spirit as a third divine agent who will replace Jesus.

title: Jesus’ Final Speech in John:  A Lead-up to the Coming of the Spirit
author: BDEhrman
description: Reads Jesus' final speech in John as a lead-up to the coming of the Spirit.
searchSummary: Introduces John's Farewell Discourse as the New Testament passage most important for tracing how the Holy Spirit entered later Trinitarian thought. Unlike the Synoptics' parables, ethical sayings, and kingdom preaching, John gives Jesus extended speeches about his identity, heavenly origin, saving mission, and signs. During his final meal, Jesus washes the disciples' feet and delivers a five-chapter address promising that the Spirit will replace him, a promise later Christians used to conceptualize Father, Son, and Spirit.

title: My Response To Conservative Critics.  An Interview on the MythVision Podcast
author: FreedomBen
description: Shares a MythVision interview responding to conservative critics.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's long MythVision Podcast interview with Derek Lambert responding to conservative criticism of his popular books. Lambert's detailed New Testament knowledge supports questions prompted especially by evangelical apologist John McLatchie's claims that Ehrman's work displays sloppy ignorance. Ehrman invites listeners to exercise their own judgment rather than accept either side's characterization, noting that the McLatchie discussion begins partway through a broader conversation about important subjects addressed across his writings.

title: You Don’t Want To Blaspheme the Spirit!  But What’s It Mean?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit and why the saying has troubled readers.
searchSummary: Explains Matthew's “blasphemy of the Holy Spirit” as attributing Jesus' Spirit-empowered works to the Devil and thereby rejecting Jesus' divine source. The saying follows the Pharisees' claim that demonic power enabled an exorcism, so it does not refer to sexual conduct or ordinary post-conversion sins. Its reference to forgiveness in the coming age concerns Jesus' expected earthly kingdom, not purgatory, and distinguishes free forgiveness from paying or suffering to atone for sin.

title: Blog Zoom Lecture This Saturday:  Jesus as a Young Boy!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Zoom lecture on stories of Jesus as a young boy.

title: The Spirit in the Life of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the Spirit's role in Jesus' life within early Christian apocalyptic expectation.

title: The Holy Spirit in Charge of the Church (?)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how early Christians understood the Holy Spirit's role in the church at the end of time.

title: What About Authors Who “Just Want to Sell Books”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to the charge that authors write controversial books merely to sell copies.
searchSummary: Rejects the accusation that writing accessible books to sell widely necessarily sacrifices scholarly integrity. Ehrman distinguishes sensational claims unsupported by evidence from trade books that present established or responsibly debated scholarship in compelling language. Using Misquoting Jesus, he shows that its central claims about New Testament manuscripts and textual variants were standard among specialists even though unfamiliar to lay readers, arguing that scholars should make important evidence interesting and available rather than conceal it from the public.

title: The Coming of the Spirit on the Day of Pentecost
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the coming of the Spirit at Pentecost through Joel and early Christian apocalyptic belief.
searchSummary: Explains how Acts interprets the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost as fulfillment of Joel's prophecy and the beginning of the worldwide Christian mission. The Spirit enables uneducated disciples to speak foreign languages, prompts Peter's sermon, produces mass conversion, and thereafter empowers miracles, guidance, and proclamation. With Jesus physically absent after his ascension, the Spirit becomes God's continuing presence in the church, helping establish later Christian reflection on the relationship among God, Jesus, and the Spirit.

title: What We Know Today About Religions and the Afterlife (in the US): Platinum Guest Post by Sharon Friedman
author: FreedomBen
description: Presents a guest overview of contemporary American religious beliefs about the afterlife.
searchSummary: Uses Pew Research Center survey data to compare present-day American beliefs about heaven across religious and nonreligious groups. Sharon Friedman notes that large majorities of Muslims and Christians affirm heaven, while belief is considerably lower among Jews, Buddhists, Hindus, Jehovah's Witnesses, agnostics, and atheists.
