Variation within groups, including Christians who reject heaven and unaffiliated respondents who accept it, raises questions about how individuals arrive at views that differ from their religious community's prevailing position.

title: Are There Actually Five Letters in 2 Corinthians (so that it is 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 Corinthians?)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores whether 2 Corinthians may be composed of as many as five separate letters.

title: Several Letters in One?  What about Second Corinthians?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the possibility that 2 Corinthians combines more than one Pauline letter.

title: The Coming of the Spirit at the End of Time
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the Spirit's arrival as part of early Christian belief that the end of time had begun.

title: Jesus according to the Christians:  A Three-Part Blog Lecture Series
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a three-part lecture series on Jesus according to early Christians.
searchSummary: Introduces a three-part public lecture series on early Christian stories about Jesus that many modern readers have never encountered. The lectures compare Jesus with ancient miracle-working divine men, explore legends about his childhood powers, and examine accounts of his activity in Hades between crucifixion and resurrection. The series uses Greco-Roman parallels and later Christian writings to illuminate portrayals of Jesus outside the familiar New Testament narratives.

title: On Being an Agnostic Atheist
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the distinction between agnosticism and atheism in personal religious identity.
searchSummary: Distinguishes agnosticism as a claim about knowledge from atheism as a position of belief. Ehrman cannot know whether any superior intelligence exists in an immense or multiple universe, making him agnostic, but he does not believe in a creator who governs the world, answers prayer, or brings good from evil, making him atheist. He occasionally calls himself a Christian atheist because he seeks to practice Christianity's best moral teachings despite rejecting its traditional supernatural claims.

title: Paul’s (Misunderstood) Message to His Corinthian Converts
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Paul's message to Corinthian converts and how it has often been misunderstood.

title: How Paul Started the Church in Corinth
author: BDEhrman
description: Reconstructs how Paul started the church in Corinth.

title: Paul and that Peculiar Church in Corinth
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Corinthian church as a key source for understanding early Christian community and the Spirit.

title: Wanna Go To Northern Italy with Me in September?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a northern Italy tour with lectures.

title: Gold Members Month of May Q&A
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the May Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: How the “Delay” of the End (Jesus’ Return) Affected Paul’s Communities
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how the delay of Jesus' return affected Pauline communities.

title: Why the Spirit Mattered for the Earliest Christians
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the Holy Spirit mattered to the earliest Christians.

title: More Recent Scholarship on Who Wrote the Pentateuch
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys more recent scholarship on the authorship of the Pentateuch.

title: Who Really Wrote the Pentateuch (if not Moses)?  The JEDP Hypothesis
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the JEDP documentary hypothesis for the sources behind the Pentateuch.

title: More Inconsistencies in the Pentateuch
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses inconsistencies in the Pentateuch to explain why scholars see multiple sources behind it.
searchSummary: Explains how inconsistencies across the Pentateuch support the Documentary Hypothesis. Genesis gives conflicting numbers of animals aboard Noah's ark, Exodus repeatedly destroys Egyptian livestock, and Genesis and Exodus disagree about whether the patriarchs knew God's name Yahweh. Ehrman argues that such seams arise when traditions from different periods and perspectives were combined, outlining the classic J, E, D, and P source model associated with Julius Wellhausen rather than Mosaic authorship.

title: Two (Contradictory?) Accounts of Creation in Genesis?
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares the two creation accounts in Genesis and their possible tensions.
searchSummary: Compares the two creation accounts in Genesis and argues that they reflect different authors and traditions. Genesis 1 and 2 conflict over the order of plants, animals, man, and woman; use different divine names; portray God differently; and pursue distinct theological interests. Rather than complementary stages of one narrative, the chapters present incompatible sequences and conceptions, providing foundational evidence that the Pentateuch compiles sources written at different times.

title: Who Wrote the Pentateuch Anyway?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks who wrote the Pentateuch if Moses did not.

title: Women and their Demons in the Life of Jesus: Guest Post by James McGrath
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents James McGrath's guest discussion of women and demons in the life of Jesus.

title: The Spirit of God in the Old Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys how the Spirit of God appears in the Old Testament.

title: How Did the Holy Spirit Get Into the Trinity?  In the Beginning….
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Holy Spirit's role in the development of the doctrine of the Trinity.
searchSummary: Explains how translation helped Christians read the Holy Spirit into Genesis and later support Trinitarian theology. Hebrew grammar presents creation as God's ordering of preexisting chaos, while ruach in Genesis 1:2 probably means a divine wind rather than a distinct Spirit. The Greek Septuagint encouraged Christians to understand pneuma as Spirit and combine it with beliefs that Christ participated in creation, allowing later readers to find Father, Son, and Spirit in the passage.

title: Was Paul Peter’s Enemy?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Paul and Peter should be understood as opponents in early Christianity.
searchSummary: Explores a forged letter attributed to Peter that portrays Paul as his enemy over the continuing authority of Jewish law. Unlike Acts, which presents Peter and Paul as harmonious advocates of a law-free gentile mission, this later text has Peter defend Moses and Jesus against Paul's allegedly lawless teaching. The post uses the contrast to show how later Christians remembered apostolic conflict and claimed Peter's authority for opposing Paul.

title: The Council of Nicaea and The Resulting View of Christ
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the Council of Nicaea and its role in shaping later views of Christ.
searchSummary: The Council of Nicaea addressed how Christ was divine, not whether he was divine or which books belonged in the New Testament. Arius taught that the Son was a subordinate divine being created before the universe, while Alexander defended a coeternal Son of the same substance as the Father. Constantine convened and influenced the council to secure unity, but its anti-Arian decision did not end the controversy.

title: YHWH and Jehovah:  Same?  Different?  Where’s Jehovah Come From?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the relationship between YHWH and Jehovah in biblical language and translation.
searchSummary: Explains that Jehovah is not the original biblical name of God. The Hebrew consonants YHWH were probably pronounced Yahweh, but Jewish readers substituted Adonai, Lord, and scribes added Adonai's vowel points as a reminder; combining those consonants and vowels through European spelling produced Jehovah. The Greek New Testament uses kurios, Lord, rather than the Hebrew Tetragrammaton, so translating its references with the constructed name Jehovah is unwarranted.

title: Jesus Under the Influence (of Women): Guest Post by James McGrath
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents James McGrath's guest discussion of women's influence on Jesus.

title: The Letter Jesus Wrote from the Cross (!)
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues the apocryphal story about a letter Jesus supposedly wrote from the cross.
searchSummary: Presents the second half of the Narrative of Joseph of Arimathea, a late apocryphal Passion Gospel that radically expands canonical traditions. Judas falsely accuses Jesus of stealing the law, the robbers Gestas and Demas respond differently at the crucifixion, and the repentant Demas is promised paradise. Jesus even writes from the cross to its heavenly gatekeepers, ordering them to admit Demas, before cosmic darkness and an earthquake accompany his death.

title: My Smithsonian Seminar: This Saturday!!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Smithsonian seminar.

title: Live Chance to Ask Me Anything!  This Sunday!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a live Ask Bart Anything event.

title: Another Letter Written By Jesus?  Stranger and Stranger…
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a later apocryphal story in which Jesus writes a letter from the cross.
searchSummary: Introduces the Narrative of Joseph of Arimathea, a late apocryphal Passion account told in the first person by the man who buried Jesus. It expands Judas's betrayal, invents detailed histories for the robbers Gestas and Demas, and has Jesus write a recommendation from the cross admitting the repentant Demas to paradise. Dependent partly on the Gospel of Nicodemus, the narrative combines legendary elaboration with a pronounced anti-Jewish purpose and may date anywhere from late antiquity to the medieval period.

title: Volunteer Needed to Read Audio Posts!
author: BDEhrman
description: Seeks a volunteer to record audio versions of blog posts.

title: Other New Testament References to Books Outside the Hebrew Bible: Platinum Guest Post by Doug Wadeson
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest discussion of New Testament references to books outside the Hebrew Bible.

title: You Call *This* a Heresy?  The Views of Arius, In His Own Words
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Arius's own words in the controversy that led to Nicaea.
searchSummary: Arius's surviving words describe the Father as uniquely eternal and incomparable, while the Son is a perfect divine creature begotten before the universe and separated from the Father by an infinity of glory. Christ created all other things but was neither coeternal nor consubstantial with God. Although this hierarchy may sound familiar to many modern Christians, Alexander condemned it as heresy and removed Arius from office.

title: A Heresy that May Not Sound Heretical to You:  Arius of Alexandria
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Arius of Alexandria and why the Arian controversy shaped the doctrine of the Trinity.
searchSummary: The Arian controversy concerned the precise relationship between God the Father and the already acknowledged divine Son, not whether Jesus was God. Arius interpreted Christ as God's first and greatest creation, begotten before the universe but subordinate to the uniquely eternal Father. Bishop Alexander regarded that view as dangerous, and the resulting conflict spread through the church until Constantine called the Council of Nicaea to seek unity.

title: Got a Question for Me?  Gold Q & A for April!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the April Gold Q&A and invites members to submit questions.

title: Did Paul the Pharisee Learn about Christianity from his Relative, the Apostle Junia?  Guest Post by James McGrath
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents James McGrath's guest proposal about Paul, Junia, and early knowledge of Christianity.

title: Do We Have Any of Jesus’ Writings?  (The Answer May Surprise You!)
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines the tradition that Jesus wrote to Abgar of Edessa.

title: Two Live Lectures on Sunday: The End is Near!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces two live lectures on apocalypticism and early Christianity.

title: Could Jesus Read?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Jesus could read in light of ancient literacy and Gospel evidence.
searchSummary: Assesses whether Jesus could read by combining ancient literacy rates with conflicting Gospel evidence. There is no reliable indication that Jesus could write, and Mark portrays Nazareth's residents as surprised by his learning without saying he read. Luke rewrites the scene to show him reading Isaiah, the New Testament's only explicit example. Ehrman slightly favors limited ability to read Hebrew Scripture, perhaps learned from a synagogue leader, while emphasizing that teaching and textual knowledge did not require literacy.

title: How Could Christ Be Both God and a Human — At Once?  The Unusual View of Origen
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Origen's unusual view of how Christ could be both divine and human.
searchSummary: Presents Origen's early-third-century explanation of Christ's simultaneous humanity and divinity. All souls originally contemplated God's Word but fell away and entered different forms of existence; one soul alone remained unwaveringly united with the Word. Like iron taking on fire's properties, it became fully suffused with divinity and then entered human life as Jesus. This allowed Christ to possess a human rational soul while manifesting God's Son, though later orthodoxy rejected Origen's preexistence and repeated-fall implications.

title: Nope Jesus is Not Yahweh
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues against the claim that the New Testament straightforwardly identifies Jesus as Yahweh.

title: Paul’s Community at Corinth
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Paul's Corinthian community as background for understanding the Spirit in 1 Corinthians.

title: Is Jesus Yahweh?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks in what sense Christians can or cannot identify Jesus with Yahweh.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: How Yahweh of the Israelites Became God of All: Platinum Guest Post by Dan Kohanski
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest account of how Israel's God came to be understood as God of all.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: Two More Live Lectures this Sunday!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces two live Zoom lectures for a New Testament course.

title: Fifty Ways to Forge a Gospel
author: admin
description: Presents James McGrath's discussion of how someone might forge a Gospel.
searchSummary: Presents James McGrath's annotated parody “Fifty Ways to Forge a Gospel,” inspired by Ehrman's argument that ancient pseudonymous writing was deceptive and condemned. Its lyrics allude to disputed canonical authorship, apocryphal dialogues and Gospels, the Gospel of Jesus' Wife, Acts, Enoch, Gnostic texts, and other ancient or modern fabrications. The commentary uses humor to show that forgery includes varied claims, techniques, and scholarly problems while emphasizing that ancient readers, like modern ones, did not approve being misled about authorship.

title: Was Marcion a Gnostic?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Marcion is usually not best classified as a Gnostic.
searchSummary: Explains why scholars no longer classify Marcion as a Gnostic despite similarities such as multiple gods, a defective creator, and escape from his power. Gnostic systems featured elaborate divine realms, sparks trapped in matter, salvation through secret knowledge, and broad use of Jewish and Christian Scripture. Marcion taught two unrelated gods, a divine Christ who only appeared human, salvation through faith in Jesus' death and resurrection, rejection of the Old Testament, and authority limited to his Gospel and Pauline collection.

title: The Earliest Views of the Trinity (Long after the New Testament)
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys early views of the Trinity that developed long after the New Testament.

title: How Can the Father and the Son Be the SAME?  Can Your Father Also Be Your Son?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the modalist view that Father, Son, and Spirit are the same divine person.

title: Are God and Christ the SAME Person?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether God and Christ were understood as the same person in early Christian debates.

title: Two Live Lectures This Sunday, On Hot Topics
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces two live Zoom lectures on New Testament topics.

title: The Importance of What Is Lost: Paul’s Letters
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why lost letters of Paul would be especially valuable for understanding early Christianity.

title: When Belief Dies Guest Post by Sam Devis!
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Sam Devis and the When Belief Dies podcast.
searchSummary: Recounts Sam Devis's loss of Christian belief after Bible college, depression, church work, chronic pain, and unanswered efforts to experience God. Because faith organized his marriage, family, employment, morality, friendships, and purpose, admitting unbelief threatened the structure of his life even though belief could not be forced. His When Belief Dies blog, podcast, and interviews create conversations about faith, religion, and nonbelief for people who feel isolated outside the Christian narrative while welcoming participants from both believing and nonbelieving perspectives.

title: Did the Disciples See Jesus Raised from the Dead?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why visions of Jesus probably led the disciples to believe in the resurrection.

title: How The Afterlife Changed After Jesus’ Life
author: BDEhrman
description: Contrasts Jesus' own afterlife expectations with later Christian beliefs about Jesus after death.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus expected bodily resurrection into God's future kingdom on earth, not immortal souls entering heaven or hell immediately after death. Hebrew tradition understood humans as animated bodies, while Jewish concern for justice eventually produced resurrection rather than Greek-style soul survival. After Easter, Jesus' followers interpreted his resurrection as the beginning of the end, but growing numbers of pagan converts brought dualistic assumptions. Christianity consequently transformed Jesus' earthly kingdom into postmortem destinations of heavenly bliss and infernal punishment.

title: A Probing Interview on “When Belief Dies Podcast”
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a probing interview on the When Belief Dies podcast.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's appearance on Sam Devis's When Belief Dies podcast, which explores questions involving faith, religion, and life. Ehrman praises Devis, who also narrates audio versions of blog posts, as a thoughtful interviewer whose questions and chosen issues are unusually penetrating. Rather than summarize the conversation's conclusions, the post directs readers to the recorded interview itself and invites them to evaluate its discussion, making the interview the substantive content associated with this brief introduction.

title: Were Jesus and Christ Two Different Beings?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains an early Christian view that separated the human Jesus from the divine Christ.

title: What Is Gnosticism?   A Video Introduction
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a video introduction to Gnosticism and early Christian views of Christ.
searchSummary: Introduces a lecture explaining Gnosticism as background for a second-century Christology in which Jesus Christ comprised two distinct beings, one human and one divine, temporarily united during Jesus' ministry. Ehrman places this view alongside alternatives that made Jesus human only, divine only, or both human and divine in another sense. Because several Christian Gnostic groups claimed this unusual position came from Jesus himself, the video examines the broader worldview that made it intelligible to its adherents.

title: A Live Lecture, this SATURDAY (April 3):  The Ethics of Paul
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a live lecture on the ethics of Paul.

title: Fantastic Story.  But History?  Some Doubts about the Triumphal Entry
author: BDEhrman
description: Raises historical doubts about the triumphal entry into Jerusalem.
searchSummary: Argues that the Gospels' triumphal entry is a distorted memory built around the historical gist that Jesus entered Jerusalem before his death. During volatile Passover celebrations, Roman troops would not have ignored crowds publicly acclaiming a new Davidic king who implied Rome's overthrow. The story instead reflects later Christian conflict with non-Christian Jews. It portrays Jewish crowds as fickle and unfaithful, first welcoming Jesus as Messiah and then demanding his death when he failed to become their expected political ruler.

title: Did Jesus Really Have a “Triumphal Entry” into Jerusalem?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the triumphal entry tradition and asks whether it happened historically.
searchSummary: Sets the historical and literary context for evaluating Jesus' triumphal entry. Passover commemorated liberation from foreign rule, drawing large crowds to Jerusalem and heightening Roman concern about revolt; Pilate stationed troops there to suppress unrest. Mark depicts crowds welcoming Jesus as the coming Davidic king. Matthew reshapes the scene by misreading Hebrew poetic parallelism as two separate animals, making Jesus ride both a donkey and its colt. This visible alteration raises questions about whether the larger remembered event is historical.

title: Modern Christians Who Follow Marcion (Unawares)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how some modern Christians unknowingly echo Marcion's view of the Old Testament.

title: Quotations of Non-Canonical Writings in the New Testament: Platinum Post by Douglas Wadeson
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest discussion of New Testament quotations from non-canonical writings.

title: Did Marcion Know the Gospels or Not??
author: BDEhrman
description: Clarifies what Marcion knew or used from Gospel traditions and Luke.
searchSummary: Clarifies that Paul used gospel to mean his preached message and probably knew no written Gospel, whereas Marcion mistakenly assumed Paul referred to a book. Marcion adopted a form of Luke but never named its author or connected it with Paul's companion. The post favors the view that Luke happened to be the Gospel used by Marcion's home church in Sinope, which he later edited and treated as Paul's authoritative Gospel.

title: Gold Members: Audio Q&A!  This week!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Gold member audio Q&A.

title: Live Lectures This Sunday, March 28!  Teachings of Paul That Are Widely Unknown.
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces live lectures on less familiar teachings of Paul.

title: More on Marcion’s Theology
author: BDEhrman
description: Gives further background on Marcion's theology and canon.

title: Lost Christian Writings I’d Love to Get My Hands On!
author: BDEhrman
description: Lists lost early Christian writings that would be especially valuable to discover.

title: A Phantom Jesus: The Teachings of the Second-Century Marcion
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Marcion's view that Christ was divine but not truly human.

title: The Value of Amulets for Reconstructing the New Testament Text: Guest Post by Brice Jones
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Brice Jones's guest discussion of amulets as evidence for New Testament textual criticism.

title: Announcing the Ehrman Blog Newsletter – Please Check Your Email!
author: Chrishuntley
description: Announces the launch of the Ehrman Blog newsletter.

title: Two Live Lectures, Sunday March 21:  The Death of Jesus and the Life of Paul.
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces live lectures on the death of Jesus and the life of Paul.
searchSummary: Announces two historical lectures prepared for an undergraduate New Testament course. The first examines what can be established about Jesus' crucifixion and how historians can approach his followers' claims that he was raised from the dead. The second reconstructs Paul's life, conversion, missionary activity, letters, and proclamation of salvation through Jesus' death and resurrection, asking whether Paul should be considered the true founder of Christianity.

title: Christ as Non-Human (but fully God) in the Early Second Century
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains early Christian views that made Christ fully divine but not genuinely human.
searchSummary: Explains docetic Christology, which held that Christ was fully divine but only appeared to possess a human body and suffer. Ignatius of Antioch attacks this view by insisting that Jesus was genuinely born, ate, drank, suffered, died, and rose bodily. Because Ignatius expected his own bodily martyrdom to imitate Christ and lead to salvation, a merely apparent crucifixion would make his sacrifice meaningless and undermine his hope for the body's redemption.

title: Was Christ So Divine That He Was Not Human?  The “Antichrists” of 1 John
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the antichrists of 1 John as opponents who denied Christ's real humanity.
searchSummary: Describes docetism, the view that Christ was completely divine and only appeared to be human. The position likely developed when some believers extended incarnation Christology beyond the Gospel of John's already elevated view of the preexistent Logos. First John attacks former community members as “antichrists” because they deny that Christ came in real flesh. Its opening emphasis on seeing, hearing, and touching Jesus counters their claim by insisting on his tangible human existence.

title: How to Make Sense of (or at least Peace with) What’s Strange in the Bible: Guest Post by Kristin Swenson
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Kristin Swenson's approach to making sense of strange features in the Bible.
searchSummary: Explains how understanding the Bible's formation helps readers address its inconsistencies, gaps, troubling ethics, and unfamiliar literary features. Using the two creation accounts in Genesis, Kristin Swenson shows that biblical books combine sources from different periods, places, and circumstances rather than presenting a single modern-style narrative. Historical and literary knowledge can therefore replace simplistic expectations with informed engagement, intellectual restraint, and a willingness to wrestle constructively with the text's diversity and difficulties.

title: Was Christ Human But Not Divine?  Another Early Christian View
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains adoptionist Christians who viewed Christ as human but not naturally divine.

title: Two More Live Lectures on Sunday, one of them very strange….
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces two live lectures for a New Testament course.

title: What Are the Sources of the Hebrew Bible?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces source-critical questions about the Hebrew Bible.

title: Christ as “Not God” in the Second Century: Early Jewish Adoptionists
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains early Jewish adoptionist views that treated Christ as human rather than divine by nature.

title: Was Matthew Influenced by Buddhist Writings?  Platinum Post by Steve Sutter
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest proposal about possible Buddhist influence on Matthew.
searchSummary: Presents proposed parallels between Buddhist writings and episodes or teachings in Matthew. Examples compare Buddha's conception, signs surrounding his appearance, care for the sick, nonviolence, generosity, imperishable treasure, and an earthquake at his death with Matthew's virgin birth, Magi, ethical teachings, parables, and crucifixion narrative. The guest author suggests that Matthew may have known Buddhist Scriptures, while offering similarities in ideas rather than evidence of direct literary dependence or shared wording.

title: Where Did the Trinity Come From?  The (Briefer) Video Version
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a shorter video version of an argument about where the Trinity came from.
searchSummary: Introduces a video lecture explaining how Christian belief moved from Jesus' divinity to the doctrine of the Trinity. Once Christians regarded Christ as God, continued to regard the Father as God, and maintained that only one God exists, they needed ways to reconcile those commitments. The lecture provides the major stages of the resulting debates, while the associated blog series promises a more detailed treatment of their theological development.

title: The Doctrine of the Trinity: Where We Are So Far
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes progress in a long thread on the doctrine of the Trinity.

title: Another Weird Event in my Life that Led Me to Be a Research Scholar
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on another unusual life event that helped lead to a research career.
searchSummary: Explains how contracting hepatitis before Ehrman's senior year of high school redirected his competitive energy from baseball into debate research. Confined from physical activity, he amassed evidence for the year's policy question, joined a partner, and helped win the state tournament. The experience made research, argument, and exposing weak reasoning compelling; combined with his new religious commitment, it propelled him toward intensive biblical study and scholarship, showing how a manageable illness produced a genuine personal benefit without explaining suffering generally.

title: God Showing Up a (Apparently) Human in the Hebrew Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores Hebrew Bible passages where God appears in apparently human form.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: TWO Live Lectures This Sunday (We’ve Changed The Plan…)!  How Do We Know about the Historical Jesus?  and Jesus, The Apocalyptic Prophet
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces live lectures on the historical Jesus and Jesus as apocalyptic prophet.

title: The Divine Realm in Antiquity (Appropriately: A Pyramid!)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the layered divine realm of antiquity as background for claims about Jesus as God.
searchSummary: Ancient people often imagined divinity as a hierarchy rather than an absolute divide between God and humanity. Supreme and Olympian gods stood above local deities, daimones, demigods, divinized rulers, and exceptional humans, with each level possessing different power and status. This graded divine realm helps explain how gentile Christians could call Jesus God without necessarily equating him with the highest deity in every respect.

title: Apologies about the Comments!
author: BDEhrman
description: Apologizes for technical problems with blog comments.

title: Christian Attitudes toward War, Through the Ages:  Platinum Post by Dan Kohanski
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest survey of Christian attitudes toward war through history.

title: The Stories We Tell: Guest Post by Robin Jones
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Robin Jones's guest reflection on stories, social concern, and Christian commitment.

title: In What SENSE is Jesus “God” in Matthew, Mark, and Luke?  My Change of Mind
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains a changed view of whether Matthew, Mark, and Luke portray Jesus as God.

title: What Did Ancient People Think It Meant To Call Someone God?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains what ancient people could mean when calling a human or heavenly being God.
searchSummary: Argues that asking whether New Testament authors considered Jesus “God” requires understanding ancient divinity as a spectrum rather than importing Nicene categories. Early Christians expressed exaltation, incarnation, and hybrid Christologies: a human could receive divine status, a heavenly being could become human, or divine sonship could begin at conception. Paul combines preexistence with later exaltation, while John presents the Logos as already God. The crucial historical question is therefore not simply whether Jesus was divine, but in what sense.

title: Wanna Go to Croatia with Me?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a possible lecture tour to Croatia.

title: More Live Lectures this Sunday:  The Gospel of John and Early Christian Gnosticism!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces live lectures on the Gospel of John and early Christian Gnosticism.
searchSummary: Announces two undergraduate lectures comparing distinctive forms of early Christianity. One examines John's presentation of Jesus as a divine being who descended from heaven, contrasting it with the other canonical Gospels and asking how Jesus can be both human and divine. The other introduces the sources and shared ideas associated with diverse Gnostic movements, explaining how their views differed from the form of Christianity that later became dominant.

title: An Intriguing but Most Peculiar Book!  Guest Post by Kristin Swenson
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Kristin Swenson's book on the strangeness of the Bible.
searchSummary: Introduces Kristin Swenson's argument that the Bible's strangeness invites informed engagement rather than unquestioning acceptance or wholesale dismissal. Its books arose across many centuries, places, languages, and communities, producing diverse voices, narrative gaps, inconsistencies, and disputed ethical claims. Swenson presents critical study as a way to examine those features, challenge inherited assumptions and literalism, and approach biblical interpretation as an active conversation grounded in the texts and their historical backgrounds.

title: The Buddhist Scriptures and the Gospel of Luke: Platinum Post by Steve Sutter
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest proposal about Buddhist scriptures and the Gospel of Luke.
searchSummary: Presents a guest comparison between Buddhist traditions and two passages in Luke. The Buddha's temptation by Mara is compared with Jesus' temptation, while Buddhist and Confucian formulations of the Golden Rule are placed alongside Luke 6:31 and earlier Greek and Jewish parallels. The post argues that these teachings were not unique to Christianity and invites consideration of similarities among ancient religious and ethical traditions without establishing direct literary dependence.

title: My Interview About Jesus for “The Dagger Squad”
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares an interview about Jesus with The Dagger Squad.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's Dagger Squad interview with Garfield A. Reid and questions from callers. The recorded program is titled Jesus, New Testament, False Prophecies, and False Doctrines, identifying the principal areas addressed in their discussion. Ehrman describes Reid as lively and engaging and the audience questions as intriguing, but the short post supplies no written account of the positions reached, directing readers to the video for the interview's arguments and answers.

title: Is the “Word” (Logos) of God in John the Wisdom (Sophia) of God in Judaism?
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares John's Logos with Jewish traditions about divine Wisdom.
searchSummary: Connects John's divine Logos with Jewish traditions about personified Wisdom rather than treating the Prologue as simply Greek philosophy. Proverbs 8 portrays Wisdom beside God before creation, assisting his work and granting life, themes closely paralleling John 1. Jewish writings could equate God's word and wisdom, while Philo described the Logos as a divine intermediary. "Logos" may also evoke Genesis, Greek intellectual culture, and a masculine term suitable for the male Christ who becomes flesh.

title: A Christian Is Not Necessarily a Disciple (Monthly Platinum Post: Douglas Wadeson)
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest argument distinguishing being Christian from being a disciple.
searchSummary: A guest writer distinguishes identifying as a Christian through belief in Christ's saving death and resurrection from living as a disciple who follows Jesus' teachings. Prosperity preaching, neglect of the poor, punitive politics, and salvation detached from conduct can preserve Christian identity while reversing Jesus' commands about mercy, generosity, forgiveness, and relinquishing wealth. The post argues that reducing faith to a past profession makes discipleship secondary, despite Gospel and James traditions that connect doing God's will with genuine faith.

title: Interested in Going to Rome with Me?
author: FreedomBen
description: Announces a possible lecture tour to Rome and southern Italy.

title: Does Luke Present Different (Inconsistent!) Views of Christ?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains whether Luke-Acts contains different or inconsistent views of Christ.
searchSummary: Explains Luke's inconsistent placement of Jesus' exalted titles at his birth, baptism, ministry, and resurrection. Luke-Acts repeatedly describes Jesus becoming Messiah, Lord, Savior, or Son of God at more than one moment, so the baptismal reading “today I have begotten you” fits Luke's flexible Christology even alongside the infancy narrative. Ehrman argues that scribes changed this wording because adoptionist Christians could use it, not because it was foreign to Luke's theology.

title: Live Lectures this Sunday!  Distinctive Messages of Luke and John
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces live lectures on the distinctive messages of Luke and John.
searchSummary: Announces two lectures designed to highlight the distinctive perspectives of Luke and John. The first compares Luke with Mark and Matthew on issues including Jesus' expectation of the end and his behavior at death. The second applies several analytical methods to John's unusual portrayal of Jesus and asks where its author obtained his information. Both lectures show why the Gospels should be interpreted as separate accounts rather than harmonized.

title: How Old Was Jesus ???
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to a reader question about Jesus' age and its possible significance.

title: But Maybe Paul Doesn’t Believe in the Incarnation….
author: BDEhrman
description: Questions whether Paul teaches incarnation in the Philippians Christ poem.
searchSummary: Evaluates the proposal that Philippians 2 portrays Jesus only as a second Adam rather than a preexistent divine being. The interpretation sees Christ refusing the equality Adam sought and reversing Adam's disobedience through humble death. Ehrman rejects it because the poem says “form,” not Genesis's “image,” attributes the desire to Eve rather than Adam, and depicts Christ becoming human. Other Pauline passages also explicitly presuppose Christ's heavenly existence, making an incarnation reading more coherent.

title: Was Christ actually God in the Flesh?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces John's fully incarnational Christology as Christ made flesh.
searchSummary: Interprets John 1:1-18 as a poetic prologue presenting an entirely incarnational Christology. The divine Logos exists with God, is itself God, creates everything, and then becomes the human Jesus who reveals the Father. Its vocabulary and staircase parallelism distinguish the poem from the rest of the Gospel, suggesting that it may be a later addition drawn from another author. Unlike exaltation Christologies, Jesus' divinity here derives from the eternal Logos becoming flesh, not elevation after resurrection.

title: Reminder!  A Live Chance to “Ask Bart Anything” (ABA) this Wednesday 2/17/2021
author: BDEhrman
description: Reminds readers about a live Ask Bart Anything session.

title: One of the Weird Events in My Life that Led Me To Be A Research Scholar
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on a strange early event that helped lead to a research career.
searchSummary: Recounts how a ninth-grade independent-study project to invent an international lunar language helped prepare Ehrman for scholarship. Although Relunar Relingua was linguistically naive, designing its grammar and dictionary forced him to think about word order, inflection, regularity, parts of speech, and shared roots. That early mental framework later helped him understand Greek and discover an aptitude for serious language study, making an attempt to escape difficult Latin an unlikely step toward his eventual career as a biblical researcher.

title: Blog Announcement!   The Full Implementation of our New Tier Membership System
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces implementation of the blog's tiered membership system.

title: The Essence of Religious Literacy: A Christian Perspective. Platinum Guest Post by Fredrick Ackun
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest reflection on religious literacy from a Christian perspective.

title: Interview about My Writing with the North Carolina Writers’ Network
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares an interview about writing, afterlife research, and related projects.
searchSummary: Presents an interview about Ehrman's research and writing, using Heaven and Hell to illustrate his approach. He discusses vivid ancient portrayals of punishment, an ideal reader open to evidence, deliberate humor and tone, careful transitions, and the sequence from a compelling idea through years of research to stressful drafting. He also explains why reconstructing afterlife beliefs requires canonical, noncanonical, Jewish, Greek, and Roman sources and distinguishes tracing a belief's development from judging whether it is true.

title: Live Lecture This Sunday!  Do Christians Need to Be Jews?  Understanding the Gospel of Matthew.
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a live lecture on Matthew and whether Christians need to be Jews.
searchSummary: Announces a lecture interpreting Matthew as a particularly Jewish Gospel. Ehrman focuses on whether Matthew's Jesus expects his followers to observe Jewish law and, if so, whether that obligation encompasses the entire Torah. The lecture uses this difficult question to explore Jesus as the Jewish Messiah, Matthew's relationship to Judaism, and the implications of reading the Gospel within its historical and religious context rather than through later Christian assumptions.

title: More Comments on Paul’s Rather Astounding Christ Poem
author: BDEhrman
description: Adds further comments on Paul's Christ poem in Philippians.

title: One of the Most Important Passages of the NT: Paul’s Christ Poem
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Paul's Christ poem as one of the New Testament's most important Christological passages.
searchSummary: Analyzes the structure and origin of Philippians 2:6-11. Its unusual vocabulary, balanced stanzas, and the exaltation section's awkward relation to Paul's appeal for selfless service suggest that Paul quotes an earlier poem. The composition presents Christ as a preexistent divine being who empties himself, becomes human, dies, and is raised to universal lordship. If it predates Paul's mid-first-century letter, it provides exceptionally early evidence that some Christians already embraced an incarnation Christology.

title: An Alternative Christology:  God Became Human
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains an incarnational Christology in which God becomes human in Christ.
searchSummary: Contrasts early exaltation Christologies, in which a human Jesus becomes divine, with incarnation Christology, in which a preexistent heavenly being becomes human. Ehrman argues that Paul viewed Christ as God's chief angel: Galatians identifies him as an angel, while Philippians depicts him abandoning divine form, entering human life, and obeying unto death. God then exalts him higher and grants him the divine title Lord, making him equal with but still distinct from God the Father.

title: Personal Post: My Work Habits
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on work habits and productivity in writing, teaching, and blogging.
searchSummary: Explains how intense focus, discipline, and deliberate time management support Ehrman's productivity as a professor, researcher, writer, and blogger. He minimizes passive distractions, protects adequate sleep, works in concentrated stretches, and schedules short household breaks to restore attention. Writing, translation, data analysis, and argument especially absorb him, while advance planning helps fit necessary work into defined periods; he also acknowledges that this highly structured, interruption-resistant approach has personal costs and does not suit everyone.

title: Platinum Members!  Vote for your Favorite Platinum Post
author: BDEhrman
description: Invites Platinum members to vote on recent guest posts.

title: The Oldest View of Christ:  Found in Only One Greek Manuscript of Luke!
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses a Greek manuscript of Luke to discuss one of the oldest views of Christ.
searchSummary: Argues that Luke's baptism originally quoted Psalm 2:7, declaring today I have begotten you, even though this wording survives in only one Greek manuscript. Earlier church fathers widely knew that form, while scribes likely harmonized Luke with Mark to suppress its adoptionist implications. The variant supports an early exaltation Christology in which Jesus became God's Son at baptism, creating tension with Luke's birth narrative and Acts' association of sonship with resurrection.

title: Ask Bart Anything!  Live Zoom Chance for you to Pick My Brain and/or Stump Me
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a live Ask Bart Anything session over Zoom.

title: When Did Jesus Become Divine?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks when Jesus came to be regarded as divine in early Christianity.
searchSummary: Traces one development of Christology by moving Jesus' divine sonship backward from resurrection to baptism, birth, and finally preexistence. Mark presents sonship at baptism, Matthew and Luke connect it with miraculous conception, and John describes the eternal Logos becoming flesh. Yet Paul, writing before the Gospels, already embraces incarnation. Ehrman therefore retains the chronological pattern as part of the story while recognizing that exaltation and incarnation Christologies coexisted earlier than a simple linear progression suggests.

title: Even Giants Have a Cross to Bear:  Platinum Post by Marie Wiley
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest reflection on suffering, miracles, and the cross.
searchSummary: Reflects on Jesus' cross as a symbol that even goodness entails suffering rather than as payment for sin. Marie Wiley explores whether pain is limited by perspective, time, unknown dimensions, divine self-experience, or human judgments that vary by victim and circumstance, while admitting such abstractions can feel morally repugnant beside actual agony. She proposes bearing suffering lovingly without welcoming it, questions selective concern for human and animal pain, and retains hope that currently unknown facts may matter.

title: Another Two Lectures on the Gospels, Live on Sunday.  Join Us!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces additional live lectures on the Gospels.
searchSummary: Announces two course lectures on central historical problems in the Synoptic Gospels. One examines evidence that Mark originally ended at 16:8, before anyone sees the risen Jesus, and asks how the absence of the later ending affects its message. The other explains the literary relationships among Matthew, Mark, and Luke, how scholars determine who copied whom, and why source relationships matter for interpreting each author's revisions and emphases.

title: Very Early Understandings of Christ in A Later Book of the NT
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains early Christology preserved in Luke-Acts despite the book's later date.

title: Jesus, Mary Magadalene, and … Sexual Innuendos?
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses Mary Magdalene, the Gospel of Philip, and modern sexualized interpretations.

title: Do You Want to Hear Two More Lectures on the Gospels?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces additional live lectures on the Gospels.
searchSummary: Announces two introductory lectures on the origins and character of the Gospels. One examines how oral stories about Jesus circulated, changed, and were sometimes invented before being written down. The other asks what kind of literature the Gospels are and how historians assess their biographical and historical value. Together the lectures explain why the transmission of tradition and the genre of the Gospels are essential for reconstructing Jesus and early Christianity.

title: How Do We Know What Christians Thought about Jesus BEFORE the New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how scholars can infer Christian views about Jesus before the New Testament writings.

title: Platinum Guest Post by Douglas Wadeson: A Christian Is Not Necessarily a Disciple, and Vice Versa. Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues a guest argument distinguishing Christians from disciples.
searchSummary: A guest writer asks whether someone can follow Jesus' moral teachings without believing he is divine, Messiah, or risen savior. Thomas Jefferson and modern Buddhists, Muslims, atheists, and former Christians can act as disciples in this limited sense, while believers may combine Christological faith with ethical transformation. The essay invites both groups to assess whether Jesus' teachings about universal concern, nonmaterialism, and service can improve personal relationships, churches, businesses, and public policy without requiring agreement about supernatural claims.

title: The Earliest Understandings of Christ
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the earliest Christian understandings of Christ after Jesus' death.

title: My Materialist View of the World
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains a materialist view of the world and its implications for mind and free will.

title: Was the King of Israel Called God??
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores whether Israelite kings or other figures could be called God.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: Want to Hear Me Give a Live Lecture?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a live lecture for readers.

title: Could Jews Consider Someone Other than God To Be God?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether ancient Jews could consider someone other than God to be divine.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: Did Humans Ever Become Divine in Judaism?  (Seems unlikely, no?)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Jewish traditions in which humans could be exalted to divine status.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: A Christian is Not Necessarily a Disciple: Platinum Post by Douglas Wadeson
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest argument distinguishing Christians from disciples.
searchSummary: Distinguishes Christian belief in Jesus' redemptive death and resurrection from discipleship expressed by following his commands. A guest writer contrasts Jesus' and the prophets' concern for the poor, mercy, forgiveness, and surrender of wealth with prosperity theology, political hostility to immigrants, inadequate health care, harsh punishment, and affluent churches. When salvation is treated as guaranteed by belief alone, conduct becomes irrelevant and Jesus' teachings can be dismissed as rules for an earlier Jewish age rather than obligations for Christians.

title: Guest Post Part 2 by New Testament Scholar Jeff Siker: Why I Am Still a Christian
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Jeff Siker's reflection on remaining Christian while doing critical New Testament scholarship.
searchSummary: Explains why New Testament scholar Jeffrey Siker remains Christian despite accepting historical-critical conclusions about Scripture. His moderate and liberal education allowed him to treat biblical differences as distinct perspectives rather than contradictions requiring reconciliation, integrating scholarship with faith instead of feeling betrayed by the church. Siker describes faith as an interpretive conversation across ancient and modern communities and grounds his continued belief especially in God's grace, resurrection hope, and response to human suffering.

title: Guest Post by New Testament Scholar Jeff Siker:  Why I am Still a Christian
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Jeff Siker's explanation of how critical New Testament scholarship can coexist with Christian faith.
searchSummary: Traces Jeffrey Siker's path from conservative Protestant youth to historically informed Christian faith. Unlike Ehrman's fundamentalist background, Siker encountered historical-critical study within a moderate tradition that did not require biblical inerrancy, so contradictions and the Bible's human character did not produce a crisis of betrayal. His education helped him move beyond literalism while integrating historical context, critical interpretation, and continued church commitment; the post sets up his fuller explanation of why he remains Christian.

title: Still Other Humans Who Became Gods: In Jesus’ Time!
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys Greco-Roman traditions about humans becoming gods in Jesus' time.
searchSummary: Roman traditions portrayed historical rulers as becoming divine as well as legendary figures such as Romulus. Julius Caesar was officially deified after death, a status promoted by Octavian, while Augustus was hailed as son of God, associated with Apollo, and worshiped in parts of the empire during his lifetime. These practices supplied a contemporary framework for understanding claims that Jesus was a divine human.

title: Could a Human Become a God in the Ancient World?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how ancient ideas of humans becoming divine help frame early claims about Jesus.
searchSummary: Greek and Roman traditions held that exceptional humans could be taken into heaven, made immortal, worshiped, and asked for protection. Livy's accounts of Romulus describe both his disappearance into the divine realm and a later appearance confirming his exalted status. Although the details differ from Christian claims about Jesus, the story shows that a human becoming a god was an intelligible ancient idea.

title: Were Ancient Pagans Sometimes Monotheists?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains ways ancient pagans could be monotheistic or henotheistic.
searchSummary: Some ancient pagans believed in one supreme divine reality without denying the existence of other gods. Philosophers sought a unifying first principle, worshipers honored the Greatest God, and inscriptions could describe lesser gods as names, powers, or messengers of the highest deity. Such henotheistic tendencies meant Christian claims about one ultimate God were distinctive but not wholly unprecedented in the Greco-Roman world.

title: Were Ancient Israelites Actually Monotheists?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why ancient Israelite monotheism was more complex than simple modern monotheism.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: Platinum Guest Post by Steve Sutter:  The Buddhist Influence on the Gospel of Luke
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest proposal about Buddhist influence on the Gospel of Luke.
searchSummary: Presents a guest argument that Buddhist writings may have influenced the Gospel of Luke through missionary and cultural exchange across the Hellenistic world. It compares Buddhist teachings with Luke's sayings about possessions, love of enemies, judging others, moral consequences, miraculous birth, and healing. Because Buddhist traditions could have reached cities such as Antioch before Luke was written, the author concludes that Luke may have borrowed some of this material.

title: The God Jesus, In Competition
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the problem of how Christians could call Jesus God while maintaining belief in one God.
searchSummary: Ehrman recalls realizing at Priene that early Christian claims about Jesus developed alongside the Roman imperial cult. Emperors were already called God, Lord, Savior, and Son of God, making Jesus and Caesar rival divine figures in the same cultural world. Because the earliest Christians were Jewish monotheists, however, explaining Jesus' divinity also requires examining Jewish traditions about divine humans and heavenly beings.

title: Gold Members Only Audio Q&A
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Gold member audio Q&A.

title: Platinum Members Webinar!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the first Platinum member webinar.

title: One of the Most Significant Passages in the NT: Paul’s Christ Poem
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Paul's Christ poem in Philippians as a major text for incarnation Christology.
searchSummary: Explains why Philippians 2:6-11 is widely regarded as a pre-Pauline Christ poem. Its balanced structure, vocabulary uncommon in Paul, and exaltation section's imperfect fit with Paul's ethical appeal indicate an earlier composition quoted in full. Christ descends from divine form into human slavery and death, then is elevated to universal lordship. Because the poem circulated before Philippians, it demonstrates that incarnation Christology was already established before Paul's letter and very early in Christian history.

title: How the Trinity Got Into the New Testament: Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues the story of how a later Trinitarian formula entered the text of 1 John.
searchSummary: Traces how a nonoriginal Trinitarian formula entered 1 John and the King James Bible through Erasmus's Greek New Testament. Working hastily from a few late manuscripts, Erasmus initially omitted the wording absent from his Greek evidence, then restored it after opponents apparently manufactured a Greek copy from the Latin Vulgate. Later printers reproduced his text for centuries, carrying this addition, the woman taken in adultery, and Mark's longer ending into familiar English Bibles despite superior manuscripts lacking them.

title: How the Trinity Got Into the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how the clearest biblical-sounding statement of the Trinity entered later manuscript tradition.
searchSummary: Introduces the manuscript history behind the Trinitarian addition in 1 John 5:7-8. The New Testament was written in Greek, but handwritten Greek and Latin copies differed, requiring editors to reconstruct earlier wording. Ehrman describes the multilingual Complutensian Polyglot, the first printed Greek New Testament, whose publication lag allowed another edition to circulate first. That later publishing sequence set the stage for an explicit statement that Father, Word, and Spirit are one to enter subsequent Greek editions and English translations.

title: Is the Trinity in the Bible?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether the doctrine of the Trinity is taught in the Bible.

title: No Virgin Births?  Then How Were Demi-gods Born In Antiquity?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how ancient demigods were conceived without matching the New Testament virgin birth stories.
searchSummary: Greek and Roman stories commonly explained extraordinary humans as children produced through sexual unions between gods and mortal women. Traditions about Alexander, Hercules, and others therefore differ sharply from Matthew's and Luke's accounts of Jesus' virginal conception. The comparison shows that divine parentage was familiar in antiquity, but a mother conceiving without sexual intercourse was not the standard pagan pattern.

title: What About All Those *Other* Virgin Births in Antiquity?
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Jesus' virgin birth traditions with other ancient birth stories.

title: With Respect to Others Who Did Not Like My Newsweek Article
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds respectfully to critics of a Newsweek article on Jesus' birth.

title: The Blog Year in Review, 2020
author: BDEhrman
description: Reviews the blog's activity, challenges, and charitable work during 2020.
searchSummary: Reviews the blog's growth and charitable achievements during 2020 despite the pandemic. A redesigned platform, tiered memberships, 289 new posts, more than 13,000 comments, and rapid membership growth pushed the archive above 2,500 posts and the community above 12,000 members. Annual charitable distributions reached $232,000 and lifetime giving exceeded $1 million. Bart credits Steven Ray and an expanded volunteer team, invites feedback, and asks readers to spread the word in 2021.

title: Responses to my Newsweek Article on Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses responses to a Newsweek article on the Christmas stories.

title: Love Your Neighbor as Yourself.  Platinum Post by Marie Wiley
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a Platinum guest reflection on loving one's neighbor.

title: Where is the Virgin Birth in John?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why John lacks a virgin birth story and what that means for John's Christology.
searchSummary: Argues that John's incarnation theology neither states nor presupposes a virgin birth. The divine Word becomes the human Jesus, but John never explains that transition through virginal conception and may even assume Joseph was Jesus' biological father. Matthew and Luke instead make Jesus God's son through miraculous conception without describing a preexistent being. Later Christian doctrine combines these distinct accounts into incarnation through the Virgin Mary, producing a synthesis that none of the individual Gospel authors expresses.

title: Does the Gospel of Mark Deny a Virgin Birth?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Mark's Gospel may imply a view inconsistent with the virgin birth.
searchSummary: Argues that Mark's Gospel may implicitly conflict with the virgin birth even though it contains no birth narrative. Mark depicts Jesus' mother and brothers trying to restrain him because they believe he is out of his mind, a conclusion supported by Greek grammar despite translations that shift the judgment to unnamed people. A mother who knew of a miraculous conception should understand Jesus' identity. Matthew and Luke omit this troubling scene while supplying their own virgin-birth accounts.

title: Want To See My New Book Manuscript?  A Blog Fundraiser
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers readers a chance to see a new book manuscript in exchange for a blog donation.
searchSummary: Offers a small number of major donors access to Bart's draft scholarly monograph on early Christian journeys through heaven and hell. The book compares the Apocalypses of Peter and Paul, Acts of Thomas, Gospel of Nicodemus, and related Greek, Roman, and Jewish traditions, arguing that their otherworldly tours shape present conduct rather than merely report geography. A $1,000 tax-deductible donation goes entirely to charity and permits reading, optional comments, and direct electronic delivery.

title: Christmas 2020
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on Christmas during the unusual and difficult year of 2020.
searchSummary: Reflects on the Christian Christmas message during the isolation, death, unemployment, and political division of the 2020 pandemic. Although Ehrman no longer believes divine help entered the world, he argues that Jesus' identification with poverty, outsiders, humility, generosity, and peace directly challenges followers who support wealth, power, exclusion, and hostility. Christians and non-Christians alike should measure holiday celebration by whether it promotes compassion for suffering people rather than hatred, exploitation, or self-centered comfort.

title: Was Jesus Born in Bethlehem?  Luke’s Version.
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Luke's account of why Jesus was born in Bethlehem despite being from Nazareth.
searchSummary: Compares Luke's and Matthew's incompatible explanations for Jesus' Bethlehem birth. Luke moves a Nazareth family through a historically impossible census and returns them home after forty days, while Matthew treats Bethlehem as their residence, sends them to Egypt, and relocates them to Nazareth years later. Combined with the mismatch between Quirinius and Herod, these contradictions suggest both authors created stories to connect Jesus with Micah's prophecy; Ehrman concludes Jesus was probably born in Nazareth.

title: Was Jesus Born in Bethlehem?  Matthew’s Version….
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Matthew's account of why Jesus was born in Bethlehem despite being from Nazareth.
searchSummary: Argues that Matthew's account of Jesus' birth in Bethlehem is historically implausible and incompatible with Luke's version. Matthew assumes that Joseph and Mary already live in a Bethlehem house, introduces a supernatural star and an otherwise unattested massacre, sends the family to Egypt, and relocates it to Nazareth only after Herod's death. The narrative solves the theological problem of a Messiah expected from Bethlehem who was widely known to come from Nazareth, but probably does not preserve Jesus' birthplace.

title: Do Christians Have to Believe in the Virgin Birth?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Christian faith requires belief in the virgin birth.

title: My Article on Christmas in Newsweek: Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the second part of a Newsweek article on Christmas and the birth stories.
searchSummary: Argues that Matthew's and Luke's infancy narratives are theologically meaningful but historically unreliable. Their invented and incompatible genealogies, Luke's unattested empire-wide ancestral census, and Matthew's impossible guiding star illustrate contradictions and implausibilities surrounding Jesus' Bethlehem birth. Ehrman contrasts Pope Benedict's devotional affirmation with critical historical judgment, suggesting believers need not ground the narratives' religious truth in factual accuracy or reject their value when their historical claims fail.

title: My Article on Christmas in Newsweek
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a Newsweek article on Christmas and historical questions about Jesus' birth.

title: Christmas from a Historical Point of View
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a historical approach to Christmas and the birth of Jesus.

title: A Holiday Season Request!
author: BDEhrman
description: Makes a holiday-season request connected with giving and support.
searchSummary: Makes a holiday and year-end appeal for additional charitable donations after a difficult 2020. Bart asks readers who valued the blog's accessible scholarship to support organizations helping people in need, explaining that all membership fees and gifts go directly to charity and may be designated for a particular beneficiary. He restates the blog's paired purposes of communicating academic knowledge and raising funds, emphasizes that charity motivates his continued work, and directs contributors to PayPal or Stripe.

title: An Apocryphal Story of Mary’s Conception of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares an apocryphal account of Mary's conception of Jesus from Pseudo-Matthew.
searchSummary: Presents the Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew's expanded account of Mary's conception of Jesus and the public defense of her virginity. An angel announces the pregnancy, Joseph initially suspects wrongdoing but is reassured in a dream, and Temple authorities compel both Joseph and Mary to drink a ritual testing water. Their innocence is vindicated when neither displays the expected sign of guilt, allowing the story to dramatize and defend Mary's holiness beyond the canonical infancy narratives.

title: A Different Account of Joseph and Mary!
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Pseudo-Matthew's expanded account of Joseph, Mary, and Jesus' birth.
searchSummary: Introduces the seventh-century Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew, a Latin reworking and expansion of the Proto-Gospel of James that strongly influenced medieval Christian art. The excerpt explains how fourteen-year-old Mary, vowed to virginity, leaves the Temple and is assigned to the elderly Joseph after a dove miraculously emerges from his branch. It also portrays Mary weaving the Temple curtain and receiving angelic confirmation that she truly merits the title Queen of Virgins.

title: Is Suffering a Problem for Those Who Suffer?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether suffering is a problem primarily for those who experience it.
searchSummary: Considers why Nick Vujicic's severe disability strengthens his Christian hope while suffering led Ehrman away from faith. Ehrman admires Vujicic's resilience and admits he cannot explain their different reactions, but exceptional success stories do not outweigh millions whose starvation, disease, violence, or disability yields no restoration. Individuals must reach their own conclusions after confronting suffering honestly; dismissive indifference and easy optimism can discourage action and thereby allow additional preventable suffering.

title: How Then Can We Believe?
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses The Brothers Karamazov to press the problem of suffering and belief.
searchSummary: Uses Ivan Karamazov's rejection of ultimate harmony to argue that no future resolution can justify a tortured child's present agony. Ehrman might accept a genuinely overwhelming divine explanation, but considers that hope unlikely, while free will addresses human cruelty without explaining droughts, disease, earthquakes, and other natural harms. The passage urges readers to face suffering directly and distrust answers that make redemption, afterlife, or a greater good too easily compensate for innocent pain.

title: Facing the Problem of Suffering Head-on
author: BDEhrman
description: Frames suffering as a direct challenge to belief in an active, loving, all-powerful God.
searchSummary: Introduces Ivan Karamazov's rebellion against a divinely governed world whose innocent suffering remains intolerable even if God eventually reveals a harmonious purpose. Ivan accepts that God may exist but refuses a final explanation that retroactively justifies atrocities against children, treating their cost as morally unacceptable. Ehrman presents this literary challenge to the comforting claim that God's hidden plan will make everything sensible and begins illustrating it through Ivan's accounts of deliberate human cruelty.

title: Are You Interested in a Platinum Membership?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the benefits of Platinum membership on the blog.

title: Human Suffering and the Christian Faith
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses God's Problem to explain how human suffering affected Christian faith.
searchSummary: Explains why innocent suffering led Ehrman to abandon belief in an active, loving, all-powerful Christian God. A Christmas Eve prayer asking God to enter the world's darkness intensified his anger at divine silence amid hunger, disease, disasters, violence, poverty, and private grief. Biblical stories portray God intervening to rescue, heal, and feed people, yet comparable help is absent for millions today. After years of considering theological answers, Ehrman found the mismatch between faith's claims and lived reality impossible to reconcile.

title: My Struggle With Why There Is Suffering
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on why suffering became the central reason for leaving Christian faith.
searchSummary: Clarifies that biblical scholarship ended Ehrman's evangelical inerrancy, not his Christianity; the problem of suffering later ended his faith. Recognizing the Bible's historically conditioned ethics and conflicting explanations opened renewed questions about punishment, free will, testing, spiritual enemies, redemption, divine companionship, afterlife, and mystery. None now explains extreme suffering to him, and he urges people to wrestle seriously rather than repeat comforting formulas, while respecting that others reach different resolutions.

title: Paul Dictated His Letters: How Does *That* Complicate Finding an Original?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Paul's dictation of letters complicates the search for an original text.
searchSummary: Examines how dictation further complicates defining the original text of Philippians. Paul may have changed his mind, misspoken, been misunderstood, or corrected a secretary's draft, making his intention, spoken words, first written form, corrections, and dispatched copy possible but conflicting originals. Because Philippians may combine two letters and extant witnesses appear much later with thousands of mostly trivial variants, scholars cannot evaluate original readings without first deciding which textual stage they seek.

title: Why Finding an “Original” Text is So Unexpectedly Complicated
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why identifying an original text is more complicated than finding the earliest copy.
searchSummary: Explains why Paul's customary use of secretaries creates multiple candidates for a letter's original text. Romans names Tertius as writer, and Galatians indicates Paul added lines in his own hand; during such production a scribe could mishear dictation, Paul could correct the draft, and the clean copy could introduce further errors. The wording Paul intended, spoke, reviewed, or finally sent may differ, so the earliest written form need not be the authoritative one.

title: What Does It Even Mean to Have an “Original” of An Ancient Writing?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks what original means when dealing with ancient writings and later copies.
searchSummary: Questions what original means for Philippians if its canonical form joins two separate Pauline letters. The earliest fragmentary witness, P46, appears about 150 years after Paul and the first complete copy about 300 years later, while neither is the physical original. Treating the later compilation as original gives an unknown editor an authorial role; treating the separate letters as originals identifies forms no surviving manuscript independently preserves.

title: Could Paul’s Letter to the Philippians be TWO Letters?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores whether Philippians may combine two separate Pauline letters.

title: A Fund-Raising Webinar:  What Can We Really Know about the Birth of Jesus??
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a fundraising webinar on what can be known about Jesus' birth.
searchSummary: Announces an intimate webinar on what can historically be known about Jesus's birth, with proceeds divided between the regional Food Bank and Doctors Without Borders. Bart plans to examine the Gospel accounts, their omissions and inconsistencies, historical context, date and place, and the virgin birth before answering participants' questions. Twelve places are awarded through two rounds of bidding, and the highest bidder also receives a private half-hour conversation with him.

title: Do We Have Paul’s Original Letter to the Philippians?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether the original form of Paul's letter to the Philippians can be recovered.
searchSummary: Clarifies that Philippians is authentically Pauline but no surviving manuscript is Paul's physical original. A first copy remains a copy, exact passages may preserve original contents while errors do not, and the earliest witness appears roughly 150 years later; the canonical letter may also combine two earlier letters. Scholars probably recover much of what Paul wrote, yet without the original they cannot directly measure their reconstruction's accuracy or know every alteration.

title: Thanksgiving 2020
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers a Thanksgiving reflection during 2020.
searchSummary: Considers how to cultivate gratitude during the loneliness, illness, loss, and economic hardship of the 2020 pandemic. Ehrman values Thanksgiving as an inclusive family holiday and remains thankful without believing in a divine giver, recognizing that circumstance and opportunity make personal success partly a matter of luck. Genuine thankfulness, he argues, should produce humility, kindness, charity, and generosity toward people with less, turning appreciation for one's own good fortune into practical help and hope for others.

title: Christian Manuscripts Used for Magic?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores Christian manuscripts used as magical objects and amulets.

title: What Really Happened at Jesus’ Trial Before Pilate?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates what historians can know about Jesus' trial before Pilate.

title: Some Feedback on the New Blog ??
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks members for feedback on the new blog site.

title: “Oral” Changes in the Christian Bible?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether oral reading and transmission affected changes in Christian texts.
searchSummary: Considers whether early Christian readers altered texts while reading them aloud to largely illiterate congregations. No recordings or reliable transcripts survive, so verbal changes cannot be demonstrated, though written quotations often paraphrase Scripture. Readers unquestionably shaped meaning through emphasis and explanation, especially when difficult texts required interpretation. Because literate leaders controlled both access to Christian writings and their public presentation, they exercised substantial authority over how communities understood Scripture and defined true belief.

title: On Ignorant Critics…
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on uninformed criticism and poor arguments against critical scholarship.
searchSummary: Uses an evangelical professor's inaccurate accusations against Ehrman to argue that all scholars have agendas and should acknowledge them honestly. Ehrman identifies his own aim as informing people about the New Testament, historical Jesus, and early Christianity rather than deconverting students. Disagreement across religious and nonreligious positions is legitimate, but responsible discussion requires accurate information, self-awareness, and genuine understanding of opposing views instead of invented motives, unsupported claims, or ignorance presented as expertise.

title: Why Scribes Changed Their Manuscripts
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why scribes changed New Testament manuscripts, including for theological reasons.

title: Peter and Mary Magdalene in Competition
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores competition between Peter and Mary Magdalene in early Christian traditions.
searchSummary: Traces competing early Christian traditions about whether Mary Magdalene or Peter first encountered the risen Jesus and therefore held priority as an apostolic witness. Mark, Matthew, John, Luke, and Paul preserve differing sequences, while later works including Pistis Sophia, the Gospel of Thomas, and the Gospel of Mary portray conflict over Mary's authority. These traditions suggest an enduring contest over status, revelation, gender, and leadership rather than a single uniform memory of the first resurrection appearance.

title: Is Mary Magdalene the Founder of Christianity?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Mary Magdalene could be seen as a founder of Christianity.

title: Women Apostles in Early Christianity
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses women apostles and Mary Magdalene's authority in early Christian texts.

title: The Gospel of Mary Magdalene
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Gospel of Mary and its portrayal of Mary Magdalene as recipient of secret teaching.
searchSummary: Introduces the second-century Gospel of Mary, a fragmentary Gnostic work in which Mary Magdalene receives a private revelation from Jesus. She comforts the fearful male disciples and describes the soul's escape from material powers, but Peter and Andrew challenge both her teaching and Jesus' decision to entrust it to a woman. Levi defends Mary and rebukes Peter, making the Gospel an important witness to debates over spiritual authority, gender, and competing disciples in early Christianity.
