title: 666: The Number of the Beast
author: admin
description: Explains 666 in Revelation through gematria and the number of the beast.
searchSummary: Explains the number 666 through ancient gematria rather than attempts to identify a modern political figure. Revelation's beast represents Rome and its emperors, especially Nero, whose Hebrew name totals 666. A spelling variation without the final letter produces 616, matching an alternative number preserved in some Greek manuscripts. The wounded-and-healed head may reflect traditions that Nero would return from death. Revelation therefore anticipates God's defeat of Roman imperial power, not a twenty-first-century enemy.

title: The Number 666 in the Context of the Book of Revelation
author: BDEhrman
description: Places 666 within Revelation and early Christian numerical interpretation.
searchSummary: Introduces the historical and symbolic framework needed to interpret Revelation's number 666. Like other ancient apocalypses, Revelation uses visions to assure suffering first-century Christians that God will soon destroy the evil powers controlling their world. The great prostitute called Babylon symbolizes Rome: the city on seven hills, supported by Satan, enriched through exploitation, and stained with Christian blood. Understanding this first-century target and Revelation's symbolic language prepares readers to identify the beast's number through gematria.

title: Interested in Volunteering for the Blog?
author: BDEhrman
description: Invites readers to volunteer for blog operations.

title: Luke and Matthew at Odds: The Genealogies
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Matthew's and Luke's genealogies of Jesus and their contradictions.
searchSummary: Compares the irreconcilable genealogies of Jesus in Matthew and Luke. Both trace Joseph's paternal line despite denying that he was Jesus' biological father, but Matthew moves from Abraham through David's son Solomon while Luke works backward through Nathan to Adam and God. Their differing scopes express Matthew's Jewish emphasis and Luke's universal one. The post rejects the common claim that Luke supplies Mary's genealogy because both texts explicitly trace Joseph.

title: Another Unusual Feature of Matthew’s Genealogy: The Women!
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines the women named in Matthew's genealogy and their significance.
searchSummary: Examines why Matthew unusually includes Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba, and Mary in Jesus' genealogy. The first four may anticipate salvation extending to gentiles, although that explanation does not include Jewish Mary. More significantly, each earlier woman was associated with a sexual situation considered scandalous by outsiders yet used to advance God's purposes. Their presence prepares readers for Mary's pregnancy before marriage, which Joseph initially suspects but Matthew attributes to divine action rather than illicit conduct.

title: A Numerical Puzzle in Matthew’s Genealogy
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the numerical puzzle in Matthew's genealogy through gematria.
searchSummary: Explains possible reasons for Matthew's carefully arranged pattern of three sets of fourteen generations in Jesus' genealogy. Fourteen is twice seven, a number associated with perfection and divinity, and it is also the numerical value of David's Hebrew name through gematria. Matthew may therefore use the number to emphasize both divine providence and Jesus' identity as Davidic Messiah, even though constructing the scheme requires omitted generations and leaves only thirteen names in the final group.

title: Curiosities and Puzzles from the Very First Passage of the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces puzzles in Matthew's genealogy, the first passage of the New Testament.
searchSummary: Examines Matthew's genealogy as a theological claim about Jesus' Jewish and Davidic credentials rather than an accurate family record. Its three groups of fourteen link Abraham, David, the Babylonian exile, and Jesus to portray Israel's history as providentially culminating in the Messiah. Yet Joseph is not Jesus' biological father, Matthew omits known generations to preserve the pattern, and the final group contains only thirteen names. These problems reveal how literary purpose shaped the genealogy's construction.

title: Ancient Numerical Interpretations of the Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains ancient numerical interpretation of Scripture through gematria.

title: Comments on the Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers guidance on commenting and participating on the new blog.

title: Why Do Some People Make Such Bad Arguments for the Superiority of their Religion?
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques weak arguments for the superiority of one's religion.

title: Speaking Event This Thursday and Friday (4 lectures, remote)
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a remote lecture series on Heaven and Hell.

title: Are the Gospels Right?  Did Pilate Really Release a Prisoner at Passover?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether Pilate released a prisoner at Passover as the Gospels claim.
searchSummary: Argues that Pilate's Passover release of Barabbas is historically implausible. No evidence shows Pilate or another Roman governor maintaining such a custom, and Pilate's brutality makes freeing a murderer who fought Roman rule especially unlikely. The episode instead became a Christian memory that absolved Pilate and blamed Jewish crowds for choosing violence over their Messiah. Barabbas means “son of the father,” and the manuscript reading Jesus Barabbas intensifies the symbolic choice between a murderous insurgent and Jesus, the self-sacrificing Son.

title: Where Did the Idea of a “Suffering Messiah” Come From?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how early Christians came to imagine a suffering messiah.
searchSummary: Traces the Christian idea of a suffering messiah to the historical collision between followers' belief that Jesus was messiah and the reality of his crucifixion. Earlier Jewish expectations envisioned a powerful ruler, and texts such as Isaiah 53 were not interpreted messianically before Christianity. Resurrection belief led Jesus' followers, and later Paul, to reread suffering passages as divine predictions and to explain his cursed death as suffering undertaken for others.

title: How Hard It is To Become an Agnostic….
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the difficulty of becoming agnostic after committed Christian faith.
searchSummary: Describes the prolonged social, moral, and religious fears that made leaving Christianity difficult for Ehrman. He worried about disappointing family, losing friendships, abandoning an ethical foundation, surrendering purpose, and risking eternal punishment if unbelief proved wrong; active church leadership temporarily helped him postpone those questions. Ultimately he concluded that benefits and fears could not determine what was true, so he examined whether he actually believed and took the life-changing step toward agnosticism despite deep roots in Christian community and identity.

title: Did Jesus’ Disciple John Write the Gospel of “John”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether the disciple John wrote the Gospel of John.
searchSummary: Argues that John son of Zebedee did not write the anonymous Fourth Gospel. John 21 distinguishes the speaking "we" from the Beloved Disciple whose testimony supports the account, so the author does not identify himself as that disciple. More decisively, John was a poor, Aramaic-speaking Galilean fisherman in a society where literary education was confined largely to urban elites; Acts itself calls him illiterate. He could not have composed a sophisticated twenty-one-chapter narrative in Greek.

title: How Were the Gnostic Gospels Discovered?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how the Nag Hammadi writings commonly called Gnostic Gospels were discovered.
searchSummary: Explains how scholars date and authenticate the Nag Hammadi codices while distinguishing those questions from interpreting their contents. Dated receipts and other papyrus scraps reused in one binding employ regnal, consular, and tax-cycle dates pointing to the mid-fourth century, although most works were composed earlier. Uncertainty about the familiar discovery story does not undermine the manuscripts' antiquity, but secure provenance remains valuable for excluding forgery and understanding which Christian writings circulated in fourth-century Egypt.

title: How Do Popular Books Get Their Titles?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how trade books get their titles and why authors often do not control them.
searchSummary: Explains how trade publishers develop titles that intrigue general readers without becoming misleadingly sensational. Editors test possibilities with colleagues, executives, authors, and marketing teams, so announced titles may change and international editions may use different names. Ehrman recounts resisting Misquoting Jesus in favor of Lost in Transmission, only to discover that the publisher's choice connected strongly with readers and helped the book succeed, illustrating why professional editorial judgment often outweighs an author's preference.

title: My Privileged View of Suffering
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on suffering from the perspective of privilege and distance from extreme hardship.
searchSummary: Defends the right of a relatively privileged person to consider suffering's religious implications without claiming authority over those who suffer more. Personal hardship does not automatically determine sound policy or theology, and the suffering person's faith need not dictate another observer's conclusion. Ehrman refuses to impose his interpretation but argues that awareness of others' pain should shape behavior; a practical response that helps people is more valuable than a ready explanation for why suffering exists.

title: The Original Blog Post!!  Misquoting Misquoting Jesus!
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts the original blog post on Misquoting Jesus and criticism of textual-criticism claims.
searchSummary: Defends Misquoting Jesus against evangelical criticism that manuscript variants are unimportant because they alter no cardinal doctrine. Ehrman did not claim that variants overturn doctrines; he argues that they affect the meaning and theology of significant passages concerning Jesus' divinity, atonement, agony, resurrection appearances, and the adulterous woman. Doctrinal impact is not the only measure of importance, because textual changes can reshape a passage, an author's theology, or an entire book.

title: Welcome to the New Blog Site!
author: BDEhrman
description: Welcomes readers to the new blog site and explains its improved features.

title: Who Would Die for a Lie?
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses apocryphal Acts traditions to revisit the claim that no one would die for a lie.

title: What Happens When Your Beliefs Contradict What You Have To Teach?  Readers’ Mailbag
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to a question about teaching religious studies when course material conflicts with personal beliefs.
searchSummary: Explains how scholars at secular research universities teach about religion without promoting or attacking personal beliefs. Ehrman argues that a professor's faith is professionally irrelevant when historical, literary, linguistic, or anthropological methods govern the classroom. He contrasts this setting with conservative institutions where critical conclusions about biblical contradictions, authorship, or historicity may conflict with doctrinal requirements, creating pressure to present both sides, obscure personal conclusions, or risk employment.

title: A Major Blog Announcement!!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the imminent launch of the redesigned blog site.

title: John, the Bedbugs, and Miracles that Convert
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the Acts of John to show how miracles could function as conversion stories.

title: Who Would *Invent* the Idea that Women (?!) Discovered Jesus’ Empty Tomb?
author: BDEhrman
description: Challenges the apologetic claim that women discovering the empty tomb could not have been invented.

title: A Celebratory Moment for the Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on Bart's sixty-fifth birthday while celebrating the blog's having raised one million dollars for charity.
searchSummary: Celebrates two coinciding milestones: Ehrman's sixty-fifth birthday and the blog's cumulative charitable revenue reaching one million dollars. The age carries personal weight because he once considered sixty-five a reasonable lifespan and because his father died at that age, while his ninety-three-year-old mother illustrates a very different trajectory. He treats the blog achievement as an unexpectedly meaningful birthday gift and thanks members whose participation directed every dollar toward hunger, homelessness, and disaster relief.

title: Hard Evidence that the Book of Acts was Written by an Eyewitness?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates an argument that Acts was written by an eyewitness because of its narrative details.
searchSummary: Rejects the argument that Acts must have been written by Paul's eyewitness companion because its later chapters accurately describe ancient geography, landmarks, and travel details. Such knowledge could come from travel, other informed people, or common information and does not establish presence at the narrated events. A fictional explosion at UNC illustrates how a story can correctly locate real people and buildings while inventing its central event, so geographical accuracy cannot by itself prove either eyewitness authorship or historical reliability.

title: Why Believe in God?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on reasons people give for believing in God.

title: The Roman Standards Worship Jesus?  From the Gospel of Nicodemus
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the Gospel of Nicodemus scene in which Roman standards bow to Jesus.
searchSummary: Presents the opening of the Gospel of Nicodemus, which claims to translate official Hebrew records about Jesus despite being written centuries later. During Jesus' trial, Pilate's courier honors him, and Roman imperial standards repeatedly bow before him even when strong Jewish men hold them. The legendary scene makes pagan symbols acknowledge Jesus' kingship and divinity while contributing to the Gospel's broader effort to defend Pilate and blame Jewish leaders for the crucifixion.

title: A Gospel of Nicodemus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Gospel of Nicodemus and its expanded passion and resurrection traditions.
searchSummary: Introduces the Gospel of Nicodemus, also called the Acts of Pilate, a highly influential apocryphal Passion narrative probably rooted in fourth-century traditions. It expands canonical trial, death, and resurrection stories with episodes such as Roman standards worshiping Jesus, Joseph of Arimathea's miraculous escape, and Jesus' descent into Hades. The work presents Jesus as divine, increasingly exonerates Pilate, assigns culpability to Jewish opponents, and claims eyewitness and official authority for its legendary account.

title: Another Important Evangelical Charity: Guest Post by Robin Jones
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Robin Jones's guest discussion of an evangelical charity.

title: The Tragedy Behind My Teaching Position
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts the tragedy and serendipity behind a first teaching position.
searchSummary: Explains how tragedy opened Ehrman's permanent UNC position. New Testament scholar John Schütz, who had created an interdisciplinary Ancient Mediterranean Religions program, suffered a bicycle injury that destroyed his short-term memory and forced disability retirement. UNC then hired Ehrman to study early Christianity within Greco-Roman religion rather than isolate canonical texts, giving him an extraordinary career opportunity rooted in another scholar's devastating loss and leaving him with enduring gratitude, admiration, and unresolved guilt despite having no responsibility for the circumstances.

title: Some Intriguing Selections from the Gospel of Peter
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares selections from the Gospel of Peter.

title: A Very Odd Saying of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces an unusual saying of Jesus preserved outside the New Testament.
searchSummary: Examines a second-century papyrus preserving Jesus' warning that sheep need not fear wolves after death, a saying also quoted in 2 Clement as a conversation with Peter. If the first-person speaker is Peter, the fragment may belong to the Gospel of Peter and could show that work contained teachings before the passion, though a post-resurrection setting remains possible. The saying is not historically reliable evidence for Jesus but may reflect later Christian persecution and illuminate a lost Gospel's scope.

title: And Now: The Gospel of Peter!
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Gospel of Peter as a major non-canonical passion and resurrection Gospel.

title: Jesus’ Twin Brother?  Really?  Readers’ Mailbag
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to questions about traditions that Thomas was Jesus' twin brother.

title: Inclusive Language in Bible Translation?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains inclusive language as a major issue in modern Bible translation.
searchSummary: Examines why inclusive Bible translation is socially important yet textually difficult. Ehrman argues that masculine-default English reflects and perpetuates unequal power, but translators must also preserve literary elegance, singular force, masculine biblical conceptions of God, and passages rooted in genuinely patriarchal social assumptions. Rendering such texts inclusively can clarify generic references to humanity while potentially concealing places where ancient authors actually addressed or privileged men.

title: Translating the Bible (and other ancient texts)
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on translating the Bible and other ancient texts into modern languages.
searchSummary: Explains why translation cannot mechanically reproduce an ancient text's exact meaning. Greek words for love and slavery carry nuances that no single English equivalent preserves, while literal translations can become wooden and idiomatic translations can become overly interpretive. Drawing on his NRSV committee experience, Ehrman presents translation as a balance between lexical precision, cultural context, readability, and the committee's principle of being as literal as possible and as free as necessary.

title: The Secret Message of the Gospel of Thomas
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the Gospel of Thomas's distinctive message about salvation and self-knowledge.

title: The Gospel of Thomas: Some Basic Information
author: BDEhrman
description: Provides basic information about the Gospel of Thomas and its sayings collection.

title: Our Most Important Gospel from Outside the NT: The Gospel of Thomas
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Gospel of Thomas as the most important non-canonical Gospel.

title: Gospel Questions and Problems
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses a class quiz to raise questions and problems about canonical and non-canonical Gospels.
searchSummary: Uses introductory Gospel questions to show how literary and historical study complicates familiar Christian narratives. Noncanonical Gospels reveal diverse early portrayals of Jesus, while the canonical works function as theological proclamations rather than neutral histories. The specific contradiction over who carried Jesus' cross—Simon of Cyrene in the Synoptics or Jesus in John—cannot be solved by having them carry it sequentially or together without creating a scene absent from every Gospel.

title: An Unusual Podcast Interview with a Muslim about How I Debate.  Check This One Out!
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares an unusual interview about debate style with a Muslim interviewer.
searchSummary: Recounts an unusual Sultans and Sneakers interview recorded in host Mahin Islam's car while driving Ehrman to the airport after an evangelical apologetics conference. Rather than debate biblical subjects, Islam asks why Ehrman participates in public debates, how he prepares, what the experience feels like, and whether he has ever recognized a decisive loss. Ehrman praises the Muslim host's broad knowledge and cross-cultural podcast format for challenging stereotypes and encouraging conversation among people with different religious and social perspectives.

title: Jesus’ Death in Mark and Luke: Why Don’t They Agree?
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Mark and Luke on Jesus' death and why their portrayals differ.
searchSummary: Explains why Mark and Luke portray Jesus' death differently and what each account offers suffering readers. Mark's abandoned Jesus does not understand his agony, but the torn Temple curtain and centurion show readers that God brings salvation through apparently meaningless suffering. Luke's calm Jesus knows God remains with him and models confidence, forgiveness, and hope of paradise. Harmonizing the accounts erases their distinct theological messages about suffering and atonement.

title: All Day Seminar (Online) for the Smithsonian: This Saturday!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces an online Smithsonian seminar on heaven and hell.

title: The Calm and Collected Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Contrasts portrayals of Jesus as calm or distressed in passion traditions.
searchSummary: Contrasts Jesus' final hours in Mark and Luke to show why each Gospel must be read on its own terms. Mark presents a silent, abandoned Jesus who dies asking why God has forsaken him. Luke replaces that portrayal with a composed Jesus who comforts women, forgives his executioners, promises paradise to a criminal, and entrusts his spirit to God. Combining their sayings into one Passion narrative obscures both evangelists' distinctive portraits.

title: The Earliest Infancy Gospel:  Some of the Critical Problems
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains critical problems raised by the Infancy Gospel of Thomas.

title: Jesus as a Boy?   The Infancy Gospel of Thomas
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Infancy Gospel of Thomas and its stories about Jesus as a child.

title: How I Do My Research
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains research habits and note-taking practices for scholarly writing.
searchSummary: Explains Ehrman's research-reading and note-taking system for mastering large scholarly bibliographies. Depending on relevance and prior knowledge, he may read an entire work or focus on its introduction, conclusion, and essential chapters, highlighting information needed for his project. The following day he converts those passages into searchable computer notes with summaries, quotations, and page references, reinforcing memory and preserving a durable record he can revisit while developing arguments or locating evidence.

title: Two More Answers from My Pop Quiz
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues explaining answers to a New Testament pop quiz.
searchSummary: Uses two introductory quiz questions to teach historical conventions and Gospel authorship. Ehrman explains why scholars prefer BCE and CE, notes that the calendar contains no year zero and misdates Jesus' birth, and discusses the traditional names Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. He emphasizes that the Gospels are internally anonymous, that their familiar attributions appear later, and that evaluating authorship, eyewitness status, sources, and accuracy requires historical evidence rather than inherited labels.

title: More Member Publications!
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares additional publications by blog members.

title: Does Basic Information about the NT *Matter*?  My Pop Quiz
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why a basic New Testament pop quiz can reveal what students know before formal study.
searchSummary: Explains why basic quiz questions about the New Testament introduce important historical and interpretive principles. Its twenty-seven books come from different authors and must first be read as individual works rather than as one unified account. Their composition in Greek reflects the eastern Roman Empire's common language and helps explain both their circulation and Christianity's expansion. Ehrman uses these facts to challenge assumptions and prepare students to study each Gospel's distinctive message.

title: Paul’s Ascent to Paradise.  Guest Post by James Tabor
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents James Tabor's guest post on Paul's ascent to paradise and its relation to ancient Jewish heavenly journeys.

title: What Is the Unforgivable Sin?  Readers’ Mailbag.
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the unforgivable sin in Matthew, why the passage does not teach purgatory, and how Jesus' apocalyptic expectation clarifies the saying.
searchSummary: Interprets the unforgivable sin in its narrative and apocalyptic contexts. The Pharisees attribute Jesus's exorcisms to demonic power, so blaspheming the Holy Spirit means rejecting God's power in Jesus as Satanic rather than committing a particular sexual or post-conversion offense. Bart also explains that forgiveness in the age to come does not describe purgatory or heaven after death; for the historical Jesus, it meant forgiveness within the imminent earthly kingdom established after God's defeat of evil.

title: My Faux Pop Quiz this Semester
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the faux pop quiz used to gauge students' starting knowledge in a New Testament course.
searchSummary: Describes how Ehrman begins a first-year seminar on Jesus with introductions, a careful explanation of the course's nonconfessional historical approach, and an ungraded quiz. The quiz reveals students' prior knowledge while providing a relaxed way to teach foundational facts about the New Testament, canonical and noncanonical Gospels, Jesus, authorship traditions, chronology, and Jewish identity. Its purpose is diagnostic and instructional rather than evaluative, preparing students for later work in scholarship and film.

title: My Early Christian Apocrypha Seminar
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a PhD seminar on early Christian apocrypha and the kinds of non-canonical texts it covers.
searchSummary: Presents the syllabus for a doctoral seminar on noncanonical Christian Gospels, Acts, epistles, and apocalypses from the early centuries. Students translate Greek texts, analyze primary sources, evaluate textual and historical scholarship, present annotated research, review a major study of canon formation, and revise a substantial term paper. Readings range from fragmentary Gospels and infancy traditions to apocryphal Acts and the Apocalypse of Peter, connecting detailed textual study with canon, forgery, and interpretation.

title: At Last.  Jesus and the Son of Man.
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Jesus' use of the Son of Man in relation to future judgment and his own role.
searchSummary: Argues that the historical Jesus distinguished himself from the Son of Man, a heavenly judge whom he expected to destroy evil and establish God's earthly kingdom. After Jesus's death, followers who believed he was raised and would return as messiah identified him with that coming figure and reshaped his sayings accordingly. Matthew therefore alters Mark's confession scene to make Jesus's identity as Son of Man explicit, reflecting later Christian belief rather than Jesus's original understanding.

title: Smith-Pettit Lecture – The History of Heaven and Hell
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a lecture on the history of heaven and hell.
searchSummary: Introduces a recorded Smith-Pettit lecture on the historical development of Christian ideas about heaven and hell. Ehrman delivered the webinar for the Sunstone Digital Symposium, an independent forum serving traditional and nontraditional Latter-day Saints while encouraging intellectual, experiential, and religious integrity. The post identifies moderator Karin Franklin Peter of the Community of Christ and presenter Lindsay Hansen Park of the Sunstone Education Foundation, situating Ehrman's afterlife history within a conversation among distinct branches and perspectives of the broader Mormon tradition.

title: The Flukes of Life and My Teaching Career
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the chance events behind a teaching career and the difficulty of academic jobs.
searchSummary: Recounts how an emergency Rutgers appointment rescued Ehrman's stalled search for an academic career. His seminary background and narrow specialization in textual criticism attracted little interest from either secular or confessional institutions, but a professor's family crisis created an immediate need to finish her New Testament courses. The temporary assignment expanded into four years of teaching, supplied the secular-university experience that later made UNC possible, and illustrates how academic careers can depend as much on timing and contingency as preparation.

title: “The Case for Christ”?  The New Testament Review Podcast
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a New Testament Review podcast episode critiquing apologetic arguments in The Case for Christ.
searchSummary: Critiques Lee Strobel's The Case for Christ as apologetics that presents a one-sided defense of evangelical claims while misrepresenting scholarship and evidence. Ian Mills and Laura Robinson challenge Strobel's pose as a skeptical investigator, his exclusion of critical voices, and false or misleading claims about Gospel dependence and the development of Alexander legends. They distinguish responsible scholarship, including evangelical scholarship, from advocacy that selectively uses research to reassure believers without accurately representing primary data or opposing interpretations.

title: How Jesus’ Apocalyptic Teachings Were Changed (even in the NT)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Jesus' apocalyptic teaching about the Son of Man was reshaped in early Christian traditions.
searchSummary: Shows how Jesus's imminent apocalyptic predictions were progressively transformed after the Son of Man and God's kingdom failed to arrive. Luke edits Mark to remove promises that Jesus's contemporaries would witness the powerful end and presents the kingdom in Jesus's ministry; John replaces future judgment with present eternal life through faith; Thomas rejects a future earthly kingdom. Bart argues that this chronological de-apocalypticizing preserves evidence that the historical Jesus originally expected the end within his generation.

title: Jesus in Scholarship and Film
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes a remote course on Jesus in scholarship and film, including canonical and non-canonical Gospels.
searchSummary: Presents a first-year seminar comparing portrayals of Jesus in canonical and noncanonical Gospels, modern historical scholarship, and film. Students study each source's distinctive Jesus, learn methods for reconstructing his life, assess cinematic interpretations, and connect Gospel passages with contemporary social issues. Discussions, position papers, quizzes, a researched essay, and an original fictional Gospel develop close reading, historical reasoning, communication, and creative interpretation without requiring students to adopt or reject a religious viewpoint.

title: A Podcast of Interest to You!  Guest post by Ian Mills and Laura Robinson
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a podcast designed to make New Testament scholarship accessible to a general audience.
searchSummary: Introduces the New Testament Review podcast as a guide to influential works, technical vocabulary, and continuing debates in New Testament scholarship. Ian Mills and Laura Robinson place each work in its original scholarly context, summarize its argument, and trace its later reception, using examples such as the Messianic Secret, the New Perspective on Paul, and criticism of "gnosticism" as a historical category. Their detailed but accessible approach connects doctoral-level disciplinary history with public understanding.

title: Did Jesus Think He Would Be the Judge of the Earth?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Jesus expected to serve as the future judge of the earth.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus expected a heavenly Son of Man to judge the earth but did not identify that figure with himself. Sayings such as Mark 8:38 distinguish Jesus from the judge and satisfy the criterion of dissimilarity because later Christians, who equated Jesus with the Son of Man, were unlikely to invent that ambiguity. Bart traces the figure to Daniel 7 and concludes that followers merged the identities only after believing the risen Jesus would return to fulfill messianic expectations.

title: How Do You Know If Jesus Said That?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how historians evaluate whether sayings attributed to Jesus go back to Jesus himself.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: A Bit of a Shocker: Jesus and the Son of Man
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Son of Man phrase and how the Gospels use it for Jesus.

title: Who Is the Son of Man?  From the Blog Readers’ Mailbag
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to reader questions about the Son of Man in the Gospels and Jesus' identity.

title: The Opening Section of the Gospel of Judas
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents the opening section of the Gospel of Judas in translation.

title: What is the Gospel of Judas About?
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes the contents and unusual claims of the Gospel of Judas.

title: Sethian Gnostics and the Gospel of Judas
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the Sethian Gnostic setting of the Gospel of Judas.

title: Will “All Israel” Be Saved? Really?  Guest Post by Jason Staples
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Jason Staples's argument about Paul's claim that all Israel will be saved.

title: Apology to the Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Apologizes for a ministry link whose statement of faith conflicted with the blog's charitable and inclusive aims.

title: What Is Gnosticism?
author: BDEhrman
description: Defines Gnosticism as background for understanding the Gospel of Judas and related early Christian texts.

title: Evangelicals Who Make the World A Better Place.  Guest Post by Robin Jones
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Robin Jones's guest post on evangelical Christians whose work aims to improve the world.

title: A Very Odd Story about the Baby Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces an unusual infancy story about Jesus from the Proto-Gospel of James.

title: When Paul Says “Israel” Does He Mean “The Jews”?  Guest Post by Jason Staples
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Jason Staples's discussion of whether Paul's language about Israel refers to Jews.
searchSummary: Explains why Paul shifts from Jews to Israel in Romans 9-11 by reconstructing the ancient distinction between the terms. Josephus and other sources treat Jews as descendants of Judah, while Israel includes the missing northern tribes whose restoration remained a prophetic hope. Jesus' twelve apostles symbolize that reunification, and Paul addresses how Gentile inclusion and Jewish response can fulfill God's promise to save a miraculously restored all Israel.

title: Seeing the Gospel of Judas for the First Time
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts seeing the Gospel of Judas manuscript for the first time as part of the National Geographic project.
searchSummary: Recounts Ehrman's first examination of the Gospel of Judas manuscript after National Geographic invited him to assess its historical significance. He traces its 1978 discovery, movement through the antiquities market, long storage in a bank vault, severe physical deterioration, and restoration under Rodolphe Kasser. Coptic expertise and radiocarbon work made forgery implausible, but participation required a restrictive nondisclosure agreement. Ehrman acknowledges that this secrecy conflicted with normal scholarship even though it protected National Geographic's substantial investment.

title: Why Do Are So Many Textual Critics Evangelicals?   Readers’ Mailbag.
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to a reader question about why many New Testament textual critics are evangelical Christians.
searchSummary: Explains why evangelical Christians are strongly represented among New Testament textual critics. Belief in verbal inspiration motivates some to recover the original words, apologetic concerns motivate others to defend the text, and the field offers a rigorous academic specialty whose methods do not directly challenge many conservative theological claims. Ehrman emphasizes that textual criticism reconstructs what authors wrote; it cannot establish whether their statements are true or whether a large manuscript count makes them trustworthy.

title: Did Paul Really Think “All Israel Will Be Saved”? Guest Post by Jason Staples
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Jason Staples's argument about Paul, Israel, and restoration eschatology.

title: When I Learned the Gospel of Judas Had Been Discovered
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts learning that the Gospel of Judas had been discovered.

title: Christianizing the Old Testament and the Museum of the Bible: Guest Post by Jill Hicks-Keeton
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques the Museum of the Bible's use of Old Testament materials through the issue of Christianizing scripture.

title: How I First Learned About the Gospel of Judas Iscariot
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts first learning about the Gospel of Judas through ancient reports about Cainite Gnostics.

title: Why Would An Atheist Teach the Bible?  Readers’ Mailbag
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why an atheist might teach biblical studies and how academic study differs from personal belief.
searchSummary: Explains why an atheist can appropriately teach the Bible in a secular university. Ehrman distinguishes studying religion from promoting it, arguing that professors teach subjects because they are historically and culturally important, not because they practice them. A nonbelieving instructor can present evidence, challenge inherited assumptions, and help students reason independently. The Bible's enormous influence makes it essential intellectual material for believers and nonbelievers alike, while religious studies encompasses far more than Christianity.

title: Proving the Bible Is True: The Museum of the Bible. Guest Post by Cavan Concannon
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Cavan Concannon's critique of the Museum of the Bible and its apologetic use of artifacts.

title: Slurs Against Religious Opponents and Makin’ Stuff Up
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how heresy hunters accused opponents of immoral practices and sometimes invented slanderous charges.
searchSummary: Challenges Epiphanius's sensational claims that the Phibionites practiced sexual rituals and possessed a Greater Questions of Mary depicting Jesus performing them. Such accusations resemble standard ancient polemics charging opponents with promiscuity, cannibalism, and other crimes, while surviving Gnostic writings generally promote bodily asceticism rather than indulgence. Because Epiphanius never witnessed the alleged rites and is the sole source for the quoted episode, the post argues that he likely fabricated both the behavior and supporting text.

title: Did Early Christian Heretics Promote Outrageous Sex Rituals?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines ancient accusations that some early Christian heretics promoted shocking sexual rituals.
searchSummary: Questions whether reports of sexually outrageous Christian heretics preserve real practices or conventional slander. Epiphanius claims personal knowledge of the Phibionites, quotes an alleged Greater Questions of Mary, and connects graphic sexual rites to their Gnostic cosmology. Ehrman notes that accusations of promiscuity, infanticide, and cannibalism were routinely exchanged among hostile groups and that Epiphanius wrote expressly to repel readers from heresy. Because the theological linkage comes from the accuser himself, neither repeated tradition nor internal coherence establishes historical truth.

title: New Book on Museum of the Bible: Guest Post by the Editors Jill Hicks-Keeton and Cavan Concannon
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a guest post on a critical book about the Museum of the Bible.

title: The Outrageous Immorality of Early Christians (!) (?)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores ancient charges that Christians were immoral and how such accusations related to Christian communities.
searchSummary: Second- and third-century outsiders accused Christians of secret sexual orgies, incest, infant murder, and cannibalism rather than admiring their communities as unusually moral. Christian writers such as Tertullian and Minucius Felix preserve these allegations while defending the movement. Night meetings, familial language, the holy kiss, and eucharistic language may have encouraged suspicion, but the charges also resemble conventional ancient slanders used against disliked groups.

title: Did the Benefits of the Christian Community Win Converts?  Readers’ Mailbag.
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to a reader question about whether the benefits of Christian community helped attract converts.

title: Would You Like a Free Three-Month Membership to the Blog?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces donated temporary memberships for readers unable to afford blog access.

title: Publications By Blog Members!  7.9.20
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares publications by blog members.

title: Why Is This Happening To Us?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on why crises and suffering lead people to ask religious and existential questions.
searchSummary: Rejects pandemic-era claims that God uses suffering to test the fortunate, create appreciation, or produce greater goods. Such explanations make victims' deaths serve observers, fail to justify starvation, disease, disasters, and cruelty, and can become morally offensive despite occasional benefits arising from hardship. Ehrman respects humble belief that suffering remains mysterious, but urges honest uncertainty, mutual support, and concrete aid instead of comforting theories that embrace or trivialize innocent pain.

title: Reason and Theology – Heaven, Hell and the Afterlife
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a podcast discussion on heaven, hell, and the afterlife.
searchSummary: Introduces a recorded discussion of Heaven and Hell: A History of the Afterlife on the Reason and Theology podcast. Three knowledgeable lay moderators grounded in Roman Catholic theology engage Ehrman in an unexpectedly wide-ranging and sometimes lively conversation about the book. The podcast's stated purpose is to make theological, philosophical, and historical questions accessible while hosting charitable exchanges between opposing viewpoints. The episode therefore places Ehrman's historical account of afterlife beliefs in dialogue with informed Catholic commitments and concerns.

title: An Intriguing New Documentary: The Search – Manufacturing Belief
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a documentary interview connected with belief, religion, and secular humanism.
searchSummary: Introduces Patrick Payne's documentary The Search: Manufacturing Belief, which combines his experiences at Catholic Cursillo retreats with interviews about religion, science, awe, and consciousness. Payne argues that structured retreat practices can manufacture overwhelming spiritual experiences through isolation, uncertainty, repetition, emotion, and group dynamics. Featuring Ehrman on the origins of sacred texts alongside scientists and secular thinkers, the film seeks common ground while interpreting spirituality through psychology, culture, and the human search for truth.

title: Are You Willing to Donate a Free Membership (or more) To Someone Who Needs It?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks readers to donate free memberships for people unable to pay during a time of crisis.

title: Do Matthew and Paul Agree on the Matter Most Important to them Both?
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Matthew and Paul on salvation, Jewish law, and what each considered central to faithfulness to God.
searchSummary: Compares Matthew and Paul on whether keeping Jewish law and doing good works lead to salvation. Matthew's Jesus tells a rich man that eternal life requires obeying commandments and that perfection involves giving wealth to the poor; Paul insists that no one is justified by works of the law and that making law observance salvific nullifies Christ's death. Because Matthew also presents Jesus' death as saving, the post asks readers to evaluate tension without automatically forcing either contradiction or harmony.

title: How Accurate are our Copies of the Hebrew Bible?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how textual evidence from the Dead Sea Scrolls complicates claims about perfectly copied Hebrew Bible manuscripts.

title: Was Jesus Connected with the Dead Sea Scrolls Community?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how the Dead Sea Scrolls illuminate the Jewish world of Jesus without making Jesus an Essene.
searchSummary: Evaluates whether Jesus was connected to the Essene community associated with the Dead Sea Scrolls. Both expected God's imminent defeat of evil and criticized Jerusalem's leadership, but Jesus ignored Essene disputes over priestly descent and calendars and rejected their strict separation from impurity. His fellowship with sinners and outcasts opposed their program of withdrawal, so the scrolls illuminate a shared apocalyptic environment without showing that Jesus belonged to Qumran.

title: Randy Alcorn’s Response to Some Blog Criticisms (part 2)
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Randy Alcorn's response to criticisms of Alcorn's review of Heaven and Hell.

title: The Importance of the Dead Sea Scrolls for Understanding Jesus: Readers’ Mailbag
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the Dead Sea Scrolls matter for understanding Jesus and early Christianity in their Jewish context.

title: Do You Have Advanced Training In any of the Blog’s Fields?
author: BDEhrman
description: Invites readers with advanced training in related fields to identify themselves for possible blog collaboration.

title: Randy Alcorn Explains His Review In Light of Readers’ Comments
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Randy Alcorn's further response to reader comments on Heaven and Hell.

title: Did You Register for the Webinar on Sunday?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reminds registered participants about logistics for an upcoming webinar on the original New Testament.

title: How Do We Interpret the Beatitudes?  Guest Post by Julius-Kei Kato
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a guest interpretation of the Beatitudes and how Matthew and Luke frame them differently.
searchSummary: A guest scholar interprets the Beatitudes through their unrealized apocalyptic setting. Jesus originally congratulated the materially poor, hungry, and grieving because God's imminent intervention would reverse their fortunes; Matthew later spiritualized parts of that concrete promise. Since the expected transformation never arrived, the essay proposes a collaborative interpretation: followers of Jesus and other compassionate people should enact the promised blessing through distributive justice and liberating action now rather than defer relief to heaven or repeat comforting abstractions.

title: What Are The Dead Sea Scrolls?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Dead Sea Scrolls, their discovery, and their importance for ancient Jewish texts.
searchSummary: Explains what the Dead Sea Scrolls are, how they were discovered, and what they reveal about the Essenes. Their Hebrew and Aramaic biblical manuscripts, commentaries, hymns, prophecies, and rules document a separatist community committed to purity, communal discipline, and imminent apocalyptic victory. The scrolls provide exceptionally early evidence for the Hebrew Bible and Jewish life around Jesus' era, although Jesus did not belong to the sect.

title: Blog Member Publications!  6.22.2020
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares another set of publications by blog members.

title: Bart’s Latest Attack on Christianity by Randy Alcorn
author: BDEhrman
description: Publishes Randy Alcorn's critical review of Heaven and Hell.
searchSummary: Reprints evangelical author Randy Alcorn's sharply critical review of Heaven and Hell after Ehrman invited a civil presentation of an opposing view. Alcorn disputes Ehrman's readings of biblical resurrection, judgment, annihilation, heaven, and hell, arguing that he neglects contrary passages and evangelical scholarship on the renewed earth. The review portrays Ehrman's historical conclusions and deconversion story as attacks on Christianity that endanger believers, while Ehrman's introduction models respectful disagreement and invites both authors to address readers' questions.

title: A Plea for Humility in the Face of the Universe
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to suffering with a call for humility and careful reflection rather than easy answers.
searchSummary: Explains why disbelief in providence leads Ehrman toward humility and care rather than selfishness. Human life occupies a moment within an immense, indifferent universe whose physical laws cannot be mastered permanently, undermining claims of cosmic importance. Because no divine caregiver will necessarily rescue people, conscious and interconnected humans must help one another; developing natural empathy reduces undeserved suffering, deepens humanity, and creates meaning during a brief life, especially for those whose privilege arose through accidents of birth.

title: Reminder!  A Webinar for You?  Topic:  Do We Have the Original New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reminds readers about a fundraising webinar on whether the original New Testament can be recovered.
searchSummary: Promotes a charitable webinar asking whether the original New Testament can be recovered from surviving manuscripts. The planned presentation covers who copied the books, how copying proceeded across centuries, the number and dates of extant witnesses, the origin and significance of hundreds of thousands of variants, and places where authorial wording may remain unknown. A lecture and participant questions support food assistance and Doctors Without Borders through registration donations.

title: Weren’t Jesus’ Followers Armed and Eager to Fight in the Garden of Gethsemane?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether armed followers in Gethsemane support the claim that Jesus sought violent revolt.
searchSummary: Rejects the claim that armed disciples in Gethsemane prove Jesus supported revolt. Although the episode appears in all four Gospels and could seem embarrassing for later Christians, Jesus' independent teachings emphasize nonviolence, and authorities would surely have arrested followers who attacked during the capture of an insurrectionist leader. The scene may have developed around Jesus' saying that those who live by the sword die by it. It became a distorted narrative memory designed to illustrate and reinforce the remembered teaching.

title: Doesn’t Jesus’ “Cleansing of the Temple” Show He Wanted a Military Uprising?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether Jesus' Temple action shows an intention to launch a military uprising.

title: Did Jesus Favor Armed Rebellion Against Rome?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines the claim that Jesus favored armed rebellion against Rome.

title: Have You Written Something You Would Like To Advertise on the Blog?
author: BDEhrman
description: Invites blog members to advertise their own published work.

title: Did the Gospel Writers Invent Barabbas?   Readers’ Mailbag
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether the Gospel writers invented the Barabbas episode in the passion narratives.
searchSummary: Concludes that the Barabbas episode is a symbolic, distorted memory rather than a historical prisoner release. No external evidence supports a Passover amnesty, Pilate was notoriously ruthless, and Rome would crucify rather than free a murderous insurgent. Later Christian storytellers used the choice to transfer responsibility from Pilate to Jewish crowds. Since Barabbas means “son of the father,” and some Matthew manuscripts call him Jesus Barabbas, the story contrasts the violent prisoner with the innocent Son whom the crowd rejects.

title: Interested in a Webinar?  Topic:  Do We Have the Original New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a fundraising webinar on how the New Testament text was transmitted.
searchSummary: Announces a fundraising webinar on whether scholars possess or can reconstruct the original New Testament. The session will explain who copied the books, how old and numerous the surviving manuscripts are, why they contain hundreds of thousands of differences, which variants matter, and whether some authorial wording remains unknown. A lecture followed by participant questions raises donations for a regional food bank and Doctors Without Borders.

title: Yet Other Accounts Of the Death of Judas
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares New Testament and later traditions about the death of Judas Iscariot.

title: But How Did Judas Die?
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Matthew and Acts on how Judas died and why the accounts are difficult to reconcile.
searchSummary: Compares Matthew's and Acts' incompatible accounts of Judas's death. Matthew says the priests buy a field with returned blood money after Judas hangs himself; Acts says Judas buys it and dies there by falling headlong and bursting open. Attempts to combine these details stretch credibility, though both stories may have developed from a tradition connecting Judas with a Jerusalem location called the Field of Blood. The precise historical circumstances remain speculative because both accounts contain legendary elements.

title: Two Ancient Jesuses and the Current Crises
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses contrasting biblical portrayals of Jesus to argue that Scripture does not speak with one uniform voice.

title: Are Bible Translators Consistent?  Readers’ Mailbag
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how manuscript variants and translation choices affect English Bibles.
searchSummary: Explains why modern translations remove some nonoriginal verses to footnotes but retain the woman taken in adultery and Mark's longer ending in the main text. Translation committees know the famous passages are scribal additions, yet their length, uniqueness, familiarity, pastoral importance, and commercial value make removing them disruptive. Ehrman understands these pressures but argues that historical consistency should not yield to readers' expectations or market concerns when presenting an author's original text.

title: Views of Suffering Among Those Who Suffer
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on how people who suffer understand suffering differently from those discussing it at a distance.
searchSummary: Responds to the claim that sufferers' continued faith refutes Ehrman's suffering-based agnosticism. Many people gain comfort from belief, while others lose faith after tragedy, but either response has no bearing on whether God exists; a victim also need not share an observer's philosophical or economic explanation. Ehrman respects believers yet finds standard theodicies unsatisfying, concluding that suffering should foster humility and compassionate action rather than confidence that another person's pain is ultimately beneficial.

title: But WHY Did Judas Betray Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines possible motives for Judas's betrayal of Jesus.

title: What Did Judas Betray?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains what Judas may have betrayed and why the issue matters for Jesus' arrest and death.

title: If We Did Have the “Original” Gospels, Would That Make Them True?
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that possessing an original Gospel manuscript would not by itself prove the historical truth of its contents.
searchSummary: Separates three questions that apologists often conflate: how well a text is attested, whether its original wording can be recovered, and whether its claims are historically accurate. Even a first-century Mark would establish only one early copy's wording for its surviving verses, not the entire Gospel's truth. Gospel reliability instead requires evaluating decades of changing oral tradition between Jesus and the evangelists, regardless of whether scholars reconstruct every word the authors wrote.

title: Would It Matter If It HAD BEEN a First-century Copy of Mark?  A Surprising Answer in the Readers’ Mailbag
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why even a first-century copy of Mark would not solve questions about the historical Jesus.
searchSummary: Explains why even an authentic first-century fragment of Mark would probably have limited consequences for textual criticism. A small scrap resembling the reconstructed text would confirm expectations, while variants would confirm that early copies differed; neither outcome would establish Gospel accuracy, eyewitness testimony, or the original wording of the entire book. Ehrman also corrects apologetic claims that he dates Mark to 200 CE, reiterating that he dates its composition to about 70 and only its earliest surviving copy much later.

title: The Remarkable Story of Masada:  Guest Post by Jodi Magness
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Jodi Magness's guest post on Masada and its archaeological and historical importance.
searchSummary: Uses Masada to compare Josephus's dramatic account of a rebel mass suicide with archaeological evidence and modern national memory. Inscribed potsherds and destruction remains cannot prove whether the suicide occurred, leaving the question dependent on Josephus's reliability. Jodi Magness also traces how Zionist treks, archaeology, the Holocaust, and Israel's early insecurity transformed violent Sicarii into heroic freedom fighters before Masada's national symbolism later declined.

title: Judas Iscariot?  What’s an Iscariot??
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores competing explanations for the meaning of Judas Iscariot's name.

title: Was Judas Iscariot “Made Up”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether Judas Iscariot was a real disciple or a figure created in later Christian tradition.
searchSummary: Argues that Judas Iscariot was historical even though no surviving account comes from an eyewitness. Mark, independent traditions used by Matthew and Luke, John, Acts, and Papias provide multiple early attestations that Judas belonged to the Twelve and betrayed Jesus. Because that tradition was widespread and potentially embarrassing to Christians, it is more credible than later anti-Jewish or Gnostic portrayals shaped by theological agendas, leaving Judas's name, discipleship, and betrayal as the most defensible historical conclusions.

title: Academic Fraud at the Highest Levels
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes allegations of academic fraud involving manuscript claims, the Museum of the Bible, and evangelical interests.
searchSummary: Describes Ariel Sabar's investigation of the alleged first-century Mark and the broader manuscript scandal involving Dirk Obbink, Hobby Lobby, and the Museum of the Bible. Obbink reportedly sold papyri from the Egypt Exploration Society that he did not own, assigned enticingly early dates, and received millions of dollars. Ehrman uses the episode to question how scholarly authority, evangelical collecting ambitions, secrecy, and enormous financial incentives allowed fraudulent claims about ancient Christian manuscripts to flourish.

title: Did Judas Really Betray Jesus?  Readers’ Mailbag
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to a reader question about whether Judas betrayed Jesus.

title: Last Chance for Webinar!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the last chance to bid for a webinar on how the New Testament was transmitted.

title: My Interview with Erstwhile-Evangelist-Now-Secular-Humanist Bart Campolo
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares an interview with Bart Campolo on deconversion, secular humanism, and Heaven and Hell.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's Humanize Me podcast conversation with Bart Campolo, a former evangelical missionary who became a secular humanist and now counsels people leaving faith. The stated occasion is Ehrman's book Heaven and Hell: A History of the Afterlife, though he notes that much of their discussion explores other shared interests. The post also situates Campolo's work within his relationship with evangelical father Tony Campolo and his broader emphasis on humane relationships, wonder, and helping others.

title: Did Some *One* Forge the Writings of “John”? Guest Post by Hugo Mendez
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Hugo Mendez's argument about authorship and the Johannine writings.
searchSummary: Concludes Hugo Mendez's reconstruction of the Johannine writings as a chain of forgeries rather than products of one community. An educated author fashioned the Gospel as eyewitness testimony to promote present eternal life; writers imitated its language and adopted its invented witness to oppose claims that Jesus had not come in flesh. Because forgery was secretive and individual, these authors may never have known one another, requiring historians to seek multiple social contexts instead of a unified Johannine church network.

title: Problems with Thinking the “Letters of John” in the NT are Forgeries?  Guest Post: Hugo Mendez
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Hugo Mendez's response to objections against viewing the letters of John as forgeries.
searchSummary: Defends the proposal that the Johannine Gospel and letters form a chain of literary forgeries built around an invented eyewitness identity. Ancient authors could imply a false author without naming one, invent realistic narrators and details, and have several writers successively adopt the same persona. Questions about 2 and 3 John already existed among Origen and Eusebius, while literary copying and shifting claims to eyewitness authority challenge reconstructions that treat these works as transparent evidence for a historical Johannine community.

title: A Bart Ehrman Webinar: How We Got the New Testament!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a fundraising webinar on the formation and transmission of the New Testament.
searchSummary: Announces a fundraising webinar centered on how the New Testament canon developed. The session will address who determined which books belonged, what authority and criteria guided those judgments, when decisions emerged, and why other early Christian writings were excluded. Limited to ten bidders, the event combines a lecture and participant questions, with all proceeds divided between a regional food bank and Doctors Without Borders and an additional private conversation offered to the highest bidder.

title: Did Paul Know that Judas Betrayed Jesus?  Readers’ Mailbag!
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Paul knew a tradition that Judas betrayed Jesus.

title: Getting a PhD in New Testament Studies
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on graduate study in New Testament and the path toward a PhD.
searchSummary: Explains the prolonged training required to become a professional scholar of the New Testament or early Christianity. Ehrman's path included an MDiv, Greek exegesis, multiple modern and ancient languages, comprehensive examinations, and a dissertation reconstructing the Gospel text used by Didymus the Blind in fourth-century Alexandria. He argues that expertise comes from mastering languages, scholarship, disciplinary history, and original research, recommending doctoral study only to those whose commitment to intellectual work justifies its years of difficulty and uncertain career prospects.

title: Are the Gospel and Epistles of John *Forgeries*??  Guest Post by Hugo Mendez
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Hugo Mendez's argument that the Gospel and Epistles of John raise forgery and authorship questions.
searchSummary: Argues that the Gospel and three Epistles of John are anonymous or implicit forgeries that falsely suggest eyewitness authorship. The Gospel's distinctive Jesus sounds like its narrator, and the otherwise unattested Beloved Disciple appears inserted into decisive scenes to create firsthand authority. Later epistle writers copied this voice and testimony while posing as the same witness. If their narrators, churches, and conflicts belong to a constructed literary world, scholars cannot safely use those details to reconstruct a historical Johannine community.

title: Was There One Author Behind the Four Johannine Writings?  A Community?  Guest Post by Hugo Mendez
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Hugo Mendez's challenge to the theory of a single Johannine author or community.
searchSummary: Explains why scholars infer a Johannine community from the Gospel and 1-3 John despite concluding that different authors wrote them. Shared expressions such as walking in light and abiding in God suggest a common tradition, while the letters describe interconnected churches, emissaries, disputes, and leaders. These features appear to document a close network shaped by Johannine theology. Hugo Mendez closes by questioning the decisive assumption: whether the epistles' vivid communal world should be trusted as historical rather than literary invention.

title: A Powerful Film and Some Raw Emotions
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on First Reformed and the raw emotions stirred by its portrayal of ministry and suffering.
searchSummary: Reflects on First Reformed, whose grieving pastor confronts environmental collapse, institutional compromise, failed prayer, and competing attempts to find meaning through religion, activism, capitalism, and sacrifice. The film affected Ehrman personally because he too pastored a small historic church while losing faith and struggling to comfort suffering parishioners. Although his circumstances differed from the protagonist's, the portrayal reopened emotional wounds from a gradual, traumatic departure from Christianity driven ultimately by apparently meaningless suffering.

title: Readers Mailbag:  Does Isaiah 53 Predict the Death and Resurrection of Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to a reader question about whether Isaiah 53 predicts Jesus' death and resurrection.
searchSummary: Explains that Isaiah 53 was not a later Christian insertion but is commonly removed from its original exilic context. The passage never calls the servant a messiah, describes suffering already endured, and identifies the servant elsewhere in Second Isaiah as Israel. Its promised vindication concerns restoration after Babylonian captivity; Christians later interpreted it as predicting Jesus because their prior belief in a crucified and risen messiah reshaped how they read Israel's Scriptures.

title: Were the Gospels Generally Written for “Communities” of Christians: Guest Post by Hugo Mendez
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Hugo Mendez's argument about whether Gospels and letters were written for specific Christian communities.
searchSummary: Surveys views about whether Gospels were written for distinct Christian communities. Most scholars retain community-specific audiences; others argue that interconnected churches made each Gospel intended for all Christians, while another approach warns that authors belonged to overlapping social networks beyond congregations. Hugo Mendez accepts particular audiences but cautions against rigid boundaries and assuming an author's ideas represented an entire church. The Gospel of John's unusual Logos theology, for example, could reflect private reading or intellectual circles rather than congregational belief.

title: Live Event on Wednesday Evening, May 6!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a virtual book-club event on Heaven and Hell.

title: WAS there a Community behind the Gospel and Letters of John?  Guest Post by Hugo Mendez
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Hugo Mendez's series on whether a Johannine community stands behind the Gospel and letters of John.
searchSummary: Defines the "Johannine community" before challenging its existence. The standard model treats the Gospel and three Epistles of John as products of one network of churches whose authors knew one another and shared distinctive theology. Hugo Mendez agrees that every author wrote within social settings, but argues that the Johannine works may come from multiple contexts, unrelated writers, and views not shared by their associates. The issue is therefore not whether contexts existed, but whether one coherent Johannine movement did.

title: Take A Final Exam on the New Testament!
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a New Testament final exam used in teaching.
searchSummary: Reproduces a New Testament final examination that moves well beyond Ehrman's introductory first-day quiz. Students define historical, literary, theological, and textual-critical terms, then write evidence-based essays on a Gospel's historical reliability, Jesus as an apocalyptic prophet, contrasting early Christian views of Judaism, or the circumstances and arguments of one undisputed Pauline letter. The format tests both broad factual command and the ability to organize detailed historical arguments under time constraints.

title: Life after Death in the Bible and Beyond: Webinar with Oxford Press
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares an Oxford University Press webinar on life after death in the Bible and beyond.

title: The Johannine Letters in Sum
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes what can be inferred about the Johannine letters and their community setting.

title: What Are The Epistles of John?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the contents and historical setting of 1, 2, and 3 John.

title: Reading the New Testament Letters in CONTEXT
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why New Testament letters need to be read in their historical and literary contexts.
searchSummary: Explains contextual analysis as a method for interpreting New Testament letters written to address occasions. Because words take meaning from their setting, scholars reconstruct the community situation implied by one side of the correspondence, much as a listener infers the unheard half of a telephone conversation. The process risks circularity, since the letter supplies evidence for the context used to explain it, but competing reconstructions can be judged by how well they account for the text's details and historical circumstances.

title: What I Do Argue in Misquoting Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Clarifies what Misquoting Jesus argues about textual variants and the New Testament.
searchSummary: Clarifies the argument of Misquoting Jesus against claims that Ehrman exaggerates New Testament corruption or lost faith because of manuscript variants. Most differences are insignificant, yet some affect important passages and individual authors' meanings even when no major doctrine depends solely on them. Ehrman believes scholars can reasonably recover most wording, but the late and incomplete evidence prevents certainty everywhere. Significance, he argues, cannot be measured only by whether a variant overturns a traditional doctrine.

title: Misquoting Misquoting Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to misunderstandings and misrepresentations of Misquoting Jesus.

title: Blog-Related Suggestions for Isolation
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers blog-related suggestions for readers during isolation.

title: The Not Old Better Show – Heaven and Hell Book Interview
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares an interview with The Not Old Better Show about Heaven and Hell and the history of afterlife ideas.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's Not Old Better Show interview with host Paul Vogelzang about Heaven and Hell: A History of the Afterlife. Although the program is aimed especially at listeners over fifty, Ehrman notes that its subjects have wider relevance. The episode combines an excerpt read from the book with a longer question-and-answer discussion, but the brief post does not summarize the historical claims addressed and instead directs readers to the recording for the substance of the conversation.

title: Do We NEED to Suffer?  The Argument from Tectonic Plates
author: BDEhrman
description: Reconsiders the argument that suffering is necessary by using tectonic plates and natural disaster.
searchSummary: Rejects the claim that earthquakes, tsunamis, and other natural suffering are necessary because tectonic plates enabled life to evolve. Free will addresses moral harms but not natural disasters, and an all-powerful creator should not be constrained to the physical conditions found on Earth. Ehrman argues that treating victims' agony as the required price of human existence diminishes divine power and elevates humanity, when the proper response is solidarity, prevention, and honest acknowledgment that believers may not understand.

title: Is There Any Point To Life?  More on Ecclesiastes
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Ecclesiastes' bleak reflections on death, meaning, and life without clear afterlife hope.

title: What Is The Meaning of Life?  The Book of Ecclesiastes
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Ecclesiastes as wisdom literature that questions easy answers about life's meaning.

title: Interested in a Webinar on My Book?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces an Oxford webinar and introduces Bart's three textbooks as resources for studying the New Testament and Bible.

title: A Good Time for Wisdom!
author: BDEhrman
description: Turns to biblical wisdom literature, especially Ecclesiastes, as a resource for thinking during crisis.

title: Q&A on Heaven and Hell
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares publisher Q&A about Heaven and Hell and the history of afterlife beliefs.
searchSummary: Answers questions about why Ehrman wrote Heaven and Hell and how Western afterlife beliefs developed. He traces a shift from Hebrew mortality, through Jewish bodily resurrection and annihilation, to Gentile Christian ideas of immortal souls entering heaven or hell. Revelation reserves endless torment for supernatural enemies, while the Apocalypse of Peter disciplines sinners through punishments. Ehrman also discusses martyrdom, demands for cosmic justice, rejection of eternal torment, and his preference for Socrates' possibilities of peaceful nonexistence or pleasant continued life.

title: More of the History Behind the Gospel of John
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses internal clues in John to reconstruct the history of the community behind the Gospel.
searchSummary: Reconstructs a later stage of the Johannine community after exclusion from its synagogue. Social separation fostered an "us versus them" worldview expressed through John's contrasts between light and darkness, God's children and the devil's children, and Jesus' followers and "the Jews." Rejection encouraged increasingly elevated Christology: Jesus became the heavenly revealer, then God's preexistent Word and equal. Stories claiming unity with the Father and the Prologue's incarnation hymn reflect this community's developing identity and conflict.

title: Easter Reflection 2020
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers an Easter reflection during the COVID crisis centered on resurrection and suffering.

title: The History Behind John’s Gospel
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how differing views of Jesus in John may reflect the history of the Johannine community.
searchSummary: Reconstructs the first two stages of the community traditionally placed behind John. Aramaic traditions first arose among Jewish believers who remained in a synagogue and used Jesus' signs to persuade other Jews that he was God's human messiah. Persistent evangelism and rejection eventually led to their expulsion, reflected retrospectively in John 9's claim that confessing Jesus brought removal from the synagogue. That social rupture then reshaped the community's identity and its developing interpretation of Jesus.

title: The Divergent Views of Christ in John
author: BDEhrman
description: Applies socio-historical method to divergent Christological views in John's Gospel.
searchSummary: Uses John's divergent Christologies to introduce a socio-historical reconstruction of its community. An early Aramaic call story presents Jesus in Jewish human terms as rabbi, Messiah, and Lamb of God, while later Greek material such as the Prologue makes him a preexistent divine equal of God. These differences may reflect traditions produced at different stages of one group's history. Changes in the community's social experience, especially its relations with other Jews, helped transform how its stories identified Jesus.

title: UGH.  Lost Comments from April 6
author: BDEhrman
description: Reports lost blog comments from April 6 and explains the technical problem.

title: The Blog Podcast and Some New Protocols
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains new blog protocols and podcast access for new and temporary members.

title: The Social History Behind the Fourth Gospel
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces socio-historical study of John by asking what social setting lies behind the Fourth Gospel.
searchSummary: Explains the socio-historical method as reading a text backward to reconstruct the social experiences that shaped its authors and sources. Gospels are literary narratives about the past, but they also reflect the later settings in which their traditions were preserved and written. Because John appears to combine sources with differing views of Jesus, scholars can ask whether those differences arose during successive stages of a community's history. Careful source analysis may therefore illuminate the social world behind the Fourth Gospel.

title: Blog Anniversary, 2020!
author: BDEhrman
description: Marks the blog's eighth anniversary and reviews its growth, changes, and charitable impact.
searchSummary: Reviews the blog on its eighth anniversary, tracing its origin as a charity project and reporting growth in posts, comments, membership, and donations. During 2019-20 it published 289 posts, surpassed 10,000 paid and free members, and distributed $189,000 to charity. Bart also discusses pandemic-era free memberships, apologizes for missed donation acknowledgments, previews a rebuilt website, thanks technical and volunteer contributors, and asks readers to promote the blog.

title: CORONA CRISIS OFFER: FREE MEMBERSHIPS TO THE BART EHRMAN BLOG!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces free temporary blog memberships during the coronavirus crisis.

title: So What Sources for Jesus’ Life *Were* Used in the Fourth Gospel?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains evidence that John used written sources for stories about Jesus' signs.
searchSummary: Identifies several written or oral sources incorporated into the Gospel of John. A missionary Signs Source may have presented seven miracles to establish Jesus as Messiah; discourse sources supplied extended teachings; a passion source resembled Mark; and separate materials likely furnished the Prologue and chapter 21. Editorial seams show these traditions were combined over time rather than composed in one sitting.
