Their varying dates and social settings prepare for reconstructing the history of the communities that preserved and reshaped them.
topics: Signs in the Gospel of John

title: Is The End Today???
author: BDEhrman
description: Notes a humorous coincidence involving the publication of Heaven and Hell and apocalyptic anxiety.

title: The Most Intriguing Evidence that John Used Sources
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents evidence that John drew on sources rather than composing every story from scratch.
searchSummary: Shows how internal inconsistencies provide strong evidence that John combined earlier written sources. Numbered "first" and "second" signs conflict with intervening miracles, geographical transitions do not follow, and the Farewell Discourse repeats questions and delays a commanded departure for three chapters. These seams make sense if chapters 15-17 came from a second account inserted between chapters 14 and 18. Source criticism thus explains repetitions and contradictions as traces of the evangelist's editorial stitching.

title: Where Did the Gospel of John Get Its Stories?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks where John's Gospel obtained its stories in light of its differences from the Synoptics.
searchSummary: Considers where John obtained traditions that differ from the Synoptic Gospels. Limited overlap and the absence of sustained word-for-word agreement suggest that John drew shared stories from independent oral traditions rather than copying Matthew, Mark, or Luke. Yet John also appears to use other written sources: the poetic Prologue differs stylistically from the narrative, the Farewell Discourse repeats similar material, and internal seams reveal incompatible passages joined together. These features point to multiple sources edited into the finished Gospel.

title: Fresh Air Interview for Heaven and Hell: Airing Tuesday!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Fresh Air interview for Heaven and Hell.
searchSummary: Announces Ehrman's Fresh Air interview with Terry Gross for the publication of Heaven and Hell: A History of the Afterlife. The post emphasizes the program's importance as the book's principal media opportunity during pandemic-related disruption and praises Gross's unusually careful preparation and questioning. It does not summarize the interview's arguments, but identifies the history of afterlife beliefs as its subject while reflecting on publishing publicity and mentioning Ehrman's planned work on Revelation and end-times expectations in popular culture.

title: Is This the Same Jesus?  John and the Synoptics (part 2)
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares John's portrait of Jesus with the Synoptic Gospels, especially in miracle stories.
searchSummary: Compares John's portrayal of Jesus' deeds and teachings with the Synoptic Gospels. Mark's private raising of Jairus' daughter follows an accidental delay, while John's Jesus deliberately lets Lazarus die and raises him publicly to prove his identity. The Synoptics reject signs as demonstrations of status and center Jesus' parables on God's coming kingdom. John instead makes spectacular signs validate extended claims that Jesus descended from God and uniquely grants eternal life, creating a fundamentally different portrait.
topics: Signs in the Gospel of John

title: Comparing John and the Synoptics
author: BDEhrman
description: Begins comparing John with the Synoptic Gospels as background for a study of Johannine writings.
searchSummary: Introduces John's distinctiveness by comparing its contents with the Synoptic Gospels. John omits the virgin birth, baptism, temptation, kingdom preaching, parables, exorcisms, transfiguration, Lord's Supper, Gethsemane prayer, and Sanhedrin trial that structure the other accounts. In their place it supplies unique signs and extended dialogues with Nicodemus, the Samaritan woman, Jewish opponents, and the disciples. Although some passion traditions overlap, most Johannine words and deeds occur nowhere else, demanding an explanation for its distinctive portrayal of Jesus.

title: Christians Against Christians: Already In the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines conflict among early Christians over law, community, and identity already within the New Testament.
searchSummary: Examines the fierce conflict behind Galatians between Paul and Christian missionaries who required gentile converts to become Jews. Paul's opponents likely argued that followers of the Jewish messiah must honor God's enduring covenant through circumcision, Sabbath, kosher practice, and other laws. Paul insisted that faith in Christ alone brought salvation, while the post emphasizes that the canon preserves his angry response but not his opponents' own defense.

title: Did Paul Really Have *That* Exalted a View of Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Concludes the discussion of Paul's high Christology in the Philippians Christ poem.
searchSummary: Argues that the Christ poem in Philippians 2:6-11 was quoted by Paul rather than inserted by a later scribe. Although its vocabulary and developed portrayal of Christ suggest an earlier composition by someone else, its ideas do not contradict Paul and the passage fits his argument about self-sacrifice, humility, and heavenly reward. Removing it disrupts the surrounding logic, unlike plausible interpolations that conflict with an author and interrupt the textual flow.

title: How To Begin with Heaven and Hell: An Excerpt
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the opening of Heaven and Hell as the book approaches publication.
searchSummary: Uses Ehrman's personal fear of hell to introduce the historical questions behind Heaven and Hell. Childhood belief, evangelical conversion, and urgency made eternal destinations central to his faith, while critical study at Princeton created anxiety that questioning Scripture might itself lead to damnation, crystallized in an overheated sauna. After leaving Christianity, he retained scholarly interest because afterlife teachings shaped early Christian literature and expansion and still influence Americans. The book asks where these powerful beliefs originated and how they changed.

title: Hard Times and Using the Blog for Charity
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on using the blog to support charity during difficult times.
searchSummary: Explains how readers can use the blog to help others during the early COVID-19 crisis while Bart continues publishing as usual. He suggests giving subscriptions to people with more time at home and donating through the blog, whose revenue goes to charities assisting people in need. Bart argues that growing the educational community attracts membership money that might not otherwise reach charity, thereby expanding its impact, while urging readers to stay safe and retain humor.

title: More Free Memberships to the Blog Available
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces more free one-year blog memberships for readers facing financial difficulty.

title: Heaven and Hell Pre-order Offer: Still Valid!!
author: BDEhrman
description: Reminds readers of a pre-order offer for Heaven and Hell.

title: Paul the Misogynist?  The Alternative Perspective
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines a more positive reading of Paul's view of women's roles in early Christian communities.

title: Paul the Feminist?  The Thecla Legends
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the Thecla legends to explore traditions portraying Paul as supportive of women's independence.

title: Paul and the Status of Women
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses Paul and women while explaining how textual critics identify later additions to manuscripts.
searchSummary: Introduces the case that 1 Corinthians 14:34-35, which commands women to remain silent in church, is an interpolation by examining Paul's broader position. Paul proclaims spiritual equality in Christ and permits women to pray and prophesy publicly, yet retains gender distinctions, head coverings, and female subordination within the present social order. This tension provides the internal evidence needed to ask whether an absolute ban on women's speech coheres with Paul.

title: Thanks to those who volunteered!
author: BDEhrman
description: Thanks volunteers who offered to help with the rebuilt blog site.

title: You Lost Me On Hello.  A Plea for Expertise
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues for the importance of expertise and informed judgment in scholarship and public life.
searchSummary: Defends the importance of expertise and warns against presenting uninformed opinion as authoritative knowledge. Drawing examples from science, history, and biblical studies, Ehrman argues that genuine expertise requires years of specialized training and does not imply superiority outside that field. People may question expert conclusions, but public criticism should begin with sufficient understanding of the relevant evidence and methods. Trusting qualified specialists is especially important when complex claims have serious consequences.

title: I Need a Volunteer!
author: BDEhrman
description: Requests a volunteer to help with the upcoming blog rebuild.

title: Jesus “Sweating Blood”: Which Text Would *Scribes* Have Preferred?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether scribes would have preferred including or omitting Luke's bloody sweat passage.
searchSummary: Applies transcriptional probability to Luke's disputed account of Jesus sweating like blood. Textual critics often prefer the harder reading because scribes tended to correct problems, but they must also ask which wording served later Christian interests. The verses strongly supported second-century opposition to Docetism by portraying Jesus as physically and emotionally human, and their earliest users cite them for that purpose. Combined with weak manuscript support and conflict with Luke's theology, this makes scribal addition more likely.

title: Smithsonian
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces cancellation of Smithsonian lectures on Heaven and Hell.

title: Lecture Cancellations and Non-Cancellations (so far)
author: BDEhrman
description: Updates readers on lecture cancellations during the emerging pandemic.

title: Did Jesus Sweat Blood?  “Intrinsic” Evidence for Textual Variants
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains intrinsic evidence for deciding whether Luke's bloody sweat passage was original.
searchSummary: Uses Luke's bloody-sweat passage to explain intrinsic probability, the question of which manuscript reading best fits an author's vocabulary, style, and theology. Comparing Luke with his Markan source shows that Luke consistently removes signs of Jesus' anguish and presents a composed, passionless Passion. Verses depicting extreme agony and angelic assistance therefore conflict with Luke's editorial pattern and are absent from important early manuscripts. Ehrman argues that textual critics must combine manuscript expertise with close literary interpretation.

title: How Manuscripts Matter for Knowing What an Author Wrote
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how manuscript evidence affects interpretation of the Philippians Christ poem.
searchSummary: Explains the external evidence textual critics use when manuscripts preserve competing readings. Raw numbers can mislead because many later copies may descend from one inferior exemplar; early witnesses usually deserve more weight, though a later manuscript may reproduce an older textual ancestor. A reading spread across independent regions is also preferable to a local variant, but manuscript evidence must eventually be combined with internal analysis of authorial style, context, and likely scribal behavior.

title: Intimate Relationships: Nonbelievers and Believers
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on relationships between believers and nonbelievers after deconversion.
searchSummary: Offers general guidance for relationships between believers and people who have lost faith. Ehrman argues that lasting intimacy depends on love, trust, respect, openness, and willingness to understand a partner's perspective without treating the relationship as a debate to be won. Concealing a major change in belief can undermine closeness and informed trust, yet every situation has unique risks involving children, community, or livelihood. He avoids prescribing one answer and recommends qualified counseling when couples cannot navigate these differences alone.

title: What Did Ancient People Think (a) God Was?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains ancient views of divine beings as background for early Christian claims about Jesus.
searchSummary: Ancient pagans and Jews often imagined a graded divine world populated by supreme gods, lesser deities, daimones, angels, and exceptional humans. Immortality, heavenly residence, power, and wisdom could make a being divine without identifying that being with the highest God. This framework helps explain how early Christians could view the resurrected and exalted Jesus as God while retaining belief in one supreme deity.

title: How Can You Tell If the Text Has Been CHANGED?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how textual critics identify passages added or omitted by scribes.
searchSummary: Explains how competing manuscript readings prove that scribes added, omitted, or altered New Testament wording and how textual critics identify the earlier form. Evidence includes manuscript age, quality, and geography; authorial vocabulary, style, theology, and context; and likely causes of accidental or purposeful change. Ehrman distinguishes manuscript-attested variants from interpolations hypothetically made before all surviving copies, for which the evidentiary burden is much higher because no extant witness preserves the supposedly earlier text.

title: Maybe the Passage wasn’t “Original”!!
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the endings of Mark and John to explain how scholars decide whether passages were original.
searchSummary: Distinguishes textual variants from interpolations while asking whether the Christ poem in Philippians 2 was inserted after Paul. Mark's longer ending and the adulterous-woman story are absent from early witnesses, but every surviving Philippians manuscript contains the poem, so rejecting it requires positing an addition before all extant lines of transmission. Such interpolations can occur, yet their universal attestation creates a heavy burden of internal proof involving contradiction, style, context, or ethical implications.

title: Paul’s Incredibly High Christology
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Paul's high Christology in Philippians, including incarnation and exaltation.
searchSummary: Surveys Pauline passages that portray Christ as a preexistent divine being. Paul calls Christ the wilderness rock, says he came from heaven and was sent in human likeness, associates him with God's Wisdom, and presents him as creation's agent. Romans 9:5 may even call him “God over all.” Ehrman concludes that Paul viewed Jesus as the Angel of the Lord who became human and was later exalted to equality with God, while remaining distinct from the Father.

title: Authors and the Fiasco of Book Tours
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on why traditional book tours are often difficult and increasingly unnecessary for authors.
searchSummary: Explains why traditional author book tours have largely declined and why many writers welcome their disappearance. Travel, small bookstore audiences, hotels, and repetitive readings consume time while producing limited sales, whereas meaningful media exposure now matters more. Ehrman illustrates the disappointment with a humorous story about a poet reading to two students who were merely studying, then lists regional events planned for Heaven and Hell despite the unusually difficult publicity environment surrounding its release.

title: A Fuller Exposition of the Christ Poem in Philippians
author: BDEhrman
description: Provides a fuller interpretation of the Philippians Christ poem and its view of Christ's descent and exaltation.
searchSummary: Interprets the Philippians Christ poem as both incarnational and exaltational. Christ begins as a divine, angelic being in God's form but not God's equal; instead of grasping higher status, he becomes human and dies obediently. God then hyper-exalts him, grants him the divine title Lord, and applies Isaiah's universal worship language to him. The passage reflects an ancient spectrum of divinity: Christ moves from a lower heavenly status to equality with God without becoming the Father.

title: Brief Video Promotion of Heaven and Hell
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a brief promotional video for Heaven and Hell.
searchSummary: Introduces a short Simon & Schuster promotional video for Ehrman's book Heaven and Hell: A History of the Afterlife before its publication. In the studio recording, his publisher asks five key questions drawn from the many issues treated in the book, offering viewers a sample of its subject matter. The written post expresses Ehrman's satisfaction with the finished volume but does not identify those questions or summarize his answers, leaving the video itself as the source for those details.

title: Did Paul Think Jesus Was a New Adam, Not a Divine Being?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether Paul viewed Jesus as a new Adam rather than as a divine being.
searchSummary: Assesses the claim that Philippians 2 presents Christ as a second Adam rather than a heavenly being. Although Paul elsewhere contrasts Adam's disobedience with Christ's obedience, the poem lacks Genesis's “image” vocabulary, attributes the desire for divine likeness to Eve, and says Christ became human. Paul also identifies Christ as the wilderness rock and the man from heaven. Ehrman therefore concludes that the poem describes a preexistent divine being entering human life, not merely an exemplary human reversing Adam.

title: Was Christ an Angel, According to Paul?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores whether Paul's language could suggest that Christ was understood as an angelic being.
searchSummary: Explains Paul's incarnation Christology through Galatians 4:14 and the Philippians Christ poem. The Greek construction in Galatians identifies Christ as an angel, probably God's chief heavenly mediator, rather than simply ranking him above angels. Philippians then describes this preexistent divine being becoming human and receiving greater glory after death. Later passages distinguish the exalted Christ from subordinate angels because his resurrection has elevated him above them, not because Paul denied his earlier angelic identity.

title: Fund-Raising Blog Dinner on March 13, Washington D.C.
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a fundraising blog dinner in Washington, D.C.
searchSummary: Announces a small fundraising dinner for blog members in Washington, D.C., centered on informal conversation about the New Testament, early Christianity, and the blog. Seven seats are available for a $200 donation plus each participant's meal cost. Additional donations provide pre-dinner drinks or, for the highest bidder, a private hour afterward. The post gives the event date, explains the first-come registration process, and asks interested members to contact Bart privately.

title: Buddhist Interview Questions on Suffering
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares Buddhist interview questions about suffering and religious explanations for it.
searchSummary: Contrasts Ehrman's naturalistic account of suffering with Buddhist explanations based on karma and liberation through Nirvana. He regards much pain as innocent and random in a material universe without supernatural direction, so humans must create meaning by enjoying brief lives and relieving others' misery. Although religions offer valuable insights without a single complete solution, Ehrman declines a comparative book requiring expertise in Buddhist sutras and identifies public education about early Christianity as his own scholarly mission.

title: More Buddhist Questions on the Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues a Buddhist magazine interview with questions about miracles, the Bible, and Christian belief.
searchSummary: Continues Ehrman's interview with editors of a Korean Buddhist magazine about Christianity from an outsider's perspective. He rejects the claim that pastors generally preach for personal profit, explains Hebrew prophets as critics of their own social and political circumstances rather than distant predictors, and compares literal and symbolic readings of miracle stories. Ehrman concludes that he does not believe miracles, spirits, or an afterlife exist and argues that mortality makes present relationships, pleasures, and help for others more precious.

title: Great Deal on My New Book!!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a pre-order deal connected with Heaven and Hell and Great Courses material.

title: Interview with Buddhists on the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces an interview with a South Korean Buddhist magazine about the New Testament and Christianity.
searchSummary: Answers a Korean Buddhist magazine's questions about Ehrman's scholarship, changing faith, American Bible reading, and Christian responses to contradiction. Ehrman explains that close study in Greek and Hebrew led him reluctantly from defending biblical inerrancy to accepting contradictions, historical errors, and scientific problems, though this did not immediately end his Christianity. He distinguishes that intellectual transition from his later agnosticism, which arose primarily from suffering rather than biblical discrepancies.

title: How Ancient is the Idea of Christ’s “Incarnation”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the Philippians Christ hymn may preserve an early idea of Christ's incarnation.
searchSummary: Argues that incarnation Christology predates the Gospel of John's explicit Logos theology. Philippians 2:6-11 appears to quote a structured composition already known before Paul's letter. It describes a divine Christ relinquishing heavenly privilege, becoming human and obedient unto death, and then being exalted to universal lordship. Because the poem is pre-Pauline, the idea of a preexistent heavenly being becoming flesh arose within the earliest decades of Christianity rather than only near the end of the first century.

title: How Do I Get To Know What Is In the Bible?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how readers can begin learning the Bible through accessible introductions and broader context.

title: Heaven and Hell: Press Release!!
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the publisher press release for Heaven and Hell.

title: Jesus Kissing Mary Magdalene: A Bizarre Scene in the Gospel of Philip
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines the Gospel of Philip passage about Jesus kissing Mary Magdalene and what it does or does not show.

title: What About Accurately Preserved *Oral* Traditions?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to arguments about accurately preserved oral traditions in Christian and Muslim contexts.

title: Sacramento Lecture: Cancelled
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces cancellation of a Sacramento lecture.

title: Raffle Winners!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces winners of a raffle for advance copies of Heaven and Hell.

title: Why Do Smart People Make Stupid Arguments?
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques bad apologetic arguments about miracles.

title: Jesus as Single: An Actual Argument!
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates the argument that Jesus was unmarried, using ancient Jewish evidence and early Christian assumptions.
searchSummary: Uses Jesus's apocalyptic ethics to argue that he was unmarried. Jesus taught followers to embody the coming kingdom's conditions before it arrived by practicing peace, justice, healing, and relief of suffering. In his response to the Sadducees, resurrected people neither marry nor have sex but live like angels. Bart reasons that if Jesus expected disciples to enact that future life in the present, his own abstention from marriage fits both his teaching and other celibate apocalyptic Jews.

title: Demons and Christians in Antiquity!  Guest Post By Travis Proctor
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Travis Proctor's guest post on demons and Christians in antiquity.

title: Was Jesus Intimate with Mary Magdalene?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether any evidence supports an intimate relationship between Jesus and Mary Magdalene.

title: So… WAS Jesus Married?
author: BDEhrman
description: Revisits whether Jesus was married.

title: A “Newly Discovered” “Gospel”: Was Jesus Married with Children?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to claims about a newly discovered Gospel portraying Jesus as married with children.

title: A Raffle!!  Would You Like a Pre-publication Copy of My  Book on Heaven and Hell?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a raffle for pre-publication copies of Heaven and Hell.
searchSummary: Offers three signed prepublication copies of Heaven and Hell through a raffle benefiting the blog. Readers may buy one, three, or five entries at tiered donation amounts before the deadline, after which winners are chosen randomly and receive the galley proofs by mail. Bart explains what the advance copies contain and provides detailed instructions for donating, saving the payment confirmation, emailing it to the fundraising address, and identifying the number of tickets purchased.

title: Want A Korean Version of My Last Book?
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers Korean translation copies of The Triumph of Christianity to interested readers.
searchSummary: Offers five Korean-language copies of The Triumph of Christianity to readers willing to make a blog donation covering at least the mailing expense. Bart notes that he cannot read the translation and invites Korean readers, or anyone interested in learning, to request one privately. The brief fundraiser establishes minimum contributions for domestic and international shipping while allowing recipients to give more, turning otherwise unused author copies into support for the blog's charitable work.

title: Rapid Fire Questions and Answers on Biblical Manuscripts
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers rapid-fire questions about biblical manuscripts, manuscript collecting, and illicit sales.

title: Other Interesting Features of the Graphic Introduction to the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes additional planned features of a graphic introduction to the New Testament.

title: How I Will Write My “Graphic Textbook of the New Testament”
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the proposed structure and coverage of a graphic textbook on the New Testament.

title: A Graphic Novel (Textbook) on the New Testament!
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a planned graphic textbook on the New Testament.

title: Volunteers Needed!  Readers for Audio Versions of the Posts.  You Interested?
author: BDEhrman
description: Seeks volunteer readers for audio versions of blog posts.

title: Want To Know About the Apostolic Fathers?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Apostolic Fathers and their importance for early Christian studies.
searchSummary: Describes an advanced doctoral seminar on the Apostolic Fathers, a diverse collection of proto-orthodox writings from around and after the New Testament period. Students translate the texts from Greek, examine authorship, dating, and textual integrity, and engage scholarship on works including 1 Clement, Ignatius, Polycarp, the Didache, Barnabas, Hermas, Papias, and Diognetus. The course uses these writings to study church hierarchy, women, martyrdom, ritual, Jewish-Christian relations, orthodoxy, and canon formation.

title: Jesus, the Supernatural, and the Historian: Guest Post 2 by James Tabor
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents James Tabor's discussion of historians, supernatural claims, and Jesus.
searchSummary: Explains that historians can investigate religious experiences and miracle reports without deciding whether supernatural realities caused them. James Tabor treats claims about healings, visions, resurrection, and ascension as historical evidence for what communities believed and reported, then evaluates the dates, tendencies, and reliability of their sources alongside comparable ancient traditions. History can reconstruct experiences and developments while remaining unable to declare demons, divine intervention, or an afterlife objectively real. That restraint differs from dogmatic denial as well as theological affirmation.

title: Guest Post by James Tabor: The Historian and the Supernatural
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents James Tabor's guest post on how historians should approach supernatural claims.
searchSummary: Defends historical investigation as evidence-based interpretation rather than either objective certainty or mere subjective opinion. James Tabor emphasizes incomplete and tendentious ancient sources, the need to evaluate authorial motives and competence, and the provisional character of scholarly consensus. Historians do not simply exclude miracle reports; they examine what texts and material evidence can support while recognizing that claims such as virgin conception, bodily resurrection, and legendary episodes exceed ordinary experience and require arguments stronger than theological presupposition.

title: So: Was Luke Luke?
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes the case against identifying Luke-Acts with Luke the companion of Paul.
searchSummary: Summarizes the case against identifying the anonymous author of Luke-Acts as Luke, Paul's Gentile physician and traveling companion. Colossians is probably not by Paul, the attribution appears only with Irenaeus about a century later, and Acts repeatedly conflicts with Paul's own accounts and theology. The Gospel remains anonymous, while Acts' first-person passages raise the possibility that its author implied participation in Paul's travels without naming himself.

title: Does the Book of Acts Accurately Record Paul’s Teachings?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether Acts accurately reports Paul's teachings.
searchSummary: Compares Paul's Areopagus speech in Acts with his argument about pagan religion in Romans. Acts portrays pagans as ignorant of the true God and says God overlooked that ignorance, whereas Romans says they knew God through creation, deliberately turned to idols, and incurred divine wrath. Although different audiences might explain the contrast, Ehrman argues that Luke's authorship of the speech better accounts for it and shows why Acts cannot be accepted uncritically as an accurate record of Paul's teaching.

title: Did *Any* Companion of Paul Write Luke and Acts?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether any companion of Paul could plausibly have written Luke and Acts.
searchSummary: Argues that no personal companion of Paul is likely to have written Luke-Acts because Acts does not accurately reflect Paul's life or central teachings. Comparisons with Paul's letters reveal disagreements about his movements after conversion, his companions, his relationship with the Jerusalem apostles, and his view of Jewish law. Acts is valuable evidence for how its author understood Paul, but its discrepancies undermine the claim of firsthand knowledge suggested by the first-person passages.

title: How Were People Crucified?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how crucifixion was carried out and why wrists rather than palms matter historically.

title: Bidding to See My New Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Follows up with readers who bid to see an advance copy of Heaven and Hell.

title: Two Brief Comments on intriguing topics: the unknowability of God and scholarly subterfuge!
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers brief reflections on divine unknowability and scholarly misconduct.
searchSummary: Offers two brief reflections on unrelated but revealing issues. First, Ehrman questions how theologians can insist that God is incomprehensible while confidently assigning God detailed attributes, intentions, and actions. Second, he directs readers to a Guardian investigation of the first-century Mark controversy, where secrecy, manuscript sales, false dating, and alleged scholarly misconduct turned an exciting claim about an early Gospel fragment into a cautionary story about evidence and academic integrity.

title: Does the Author of Acts Identify Himself?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Acts does not identify its author as Luke or any companion of Paul.
searchSummary: Examines the first-person “we-passages” in Acts and argues that they make a deliberate claim that the author accompanied Paul. Their abrupt appearances and disappearances, unexplained shifts between “we” and third-person narration, and realistic but narratively unnecessary details are difficult to reconcile with a straightforward eyewitness diary. Ehrman proposes that the author selectively inserted himself into the story to authenticate his account and give Paul's activities vivid historical authority, even though the claimed presence and other narrative assertions may be false.

title: A Revelatory Moment about “God”
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on a personal shift in thinking about God and superior beings.
searchSummary: Explains why reflection on consciousness made Ehrman emphasize agnosticism more strongly than atheism. Just as rocks, plants, and animals cannot comprehend higher cognitive forms, humans may be incapable of recognizing superior orders of intelligence or existence, making confidence that humanity occupies reality's pinnacle unwarranted. This possibility does not validate biblical deities or traditional religion; it instead exposes human epistemological limits and hubris, leaving Ehrman unable to determine whether unimaginable beings exist above the material world people can investigate.

title: Did Paul Write Colossians? According to Most Scholars No – Paul did Not Write Colossians
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why many scholars think Paul did not write Colossians.
searchSummary: Presents the cumulative scholarly case that Paul did not write Colossians. Detailed stylistic analysis finds striking differences in conjunctions, infinitives, relative clauses, sentence structure, and other habits, while the letter's realized resurrection, exalted Christology, treatment of forgiveness, household code, and long-term social outlook diverge from undisputed Paul. Together these features indicate that a later admirer developed Pauline ideas in new directions while writing under the apostle's name.

title: Would You Like to Read My New Book NOW Instead of When It Gets Published???
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers readers a chance to bid for early access to Heaven and Hell.

title: Problems with Thinking That Luke Wrote Luke (and Acts)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains problems with the traditional claim that Luke wrote the Gospel of Luke and Acts.
searchSummary: Challenges a key premise behind attributing Luke-Acts to Luke the Gentile physician. Luke is named as Paul's coworker in Philemon, but only Colossians calls him a physician and implies that he was Gentile. Because Colossians and 2 Timothy were probably written in Paul's name by later Christians, they cannot establish the identity needed for the traditional authorship argument. Differences in Colossians' style and theology support its non-Pauline authorship.

title: Once More on the Credibility of Miracles: Guest post by Darren Slade
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Darren Slade's guest post on miracle claims and historical credibility.
searchSummary: Summarizes Darren Slade's argument that sincere eyewitness testimony cannot by itself establish a miracle. Memory distortion, source confusion, suggestion, interviewer bias, obstructed observation, fraud, and postevent information must be investigated through rigorous, independent fact-finding. Craig Keener's acceptance of modern Christian miracle reports at face value, while discounting comparable claims from other religions, therefore cannot authenticate New Testament miracles; without corroborating evidence that rules out natural explanations, the rational response is to withhold judgment.

title: Did “Luke” Really Write Luke?  And the book of Acts?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Luke wrote the Gospel of Luke and Acts.
searchSummary: Introduces the traditional reasoning used to identify the anonymous author of Luke-Acts as Luke, a Gentile physician who traveled with Paul. The argument connects Acts' first-person travel passages, its Gentile emphasis, references to Luke in Pauline letters, and perceived medical language. The post emphasizes that the attribution first appears with Irenaeus about a century after the Gospel was written and begins evaluating whether the first-person passages really provide eyewitness evidence.

title: Misunderstandings???
author: BDEhrman
description: Clarifies a misunderstanding about authorship of a previous blog post.

title: Was Christianity a Missionary Religion with No Missionaries?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how early Christianity could be missionary without a formal missionary system.
searchSummary: Explains how early Christianity expanded despite having almost no organized missionaries after Paul. Rather than relying on public campaigns, ordinary Christians shared their faith through overlapping networks of relatives, friends, neighbors, coworkers, and household dependents. Each conversion opened further relationships through which stories and personal experiences could spread. Because Christianity demanded exclusive allegiance, every convert both enlarged the church and reduced pagan participation, allowing steady interpersonal growth to transform the religious landscape over several centuries.

title: Why Do Christians Try to Convert People?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Christians try to convert others and how that differs from Greco-Roman religious practice.
searchSummary: Explains why Christianity developed an evangelistic mission unlike Roman pagan cults and ancient Judaism, neither of which generally organized efforts to win converts. Ehrman connects Christian proselytizing to an apocalyptic message in which only those saved through Christ would escape divine judgment. Christianity's command to love all people reinforced that urgency: if nonbelievers faced destruction or eternal punishment, persuading them to worship the Christian God became an act of concern for their salvation.

title: Blog Year in Review, 2019!
author: BDEhrman
description: Reviews the blog's activity, reach, and charitable work during 2019.
searchSummary: Reviews the blog's educational and charitable performance during 2019. Bart describes its commitment to presenting critical scholarship, reports 268 posts and 14,801 reader comments for the year, and notes more than 8,300 members. The blog raised $167,000 that year and over $825,000 since launch for five charities. He discusses plans for substantial growth, recognizes Steven Ray and new volunteers, invites suggestions, and asks members to promote the blog and give subscriptions.

title: The Case Against Miracles:  Guest Post by John Loftus
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents John Loftus's guest post on arguments against miracles.

title: End of the Year Final Exam!
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares an end-of-year final exam on Jesus, the Gospels, and early Christianity.
searchSummary: Presents the possible essay questions for a final examination in a course on Jesus in scholarship and film. Students apply Gospel-study methods, compare distinctive portrayals, evaluate contradictions and historical reliability, assess criteria for reconstructing Jesus, compare a film with an ancient Gospel, debate Jesus as an apocalyptic prophet, or contrast modern historical reconstructions. Ehrman favors essays because they reveal how much students understand and how well they can develop evidence-based written arguments.

title: The Life and Message of Paul
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys Paul's life and message within a broader introduction to the New Testament.

title: Why Does Matthew Have the Story of the “Wise Men”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Matthew includes the story of the wise men in the birth narrative.
searchSummary: Explains how Matthew's legendary story of the Magi introduces major themes of the Gospel. Pagan astrologers recognize and worship the infant Jewish Messiah, while Herod, chief priests, and Scripture experts know the prophetic location of his birth but either ignore or seek to kill him. This irony anticipates Jesus' fulfillment of Jewish Scripture, rejection by Jewish leaders who know but fail to follow God's law, and acceptance by gentiles who initially lack that scriptural knowledge.

title: Christmas 2019
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the meaning and emotional ambiguity of Christmas.
searchSummary: Confronts Christmas loneliness, materialism, and temporary goodwill while seeking limited reasons for hope. Ehrman recommends silently accompanying severe sufferers rather than offering easy solutions, contrasts consumer desire with the Christian story of selfless giving, and questions why generosity and kindness appear seasonally. Yet repeated holiday practices may cultivate lasting habits, much as a small exercise routine can grow, so obligatory gifts and brief decency might teach some people to give freely and care for others throughout the year.

title: More on the Case Against Miracles: Michael Shermer Guest Post
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Michael Shermer's guest foreword on arguments against miracles.

title: The Case Against Miracles
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces The Case Against Miracles and its challenge to miracle claims.

title: Guided Tours of Heaven and Hell in a Christian Mode
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains early Christian guided tours of heaven and hell as otherworldly journey traditions.
searchSummary: Explains how Christian tours of heaven and hell adapted older journey traditions to enforce distinct beliefs and conduct. The Acts of Thomas makes faith, obedience, and charity decisive; the Apocalypse of Peter matches specific sins with punishments; and the Apocalypse of Paul targets immoral clergy and theological heresy. Comparing these works with Lucian and Virgil shows how persecution, ecclesiastical conflict, asceticism, and attitudes toward wealth shaped Christian visions that later contributed to Western doctrines of heaven, hell, and purgatory.

title: Guided Tours of Heaven and Hell:  My Scholarly Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a scholarly book project on early Christian tours of heaven and hell.
searchSummary: Outlines a scholarly project comparing early Christian journeys through heaven and hell with Greek, Roman, and Jewish precedents. The Apocalypse of Peter, Acts of Thomas, Apocalypse of Paul, and Gospel of Nicodemus portray differentiated rewards and punishments while advancing specific ethical and theological agendas. Ehrman moves beyond debates over whether Christian tours originated in Orphic or Jewish traditions, asking how each narrative functioned within its religious world and instructed readers to live in light of death and judgment.

title: UpcomingTours, Lectures, and Book Readings
author: BDEhrman
description: Lists upcoming tours, lectures, and book readings.

title: Heaven and Hell in a Nutshell: Getting into the Kernel
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes central arguments of Heaven and Hell about changing afterlife beliefs.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus taught bodily resurrection into God's earthly kingdom for the righteous and permanent annihilation for opponents, not immortal souls experiencing heaven or eternal torment. This Jewish apocalyptic expectation developed from demands for justice and differed from Greek dualism. As Gentile converts adopted Christianity and the anticipated judgment failed to arrive, they reinterpreted Jesus through Platonic assumptions, producing heaven and hell. Ehrman concludes with Socrates that death is either peaceful nonexistence or welcome continued life, leaving nothing to fear.

title: Heaven and Hell in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Heaven and Hell and its basic questions about afterlife belief.
searchSummary: Traces early Western afterlife ideas from Hebrew mortality and Homer's shadowy Hades to Plato's system of moral rewards and punishments. Most Hebrew writings treat death as the end, with Sheol meaning the grave or an inactive netherworld, while Homer sends nearly everyone to the same diminished existence. Plato instead makes the immortal soul decisive and uses postmortem judgment to promote virtue, reason, and detachment from bodily pleasure. This development supplied concepts later transformed within Judaism and Christianity.

title: Why Would an Agnostic-Atheist Be A Bible Scholar??
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why agnosticism or atheism need not prevent serious study of the Bible.
searchSummary: Explains why an agnostic can remain professionally committed to biblical scholarship. In a secular research university, scholars study historically and culturally important subjects without needing to believe their religious, political, or philosophical claims. The Bible, Christianity, and Jesus have profoundly shaped Western history and remain intellectually compelling objects of historical and literary study. Ehrman's loss of faith changed the reasons for his work, but not its academic legitimacy, importance, or fascination.

title: Update on My Next Book: The Joys of Academic Writing
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes progress on academic writing and a forthcoming monograph.
searchSummary: Describes a secluded writing retreat where Ehrman begins his scholarly book on ancient journeys to the afterlife after two years of intensive research. Work in Greek, Latin, French, German, and Italian led him to divide a comparative opening chapter into separate treatments of pagan and Jewish-Christian traditions. Unlike rapidly drafted trade books, this monograph requires slow, exact prose and original knowledge creation, but the difficulty renews his sense that rigorous academic scholarship is his central vocation.

title: Why Are Their Differences in the Gospels?  Does it Affect Their Inspiration?  Guest Post by Mike Licona
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Mike Licona's view that Gospel differences need not undermine inspiration.
searchSummary: Presents Mike Licona's argument that ancient biographical conventions explain many Gospel differences without destroying their historical value. Comparing Plutarch's transfer of an emissary's actions to Pompey with Matthew's transfer of intermediaries' words to the centurion, Licona identifies compression, conflation, displacement, and invented contexts as accepted compositional devices. He concludes that the Gospels preserve a substantial historical core while rhetorically shaping details, though he does not claim this resolves every discrepancy.

title: Do You Want (and Need) a Free Membership to the Blog?  Gift Memberships 2019
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces donated free memberships for readers who need access to the blog.

title: Does the New Testament Condemn “Homosexuals”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether New Testament passages condemn homosexuality and how translation affects the issue.
searchSummary: Argues that translating arsenokoites as homosexuals in 1 Corinthians 6:9 and 1 Timothy 1:10 claims more certainty than the evidence allows. The rare Greek compound may concern male sexual behavior, exploitation, prostitution, or another practice, while its etymology and sparse later uses cannot establish a precise meaning. Ehrman also stresses that ancient authors lacked the modern concept of sexual orientation, making broad condemnations of gay identity historically and linguistically misleading.

title: One of the Blog’s Main Charities: Urban Ministries of Durham
author: BDEhrman
description: Highlights Urban Ministries of Durham as one of the blog's major charities.
searchSummary: Profiles Urban Ministries of Durham, one of five charities supported by the blog's membership fees and donations. Bart explains the foundation's direct distribution model, its cumulative giving above $800,000, and UMD's work addressing local hunger, homelessness, employment, and permanent housing. Statistics supplied by its development director document shelter stays, job placements, meals, pantry use, and volunteer service. Readers may donate directly during a matching campaign or designate a blog contribution for UMD.

title: An Older Manuscript Controversy about the Dead Sea Scrolls
author: BDEhrman
description: Revisits an older controversy over access to the Dead Sea Scrolls.
searchSummary: Recounts a modern controversy over who produced the Dead Sea Scrolls and the criminal campaign waged in defense of Norman Golb's minority theory. Golb's son Raphael used false identities, harassment, and forged messages to discredit scholars who favored the Essene hypothesis, including messages falsely admitting plagiarism in another scholar's name. His conduct led to convictions for identity theft, forgery, impersonation, harassment, and unauthorized computer use, illustrating how a manuscript dispute escaped scholarly boundaries.

title: Final Tribute To Larry Hurtado
author: BDEhrman
description: Pays tribute to Larry Hurtado and his contributions to New Testament scholarship.

title: Is the Bible Inerrant?  Guest Post by Mike Licona
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Mike Licona's defense of biblical inerrancy.

title: Why Don’t You Just Believe?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to a reader question about why critical scholarship did not lead back to belief.

title: Who Was Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Provides a broad historical overview of Jesus within an introduction to the New Testament.
searchSummary: Reconstructs Jesus as a Galilean Jewish apocalyptic preacher whose message centered on God's imminent earthly kingdom. After joining John the Baptist, Jesus taught repentance, love, care for the poor and suffering, and preparation for judgment; he expected the wicked to be destroyed and the righteous bodily raised. His actions and predictions in Jerusalem alarmed local leaders, and Pilate crucified him as a prospective king. Followers' subsequent resurrection claims launched Christianity.

title: Thanksgiving 2019
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers a Thanksgiving reflection on holidays, gratitude, and personal circumstances.
searchSummary: Reflects on gratitude without belief in a divine giver and on the hidden suffering beneath familiar holidays. Ehrman distinguishes thanking particular people from feeling grateful for health, opportunity, temperament, consciousness, and existence produced largely by chance, while acknowledging that others have little reason for celebration. Meditation deepens his appreciation for the brief fact of being alive, and Thanksgiving becomes an occasion to focus on whatever good exists without denying tragedy or treating personal fortune as deserved.

title: Setting Dates for the Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how scholars date the Gospels.

title: The Annual Meeting of Biblical Scholars, and ALL Those Books!!
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the annual biblical-studies meeting and the flood of new scholarly books.
searchSummary: Reflects on the abundance of books displayed at the Society of Biblical Literature meeting and the economic structures behind academic publishing. The display reveals both valuable new scholarship and the impossibility of keeping up with every relevant work. Publishers need saleable titles, while scholars need books for employment, tenure, and promotion, so many publications repeat established work or address narrow questions without substantially advancing knowledge. Ehrman argues that scholarly books should contribute something genuinely new.

title: Maybe Jesus DOES Talk about “Homosexuality”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates a claim that Jesus addressed homosexuality indirectly.

title: Do Textual Variants Actually *Matter* For Much??
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why some textual variants matter for New Testament interpretation.
searchSummary: Argues that textual variants can be highly significant even when no single reading overturns a major Christian doctrine. Most variants are trivial, and theology normally rests on multiple passages and traditions, but doctrinal impact is an inadequate measure of importance. Readings involving the Trinity, Jesus' emotions and divine sonship, Luke's view of atonement, resurrection appearances, and the woman taken in adultery can materially change how individual books and authors are interpreted.

title: Introduction to the Manuscripts of the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the manuscript evidence for the New Testament.
searchSummary: Introduces how hand copying transmitted New Testament books and produced hundreds of thousands of mostly minor differences among surviving witnesses. More than 5,600 Greek manuscripts and ancient translations provide abundant evidence, but the earliest Christian copyists lacked professional training and complete witnesses appear centuries after composition. Textual methods usually recover the oldest known and probably original wording, yet changes before the surviving record prevent absolute certainty in some passages.

title: Two More Openings for Blog Dinner in Durham, December 3.  Interested?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces open seats at a Durham fundraising blog dinner.
searchSummary: Reopens two seats for a members-only fundraising dinner in Durham after cancellations. For a $100 blog donation plus the cost of their meals, participants can join Bart for informal conversation about the New Testament, early Christianity, and the blog. Optional additional donations provide drinks beforehand, while the highest bidder can arrange a private hour afterward. The notice repeats the original event details and asks interested members to contact Bart privately before the remaining places fill.

title: How Did We Get The 27 Books of the New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how the twenty-seven books of the New Testament came to form the canon.
searchSummary: Explains that the New Testament developed gradually from writings produced by different authors rather than arriving as a unified book. Christians debated which Gospels, letters, and apocalypses carried apostolic authority, and no early council settled the matter. Church leaders favored works considered ancient, apostolic, widely used, and orthodox. Athanasius first listed the familiar twenty-seven books in 367, but his judgment only contributed to the broader consensus that eventually preserved these works while others disappeared.

title: Is the Bible Inspired by God?  Guest Post by Evangelical Apologist Mike Licona
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Mike Licona's evangelical argument for biblical inspiration.

title: Jesus and “Homosexuality”
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Jesus said anything about same-sex relations.

title: The Gospel of Thomas and the Other Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares the Gospel of Thomas with the canonical Gospels and other early Jesus traditions.

title: The Coming Armageddon:  I Need Some Suggestions!
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks readers for suggestions for a trade book on Revelation and modern apocalyptic expectation.
searchSummary: Describes an early plan for a trade book about Revelation, end-time expectations, and modern apocalyptic culture. Rather than only tracing repeated Christian claims that biblical prophecies would be fulfilled in each interpreter's lifetime, the project might explore secular expressions of impending catastrophe in literature, film, politics, and public policy. Examples range from technological and nuclear fears to climate change. The post asks readers to recommend powerful fiction, nonfiction, and films about the belief that the end is near.

title: Are Same-Sex Relations Condemned in the Old Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Old Testament passages commonly used in debates over same-sex relations.

title: A Synopsis of Each New Testament Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Provides a brief synopsis of each New Testament book.

title: Blog Fund-Raising Dinner, December 3
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Durham fundraising dinner for the blog.
searchSummary: Introduces a members-only fundraising dinner in Durham designed for informal conversation with Bart about the New Testament, early Christianity, and the blog. Seven seats are available for a $100 donation plus each participant's meal cost. An additional donation permits drinks beforehand, and the highest bidder can arrange a private hour after dinner. Bart presents the experiment as both a chance to meet members and a way to support the blog's charitable mission, with registration handled privately.

title: One C. S. Lewis Writing I Relate To
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on C. S. Lewis, apologetics, and changing relationships to Christian arguments.
searchSummary: Assesses C. S. Lewis as a brilliant writer and communicator whose popular apologetics Ehrman once revered but now considers philosophically amateur and largely unpersuasive. Ehrman nevertheless identifies strongly with Lewis's poem As the Ruin Falls, especially its confession that professed love often masks self-interest and a desire for comfort. He reads the poem metaphorically toward loved ones and the world, while rejecting its conclusion that God sends suffering and should be thanked for the pain people endure.

title: What Is the New Testament?  A Broad Overview
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers a broad overview of the New Testament and its major writings.

title: Losing *Your* Faith?
author: BDEhrman
description: Addresses readers who are struggling with doubt or losing faith.
searchSummary: Directs people experiencing religious doubt or loss of faith to public resources connected with the Clergy Project. Linda LaScola's Rational Doubt blog publishes accounts by religious professionals who no longer believe, while Caught in the Pulpit, coauthored with Daniel Dennett, examines clergy who remain in ministry during deconversion. Although the Clergy Project itself serves religious professionals, these materials make their experiences accessible to anyone struggling with belief and help readers recognize that such transitions are shared rather than isolated.

title: Sex and Gender in the Ancient World
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains ancient assumptions about sex and gender as background for biblical passages.

title: Why I’m To Be Pitied for Being the Wrong *Kind* of Fundamentalist!
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to criticism by reflecting on fundamentalism and forms of biblical literalism.
searchSummary: Rejects an evangelical critic's pity for Ehrman as the product of mistaken assumptions about his life and fundamentalist background. Louis Markos argues that biblical contradictions disappear when Scripture is judged by premodern rather than modern standards, but Ehrman considers that approach intellectually and practically untenable. Historical interpretation should reconstruct ancient assumptions, while modern people should still evaluate factual, scientific, and moral claims using present knowledge rather than adopting ancient ignorance merely to preserve inerrancy.

title: Women Are To Be Silent and Submissive!
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Genesis has been used to support women's subordination.

title: Why Women Are To Be Subservient to Men
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores ancient arguments for women's subordination and their relevance to modern biblical interpretation.

title: What Does the Name Judas “Iscariot” Mean?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains competing interpretations of the name Judas Iscariot.

title: Video Debate with Peter Williams: Can We Trust the Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a video debate with Peter Williams on whether the Gospels can be trusted.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's Big Conversation debate with evangelical New Testament scholar Peter Williams over whether the Gospels can be trusted historically. Ehrman argues that Williams's defense overlooks the actual reasons scholars question Gospel reliability, answering objections that critics do not ordinarily make while leaving their central arguments unaddressed. He characterizes this as a straw-man approach likely to reassure readers already inclined to trust the Gospels, then invites viewers to watch the extended exchange and judge the competing positions themselves.

title: The Quest for the Historical … Judas Iscariot
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether Judas Iscariot was a historical figure.
searchSummary: Explains how historians assess whether Judas Iscariot existed despite having no eyewitness account and no mention in Paul. The surviving Gospels are decades later, Matthew and Luke depend largely on Mark, and later portrayals often reflect anti-Jewish or Gnostic agendas, so source independence and authorial bias must be weighed carefully. Even with those limitations, critical comparison supports three historical conclusions: Judas Iscariot existed, belonged to Jesus' twelve disciples, and handed Jesus over to the authorities.

title: Can My Undergraduate Students Continue Believing the Bible is Inerrant?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on whether students can remain committed to biblical inerrancy after critical study.

title: Who Would Invent the Story of Women at the Tomb??
author: BDEhrman
description: Challenges the claim that women at the empty tomb could not have been invented.

title: A New Way of Explaining Contradictions in an “Inerrant” Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines evangelical attempts to reconcile Gospel contradictions with inerrancy.
searchSummary: Examines Mike Licona's use of ancient biographical conventions to acknowledge Gospel alterations while retaining inerrancy. Licona treats differing details as literary shaping that preserves a story's essential gist, even when Matthew reverses Mark's instruction about carrying a staff or changes when Jairus's daughter died. Ehrman accepts that ancient authors modified sources but argues that explaining a contradiction does not erase it, questioning how an opposite report remains historically accurate or without error.

title: Modern Evangelical Christian Apologetics
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces modern evangelical apologetics and its defense of Christian claims.
searchSummary: Describes newer evangelical approaches to Gospel contradictions that move beyond insisting every detail can be harmonized. Some defenders locate inerrancy in a passage's central affirmation rather than incidental chronology, while others use ancient literary practices to explain why authors changed details. Ehrman welcomes the greater historical sophistication but questions whether a text can contain incorrect statements yet remain error-free, emphasizing that identifying why contradictions arose does not make the contradictions disappear.

title: But the Women Who Did *NOT* Doubt the Resurrection
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines resurrection narratives where women believe while other disciples doubt.

title: Startling and Disturbing Development Involving Manuscripts at the Museum of the Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Reports new developments in the First-Century Mark manuscript controversy.
searchSummary: Reports the Egypt Exploration Society's finding that Dirk Obbink unlawfully offered thirteen Oxyrhynchus papyri for sale to Hobby Lobby and the Museum of the Bible. The group included the tiny Mark fragment once advertised as first-century but later dated to the late second or early third century. Ehrman explains that Obbink had temporary access to publish the papyrus but did not own it, making the episode a major scandal involving provenance, scholarly trust, and illicit manuscript commerce.

title: Why Would Jesus’ Disciples Doubt the Resurrection?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores why the Gospels portray some disciples as doubting the resurrection.

title: More Free Memberships Available, 2019
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces more donated free memberships for readers unable to pay.

title: Crazy Things Textual Scholars Say
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques exaggerated or misleading claims made by textual scholars.
searchSummary: Rejects unsupported claims that scholars know 99 percent of the New Testament's original wording. A precise accuracy rate requires comparing copies with the missing originals; manuscript agreement or scholarly consensus can be measured, but neither proves agreement with an unavailable model, and a small disputed percentage could include crucial words. Ehrman considers it reasonable that scholars usually approximate the authors' text, but labels numerical certainty an invented reassurance rather than a defensible statistic.

title: My Trip To Rome: Interested in Joining?
author: BDEhrman
description: Invites readers to join a Rome and southern Italy tour.

title: Did God Want Us To Have His Word?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on whether God would preserve the exact words of the New Testament.
searchSummary: Challenges the theological claim that God must have preserved every original New Testament word for modern readers. Today's Greek text is an eclectic scholarly reconstruction assembled reading by reading from manuscripts, translations, and church-father quotations; no single ancient witness contains that complete form, and experts often disagree. If divine preservation required exact wording, earlier Christians lacked it for centuries, so confidence should rest on historical evidence and a practical probability of approximation rather than theological necessity.

title: What I think of the Bible as Both a Critical Scholar and A Christian: Guest Post by Judy Siker
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Judy Siker's account of reading the Bible as both critical scholar and Christian.
searchSummary: Explains how Judy Siker's Christian faith is enriched rather than destroyed by critical biblical scholarship. She treats questions, ambiguity, and continuing inquiry as essential to both academic learning and religious life, while rejecting the demand that sacred Scripture be historically perfect, internally consistent, or a direct answer book for modern issues. Siker understands the Bible as an imperfect collection of human reflections on experiences of God, whose complexity invites sustained study rather than unquestioning certainty.

title: Misconstruing My Words.  Can We Know What the Authors of the New Testament Originally Said?
author: BDEhrman
description: Clarifies claims about whether scholars can recover the original wording of the New Testament.
searchSummary: Clarifies that Ehrman does not claim scholars have no idea what New Testament authors wrote. Thousands of manuscripts contain hundreds of thousands of mostly insignificant differences, and scholars usually agree on a likely text, but some meaningful readings remain disputed or unknowable and agreement cannot create absolute certainty. That limitation is ordinary for ancient literature but especially challenges claims that every biblical word is divinely inspired and certainly preserved.

title: Modern Defenders of the Faith: Why Not Just Tell the Truth?
author: BDEhrman
description: Challenges defenders of inerrancy to acknowledge Gospel contradictions honestly.
searchSummary: Corrects apologists who misrepresent Ehrman's move from fundamentalism to agnosticism. He rejected inerrancy after recognizing biblical contradictions, historical errors, and differing theologies, but continued believing in Jesus' divinity and resurrection for years; those beliefs weakened later through separate historical scrutiny, and suffering ultimately drove his agnosticism. Ehrman agrees Christian faith need not depend on inerrancy but objects when William Lane Craig and Craig Evans use a false chronology to diagnose his theology.

title: Who Wrote the Pentateuch?  The JEDP Hypothesis
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the Documentary Hypothesis for the authorship of the Pentateuch.

title: Blog Dinner in Chicago (Oct. 18): Full!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces that the Chicago blog dinner is full.

title: How Did We Get *These* 27 Books in the New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how the New Testament canon came to consist of twenty-seven books.
searchSummary: Corrects the popular claim that Nicaea or Constantine selected the New Testament books. Different early Christian communities recognized different writings as Scripture, and the victorious proto-orthodox tradition gradually established the collection that prevailed. Athanasius first listed the familiar twenty-seven books in 367, nearly three centuries after most were written. Leaders generally favored works they considered ancient, apostolic, widely used across churches, and theologically orthodox, although judgments and accepted collections continued to vary.

title: Blog Dinner, Chicago IL, Friday October 18
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Chicago blog dinner for members.

title: How Can You Still Believe?  Guest Post by Judy Siker
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Judy Siker's response to how critical scholarship can coexist with Christian faith.
searchSummary: Traces Judy Siker's development as both a New Testament scholar and a practicing Christian minister. Raised in a moderate Protestant setting that allowed questions, she encountered historical-critical study in college as an illuminating response to difficulties in biblical narratives rather than an attack on faith. Continued academic training exposed contradictions and the human dimensions of Scripture but deepened her curiosity and commitment, preparing her fuller account of how scholarly inquiry and belief can coexist.

title: If the Old Testament is Not Accurate — Where Did Israel Come From?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why problems with the conquest of Canaan raise historical questions about Israel's origins.

title: Did The Israelites Really Conquer Canaan?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether the biblical conquest of Canaan happened as described.

title: Is It Ever Right to Lie?  Or Was It?  Even in Early Christianity?  The Relevance for Forgery.
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines ancient Christian views on lying and their relevance to forgery.
searchSummary: Examines Christian ethics of lying to explain how forgers might justify false identities. Augustine prohibited all intentional deception, but most ancient thinkers allowed lies that prevented harm or benefited another person. Readers who detected forgery often felt betrayed, yet authors had varied motives, including profit, rivalry, institutional prestige, and promoting moral or religious teaching. Ehrman suggests that unknown writers lacking authority could view an assumed famous name as a permissible way to communicate truths they believed their communities urgently needed.

title: Why It Is Hard To Publish a Translation of an Ancient Text
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why publishing translations of ancient texts is difficult and labor-intensive.
searchSummary: Explains why publishing a translation is harder than understanding Greek privately or discussing alternatives in a seminar. Ehrman's Loeb Apostolic Fathers required selecting a Greek text, researching each work, and making thousands of final English choices where several renderings captured different nuances. The obligation to print one imperfect option, knowing other scholars might disagree, made the project painstaking despite his fluency and ultimately led him to swear off further translations.

title: My Speaking Schedule for this Academic Year (so far)
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a speaking schedule for the academic year.

title: Hey!  Wanna Go With Me To Rome ?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a lecture trip to Rome and southern Italy.

title: A Recent Argument that Ancient Pseudepigraphy Was NOT Deceptive (or Meant to Be)
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to the argument that ancient pseudepigraphy was not intended to deceive.
searchSummary: Evaluates Irene Peirano's argument that some Latin pseudepigrapha were transparent literary impersonations rather than intended deceptions. She connects them to rhetorical training in imitation and interprets obvious anachronisms as clues inviting educated readers to enjoy the performance. Ehrman finds no ancient author or reader explicitly describing this practice, distinguishes classroom exercises from publication, and reads the Heraclides episode as a deliberate trap. He also argues that the model does not fit Christian prose, uneducated apostolic names, or poor stylistic imitation.

title: What Motivated Some Ancient Authors to Lie About Themselves?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains possible motives for ancient authors who wrote falsely in another person's name.
searchSummary: Distinguishes a forger's intention to deceive from the motivation behind that deception. Evidence offers little approval for false authorial claims, while fiction operated under a different reader-author agreement. Forgers sought profit, defended philosophical or religious positions, defamed opponents, or commonly borrowed authority so unknown ideas would circulate. Each goal depended on readers accepting the claimed identity. Ehrman concludes that even noble motives do not erase deception: authors knew they wrote the works and that the named authorities did not.

title: My Approaching Birthday
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on an approaching birthday and the passage of time.
searchSummary: Reflects on how approaching age sixty-four has narrowed Ehrman's priorities toward meaningful work, health, family, friendship, serious literature, and service. Awareness of limited time leads him to reduce shallow entertainment while continuing research, teaching, writing, and public communication that he genuinely enjoys. He presents the blog as both an accessible bridge between scholarship and general readers and a charitable project, asking members to mark his birthday by supporting organizations that assist people in need.

title: How Many Books in the New Testament Were Forged?
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers how many New Testament writings are considered forged.
searchSummary: Classifies New Testament writings by how their authorship is presented. Ehrman identifies anonymous works later falsely attributed to famous figures, Revelation as probably written by a different John, seven undisputed Pauline letters as correctly named, and ten to thirteen writings as forged or implicitly deceptive. His latter category includes disputed Pauline letters, James, Peter, Jude, and claims embedded in Acts, Hebrews, and 1 John. The resulting totals illustrate how little surviving early Christian literature securely bears its actual author's name.

title: Were Ancient Readers Interested in Detecting Forgeries?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether ancient readers cared about detecting forged writings.
searchSummary: Shows that Greek, Roman, and Christian readers actively investigated authorship and treated false claims as deception. Critics used style, content, theology, historical setting, and anachronism to identify works as lies or illegitimate offspring. Galen documented his authentic books after encountering false works, Dionysius trapped Heraclides with a forged play, and Salonius confronted Salvian over a pseudonymous Christian letter. Ehrman argues that these reactions refute claims that informed ancient readers routinely accepted false attribution as harmless literary convention.

title: My Lecture in Quebec:  Did Ancient Authors Try To Deceive Their Readers?
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a lecture on whether ancient authors tried to deceive readers through pseudepigraphy.
searchSummary: Argues that publishing under another famous person's name was normally understood in antiquity as intentional literary deceit and can properly be called forgery. Ehrman separates false authorial claims from anonymity, later attribution, homonymity, pen names, fabrication, textual alteration, and plagiarism. Ancient terminology, authenticity criticism, and authors' motives all support the conclusion that readers were meant to believe the false identity. Detecting forgery should relocate a work to its genuine historical context, not make scholars dismiss its literary or theological value.

title: A New and Important Book on the Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Reviews John Barton's general-audience book on the Bible.
searchSummary: Reviews John Barton's A History of the Bible as an accessible, scholarly introduction to the Bible's origins, interpretation, and religious authority. Bart highlights Barton's candid treatment of morally troubling passages and other complications while praising his balanced presentation of scholarship. The review also contrasts Jewish and Christian readings of the Hebrew Bible and explains Barton's view that biblical authority rests within developing faith traditions rather than literal inerrancy.

title: My Conference on Pseudepigraphy
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes a Quebec conference on pseudepigraphy in antiquity.
searchSummary: Reflects on an international conference devoted to known ancient pseudepigrapha and the functions of false authorial claims. Ehrman describes the benefits of focused scholarly exchange and regrets American academics' comparative weakness in spoken languages. He then traces his own forgery research from Wolfgang Speyer's foundational study through years of Greek, Latin, and secondary-source work. That investigation produced Forged for general readers first and the longer Forgery and Counterforgery for scholars, challenging inherited claims that pseudonymous writing was accepted and transparent.

title: Did the Exodus Happen?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates historical problems with the biblical Exodus.

title: Now: Literary Inconsistencies in the Old Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains literary inconsistencies in the Old Testament, especially in the Pentateuch.
searchSummary: Surveys literary inconsistencies in the Pentateuch that led scholars to posit multiple edited sources. Genesis 1 and 2 differ over creation order, divine names, portrayals of God, and theological interests; the flood gives conflicting animal counts; Exodus repeatedly destroys Egyptian livestock and contradicts Genesis about knowledge of Yahweh. Ehrman argues these are not isolated difficulties but seams produced when traditions from different authors and periods were combined into the present books.

title: What About the Original *Old* Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains textual problems in the Old Testament manuscript tradition.

title: Some Pitfalls of Writing for a General Audience
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains pitfalls scholars face when writing for general audiences.
searchSummary: Examines why scholars often distrust colleagues who write for general audiences and why successful trade writing remains difficult.
