Popularizers may abandon peer-reviewed research, rely on credentials without continued expert scrutiny, or discover that clarity and compelling narrative require skills graduate training never taught. Ehrman tries to maintain both scholarly production and public communication, arguing that wider audiences deserve access to expertise while acknowledging the reputational, professional, and market risks of moving away from original scholarship.

title: Why Don’t More Scholars Write Trade Books?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why many scholars avoid writing trade books for general readers.
searchSummary: Explains why many scholars neither write trade books nor regard them as prestigious academic work. Graduate education trains researchers to produce new knowledge for specialists, while popular books usually do not advance a field and may be dismissed as simplified, sensationalized, or commercially motivated. Bart acknowledges poorly qualified popularizers and professional jealousy, but defends responsible experts who communicate genuine scholarship to general readers without distorting evidence for attention or sales.

title: How Did We Get Chapters and Verses?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains where biblical chapters and verses came from.

title: Blog Dinner, Washington DC.  September 6, 2019
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Washington, D.C., fundraising blog dinner.

title: A Readable Edition of the “Lost” (i.e. non-canonical) Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes a readable translation edition of non-canonical Gospels.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman and Zlatko Plese adapted their scholarly Apocryphal Gospels edition into a trade book for general readers. The original facing-page Greek, Latin, and Coptic volume served specialists, while most readers wanted accessible English translations and concise introductions without technical apparatus. Their popular edition gathered nearly all significant noncanonical Gospels in one volume, added the Gospel of the Savior, and rewrote scholarly introductions for nonspecialists.

title: The Scholarly Edition of the Apocryphal Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the scholarly edition of the Apocryphal Gospels.
searchSummary: Recounts how Ehrman and Coptic specialist Zlatko Plese created a multilingual scholarly edition of roughly forty noncanonical Gospels. After the Loeb series declined the proposal, Oxford accepted a broader collection including Greek, Latin, and Coptic works ranging from complete texts to tiny fragments. They divided the languages, supplied fresh facing-page translations, introductions, textual apparatuses, and notes, producing a resource that later inspired a separate popular edition.

title: Why It’s Hard to Publish a Translation: Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Revisits the difficulty of publishing a Greek-English translation of ancient texts.
searchSummary: Explains why producing the Loeb Apostolic Fathers was far harder than reading Greek or discussing translations in a classroom. Publishing required Ehrman to choose one English rendering for every word and sentence despite several defensible alternatives, alongside reconstructing texts and researching introductions. The thousands of irreversible interpretive decisions made the two-volume project demanding but intellectually invigorating, and briefly convinced him never to undertake another major translation.

title: Can We Reconstruct the Entire New Testament from Quotations of the Church Fathers?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why patristic quotations cannot reconstruct the whole New Testament.

title: Did Superior Health Care Lead to the Dominance of Christianity?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates the claim that Christian health care helped Christianity grow.
searchSummary: Evaluates and rejects the theory that superior Christian health care during Roman epidemics substantially drove the religion's growth. Ehrman argues that praise of Christian nursing and condemnation of pagan neglect come from biased Christian sources, while close contact with sufferers also caused many Christian caregivers to die. Because no outside evidence shows pagans converting for medical support, he concludes that health care is an inadequate explanation and points instead to conversion accounts emphasizing Christian miracle claims.

title: On Producing a New Translation of Ancient Texts
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the work involved in producing a new translation of ancient texts.
searchSummary: Recounts how complaints about Kirsopp Lake's dated Loeb Apostolic Fathers edition led Ehrman into professional translation. His graduate students questioned its English, introductions, and textual decisions, and a chance conversation with a Harvard editor opened discussion of a replacement. Although initially uninterested, Ehrman proposed a completely new Greek-English edition with updated scholarship and reconstructed texts, beginning a project that later helped inspire his editions of apocryphal Gospels.

title: My Two Books on Forgery
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Forged and Forgery and Counterforgery as popular and scholarly treatments of ancient forgery.
searchSummary: Explains how one research project produced Ehrman's popular Forged and scholarly Forgery and Counterforgery. Dissatisfied that New Testament scholars repeated unsupported claims that ancient pseudepigraphy was acceptable, he returned to Wolfgang Speyer's work and spent years examining pagan, Jewish, and Christian evidence in several languages. A fellowship enabled concentrated study of ancient references and modern scholarship. Although originally planning the academic monograph first, editorial advice led him to write the accessible trade book before completing the more comprehensive scholarly analysis.

title: Writing Scholarly and Popular Books on the Same Topic
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the challenge of writing scholarly and popular books on the same topic.
searchSummary: Explains how a scholar can write both academic and popular books on related subjects without simply producing simplified duplicates. Ehrman traces his technical work in textual criticism through The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture and other publications to Misquoting Jesus, which made the field's broader problems accessible to nonspecialists. His current afterlife projects similarly pair a wide historical trade book with a focused monograph, using different evidence, depth, and purposes for distinct audiences.

title: Does Isaiah 53 Predict Jesus’ Suffering and Death or Has Isaiah 53 Been Debunked?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether Isaiah 53 predicts Jesus' suffering and death.
searchSummary: Argues from the literary and historical context of Second Isaiah that the suffering servant is Israel, not a prediction of Jesus as a future suffering messiah. The servant has already suffered, will later be vindicated, and is explicitly identified as Israel in surrounding passages. No pre-Christian Jewish evidence reads Isaiah 53 messianically; that interpretation arose when Christians sought scriptural support for a crucified messiah whom they believed God had raised.

title: An Opening for the Blog Dinner NYC August 27
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces an opening at a New York City blog dinner.

title: Does Your Soul Go To Heaven?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how resurrection of the dead differs from the idea of the soul going to heaven.
searchSummary: Distinguishes the Jewish and early Christian resurrection of the body from the popular belief that an immortal soul goes directly to heaven. Jesus, Paul, and New Testament writers expected persons to receive eternal embodied life, a claim most Greeks and Romans considered absurd because they separated a decaying body from a surviving soul. Although bodily resurrection appears explicitly only in Daniel within the Hebrew Bible, Ehrman traces its roots to God's life-giving creation and prophetic restorations of the dead.

title: An Alternative View of Suffering and the Idea of Resurrection
author: BDEhrman
description: Connects belief in resurrection with Jewish attempts to explain suffering and divine justice.
searchSummary: Explains how Jewish apocalypticism transformed the problem of righteous suffering and generated belief in bodily resurrection. Rejecting the prophetic claim that pain simply punishes sin, apocalyptic thinkers blamed temporary cosmic rule by Satan and demonic forces, which prosper the wicked and persecute God's faithful. God would soon overthrow evil, restore paradise, raise the righteous to immortal earthly life, and resurrect the wicked for judgment, ensuring that those who died unjustly still receive vindication.

title: Resurrection from the Dead: Were Jews Influenced by Zoroastrianism?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether Persian religion influenced Jewish resurrection beliefs.
searchSummary: Reconsiders the common claim that Jewish belief in bodily resurrection came from Zoroastrianism. The doctrine envisioned God raising both righteous and wicked people at history's end, rewarding the faithful and punishing opponents, and it later contributed to Christian heaven-and-hell beliefs. Yet Persian influence is difficult to establish because early Zoroastrian evidence is lacking and Jewish resurrection texts appeared long after Persian rule. Ehrman instead emphasizes an internal Jewish response to righteous suffering under a sovereign God.

title: Learning New Things
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on scholarly curiosity and the experience of learning new things.
searchSummary: Celebrates renewed intellectual curiosity through Ehrman's decision to study Homeric Greek and literary Latin after decades specializing in New Testament Greek. Daily work on Homer and Virgil expands his knowledge of classical antiquity, supports research on ancient afterlife traditions, and reveals why canonical literature continues addressing suffering, loyalty, value, and human purpose. He urges people to identify their own neglected interests, deliberately make time for them, and experience the energy that comes from learning something genuinely new.

title: Blog Dinner for NYC Full!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces that the New York City blog dinner is full.

title: Join Me In Egypt?  Tour in October 2020!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a planned Egypt lecture tour.

title: Do You Need a Free Membership?
author: admin
description: Announces available free memberships for readers unable to pay.

title: How Views of the Afterlife Changed
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how early Christian views of heaven, hell, and judgment differed from Greek and Roman afterlife ideas.
searchSummary: Shows how Christian depictions of heaven and hell changed as communities' concerns shifted. The Acts of Thomas grades rewards and punishments while promoting conversion, asceticism, and almsgiving; the Apocalypse of Peter expands the catalog to moral and religious offenses; and the later Apocalypse of Paul focuses on corrupt church officials and reserves its worst torments for Christological and Eucharistic heresy. These evolving journeys use the afterlife to define each period's most urgent standards of Christian behavior, authority, and doctrine.

title: Who Has The Answer For a Happy Afterlife?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains afterlife journeys in Acts of Thomas and their claims about who attains a happy afterlife.

title: Last Minute (well, sort of): Another Blog Dinner Option.  NYC, August 27
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a New York City blog dinner option.

title: An Ancient Author Trying to Justify His Deceit
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes an ancient author caught defending deceit after pseudonymous writing.
searchSummary: Analyzes Salvian's attempted defense after his pseudonymous Letter of Timothy to the Church was exposed. Salvian claimed the name symbolically meant honoring God and reflected personal humility, yet also admitted that an obscure author's identity would weaken the work's authority. Ehrman rejects appeals to pen names, self-effacement, or manuscript placement because anonymity could have achieved concealment without invoking Paul's famous companion. Salonius's objection and Salvian's contradictory explanation show that prestigious pseudonyms attracted readers precisely by deceiving them about authorship.

title: A Christian Forger Caught in the Act
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a case of a Christian forger caught falsely writing in another person's name.
searchSummary: Describes the documented case of an ancient Christian forger being identified and challenged. Around 440, Salvian of Marseille published an ascetic appeal for radical almsgiving as Timothy, but his former student and bishop Salonius detected the fraud. Salvian's surviving defense says content matters more than authorship while admitting that his obscurity would reduce the book's influence. His further claim that Timothy was merely a symbolic pen name conflicts with the apostolic authority the identity supplied, revealing both motive and deception.

title: Blog Dinner in D.C.: Full!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces that the Washington, D.C., blog dinner is full.

title: Who Is The Enemy?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on being labeled an enemy of Christian faith and how context affects religious criticism.
searchSummary: Examines why identical critical claims about the Bible can appear acceptable from a believer but threatening from a former believer. Using forgery and inspiration as examples, Ehrman argues that critical findings do not logically require rejection of faith; scholars such as Bruce Metzger could accept biblical myths or pseudepigrapha as inspired. Nevertheless, because Ehrman left Christianity and presents scholarship publicly, believers may treat his historical conclusions as hostile evidence against faith even when those conclusions are widely shared.

title: Some Very Strange Journeys to Heaven and Hell
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces unusual Christian journeys to heaven and hell in apocryphal literature.
searchSummary: Examines two near-death journeys in the Acts of Thomas that contrast Christian salvation with pagan afterlife traditions. King Gundaphorus's deceased brother sees a heavenly palace created through almsgiving, prompting conversion and charity, while a murdered woman tours punishments matched to sins and returns warning others to repent. Ehrman argues that the stories transform older Greek and Roman journey forms into evangelistic narratives where belief in Christ, ascetic conduct, and care for the poor determine eternal bliss or torment.

title: Why Did the Author of James Claim to be James in Particular?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the author of James may have chosen James's name for an anti-Pauline forgery.

title: Is the Author of James Rejecting Paul Himself?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether James is rejecting Paul directly or later interpretations of Paul.

title: Scribes Who Changed Their Texts on Purpose
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why scribes sometimes changed New Testament texts intentionally.
searchSummary: Explains an apparently intentional change to Jesus' final words in Mark from "forsaken me" to "mocked me." Matthew's dependence on Mark, the Aramaic wording, and overwhelming manuscript evidence establish "forsaken" as original, although "mocked" suits the surrounding scene. A second-century scribe may have preferred "mocked" because Gnostic Christians used "left behind" to claim that the divine Christ departed from the human Jesus at crucifixion. The altered reading blocks that theological interpretation.

title: The Close Connections of James and Paul
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares James and Paul to argue that James responds directly to Pauline letters.

title: Is James Responding to Paul?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the case that James was written to oppose Pauline teaching.

title: But WHY Doesn’t Torture Hurt??  Guest Post by Stephanie Cobb
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Stephanie Cobb's explanation of why martyrdom accounts portray torture as painless.

title: My Current Research Projects, 7/2019
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys current research projects, including work on afterlife journeys and related scholarship.

title: Does James (the Book)  Have the Same Concerns as James (the Man)?  Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares the concerns of the letter of James with what can be known of James the brother of Jesus.

title: Does the Book of James Have the Same Concerns as the Historical James?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether the book of James reflects the historical James's concerns.
searchSummary: Argues that the letter of James does not reflect the concerns historically associated with James, Jesus' brother. Early sources portray James as defending Jewish identity through Torah observance, including dietary and ritual practices, but the letter treats law chiefly as a universal moral code centered on love and the Decalogue. This mismatch strengthens the case that the historical James did not write the New Testament work bearing his name.

title: The Brother of Jesus and the Book of James
author: BDEhrman
description: Begins the argument that James the brother of Jesus did not write the letter of James.

title: How Could Torture Not Hurt??  Guest Post by Stephanie Cobb
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Stephanie Cobb's discussion of painlessness in early Christian martyrdom accounts.

title: Could Most People Write in Antiquity?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains ancient literacy rates as background for whether James could have written the letter.
searchSummary: Explains why reading, writing, and literary composition were distinct and increasingly rare skills in antiquity. Literacy was concentrated among wealthy urban elites, perhaps reaching only three percent in Roman Palestine, while advanced Greek composition required years of education unavailable to rural laborers. Most Galileans spoke Aramaic and had little Greek. Applied to New Testament authorship, this evidence makes it highly unlikely that Peter, an impoverished fisherman, produced the refined Greek prose of 1 Peter.

title: Did James Write James?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the authorship question for the New Testament letter of James.

title: Is History a Four-Letter Word?
author: BDEhrman
description: Defends the importance of history for understanding ancient texts and human life.
searchSummary: Argues that treating the Bible as exempt from skeptical historical inquiry is a confessional choice, not an academic method. Historical sources err, so investigators must question, compare, and test them rather than assuming trustworthiness in advance. Applying criticism to the Quran, Book of Mormon, and noncanonical Christian texts while shielding the New Testament reveals inconsistent theological privilege. Because Christianity makes claims about divine action in the past, understanding those claims historically requires critical procedures used for every other source.

title: Changing Your Mind.  Or Not.
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on changes of mind and diverging life paths.
searchSummary: Asks why some people revise deeply held beliefs while others preserve views learned in adolescence despite decades of evidence and experience. Encounters with an evangelical scholarly opponent and a hostile former Moody classmate remind Ehrman that his search for truth made him an enemy within communities he once shared, even though he feels no comparable animosity. He finds it implausible that one inherited worldview alone escaped error and troubling that exclusive certainty can prevent examination while condemning everyone outside it.

title: Did It Hurt to Be Martyred?  The Surprising Answer.  Guest Post by Stephanie Cobb.
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Stephanie Cobb's argument about whether early Christian martyrs experienced pain.

title: Was James the Actual Brother of Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether James was literally Jesus' brother and how ancient traditions understood the relationship.

title: Is the Book of James Attacking the Teachings of Paul?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether James attacks Paul's teaching on faith, works, and law.
searchSummary: Asks whether the letter of James contradicts Paul by insisting that faith without works cannot save. Although both invoke Abraham and Genesis 15:6, Paul means trust in Christ apart from Jewish legal observance, whereas James means intellectual belief accompanied by charitable deeds. The post concludes that James attacks a later misunderstanding of Paul that separated belief from moral conduct, rather than Paul's actual argument about circumcision, Sabbath, and kosher law.

title: One of My Favorite Letters in the New Testament: The Book of James
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the letter of James and its relationship to Paul.

title: Sad News From Larry Hurtado
author: BDEhrman
description: Reports Larry Hurtado's illness and reflects on his scholarly blogging.

title: The Legality, Morality, and Scandal of Acquiring Ancient Manuscripts: Guest Post by Jennifer Knust
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Jennifer Knust's investigation into the legality and morality of acquiring ancient manuscripts.
searchSummary: Argues that the market for rare manuscripts can conceal theft, coercion, and the human histories behind cultural objects. Knust connects Nazi-era seizure of the Rosenthal collection with disputed Museum of the Bible acquisitions, showing how dealers, auction houses, institutions, and nondisclosure agreements obscure provenance. Restitution becomes possible only when records, law, and accountability converge. She urges scholars and collections to investigate ownership histories openly rather than treating possession or educational value as sufficient justification for retaining questionable objects.

title: Christian Manuscripts and Nazi Loot: Guest Post by Jennifer Knust
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Jennifer Knust's research into a Christian manuscript's possible connection with Nazi looting.
searchSummary: Investigates whether Duke's Greek manuscript 018 may have passed through the Nazi looting of the Jewish-owned Ludwig Rosenthal Antiquariat. Archival research establishes that the store's enormous collection was seized and dispersed under Aryanization, though it does not yet reveal exactly when Raphael King acquired Duke's manuscript. The timing determines whether the transfer was legitimate or tainted by confiscation. Knust narrows the possibilities while emphasizing how little Nazi-looted cultural property was ultimately returned to its owners.

title: Tracking Down Stolen Manuscripts: Guest Post by Jennifer Knust
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Jennifer Knust's investigation into stolen manuscripts and the modern manuscript trade.
searchSummary: Introduces provenance research through two manuscript controversies: the falsely promoted “first-century Mark” fragment and Duke's medieval Greek menologion. Knust explains that manuscripts are valuable commodities capable of supporting careers, institutions, theological claims, and fortunes, which creates incentives for theft and concealment. The physical objects carry histories extending beyond their texts, including the lives of prior owners. She argues that scholars and institutions must investigate those histories and ask who bears the cost of acquiring treasured artifacts.

title: Heightened Opposition to Jews in Early Christianity
author: BDEhrman
description: Traces increasing anti-Jewish rhetoric in early Christianity.

title: When Christians Went on the Attack Against Jews
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Christian claims over the Jewish Bible contributed to attacks on Jews.

title: Is the Qur’an More Reliable than the New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds cautiously to a question about the reliability of the Qur'an compared with the New Testament.

title: Why Was the World Created in 4004 BC?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the historical calculation that placed creation in 4004 BC.

title: Would You Be Willing To Donate a Membership?
author: BDEhrman
description: Invites readers to donate memberships for people unable to afford access.
searchSummary: Requests donations of annual memberships for people who want to join the blog but cannot afford its fee. Bart recounts how the program began with anonymous donors and now supplies roughly seventy to eighty memberships a year after confirming applicants' financial need. Readers can contribute in $25 increments, notify him privately of the number sponsored, and donate through the site. Their gifts provide access while also sending the resulting funds to charity.

title: Do You Need a Free Membership?
author: admin
description: Announces free memberships for readers unable to afford the blog.

title: Is There a Way to Know if a Manuscript is the “Original”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains whether a manuscript could ever be identified as the original.
searchSummary: Argues that even an extremely early Gospel manuscript probably could not be proven to be the author's original. Paleographic dates span decades and invite disagreement, an apparent authorial signature could itself be copied, and agreement with later witnesses would show textual proximity rather than autograph status. A divergent fragment might instead be classified as another Gospel, so competing interpretations would remain possible even if scholars unknowingly possessed the actual original.

title: Flat-out Lies or Willful Ignorance.  How Do They Get Away With It?
author: BDEhrman
description: Criticizes misleading claims about the alleged first-century copy of Mark.
searchSummary: Corrects Scott Carroll's claim that Ehrman dates Mark to about 200 CE and treats it as the final Gospel written. Ehrman has long dated Mark to around 70 and regarded it as the earliest canonical Gospel; 200 referred only to the approximate date of its earliest known manuscript at the time. He argues that Carroll's misrepresentation turned the rumored first-century fragment into evangelical propaganda even after the scrap proved considerably later and historically modest.

title: The Hobby Lobby, Biblical Manuscripts, and Academic Scandal
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the Hobby Lobby and Museum of the Bible scandal surrounding biblical manuscripts.
searchSummary: Examines the ethical and academic failures surrounding the tiny Mark fragment eventually published as P137. Once promoted as a first-century discovery, it was dated instead to the late second or early third century and traced to the Egypt Exploration Society's collection. Ehrman describes how weak provenance practices, Hobby Lobby's collecting program, Scott Carroll's purchase, Dirk Obbink's unauthorized sale, and Dan Wallace's premature announcement combined to produce a major manuscript scandal.

title: Finally!  Now We Know.  The “First-Century Copy” of Mark
author: BDEhrman
description: Reports confirmation about the so-called first-century copy of Mark and its actual status.
searchSummary: Explains the documentary evidence revealing what happened to the alleged first-century Mark. The fragment belonged to the Egypt Exploration Society, which had given Dirk Obbink temporary custody to prepare it for publication, yet Obbink represented it as his own and sold it to the Green Collection or Museum of the Bible. He also supplied an implausibly early date. The episode transformed a sensational manuscript announcement into evidence of unauthorized sale, misrepresentation, and failed scholarly oversight.

title: Why Christians Needed an Old Testament: Pagan Attacks on the Faith
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Christians needed the Old Testament in responding to pagan critics.

title: The Jewish Bible in the Gentile Churches
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Gentile Christian churches came to claim the Jewish Bible as their own scripture.

title: Feedback on the Blog?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks readers for feedback while work continues on a book about journeys to heaven and hell.

title: Why Paul Did Not Write 2 Thessalonians: A Final Post
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes the final case that Paul did not write 2 Thessalonians.
searchSummary: Concludes the case against Pauline authorship of Second Thessalonians by answering proposed alternatives. Reversing the letters' order or assigning them to different audiences does not resolve their conflicting timetables for the end, and ancient evidence shows that successful forgeries could circulate during an author's lifetime. A later setting remains entirely plausible because apocalyptic expectation continued after Paul, allowing another Christian to use his name to authorize a less imminent eschatology.

title: Does Paul Think the End is Coming Soon?  Does 2 Thessalonians?
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares 1 and 2 Thessalonians on the timing of the end as evidence for disputed authorship.
searchSummary: Argues that Second Thessalonians opposes belief in an immediately approaching Day of the Lord rather than a claim that salvation has already arrived. Its author supplies events that must occur first, including rebellion and the man of lawlessness, whereas First Thessalonians warns that the end will come unexpectedly like a thief. This conflicting timetable, especially when the disputed letter claims Paul had already taught it, strongly suggests a later author revising Paul's imminent expectation.

title: 2 Thessalonians as a Forgery?  Does the Author “Write” Like Paul?
author: BDEhrman
description: Analyzes whether the writing style of 2 Thessalonians supports viewing it as a forgery.
searchSummary: Presents detailed stylistic evidence that 2 Thessalonians was written by someone imitating Paul. Although the author borrows the structure, vocabulary, and sentences of 1 Thessalonians, the freely composed material differs sharply from Paul's undisputed letters. Measurements of embedded clauses, genitive constructions, and coordination versus subordination reveal an unusually complex style shared with Colossians and Ephesians. Ehrman argues that these patterns, combined with deliberate borrowing and theological differences, strongly support forgery rather than Pauline authorship.

title: Is 2 Thessalonians a Forgery Based on 1 Thessalonians?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why 2 Thessalonians may be a forgery based on 1 Thessalonians.
searchSummary: Argues that Second Thessalonians closely copies First Thessalonians as a deliberate imitation rather than as another letter by Paul. The two share distinctive openings, endings, phrases, structure, double thanksgivings, eschatological instruction, and warnings against idleness to a degree unmatched among Paul's other related letters. Borrowing explains why the work sounds Pauline, while differences in its independently composed style and theology reveal a later author using the authentic letter as a model.

title: How “Jews” Became “Children of the Devil” in the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how the Gospel of John's language about Jews contributed to Christian anti-Judaism.
searchSummary: Traces how Jewish followers of Jesus reinterpreted Scripture after his crucifixion and resurrection, laying foundations for Christian anti-Judaism. Passages about righteous sufferers were newly read as predictions that the Messiah had to die, but most Jews rejected this unprecedented claim. Christians increasingly explained that rejection as rebellion against God, moved from a Jewish sect toward separation, and eventually claimed that God had rejected the Jews. John expresses the hardened result by portraying Jesus' Jewish opponents as children of the devil.

title: Should the Old Testament Even Be in the Bible?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines why Christians kept the Old Testament and how figures such as Marcion challenged that choice.
searchSummary: Explains why early Christians disagreed over retaining the Hebrew Bible after many ceased observing its laws. Jesus' Jewish followers upheld Torah, Paul exempted gentile believers, and Jewish Christian groups continued requiring observance; Marcion instead rejected the Old Testament and distinguished its creator from Jesus' God. Emerging orthodox leaders kept Israel's Scriptures but claimed them as Christian, a development the post connects to later Christian anti-Judaism.

title: When Were Matthew and Mark First Seen as Scripture: Guest Post on Papias by Stephen Carlson
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether Papias shows that Matthew and Mark were already treated as scripture.
searchSummary: Argues that Papias's “dominical oracles” were Old Testament prophecies about Christ rather than New Testament Gospels treated as Scripture. On this reading, Papias says Matthew compiled such passages in Hebrew and excuses Mark for preserving only some because Peter had not arranged them. Eusebius later misunderstood Papias through a developed Christian use of “oracles” for both Testaments. Papias therefore may have known the canonical Mark but apparently was unaware of the canonical Greek Matthew.

title: 2 Thessalonians: When Scholars Began To Doubt It Was Authentic
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains when scholars began doubting Pauline authorship of 2 Thessalonians.
searchSummary: Traces the scholarly debate over Second Thessalonians from early nineteenth-century doubts to the modern case for non-Pauline authorship. Schmidt first identified the conflict between the imminent end in First Thessalonians and the warning against that view in Second Thessalonians, initially proposing interpolation rather than total forgery. Later scholars increasingly focused on the disputed letter's unusually close imitation of its predecessor, non-Pauline features, and theological divergence, though defenders of authenticity remain.

title: Did Paul Really Write 2 Thessalonians?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces arguments that Paul did not write 2 Thessalonians.
searchSummary: Introduces the central reason many scholars doubt that Paul wrote Second Thessalonians. First Thessalonians expects Jesus to return suddenly and imminently, but the second letter says recognizable events, including rebellion and the man of lawlessness, must occur first. Its claim that Paul always authenticates letters with a handwritten ending is also historically inaccurate, making better sense as a later writer's attempt to reassure readers that his own Pauline letter was genuine.

title: Is There a “Best” Bible Translation Out There?  A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers whether there is a best Bible translation and discusses the NRSV.

title: How Do We know When Manuscripts Were Written? Guest Post by Brent Nongbri
author: admin
description: Presents Brent Nongbri's discussion of how scholars date ancient manuscripts.

title: Is the Old Testament a Christian Book?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores why Christians came to regard the Old Testament as a Christian book.

title: Why Do Christians Have an Old Testament?  Another Trade Book.
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a possible trade book on why Christians have an Old Testament.
searchSummary: Outlines Bart's proposed trade book about why Christians claimed the Jewish Scriptures as their Old Testament while declining to follow Jewish law and practice. He connects early Christian interpretations of Scripture and rejection of non-Christian Judaism with the later history of anti-Jewish hostility. The post also explains how a preliminary statement of a book's purpose, scope, importance, and structure becomes a prospectus used to seek a publishing contract.

title: The Blog Podcast: A Milestone!
author: BDEhrman
description: Marks a milestone for the Bart Ehrman Blog Podcast.

title: God’s Library Part 1: Finding Ancient Christian Manuscripts in Egypt.  Guest Post by Brent Nongbri
author: admin
description: Introduces Brent Nongbri's work on finding and dating ancient Christian manuscripts from Egypt.
searchSummary: Presents early Christian manuscripts as archaeological objects whose manufacture, dating, provenance, and discovery contexts matter alongside their texts. Nongbri surveys major Egyptian collections and explains how nineteenth-century cotton expansion encouraged digging for fertilizer, exposing manuscripts while also enabling looting. Archival evidence about dealer and missionary David Askren shows how finds entered Western collections, including leaves of an early Pauline codex purchased by Michigan. Such records reconstruct the modern movement and acquisition of ancient books.

title: Interview for “Letters & Politics” on The Triumph of Christianity
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares an interview about The Triumph of Christianity and the Christianization of the Roman Empire.
searchSummary: Introduces a Letters & Politics interview with host Mitch Jeserich about Ehrman's book The Triumph of Christianity. The conversation concerns how Christianity displaced the religions of the Roman Empire and became the dominant religion of the West, the central historical problem investigated in the book. Because the short post provides only the interview's setting and broad subject, it directs readers to the recording rather than detailing Ehrman's explanation of the social, demographic, political, or religious forces involved in that transformation.

title: An Official Copy of Jesus’ Death Sentence:  Another Forgery?
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses a modern forgery claiming to preserve an official death sentence for Jesus.

title: When You Feel Like You’re Talking to a Wall
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on debate frustrations when arguments do not seem to be heard.
searchSummary: Explains why proposed harmonizations of Gospel contradictions can feel linguistically impossible. Claims that Matthew's “just died” means “about to die,” Luke's immediate return to Nazareth allows years in Bethlehem and Egypt, or “while they were talking” permits a month-long Galilean interval violate ordinary speech and Greek usage. Ehrman argues that theoretically possible additions unsupported by any comparable usage are not sensible readings, while acknowledging that committed readers on both sides may feel unheard.

title: Was Jesus Perfect?  Then How Was He Human??  Guest Post: Jeffrey Siker
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Jeffrey Siker's question about Jesus' humanity and later claims of sinlessness.

title: Were Miracle Stories Originally in the Gospels?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether miracle stories belonged to the Gospels from their earliest forms.

title: Being Willing to Accept the Truth
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on intellectual honesty and willingness to accept evidence in debates about contradictions.
searchSummary: Argues that recognizing biblical contradictions does not require anti-Christian bias and should not be extended to every difference. Ehrman's Christian seminary teachers accepted discrepancies through rigorous scholarship, while he himself rejects proposed contradictions such as two differently located versions of the Beatitudes that Jesus could have delivered separately. The Jairus narratives concern the same event and conflict, however; improbable duplicate-event solutions reveal that fundamentalist inerrancy has far more at stake than critical inquiry.

title: Do My Biases Mean I *Have* to Find Contradictions?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to the charge that critical scholars find contradictions because of bias.
searchSummary: Examines how theological commitments shape debates about biblical contradictions. Ehrman argues that inerrancy requires Matthew Firth to reconcile every apparent conflict, whereas Ehrman's beliefs do not depend on whether any particular passage contradicts another; he remained a Christian long after accepting the Jairus discrepancy. His stated bias favors scholarship unconstrained by dogma: theological conclusions may respond to historical evidence, but religious commitments should not predetermine what historical or literary analysis is allowed to find.

title: How Jesus Became Perfectly Sinless: Guest Post by Jeff Siker
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Jeff Siker's account of how early Christians came to view Jesus as sinless.

title: An Eyewitness to the Crucifixion?  Another Modern Forgery
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines a modern forgery claiming eyewitness testimony to Jesus' crucifixion.
searchSummary: Identifies The Crucifixion of Jesus, by an Eye-Witness as a nineteenth-century forgery masquerading as a Latin letter by an Essene who saw Jesus survive crucifixion. The text misunderstands the Essenes, names four Gospels written decades after its alleged date, and replaces miracles with distinctly modern rationalist explanations. Its story was condensed from K. H. Venturini's earlier historical fiction, showing that an elaborate discovery account and claimed eyewitness narrator can disguise a modern fabrication as ancient testimony.

title: Judging the Debate!
author: BDEhrman
description: Invites readers to judge a debate over contradictions in the Gospels.
searchSummary: Invites readers to evaluate the completed Gospel-contradictions debate with Matthew Firth, including which arguments persuaded them and why. Ehrman reflects that confirmation bias usually prevents opponents and committed audiences from changing their minds, yet debates can help undecided or genuinely open readers and may plant ideas that mature later. He asks whether the written format was useful and worth repeating, while noting that the fundraiser generated several thousand dollars for charity.

title: When Did Jesus Become Sinless?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks when Christians began to think Jesus was sinless.

title: Did Jesus Go to India?  A Modern Gospel Forgery.
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses a modern Gospel forgery claiming Jesus traveled to India.

title: Contradictions in the Gospels – Rev Matthew Firth’s Final Response
author: admin
description: Presents Matthew Firth's final response in a debate over Gospel contradictions.
searchSummary: Presents Matthew Firth's final defense that Ehrman has shown apparent but not logically necessary Gospel contradictions. Firth argues that Luke omits known intervals that can accommodate Galilean events, Matthew's Greek can portray Jairus's daughter near death, and Levirate marriage can reconcile Joseph's genealogies. He faults surface readings and modern expectations, maintaining that ancient selective narration and plausible unstated circumstances prevent the accounts from becoming mutually exclusive.

title: What Kind of Book Was Papias Writing?  Guest Post by Stephen Carlson
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Stephen Carlson's reconstruction of Papias's book.

title: Wine Flowing in the Kingdom: Guest Post on Papias by Stephen Carlson
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Papias's extravagant kingdom saying about miraculous abundance.

title: Early Christian Liars
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how early Christian forgers could justify lying in the names of famous figures.
searchSummary: Examines whether Christian forgers could justify deceiving readers in order to promote teachings they considered true. Ehrman contrasts Augustine's absolute rejection of lying with the widespread view that deception can sometimes serve a worthy end. He argues that forged writings used false apostolic identities to make their teachings authoritative, even though ancient critics condemned the practice as lying. Whatever their motives, these authors violated the expectation of honesty and treated readers in ways they would not have wished for themselves.

title: Could Christian Forgers Justifying Lying?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Christian forgers believed lying could be justified.
searchSummary: Explores how Christian authors who forged apostolic writings may have reconciled deception with their religious convictions. Ehrman emphasizes that ancient critics regarded false authorial claims as lying and condemned exposed forgers, yet numerous Christian Gospels, letters, treatises, and apocalypses used prestigious names to authorize their teachings. Examples such as the authors of Paul and Thecla and Salvian suggest that forgers could appeal to good intentions or a "noble lie," believing that promoting truth justified deception about authorship.

title: Why Did Ancient Christian Forgers Commit Forgery?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains motives behind ancient Christian literary forgery.
searchSummary: Considers why ancient Christian forgers knowingly claimed famous identities despite moral teachings against lying. Ancient sources treated forgery as deliberate deception, but philosophers and theologians disagreed over whether beneficial lies could be justified. Ehrman contrasts Augustine's absolute prohibition with scriptural examples and thinkers such as Clement and Origen, who accepted medicinal deception. Because the forgers left no explanation, their motives remain uncertain, but they may have believed that spreading authoritative religious truth justified concealing their identities and misleading readers.

title: Contradictions and Contradictions: Final Response to Matt Firth
author: BDEhrman
description: Gives a final response to Matthew Firth on contradictions in resurrection accounts.
searchSummary: Gives Ehrman's final response to Matthew Firth's harmonizations, asking what evidence could ever qualify as a contradiction if authors are presumed not to mean what they say or unattested events may always be inserted. Luke's narrative keeps disciples in Jerusalem, its infancy sequence excludes years in Egypt, Matthew's Greek says Jairus's daughter had died, and no parallel supports the proposed genealogy. Ehrman argues that theological confidence in consistency cannot substitute for historical and grammatical evidence.

title: Constantine and the Christian Faith: My Fourth Smithsonian Lecture
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Constantine's conversion and its significance for the Christian faith in the Roman Empire.
searchSummary: A Smithsonian lecture corrects common misconceptions about Constantine and explains why his conversion remains pivotal. Constantine did not make Christianity Rome's official religion, single-handedly cause its triumph, or merely pretend to convert for political advantage. His adoption of Christianity in 312 nevertheless redirected imperial support toward the church, while official establishment and broader suppression of other religions came only near the end of the fourth century.

title: Death and the Meaning of Life
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on how afterlife beliefs shape ideas about the meaning of life.
searchSummary: Homer, Plato, and Virgil used journeys to the underworld to express competing accounts of life's meaning. Homer presents death as the great equalizer, making present life the only arena of experience, while Plato and Virgil connect conduct with postmortem reward or punishment. These alternatives raise enduring ethical questions about pleasure, justice, responsibility for others, and whether an afterlife is necessary for moral order.

title: Similarities and Differences: Which Matter the Most?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on how similarities and differences shape scholarly and personal interpretation.
searchSummary: Explains how recognizing meaningful differences transformed Ehrman's approach to the Bible and later comparative research. Evangelical interpretation treated Scripture as one consistent divine work whose passages explain each other, but noticing contradictions and distinct authorial perspectives opened critical study and preserved what each text actually says. His research on Greek, Roman, Jewish, and Christian journeys through the afterlife likewise uses shared features to make comparison possible while emphasizing differences that reveal each account's distinctive worldview and purpose.

title: Contradictions in the Gospels – Rev Matthew Firth’s Second Response
author: admin
description: Presents Matthew Firth's second response in the debate over Gospel contradictions.
searchSummary: Presents Matthew Firth's second defense of Gospel consistency. He inserts unreported intervals into Luke to accommodate Matthew's Egypt and Galilee episodes, interprets Jairus's words as compatible reports from an emotional conversation, treats Matthew's abbreviation as accepted telescoping, and invokes Levirate marriage for Joseph's two fathers. Because each conflict has a possible reconstruction, Firth concludes that no necessary contradiction or historical uncertainty has been established, even without parallel examples for his genealogy solution.

title: Paul in Hell.   The Apocryphal Apocalypse of Paul.
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Apocalypse of Paul as an apocryphal tour of hell.
searchSummary: Summarizes the Apocalypse of Paul, a widely translated and influential guided tour of temporary heavenly rewards and hellish punishments before bodily resurrection. Building on the Apocalypse of Peter, it praises ascetics but condemns inconsistent Christians, sexually immoral clergy, unjust bishops, corrupt deacons, and failed monks. Its fiercest polemic targets those denying Christ's flesh, Mary's role, the Eucharist, or bodily resurrection, assigning them torments worse than murderers. The narrative thus makes orthodox doctrine and disciplined church life decisive for eternity.

title: Papias and the Writers of the New Testament: Guest Post by Stephen Carlson
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Stephen Carlson's discussion of Papias and claims about New Testament authors.

title: Why Did Christianity Take Over the World?  Smithsonian Lecture 3.
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Christianity took over the Roman Empire in a Smithsonian lecture.

title: Are These Really Contradictions?  My Response to Matt Firth
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to Matthew Firth's challenges about alleged Gospel contradictions.
searchSummary: Responds to Matthew Firth's first proposed reconciliations of four Gospel contradictions. Ehrman argues that Greek grammar makes Jairus's daughter already dead in Matthew, abbreviation explains but does not remove Matthew's change to Mark, Levirate marriage lacks evidence and cannot make deceased Heli Joseph's legal father, and Luke's temporal constructions exclude Matthew's years in Egypt or trip to Galilee. Plausible literary motives cannot make incompatible narrative facts agree.

title: The Radical Implications of the Resurrection
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the theological implications early Christians drew from belief in Jesus' resurrection.
searchSummary: Explains how resurrection belief radically transformed the disciples' understanding of Jesus as messiah. Crucifixion had disproved their hope that he would become Israel's king, but belief that God raised and exalted him recast Jesus as a divine Son of God, heavenly Son of Man, and ruler of all. This reinterpretation moved from an expected human king in a coming earthly kingdom toward the exalted Christology that eventually supported belief in Christ's eternal equality with God.

title: Why Are the Gospels Anonymous?
author: admin
description: Explains why the Gospels are anonymous and how their traditional names arose.

title: Contradictions in the Gospels – Rev Matthew Firth’s Response
author: admin
description: Presents Matthew Firth's first response in the debate over Gospel contradictions.
searchSummary: Presents Matthew Firth's opening response denying contradictions in four Gospel examples. He uses Greek ambiguity, emotional dialogue, and Matthew's telescoping to reconcile Jairus's daughter; hypothetical Levirate marriage to align Joseph's genealogies; omitted years to fit Egypt into Luke's infancy sequence; and an unstated interval to allow Matthew's Galilean resurrection appearance within Luke. Firth treats these reconstructions as plausible ways both accounts can remain true despite their surface differences.

title: Contradictions in the Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Opens a debate over whether the Gospels contain contradictions.
searchSummary: Opens a debate by identifying four Gospel contradictions: Jairus approaches Jesus before his daughter's death in Mark but afterward in Matthew; Matthew and Luke trace Joseph through incompatible fathers; Luke returns Jesus' family to Nazareth while Matthew sends them to Egypt; and Matthew directs disciples to Galilee after the resurrection while Luke requires them to remain in Jerusalem. Ehrman urges readers to compare the passages directly before assessing whether reconciliation is possible.

title: What Is a Contradiction?
author: BDEhrman
description: Defines what counts as a contradiction before a debate on Gospel discrepancies.
searchSummary: Defines a contradiction as two statements that cannot both be literally true under a sensible reading. Ehrman separates contradictions from omissions, such as Mark and John not mentioning a virgin birth, and from historically suspicious developments, such as divine self-claims appearing only in John. Because ingenious duplicate-event scenarios can technically rescue nearly any conflict, judgments also involve plausibility; the planned debate concerns Gospel consistency rather than whether Scripture is inspired.

title: Who Were The “Pagans” Christians Were Converting?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the pagan religious world into which Christianity spread.
searchSummary: Introduces a lecture on the largely pagan population Christianity converted as it spread through the Roman Empire. Ehrman explains that “paganism” was a Christian umbrella term for thousands of traditional, non-Jewish and non-Christian religious practices rather than a single religion. The lecture asks what these diverse traditions shared, how Christians connected their message to people who regarded ancestral rituals as naturally valid, and how converts could be persuaded that Christianity demonstrated a superior divine power.

title: A Papias Mystery: What Was the Book He Wrote?  Guest Post by Stephen Carlson
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Stephen Carlson's discussion of what Papias's lost book may have been.

title: Fund Raising Event on the Blog: Contradictions in the Gospels??
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a fundraising debate on contradictions in the Gospels.
searchSummary: Announces a charitable written debate with Anglican priest Matthew Firth over whether the New Testament Gospels contain contradictions. Ehrman expects neither committed side to change its mind because sufficiently inventive explanations can preserve any prior conclusion, but sees value for undecided readers and fundraising. The post outlines three rounds of examples and responses, cordial participation, timing, word limits, organizers, and supported charities rather than arguing any particular textual case.

title: Enoch’s Vision of the Realms of the Dead
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Enoch's vision of the realms of the dead in relation to ancient afterlife journeys.

title: Christianity’s Most Important Convert: Lecture at the Smithsonian
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a Smithsonian lecture on Paul as Christianity's most important convert.

title: Jesus “Only” Adopted to be the Son of God?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reconsiders whether Jesus was understood as adopted as God's Son.
searchSummary: Corrects the modern assumption that an adopted son held lower status than a biological son in Roman society. Adult adoptees were deliberately selected to inherit a powerful father's status, property, clients, and authority, as Augustus inherited Caesar's position; adoption could therefore convey exceptional honor. Christians who said God adopted Jesus at the resurrection meant that he received God's power and privileges as sole heir, making adoptionist Christology a remarkable claim of divinity rather than a weak one.

title: Papias.  How Do We Know His Context?  Guest post by Stephen Carlson
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Papias's fragmentary context is difficult to reconstruct.
searchSummary: Explains why Papias's fragmentary comments about Mark cannot be understood apart from their lost original context and later quotation by Eusebius. Unidentified figures, earlier remarks, and terms such as "dominical oracles" make the excerpt ambiguous, while transmitters reused Papias for their own purposes. A broad survey of nearly one hundred ancient and medieval testimonies distinguishes reception reports from reliable textual fragments. Reconstructing their sequence and Papias's genre is necessary before using his statement to explain Gospel origins.

title: The Writings of Papias: Guest Post by Stephen Carlson
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Papias and his reported comments on the origins of Matthew and Mark.
searchSummary: Explains why Papias's famous comments about Matthew and Mark cannot be interpreted apart from their lost contexts. An elder's original remarks were selected and reshaped by Papias, whose own account was then excerpted by Eusebius for a fourth-century discussion of canonical books. Because each author had a different purpose and most of Papias's work is lost, the surviving passage is a layered joint production rather than a self-contained eyewitness tradition about Gospel origins.

title: A Blog Anniversary!  Seven Years!
author: BDEhrman
description: Marks the blog's seventh anniversary and reflects on its development and charitable purpose.
searchSummary: Celebrates the blog's seventh anniversary by recounting its origins as a way to share scholarship with general readers while raising money for charity. Bart reports more than 7,100 paying members, 2,013 posts, 80,459 comments, $158,000 distributed during the year, and over $700,000 in lifetime giving. He discusses the work required, thanks Steven Ray, invites feedback and donations, and asks members to promote the blog and give subscriptions to potential readers.

title: Revelation as a Blueprint for our Future
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Revelation should not be read as a blueprint for the modern future.
searchSummary: Contrasts modern futuristic readings of Revelation with historical interpretation of ancient apocalyptic literature. Hal Lindsey's claim that Revelation's locusts are attack helicopters ignores their stated inability to kill or destroy vegetation. Revelation instead addressed first-century Christians under Roman power, using symbols such as Nero's 666 and Babylon as Rome to promise God's victory over oppression. The proposed book would also examine how mistaken end-time readings have influenced modern American religion, politics, and culture.

title: - The Bart Ehrman Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Repeats a discussion of modern readings of Revelation as a blueprint for the future.
searchSummary: Contrasts modern futuristic readings of Revelation with historical interpretation of ancient apocalyptic literature. Hal Lindsey's claim that Revelation's locusts are attack helicopters ignores their stated inability to kill or destroy vegetation. Revelation instead addressed first-century Christians under Roman power, using symbols such as Nero's 666 and Babylon as Rome to promise God's victory over oppression. The proposed book would also examine how mistaken end-time readings have influenced modern American religion, politics, and culture.

title: My Very First Post: Do Textual Variants Matter??
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts the blog's first post on whether textual variants matter.
searchSummary: Defends the significance of New Testament variants against claims that none matters because no cardinal doctrine is overturned. Doctrines depend on multiple passages, but disputed readings still affect the meaning and theology of texts concerning Jesus' divinity, atoning death, agony, resurrection appearances, and the adulterous woman. Ehrman's claim is not that variants destroy Christian belief; it is that some reshape passages or books, remain unresolved, and matter independently of doctrinal consequences.

title: The Odd Modern Way of Reading the Book of Revelation
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques modern readings of Revelation that treat it as a literal forecast of current events.
searchSummary: Traces the modern rise of reading Revelation as a detailed blueprint for events about to occur. Earlier Christians usually interpreted its symbols across church history, while nineteenth-century dispensational premillennialism introduced a sequence of eras culminating in the Rapture, Tribulation, and millennium. John Nelson Darby spread this scheme in America, and twentieth-century wars, depression, and nuclear danger made its pessimistic outlook more attractive. The post contrasts this movement with scholars' first-century historical interpretation of Revelation.

title: A Roman Vision of Heaven and Hell
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a Roman vision of the afterlife as background for heaven and hell traditions.
searchSummary: Begins Virgil's Roman vision of the afterlife by following Aeneas and the Sibyl into the underworld in Book 6 of the Aeneid. Seeking his dead father and knowledge of his destiny, Aeneas learns that entering Hades is easy but returning is reserved for exceptional figures. After completing the required rites, he crosses the Styx, encounters improperly buried and tragically dead souls, and sees former warriors reduced to powerless shades, preparing for Virgil's differentiated punishments, rewards, purification, and reincarnation.

title: Did Ancient Greeks Invent Heaven and Hell?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores whether Greek traditions helped shape later ideas of heaven and hell.
searchSummary: Locates a major source of later heaven-and-hell beliefs in post-Homeric Greek thought, especially Plato's myth of Er. A slain soldier revives after witnessing souls judged, rewarded in heaven, punished below for a thousand years, and then reincarnated after choosing new lives. Plato presents the story as morally true rather than literal history: immortal souls make virtue and wisdom more important than bodily pleasure. Ehrman argues that such familiar Greek concepts were later adapted by some Jews and Christians.

title: Armageddon and American Politics
author: BDEhrman
description: Connects modern interpretations of Armageddon with American politics and public policy.

title: Did Jesus Pray “Father Forgive Them” from the Cross?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines the textual variant in Luke where Jesus asks forgiveness for those killing Jesus.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus' prayer for his executioners in Luke 23:34 was written by Luke but omitted by some early scribes. Prayer, forgiveness, ignorance, and Jesus' composure fit Luke's themes, while the nonverbal parallel with Stephen's prayer is more characteristic of Luke than scribal harmonization. Early Christians interpreted the prayer as seeking forgiveness for Jews, giving increasingly anti-Jewish scribes a strong motive to remove it.

title: Secular Versions of the Coming Apocalypse
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores secular versions of apocalyptic expectation and coming catastrophe.

title: Fundamentalist Visions of the End of the World
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains fundamentalist readings of Revelation as predictions of the imminent end.
searchSummary: Shows how fundamentalist expectations of an imminent end moved from the margins into popular culture. Tim LaHaye's Left Behind novels and Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth presented Revelation as a forecast of the Rapture, Tribulation, Antichrist, and modern geopolitical conflict, reaching tens of millions of readers. Earlier movements and figures also set failed dates for the end. Although most Christians historically rejected such expectations, growing evangelical communities have made this nineteenth-century interpretive system increasingly influential.

title: Expecting the Apocalypse: My Idea for the Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a proposed book on Revelation and modern expectations of apocalypse.
searchSummary: Introduces a proposed trade book tracing how a nineteenth-century interpretation of Revelation shaped religious end-time expectations, secular culture, and American policy. The project would explain this reading's origins, modern development, and scholarly problems. Edgar Whisenant's widely circulated prediction that the Rapture would occur in September 1988 illustrates its appeal: he combined Revelation, Jesus' apocalyptic sayings, Israel's 1948 founding, and a forty-year generation to produce a failed date that nevertheless prompted some believers to reorganize their lives.

title: An Early Otherworldly Journey
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces ancient otherworldly journey traditions relevant to heaven and hell research.

title: Very Funny…
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a humorous item from the blog archive.

title: My Doubts about the Son of God: A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a personal reflection on doubts about Jesus as Son of God.
searchSummary: Recounts the theological doubts that arose when Ehrman's biblical studies led him to recognize errors and contradictions in Scripture. Because Jesus is rarely called God and divine self-claims appear primarily in the late Gospel of John, he began questioning a belief central to his evangelical identity. His painful exchange with former mentor Evan Goranson over whether Jesus actually spoke John 14:6 illustrates both the historical issue and the personal cost of intellectual change.

title: The Protestant Obsession with Origins
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the Protestant scholarly fascination with origins in religious and biblical studies.
searchSummary: Traces modern scholarship's interest in Christian origins to Protestant efforts to recover an original, uncorrupted faith through Scripture alone. This search encouraged textual critics to reconstruct original wording, Gospel scholars to identify earliest accounts, and historians to recover Jesus' teachings and earliest Christianity. Nineteenth-century scholars then broadened the inquiry by examining Christianity's roots in Judaism and Greco-Roman religion, though some portrayed Judaism unfairly as a degraded precursor rather than a developing tradition in its own right.

title: Who Cares How It All Started?
author: BDEhrman
description: Questions whether tracing origins is always the best way to understand afterlife journey traditions.
searchSummary: Questions why modern scholarship often treats the origin of an idea as its most revealing feature. Ehrman traces the Western passion for origins tentatively through nineteenth-century science, the Enlightenment, the Reformation's recovery of original Christianity, and Renaissance classicism, then notices the irony of seeking the origin of origin-seeking itself. Lacking expertise for that sweeping intellectual history, he narrows the project to why late nineteenth-century scholars became preoccupied with pagan or Jewish sources for Christian journeys to the underworld.

title: The Passion for Origins
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how scholarly interest in afterlife journeys became focused on questions of origins.

title: Do Any Ancient Jewish Sources Mention Jesus?  Weekly Mailbag
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers whether first-century Jewish sources mention Jesus, especially Josephus.

title: The Original Obsession with Trips to the Afterlife
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the early Christian fascination with journeys to heaven and hell.
searchSummary: Reviews the ancient tradition of journeys to the afterlife and questions scholarship's long preoccupation with identifying its single origin. From Homer and Plato through Jewish apocalypses and Christian texts such as the Apocalypses of Peter and Paul, Acts of Thomas, and Martyrdom of Perpetua, visitors observe the dead and report rewards or punishments. Ehrman traces German scholarship's Orphic-Pythagorean theory but argues that source genealogy alone cannot explain these narratives' meanings, differences, social functions, or enduring religious importance.

title: My Next Scholarly Book: Visits to Heaven and Hell
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a scholarly project on visits to heaven and hell in early Christian tradition.

title: Heaven and Hell, Finally
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces completion of the trade book on heaven, hell, and the afterlife.
searchSummary: Announces the completed manuscript and final title of Heaven and Hell: A History of the Afterlife, then summarizes the book's thesis and Bart's motivation for writing it. The book traces changing beliefs about death from Greek and Hebrew sources through Jesus and early Christianity, arguing that familiar ideas of eternal heaven and hell are neither consistent across the Bible nor the teachings of the historical Jesus.

title: Homosexuality and the New Testament.  Guest Post by Jeff Siker.
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Jeff Siker's guest post on homosexuality and the New Testament.
searchSummary: Guest contributor Jeff Siker examines New Testament passages commonly applied to homosexuality. He argues that Romans and Pauline vice lists address ancient practices such as idolatrous sex, pederasty, prostitution, and exploitation, while disputed Greek terms resist confident modern translation. Because biblical authors lacked a concept of sexual orientation or committed same-sex marriage, Siker recommends interpreting Scripture alongside historical context, reason, experience, and testimony from LGBT Christians rather than treating isolated verses as comprehensive judgments.

title: Homosexuality in the Bible (and the Christian Church)
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to a question about homosexuality in the Bible and the Christian church.

title: University Professors and their Research
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on university research, burnout, and the role of writing in academic life.
searchSummary: Explains why research universities give professors lighter teaching loads and periodic academic leave. Unlike teaching-centered colleges, Research 1 institutions expect faculty not merely to transmit knowledge but to produce it through internationally recognized scholarship, which requires protected time away from classes and administration. Ehrman's leave supports a monograph, trade books, course development, proposals, reviews, and related projects, ultimately keeping his teaching current and preparing the next generation of researchers rather than functioning as a vacation from professorial work.

title: A Return to the Historical Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Returns to historical Jesus research through twentieth-century developments in Gospel study.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: The Gospel Writers as Editors Rather than Authors
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Gospel writers as editors who shaped inherited traditions.
searchSummary: Explains how redaction criticism treats Gospel writers as purposeful editors who reshape inherited traditions rather than passive compilers. Changes, omissions, additions, and even decisions to retain a source reveal each author's theological and literary interests. Although intact written sources survive mainly for comparing Matthew and Luke with Mark, recurring vocabulary, framing, and motifs can help scholars tentatively distinguish tradition from editorial work within Mark or John, enabling source reconstruction and analysis of how those writers formed their narratives.

title: A New Way of Looking at the Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces redaction criticism as a new way of reading the Gospels.
searchSummary: Traces Gospel scholarship from source criticism and the collapse of an early historical-Jesus quest through form criticism to redaction criticism. Form critics emphasized oral stories shaped by Christian communities, often treating Gospel authors as little more than collectors. Beginning in the 1950s, redaction critics returned attention to the extant narratives and examined how writers added, removed, rearranged, or altered inherited sources. Comparing Matthew and Luke with Mark thereby identifies each evangelist's distinctive theology and literary aims.

title: Non-Christian Sources for Jesus: An Interview with History.com
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a History.com interview about non-Christian sources for Jesus.
searchSummary: Presents Ehrman's History.com interview about non-Christian evidence for the historical Jesus. He explains why the absence of archaeological remains is unsurprising, evaluates Josephus as indispensable but biased, and treats Tacitus as an independent Roman witness to Jesus' execution under Pontius Pilate. Roman references cannot reconstruct Jesus' teachings or deeds, but they corroborate basic Christian claims about his existence, Judean setting, execution, and subsequent movement while showing that informed ancient writers did not regard him as invented.

title: If the Quest for the Historical Jesus Failed… What Then?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains what scholars did after confidence in Mark as straightforward history collapsed.
searchSummary: Explains how recognition of Mark's theological framework led scholars from failed biographies of Jesus to form criticism. Schmidt distinguished Mark's editorial transitions from inherited story units, while Dibelius and Bultmann examined oral traditions shaped by recurring community needs. Healing and controversy stories developed recognizable forms suited to worship, preaching, and disputes. Form critics therefore classified stories and reconstructed their social settings, often concluding that Gospel narratives evolved to address early Christian life rather than simply preserve historical events.

title: The Death Knell for the Study of the Historical Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Wrede's study of Mark challenged older quests for the historical Jesus.
searchSummary: Describes how Wrede and Schweitzer undermined attempts to reconstruct Jesus by treating Mark as an unbiased historical source. Wrede exposed Mark's theological shaping, while Schweitzer showed that earlier scholars repeatedly created Jesus in their own intellectual image and emphasized his apocalyptic setting. Historical-Jesus research then receded as scholars investigated oral traditions and how communities changed stories before the Gospels. The post stresses that these conclusions reflect longstanding critical scholarship rather than novel attacks on Christianity.

title: Wrede’s Revolutionary Claim about the “Messianic Secret”
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Wrede's claim that Mark created the motif of Jesus hiding the messianic identity.
searchSummary: Explains Wrede's claim that Mark's messianic secret is a theological invention designed to reconcile changing Christian beliefs. The earliest followers allegedly thought Jesus became God's Son at resurrection, whereas Mark's community believed he already held that identity during ministry. Mark therefore portrays Jesus commanding silence until after resurrection, especially following the Transfiguration. Because this secrecy does not plausibly describe Jesus' public activity, it demonstrates that Mark reshaped history to explain why Jesus' messiahship became known only later.

title: Is It Plausible that Jesus Kept the Whole Thing a Secret??
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether it is plausible that Jesus kept the messianic identity secret throughout the ministry.

title: Why Textual Criticism Seemed to Be on Death’s Door
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why New Testament textual criticism once seemed to have reached a dead end.

title: Who CARES if Mark was the First Gospel Written?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Mark's priority matters for interpreting the Gospels and the historical Jesus.
searchSummary: Explains why Markan priority matters for interpreting the Synoptic Gospels and reconstructing Jesus. Because Matthew and Luke independently edit Mark, redaction criticism can identify their distinctive concerns through what they add, remove, or alter. Nineteenth-century scholars instead treated Mark's early, terse narrative as an essentially accurate historical framework and supplied psychological motives for its gaps. Wrede's analysis of the messianic secret overturned that confidence by showing that Mark also organizes Jesus' life around a theological agenda.

title: Editorial Fatigue in Luke:  More from Blog Guest Mark Goodacre
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Mark Goodacre's argument from editorial fatigue in Luke.
searchSummary: Uses Mark Goodacre's examples of editorial fatigue in Luke to argue that Luke copied and incompletely revised Mark. In the Sower parable, Luke's interpretation retains explanations for details removed or changed in his retelling; in the paralytic story, characters climb onto a house whose introduction Luke omitted, and Jesus answers thoughts Luke made audible. These continuity errors arise naturally when an editor begins revising a source but later lapses into its wording, supporting Markan priority.

title: A New Argument that Mark Was the First Gospel (Editorial Fatigue):  Guest Post by Mark Goodacre!
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Mark Goodacre's argument from editorial fatigue that Mark was the first Gospel.
searchSummary: Introduces editorial fatigue as Mark Goodacre's additional argument that Matthew copied Mark. Matthew changes a story's opening but later reproduces Markan details inconsistent with that revision: crowds witness a healing that Jesus orders kept secret, and Herod both wants John killed and grieves when it happens. Matthew also corrects Herod's title from king to tetrarch before lapsing back. Such continuity errors are best explained when a reviser initially alters a source but subsequently follows it mechanically.

title: Pursuing My Passion for Textual Criticism
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on moving from textual criticism into broader work on early Christianity.
searchSummary: Traces Ehrman's early fascination with textual criticism from Moody Bible Institute through graduate study with Bruce Metzger. The contrast between largely uniform medieval Byzantine manuscripts and significantly different early witnesses challenged fundamentalist preference for the King James textual base and made recovering inspired wording a historical puzzle. Greek study, a master's thesis, Didymus the Blind's quotations, and later books developed that interest before Ehrman shifted toward broader early Christian history.

title: On Being Just a Textual Critic
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on academic identity and the limits of being known only as a textual critic.
searchSummary: Rejects the claim that Ehrman's specialization in textual criticism leaves him unqualified to interpret early Christian texts or reconstruct history.
