Textual criticism identifies an author's probable wording, but his formal graduate training centered overwhelmingly on historical exegesis and early Christian history; he developed textual expertise largely through independent study under Bruce Metzger. He argues that critics mistake his dissertation specialty for the boundaries of his education, overlooking years of seminars and examinations across the New Testament and ancient Christianity.

title: Mark: The First Gospel in 19th Century Research
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how nineteenth-century research came to see Mark as the first Gospel.
searchSummary: Presents three major arguments that Mark was written before and used by Matthew and Luke. Patterns of wording, narrative sequence, and the tendency of later evangelists to smooth Mark's awkward language and difficult ideas are best explained by Markan priority. Mark's relative brevity does not indicate condensation because its individual shared stories are usually longer. This conclusion allowed scholars both to study Matthew's and Luke's editorial changes and, initially, to treat Mark as the earliest and most historically reliable Gospel.

title: The Beginning of the Quest of the Historical Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Wrede and the beginning of a major turn in historical Jesus research.
searchSummary: Traces the historical-Jesus quest from Reimarus's political revolutionary to Wrede's critique of Mark. Enlightenment scholars recognized contradictions and sought the earliest Gospel, eventually treating Mark's terse narrative as an unbiased historical framework whose gaps could be filled through psychological reconstruction. Schweitzer surveyed and criticized these attempts, while Wrede demonstrated that Mark's messianic secret reflects theological shaping rather than straightforward reporting. That insight destabilized the assumption underlying many nineteenth-century lives of Jesus.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: Mark’s Central Focus on Jesus’ Death
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Mark's Gospel centers Jesus' death within the Messianic Secret.
searchSummary: Explains that Jesus' suffering and death form the organizing center of Mark's Gospel. Three passion predictions are followed by disciples misunderstanding messiahship as power and status, while Jesus defines discipleship as suffering, service, and self-sacrifice. The narrative then moves through Jerusalem conflict, apocalyptic teaching, betrayal, trial, denial, and crucifixion. Mark resolves the scandal of a defeated Messiah by presenting death as Jesus' necessary mission, the very truth that nearly every character fails to understand.

title: How No One Understands Jesus in Mark’s Gospel
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Mark's portrayal of disciples and others failing to understand Jesus.
searchSummary: Shows how misunderstanding Jesus functions as a central theme in Mark. God, demons, the narrator, and readers know his identity, but family, neighbors, leaders, and disciples remain blind. A two-stage healing symbolizes Peter's partial recognition: he names Jesus as Messiah yet rejects the suffering and death that define Mark's Messiah. Jesus rebukes him because conventional expectations of power obscure the Gospel's paradox. Mark portrays genuine understanding as recognizing Jesus specifically as the suffering Son of God.

title: How Do We Explain the Messianic Secret?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Messianic Secret as a key problem in interpreting Mark.
searchSummary: Introduces Mark's messianic secret against ancient Jewish expectations of a Messiah. Mark repeatedly has Jesus silence those who recognize him, a feature not prominent in the other Gospels. The problem is that Jews expected an anointed Davidic king, priestly leader, or heavenly conqueror, not a lower-class man defeated and crucified by Rome. Mark's secrecy motif helps explain how this rejected and executed Jesus could nevertheless be proclaimed Messiah, preparing for a fuller account of the device.

title: Guest Post!  Joel Marcus on His New Book on the John the Baptist
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Joel Marcus's guest post on a new book about John the Baptist.

title: The Aberrant View of the Afterlife in the Apocalypse of Peter
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the unusual universalist strand in the Apocalypse of Peter's afterlife teaching.

title: Finally.  Why Did the Apocalypse of Peter Not Make It Into the Canon?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the Apocalypse of Peter may have failed to enter the New Testament canon.
searchSummary: Examines a textual detail that may help explain the Apocalypse of Peter's exclusion from the canon. A Greek fragment says Christ will release condemned people from torment when the elect request their salvation, whereas other surviving versions omit this passage. The teaching could make salvation depend on the saints' petitions and appear to overturn God's judgment selectively. Such theological concerns may have contributed to orthodox resistance even though the work had earlier circulated as Scripture.

title: Other Manuscripts of the Apocalypse of Peter, And Why It Matters
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares manuscript witnesses to the Apocalypse of Peter and why their differences matter.
searchSummary: Explains why scholars consider the Ethiopic Apocalypse of Peter closer to the original than the shorter Greek manuscript, despite its translation through Arabic. Ancient line counts, church-father quotations, and older Greek fragments align with the Ethiopic form, showing that the Akhmim Greek text was heavily edited and perhaps adapted to accompany the Gospel of Peter. One early fragment preserves an otherwise lost passage about hell that may explain the apocalypse's exclusion from the New Testament.

title: Don’t Trust What You Read!
author: BDEhrman
description: Retracts an earlier claim about Mark 7 after readers pointed to contrary evidence in the Letter of Aristeas.

title: How Do We Know What Was Originally in the Apocalypse of Peter?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the problem of reconstructing the original Apocalypse of Peter from surviving evidence.
searchSummary: Introduces the manuscript problem of reconstructing the Apocalypse of Peter after its disappearance from common use. An Akhmim Greek version presents a shorter, differently ordered tour of heaven and hell, while an Ethiopic text translated through lost Arabic and Greek stages preserves a longer account with future post-judgment punishments. Although the Greek witness appears more direct, the later translation may retain an earlier textual form, so language and date alone cannot decide which version is original.

title: How Does A Book Actually Get Published?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the process by which a trade book moves from manuscript to publication.
searchSummary: Explains the extensive editorial and production process that begins after an author completes a trade-book draft. Ehrman describes repeated self-revision, feedback from specialists and blog readers, review by his agent and editor, copyediting, typeset proofs, corrections, cover design, blurbs, indexing, and final title decisions. These stages can take about a year because each contributor checks accuracy, clarity, style, and physical presentation while the publisher also chooses a release date suited to its production schedule and market.

title: If Jesus Wasn’t God, Was He Necessarily Either a Calloused Liar or a Raving Lunatic?
author: BDEhrman
description: Challenges the argument that Jesus must be either God, liar, or lunatic.
searchSummary: Rejects C. S. Lewis's claim that Jesus must be liar, lunatic, or Lord because he called himself God. The argument assumes that John's divine self-declarations preserve Jesus' words, yet the earlier Synoptic Gospels never report such claims and portray his identity differently. John's high Christology developed decades later and places its theology on Jesus' lips. The missing alternative is therefore "legend": Jesus was historical, but the claim that he publicly identified himself as God probably was not.

title: Was Jesus A Great Moral Teacher?  A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether Jesus can be understood as a great moral teacher apart from later doctrine.
searchSummary: Affirms Jesus as a moral teacher while explaining that his reason for ethics differs from modern programs for social well-being. Jesus expected God to destroy evil and establish the kingdom, so people prepared by loving God and neighbor and by embodying its peace, healing, justice, generosity, and inclusion in advance. After his death, followers shifted the path to salvation from obeying God's law and aiding others to believing in Jesus' death and resurrection, changing Jesus' religion into Christianity about him.

title: Readers’ Mailbag 1/20/2019: The Only Story of Jesus as a Boy in the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Luke's story of the twelve-year-old Jesus as a feature of Greco-Roman biography that anticipates his adult identity and mission.
searchSummary: Explains why Luke includes the New Testament's only story about Jesus as a boy. Ancient Greco-Roman biographies used childhood episodes to reveal a great person's fixed character and future identity rather than trace psychological development. Luke frames Jesus' life in that biographical pattern through a miraculous birth, a youthful episode, adult ministry, and ascension. Finding twelve-year-old Jesus in his Father's house after three days anticipates his later identity and mission.

title: The Dangers of Fundamentalism
author: BDEhrman
description: Defines fundamentalism and explains why it can be dangerous.

title: Your Thoughts on the Blog?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks readers for feedback on what works well on the blog.

title: Does Eternal Punishment Even Make Sense?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether eternal punishment makes theological and moral sense.

title: Eternal Torment Even for Christians?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores early Christian claims that even Christians could face eternal torment.
searchSummary: Shows how the Apocalypse of Paul extended hell to sinful Christians, corrupt clergy, failed ascetics, and doctrinal heretics after Christianity became an imperial religion. Its graded heaven rewards chastity, repentance, and greater ascetic sacrifice, while boiling rivers and tailored tortures punish misconduct within the church. The harshest penalty targets Christians denying Christ's flesh, Mary's maternity, Eucharistic presence, or bodily resurrection. Unlike the earlier Apocalypse of Peter, the work insists that Christian identity alone cannot secure salvation without conduct and orthodoxy.

title: What *Greek* Version of the New Testament Do I Use?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains which Greek New Testament text is used for personal translations.
searchSummary: Explains which Greek New Testament Ehrman and other translators use when rendering passages themselves. The United Bible Societies edition reconstructs authorial wording from manuscripts, ancient translations, and church-father quotations, presents major variants, and rates editorial confidence. Scholars usually consult the Nestle-Aland edition, which prints the identical Greek text but supplies a much fuller and more technical apparatus, while translators often prefer the UBS presentation focused on consequential choices.

title: The Happy News!  No One Stays In Hell!
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains early Christian universalism and the claim that no one remains in hell forever.
searchSummary: Explores early Christian universal salvation through Gregory of Nyssa and the Gospel of Nicodemus. Gregory portrays postmortem suffering as purification that eventually eliminates evil and restores everyone. In the Gospel's Harrowing of Hell, Christ breaks Hades's gates, frees its captives, raises Adam, and calls all who died to follow him. Although the ending highlights Israel's righteous saints, personified Hades repeatedly declares itself completely emptied, suggesting that Christ's death and descent make even pagans righteous and leave no soul permanently damned.

title: Did We Exist Before We Were Born?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Origen's view of preexistent souls as part of universal salvation.

title: Does Everyone Get Saved in the End?
author: BDEhrman
description: Returns to whether the Apocalypse of Peter teaches universal salvation.

title: Fundamentalist Arguments Ad Absurdum about the “Original” Text of the NT
author: BDEhrman
description: Challenges fundamentalist arguments about the original New Testament manuscripts.
searchSummary: Rejects an argument that uncertainty about New Testament wording makes all ancient history unknowable. Historians distinguish reconstructing a source's text from evaluating whether its claims are true, using multiple sources, context, bias, and comparison rather than inspiration; the same textual limitations affect Plato and other ancient writers. Numerous New Testament manuscripts neither guarantee original wording nor historical reliability, just as exact knowledge of Mein Kampf's text does not make its contents trustworthy.

title: My Pod Cast Interview with Sam Harris
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a Sam Harris podcast interview covering The Triumph of Christianity and related topics.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's Waking Up podcast interview with Sam Harris, nominally organized around The Triumph of Christianity but extending across many subjects. Their discussion includes Ehrman's autobiography, miracles, New Testament composition, Jesus' resurrection, heaven and hell, Revelation and the end times, biblical contradictions, messianic ideas, Jesus' historical existence, and Constantine's conversion. The brief post demonstrates the conversation's breadth but does not summarize the arguments or conclusions offered on any individual issue, directing readers to the recording.

title: Hey, They’re Free!   Memberships Still Available for Those Who Can’t Afford Them
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces that free memberships remain available for readers who cannot afford them.

title: My Research Goals for 2019
author: BDEhrman
description: Lays out research goals for 2019, especially work on heaven, hell, and afterlife journeys.

title: Blog Year in Review, 2018
author: BDEhrman
description: Reviews the blog's 2018 growth, topics, and charitable work.
searchSummary: Reviews the blog's seventh calendar year, including its broad coverage of early Christianity, publishing rhythm, reposting policy, reader questions, and membership growth. Bart reports more than 250 posts during 2018, 76,375 lifetime comments, 6,729 members, and $154,000 raised that year for five charities. He describes the educational and charitable missions, encourages donations and word-of-mouth promotion, and thanks Steven Ray and members for sustaining the community.

title: Were There *Other* Virgin Births in Antiquity?
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares New Testament virgin birth stories with other ancient birth traditions.
searchSummary: Claims that pagan religions routinely featured virgin-born savior gods rest on modern repetition rather than ancient evidence. Ehrman critiques popular mythicist arguments that figures such as Osiris, Dionysus, and Mithras shared Jesus' birth, death, and resurrection story, noting that their authors do not cite primary sources. Pagan tales did describe divine-human offspring, but typically through sexual relations between a god and a mortal woman.

title: Was Jesus Born of a Virgin in the Gospel of John?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains whether John's Gospel contains or implies a virgin birth.
searchSummary: Explains that John presents incarnation without a virgin birth. Its Prologue makes Jesus the human embodiment of God's preexistent Word, but never describes Mary's conception as virginal; John 8 may even preserve accusations of illegitimate birth. Matthew and Luke describe miraculous conception without teaching that Jesus preexisted, whereas John describes preexistence without miraculous conception. The Nicene formulation that Christ became incarnate through the Virgin Mary combines these different Gospel views into a doctrine that no single evangelist states.

title: Does Mark’s Gospel Actually *Deny* the Virgin Birth?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Mark may imply a view inconsistent with the virgin birth.
searchSummary: Argues that Mark may implicitly deny the virgin birth even though it never discusses Jesus' conception. Greek grammar indicates that Jesus' family, including his mother, tries to restrain him because they believe he is out of his mind; translations that attribute the judgment to unnamed people soften the passage. Mary would presumably understand Jesus if she knew of a miraculous birth. Matthew and Luke omit Mark's scene and instead portray his mother and origins very differently.

title: Christmas Reflection 2018
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on Christmas, incarnation, and changing personal meanings of the holiday.
searchSummary: Reinterprets Christmas as a story of grace after Ehrman abandoned belief in the incarnation and rejected atonement through an innocent person's torture. The holiday's enduring value lies in freely giving oneself for others, recognizing undeserved kindness, and practicing love without seeking reward, whether or not God literally sent a divine child. Amid materialism, family strain, anxiety, and loneliness, he hopes people can receive and extend small or transformative acts of grace that embody the story's moral meaning.

title: The Gospel of Luke without a Birth Story
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores the possibility that Luke originally circulated without its birth narrative.
searchSummary: Explores whether an early edition of Luke circulated without the birth narrative and began with John the Baptist and Jesus' baptism. Marcion may have inherited rather than shortened such a text. Without chapters 1-2, the early baptismal reading today I have begotten you would make Luke especially open to adoptionist interpretation, where God selects and empowers a human Jesus as Son, though the post does not claim this was necessarily Luke's own theology.

title: Did Luke Originally Tell the Birth Story?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Luke's birth narrative belonged to the Gospel from the beginning.
searchSummary: Argues that Luke's birth narrative may have been added after the Gospel's first publication. Chapter 3 reads like a formal beginning, key infancy traditions disappear from the remainder of Luke-Acts, and summaries in Acts start Jesus' story with John the Baptist. The genealogy also belongs more naturally after a baptism declaring Jesus God's Son if the narrative originally moved directly from Luke's preface to chapter 3.

title: Last Minute Christmas Presents!!
author: BDEhrman
description: Suggests gift memberships as last-minute Christmas presents.

title: The Virgin Birth in Matthew and Luke
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares the virgin birth traditions in Matthew and Luke.
searchSummary: Compares the different theological functions of the virgin birth in Matthew and Luke. Matthew uses Isaiah 7:14 and other fulfillment citations to present Jesus' birth as part of God's scriptural plan, despite the Hebrew verse referring to a young woman in Isaiah's own time. Luke instead says conception by the Holy Spirit is why Jesus is literally called God's Son. Later Christians combine these distinct claims with John's incarnation theology, but neither birth account explicitly makes the other's point.

title: Was the Apocalypse of Peter Originally Part of the New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether the Apocalypse of Peter was once considered part of the New Testament.
searchSummary: Surveys evidence that many early Christians treated the Apocalypse of Peter as Scripture before its support declined. Canon lists, theologians, preachers, and church communities in Rome, Alexandria, Asia Minor, North Africa, and Palestine cited or used it from the second through fifth centuries, sometimes alongside Revelation. Later writers increasingly called it inauthentic or apocryphal, but they did not explain why. Its changing status illustrates that the New Testament boundaries remained disputed across regions and generations.

title: How Would an Early Christian “Know” Which Books Peter Wrote?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how early Christians evaluated which writings attributed to Peter were authentic and canonical.
searchSummary: Explains that ancient Christians generally judged claimed apostolic authorship through a book's circulation, users, theology, and usefulness rather than modern literary or historical analysis. The Gospel of Peter was rejected after Serapion found potentially unorthodox teaching, while widely used and orthodox 1 Peter was accepted as apostolic and canonical. This reasoning makes the eventual acceptance of disputed 2 Peter, despite the Apocalypse of Peter's earlier prominence, an important puzzle in the history of canon formation.

title: The Books of Peter
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys writings attributed to Peter while asking why some became canonical and others did not.

title: Jesus’ Birth in Matthew and Luke: A Study in Contrasts
author: BDEhrman
description: Contrasts Matthew's and Luke's accounts of Jesus' birth.
searchSummary: Argues that discrepancies between Matthew's and Luke's infancy narratives are valuable for interpreting each Gospel independently and assessing history. Their genealogies differ, Matthew assumes Bethlehem was the family's home while Luke starts in Nazareth, and Matthew's flight to Egypt conflicts with Luke's prompt return north after Temple rites. Although both want Jesus born in Bethlehem despite his known association with Nazareth, their incompatible explanations reveal distinct agendas rather than complementary portions of one historical account.

title: Jesus’ Birth as “The Fulfillment of the Prophecies”
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Matthew presents Jesus' birth as fulfillment of scripture.
searchSummary: Explains Matthew's distinctive claim that events surrounding Jesus' birth fulfill Scripture in two ways. Some passages are treated as predictions, while earlier events such as Israel's exodus gain fuller meaning when repeated in Jesus. Isaiah 7:14 originally concerns a pregnant young woman and an immediate political crisis, not a future virgin-born Messiah. Matthew, reading the Greek translation's term for maiden as “virgin,” either misinterprets Isaiah or intentionally gives the ancient text a new, christological meaning.

title: The Birth of Jesus in Matthew
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Matthew's version of Jesus' birth and its distinctive features.
searchSummary: Reconstructs Matthew's infancy narrative on its own terms rather than combining it with Luke. Joseph and Mary live in Bethlehem, receive the Magi in their house months after Jesus' birth, escape Herod's massacre by fleeing to Egypt, and later relocate to Nazareth because Archelaus makes returning home unsafe. The supernatural star, unattested massacre, fulfillment citations, and chronology create historical problems, but the account consistently assumes Bethlehem—not Nazareth—was the family's original residence.

title: Free Memberships for Those Who Need Them!
author: admin
description: Announces free memberships for readers who need them.

title: The Birth of Jesus in Luke
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Luke's version of Jesus' birth.
searchSummary: Reconstructs Luke's distinctive account of Jesus' birth, including the annunciation, journey from Nazareth to Bethlehem, manger, shepherds, Temple presentation, and return home. The narrative explains how someone known as Jesus of Nazareth could have been born in David's city. The post argues that Luke's worldwide census is historically implausible and chronologically incompatible with both Herod's reign and Quirinius' governorship, indicating a theological story rather than historical reporting.

title: What Can We Know about Jesus’ Birth?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces what historians can and cannot know about Jesus' birth.

title: Another Chance: Donating Free Memberships
author: BDEhrman
description: Invites donations to provide free blog memberships.
searchSummary: Renews an appeal for members to fund free annual subscriptions for readers unable to afford the blog. Because donations had fallen below prior years and the public offer of free memberships was approaching, Bart worries that deserving applicants might have to be turned away. He asks contributors to sponsor subscriptions in $25 increments, email him privately with the number intended, and use the site's donation form, while thanking those who had already participated.

title: Did Jesus Write Anything in the New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether any New Testament writing claims to be by Jesus.
searchSummary: Explains why the only New Testament scene of Jesus writing, the woman caught in adultery, was not part of John's original Gospel. The story is absent from the earliest manuscripts, uses non-Johannine language, and appears in different locations in later copies, indicating that scribes inserted a circulating oral tradition. Although its mercy, suspense, and unanswered question about Jesus' writing made it beloved, textual evidence leaves little doubt that the passage was added and raises whether it belongs in the Bible.

title: An Intriguingly Legendary Account of Jesus’ Death
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a legendary apocryphal account of Jesus' death.
searchSummary: Presents a legendary account of Jesus' trial and crucifixion from the Narrative of Joseph of Arimathea. Judas frames Jesus for stealing the law, Gestas mocks him from one cross, and the repentant Demas recognizes his divine authority and asks for mercy. Jesus promises Demas paradise and writes to its angelic gatekeepers ordering his admission, turning the canonical exchange with the good robber into an elaborate story of forgiveness, judgment, and heavenly access.

title: Did Jesus Write a Letter to Joseph of Arimathea
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Narrative of Joseph of Arimathea, in which Jesus writes from the cross to the guardians of paradise.
searchSummary: Explains the Narrative of Joseph of Arimathea, a late apocryphal Passion Gospel that supplements and contradicts canonical accounts. It invents biographies for the robbers Gestas and Demas, makes Judas falsely accuse Jesus of stealing the law, and later has Jesus write from the cross to secure paradise for the repentant Demas. The work depends partly on the Gospel of Nicodemus, displays strong anti-Jewish rhetoric, and probably originated sometime between late antiquity and its medieval attestation.

title: Do Any Forgeries Claim to be Written by Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines ancient forgeries that claim to have been written by Jesus.
searchSummary: Describes the apocryphal correspondence between Jesus and King Abgar of Edessa, a prominent ancient forgery written in Jesus' own name. Abgar asks Jesus for healing, and Jesus promises to send a disciple after completing his mission and ascending. Ehrman traces the letters' relationship to the later Abgar legend, their independent manuscript circulation, probable third-century Syrian origin, and protective use in inscriptions and amulets. The post includes translations of both forged letters preserved by Eusebius.

title: Gift Memberships 2018!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces holiday gift memberships for readers unable to afford the blog.

title: Could Peter Have “Written” 1 and 2 Peter Some Other Way?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Peter could have produced 1 and 2 Peter through alternate means.
searchSummary: Rejects proposals that Peter produced 1 or 2 Peter by learning literary Greek, dictating through Silvanus, translating from Aramaic, or commissioning an unnamed author. First Peter is an original, rhetorically skilled Greek composition grounded in the Septuagint, while Acts identifies Peter as illiterate. “Through Silvanus” denotes delivery rather than secretarial authorship, and antiquity offers no accepted parallel for another person composing such a letter under Peter's name. Ehrman therefore classifies the work as pseudonymous forgery.

title: Were First-Century Jewish Boys Taught to Read and Write?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains whether first-century Jewish boys were generally taught to read and write.
searchSummary: Rejects the assumption that first-century Jewish boys routinely learned to read and write. Studies place literacy in Roman Palestine around three percent, mostly among urban elites, with writing far rarer than reading and Greek literary composition exceptionally uncommon. Archaeology depicts Peter's Capernaum as an impoverished, isolated, Aramaic-speaking village without elite buildings, inscriptions, or educational evidence. As a working fisherman, Peter almost certainly lacked the schooling necessary to compose sophisticated Greek letters attributed to him.

title: Seriously.  How Many People in Antiquity Could Write?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines ancient literacy rates in relation to whether Peter could have written 1 Peter.
searchSummary: Contrasts modern mass literacy with ancient education to show why few people could produce written works. Even in favorable settings perhaps ten percent could read, mainly upper-class men, while writing and composition were taught separately and reached far fewer students. Creating a sustained argument in a second language required still more training. Ehrman applies this framework to Peter, arguing that an Aramaic-speaking rural fisherman could not plausibly acquire the advanced literary Greek displayed in 1 Peter.

title: Who Wrote 1 Peter?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the author of 1 Peter was probably not Peter.
searchSummary: Explains why 1 Peter is probably a pseudonymous late-first-century work. Its polished Greek, rhetorical skill, and detailed use of the Greek Old Testament do not fit an illiterate Aramaic-speaking fisherman from Galilee. Identifying Silvanus as secretary or carrier does not explain who composed the letter's arguments and scriptural interpretations. Given the many other writings falsely attributed to Peter and the letter's apparent setting after Jerusalem's destruction, Ehrman judges authorship by a later Christian more likely.

title: The Situation Behind the (“Forged”) Book of 1 Peter
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the social setting and persecution concerns behind 1 Peter.
searchSummary: Reconstructs 1 Peter's setting as local, grassroots hostility against Gentile converts who withdrew from former social and civic practices. The author strengthens community identity by portraying believers as God's chosen household, temple, priesthood, and children who share Christ's suffering. They should avoid wrongdoing, obey authorities, explain their hope gently, and use honorable conduct to silence accusations. Their present trials will end in salvation, and the letter seeks both cohesion under pressure and reduced conflict with outsiders.

title: The So-Called First Letter of Peter
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces 1 Peter as a writing attributed to Peter and centered on suffering.
searchSummary: Introduces 1 Peter as a circular letter to Christians in several provinces of Asia Minor who are called exiles and aliens. Those labels may partly describe socially marginal residents, but they chiefly express believers' temporary distance from their heavenly home. The recipients face suffering and suspicion, and the letter repeatedly urges respectable conduct, submission within households, and obedience to authorities. These instructions aim not merely at morality but at preventing persecution and discrediting accusations against the community.

title: Thanksgiving Musings 2018
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers Thanksgiving reflections on gratitude amid hardship.
searchSummary: Reflects on the relationship between gratitude, generosity, circumstance, and need. Ehrman notes that thankfulness and giving come easily when life is abundant, while the poor widow who sacrifices everything may display greater generosity than a wealthy donor's much larger gift. Remembering people who remain grateful and giving despite hardship can help fortunate people resist greed, appreciate what they possess, and convert personal thankfulness into concrete goodness toward others rather than treating the universe as centered on themselves.

title: Deciding on Which Books Should Be in the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains early Christian debates over which Petrine writings belonged in the New Testament.
searchSummary: Explains that the New Testament canon emerged from prolonged disagreement rather than a single early decision. Different churches treated works such as the Shepherd of Hermas, Barnabas, 1 Clement, and noncanonical Gospels as Scripture, while Athanasius first listed the familiar twenty-seven books only in 367. Proto-orthodox leaders generally favored writings considered ancient, apostolic, broadly used, and theologically acceptable, and the tradition that prevailed in wider doctrinal conflicts ultimately shaped the received collection.

title: Question: How Do I Read Books?
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes a method for reading books efficiently and purposefully.
searchSummary: Explains that efficient nonfiction reading requires different levels of attention for different books. Ehrman reads unfamiliar, important works completely and takes extensive notes, but skims the table of contents, introduction, conclusion, and selected chapters when he already knows the field or needs only the author's thesis. Reviews or assistant-produced synopses can help identify relevance, allowing him to concentrate detailed reading on genuinely useful evidence and avoid treating every publication as equally important.

title: Early Debates about the Gospel of Peter
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains early debates about the Gospel of Peter and its Christology.

title: Now, The Gospel of Peter
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Gospel of Peter as part of a broader comparison of Petrine writings.

title: Interested in Taking a Trip With Me to Greece and Turkey?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a lecture trip to Greece and Turkey following the journeys of Paul.

title: Introducing the Book of 2 Peter
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces 2 Peter as part of the question why some Petrine writings entered the canon.

title: Introducing the Apocalypse of Peter
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Apocalypse of Peter and its graphic descriptions of punishment after death.
searchSummary: Introduces the Apocalypse of Peter, an early Christian account of heaven and hell that some second- and third-century churches accepted as Scripture. Presented as Peter's vision, it assigns punishments suited to particular sins and promises eternal blessing to Christ's righteous followers. Although the work influenced later otherworldly journeys, including traditions behind Dante, it was ultimately excluded from the New Testament. Its seemingly strong canonical credentials make the reasons for that exclusion historically difficult to explain.

title: A Very Perplexing Question
author: BDEhrman
description: Raises the canon question of why the Apocalypse of Peter was excluded while 2 Peter was included.
searchSummary: Introduces a research problem concerning why 2 Peter entered the New Testament while the once-prominent Apocalypse of Peter did not. Both works claimed the apostle's authority, yet ancient canon lists and communities assessed them differently over time. The question emerged during research on early Christian journeys through heaven and hell and draws on longstanding study of competing canon lists, regional disagreements, selection criteria, and the uncertain process by which the twenty-seven-book collection became established.

title: Thanksgiving and the Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on Thanksgiving, Christmas commercialization, and blog giving.
searchSummary: Presents Thanksgiving as an opportunity for fortunate people to acknowledge their blessings and help those experiencing hunger, homelessness, illness, loneliness, displacement, or war. Ehrman values the holiday's relative freedom from commercialization and connects gratitude with the blog's charitable purpose, which directs all membership and donation revenue to organizations serving people in need. He asks appreciative readers to support an ambitious annual fundraising goal while inviting suggestions that could make the blog more useful and sustainable.

title: Old and Ongoing Criticisms!
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers recurring criticisms about secretaries, authorship, and ancient writing.

title: The De-apocalypticized Jesus of the Gospel of John
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how John's Gospel moves Jesus away from the apocalyptic message found elsewhere.
searchSummary: Explains how John transforms Jesus' apocalyptic message from future intervention into present spiritual reality. Remnants of resurrection, return, and a "last day" remain, but the Gospel chiefly promises that believers already possess eternal life and have passed from death to life, while unbelievers already remain under God's wrath. Unlike the Synoptics' coming kingdom and final judgment, John locates salvation and condemnation in present responses to Jesus, substantially de-apocalypticizing earlier Christian expectations.

title: How Christianity Grew and Grew
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Christian growth through conversion, miracles, and social expansion.
searchSummary: Pairs a legendary account of conversion through miracles with estimates of Christianity's historical growth. In the Acts of John, the apostle defeats Artemis, damages her temple, raises its priest, and prompts pagans to worship the apparently stronger God. Ehrman then explains that expansion from a few followers to millions required sustained growth of roughly 30–35 percent per decade, not continual mass conversions. The estimates show Christians remained a tiny imperial minority through the first two centuries before eventually becoming dominant.

title: Today You Will Be With Me in Paradise?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Jesus' promise of paradise to the crucified criminal in Luke.
searchSummary: Examines whether Jesus tells the crucified criminal, 'Today you will be with me in paradise,' or merely says that he is speaking 'today.' The post argues from Luke's repeated use of 'today' and the death of Stephen in Acts that Luke expects believers to enter paradise immediately after death, rather than waiting for a future bodily resurrection and final judgment.

title: Miraculous Conversions in the Book of Acts
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains miraculous conversions in Acts as evidence of early Christian claims about divine power.
searchSummary: Examines Acts' recurring claim that spectacular miracles produced Christian conversions. Pentecost, Peter's healing of a lame man, cures associated with Peter's shadow, and healings through objects connected with Paul lead crowds to accept the apostles' message. Later Christian narratives use the same pattern, suggesting that miracle stories remained an important explanation for Christianity's appeal. Ehrman distinguishes the historical question of whether such events occurred from the evidence that belief in miracles helped people embrace the faith.

title: Jews and Gentiles in Paul’s Churches
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the mix of Jews and Gentiles in Paul's churches.

title: Jesus and Hell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Jesus' teaching on hell for a New Testament textbook box.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus' references to Gehenna describe destruction rather than everlasting conscious torment. The valley outside Jerusalem, associated with child sacrifice and denied burial, represented an unholy fate where corpses were consumed by worms and fire. Jesus says the worms and flames continue, not that their victims remain alive. His warning that God can destroy both body and soul indicates that the wicked will be annihilated and never restored at the resurrection, while the righteous receive life in God's kingdom.

title: The Value of Eyewitness Testimony
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the value and limits of eyewitness testimony for historical Jesus research.
searchSummary: Uses an early controlled experiment to challenge the assumption that eyewitness reports are inherently accurate. Students who observed a carefully staged classroom altercation misreported between 26 and 80 percent of its details, and subsequent legal and psychological research has repeatedly found serious eyewitness error. Direct testimony about Jesus would be historically valuable because of its proximity to the events, but the identity of a witness would not guarantee that the person's perception, memory, or later account was reliable.

title: Discovery of the Nag Hammadi Library and Some Crucial Missing Parts!
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the discovery of the Nag Hammadi Library and missing parts of the story.

title: The Difference Between Eschatology and Apocalypticism
author: BDEhrman
description: Distinguishes eschatology from apocalypticism in discussions of Jesus and John the Baptist.

title: My Own Translation of the New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers whether a personal English translation of the New Testament will be published.

title: Jesus’ Apocalyptic Message in Matthew
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Matthew's heightened apocalyptic message.
searchSummary: Explains how Matthew intensifies the apocalyptic message already found in Mark. John the Baptist announces that divine wrath and judgment are imminent, ancestry from Abraham cannot secure salvation, and people must demonstrate repentance through worthy conduct. Jesus continues this urgent proclamation throughout the Gospel with even greater force. Matthew therefore portrays the present world as controlled by evil powers that God will soon overthrow when his kingdom arrives on earth.

title: Did Jesus Call Himself God?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether the historical Jesus called himself God.
searchSummary: Compares Jesus' self-presentation in John with the Synoptic Gospels. Matthew, Mark, and Luke center his teaching on God's coming kingdom and never have him call himself God. John instead makes Jesus' heavenly origin and relationship to the Father his primary message, including claims to preexist Abraham, share God's name, be one with the Father, and reveal him directly. These sayings fit John's divine Christology but their absence from earlier accounts raises doubts that the historical Jesus spoke them.

title: How Reliable are Oral Traditions?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why oral traditions about Jesus may change as they are retold.

title: Talking Dogs and Resurrected Slaves
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces miraculous stories in non-canonical Christian texts as examples of oral and literary tradition.

title: The New Edition of My New Testament Textbook
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the seventh edition of a New Testament textbook.

title: Yet Other Apocryphal Books
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes additional apocryphal books accepted in some Christian traditions.

title: Blog Dinner!  Denver, November 15
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Denver blog dinner during a speaking trip.

title: The Digital Bible (by Jeff Siker)
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Jeff Siker's reflection on digital Bible resources.

title: More Apocrypha: A Letter of Jeremiah, (Fascinating) Additions to Daniel, and 1 Maccabees
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes the Letter of Jeremiah, additions to Daniel, and 1 Maccabees.

title: More Books of the Apocrypha:  Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, and Baruch
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, and Baruch among the Old Testament Apocrypha.

title: Some of the Apocrypha: Tobit, Judith, and Additions to Esther
author: BDEhrman
description: Begins describing Tobit, Judith, and additions to Esther in the Old Testament Apocrypha.

title: What Is the Apocrypha (of the Old Testament)?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains what the Old Testament Apocrypha are and why some churches include them.

title: Did Paul Believe that the Fleshly Body Would be Resurrected
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Paul's view of the future resurrection body.
searchSummary: Clarifies Paul's distinction between “body” and “flesh” in his teaching about resurrection. Flesh is not bodily tissue but humanity's sinful, corrupted dimension, which must be destroyed; the body is God's creation and must be redeemed. Ancient people could regard spirit as refined material, so a “spiritual body” remained a real, physical body transformed beyond mortality. Later theologians such as Tertullian confused these categories by defending resurrection of the flesh while believing they were preserving Paul's position.

title: Mapping the Diversity of Earliest Christianity
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses the diversity of earliest Christianity and how oral traditions circulated.
searchSummary: Revisits Destro and Pesce's proposal that the Gospels' differing geographical interests reveal diverse groups of Jesus' followers from the earliest period. Mapping Mark, Matthew's and Luke's special sources, and John produces distinct regional patterns for Jesus' deeds, teachings, and appearances. Local adherents may have preserved different memories and developed different interpretations before these traditions were combined in written Gospels. Christianity therefore may have begun as scattered, loosely connected Palestinian communities rather than a single unified movement directed from Jerusalem.

title: What’s the Story of Lazarus and the Rich Man All About?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Luke's parable of Lazarus and the rich man in relation to afterlife judgment.
searchSummary: Interprets Luke's parable of Lazarus and the rich man as a warning about wealth, poverty, and responsibility to the needy. The post connects the rich man's fate with Luke's blessings on the poor, woes against the rich, and commands to surrender possessions. It also argues that the parable reflects Christian knowledge of Jesus' resurrection and helped establish later beliefs in immediate reward and punishment after death.

title: The Fate of the Rich and the Poor: Another Story
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares an Egyptian story of rich and poor after death with Luke's parable.
searchSummary: Explains that Luke's story of Lazarus and the rich man is a parable about conduct in the present, not a literal map of the afterlife. The post compares it with an Egyptian tale in which a righteous poor man is rewarded and an unrighteous rich man punished after death. This parallel helps frame the biblical story's reversal of earthly fortunes while leaving Luke's distinctive lesson about wealth for further analysis.

title: Heaven, Hell, and the Parable of Lazarus and the Rich Man
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Luke's distinctive teaching on immediate postmortem rewards and punishments.
searchSummary: Introduces Luke's parable of Lazarus and the rich man as a distinctive New Testament portrayal of rewards and punishments immediately after death. Lazarus is carried to paradise with Abraham, while the rich man suffers in Hades and cannot cross the chasm between them. The post argues that this view differs from the historical Jesus' teaching and cautions that the parable conveys a spiritual lesson rather than a literal description of the afterlife.

title: A Bit of Fun with 666!
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers a playful reflection on 666 and its symbolic uses.
searchSummary: Invites readers to invent humorous or serious ways of connecting the number 666 with contemporary people and institutions. Examples playfully derive three sixes from the letters in Fox, UNC Religious Studies' telephone number, and the six-letter names Ronald Wilson Reagan. The post frames the exercise as nonpartisan fun, welcoming jokes from different political and religious perspectives while excluding abuse. It illustrates how easily interpreters can manipulate names and numbers to identify a favored modern candidate as Revelation's beast.

title: If Jesus Wasn’t Really Raised from the Dead, What Happened?
author: BDEhrman
description: Considers alternatives to the claim that Jesus was literally raised from the dead.

title: Who Wrote the Book of Revelation?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains questions about the authorship of Revelation and its place in the canon.
searchSummary: Argues that Revelation was written neither by the author of the Gospel of John nor by Jesus' disciple John, son of Zebedee. Dionysius of Alexandria already distinguished the books through their self-presentation and different Greek styles; modern scholars also note their contrasting eschatology. Revelation's author wrote error-filled Greek as a second language and openly called himself John. The Galilean fisherman John almost certainly lacked the elite education required to compose such a work, leaving another early Christian John as author.

title: The Lake of Fire in Revelation
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the lake of fire in Revelation as part of its final judgment imagery.
searchSummary: Argues that Revelation's lake of fire represents the annihilation of condemned humans rather than their eternal conscious torment. The Beast, false prophet, and Devil are supernatural enemies tormented forever, but human opponents die before judgment. After the millennium, the dead are judged by their deeds; those absent from the book of life enter the lake described as the second death. Death and Hades themselves are also destroyed, signaling the permanent elimination of everything opposed to God's life-giving kingdom.

title: The Afterlife in Revelation
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses afterlife scenes in Revelation, especially the souls of martyrs.
searchSummary: Examines Revelation's intermediate afterlife before the final judgment. Christian martyrs rest under heaven's altar awaiting vindication, while the book does not say where other deceased believers remain. Supporters of Rome undergo temporary fiery torment without rest, contrasting with the martyrs' privileged state. The smoke rising forever symbolizes irreversible destruction, as in Isaiah's prophecy against Edom, rather than endless burning. Revelation later subjects these enemies to final judgment and annihilation, after which the righteous inherit life in the New Jerusalem.

title: More on the Symbolism of Revelation
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Revelation's symbolism works and whether it was meant to conceal its message.
searchSummary: Explains why Revelation's symbolism is neither a secret code shielding its author from Roman authorities nor a literal forecast of modern events. Bizarre imagery suits revelations of hidden heavenly realities, while references to the city on seven hills make Rome readily identifiable. Hal Lindsey's interpretation of demonic locusts as attack helicopters fails because the creatures cannot kill or damage vegetation. Reading the book in its historical context instead presents a symbolic assurance of God's sovereignty over first-century evil and oppression.

title: More Symbolism in Revelation: 666, The Number of “The Beast”
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the number 666 and the symbolic identification of the beast.
searchSummary: Uses Revelation's beast and the numbers 666 and 616 to demonstrate the book's symbolic method. The beast represents Rome and its rulers, while gematria identifies Nero: the Hebrew letters of Caesar Neron total 666, and the alternative Nero spelling totals 616. This first-century solution is stronger than attempts to identify modern leaders. Because Revelation openly communicates through symbols, its lake of fire and New Jerusalem likewise portray ultimate annihilation and unimaginable life rather than literal geography of the afterlife.

title: Symbolism in Revelation: The Whore of Babylon
author: BDEhrman
description: Interprets the Whore of Babylon as part of Revelation's symbolic critique of Rome.
searchSummary: Interprets Revelation's prostitute of Babylon as a symbol for Rome rather than a literal future woman. The beast supporting her connects the city with Satan; its seven heads represent Rome's seven hills, and the angel identifies her as the city ruling earthly kings. Babylon recalls the empire that destroyed Jerusalem's first temple, while Rome destroyed the second. Her wealth and drunkenness with martyrs' blood portray Roman exploitation and persecution, illustrating how Revelation itself supplies clues for reading its visions figuratively.

title: Overview of the Book of Revelation
author: BDEhrman
description: Gives an overview of Revelation with attention to afterlife and judgment.
searchSummary: Surveys Revelation's narrative as preparation for interpreting its lake of fire. John's heavenly visions unfold through catastrophic seals, trumpets, and bowls before Christ defeats Babylon, the Antichrist, and their forces. Satan is bound during a thousand-year reign with the martyrs, released briefly, and finally condemned. After the resurrection and judgment, the righteous inhabit the New Jerusalem without suffering or death. Because this chronology and imagery are openly symbolic, the post questions whether the lake of fire should be read literally.

title: Studying the Bible as Theology and/or History
author: BDEhrman
description: Distinguishes studying the Bible historically from studying it theologically.
searchSummary: Separates historical study of the Bible from theological judgment. Historians investigate publicly accessible evidence to reconstruct what probably happened, describe competing beliefs, and explain how scriptural claims developed; they cannot determine which religion is true, whether God caused an event, or what ultimate meaning it has. Believers can practice history, but supernatural conclusions belong to their faith rather than the discipline. Ehrman's textbook therefore neither promotes nor attacks belief while treating biblical writings within ancient Israelite and Christian history.

title: How I Take Notes on What I Read for a Trade Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains note-taking practices for writing a trade book on the afterlife.
searchSummary: Explains how Ehrman records and organizes several years of research for a trade book. He builds expanding bibliographies, personally reads relevant sources, and creates searchable word-processing notes ranging from a sentence to many pages according to each work's importance. Graduate assistants may collect references or prepare summaries that help prioritize his reading, but they do not replace it; topical folders preserve scholarship, primary texts, ideas, outlines, and chapters that later shape the book's organization.

title: How Do We Know When the Gospels Were Written?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how scholars date the Gospels and why the question matters.

title: Writing a Historical-Critical Textbook that Isn’t *Critical*
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the challenge of writing a historical-critical New Testament textbook without sounding destructive.
searchSummary: Describes the challenge of writing an introductory historical-critical Bible textbook that is accessible, accurate, and sensitive to students with traditional beliefs. A historical approach must present Scripture as a diverse collection produced by different authors, periods, genres, audiences, and purposes, while also acknowledging internal discrepancies and conflicts with archaeological evidence. Because readers may interpret Ehrman's agnosticism as hostility, he works to soften the presentation without concealing critical conclusions or sacrificing the book's educational purpose.

title: A Peculiar Story of Peter’s Martyrdom
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents an early and unusual account of Peter's martyrdom.

title: Who Was the First Bishop of Rome?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether Peter was the first bishop of Rome.
searchSummary: Conflicting later traditions name Peter, Linus, or Clement as Rome's first bishop, but first- and early second-century evidence shows no solitary leader there. Paul, Ignatius, 1 Clement, and the Shepherd of Hermas describe a congregation or groups of presbyters and bishops rather than a monarchic episcopate. Rome's dispersed house churches likely developed unified leadership only around the middle of the second century, long after Peter's death.

title: Peter: First Bishop (Pope) in Rome?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the historical question of Peter as Rome's first bishop and martyr.
searchSummary: Peter's prominence allowed major churches to claim connections with him, but the Roman church existed before he arrived and was not founded by him. Paul's letter to Rome mentions many believers but not Peter, while later tradition linked Peter and Paul to the capital to bolster Roman authority. The earliest congregation was probably established by otherwise unknown converts traveling to Rome, so Peter cannot historically be identified as its founding bishop.

title: Opportunity Knocking:   A Chance to Read a Draft of My Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers readers a chance to read and comment on a draft of the afterlife book.

title: Would the Disciples Die for A Lie?  Proofs for the Resurrection.
author: BDEhrman
description: Challenges the argument that the disciples' deaths prove the resurrection.

title: Did Jesus Believe Sinners Would Be Annihilated?  The Sheep and the Goats
author: BDEhrman
description: Interprets Matthew's sheep and goats passage in relation to judgment and annihilation.
searchSummary: Argues that Matthew's parable of the sheep and goats teaches the permanent annihilation of the wicked rather than eternal conscious torment. The Son of Man rewards people who aided those in need and condemns those who did not, a salvation standard likely traceable to Jesus because it does not require faith in his death or resurrection. “Eternal punishment” contrasts with eternal life: the unending fire destroys sinners permanently, while the righteous enter God's earthly kingdom.

title: Gehenna:  Where You Do Not Want to Go
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Gehenna as destruction and dishonor rather than eternal fiery torment.

title: Jesus on Gehenna
author: BDEhrman
description: Begins explaining Jesus' use of Gehenna in teachings about judgment.

title: Looking for Feedback on My Views about Jesus and the Afterlife
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Jesus taught the annihilation of sinners rather than their eternal torment and seeks feedback on that reading.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus expected sinners to be permanently destroyed at the coming judgment rather than consciously tormented forever. Images of the broad road, burned trees and weeds, discarded fish, and exclusion from the kingdom depict death and annihilation, while the righteous receive unending embodied life. Bart presents this as a developing thesis for his afterlife book, distinguishing an eternal consequence from eternal suffering and situating Jesus's teaching within Jewish apocalyptic expectations.

title: Did My Loss of Faith Affect my Scholarship?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on whether losing Christian faith changed scholarly conclusions.
searchSummary: Argues that Ehrman's loss of Christian faith had almost no effect on his mature historical scholarship. Before becoming agnostic, he already accepted textual uncertainty, biblical discrepancies, disputed authorship, an apocalyptic Jesus, diverse New Testament theologies, and competing early Christian movements. Those conclusions arose through critical study and can be shared by believers and nonbelievers alike. His teaching therefore aims to develop historical knowledge and careful thinking, not to convert or deconvert students, though scholarship may require revising fundamentalist beliefs.

title: Opening for Dinner in Durham
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces an opening at a Durham blog dinner.

title: Thomas and His Identical Twin Jesus, in the Acts of Thomas
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the Acts of Thomas and its portrayal of Thomas as Jesus' twin.

title: Did Jesus Have a Twin Brother?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores early Christian traditions claiming Jesus had a twin brother.

title: Progress Report on the Afterlife
author: BDEhrman
description: Gives a progress report on the trade book about heaven, hell, and the afterlife.
searchSummary: Reports progress on Bart's draft of the trade book later titled Heaven and Hell and explains what he means by the “invention” of afterlife beliefs. He argues that ideas such as resurrection, heaven, and hell emerged in particular historical settings without thereby judging their truth. The post also describes his shorter-chapter writing strategy and the successive rounds of fact-checking, annotation, stylistic editing, expert review, and publisher feedback still required.

title: Thomas, the Synoptic Gospels, and Q
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how the Gospel of Thomas relates to the Synoptic Gospels and Q.
searchSummary: Compares the sayings Gospel of Thomas with the hypothetical Q source and the Synoptic Gospels. Q cannot confidently be reconstructed as sayings-only or lacking a passion narrative, and its apocalyptic expectation differs sharply from Thomas's denial of a future Son of Man judgment. Thomas itself likely dates to the second century, but individual sayings may preserve older, simpler forms of parables also found in the Synoptics, so each tradition must be evaluated independently for possible historical antiquity.

title: Thomas: The Most Important Gospel Outside the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Gospel of Thomas and its distinctive message.

title: The Gospel of Thomas: An Overview
author: BDEhrman
description: Provides an overview of the Gospel of Thomas and Thomasine Christianity.

title: Thomasine Christians and Others, From After the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Thomasine Christianity and introduces other Gnostic texts that do not fit neatly into Sethian, Valentinian, or Thomasine groupings.

title: The Valentinian Gnostics from After The New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Valentinian Gnostics from a reader on early Christianity after the New Testament.

title: The Sethian Gnostics, from After The New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Sethian Gnostics and their place in discussions of Gnosticism.

title: Proselytizing on the Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Reiterates the blog policy against proselytizing in comments.

title: Our Knowledge of Gnosticism
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Nag Hammadi texts changed scholarly knowledge of Gnosticism.

title: What Was Discovered in the Nag Hammadi Library?
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the contents of the Nag Hammadi Library, including the Gospel of Thomas.

title: How the Gospel of Thomas Was Discovered
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts the discovery of the Gospel of Thomas and the Nag Hammadi codices.

title: Finishing my Dissertation
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes finishing a dissertation on Didymus the Blind's Gospel quotations.
searchSummary: Describes how Bruce Metzger's limited but careful supervision enabled Ehrman to finish an independent dissertation on Didymus the Blind's Gospel text. Metzger read chapters, answered questions, and corrected prose without controlling the research, remaining on the committee after David Adams became official adviser. Ehrman published the method as an article and the study as his first book, then persuaded Gordon Fee to launch a continuing series for similar patristic textual studies that Ehrman later helped author and edit.

title: The Core of My Dissertation on The Gospel Quotations of Didymus the Blind
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the central argument of a dissertation on Didymus the Blind's Gospel quotations.
searchSummary: Explains the detailed research behind Ehrman's dissertation on Gospel quotations in Didymus the Blind. He extracted and classified every citation, compared its Greek wording with numerous manuscripts, catalogued differences, applied statistical analysis, and reconstructed the textual history of fourth-century Alexandria. The project also produced a new method for grouping New Testament manuscripts, illustrating why dissertations demand sustained technical specialization and serve both to advance a narrow area of scholarship and to establish the researcher's professional expertise.

title: Bruce Metzger and Me: Finding a Dissertation
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts finding a dissertation topic under Bruce Metzger's direction.
searchSummary: Recounts how Ehrman chose a dissertation on New Testament quotations in Didymus the Blind under Bruce Metzger. Gordon Fee showed that patristic citations can reveal a geographically and chronologically located biblical text, although memory, paraphrase, and adaptation make reconstruction difficult and older studies methodologically weak. Newly discovered Toura commentaries offered untouched evidence, and Ludwig Koenen lent Ehrman the handwritten copy of an unpublished volume needed to analyze the complete collection.

title: Is 1 Clement Older than Some Books of the New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the dating of 1 Clement and its relationship to some New Testament writings.
searchSummary: Evaluates the date of 1 Clement, traditionally placed around 95-96 CE but theoretically possible anywhere from about 65 to 170. The supposed persecution under Domitian does not securely establish the date, yet internal evidence still points near the end of the first century: Peter and Paul belong to the author's generation, apostolically appointed leaders remain alive, and Rome lacks a single bishop. Corinth's described age and leadership succession make a pre-70 date unlikely.

title: Did a “Pope” Write the First-Century Book of 1 Clement?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether Clement of Rome wrote 1 Clement and whether pope is anachronistic.
searchSummary: Examines whether the anonymous Roman church letter known as 1 Clement was actually written by Clement. Later sources identify Clement as Paul's companion or an early bishop, and the Shepherd of Hermas may portray a Clement responsible for correspondence with other churches. Yet the letter itself names no author, and its interchangeable use of presbyter and bishop suggests Rome had no single pope-like leader, leaving Clement's involvement plausible but impossible to establish confidently.

title: The Letter of First Clement: An Overview
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces 1 Clement and the Apostolic Fathers.
searchSummary: Provides an overview of 1 Clement, an anonymous Roman letter responding to the removal of presbyters from leadership in Corinth. Drawing extensively on the Septuagint, Hellenistic rhetoric, and examples from nature, the author argues that God's people and creation should display harmony, order, humility, and freedom from envy. The lengthy appeal ultimately urges the Corinthians to reverse their leadership revolt, reinstate the displaced presbyters, and restore peace within the church.

title: Blog Dinner in Durham in September is Full!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces that the Durham blog dinner is full.

title: Was Jesus Thought To Be a Miracle Worker in His Own Lifetime?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether Jesus was regarded as a miracle worker during Jesus' lifetime.

title: The Message of Jesus’ Miracles
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the message conveyed by stories of Jesus' miracles.

title: Blog Dinners Next Month.  Interested?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces upcoming blog dinners for members.

title: Is There Sarcasm in the New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers whether sarcasm appears in the New Testament.
searchSummary: Shows how literary and historical context can reveal sarcasm in New Testament writings despite the loss of ancient tone and facial cues. Jesus' image of someone with a log in his eye judging another's speck mocks hypocrisy. Paul sarcastically calls the Corinthians rich and kingly to challenge their belief that they already possess heavenly glory, and his wish that circumcision advocates be "cut off" in Galatians carries a deliberately cutting double meaning.

title: Jesus and His Miracles: Some Interesting Features
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses notable features of Gospel miracle stories about Jesus.

title: Did the Original Gospels Describe Jesus’ Miracles?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why independent Greek manuscripts, ancient translations, and patristic quotations show that miracle stories belonged to the Gospels from the start.

title: More Free Memberships Available
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces additional free memberships for readers unable to pay.

title: More on the Historical Problem of Miracles
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why miracles pose special problems for historical demonstration.

title: History is not the Past!  Proving Jesus’ Resurrection and Other Miracles
author: BDEhrman
description: Distinguishes history from the past while explaining why historians cannot prove miracles.

title: My First Taste of Critical Scholarship
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the difference between knowing biblical content and understanding critical scholarship.
searchSummary: Recounts Ehrman's difficult first encounter with historical-critical scholarship through Hans Conzelmann's study of Luke. Rather than harmonizing the Gospels, redaction criticism examines how Luke deliberately changed Mark to express a distinctive theology, including a revised understanding of history and Jesus' delayed return. The method initially seemed incoherent because its assumptions contradicted Ehrman's evangelical training, but sustained study eventually allowed him to understand its logic and transformed his approach to Gospel interpretation.

title: Upcoming Speaking Events, Fall 2018
author: BDEhrman
description: Lists upcoming speaking events for fall 2018.

title: Did Peter Use a Secretary for his Writings?  A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether Peter could have used a secretary to produce writings attributed to him.
searchSummary: Addresses whether 1 Peter 5:12 identifies Silvanus as Peter's secretary. The phrase translated “through Silvanus” normally names the person carrying and authenticating a letter, not its composer. Silvanus also appears to have been an Aramaic-speaking Palestinian unlikely to possess the required literary Greek. More broadly, ancient secretaries usually took exact dictation and only rarely edited elite correspondence; evidence does not support their routinely composing complex works for illiterate figures. Pseudonymous authorship remains the stronger explanation.

title: Finishing my Work on the Afterlife
author: BDEhrman
description: Reports nearing completion of research for the afterlife book.

title: Traditions About Jesus that Are Probably Not Historical
author: BDEhrman
description: Gives examples of Gospel traditions about Jesus judged unlikely to be historical.

title: How a Book Gets Its Title
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how publishers and authors arrive at book titles.
searchSummary: Explains the collaborative and uncertain process of naming a trade book. Publishers seek titles that attract nonspecialists without excessive sensationalism, and editors, marketing teams, international branches, and authors may revise choices even after advance listings appear. Ehrman recounts preferring Lost in Transmission to Misquoting Jesus because it better described scribal changes, but the publisher rejected its possible association with automobile racing; the eventual bestseller showed that the more provocative title worked better than he expected.

title: The Trickiest Criterion for Determining What Happened in the Life of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains a difficult criterion used to evaluate historical traditions about Jesus.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: An Important Criterion for Establishing What Actually Happened
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains a historical criterion used to judge whether Gospel traditions go back to Jesus.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: Rules of Thumb for Reconstructing the History behind the Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Lays out rules of thumb for using the Gospels as historical sources.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: The Historian’s Wish List
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains what historians ideally want from sources and how the Gospels measure up.
searchSummary: Describes the kinds of sources historians would ideally possess when reconstructing Jesus' life. Reliable evidence would be numerous, early, independent, mutually consistent, internally coherent, and relatively unbiased. The Gospels offer several independent accounts, an unusual advantage for an ancient person, but they were written decades later by committed followers drawing on changing oral and written traditions rather than eyewitness documentation. The task is neither automatic acceptance nor despair, but disciplined use of imperfect faith documents to identify probable historical information.

title: What I Saw at St. Catherine’s Monastery at Mount Sinai
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes seeing St. Catherine's Monastery and its manuscripts at Mount Sinai.

title: Visiting the Monastery at Mount Sinai: A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts an account of visiting St. Catherine's Monastery at Mount Sinai.

title: A Key Contradiction in the Birth Narratives of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains a key contradiction between Matthew's and Luke's birth narratives.
searchSummary: Compares Matthew's and Luke's accounts of Jesus' birth and argues that they cannot be combined into a single coherent chronology. Matthew appears to place the family in Bethlehem before the flight to Egypt and later relocation to Nazareth, while Luke begins them in Nazareth and returns them there about a month after the birth. The post identifies this conflict, not merely their different characters and episodes, as a genuine contradiction.

title: Are Matthew and Paul at Odds on the Most Important Issue?
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Matthew and Paul on salvation, law, and what matters most.
searchSummary: Compares Matthew and Paul on the relationship between law, good deeds, and salvation. Matthew's Jesus tells the rich man that keeping the commandments brings eternal life and giving possessions to the poor brings perfection; Paul says no one is justified by works of the law and that justification through law would make Christ's death pointless. Because Matthew also treats Jesus' death as salvific, the post asks whether their views can be reconciled without assuming either harmony or contradiction in advance.

title: Are the Gospels Principally Concerned to Show What Actually Happened?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the Gospels were not written primarily as neutral historical reports.
searchSummary: Argues that Gospel contradictions matter because they reveal theological storytelling and limit using the narratives as neutral historical reports. Differences over chronology, Jesus's death, and especially his identity show authors adapting traditions to communicate distinct claims. John's Jesus repeatedly declares heavenly preexistence and equality with God, teachings absent from Mark, Q, M, L, Matthew, and Luke; this makes it more plausible that Johannine tradition transformed Jesus's message than that every earlier source omitted its most remarkable feature.

title: Why Contradictions Matter for Understanding the Life of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why contradictions matter for reconstructing Jesus' life historically.
searchSummary: Explains how contradictions affect historical reconstruction of Jesus' life through Matthew's and Luke's infancy narratives. Their conflicting sequences, lack of outside corroboration, and implausibilities prevent both accounts from being wholly accurate; even their agreements on virgin birth and Bethlehem serve strong theological claims about Jesus as God's messiah. Ehrman concludes that historically uncheckable agreements cannot simply outweigh demonstrable problems, making the narratives more likely later legends expressing theology than reports of actual events.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: Student Excuses: A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a memorable student excuse from a teaching career.
searchSummary: Recounts the most memorable excuse Ehrman received for a missed examination. A Rutgers student claimed that a suicidal chemist's explosion sent a water heater through his house, collapsing the ceiling on him; the student had already experienced other unusual ambulance incidents. Although the story sounded improbable, he offered documentation, received permission to take a makeup final, and earned a high grade. Ehrman treats the episode humorously as an example of creativity, fairness, and teaching's unpredictable human side.

title: The Historical Significance of Contradictions
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how biblical contradictions can help historians analyze sources.
searchSummary: Shows how biblical contradictions undermine straightforward historical use of the Pentateuch. Conflicting creation orders, Noah's animal counts, repeated destruction of Egyptian livestock, and disagreement over when Yahweh's name became known led scholars to identify multiple sources rather than Mosaic authorship. Ehrman argues that these editorial seams make the narratives problematic evidence for what happened in the past and suggest that substantial portions function as story rather than objective history.

title: Balancing the Scholarly and the Popular
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on balancing scholarly writing with books for general readers.
searchSummary: Reflects on the difficulty of sustaining both a peer-reviewed scholarly career and a program of books for general readers. While serving as an editor for a leading patristics journal, Ehrman contrasts rigorous expert review with public writing and notes that few academics continue both after entering trade publishing. Each form demands different assumptions, language, pacing, and skills, yet he remains committed to creating new knowledge and making serious scholarship understandable beyond the academy despite skepticism from colleagues.

title: The Broader Significance(s) of Contradictions
