author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why contradictions matter beyond debates over inerrancy.
searchSummary: Explains that biblical contradictions matter beyond disproving fundamentalist inerrancy. Christians have long developed sophisticated ways to retain scriptural authority despite discrepancies, but contradictions also complicate reconstruction of Christian origins and interpretation of the Bible's competing moral and theological messages. Ehrman argues that believers and nonbelievers alike should study the Bible as a multi-author foundation of Western culture, recognizing its diversity rather than treating it as one unified historical account or message.

title: The Strangest Moment of My Teaching Career
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts an unusual classroom incident from university teaching.
searchSummary: Describes a parent's only call to Ehrman during decades of teaching and the strange resolution of a failing grade. A mother asked him to pass her daughter so she could remain in college, but he refused to add points without academic justification. When he reviewed the teaching assistant's calculations, he discovered a four-point arithmetic error that raised the grade to passing. The incident illustrates the importance of standards, compassion, and verifying assessment records before treating results as final.

title: If the Bible is Contradictory, How Can it Be Authoritative?
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses how biblical contradictions affect claims about scriptural authority.
searchSummary: Asks how Scripture can function as final authority when its books give irreconcilable instructions and beliefs. Examples include kosher and Sabbath laws, monotheism, Jesus' identity, present versus future eternal life, violence versus love, women's speech, family loyalty, political obedience, and Torah observance. Because readers must select, reject, or reinterpret conflicting passages, Ehrman argues that they themselves exercise the decisive authority, raising ethical and theological problems that cannot be solved merely by asserting biblical inerrancy.

title: Are Contradictions the Real Point?
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that contradictions are not the endpoint but a starting point for interpretation.
searchSummary: Clarifies that contradictions challenge one fundamentalist model of inspiration, not every belief that Scripture is inspired. Ehrman traces alternatives he held as a Christian: allowing minor or historical mistakes, preserving only faith and practice, emphasizing an overall message, or treating fallible words as a medium through which God speaks. Though ingenious theories could claim God intentionally inspired contradictions, their greater importance lies in how discrepancies affect historical reconstruction and interpretation of the Bible's messages.

title: Internal Discrepancies in the Gospel of John
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines internal discrepancies within John's Gospel.
searchSummary: Uses internal discrepancies to argue that John's author spliced together multiple written sources. Numbered signs conflict with intervening miracles, geographical movements are incoherent, and Jesus says no disciple has asked where he is going shortly after Peter and Thomas do so. The Farewell Discourse also commands departure three chapters before anyone leaves. These problems become coherent if chapters 15-17 represent a second version inserted between an original ending in chapter 14 and the departure in chapter 18.

title: Why Does Luke Appear to Contradict Himself?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Luke-Acts may contain internal tensions created by the author's sources.
searchSummary: Explains internal tensions in Luke-Acts as the likely result of the author's use of multiple sources with different early Christian views. Speeches and narratives variously place Jesus' status as Messiah, Lord, Savior, and Son of God at his birth, baptism, ministry, resurrection, or future return. The post argues that incorporating inherited traditions without fully reconciling their Christologies produced these discrepancies.

title: Sources for the Hebrew Bible: A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts an explanation of source theories behind the Hebrew Bible.

title: Does Luke Flat Out Contradict Himself?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines a contradiction between Luke and Acts about Jesus' ascension.
searchSummary: Examines the apparent conflict between Luke, where Jesus seems to ascend on the day of his resurrection, and Acts, where the ascension occurs forty days later. Because key ascension language in Luke 24:51 is absent from important manuscripts, the post argues that a later scribe probably added it to emphasize Jesus' bodily ascension against docetic beliefs. On that reading, Luke originally contained no contradictory ascension account.

title: New Rules for Comments on the Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces new rules for comments on the blog.

title: How I Write: The Crucial Phase
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains a crucial phase in the process of writing a book.
searchSummary: Explains Ehrman's outline-centered method for turning years of research into a rapidly written trade-book draft. After defining a thesis, chapters, sections, and subsections, he rereads every primary source and scholarly note, inserts relevant evidence and quotations into separate chapter outlines, and repeatedly reorganizes and trims them. The resulting outlines may nearly equal the chapters in length, but they eliminate uncertainty about content and sequence, letting him concentrate on prose and complete the first draft in several intense weeks.

title: Does the Book of Acts Portray the *Teachings* of Paul Accurately?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether Acts accurately portrays Paul's teachings.
searchSummary: Compares Paul's teaching about pagan religion in Acts 17 with his argument in Romans 1 to test whether Acts preserves his views accurately. Acts says pagans were ignorant of the creator and that God overlooked their error, while Romans says they knowingly rejected God and faced divine wrath. The contrast, along with the similar voices given to different speakers, suggests Luke composed the speeches. Ehrman therefore recommends reconstructing Paul's theology primarily from his undisputed letters rather than Acts.

title: Does the Book of Acts Accurately Portray the Life and Teachings of Paul?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the problem of Acts as a historical source for Paul's life and message.
searchSummary: Evaluates Acts' portrayal of Paul's life and relationship to Jewish law by comparing it with Paul's own letters. Differences concern travel companions, whether Paul consulted Jerusalem's apostles after his conversion, and whether he remained fully law-observant while preaching to Gentiles. Ehrman argues that Luke reshaped events to emphasize apostolic unity and continuity with Judaism, whereas Paul's letters reveal sharper conflicts and a stronger rejection of law observance for Gentile converts. Acts is broadly informative but unreliable in important specifics.

title: Why I Am Obsessed with Jesus: A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains that the historical gap between Jesus as an apocalyptic preacher and the divine Christ proclaimed by Christians drives continuing interest in Jesus.
searchSummary: Explains why Jesus remains Ehrman's dominant scholarly interest despite his atheism. The historical Jesus was an apocalyptic Jewish preacher who did not claim to be God, yet his followers' later declaration of his divinity made Christianity's Gentile growth and eventual transformation of Western civilization possible. Ehrman's fascination therefore centers on the enormous historical consequences of the gap between the human Jesus reconstructed by historians and the divine Christ worshiped by Christians.

title: How Does an Author Write a Trade Book?  Phase 2.
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the second phase of writing a trade book.
searchSummary: Describes outlining as the second of Ehrman's three major book-writing phases, following research and preceding drafting. After eighteen months of reading and organized notes on ancient afterlife traditions, he reassesses the book from scratch because sustained research has changed what he knows and wants to argue. He contrasts this mature plan with the preliminary prospectus used to secure a trade-book contract, showing how evidence transforms an initial chapter sketch into the book that will actually be written.

title: The Name Judas Iscariot: What Does It Mean?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores the meaning of the name Judas Iscariot.

title: Taking the Temperature of the Blog: June 2018
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks readers for feedback on the blog's direction and usefulness.

title: Why Would I Call Myself Both an Agnostic and an Atheist?  A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the distinction between being agnostic and being atheist.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman identifies as both agnostic and atheist by treating the labels as answers to different questions. Atheism describes his lack of belief in traditional gods, while agnosticism expresses his inability to know whether some greater spiritual intelligence exists in the universe. He usually emphasizes agnosticism because intellectual humility better reflects the limits of human knowledge, even though others may reasonably prefer to foreground what they do not believe rather than what they cannot know.

title: Two Rather Bizarre Accounts of How Judas Died
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares two strange later accounts of Judas's death.

title: Can We Know Anything Historically About How Judas Iscariot Died?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether historians can know how Judas Iscariot died.
searchSummary: Compares Acts' account of Judas buying a field and dying there violently with Matthew's account of priests buying it after Judas returns the money and hangs himself. The independent traditions agree only that Judas's death was associated with a Jerusalem place called the Field of Blood. A possible historical reconstruction suggests a potter's field known for red clay where Judas died, perhaps by suicide, after which Christians developed different explanations connecting its name with his blood or Jesus' blood money.

title: The Death of Judas in Matthew
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Matthew's account of Judas's death.
searchSummary: Explains Matthew's account of Judas returning his blood money, hanging himself, and indirectly funding the purchase of a potter's field. Matthew blends scriptural allusions to portray Jerusalem's destruction as punishment for shedding innocent blood and stresses that both Judas and Pilate recognize Jesus' innocence. Responsibility is therefore shifted toward Jerusalem's Jewish leaders and crowds, a polemical interpretation that later contributed to antisemitism. Whether Judas's remorse was genuine or historically grounded remains uncertain.

title: Self-Reflection on The Process of Writing a Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the research and writing process for a book.
searchSummary: Reflects on which stages of writing Ehrman finds most and least satisfying. Close research reading and rapid drafting are difficult for different reasons: one is a prolonged grind, while the other demands intense focus and creates anxiety despite his speed. He most enjoys the creative middle stage, when completed notes become detailed chapter outlines and he decides what matters, how the argument should flow, and how to make the material compelling for general readers.

title: Why Did Judas Iscariot Betray Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines possible reasons Judas betrayed Jesus.

title: Past and Present: One of My Debates with Dinesh D’Souza
author: BDEhrman
description: Revisits debates with Dinesh D'Souza in light of suffering and public controversy.
searchSummary: Introduces a recorded debate between Ehrman and evangelical commentator Dinesh D'Souza over whether extensive suffering should affect belief in God. D'Souza maintains that pain and misery are compatible with Christian faith, while Ehrman argues that they count strongly against an active, loving, all-powerful deity. Recorded at Gordon College in 2010, the exchange is one of three debates between them and presents their opposing arguments directly rather than summarizing a new written position.

title: Did the Gospels Originally Have Titles?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains whether the Gospels originally had titles.

title: Non-Disclosure Agreements
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses non-disclosure agreements surrounding the First-Century Mark controversy.
searchSummary: Uses Ehrman's experience with the Gospel of Judas to distinguish a reasonable non-disclosure agreement from the secrecy surrounding the alleged first-century Mark. National Geographic's agreement protected a funded restoration and ended when the manuscript was publicly released. By contrast, Dan Wallace continued withholding who required his agreement, when it began, and why, even after the Mark fragment appeared. Ehrman questions whether law still required the silence and calls for a full account of the affair.

title: What the New Fragment of Mark’s Gospel Looks like (the so-called First-Century Mark)
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the published fragment once promoted as a first-century copy of Mark.
searchSummary: Introduces P137, the papyrus fragment once promoted as a first-century copy of Mark but published as a late-second- or early-third-century manuscript. Discovered among the Oxyrhynchus papyri, it preserves only portions of Mark 1:7-9 and 1:16-18 on a tiny two-sided scrap. Ehrman explains its transcription and surviving wording while stressing that, despite the failed publicity, it remains important as probably the earliest known physical witness to Mark alongside P45.

title: Did Jesus Do “Signs” To Prove Who He Was?  A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares John's signs with Synoptic miracle traditions.
searchSummary: Explains why John's miracles function as "signs" of Jesus' identity, unlike miracles in the Synoptic Gospels. The Synoptic Jesus refuses requests for supernatural proof and offers only his death and resurrection as a sign. John instead presents seven spectacular deeds specifically to demonstrate that Jesus is Messiah and Son of God, matching the Gospel's focus on his divine self-revelation. A hypothetical written Signs Source may have supplied these stories before they were incorporated into the finished Gospel.
topics: Signs in the Gospel of John

title: Doing Research for a Trade Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how research for a trade book begins.
searchSummary: Explains Bart's research process for a general-audience book through his work on the history of the afterlife. He describes identifying indispensable scholarship, avoiding distracting research paths, taking different levels of notes according to a source's relevance, and tracing citations to earlier studies. Alongside modern scholarship, he systematically gathers and evaluates ancient evidence from biblical, Mesopotamian, Greek, Roman, Jewish, and early Christian writings before deciding what the book will argue.

title: We Do *NOT* Have a First-Century Copy of the Gospel of Mark
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the claimed first-century copy of Mark does not exist.
searchSummary: Announces that the published Oxyrhynchus fragment is the manuscript Dan Wallace had promoted as a first-century copy of Mark, but its editors date it to the second or third century. Wallace apologizes for repeating information he had not personally verified and explains how an undisclosed representative encouraged the announcement before he signed a non-disclosure agreement. His account reveals that the unnamed papyrologist had already become less certain of the early date before the 2012 debate.

title: Why Didn’t the Gospel Writers Tell Us Who They Were?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the Gospel writers remained anonymous.

title: Why Would an Ancient Author Write a Book Anonymously?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why ancient authors sometimes wrote anonymously.

title: Do We Know Why Jesus Went to Jerusalem?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores historical reasons Jesus went to Jerusalem.

title: The Tricks of Writing for a General Audience
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how scholars learn to write clearly for general audiences.
searchSummary: Explains why writing successfully for nonspecialists requires more than removing academic jargon. Authors must recognize what readers do not know, explain scholarly foundations clearly without condescension, respect their intelligence, and show why an unfamiliar issue matters. Graduate training teaches insiders to communicate efficiently with other experts, not to reconstruct that background for outsiders; scholars therefore often fail either by assuming too much knowledge or by never generating interest in a subject that already fascinates specialists.

title: How a Book Gets Written
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the practical process of writing a book.
searchSummary: Explains the skills required at every stage of producing a trade book. An author must define a central point, select and evaluate primary and secondary sources, take useful notes, organize chapters and subarguments, write lively prose for nonspecialists, revise repeatedly, and respond intelligently to expert and editorial feedback. Because weakness at any stage can undermine the result, Ehrman portrays book writing as an integrated process extending from research design through polishing and later production rather than simply composing pages.

title: Back in Business!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the blog's return after a brief technology-related hiatus.

title: How I Write a Trade Book for a General Audience
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the process of writing a trade book for general readers.
searchSummary: Explains how Ehrman chooses a trade-book topic by combining his expertise, intellectual interest, and likely value to general readers. Some books answer questions the public already asks, such as how the canon formed or what scholars think about Jesus. Others make a technical issue compelling by revealing its stakes, as Misquoting Jesus does with manuscript variation. His planned afterlife book uses a familiar concern but promises a surprising historical explanation for beliefs many readers assume come directly from the Bible.

title: Technology Challenge at the Beach
author: BDEhrman
description: Reports a temporary technology problem preventing normal blog posting.

title: My Life!  An Interview with Frank Statio on “The State of Things”
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a radio interview about religious autobiography and The Triumph of Christianity.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's public-radio interview with Frank Stasio on The State of Things. The conversation primarily traces his religious journey from Christian fundamentalism to atheism before turning near the end to The Triumph of Christianity, his then-new account of Christianity's historical expansion. Ehrman praises Stasio's ability to reach the center of an issue and sustain an engaging discussion, presenting the recording itself as the source for listeners interested in his biography, deconversion, and scholarship.

title: Does Paul Condemn Slavery?   The Case of Philemon and Onesimus.
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Paul's letter to Philemon and whether it condemns slavery.

title: A Different First-Century Mark?  An Interesting Piece of Sleuth Work
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses Brent Nongbri's sleuthing about a different possible early Mark fragment.
searchSummary: Shares Brent Nongbri's investigation of a different papyrus once claimed to preserve first-century notes or a precursor of Mark from mummy cartonnage. The supposed Christian undertext was unreadable, linguistically incoherent, and incompatible with the papyrus's Ptolemaic upper text; specialists concluded that the claim was wishful thinking or a hoax. Nongbri also traces the artifact's ownership and discovers ambiguity over whether the published article was written by conservator Anton Fackelmann or his untrained son.

title: Why Would It Matter If There Were a First-Century Copy of Mark?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why a first-century copy of Mark would matter for apologetic and historical claims.
searchSummary: Asks what a genuine first-century fragment of Mark would actually change. A small scrap closely matching the reconstructed text would confirm current expectations, while one containing variants would confirm that early copies differed; neither result would reveal Mark's sources or prove historical reliability. Ehrman argues that only a lengthy and unmistakable copy with radically unexpected wording could significantly revise scholarship, and that evangelical claims instead inflate the fragment's value for apologetic purposes it cannot support.

title: Bogus Christian Apologetics and a First-Century Fragment of Mark
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques apologetic claims about an alleged first-century fragment of Mark.
searchSummary: Critiques apologetic claims that an alleged first-century Mark fragment would prove the Gospel's eyewitness basis and historical reliability. Ehrman notes that the evidence remained unpublished, its dating and experts unidentified, and the cited semiotics credential irrelevant to manuscript dating. Even if authentic, an early copy would show only that Mark, usually dated around 70, circulated soon afterward. It could not identify the Gospel's sources, bridge the gap to Jesus, or refute scholars' reasons for questioning eyewitness authorship.

title: Seeing Capernaum and the “Jesus Boat”: A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts travel reflections on Capernaum and the so-called Jesus Boat.

title: Are Christians Intolerant?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines ancient Christian intolerance toward other religions.
searchSummary: Christian writers appealed for religious freedom while their movement faced persecution, but some advocated coercion after Christian emperors gained power. Lactantius argued that religion must be voluntary, whereas Firmicus Maternus later urged emperors to suppress pagan worship and invoked biblical commands for violence. Gregory of Nazianzus and others still opposed compulsion, showing that late antique Christianity contained competing approaches to religious tolerance.

title: When Christianity Became the “Official” Religion of Rome
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains when Christianity became the official religion of the Roman Empire.
searchSummary: Christianity became effectively Rome's official religion under Theodosius I near the end of the fourth century, not under Constantine. Theodosius penalized apostasy, prohibited sacrifice and temple worship, and eventually banned even private pagan rites, while imposing fines and confiscation. Enforcement varied across the vast empire, pagan practices continued, and Christians who had once demanded religious liberty increasingly debated whether imperial power should force conversion.

title: Making Rome Pagan Again
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Julian's attempt to restore pagan religion after Constantine.
searchSummary: Julian attempted to restore traditional Roman religion during his brief reign after decades of Christian imperial support. He reopened temples, revived sacrifices, withdrew Christian privileges, restricted Christian teachers of pagan classics, and promoted pagan charity to compete with the church. Rather than systematically executing Christians, he used policy, education, and persuasion in hopes of weakening Christianity and renewing devotion to the gods.

title: The Beginning of the End of Paganism
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the fourth-century decline of paganism as Christianity gained imperial power.
searchSummary: After Constantine's death, his sons fought violently for control while expanding imperial support for Christianity. Constantius II backed Arian Christianity and issued laws closing temples, banning sacrifices, and threatening pagan worshipers with severe penalties, although limited enforcement allowed traditional practices to continue. These measures reveal the emperor's anti-pagan policy and mark an early stage in Christianity's growing dominance of the Roman Empire.

title: Did Constantine Outlaw the Pagan Religions?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Constantine did not outlaw pagan religions.
searchSummary: Ehrman examines disputed evidence that Constantine outlawed pagan sacrifice and concludes that he probably favored persuasion over coercion. Eusebius and a later law of Constantius imply a ban, but no Constantinian prohibition survives in the Theodosian Code, and Libanius remembered his tolerance. Constantine's own letter explicitly allowed people to retain their religious convictions, even while presenting Christianity as the truth.

title: Fresh Air – Christianity’s Path From ‘Forbidden’ To A ‘Triumph’
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a Fresh Air interview on The Triumph of Christianity.
searchSummary: Presents Ehrman's appearance on NPR's Fresh Air with Terry Gross about The Triumph of Christianity and the religion's movement from a forbidden faith to dominance in the Roman world. Ehrman notes that the broadcast runs about forty-five minutes although their conversation lasted twice as long, allowing editors to select from a much broader discussion. The post provides an embedded recording and a link to NPR's transcript rather than reproducing the interview's arguments in the article itself.

title: What It Takes to be a Graduate Student
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the demands and difficulties of pursuing graduate study in New Testament or early Christianity.
searchSummary: Explains why doctoral education in early Christianity is both transformative and exceptionally demanding. Students complete intensive seminars, master modern and ancient languages, prepare broad multilingual bibliographies, pass written and oral examinations, propose original research, and produce and defend a book-length dissertation, commonly over many years. Graduate teaching likewise forces faculty to learn from specialized student projects, while the program's rigor establishes real expertise rather than elitist status; Ehrman admires those committed enough to endure the preparation.

title: The Different Terms for Literary Deception
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains terminology scholars use for different kinds of literary deception.
searchSummary: Defines a detailed vocabulary for distinguishing forms of ancient literary deception, including falsification, fabrication, plagiarism, anonymity, pseudonymity, false attribution, and several kinds of forgery. Ehrman stresses that these labels describe different authorial and editorial practices and should not be used interchangeably. Applying the taxonomy to the New Testament, he classifies its books as correctly named, anonymous and later attributed, implicitly forged, or explicitly forged. He concludes that roughly thirteen of the twenty-seven writings represent some form of forgery.

title: Different Kinds of Literary Deceit
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains different forms of literary deceit in ancient writing.
searchSummary: Explains why the study of ancient literary deceit requires a consistent vocabulary. Scholars sometimes deny that practices such as plagiarism or forgery existed in antiquity and often use the same labels for distinct phenomena. Using Tertullian's account of the Acts of Thecla, Ehrman distinguishes fabrication, the invention of supposedly historical stories, from forgery, a false claim to be a known author. He proposes a taxonomy encompassing falsification, pseudonymity, false attribution, several forms of forgery, and related practices.

title: A Forger Fooled By Forgery
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces an example of a forger being fooled by another forgery.
searchSummary: Recounts an ancient story in which Heraclides Ponticus, himself associated with deception, plagiarism, and forged plays, became the victim of another forger. His former student Dionysius wrote a play under Sophocles' name, allowed Heraclides to cite it as authentic, and then exposed the trick through embedded acrostics. Ehrman discusses doubts about the anecdote's historicity and related literary hoaxes, using the episode to illustrate the irony of a practiced deceiver being publicly deceived by forgery.

title: Additional Free Memberships Available
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces additional free memberships for readers unable to pay.

title: My Book on Literary Forgery
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Forgery and Counterforgery and its study of literary deceit in early Christianity.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's scholarly monograph Forgery and Counterforgery and its investigation of Christian literary forgeries from the first four centuries. He emphasizes the extraordinary prevalence of anonymous, falsely attributed, and forged writings in early Christianity and the lack of comprehensive modern study. The book places canonical and noncanonical cases within broader Greco-Roman and Jewish practices, examining authors' motives, ancient judgments and detection methods, and the use of prestigious assumed identities to claim authority in theological, institutional, and communal disputes.

title: Some Academic Good News
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares good news from academic life.
searchSummary: Clarifies why a research professor's apparently light teaching calendar does not amount to abundant free time. Courses, graduate advising, examinations, theses, dissertations, and administration accompany original scholarship required for tenure and promotion, often producing sixty-hour weeks throughout summers and semesters. Ehrman's National Humanities Center and Guggenheim fellowships provide two years for a major scholarly book, yet he still expects continuing obligations to graduate students, illustrating how research leave reallocates academic labor rather than ending it.

title: My Testier Days: A Response to a Critique of How Jesus Became God
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on earlier responses to criticism of How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Revisits Ehrman's forceful response to Robert Barron's critique of How Jesus Became God and acknowledges the testy tone of his earlier writing. He argues that Barron wrongly attributes to the book a hallucination theory, claims of novelty, and a reconstruction resembling the Passover Plot, although Ehrman explicitly avoids theological judgments about resurrection and divinity. The post defends serious historical disagreement while rejecting criticism based on caricature rather than careful reading.

title: Q&A with Bart on The Heretic Happy Hour
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a Heretic Happy Hour Q&A on The Triumph of Christianity and related topics.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's twenty-five-minute call-in appearance on the Heretic Happy Hour podcast. The hosts ask numerous questions covering a range of issues, including but not limited to his book The Triumph of Christianity: How a Forbidden Religion Swept the World. Ehrman describes the episode as interesting and enjoyable, but the short post does not list the individual questions or summarize his responses, so the linked program supplies the substantive discussion and any conclusions about Jesus, Christianity, or the book.

title: Why Should Faith and the Afterlife Matter?  Readers’ Mailbag April 15, 2018
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to a reader question about why faith and afterlife beliefs matter.

title: Jesus as God in the Synoptics: A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains a changed view about whether the Synoptic Gospels portray Jesus as divine.
searchSummary: Explains a change in judgment about whether the Synoptic Gospels portray Jesus as divine. Miracles, forgiveness, and worship do not individually prove divinity, but combined with Jesus's divine sonship they suggest an exalted being: Mark presents adoption at baptism, while Luke and Matthew connect sonship with conception or birth. This differs from John's preexistent Word who becomes human, demonstrating that calling Jesus “God” requires asking what kind of divinity each Gospel imagines.

title: Blog Lunch in Houston Thursday April 19?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Houston blog lunch during Rice University lectures.

title: Is There a Time and Place for Heaven and Hell?
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses American beliefs about heaven and hell in light of survey data.
searchSummary: Questions how literal heaven and hell can fit within understandings of space and time. Ancient biblical cosmology placed God's realm above a flat earth and the dead beneath it, but neither direction leads to another world in a universe whose time began and may end. Believers may relocate the afterlife to a dimension, yet that reinterprets authorities who envisioned places and endless duration. Ehrman asks whether inherited cosmology should govern belief or give way to conclusions based on current knowledge.

title: The Thinking Atheist Interview: The Triumph of Christianity
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a Thinking Atheist interview on The Triumph of Christianity.
searchSummary: Introduces Seth Andrews's interview with Ehrman about The Triumph of Christianity: How a Forbidden Religion Swept the World. The post identifies Andrews as host of The Thinking Atheist, a media channel that challenges religious claims and favors science, reason, evidence, and continued inquiry over faith as a way of determining truth. It provides the interview itself rather than a written account of Ehrman's explanation for Christianity's expansion and eventual dominance.

title: Degrees of Punishment and Purgatory
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores degrees of punishment, purgatory, and the variety of biblical afterlife views.

title: Who Invented the Idea of a Suffering Messiah?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Christians came to understand the messiah as suffering and dying.
searchSummary: Argues that Christians, rather than pre-Christian Jews, developed the idea of a messiah who suffered and died for others. Jewish expectations centered on a powerful ruler, while Isaiah 53 describes Israel's past suffering and never names a messiah. Jesus' execution shattered his followers' hopes, but resurrection belief restored their conviction and prompted them to reinterpret suffering texts as prophecy, enabling Paul to understand the crucifixion as bearing a curse for others.

title: The Unforgivable Sin and Purgatory
author: BDEhrman
description: Connects the unforgivable sin to later ideas about purgatory.

title: The Sixth Anniversary of the Blog!
author: BDEhrman
description: Marks the blog's sixth anniversary and reflects on its progress.
searchSummary: Marks the blog's sixth anniversary with statistics on publishing, engagement, membership, and fundraising. During the year Bart produced 275 posts, handled more than 15,000 comments, reached roughly 5,500 members, and raised a record $137,000 for charity. He considers a possible sustaining-membership program, asks readers to promote the blog, give subscriptions, donate, and suggest improvements, and thanks Steven Ray and the community while reaffirming the blog's educational and charitable purposes.

title: Making the Bestseller List
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on media attention and reaching the bestseller list.
searchSummary: Celebrates The Triumph of Christianity reaching number eleven on the New York Times hardcover nonfiction bestseller list after Bart's Fresh Air appearance. He emphasizes the importance of media exposure for trade-book sales and notes additional publicity through Sam Harris's podcast and History.com. An excerpt from his History essay frames the book's central question: how a tiny group of Jesus's followers grew into the dominant religion of the Roman Empire.

title: Did Jesus Teach About Purgatory?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Jesus taught anything like purgatory.

title: An Easter Reflection 2018
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on Easter and the centrality of Jesus' resurrection for Christianity.

title: The First Intimation of Purgatory?
author: BDEhrman
description: Traces early hints of the idea that became purgatory.

title: The Birth of Purgatory
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the development of purgatory as a third postmortem state.

title: The Martyr Perpetua and Her Estranged Family
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses Perpetua's martyrdom and her estranged family.

title: The Martyrdom of Perpetua
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Martyrdom of Perpetua in a discussion of afterlife views.

title: Forgery Lecture
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a public lecture on literary forgery in early Christianity.
searchSummary: Announces a Rice University lecture on the forms of literary deceit found in Christian writings from the first four centuries. Ehrman argues that calling a falsely authored work a forgery is clearer than the technical label pseudepigraphon and reflects ancient judgments that such claims were lies. The lecture distinguishes types of forgery, including authorial claims inserted by editors, from other practices such as plagiarism, fabricated narratives, textual falsification, and mistaken attribution, providing a more precise framework for evaluating deceptive literature.

title: How Were Books Published in the Ancient World?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how books were published and circulated in the ancient world.
searchSummary: Explains how ancient books entered circulation without publishers, printing presses, copyright, or standardized copies. Authors shared finalized texts with associates, after which professional scribes, literate slaves, or ordinary readers copied and distributed them individually. Early Christian writings moved between congregations through repeated copying, introducing accidental and sometimes deliberate changes beyond an author's control; surviving manuscripts therefore differ, and textual scholars must compare later copies to reconstruct the earliest attainable wording of New Testament and other ancient works.

title: Ehrman & Licona: Are the Gospels Historically Reliable? Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the second part of a debate with Mike Licona on Gospel reliability.
searchSummary: Presents the second portion of Ehrman's debate with Mike Licona over the historical reliability of the Gospels. This segment largely features audience questions directed to both speakers, allowing them to clarify, defend, and challenge their positions after the principal presentations. Ehrman notes that viewers can understand much of it without watching the first part and supplies the video. The post does not summarize the answers, instead inviting readers to evaluate how each scholar handles probing questions.

title: The Miracle of New Life
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on new life as a nonliteral miracle.
searchSummary: Distinguishes literal supernatural miracles from the metaphorical wonder Ehrman finds throughout the natural world. Historical testimony cannot establish divine intervention when mistaken observation, deception, or other natural explanations remain more probable, yet galaxies, brains, consciousness, bodies, and life itself still inspire awe without requiring God. The birth of his children, and now a grandson, represents his closest experience of a miracle: a naturally explicable but personally incomprehensible appearance of new life that deepens gratitude and amazement.

title: The Marvels of Media Attention
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how media attention can affect the reach of trade books.
searchSummary: Explains why national media attention, rather than quality or paid advertising alone, largely determines whether a trade book reaches a substantial audience. Bart recounts learning this distinction after his first general-audience book and illustrates it with The Triumph of Christianity, whose Amazon ranking rose dramatically following a Fresh Air interview. He discusses authors' desire to be read, publishers' publicity efforts, and the continuing influence of major reviews, radio, television, podcasts, and social media.

title: Fresh Air Interview Tuesday March 20
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Fresh Air interview on The Triumph of Christianity.
searchSummary: Announces Ehrman's scheduled Fresh Air interview with Terry Gross, recorded principally to discuss his book The Triumph of Christianity. He notes that the original conversation lasted an hour and a half and would therefore be edited before broadcast. The very short post provides no account of the questions, arguments, or historical conclusions covered in the interview, identifying only its principal book-related focus and directing readers to the forthcoming program for the substance of their exchange.

title: Jesus and My First Girlfriend: A Blast From The Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a personal story about Jesus and a first girlfriend.
searchSummary: Recounts how Ehrman's first serious girlfriend unintentionally exposed the shallowness of his early born-again understanding. After converting at sixteen, he tried to persuade his Jewish former girlfriend that salvation required accepting Jesus, but could not answer why someone who already had God needed Jesus as well. His improvised response revealed how little he understood and helped motivate the intensive biblical and theological study that soon took him to Moody Bible Institute and supplied the confident answers he initially lacked.

title: Ehrman & Licona: Are the Gospels Historically Reliable? Part 1
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the first part of a debate with Mike Licona on Gospel reliability.
searchSummary: Introduces the first portion of Ehrman's public debate with Mike Licona on whether the Gospels are historically reliable. Hosted at Kennesaw State University before an audience largely sympathetic to Licona, the event includes extensive argument, rebuttal, and later audience questions. Ehrman emphasizes that the disagreement became animated while remaining friendly because the two scholars have a good personal relationship. The post provides the opening video and postpones the remainder of the exchange to a subsequent installment.

title: Scribes Who Injected the Idea of Atonement into Luke’s Gospel
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how scribes added atonement language to Luke's Gospel.
searchSummary: Argues that scribes added familiar Last Supper language about Jesus' body given and blood shed 'for you' to Luke 22. Elsewhere Luke-Acts presents Jesus' death as exposing human guilt and prompting repentance, not as an atoning sacrifice that itself removes sin. The addition aligned Luke with Pauline language and helped proto-orthodox Christians stress Jesus' real flesh, blood, and sacrificial death against docetic Christologies.

title: What Happened at the Last Supper?  A Textual Problem in Luke
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines a textual problem in Luke's Last Supper account.
searchSummary: Examines whether Luke's Last Supper originally described a cup, then bread, then another cup, or only the first cup and bread. The longer reading contains language familiar from 1 Corinthians, while important early witnesses omit it. The post argues that scribes had little reason to remove the disputed words but understandable reasons to add them, making the shorter and less familiar account more likely original.

title: The Golden Rule
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the Golden Rule in the Didache and its relation to Jesus traditions.
searchSummary: Explains why the Didache states the Golden Rule negatively even if its author knew Matthew's positive formulation. The rule circulated for centuries in Greek, Chinese, Jewish, and oral traditions, most often as a prohibition against doing what one hates, and the Didachist rephrased sayings rather than copying Matthew as Matthew copied Mark. Jesus' version was therefore neither the first expression nor the only form available, although he joined other Jewish teachers in making love of neighbor a summary of Torah.

title: Once More: The Interesting Text Called the Didache
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Didache and its form of the Golden Rule.

title: A Privileged View of Suffering
author: admin
description: Reflects on suffering from the perspective of privilege.
searchSummary: Defends a privileged person's right to reflect on others' suffering and its implications for belief in a caring, powerful God. People experiencing poverty or pain do not exclusively determine sound economic policy or theology, and their faith need not dictate another observer's conclusion. Ehrman refuses to impose his views on sufferers but argues that awareness of unequal hardship should govern his own conduct; compassionate response and practical aid matter more than claiming a ready explanation.

title: My Scholarly Project on the Afterlife
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a research proposal for a scholarly project on afterlife journeys.
searchSummary: Proposes a study of Christian journeys to heaven and hell within their pagan and Jewish settings. Moving from undifferentiated underworlds in Gilgamesh and Homer through moral judgment in Plato to detailed Christian punishments in the Apocalypses of Peter and Paul, Ehrman examines how such narratives promoted ethical and doctrinal priorities. The project asks how persecution, church conflict, asceticism, and charity shaped afterlife imagination and how these texts influenced religion, literature, art, near-death accounts, and doctrines of heaven, hell, and purgatory.

title: My Upcoming Writing Plans: The Afterlife and the Afterlife
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains plans for trade and scholarly books on the afterlife.

title: Why Women Came to be Silenced
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why women came to be silenced in early Christian communities.
searchSummary: Women held significant roles in early house churches partly because those gatherings occupied domestic space where women exercised greater responsibility. As Christianity grew more public, hierarchical, and concerned with social respectability, converts imported Roman gender assumptions and used scripture to defend male authority. Waning apocalyptic expectations and opposition to celibate women's independence ultimately restricted women from teaching, evangelizing, and leading, Christianizing the surrounding culture's patriarchal norms.

title: The Surprising Understanding of Gender in the Ancient World
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains ancient views of gender that shaped women's roles in early Christianity.

title: Reading The Triumph of Christianity at Quail Ridge Books
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a Quail Ridge Books reading from The Triumph of Christianity.
searchSummary: Presents a recording of Ehrman's February 2018 appearance at Quail Ridge Books in Raleigh for The Triumph of Christianity: How a Forbidden Religion Swept the World. He explains that the event combined approximately thirty minutes of readings from the new book with an audience question-and-answer session. The brief accompanying post does not summarize the book's historical argument, instead directing readers to the embedded video of the complete public program.

title: Early Christology: How I Changed My Mind
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on changing views about early Christology while writing How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Explains Ehrman's change from treating humanity and divinity as mutually exclusive categories to recognizing an ancient spectrum of divine status. Early Christians developed exaltation Christologies, incarnation Christologies, and hybrids in which Jesus became God's son at resurrection, baptism, birth, or through preexistence and incarnation. Because Jewish and pagan sources allowed different levels of divinity, the proper historical question is not simply whether a New Testament author calls Jesus God, but in what sense.

title: Futuristic Interpretations of the Book of Revelation
author: admin
description: Explains futuristic interpretations of Revelation and their relation to modern expectations.
searchSummary: Critiques futuristic interpretations that treat Revelation's visions as literal predictions of events in the reader's own era. The claim that chapter 9's locusts represent modern attack helicopters maps selected physical features onto military technology. It fails, however, because Revelation says the creatures cannot harm vegetation or kill people and can only torture them for five months. Ignoring those details distorts the text. A historical reading better understands the imagery as a metaphorical assurance of God's sovereignty over an evil world.

title: What Did Jesus Look Like?
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses what historians can infer about Jesus' physical appearance.

title: Do We Know How Paul Died?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines what can and cannot be known about Paul's death from early sources.

title: The Legend of Peter’s Martyrdom
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains legendary traditions about Peter's martyrdom and their value for resurrection arguments.

title: My Interview with Michael Shermer
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a Michael Shermer interview on The Triumph of Christianity and related topics.
searchSummary: Summarizes the subjects of Ehrman's Science Salon interview with skeptic and historian of science Michael Shermer, prompted by The Triumph of Christianity. Their wide-ranging conversation addresses modern atheism, religion and politics, the problem of evil, early explanations of Jesus as both human and divine, pagan beliefs about gods and the afterlife, and Christian appeals used in converting pagans. The post situates these issues within Shermer's work investigating supernatural and pseudoscientific claims through scientific skepticism.

title: Pilate’s *Own* Account of Why He Crucified Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses an apocryphal account in which Pilate explains why Jesus was crucified.
searchSummary: Presents the Report of Pontius Pilate, a fictional letter to Emperor Tiberius that recounts Jesus' ministry, death, and resurrection from the governor's perspective. Pilate describes spectacular healings, insists that Jewish pressure forced the crucifixion, and reports cosmic signs, angels, resurrected patriarchs, and divine punishment after Jesus rises. The narrative's central purposes are to magnify Jesus' supernatural power, absolve Pilate, and transfer responsibility for his death to Jewish opponents.

title: The Ironies of Jesus’ Trial
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares John's portrayal of Jesus' trial before Pilate with the other Gospels.
searchSummary: Examines John's distinctive trial narrative, where Jesus dies while Passover lambs are being prepared rather than after the Passover meal. Pilate repeatedly moves between Jesus and Jewish accusers, declares him innocent, and discusses kingship and truth. The timing and dialogue create theological irony: leaders seeking ritual purity and Passover salvation reject Jesus, whom John identifies as God's true sacrificial lamb. The narrative's chronology and characterization serve John's claim that Jesus' death provides salvation.

title: The Increasing Innocence of Pilate in the Death of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Traces the Gospels' increasing portrayal of Pilate as reluctant to execute Jesus.

title: Why Discrepancies Matter for Interpretation
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Mark's and Luke's different passion narratives matter for interpretation.
searchSummary: Explains how Mark's and Luke's contrasting passion narratives offer different theological responses to human suffering. Mark's abandoned and anguished Jesus suggests that God can bring salvation from suffering even when divine help is imperceptible; Luke's calm and compassionate Jesus models confidence that God remains present. Combining the accounts erases the distinct message each Gospel communicates to suffering readers and communities.

title: Why Differences and Discrepancies Matter Theologically/Religiously
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Gospel discrepancies matter theologically and religiously, not only historically.
searchSummary: Argues that Gospel discrepancies can be theologically valuable because differences reveal each author's distinctive message and purpose. Mark portrays Jesus dying in anguish and apparent abandonment, while Luke presents him as composed, compassionate, and confident in God. Treating every detail as part of one harmonized account obscures both portrayals and replaces the individual Gospels with a new composite narrative of Jesus' death.

title: A Welcome Review of The Triumph of Christianity
author: BDEhrman
description: Notes a New York Times review of The Triumph of Christianity and its discussion of Christian exclusivity.
searchSummary: Reproduces Tom Bissell's favorable New York Times review of The Triumph of Christianity. The review praises Ehrman's accessible historical synthesis and explains his account of Christianity's expansion through missionary exclusivity, steady exponential growth, and the gradual displacement of pagan worship. It also highlights Constantine's privileges for Christianity, the religion's appeal across social groups, its care for the needy, and the reversal by which Christians who once sought religious liberty later suppressed traditional religions after gaining imperial power.

title: Being Blindstruck by Triumph
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the origin of the idea for The Triumph of Christianity.

title: The Conversion of Constantine
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Constantine's conversion as a decisive event in the rise of Christianity.
searchSummary: Explains why Constantine's conversion in 312 transformed Christianity without immediately making it Rome's official religion or single-handedly ensuring its success. Imperial policy shifted from persecution to legal recognition, privilege, funding, and elite support, accelerating growth already underway. Ehrman contrasts exclusive Christian conversion with additive pagan worship, where adopting one deity did not require abandoning others, and situates Constantine's decision within an ancient world where religion, government, public welfare, and imperial security were inseparable.

title: Beginning the Triumph of Christianity
author: BDEhrman
description: Marks the first public book talk for The Triumph of Christianity.

title: How Was Jesus *Really* Born?  The Proto-Gospel of James
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Proto-Gospel of James and its expanded account of Jesus' birth.

title: Small Differences that Make a Difference
author: BDEhrman
description: Shows how small textual variants can affect interpretation of Jesus' birth story.
searchSummary: Examines a small variant in Luke 2 that changes Mary giving birth after arriving in Bethlehem to giving birth while traveling there. The latter reading in Codex Bezae resembles the Proto-Gospel of James, where labor begins en route and Jesus is born in a cave outside Bethlehem. Ehrman considers whether the scribe knew that noncanonical account, inherited another tradition, or independently heightened the narrative, showing how one phrase can alter geography and the story's relationship to prophecy.

title: Jesus Kissing Mary Magdalene: A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a discussion of the Gospel of Philip passage about Jesus kissing Mary Magdalene.

title: Do We KNOW the Original Words of the NT?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to claims that scholars can know the original words of the New Testament with virtual certainty.
searchSummary: Argues that abundant New Testament manuscripts do not establish certain knowledge of the authors' exact wording. Philippians circulated for about 150 years before the earliest fragmentary witness and 300 years before a complete copy, so an altered early exemplar could transmit changes to every surviving descendant without detection. Ehrman does not claim the reconstructed text is wrong; he claims certainty is unavailable, a problem sharpened when critics simultaneously insist nothing remains to investigate yet fund textual research.

title: On Being Controversial
author: admin
description: Reflects on the unexpected controversy surrounding Misquoting Jesus.

title: Do the Differences in Our Manuscripts Matter?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why manuscript differences can matter despite many insignificant variants.
searchSummary: Responds to claims that New Testament variants are insignificant because none overturns a cardinal Christian doctrine. Ehrman agrees that most differences are trivial and that doctrines usually draw support from multiple passages, but argues that interpretation matters independently of doctrinal survival. Variants can determine Luke's view of atonement, John's language about Jesus as God, or Luke's portrayal of Jesus' suffering. Losing entire biblical books would likewise be significant even if every doctrine remained defensible elsewhere.

title: Conservative Reactions to Misquoting Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes conservative evangelical reactions to Misquoting Jesus.

title: Misquoting Jesus and My Fundamentalist Faith
author: BDEhrman
description: Connects Misquoting Jesus with earlier fundamentalist assumptions about scripture.

title: Jesus and Paul: Similarities and Differences
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares the teachings of Jesus and Paul.
searchSummary: Compares Jesus and Paul as Jewish apocalyptic preachers who expected imminent divine intervention, emphasized faith, and treated love of neighbor as the law's fulfillment. They diverge over the coming judge, salvation, and Jesus' significance: Jesus proclaims a distinct Son of Man and prepares people through obedience to his interpretation of Torah, while Paul identifies Jesus as judge and centers faith, baptism, death, and resurrection. The evidence supports both continuity and transformation rather than one uncontested verdict.

title: What Is My Best Book for a General Audience?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on which general-audience book may be the strongest work.
searchSummary: Considers which of Bart's books is most useful, most popular, and best for general readers, beginning with Misquoting Jesus as his clear bestseller. He explains how he made the technical field of New Testament textual criticism accessible by identifying the questions that first fascinated him: scribal changes, famous passages absent from the earliest manuscripts, and uncertainty about original wording. The post distinguishes trade books from his scholarly monographs and textbooks.

title: Are Paul and Jesus on the Same Page?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Jesus and Paul represented the same religious message.
searchSummary: Contrasts Jesus' and Paul's responses to the question of eternal life through the rich man narrative. Jesus requires keeping Torah's commandments and surrendering wealth to the poor, whereas Paul teaches that justification cannot come through law but requires faith in Christ's death and resurrection and baptism. Jesus' invitation to follow him does not erase that difference, leaving his message about obedience before the Son of Man's kingdom distinct from Paul's gospel of salvation through the returning crucified and risen Christ.

title: Is Paul Given Too Much Credit?
author: BDEhrman
description: Questions whether Paul receives too much attention compared with other early Christian writings.
searchSummary: Questions whether scholars overstate Paul's influence on the Apostolic Fathers and early Christianity more broadly. Most writings in the collection neither name nor clearly use Paul, yet scholarship often treats that absence as a puzzle because the New Testament canon makes him appear uniquely dominant. Ehrman argues that Paul's own opponents and the loss of nearly all other pre-70 Christian writings should caution against assuming that familiar early Christian ideas originated with him or spread everywhere through his influence.

title: Was Jesus Given Special Treatment?
author: BDEhrman
description: Revisits whether Jesus received special burial treatment after crucifixion.
searchSummary: Warns against assuming that Jesus received exceptional burial treatment because later history made him uniquely important. Bart asks whether Pilate routinely released every crucified Jew, why no source records such a policy, and why only Jesus rather than the two men beside him would be spared normal exposure. Since Joseph of Arimathea is otherwise unattested and the Gospels were written decades later, Bart considers the burial benefactor probably legendary rather than evidence of Pilate's special accommodation.

title: Pilate, Who Never “Learned His Lesson”
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Pilate's character in Josephus to question claims about Jesus' burial.
searchSummary: Rejects the claim that Pilate learned to respect Jewish customs and therefore would have permitted Jesus's burial. Josephus records that Pilate later funded an aqueduct from the Temple treasury and used disguised soldiers to beat protesting Jews, causing numerous deaths. Together with Philo's condemnation of Pilate's corruption, cruelty, and executions, the episode portrays a consistently brutal governor rather than one likely to depart from Roman crucifixion practice out of sensitivity to Jewish burial expectations.

title: Pontius Pilate: A Sensitive Guy….
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether Pilate was likely to permit burial for a crucified victim.
searchSummary: Argues that Pilate's handling of Roman standards does not show sensitivity to Jewish customs or make Jesus's burial likely. Josephus says Pilate knowingly introduced imperial images at night, resisted six days of protest, and threatened mass execution before demonstrators offered their necks rather than yield. Bart concludes that Pilate withdrew to avoid the political consequences of slaughtering Judea's leaders, not because he learned respect for Jewish law, and remained brutal afterward.

title: Illuminating Exercises: The Position Paper Assignments for My NT Greek Class
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes position-paper assignments for a Greek New Testament course.
searchSummary: Presents weekly analytical exercises for an advanced course in New Testament Greek. Students compare Christologies, miracle stories, infancy narratives, Jesus and Paul on Jewish law, Gospel passion accounts, and the eschatology of 1 and 2 Thessalonians. They also evaluate difficult textual variants, analyze Paul's argument in Romans, and collate Greek manuscripts letter by letter. The assignments integrate close reading, exegesis, historical interpretation, textual criticism, and direct work with handwritten witnesses.

title: Was Paul a Misogynist?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Paul wrote the command for women to be silent in church.

title: Paul and His Female Disciple Thecla
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Thecla traditions as background for debates about Paul and women.

title: Paul’s Views of Women
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses Paul's views of women and the possibility of later textual additions.

title: Pre-order Triumph of Christianity and Get Some Serious Perks!!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces preorder perks for The Triumph of Christianity.

title: Request for Help!   Your Favorite Podcasts.
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks readers for podcast recommendations before publication of The Triumph of Christianity.

title: Accessing the Bart Ehrman Blog Podcast
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how to access the Bart Ehrman Blog Podcast.

title: My Greek New Testament Course
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a Greek New Testament course focused on textual criticism and close reading.
searchSummary: Presents the syllabus for an advanced Greek New Testament course requiring prior study of the language. Students improve Koine Greek through translation, learn textual criticism and manuscript reading, and interpret passages through grammar, vocabulary, and literary structure. Position papers, manuscript collations, quizzes, a textual-variant research paper, and a translation examination connect linguistic proficiency with reconstructing early wording, explaining scribal changes, and evaluating the theological or historical significance of competing readings.

title: The Blog Podcast
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Bart Ehrman Blog Podcast and its production.

title: Were Cut and Paste Jobs Common in Antiquity?  Guest Post by Brent Nongbri
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Brent Nongbri's guest post on ancient cut-and-paste literary practices.

title: More Cutting and Pasting?  Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores whether Philippians may be a composite letter.

title: Can Historians Be Neutral?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains whether historians can be neutral when evaluating controversial evidence.
searchSummary: Rejects simple claims of objectivity because every historian brings assumptions and perspective, while still insisting that arguments can be evaluated fairly. Ehrman recommends becoming deliberately disinterested by researching and presenting the strongest case for the opposing position before deciding. His student debates require participants to write persuasively against the side they will defend orally. This exercise exposes valid contrary evidence, reduces confirmation bias, and helps historical, religious, or political judgments rest on comparative argument rather than prior comfort.

title: My Long Favorite Pauline Letter: Philippians
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Philippians as a possible composite Pauline letter.

title: January Dinner Full!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces that the January blog dinner is full.

title: February Dinner Full!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces that the February blog dinner is full.

title: Speaking Engagements and Blog Dinners for January and February
author: BDEhrman
description: Lists speaking engagements and blog dinners for early 2018.

title: Is 2 Corinthians *FIVE* Letters?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the theory that 2 Corinthians may combine multiple Pauline letters.

title: Did Romans Allow Jews to Bury Crucified Victims?  Readers’ Mailbag January 1, 2018
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether Romans allowed burial of crucified Jewish victims.
searchSummary: Reassesses Josephus's statement that Jews buried crucified offenders before sunset. Bart questions whether Josephus means Roman victims, exaggerates Jewish piety and Roman mercy, or describes a universal practice; mass crucifixions during war plainly remained unburied. Even if lesser offenders sometimes received burial in peaceful conditions, Bart argues that Jesus was executed as a rival king and enemy of the state, precisely the kind of victim Rome exposed to deter resistance.

title: Year in Review 2017!
author: BDEhrman
description: Reviews the blog's 2017 activity and charitable results.
searchSummary: Reviews the blog's performance during 2017, when it published more than 270 posts, received 15,500 comments, and raised $134,000 for charity, pushing lifetime distributions above $500,000. Bart reflects on the time required to write posts and answer readers while making scholarship accessible. He explores tiered monthly sustaining memberships as a way to increase donations without raising the basic price, invites suggestions, and thanks Steven Ray and the participating community.

title: Are There Cut-and-Paste Jobs in the New Testament?  The Case of 2 Corinthians
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces 2 Corinthians as a possible cut-and-paste composition.

title: The Virgin Birth and the Gospel of John: A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a discussion of John and the absence of a virgin birth story.
searchSummary: Argues that John's Christmas reading describes incarnation, not virgin birth. The Prologue presents the preexistent divine Word becoming the human Jesus but says nothing about Mary conceiving without sex; John may even preserve awareness of accusations about Jesus' parentage. Matthew and Luke teach virginal conception without a preexistent Christ, whereas John teaches preexistence without virginal conception. The later creed combines these separate traditions into incarnation through Mary, a doctrinal synthesis absent from every individual Gospel.

title: Did They Crucify the Wrong Guy?  Jesus’ Identity Switch.
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains a Coptic Apocalypse of Peter tradition in which Jesus and Christ are separated at the crucifixion.
secondaryKeywords: Second Treatise of the Great Seth

title: Did Jesus’ Death Matter?  The Intriguing View of the Coptic Apocalypse of Peter
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines the Coptic Apocalypse of Peter's view of Jesus' death and salvation.

title: Christmas Reflection 2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on Christmas from a secular humanist and formerly Christian perspective.
searchSummary: Explains why Christmas still attracts Ehrman as a secular humanist who considers its biblical stories largely unhistorical. Family memories, shared food, goodwill, meaningful giving, and the image of a loving God embody values he cherishes, even while he rejects commercialization and acknowledges the season's loneliness and pain for many people. If he believed in God, he would proclaim this compassionate figure who brings peace, healing, and wholeness rather than wrath, punishment, violence, and eternal torment.

title: Is the Christmas Story a Myth?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains different senses of myth in relation to the Christmas story.

title: Is the Didache One Document or Three?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether the Didache is a single document or a compilation of sources.

title: The Ethical Teachings of the Didache
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents ethical teaching from the Didache's two-ways section.

title: Blog Christmas Gift Idea #2:  Gift Subscriptions
author: BDEhrman
description: Suggests blog gift subscriptions as Christmas presents.

title: Blog Christmas Gift Idea #1!    Free Memberships Still Available!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces that free memberships remain available before Christmas.

title: Managing the Time!  Readers’ Mailbag December 17, 2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to a reader question about time management.
searchSummary: Explains how years of competing academic, employment, ministry, and family demands taught Ehrman to manage time through intense concentration and advance planning. While preparing doctoral examinations, he calculated every available study hour and assigned specific time limits to a large multilingual bibliography. That discipline now lets him complete blog and scholarly tasks quickly, although interruptions can be jarring and the approach has personal costs; his main practical advice is to focus fully on one task before moving to the next.

title: A Final Statement on a Different Approach to the Synoptic Problem: Evan Powell
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Evan Powell's final statement on an alternative Synoptic Problem proposal.
searchSummary: Presents Evan Powell's defense of an alternative Synoptic solution in which Luke used Mark and Matthew later used both Mark and Luke. He argues that standard Two-Document, Farrer, and Griesbach theories each require implausible editorial behavior and that the Matthew-last proposal offers a simpler, more comprehensive account. The essay answers Mark Goodacre's objection that Matthew treats sources inconsistently and encourages readers to consider Alan Garrow's statistical case rather than limiting analysis to established hypotheses.

title: Brief Reply to Garrow
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares Mark Goodacre's brief reply to Alan Garrow on Matthew and Luke.

title: Back Again: Did Matthew Use Luke?  Alan Garrow’s Reply to Mark Goodacre
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Alan Garrow's reply to Mark Goodacre on whether Matthew used Luke.
searchSummary: Presents Alan Garrow's response to Mark Goodacre in a debate over whether Matthew knew and used Luke. Garrow distinguishes the reconstructed Q document from a broader collection of shared resources and argues that Matthew plausibly conflated Mark, Luke, and material such as the Didache. He contends that this model avoids editorial difficulties in both the Farrer and Two-Document hypotheses while explaining close verbal agreements between Matthew and Luke.

title: Did Matthew Copy Luke?  Mark Goodacre’s Rebuttal
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Mark Goodacre's rebuttal of the claim that Matthew copied Luke.
searchSummary: Presents Mark Goodacre's critique of Alan Garrow's claim that Matthew copied Luke while also using Mark and the Didache. Garrow explains high verbal agreement as Matthew copying Luke without another source and lower agreement as source conflation. Goodacre argues that passages where Matthew also follows Mark can still agree closely with Luke, while single-source passages can agree loosely, so Garrow's proposed relationship between source distraction and verbal agreement does not hold.

title: A $1000 Challenge to Me:  Did the Author of Matthew Use Luke?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a blog challenge over whether Matthew used Luke.
searchSummary: Introduces a scholarly challenge to Alan Garrow's claim that Matthew used both Mark and Luke, eliminating the need for the hypothetical Q source. A blog member offers a charitable donation for an expert response, while Ehrman cautions that arguments persuasive to nonspecialists may contain problems readily visible to trained scholars. Synoptic Problem specialist Mark Goodacre volunteers to evaluate Garrow's case, with Garrow and the questioner invited to reply; the actual refutation is reserved for the following post.

title: The Pope and the Lord’s Prayer
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Pope Francis's comments on the Lord's Prayer and translation.
searchSummary: Evaluates Pope Francis's proposal to render the Lord's Prayer as asking God not to let believers fall into temptation. Ehrman explains that Matthew's Greek unambiguously says, Do not bring us into temptation or trial, without mentioning Satan. Because the petition appears in both Matthew and Luke and fits Jesus' apocalyptic message, he considers it likely historical and interprets it as asking God to spare followers from end-time testing.

title: Is the Blog Meaningful for You?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the blog's meaning for readers and its charitable purpose.
searchSummary: Uses feedback from a member dinner to make a year-end appeal and explain the charities supported by the blog. Bart asks readers who find the scholarship meaningful to make a personally generous donation, noting that giving had declined and that fundraising motivates his substantial writing and moderation work. He describes Urban Ministries of Durham, the regional Food Bank, CARE, and Doctors Without Borders, explaining their local and international work against hunger, homelessness, poverty, emergencies, and medical crises.
secondaryKeywords: Food Bank of Central and Eastern North Carolina

title: Free Memberships for those Who Need Them!
author: admin
description: Announces free memberships for readers unable to pay.

title: A Very Strange Saying:  From the Gospel of Peter?
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses a strange saying that may come from the lost Gospel of Peter.

title: The Exasperatingly Fragmentary Gospel of Peter: Readers’ Mailbag December 4, 2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the fragmentary state of the Gospel of Peter.

title: Could Q Have Been Lost?  Readers’ Mailbag December 3, 2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to whether a hypothetical Q source could have been lost.

title: Last Minute: Dinner on Thursday?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a last-minute dinner opening in Durham.

title: Redaction Criticism of the Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains redaction criticism and how Gospel writers shaped inherited sources.
searchSummary: Explains redaction criticism as the study of how Gospel authors edited inherited sources to express their own theology. Because Matthew and Luke used Mark, their additions, deletions, and alterations can disclose distinctive emphases that harmonization obscures. Comparing Mark's and Luke's passion narratives reveals different portrayals of Jesus, while Matthew's added genealogy and infancy stories establish Jesus as Jewish, Davidic, and messianic. Gospel differences therefore provide positive interpretive evidence rather than merely demonstrating contradiction.

title: And Then There Was Q
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Q as a proposed sayings source behind Matthew and Luke.

title: Arguments for Markan Priority (that Mark was the first Gospel written)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains arguments for Markan priority in the Synoptic Problem.
searchSummary: Explains why most scholars regard Mark as the earliest Synoptic Gospel and a source for Matthew and Luke. Their patterns of verbal agreement, shared narrative sequence, and smoothing of Mark's awkward or difficult wording fit independent use of Mark better than competing directions of dependence. Mark's brevity also does not make it an abridgment, since its versions of shared stories are usually longer. Together these observations support Markan priority as the most economical explanation of the Synoptic relationships.

title: Jesus’ Death and Resurrection in Mark: Another Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Mark's death and resurrection narrative reveals Jesus' identity.
searchSummary: Explains how Mark reveals the meaning of Jesus' death and resurrection despite the disciples' continuing failure to understand. The torn Temple curtain presents Jesus' death as the sacrifice opening access to God, while a gentile centurion becomes the first human to recognize the suffering Son. At the empty tomb, the women flee without telling anyone, leaving the disciples ignorant. The abrupt ending reinforces Mark's irony: readers understand Jesus' identity, resurrection, gentile mission, and costly discipleship when his followers do not.

title: Mark’s Suffering Son of God: A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Mark's portrayal of Jesus as the suffering Son of God.
searchSummary: Presents Mark's Jesus as the suffering Son of God whose death defines both messiahship and discipleship. After each of three passion predictions, the disciples seek power or reject suffering, and Jesus answers that followers must embrace service, loss, and self-sacrifice.
