The narrative then advances through Jerusalem conflict, apocalyptic teaching, abandonment, trial, and crucifixion. Mark overturns expectations of a triumphant Messiah by making rejection and death the necessary expression of Jesus' mission and the pattern for his followers.

title: Jesus in Mark: Who Knew?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains who understands Jesus' identity in Mark and who does not.
searchSummary: Examines Mark's theme that almost no character understands Jesus' identity. God, demons, the narrator, and readers know he is God's Son, while family, neighbors, authorities, and disciples remain confused. The gradual healing of a blind man symbolizes Peter's partial insight: he recognizes the Messiah but rejects the suffering that Mark considers essential. Peter's incomplete perception becomes satanic misperception because Mark defines Jesus not as a conventional powerful deliverer but as the suffering Son of God.

title: The Women in Matthew’s Genealogy: Answer to a Reader
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines the women in Matthew's genealogy and possible implications for Jesus' birth.
searchSummary: Examines why Matthew includes Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba, and Mary in a genealogy that would normally name only men. The first four may signal that gentiles have always participated in God's saving plan, though Mary herself was Jewish. More persuasively, each earlier woman was connected with a sexual situation outsiders could regard as scandalous, yet God used it to advance divine purposes. They therefore prepare readers to reinterpret Mary's premarital pregnancy as miraculous rather than illegitimate.

title: Jesus’ (Young?) Mother and (Half?) Brothers? The Proto-Gospel of James
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses the Proto-Gospel of James on Mary's age and Jesus' family.

title: Jesus’ Mother and Brothers in Mark
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Mark's reference to Jesus' mother and brothers.
searchSummary: Examines why Mark calls Jesus "the son of Mary" and names his brothers and sisters without mentioning Joseph. Mark contains no birth narrative and portrays Jesus' mother and brothers as believing he is out of his mind, suggesting that Mary knows nothing of a miraculous conception. Explanations based on Joseph's death or a virgin birth are therefore weak. The post considers, without endorsing, whether unknown paternity and later efforts to reinterpret unusual birth circumstances could explain Mark's wording.

title: Jesus Rejected by His Own Townspeople in Mark
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Mark's story of Jesus being rejected by the people of Nazareth.
searchSummary: Analyzes Mark's account of Jesus being rejected in Nazareth as groundwork for comparison with Luke. His townspeople know him as an ordinary manual worker from an unremarkable family, take offense at his teaching, and limit his miracles through unbelief. Mark's statement that Jesus could perform only a few healings creates tension between divine power and human faith. The story may combine an inherited claim that rejection prevented miracles with Mark's qualification that Jesus nevertheless retained some power.

title: Paul’s Exalted Self-Image: The Fulfillment of Ancient Prophecy
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes Paul's sense of mission as fulfillment of ancient prophecy.

title: What Is the Original Text of the Gospels?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the difficulty of defining the original text of the Gospels.
searchSummary: Explores why original text is difficult to define for a Gospel shaped by drafting, revision, sources, dictation, and later editions. For John, the first draft, corrected publication, possible second edition with chapter 21, incorporated signs source, spoken dictation, and secretarial transcription represent different textual stages. Scholars may instead seek the initial text behind all surviving copies, but that ancestor could itself be a later altered copy, leaving earlier forms unrecoverable.

title: How Do I Read Books?  A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts advice on how to read books efficiently.
searchSummary: Explains that scholarly books should be read according to their importance, novelty, and relevance rather than with a single universal method. Ehrman reads essential unfamiliar works completely, highlights them, and records detailed notes, while familiar or less useful books may require only their table of contents, introduction, conclusion, reviews, or selected chapters. This deliberate triage allows researchers to master large bodies of scholarship while preserving close attention for sources that contribute evidence or arguments they genuinely need.

title: Getting Together and Speaking Gigs
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces speaking events and opportunities to meet blog members.

title: Ehrman vs Licona Debate on the Resurrection
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a debate with Mike Licona on the resurrection.
searchSummary: Presents an audio debate between Ehrman and conservative Christian scholar Mike Licona over whether historical evidence establishes that Jesus rose from the dead. Recorded for Justin Brierley's Unbelievable program after Licona published a major historiographical study, the exchange moves through several related questions and increasingly direct scholarly challenges. The post identifies the participants and their central disagreement but does not summarize their arguments, instead providing the recording for readers to assess the historical and methodological case themselves.

title: Why Do Translators Include Passages They Know Are Not Original?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why translators sometimes include passages judged not original.
searchSummary: Explains why translations inconsistently retain famous passages scholars regard as nonoriginal. The NRSV relegates the Trinitarian addition in 1 John to a note but prints the woman taken in adultery and multiple endings of Mark in brackets because they are ancient, beloved, and expected by readers. Ehrman presents both pastoral and commercial explanations: translators want to serve churches and ensure adoption, even when familiar tradition complicates textual consistency.

title: 666 and Scribal  Changes of the Text
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses how scribal changes affected the number of the beast in Revelation.
searchSummary: Explains why discovery of an early manuscript reading 616 does not displace 666 as Revelation's number of the beast. Both numbers can encode Nero Caesar through alternative Hebrew spellings, but 666 appears in far more witnesses and in the earlier papyrus P47, while its triple six carries symbolic contrast with the divine number seven. Ehrman concludes that 666 was probably original and that scribes who spelled Nero without a final consonant produced the meaningful alternative 616.

title: More on 666: The Number of the Beast: A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to questions about 666 and 616 in Revelation.
searchSummary: Explains Revelation's number of the beast through ancient gematria. Rather than identifying a modern dictator or politician, the beast symbolizes Rome and its persecuting rulers. The Hebrew letters of Caesar Neron add to 666, while the alternative spelling Nero omits a letter worth fifty and yields 616, the reading found in some manuscripts. Traditions that Nero would return from death may explain the beast's healed wound. Revelation thus anticipates God's overthrow of Roman imperial power and vindication of persecuted Christians.

title: Were All Textual Changes Made by Scribes by 300 CE? Readers’ Mailbag November 5, 2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains whether major scribal changes were already made by 300 CE.

title: Did Jesus Mean that Literally?  Rewards and Punishments in the Afterlife
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Jesus' afterlife language about rewards and punishments should be read literally.
searchSummary: Argues that Matthew's sheep-and-goats judgment is a literal eschatological prediction rather than a parable, despite its figurative animal comparison. Unlike everyday stories conveying hidden lessons, the scene describes a unique future event consistent with multiply attested sayings about the Son of Man as judge. Ehrman concludes that Jesus probably expected genuine eternal reward and punishment, but at history's end rather than immediately after individual death. The judgment concerns resurrected bodies, not disembodied souls traveling to heaven or hell.

title: Another Translation Project:  The Apocryphal Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the translation project behind an edition of the Apocryphal Gospels.
searchSummary: Recounts the development of Ehrman and Zlatko Plese's multilingual edition of early non-canonical Gospels. Ehrman explains why moving beyond a Greek-Latin Loeb proposal allowed them to include important Coptic works, how they divided the translation work according to expertise, and what scholarly apparatus accompanied each text. He also distinguishes the academic edition, The Apocryphal Gospels, from its later reader-oriented counterpart, The Other Gospels.

title: The Loeb Apostolic Fathers: The Challenges (Again)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains challenges in producing a facing-page translation of the Apostolic Fathers.
searchSummary: Describes the scholarly and practical decisions required to produce Ehrman's facing-page Loeb edition of the Apostolic Fathers. The work involved establishing the original-language text from variant manuscripts, selecting readings for a concise critical apparatus, choosing between literal and idiomatic translation, translating each passage carefully, and introducing every document and the collection. Ehrman presents translation as painstaking scholarship that combines textual criticism, historical research, interpretation, and English style.

title: The Apostolic Fathers: Serendipity Strikes
author: admin
description: Recounts how the Loeb Apostolic Fathers translation project came about.
searchSummary: Recounts how a graduate seminar and a chance taxi conversation led Ehrman to produce a new Loeb edition of the Apostolic Fathers. His students identified dated introductions, antiquated English, newly discovered manuscripts, and questionable renderings in Kirsopp Lake's 1912 edition. After Ehrman raised those problems with Harvard University Press at a scholarly meeting, the Loeb editor unexpectedly invited him to propose the replacement translation project.

title: Taking the Temperature of the Blog October 2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks readers for feedback on the blog.

title: Translating the Apostolic Fathers: A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts reflections on translating the Apostolic Fathers.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's translation of the Apostolic Fathers by distinguishing the ability to read an ancient language from the demands of publishing a reliable translation. He explains the Loeb Classical Library's facing-page format, its manuscript apparatus, and the importance of Kirsopp Lake's earlier edition. The post also identifies the works collected as the Apostolic Fathers and explains why scholars call their authors early proto-orthodox Christians rather than direct companions of Jesus' apostles.

title: The Sheep and the Goats
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the sheep and goats passage as a teaching about final judgment.
searchSummary: Interprets the sheep and goats as Jesus' description of the Son of Man's judgment rather than a parable about souls entering heaven or hell at death. People from all nations receive eternal life or punishment according to whether they fed, clothed, welcomed, visited, and cared for anyone in need. The criterion is compassionate conduct, not Christian belief or knowledge of Jesus; the passage concerns those alive at history's end and does not explain the fate of people who die beforehand.

title: The Son of Man, Pericopes, and the Complexities of Biblical Scholarship
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why terms like Son of Man and pericope make biblical scholarship hard to communicate.
searchSummary: Explains why scholarly conclusions can seem arbitrary when their underlying layers of evidence and method remain unstated. Using Gospel pericopes, Ehrman shows that adjacent passages may have circulated independently before an evangelist joined them, so one saying cannot automatically determine the original meaning of another. Matthew's placement of Son of Man passages reflects his editorial understanding, but historians must analyze each tradition's literary form, transmission history, and probable origin before attributing its claims to Jesus.

title: The Academic Study of the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces academic study of the New Testament for students without prior background.
searchSummary: Contrasts devotional reading of the New Testament with academic historical study. Church readers may ask what the Lord's Prayer teaches believers, while historians ask about its sources, versions, apocalyptic setting, and connection to Jesus. Students with extensive religious training can struggle because they must suspend familiar assumptions before understanding these questions, whereas newcomers often learn the historical approach more readily. Ehrman presents the approaches as different in purpose, evidence, and conclusions rather than inherently unequal.

title: Was My Weird Background a Help or a Hindrance: Mailbag October 22, 2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on whether a fundamentalist background helped or hindered scholarly work.
searchSummary: Evaluates how Ehrman's fundamentalist education both helped and hindered his development as a secular biblical scholar. Moody Bible Institute gave him unusually deep knowledge of Scripture, disciplined study habits, and practical ministry experience, but it organized every subject through assumptions he later had to overturn. Becoming a critical scholar therefore required not merely adding information but reconstructing an entire intellectual, ethical, political, and social worldview, a disruptive paradigm shift that colleagues with less rigid religious backgrounds generally did not face.

title: Decent Burials for Crucified Victims: A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses evidence about whether crucified victims could receive decent burial.
searchSummary: Reviews four arguments for allowing Jesus a decent burial: Jewish law, Yehohanan's buried remains, Josephus's rescue of crucified associates, and Philo's report of holiday clemency. Bart finds none closely analogous because Romans controlled Jesus's body, Yehohanan's circumstances are unknown, Josephus sought to halt executions, and Philo describes an exceptional imperial birthday concession to relatives. He concludes that prompt burial remains conceivable but historically unusual and improbable.

title: Jesus, the Sheep, and the Goats
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Matthew's sheep and goats passage likely goes back to Jesus.
searchSummary: Uses the criterion of dissimilarity to argue that Jesus probably taught the sheep-and-goats judgment in Matthew 25. The passage makes care for hungry, sick, imprisoned, poor, and displaced people, rather than belief in Jesus' death and resurrection, the basis for entering eternal life. Because later Christians centered salvation on faith in Christ, they were unlikely to invent this formulation. The saying therefore reflects Jesus' expectation that the coming Son of Man would judge people by compassionate treatment of the needy.

title: How Do We Know What Jesus Said or Did?  The Criterion of Dissimilarity in Practice
author: BDEhrman
description: Demonstrates the criterion of dissimilarity with Gospel traditions about Jesus.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: Are Jews and Christians Monotheists?  Mailbag October 15, 2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores whether Judaism and Christianity should be described as monotheistic or henotheistic.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: Were the Disciples Martyred for Believing the Resurrection? A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Revisits the claim that apostles died for belief in the resurrection.

title: How Old Was Jesus at His Baptism, Start of His Ministry & Death?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines what can be known about Jesus' age at baptism, ministry, and death.

title: Explaining Jesus’ Apocalyptic Assumptions
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the apocalyptic assumptions behind Jesus' teaching.
searchSummary: Explains the assumptions behind Jesus's apocalyptic understanding of resurrection and eternal life. Because God created the material world and body as good, evil resulted from rebellious angels or humans rather than a defect in God; divine sovereignty therefore required their restoration. Bart argues that Jesus and related Jewish apocalypticists expected God to defeat evil, raise the dead into perfected immortal bodies, and renew earthly creation, not release disembodied souls to transcend material existence.

title: The Preaching of Jesus in a Nutshell
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Jesus' preaching about the kingdom, judgment, wealth, and the afterlife.
searchSummary: Summarizes Jesus' preaching as an apocalyptic announcement of God's imminent earthly kingdom. The Son of Man would overthrow evil powers, reverse the fortunes of rich and poor, and judge people within Jesus' generation; preparation required loving God and neighbor through radical care for those in need. Followers already previewed the kingdom through peace, generosity, healing, and inclusion, but these ethics sought readiness for divine intervention rather than gradual social reform during a long future Jesus did not expect.

title: The Skeletal Remains of Yehohanan: Readers Mailbag October 8, 2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses the crucified remains of Yehohanan and what they imply about burial practices.
searchSummary: Evaluates the archaeological remains of Yehohanan, whose ankle still held a crucifixion nail, as evidence for Jesus's burial. Bart argues that this solitary case cannot establish a pattern because Yehohanan's social status, offense, and time on the cross are unknown. Disputed broken bones may belong to another person or reflect removal after death. He concludes that the find does not show same-day burial or closely parallel Jesus's execution as an enemy of Rome.

title: Reasonable Doubts – How Jesus Became God
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a Reasonable Doubts interview on How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Introduces a Reasonable Doubts podcast interview about How Jesus Became God. Ehrman discusses how followers transformed their understanding of Jesus from an apocalyptic Jewish prophet into a divine figure, the historical problem at the center of the book. The post identifies hosts Jeremy Beahan and Justin Schieber, notes the program's recognition as a religious podcast, and provides the complete recorded conversation rather than developing a separate written argument.

title: Is This the Same Teacher?  Jesus in John and the Synoptics.
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Jesus' teaching in John with the Synoptic Gospels.
searchSummary: Contrasts Jesus' teachings in John with the Synoptic Gospels. The Synoptics emphasize parables, repentance, God's coming kingdom, and future resurrection, whereas John concentrates on Jesus' heavenly identity and present salvation. Its seven symbolic "I am" sayings and absolute claims may identify Jesus with God's revealed name. Believers already possess eternal life and belong to the world above, transforming apocalyptic dualism between present and future ages into a spatial division between the world below and heaven.

title: Jesus’ Miracles in John and the Synoptics
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Jesus' miracles in John with miracle stories in the Synoptic Gospels.
searchSummary: Compares Mark's raising of Jairus' daughter with John's raising of Lazarus to show how each Gospel uses miracles differently. Mark's delay is accidental and the healing private; John's Jesus deliberately waits for Lazarus to die, then raises him before a crowd so people will believe. The Synoptic Jesus refuses miraculous proof of his identity, while John calls such deeds "signs" and makes them public demonstrations that Jesus is Messiah and Son of God.
topics: Signs in the Gospel of John

title: (Birthday) Gifts and (Speaking) Gigs
author: BDEhrman
description: Mentions birthday-related blog giving and upcoming speaking events.

title: Differences Between John and the Synoptics
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains major differences between John and the Synoptic Gospels.
searchSummary: Catalogs major content differences between John and the Synoptic Gospels to explain why John is less useful for reconstructing Jesus' historical teaching. John lacks their virgin birth, baptism, temptation, parables, exorcisms, transfiguration, Lord's Supper, Gethsemane prayer, and Sanhedrin trial. Conversely, most of John's signs and extended dialogues appear nowhere else. Shared material concentrates in the passion narrative, but the overall selection of Jesus' words and deeds creates a substantially different account from the earlier Gospels.

title: Lunch in Boston?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks about arranging a blog lunch in Boston.

title: An Introduction to the Gospel of John
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces John's Gospel and explains why it is used cautiously for historical Jesus questions.
searchSummary: Introduces John as an ancient biography whose Prologue identifies Jesus as God's preexistent creative Word made human. Chapters 1-12 recount a multi-year public ministry in which seven signs validate Jesus' claims to heavenly origin, while Jewish opponents reject him. Chapters 13-17 compress his final meal, foot washing, Farewell Discourse, promise of the Spirit, and prayer into one evening. Chapters 18-21 narrate arrest, trial, crucifixion, resurrection, and appearances that confirm Jesus is alive and divine.

title: Jesus’ Teaching About the Kingdom of God
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Jesus' teaching about the kingdom of God in relation to afterlife expectation.
searchSummary: Explains that Jesus' kingdom of God was not heaven as the destination of a soul after death or merely God's rule within an individual heart. Drawing on Jewish royal and apocalyptic traditions, Jesus announced an earthly realm where God would rule through chosen representatives, people would enter or be excluded, and the faithful would eat, drink, and govern. Its arrival would overthrow present oppressive powers in an imminent judgment, making the news hopeful for sufferers but threatening for existing rulers.

title: Paul on Trial for the Resurrection
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Paul's trial in Acts to illustrate debates over resurrection among Jewish groups.
searchSummary: Uses Paul's trial before the Sanhedrin in Acts 23 to illustrate ancient Jewish disagreement over resurrection. In the story Paul divides Pharisees and Sadducees by claiming he is prosecuted for the Pharisaic hope of resurrection, prompting Roman intervention. Ehrman doubts the scene is historical because Pharisees apparently did not serve on the aristocratic council, yet its theological contrast is plausible: Pharisees expected a future resurrection and judgment, while Sadducees denied resurrection and probably any meaningful afterlife.

title: Is Luke’s Christology Consistent?   A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores whether Luke's Christology is internally consistent.
searchSummary: Explores Luke's inconsistent placement of when Jesus becomes Messiah, Lord, Savior, and Son of God. Luke-Acts associates these identities variously with Jesus' birth, lineage, baptism, ministry, and resurrection rather than reserving each title for one moment. This pattern supports the baptismal reading 'Today I have begotten you' as compatible with Luke's Christology, while explaining why later scribes concerned about adoptionism may have changed it.

title: Did Luke Have a Doctrine of the Atonement?  Mailbag September 24, 2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Luke-Acts lacks a clear doctrine of atonement.
searchSummary: Argues that Luke-Acts does not present Jesus' death as an atoning sacrifice. Luke removes or changes Mark's atonement language, and the apostles' speeches in Acts emphasize resurrection and repentance rather than forgiveness produced by the crucifixion. The Last Supper words about Jesus' body and blood being given 'for you' were likely added by scribes to align Luke with sacrificial theology and affirm Jesus' physical body against docetic Christians.

title: Does the Book of Acts Underplay the Significance of Jesus’ Death?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Acts underplays the saving significance of Jesus' death.
searchSummary: Argues that Acts emphasizes Jesus' resurrection while largely omitting Paul's understanding of his death as an atoning sacrifice. Its missionary speeches portray the crucifixion chiefly as an unjust human act reversed by God, who raises and exalts Jesus; sinners receive forgiveness through repentance and baptism rather than faith in the saving power of his death. Peter's Pentecost speech even says God made Jesus Lord and Messiah at the resurrection, revealing a distinctive theology of salvation and exaltation.

title: Two Other Ancient Jewish Sects
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Essenes and the Fourth Philosophy as ancient Jewish sects.
searchSummary: Surveys the Essenes and the Fourth Philosophy as two Jewish movements described by Josephus. The Essenes associated with Qumran maintained communal property, strict purity, rigorous law observance, and an imminent apocalyptic hope reflected in the Dead Sea Scrolls. The Fourth Philosophy encompassed resistance movements such as Sicarii and Zealots, who defended Israel's divine claim to the land through assassinations, kidnappings, revolt, and ultimately violent opposition to Rome.

title: Ancient Jewish Sects:  Pharisees and Sadducees
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Pharisees and Sadducees as Jewish sects with different views of resurrection.
searchSummary: Introduces the Pharisees and Sadducees as small but influential Jewish sects that differed over obedience, authority, and political accommodation. Pharisees developed an oral law to clarify Torah and preserve purity in daily life, while Sadducees centered on the priesthood, Temple, and written Torah alone. Their different approaches also shaped beliefs about resurrection and angels, with Pharisaic traditions eventually contributing to rabbinic Judaism after the Temple's destruction.

title: Reviewing the Afterlife
author: BDEhrman
description: Returns to the development of afterlife views in ancient Judaism and Christianity.

title: How Changing My Views Affected My Relationships
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on how leaving conservative Christianity affected relationships.
searchSummary: Explains how Ehrman's changing biblical views disrupted friendships, church ties, and family relationships. As graduate study exposed Gospel discrepancies and other historical problems, he shifted from outspoken evangelical inerrancy to liberal Christianity, contradicting beliefs he had once persuaded others to accept. Some friendships disappeared, family arguments continued for years, and he changed churches. He eventually concluded that preserving loving relationships matters more than persuading relatives to share religious conclusions, and that many meaningful connections can flourish without discussing disputed beliefs.

title: My Favorite Anecdote about Jesus and the Afterlife: Teeth Will Be Provided!
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a humorous anecdote about Jesus, resurrection, and the afterlife.

title: Controversy Sells!
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on whether controversy helps generate reader interest in the afterlife book.

title: My Major Anxiety for my Book.  Are People Interested in the Afterlife?
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses anxiety over whether readers will care about a book on the afterlife.

title: Too Much Money and the Afterlife
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Lucian's satire to connect wealth with afterlife punishment.
searchSummary: Compares Lucian's satire of a rich tyrant losing everything at death with the Acts of Thomas story of King Gundaphorus gaining a heavenly palace through charity. Thomas spends the king's building funds on the poor, and a near-death visitor reveals that these gifts constructed an eternal residence, prompting Gundaphorus's conversion. Unlike Lucian's philosophical warning against attachment, the Christian narrative treats wealth as useful only when surrendered to the needy and promises greater heavenly joy in exchange for earthly possessions.

title: What Did the Angels Tell the Shepherds?  It Depends.  Mailbag Sept. 10, 2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains a translation problem in the angels' announcement to the shepherds.
searchSummary: Explains why Luke 2:14 appears in English as either goodwill to people or peace among people of goodwill. The alternatives translate two Greek manuscript readings that differ by a final sigma, not competing interpretations of one text. Although most later manuscripts support the familiar wording, the earliest and strongest witnesses favor people of goodwill, and corrections in Vaticanus and Sinaiticus show later scribes deliberately moving toward the better-known reading.

title: Fun with the Jewish Christian Gospels: A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a discussion of Jewish Christian Gospels outside the New Testament.
searchSummary: Explores the lost Jewish-Christian Gospels, preserved only in quotations by church fathers who often confused their titles and relationships. Focusing on the Gospel of the Ebionites, the post shows how its baptism account combines the different heavenly declarations found in Matthew, Mark, and Luke by having the voice speak three times. This may reflect an early attempt to harmonize discrepant canonical traditions, although uncertainty about the Gospel's sources and form prevents a simple conclusion.

title: A Satirical Lesson about the Afterlife
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Lucian's afterlife satire to show moral lessons in journeys to the dead.
searchSummary: Explains how Lucian's satirical Voyage to the Underworld uses death to criticize attachment to wealth and power. The tyrant Megapenthes mourns everything stripped from him and is sentenced to remember his losses forever, while the impoverished cobbler Mycillus welcomes an egalitarian Hades free from hunger and cold. Rather than offering literal geography of the afterlife, the story teaches a philosophical lesson for present life: possessions, status, and domination inevitably disappear, so lasting well-being requires valuing what death cannot take.

title: Looking at Hell
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes ancient and Christian ideas about hell.
searchSummary: Uses a murdered woman's near-death journey in the Acts of Thomas to show how Christians transformed older underworld tales. She sees adulterers, slanderers, and other sinners suffering bodily punishments matched to their offenses, then returns to life and converts after Thomas warns of worse torments. Unlike Homer's undifferentiated, tedious Hades, this narrative separates believers from sinners and makes eternal destiny a choice. Its graphic hell promotes Christian faith and conduct among living readers more than detached information about death.

title: Problems with Some Bible Translations, including the King James: A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains problems in Bible translations, including the King James Version.
searchSummary: Explains Ehrman's preference for the NRSV and objections to using the King James Version or paraphrases for academic study. The KJV relies on manuscripts unavailable to modern scholarship and uses English whose meanings have changed since 1611. Although readable, the NIV can smooth tensions because its translators shared evangelical commitments. Ehrman argues that translations should prioritize philology, textual evidence, accuracy, and readable modern English rather than inherited wording or theological harmonization.

title: Speaking in Tongues and Virgin Births: Readers’ Mailbag September 3, 2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to questions about speaking in tongues and virgin birth claims.

title: Life in Hades
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains life in Hades through Odysseus's encounter with the dead.

title: The Body and Soul in Hades
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains body and soul in Hades through scenes from the Odyssey.

title: The First Recorded Visit to the Realm of the Dead (in Western literature)
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Odysseus's journey to the realm of the dead.

title: My Graduate Level New Testament Course
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes a graduate seminar on problems and methods in New Testament studies.
searchSummary: Presents a graduate seminar introducing major problems and methods in New Testament scholarship while preparing students for research and teaching careers. Topics include canon, textual criticism, Gospel sources, the historical Jesus, Acts and Paul, Pauline communities and authorship, and Revelation. Students translate Greek, survey scholarship, write and present professional book reviews, compile bibliographies, design an undergraduate syllabus, and compare textbooks, developing both disciplinary breadth and the ability to communicate research clearly.

title: Journeys to Heaven and Hell: A Sketch of My Project
author: BDEhrman
description: Sketches a scholarly project on journeys to heaven and hell.
searchSummary: Sketches a comparative study of ancient journeys to heaven and hell that emphasizes their moral and religious purposes. Earlier Near Eastern and Homeric accounts portray one bleak fate for everyone; Plato and Virgil distinguish rewards and punishments; Christian texts increasingly tailor torments and blessings to behavior, charity, church leadership, and doctrine. Moving beyond debates over pagan or Jewish origins, Ehrman proposes to show how thirty narratives reveal diverse afterlife concepts and competing priorities within early Christianity and its surrounding cultures.

title: Could Moses Write Hebrew & What Language Could Moses Speak
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers what can be known about Moses, Hebrew, and ancient literacy.
searchSummary: Asks when written Hebrew emerged and whether a hypothetical Moses could have written the Pentateuch. Joseph Lam explains that possible Hebrew inscriptions appear in the tenth or ninth centuries BCE, while unambiguous examples become plentiful in the eighth; earlier short Canaanite inscriptions are difficult to classify. A Moses raised in a thirteenth-century Egyptian court would probably have written Egyptian or Canaanite, not the classical first-millennium Hebrew preserved in the Pentateuch, which therefore cannot be his original composition.

title: My New Scholarly Project
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a scholarly project on afterlife views and otherworldly journeys.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's decision to undertake a scholarly study of early Christian guided journeys to heaven and hell alongside his trade book on afterlife origins. Reenergized after considering a slower publishing schedule, he identifies katabasis and anabasis traditions from Christianity's first centuries as important but comparatively understudied material. The proposed project, Observing the Dead, will analyze narratives anticipating Dante and provide the substantial original research needed for a fellowship-supported year away from teaching, allowing sustained investigation and writing.

title: Do Later Manuscript Discoveries Ever Support Proposed Interpolations?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how later manuscript discoveries can support conjectures about interpolations.
searchSummary: Surveys cases where scholars conjectured that words were interpolated before later-discovered manuscripts were found without them. Jan Krans shows that such confirmation occurs, but often reflects coincidental accidental omission, especially in omission-prone Codex Sinaiticus, rather than proof that the conjecture recovered the original. Manuscripts also later attest conjectured additions and substitutions. Of numerous examples, he considers only the omission of hearts in 2 Corinthians 3:3 a serious candidate for the authorial text.

title: Are There Passages Where *Every* NT Manuscript Gives the “Wrong” Reading?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores whether all surviving New Testament manuscripts can preserve a wrong reading.
searchSummary: Explains conjectural emendation, where scholars judge every surviving manuscript to preserve a corrupted reading and propose lost original wording. Jan Krans rejects the assumption that complete preservation is guaranteed and separates diagnosing corruption from identifying its remedy. Examples in Acts and 1 Corinthians contain phrases that are misplaced, ungrammatical, or nonsensical, prompting multiple competing corrections. Such cases are rare, and scholarly majorities are difficult to measure, but some primitive errors receive substantial specialist support.

title: Was John the Son of Zebedee Capable of Writing a  Gospel?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether John son of Zebedee could have written a Greek Gospel.
searchSummary: Explains why John son of Zebedee could not plausibly have written the Greek Gospel attributed to him. As an illiterate Aramaic-speaking fisherman from rural Galilee, he lacked the years of elite education required to read, compose prose, and master a foreign literary language. Living or preaching among Greek speakers would not supply that training, and no evidence shows ancient adult education producing such authors. The Gospel's accessible Greek does not make its sustained literary composition possible for an uneducated laborer.

title: Physical Persecution and the Physical Resurrection of the Dead
author: BDEhrman
description: Connects physical persecution with the emergence of bodily resurrection belief.
searchSummary: Proposes that persecution for religious fidelity helped generate Jewish belief in bodily resurrection during the Maccabean crisis. Earlier prophets explained suffering as God's punishment for sin, but that model failed when Jews were tortured and killed precisely for obeying God's law. If a just and sovereign God did not vindicate them in this life, vindication had to follow death. Because their suffering was physical, the hoped-for reward likewise became physical: restored bodies enjoying the life their persecutors had denied them.

title: A Resurrection for Tortured Jews (2 Maccabees)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains resurrection hope in 2 Maccabees in response to Jewish martyrdom.
searchSummary: Shows how 2 Maccabees connects martyrdom under Antiochus IV with hope for bodily resurrection. Eleazar, seven brothers, and their mother endure torture and death rather than violate Jewish law, while the brothers expect God to restore the tongues, hands, and lives taken from them. The text promises resurrection specifically to those faithful unto death and anticipates punishment for Antiochus without clearly describing hell. Ehrman argues that persecution for keeping God's law fostered Jewish belief in physical vindication after death.

title: Interpolations and Textual Corruptions: The Blurry Lines
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the blurry line between interpolations and textual corruptions.
searchSummary: Distinguishes a textual corruption, introduced by a copyist after a work circulated, from an interpolation added during editing before the textual form behind all surviving manuscripts was published. The post explains why suspected additions such as Luke's infancy narrative should not be bracketed like passages absent from important manuscripts. It also discusses the blurred boundary created by early scribal changes that may underlie every surviving copy and require conjectural emendation.

title: Is There Evidence that Luke Originally Did Not Have the Story of Jesus Birth?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines evidence that Luke may originally have lacked the birth narrative.
searchSummary: Examines evidence that an early edition of Luke may have circulated without chapters 1-2. Marcion's Gospel lacked the infancy narrative, though opponents accused him of removing it, and the surviving manuscripts cannot settle the issue. Without those chapters, Luke begins with Jesus' baptism and the probable reading 'Today I have begotten you,' making the Gospel especially compatible with an adoptionist understanding of Jesus as God's chosen Son.

title: Did Luke’s Gospel Originally Have The Birth Story?  Readers Mailbag and a Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether translations should mark Luke's birth narrative as possibly secondary.
searchSummary: Introduces the case that Luke may originally have begun with John the Baptist in chapter 3 and received its infancy narrative in a later edition. The formal opening at Luke 3:1, the disappearance of infancy themes from Luke-Acts, summaries beginning with John's baptism, and the genealogy's placement after Jesus is called God's Son all support this possibility. The post frames the separate question of whether translations should mark the chapters as secondary.

title: A New Blog Podcast!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a new blog podcast featuring readings of past posts.
searchSummary: Announces the Bart Ehrman Blog Podcast, a weekly audio project created, managed, financed, and narrated by blog member John Mueller. Each fifteen-to-twenty-minute episode reads two previously published posts, combining recent material with selections from the archive, and is distributed through major podcast platforms. Ehrman explains that the project aims to broaden awareness, increase blog membership, and generate more charitable revenue, while noting that its continuation would depend on whether it ultimately helps rather than harms membership.

title: Was Resurrection a Zoroastrian Idea?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether Jewish resurrection belief came from Zoroastrian influence.
searchSummary: Questions the longstanding theory that Jews borrowed bodily resurrection from Zoroastrian religion during Persian rule. Jewish texts from the Persian period show no such belief, resurrection emerges roughly 150 years after Persian control ended, and surviving Zoroastrian manuscripts are too late to establish an earlier doctrine of final resurrection and judgment. Because tracing every idea to an external source creates an endless regress, Ehrman considers the growing scholarly view that resurrection arose through developments within Judaism during the Maccabean period.

title: Daniel and a New Doctrine of Resurrection From the Dead
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Daniel 12 as the first clear Hebrew Bible reference to resurrection of the dead.
searchSummary: Explains Daniel 12 as the Hebrew Bible's earliest clear teaching of individual bodily resurrection. Written amid persecution under Antiochus IV, it predicts that many who sleep in the dust will awaken, some to everlasting life and others to shame, while the wise become radiant like heavenly beings. The passage transforms older expectations of Sheol by promising divine reversal beyond death. It offers persecuted Jews hope that fidelity to God will receive eternal reward and that their oppressors will face judgment.

title: A Resurrection of the Dead in the Prophet Ezekiel?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Ezekiel's dry bones vision teaches resurrection of the dead.
searchSummary: Distinguishes Ezekiel's valley of dry bones from the later Jewish doctrine of individual resurrection. Ezekiel addresses exiles who regard Israel as a dead nation; reconstructed bones, flesh, breath, and opened graves symbolize God's promise to restore the people to their land after Babylonian captivity. The vision does not predict dead individuals returning for eternal life. Centuries later, Daniel develops literal personal resurrection as a way for God to reward righteous people who die under persecution.

title: Charges and Anti-Supernatural Biases!  Readers Mailbag August 6, 2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Corrects a claim about Ehrman's view of Gnosticism and explains why critical scholars date much of Daniel to the Maccabean period.
searchSummary: Answers two examples of poor historical argument. Ehrman rejects N. T. Wright's claim that he considers Gnosticism the original Christianity, identifying it as a straw man contradicted by his published view that Gnosticism arose later. He then explains why Daniel's detailed knowledge of Antiochus Epiphanes, its later Aramaic, and the pattern of accurate retrospective prophecy support a second-century date. Historical contextualization is not anti-supernatural bias, even when theological readers prefer divine prediction.

title: How Women Came to Be Silenced in Early Christianity: A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts an explanation of how women came to be silenced in early Christianity.
searchSummary: Women held significant roles in early house churches partly because those gatherings occupied domestic space where women exercised greater responsibility. As Christianity grew more public, hierarchical, and concerned with social respectability, converts imported Roman gender assumptions and used scripture to defend male authority. Waning apocalyptic expectations and opposition to celibate women's independence ultimately restricted women from teaching, evangelizing, and leading, Christianizing the surrounding culture's patriarchal norms.

title: The Origins of Heaven and Hell
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the emergence of differentiated afterlife beliefs in Judaism and Christianity.
searchSummary: Explains how Jewish apocalypticism replaced the Hebrew Bible's largely undifferentiated Sheol with rewards for the righteous and punishment for the wicked. Traditional prophetic theology attributed Israel's suffering to God's discipline for disobedience, but persecution under Antiochus Epiphanes made faithful Jews suffer precisely for keeping God's law. Apocalyptic thinkers resolved this injustice by promising that God would intervene, raise the dead, reverse present fortunes, and judge everyone according to allegiance. Daniel preserves the earliest Hebrew expression of this differentiated afterlife.

title: The First Apocalypse: The Book of Daniel
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Daniel as the first surviving Jewish apocalypse.

title: A New Attack on My Views
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to an anonymous critique of views on the New Testament.
searchSummary: Reports an anonymously authored book claiming to resolve Gospel contradictions through a novel metaphysical interpretation and challenging Ehrman to respond. Ehrman finds the author's refusal to identify himself unusual and doubts that the advertised method will prove promising, but has not read the book and therefore offers no substantive judgment. He invites readers who examine it to explain its approach, identify worthwhile arguments, and suggest specific issues that merit a later response.

title: A New Genre in Jewish Antiquity: The Apocalypse
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains apocalypse as a new Jewish literary genre connected with afterlife hope.

title: The Books of 1 and 2 Maccabees
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes 1 and 2 Maccabees as sources for the Maccabean revolt and resurrection belief.
searchSummary: Introduces 1 and 2 Maccabees as independent historical accounts of the revolt against Antiochus IV and explains their different purposes. First Maccabees offers a largely chronological Hebrew narrative from the revolt's origins through the Hasmonean successors, while Greek 2 Maccabees abridges another work and interprets the struggle theologically. Its accounts of Eleazar, seven brothers, and their mother portray fidelity to Jewish law through torture and death as grounded in hope for future bodily resurrection and eternal reward.

title: Background to The Christian Afterlife: The Maccabean Revolt: A Blast from the (Recent) Past!
author: BDEhrman
description: Reintroduces the Maccabean revolt as background for Christian afterlife beliefs.
searchSummary: Connects the Maccabean crisis to Judaism's developing belief in resurrection and a transformed afterlife. Persian and Hellenistic rule culminated in Antiochus IV's attack on Jewish worship, prompting the Maccabean revolt, Temple rededication, and Hasmonean independence. The conflict and persecution created the historical setting in which older ideas of Sheol gave way to apocalyptic expectations that God would vindicate the faithful, a framework later prominent in the New Testament.

title: Lecture at Washington & Jefferson College
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a lecture on authorship and forgery in the Bible.
searchSummary: Introduces a recorded lecture based on Forged about scholarship's conclusions regarding biblical authorship. Ehrman explains that the lecture asks how ancient people understood works written under the false identity of a famous author, whether they considered that practice deceptive, how common it was, and whether they approved or condemned it. It then applies those questions to early Christianity and asks whether some New Testament books should be classified as forgeries. The post also describes the lecture's Phi Beta Kappa setting.

title: Threads and Comments on the Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains blog threads, comments, and how readers can participate.

title: Teaching Religion as an Agnostic
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on teaching religion as an agnostic.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman's move from Christianity to agnosticism did not change his teaching in a secular research university. Religious studies examines histories, texts, beliefs, practices, and cultural effects rather than promoting a faith, so personal belief is no more required than Marxism for teaching economic theory. Ehrman presents current scholarship about Jesus, the Gospels, Acts, Paul, and Revelation on evidentiary grounds; only developments in scholarship, not his personal religious outlook, alter the classroom material.

title: Was There a “Moment” When I Left the Faith?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains leaving faith as a gradual process rather than a single moment.
searchSummary: Identifies a memorable stage in Ehrman's gradual movement from liberal Christianity to agnosticism rather than a sudden break caused by biblical contradictions. At his Episcopal church he increasingly interpreted the Nicene Creed metaphorically until he realized the only statement he literally accepted was that Jesus had been crucified and buried. Feeling hypocritical reciting beliefs and worshiping a God he no longer thought active or real, he left despite the congregation's willingness to welcome his doubts and began calling himself agnostic.

title: Leaving the Faith
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes leaving Christian faith while retaining values once tied to belief.
searchSummary: Explains why the problem of innocent suffering, rather than biblical criticism, ultimately led Ehrman to leave Christianity. He could retain awe, gratitude, love, purpose, and enjoyment without believing God supplied them, but could not reconcile an intervening, prayer-answering deity with starvation, disease, genocide, disaster, and the equal suffering of believers and unbelievers. Thanking God for personal privilege seemed morally troubling when others received no rescue. He therefore stopped believing in the active God at the heart of his Christian tradition.

title: Growing into Unbelief
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes growing into unbelief after moving away from literal Christian claims.
searchSummary: Traces Ehrman's gradual movement from liberal Christianity toward unbelief. He increasingly interpreted creation, God, Jesus, communion, and morality nonliterally, questioned whether Jesus voluntarily died for sins, and rejected claims that the Holy Spirit guarantees correct interpretation because Spirit-filled Christians reach contradictory conclusions. As traditional doctrines became metaphorical or implausible, he asked what he still believed that a non-Christian could not also affirm. The accumulation of these doubts made continued Christian identity progressively harder to justify.

title: Apocalypticism in a Modern Idiom
author: BDEhrman
description: Recasts apocalyptic thought in modern terms while discussing suffering and divine justice.

title: Important Announcement about the Blog!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces an off-grid hiking break from the blog.

title: Did Paul Think Jesus’ Body Remained in the Grave?  Mailbag July 14, 2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Paul thought Jesus' body remained in the grave.
searchSummary: Answers whether Paul thought Jesus's corpse remained in its grave after a merely spiritual resurrection. Bart argues from Romans, 1 Thessalonians, and 1 Corinthians that believers' physical bodies would be transformed into immortal spiritual bodies like Jesus's; Paul therefore understood Jesus's actual body as raised and glorified, not abandoned. A second answer recounts how Bart financed twelve years of higher education through savings and sustained employment rather than parental payments.

title: The Essence of Biblical Apocalyptic Thought
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes core features of biblical apocalyptic thought.

title: The Origins of Apocalypticism
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how apocalypticism arose in response to suffering and failed prophetic explanations.
searchSummary: Explains how Jewish apocalypticism arose when historical experience contradicted the prophets' claim that national suffering punished disobedience. Under Antiochus Epiphanes, faithful Jews suffered precisely for keeping Torah, prompting belief that hostile supernatural powers temporarily controlled the world. Unlike the prophetic call to repent, apocalypticists blamed God's enemies and expected imminent divine intervention to destroy evil governments, vindicate the righteous, and establish God's kingdom, a framework later shared by Jesus, Paul, and early Christians.

title: Apologies to All Colombians
author: BDEhrman
description: Corrects a misspelling of Colombia.

title: Explaining a Columbian Mudslide
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses a Colombian mudslide to probe biblical explanations of suffering.
searchSummary: Uses the 1985 Colombian mudslide that killed approximately 23,000 people to test biblical explanations of suffering. Punishment, Adam and Eve's sin, testing, redemptive outcomes, and Job's unquestionable divine mystery all fail to explain why particular innocents and children died or make their deaths morally acceptable. The disaster helped convince Ehrman that many biblical answers were wrong or inapplicable, while he temporarily retained an apocalyptic view that anti-divine cosmic forces, rather than God, caused catastrophe.

title: The Variety of Views of Suffering in the Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys varied biblical explanations for suffering.
searchSummary: Surveys conflicting biblical explanations of suffering and evaluates their moral and intellectual appeal. Punishment for sin dominates the prophets, Joseph illustrates suffering producing greater good, Job offers testing and an unanswerable God, and Ecclesiastes recommends enjoying a brief, incomprehensible life. Inspired-Bible readers may combine these as partial truths, while historical readers see alternative human responses; Ehrman rejects several as offensive or implausible but finds resignation and another forthcoming apocalyptic answer more compelling.

title: Teaching about How The Bible Explains Suffering
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on teaching biblical approaches to suffering and their effect on faith.
searchSummary: Recounts how teaching a Rutgers course on suffering focused Ehrman's own theological struggle. Comparing biblical and modern responses showed students that Scripture contains diverse, sometimes incompatible explanations and required them to evaluate punishment, faith, and other claims rather than assume one answer. Contemporary Ethiopian famine made the issue concrete for students who initially saw no problem, while the course led Ehrman, then still Christian, toward an apocalyptic explanation he retained for several years.

title: Is Suffering Our Fault?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether human-caused suffering removes the problem of divine responsibility.
searchSummary: Distinguishes human-caused moral evil from natural suffering that free will cannot explain. People can inflict or now alleviate hunger, violence, and deprivation, but birth defects, ancient starvation, earthquakes, weather, and tsunamis long preceded modern capacity to prevent them. Claims that tectonic plates make suffering necessary constrain an all-powerful creator and conflict with a painless heaven. Free agency therefore supplies a response—using available power to help—not a complete explanation for why suffering exists.

title: Why Would I Call Myself Both an Agnostic or an Atheist?  A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the distinction between agnosticism and atheism.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman can call himself both agnostic and atheist by separating knowledge from belief. He lacks belief in traditional gods and is therefore atheist, but cannot know whether some greater power or intelligence exists and is therefore agnostic. He tends to prefer the latter label because scholarly concern for knowledge and humility before an immense, poorly understood universe matter more to him than emphasizing disbelief, while accepting that others may reasonably choose a different description.

title: Why Was Marcion Declared a Heretic?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Marcion was declared a heretic.
searchSummary: Explains how Marcion became the first known Christian condemned by a council after the New Testament period. He taught that Jesus' loving God differed from the just creator of Jewish Scripture, that Christ only appeared human, and that salvation came through faith rather than the creator's law; his canon contained an edited Luke and ten Pauline letters. Marcion convened Roman leaders hoping for approval in 144, but they rejected and expelled him. His movement nevertheless established churches across the world.

title: Do I Need to Suffer Myself to Question Whether God Exists?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to the idea that only personal suffering can raise doubts about God.
searchSummary: Explains that Ehrman's doubts about God arose not from exceptional personal tragedy but from confronting the immense suffering of others. He rejects the idea that suffering matters only when it affects oneself and questions thanking God for personal blessings while others starve or endure disaster. Although religious belief can comfort sufferers, he argues that comfort does not establish truth, and their anguish remains a serious challenge to belief in a loving God who governs the world.

title: Why Not Believe in a Different Kind of God?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether suffering is still a problem if God is understood differently.
searchSummary: Examines whether adopting a different concept of God avoids the problem of suffering. Ancient polytheism could blame hostile or limited deities, while monotheism creates tension between one loving, powerful God and widespread pain. Deism removes divine responsibility by making God an uninvolved creator, but Ehrman sees no evidence or practical reason for that belief. He concludes that such a deity would explain little, affect nothing in daily life, and function much like atheism.

title: The Classic “Problem” of Suffering
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the classic problem of suffering for belief in a loving and powerful God.
searchSummary: Defines the classical problem of suffering, or theodicy, through three apparently incompatible claims: God is all-powerful, God is all-loving, and suffering exists. Limiting divine power or love, denying suffering, or explaining it through punishment and eventual justice each creates further difficulties, especially when righteous people suffer while the wicked prosper. Drawing on Leibniz, Kushner, Wiesel, and Epicurus, Ehrman asks whether proposed solutions are genuinely satisfying rather than merely familiar or comforting.

title: Two Unsatisfactory Solutions to the Problem of Suffering
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates two unsatisfactory attempts to solve the problem of suffering.
searchSummary: Rejects two responses to suffering that overlook or worsen concrete human pain. A scholar's unified biblical narrative makes every biblical explanation part of God's grand design but smooths over Scripture's diverse views and fails to address individual victims of disease, disaster, hunger, and death. A grieving mother's belief that God killed her daughter to punish broken promises illustrates how biblical punishment theology can become cruel and harmful. Examining the problem can at least eliminate such damaging answers.

title: The Kind of Suffering that is a Problem
author: BDEhrman
description: Defines the suffering that creates a serious problem for belief in God.
searchSummary: Clarifies that the theological problem is not ordinary hardship but extreme, gratuitous suffering that appears to benefit no one: starvation, birth defects, disease, genocide, displacement, and natural catastrophe. Ehrman rejects claims that victims endured such horrors to ennoble comfortable observers. This suffering specifically challenges belief in a God who is both all-powerful and lovingly active in the world. He does not yet deny that an answer exists, but insists that the conflict constitutes a genuine problem.

title: My Role in Editing My Most Important Book that No One Has Heard Of.
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses editing a major scholarly volume honoring Bruce Metzger.

title: Why I Was Afraid to Become an Agnostic
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains fear of becoming agnostic during graduate study and pastoral work.
searchSummary: Describes the fears that delayed Ehrman's movement toward agnosticism while he served as a pastor and pursued doctoral study. Leaving threatened family ties, friendships, moral grounding, purpose, divine love, and assurance about the afterlife, including a persistent fear of hell. Church responsibilities temporarily kept deeper doubts at bay. Ehrman eventually concluded that social benefits and frightening consequences could not determine truth; he had to examine whether he actually believed, making the decision one of his most difficult transformations.

title: Why Even Bother Being a Liberal Christian?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the purpose of liberal Christianity after abandoning literal beliefs.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman remained a liberal Christian after rejecting biblical inerrancy, traditional Christology, hell, creationism, and other doctrines. Everyone interprets life from inherited assumptions, and Christianity remained the tradition he understood, valued, and intentionally reinterpreted rather than replacing with another imperfect worldview. He treated God as ultimate goodness, Jesus as self-giving love, confession as moral honesty, prayer as alignment, communion as commitment, and Scripture as human spiritual insight until suffering finally undermined belief in a loving God.

title: Was Jesus Made Up?  A Blast from the Past.
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to mythicist claims that Jesus was invented.
searchSummary: Argues that literary patterns and pagan parallels cannot establish that Jesus was invented. Gospel writers may shape Jesus as a new Moses, but historical people routinely acquire patterned biographies, and similar miraculous traditions surround acknowledged figures such as Alexander, Vespasian, and Apollonius. The alleged parallels are also incomplete: pagan supernatural births generally involve divine sex rather than virginal conception, and comparable divine men do not undergo Jesus' bodily resurrection. Each tradition must be evaluated rather than treated as interchangeable mythology.

title: How Biblical Discrepancies Can Be Theologically Liberating for a Christian
author: BDEhrman
description: Shows how Gospel discrepancies can be theologically liberating rather than destructive.
searchSummary: Argues that recognizing Gospel discrepancies can deepen rather than destroy Christian theological reading. Combining Mark's anguished Jesus with Luke's calm, confident Jesus into one passion narrative creates a fifth Gospel and erases each author's distinctive message; reading them separately preserves their literary and theological integrity. Ehrman describes this historical-critical approach as liberating during his Christian years, allowing diverse fallible books to inform reflection without demanding historical inerrancy, and reiterates that unrelated suffering later ended his faith.

title: How Did Judas Iscariot Die?  Readers’ Mailbag June 18, 2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares accounts of Judas's death in Matthew, Acts, and Papias, then explains how evangelicals approach New Testament textual variants.
searchSummary: Answers questions about Papias's gruesome account of Judas's death and evangelical responses to New Testament manuscript differences. Papias preserves a third, nonhistorical tradition in which Judas becomes grotesquely swollen, emits worms and pus, and dies amid a lasting stench, using conventional imagery for an evil person's fate. Evangelicals generally hold that God inspired the original wording while allowing scribal mistakes, trusting textual critics to reconstruct it and maintaining that variants do not undermine central doctrines.

title: A Very Different Portrayal of Jesus’ Death
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Gospel portrayals of Jesus' death, especially in Mark and Luke.
searchSummary: Compares Luke's passion narrative with Mark's and argues that each conveys a distinct response to suffering. Luke's Jesus comforts others, forgives his executioners, promises paradise, entrusts himself to God, and is declared innocent, remaining calm and assured throughout. The post suggests that Luke portrays Jesus as the ideal martyr, teaching persecuted Christians to face suffering with compassion, confidence in God's presence, and hope of imminent reward.

title: How a Non-Historical Account Can Be Meaningful: The Death of Jesus in Mark
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Mark's non-historical portrayal of Jesus' death can still be meaningful.
searchSummary: Shows how a nonhistorical Gospel narrative can convey theological meaning by examining Jesus' death in Mark. Betrayed, abandoned, mocked, and silent, Jesus finally asks why God has forsaken him and dies in anguish. The torn Temple curtain and gentile centurion reveal to readers what the characters miss: his death provides atonement, access to God, and salvation extending beyond Judaism. Mark's portrayal also offers persecuted Christians a model in which unexplained suffering can serve redemptive purposes.

title: A New Way of Reading the Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes a new historical-critical way of reading the Bible.
searchSummary: Explains historical criticism as reading each biblical author on individual terms rather than harmonizing the canon into one message. Contradictions and major theological differences reveal that Mark, Luke, John, Paul, and others wrote at different times for different circumstances and did not expect later readers to interpret them through one another. The method does not prohibit theological or devotional readings, but it resists creating agreement where none originally existed. Each work's distinctive claims must be understood before later canonical synthesis.

title: More of What I Believed When I Was a Committed (non-fundamentalist) Christian
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains beliefs held as a committed non-fundamentalist Christian.
searchSummary: Explains the liberal Christian beliefs Ehrman retained for years after rejecting biblical inerrancy. He understood Jesus' death as a model of self-sacrificial love, resurrection and second coming as symbols of God's eventual triumph over evil, and the flawed yet inspired Bible as a source of profound insight. Faith emphasized care for vulnerable people, social and political responsibility, possible personal existence after death, openness to doubt, and living after Jesus' example rather than possessing certain answers to every theological question.

title: What I Believed as a Committed but but non-Fundamentalist Christian
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the transition from fundamentalism to committed but non-fundamentalist Christianity.
searchSummary: Describes Ehrman's faith while serving churches during graduate school, after he had left fundamentalism but remained a committed Christian. He accepted science and evolution while believing a personal God guided the world in mysterious ways, and viewed Jesus as a human revelation of God's concern for sick, poor, hungry, and marginalized people. Although Jesus mistakenly expected an imminent apocalypse, Ehrman retained the underlying conviction that God would ultimately defeat evil, reverse suffering, vindicate the faithful, and overcome death.

title: Can (or Should) We Change the Canon of Scripture? A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether the canon of Scripture could or should be changed.
searchSummary: Explains why modern conclusions about disputed authorship are unlikely to alter the New Testament canon. Ancient church leaders valued books considered early, widespread, orthodox, and apostolic, but often inferred authorship from acceptable content rather than rigorous literary analysis. Scholars now reject traditional attributions for Hebrews, Revelation, and numerous letters, yet the canon is grounded in longstanding religious claims about inspiration and authority. Historical scholarship can reassess authorship, but no effective mechanism exists to add or remove books.

title: Update on my Publication Plans
author: BDEhrman
description: Updates publication plans for The Triumph of Christianity and the afterlife book.
searchSummary: Explains why Simon & Schuster delayed The Triumph of Christianity despite having a completed, edited manuscript ready for production. Political news and a crowded publishing season threatened to limit media attention, so the press chose a later date in hopes of improving visibility and sales. Ehrman contrasts his impatience with the strategic benefit, then reports extensive primary and secondary research for his next afterlife book, including Mesopotamian, Egyptian, Greek, Roman, Jewish, and early Christian sources.

title: What I Came To Believe About the Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains changing views about the Bible after abandoning inerrancy.

title: What Really Happened to Me: Demythologizing the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains demythologizing as a way to read the New Testament without literalism.

title: Why Have I Stopped Explaining How I Lost My Faith?  Readers’ Mailbag June 4, 2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the thread on losing faith paused while discussing biblical discrepancies.
searchSummary: Answers questions about Ehrman's post-fundamentalist Christianity and an apparent internal contradiction in Mark's crucifixion chronology. He explains that accepting biblical errors led to years of liberal Christian faith, not immediate agnosticism. Mark's “day of Preparation” means Friday before the Sabbath, while John's Friday is also preparation for Passover; thus Mark remains internally consistent but contradicts John over whether Jesus died on Passover or the preceding day.

title: Why It Didn’t Happen that Way.  The Stories of Jesus’ Birth
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Matthew's and Luke's birth narratives cannot both be historically accurate.
searchSummary: Argues that Matthew's and Luke's birth narratives cannot both be historically accurate and that harmonizing them creates a story found in neither Gospel. Luke's empire-wide ancestral census is unattested and implausible, while its chronology places Quirinius roughly a decade after Herod's death. Despite these problems, both narratives communicate theological claims that Jesus was born of a virgin and in Bethlehem, though they explain those claims in incompatible ways.

title: Another “True” Story that Didn’t Happen?  Jesus’ Birth in Luke
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Luke's birth narrative as a theologically meaningful story with historical problems.
searchSummary: Compares Matthew's and Luke's narratives of Jesus' birth to show that their familiar elements come from separate and difficult-to-reconcile stories. Matthew begins the family in Bethlehem, sends them to Egypt, and later relocates them to Nazareth; Luke begins them in Nazareth, brings them to Bethlehem for a census, and returns them home after the Temple rites. The post argues that a story can convey theological meaning without being historically accurate.

title: Is Theological “Truth” More Important than Historical Accuracy?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores whether theological truth can matter more than historical accuracy in Gospel narratives.
searchSummary: Uses the conflicting Passover chronologies in Mark and John to show how theological truth could outweigh historical accuracy for Gospel writers. Mark places Jesus' crucifixion after the Passover meal; John moves it to the afternoon when temple lambs were slaughtered. The change allows John's "Lamb of God" to die alongside the Passover lambs, making Jesus' death symbolize salvation. The irreconcilable dates suggest that John or his tradition altered history to communicate a theological claim.

title: An Example of a True Story that Didn’t Happen: Part 1
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the idea of a Gospel story that can be meaningful without being historically accurate.
searchSummary: Explains how contradictory Gospel accounts can convey theological truths without being fully historical. Beginning with Jesus' death, Ehrman establishes that two incompatible versions of one event cannot both be accurate and prepares to compare Mark's and John's Passover chronologies. The disagreement does not deny that Jesus died; instead, it shows that narrative details may have been shaped to communicate an author's meaning rather than preserve objective history.

title: Would I Be Personally Devastated if the Mythicists Were Right? A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on whether mythicist claims would be personally devastating if true.
searchSummary: Explains that Ehrman would not be emotionally devastated if evidence established the mythicist position. He warns that Christian apologists and atheist mythicists can use history to confirm beliefs held before investigation, while scholars often recreate Jesus in their own image. His historical work instead changed his preferred portrait of Jesus into an apocalyptic prophet he considers mistaken. Although nonexistence could suit his agnosticism, the evidence supports a historical Jesus, and conclusions should change only when evidence warrants it.

title: True Stories that Didn’t Happen
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how stories can function as true myths without having happened historically.

title: The Gospels as Myths
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the rise of interpreting Gospel miracle stories as myths.

title: The Gospels as Natural Histories
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the Enlightenment move toward natural explanations of Gospel miracle stories.

title: The Gospels as Supernatural Histories
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains older readings of the Gospels as supernatural histories.

title: Can Myths Be True and Meaningful?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to whether myths can be both meaningful and true.
searchSummary: Argues that a Gospel story can be historically inaccurate yet remain meaningful and valuable. Fiction, art, and personal memory shape human understanding without depending on perfect factual correspondence, and biblical narratives likewise preserve communities' transformative memories of Jesus. Historical criticism properly tests discrepancies and implausibilities, but it is only one way to read these writings. Reducing truth to brute past events overlooks literary power, remembered identity, and the capacity of nonhistorical narratives to communicate enduring insight.

title: Appreciating the Myths of the Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how biblical myths remained meaningful after abandoning inerrancy.
searchSummary: Presents Genesis 1–11 as myth rather than scientific explanation or conventional history. Myth means an imaginative story about divine activity that explains the world and humanity's place within it, not a worthless falsehood. Creation, Eden, Cain and Abel, and the flood express theological claims about Sabbath, human status, moral knowledge, disobedience, and punishment. Reading these narratives within their literary form allows their intended lessons to emerge without requiring their events to be historically or scientifically demonstrable.

title: Becoming a Non-Fundamentalist Christian
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes becoming a non-fundamentalist Christian after recognizing biblical mistakes.

title: Fundamentalism and the Truth of the Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why problems in the Bible can challenge fundamentalist claims about truth.

title: Eyewitnesses and the Gospels: A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a discussion of eyewitnesses, oral tradition, and the Gospels.
searchSummary: Explains why the possible survival of eyewitnesses when the Gospels were written does not mean the evangelists consulted them. Jesus' earliest followers were largely Aramaic-speaking Galileans, while the Gospel authors were educated Greek-speaking Christians writing elsewhere decades later; none claims direct interviews with eyewitnesses. The Gospels instead draw on oral traditions that circulated across languages and communities, allowing stories to change or arise before reaching the writers.

title: Finding More Problems in the Old Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes further Old Testament problems encountered during graduate study.
searchSummary: Uses Pentateuchal contradictions to explain Ehrman's move away from conservative evangelicalism. Noah receives conflicting animal counts, Egyptian livestock repeatedly die, and Genesis and Exodus disagree about whether the patriarchs knew Yahweh's name, indicating sources with different perspectives edited together.
