Ehrman concludes that the Bible is a fallible human collection rather than a single Mosaic revelation, though accepting that judgment initially changed the form of his Christianity rather than ending his faith.

title: Finding Problems in the Old Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Old Testament study raised problems for biblical inerrancy.
searchSummary: Describes the Old Testament problems that undermined Ehrman's belief in Mosaic authorship and biblical inerrancy. Anachronistic camels, Philistines, and Beersheba place Genesis traditions after Moses, while Genesis 1 and 2 conflict over creation order, divine names, portrayals of God, and theological purpose. These tensions suggest that the Pentateuch combines authors from different periods rather than presenting one consistent account written by Moses.

title: How I First Realized There Are Mistakes in the Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts first realizing that the Bible contains mistakes.
searchSummary: Recounts the interpretive problem that first led Ehrman to accept that the Bible could contain mistakes. Mark places David's eating of sacred bread during Abiathar's high priesthood, although 1 Samuel names Ahimelech. After constructing a complicated defense, a professor's suggestion that Mark simply erred proved more convincing. Accepting that small error opened the possibility of other factual mistakes and contradictions involving seeds, crucifixion chronology, Jesus' birth narratives, and Paul's movements after conversion.

title: My Resistance to Change at Princeton Seminary
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes resistance to changing views during Princeton Seminary.
searchSummary: Explains how close study at Princeton Seminary gradually overcame Ehrman's resistance to evidence challenging biblical inerrancy. Initially he treated apparent contradictions, historical impossibilities, and differing Gospel perspectives as problems that faith required him to explain away. Reading Hebrew and Greek under critical scholars led to a methodological shift: instead of assuming the Bible could contain no errors, he allowed the question to remain open and tested the texts, after which mistakes became visible and his understanding of Scripture changed fundamentally.

title: My Encounter with the Enlightenment
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how exposure to Enlightenment ideas changed views of truth and objectivity.
searchSummary: Explores a paradox in conservative evangelical appeals to objective truth. The Enlightenment promoted evidence, reason, and open inquiry in place of inherited authority, producing scientific and historical conclusions many fundamentalists reject. Yet Christian apologetics adopts the same premise that religious claims can be objectively demonstrated. Ehrman argues that accepting proof also permits disproof; his commitment to objective investigation eventually exposed weaknesses in his evangelical claims and helped produce a crisis of faith.

title: Mythicists and the Virgin Birth: Readers’ Mailbag May 6, 2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about mythicist claims, the virgin birth, and textual criticism.
searchSummary: Addresses mythicist claims about Jesus' virgin birth and the use of ancient New Testament translations in textual criticism. Ehrman argues that Matthew and Luke's nonsexual conception has no precise Greco-Roman parallel and developed too late to explain the invention of Jesus. He then explains how Latin, Syriac, and Coptic versions can preserve evidence for early Greek readings, although scholars must first reconstruct those translations from later, scribally altered manuscripts before retroverting them into Greek.

title: What Happened Next: My Life After Moody Bible Institute
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues an autobiographical account of life after Moody Bible Institute.
searchSummary: Recounts how transferring from Moody Bible Institute to Wheaton College broadened Ehrman's education while he remained a conservative evangelical. Literature, science, classics, philosophy, and intellectual history exposed him to worldviews and questions beyond Bible and theology, while Greek professor Gerald Hawthorne modeled learned Christian faith that admitted uncertainty. Hawthorne's openness showed that serious believers could value questions rather than possess every answer, helping begin the intellectual transformation that eventually led Ehrman to reconsider the foundations of his Christianity.

title: The Life Story I Tell My Students
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the life story told to students on the final day of class.
searchSummary: Summarizes the life story Ehrman tells students to explain his beliefs, beginning with an Episcopal childhood and a born-again conversion through Youth for Christ. At seventeen he entered Moody Bible Institute, where intensive Bible study, memorization, work, and fundamentalist training transformed an ordinary student into a driven scholar determined to teach New Testament. Transferring to Wheaton for a liberal-arts degree then introduced a broader intellectual environment that began loosening the rigid certainty established at Moody.

title: Spilling the Beans on my Beliefs on the Last Day of Class
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the final New Testament class addresses personal beliefs.
searchSummary: Explains Ehrman's practice of offering an optional final class in which he discusses his personal beliefs and how they changed. During the semester he keeps those views separate from historical evidence so students evaluate arguments without accepting or rejecting them because of his identity. The final session addresses why he studies the New Testament and historical Jesus as an agnostic and gives interested students a fuller personal account without making it part of course requirements or assessment.

title: Can Teaching Be Objective?
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses objectivity and subjectivity in teaching religion.
searchSummary: Reflects on whether teaching can be objective by contrasting Socratic emphasis on evidence with Kierkegaardian attention to a teacher's subjectivity. Ehrman accepts that background and beliefs affect judgment, yet withholds his own religious views during the semester so students do not embrace or resist arguments merely because of his position. His pedagogical goal is to help them weigh evidence, challenge assumptions, and revise conclusions independently before he discusses his personal outlook on the final day.

title: The Text of the New Testament:  Are the Textual Traditions of Other Ancient Works Relevant?  A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares New Testament textual traditions with other ancient works.
searchSummary: Explains why the New Testament's superior manuscript attestation does not guarantee its original wording. Classical scholars also debate Homer, Plato, and other texts, and being better documented than those works does not itself provide sufficient evidence; 94 percent of Greek New Testament manuscripts date after the ninth century. Numerous late witnesses illuminate medieval transmission, but confidence about the authors requires early, extensive copies that largely do not survive.

title: Teaching the Bible as a Historical Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains teaching the Bible historically in a secular university.
searchSummary: Explains how a secular university can teach the Bible historically and literarily without promoting or undermining religion. Students examine sources, contradictions, authorship, theology, and historical reliability using methods applied to other ancient religious texts, while their professor neither discloses nor asks them to adopt personal beliefs. Because many arrive with lifelong commitments, the material challenges assumptions and encourages thought. Its educational purpose is humanistic inquiry, not conversion, deconversion, or a claim that historical study is the only valid approach.

title: Teaching Religion in a Secular Environment
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on teaching religion in a secular environment.
searchSummary: Describes Ehrman's unexpected transition from confessional education to teaching religion at Rutgers, his first secular university. That contrast clarified the difference between promoting faith and studying religion historically in a state institution. He argues that professors should teach about religious texts, beliefs, and practices without advocating personal commitments, both because scholarly expertise does not require adherence and because church-state separation makes taxpayer-supported proselytizing inappropriate. His colleagues' personal beliefs therefore remain professionally irrelevant.

title: How We Got Our 27-Book New Testament: The Case of Didymus
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Didymus the Blind to illustrate how the New Testament canon developed.
searchSummary: Uses Didymus the Blind to challenge the claim that Athanasius settled the New Testament canon for fourth-century Christianity. Although Athanasius listed the familiar twenty-seven books in 367, Didymus, another Alexandrian authority, quoted works such as the Shepherd of Hermas and 1 Clement as Scripture. Early biblical manuscripts likewise included some later-excluded works. This evidence shows that competing canonical boundaries persisted even within Alexandria and became the subject of Ehrman's first published academic article.

title: My “Preparation” to Teach in a Secular Research Institution
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes preparation for teaching in a secular research institution.
searchSummary: Explains how Ehrman's entirely Christian education and specialized training in New Testament textual criticism initially complicated his academic job search. Concerned that employers would see him only as a manuscript technician, he published graduate research across broader areas to demonstrate competence in interpretation, theology, and history. The post frames his eventual move into secular teaching by showing how he deliberately developed a wider scholarly profile despite having no personal experience in a secular university classroom.

title: About Graduate Studies:  A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Gives advice about pursuing graduate study in New Testament and early Christianity.
searchSummary: Warns that doctoral study in early Christianity is too long, difficult, and uncertain to pursue without an overriding intellectual commitment. Students spend years in seminars, languages, comprehensive examinations, a research proposal, and a publishable dissertation, emerging as experts through sustained labor rather than credentials alone. Ehrman also emphasizes that graduate students broaden their professors' knowledge through specialized projects, but advises prospective candidates to choose another path if they can imagine a satisfying alternative, especially given the absence of guaranteed employment.

title: How Does A Book Become A Bestseller?  Readers’ Mailbag April 21, 2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how media exposure helped Misquoting Jesus become a bestseller.

title: Background to a Different View of the Afterlife: The Maccabean Revolt
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the Maccabean revolt as background for new Jewish afterlife beliefs.
searchSummary: Explains the political and religious background behind Judaism's developing belief in resurrection. Hellenization under the Seleucids and Antiochus IV's assault on Jewish practices provoked the Maccabean revolt, Temple rededication, and Hasmonean independence, while the new rulers' non-Zadokite high priesthood generated further conflict. These crises helped produce the apocalyptic framework through which persecuted Jews expected God to vindicate the faithful beyond death rather than consign everyone alike to Sheol.

title: Dinner With Me?  A Blog Idea.
author: BDEhrman
description: Proposes fundraising dinners with blog members.
searchSummary: Presents a reader's proposal for auctioning several places at a private group dinner with Bart as a blog fundraiser. The highest bidders would make charitable donations in exchange for conversation and a meal, probably in North Carolina or another central location. Bart has not committed to holding the event and instead asks members whether the idea is attractive, financially worthwhile, and logistically workable, inviting suggestions that could shape a later version.

title: Job and the God Who Refuses To Answer
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Job's unanswered demand for a response from God.
searchSummary: Interprets God's whirlwind speeches as a refusal to explain Job's innocent suffering. God overwhelms Job with questions about creation and compels submission, but never identifies sin, testing, demonic action, or any other cause. Job repents of challenging the Almighty rather than of wrongdoing. Ehrman argues that divine power alone does not establish justice: if God may torment innocents without accountability, might appears to make right, leaving human beings unable to understand divine morality by the standards God supposedly gave them.

title: Was Job Really Innocent?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Job is truly innocent in the book's competing explanations of suffering.
searchSummary: Presents Job's insistence that he is innocent and cannot honestly repent of sins he did not commit. He describes God as a violent attacker who torments him without cause, while wicked people often prosper and no afterlife restores justice. Job knows that divine power would overwhelm any attempt to plead his case, but power does not erase his innocence. Elihu then repeats the friends' claim that suffering punishes sin before God appears to answer Job directly.

title: Bart Ehrman Resurrection of Jesus: A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a discussion of Jesus' resurrection and historical explanation.

title: Did David Exist?  And When Did I Know I Lost My Faith?  Mailbag April 15, 2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about David's historicity and the process of losing faith.
searchSummary: Answers separate questions about Israel's early kings and the moment Ehrman recognized he had left Christianity. The Tel Dan inscription supports a Davidic dynasty, though most biblical narratives about Saul, David, and Solomon may be legendary. Ehrman's personal turning point came while reciting the Nicene Creed and realizing he literally accepted almost none of it beyond Jesus' execution and burial. Participating in worship then felt hypocritical, so he stopped attending despite recognizing that others sustain church membership through nonliteral interpretation.

title: Job’s So-called Friends (With Friends Like These….)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the role of Job's friends in the poetic dialogues.
searchSummary: Introduces the poetic dialogues of Job as a distinct treatment of innocent suffering from the book's framing tale. Job's three friends, followed by Elihu, insist that God punishes wrongdoing and therefore accuse Job of hidden sins, despite the reader's knowledge of his innocence. Job curses his birth and contests their punishment theology. The dialogues ultimately move toward God's appearance, where divine power silences Job without supplying a reason, suggesting that innocent suffering receives no explanatory answer.

title: Why I Find the Story of Job is Disturbing
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the framing story of Job is troubling.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman now finds Job's framing story morally disturbing rather than inspiring. God permits the destruction of an innocent man's health, property, servants, and children to test his loyalty and win a wager, then treats new children as replacements for those killed. Because the Hebrew Bible offers no compensating heavenly reward, justice must occur during earthly life. Restoring Job's possessions and family, however, cannot undo the murdered children's suffering or make the original test morally acceptable.

title: Understanding the Story of Job
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the narrative and poetic layers of Job.
searchSummary: Retells Job's prose folktale, in which the Adversary serves on God's heavenly council and receives permission to test whether Job's piety depends on prosperity. Job loses property, servants, children, and health but refuses to curse God, so God restores and doubles his possessions. The story presents innocent suffering as a test of disinterested faith, yet explicitly attributes Job's undeserved misery to God's authorization. Ehrman questions a deity who inflicts devastation merely to prove Job's loyalty.

title: The Two Books of Job: A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Job contains different perspectives on afterlife and suffering.
searchSummary: Explains why scholars identify two works with conflicting views of suffering within Job. The prose frame uses Yahweh, portrays a patient Job, and explains his losses as a divinely authorized test of faith. The poetic dialogues prefer other divine names, portray Job loudly protesting his innocence, omit the Adversary and any test, and offer no understandable reason for his pain. Combining these distinct authors and genres created the apparent inconsistency that often confuses readers.

title: My Meditation Practice and Women at the Empty Tomb: Readers Mailbag April 9, 2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about meditation and women at the empty tomb.

title: The Afterlife (or not) in Ecclesiastes
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Ecclesiastes' denial or skepticism about afterlife hope.
searchSummary: Explains Ecclesiastes' rejection of moral retribution in both life and death: righteous people suffer, wicked people prosper, chance governs outcomes, and no afterlife corrects the imbalance. Because life is fleeting, the Teacher advises enjoying its ordinary goods while they last. Suffering likewise has no comprehensible divine purpose; people should alleviate it where possible without pretending to explain it. Ehrman finds this more acceptable than Job's God, who causes pain and then refuses to justify it.

title: Ecclesiastes and the Meaning of Life
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Ecclesiastes on Sheol, death, and the meaning of life.

title: Life After Death According to Samuel
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines the story of Saul consulting Samuel through a medium.

title: Our Fifth Year Anniversary!
author: BDEhrman
description: Marks the blog's fifth anniversary and summarizes its output and charitable results.
searchSummary: Celebrates the blog's fifth anniversary with totals of 1,462 posts, nearly 50,000 approved comments, $117,000 raised during the year, and $410,000 distributed since launch. Bart says continued interest and charitable impact make the demanding schedule sustainable. He asks readers to recruit members, give subscriptions, suggest improvements, and donate, while expressing appreciation for the community's civil inquiry and participation and affirming plans to continue publishing and helping people in need.

title: Is Mark’s Gospel Unsophisticated?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates Mark's literary sophistication and narrative artistry.
searchSummary: Argues that Mark's apparently simple style conceals deliberate literary artistry. The baptism and crucifixion mirror one another through the Spirit, a ripping open, a voice, and identification of Jesus as God's Son. God reveals Jesus' identity privately at the beginning; a Roman centurion recognizes it publicly only at his death, when the torn Temple curtain signifies access to God. This framing supports Mark's themes of universal misunderstanding, the crucified Son, and the abrupt silence at the empty tomb.

title: Recent Manuscript Discoveries: A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a discussion of manuscript discoveries, including the Gospel of Jesus' Wife and Mark claims.
searchSummary: Revisits two highly publicized manuscript claims: the Gospel of Jesus' Wife, now recognized as a modern forgery, and the still-unpublished first-century fragment of Mark. Ehrman summarizes evidence against the former and the unanswered questions surrounding the latter's size, date, verification, and significance. He argues that a small early Mark scrap would probably confirm what scholars already believe and sharply rejects comparisons with the Dead Sea Scrolls, which transformed knowledge through extensive, much earlier textual evidence.

title: Returning from the Dead in the Hebrew Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys Hebrew Bible stories in which the dead are revived or contacted.

title: The Afterlife in the Hebrew Bible: Sheol
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Sheol as the Hebrew Bible's realm of the dead, not a place of reward or eternal punishment.
searchSummary: Explains that the Hebrew Bible does not teach the Christian division of immortal souls between heaven and hell. Its dominant view sends the whole deceased person to Sheol, understood as grave, pit, darkness, watery netherworld, or inactive realm cut off from God, without separating body from soul or distinguishing righteous from wicked. King James translators rendered Sheol as "hell" where punishment seemed implied, showing how translation imported theology absent from Hebrew. Marginal biblical views include extinction and bodily resurrection.

title: Eternal Life and Damnation
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares the Apocalypse of Peter and Apocalypse of Paul on eternal reward and punishment.
searchSummary: Examines an early Christian tension over whether eternal destiny depends on moral conduct or correct belief. The Apocalypse of Peter punishes characteristic wrongdoing, whereas the Apocalypse of Paul targets compromised Christians, corrupt clergy, and theological heretics. Ehrman contrasts Jesus' emphasis on loving God, serving neighbors, and aiding the needy with John's insistence on belief in the Son and 2 Thessalonians' vengeance against unbelievers. Revelation combines both tendencies, leaving unresolved whether salvation requires behavior, doctrine, or some relationship between them.

title: Was Jesus a Myth or a Historical Figure? Robert Price and I Debate This Very Interesting Question
author: BryanS
description: Shares a debate with Robert Price over whether Jesus existed.
searchSummary: Presents Ehrman's debate with mythicist Robert Price over whether Jesus was invented or historical. Ehrman represents the overwhelming specialist consensus and points viewers toward evidence involving Paul, James, early traditions, Nazareth, crucifixion, and ancient parallels, followed by extended questions from the audience. He explains that expertise is not infallible but remains essential for evaluating difficult historical claims, and that his agnosticism does not prevent him from concluding that Jesus clearly existed even if he was not divine.

title: Questions on the Resurrection and My Personal Spiritual Experiences: Readers’ Mailbag
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about Jesus' resurrection and personal spiritual experiences.
searchSummary: Distinguishes historically probable resurrection belief from later physical details and clarifies the basis of Ehrman's former faith. Independent sources establish that Jesus' followers claimed appearances convinced them he was raised, while stories such as eating fish may serve later arguments for bodily resurrection and lack comparable explanatory necessity. Ehrman's evangelical faith rested on powerful spiritual experiences as well as Scripture. Biblical problems changed his theology but did not end belief; suffering eventually undermined faith in an active, prayer-answering God.

title: Another Gory Account of the Afterlife: The Apocalypse of Paul
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Apocalypse of Paul as a later Christian tour of heaven and hell.
searchSummary: Examines the influential Apocalypse of Paul, a late antique Christian tour of heaven and hell that expands traditions from the Apocalypse of Peter. Paul sees temporary rewards and torments before bodily resurrection, with graphic punishments aimed especially at compromised clergy, failed ascetics, and heretics who deny Christ's flesh, Eucharistic presence, or physical resurrection. The work uses embodied afterlife suffering to defend orthodox doctrine and Christian discipline, while attributing its revelation pseudonymously to Paul.

title: Touring Hell: The Apocalypse of Peter
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Apocalypse of Peter as an early Christian tour of hell and heaven.
searchSummary: Introduces the Apocalypse of Peter, the earliest surviving Christian guided tour of heaven and hell and a work some fourth-century communities nearly accepted as scripture. In Peter's purported vision, Jesus reveals distinct destinies for blessed and damned souls, with sinners physically punished in ways matching their offenses. The lurid torments serve a practical moral warning: avoid sin to gain paradise. By writing in Peter's voice, the unknown author gives this invented revelation apostolic authority.

title: The Burial of Jesus: A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts an early discussion of Jesus' burial.
searchSummary: Explains why Bart changed from accepting Joseph of Arimathea's burial and the empty tomb as historical facts to doubting both traditions. Roman crucifixion normally denied victims honorable burial, only one crucified skeleton has been recovered, and Joseph is unattested outside later Gospel accounts or their derivatives. Bart considers a common grave more historically plausible, while acknowledging uncertainty and suggesting that Isaiah's rich-man burial language may have influenced the developing story.

title: Does Jesus Claim to Be God in Mark?  And My Former Converts.  Mailbag March 19, 2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about Jesus' divine identity in Mark and past evangelical ministry.
searchSummary: Argues that forgiving the paralytic in Mark 2 does not mean Jesus claims to be God. Jesus says the Son of Man has authority on earth to pronounce forgiveness, comparable to authority exercised by Temple priests, and his healing verifies that delegated authority. Mark may consider Jesus divine in some sense, but that differs from portraying him publicly declaring himself God as John does. The post also briefly reflects on Ehrman's relationships with people he once tried to convert.

title: A Final Word (I Think!) on Group Visions
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to critiques of using visions to explain resurrection belief.

title: What Really Happens With Group Visions
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how group visions or shared visionary experiences may occur.
searchSummary: Clarifies that a “group vision” need not mean several brains independently produced the same hallucination at the same instant. Studies of a nonexistent film of an Amsterdam plane crash show how suggestion, hearsay, inference, and vivid imagination can give many people detailed memories of something none witnessed. Ehrman proposes that one person's experience of Jesus could similarly spread through a group until others sincerely remembered sharing it, because false memories can feel as vivid and certain as accurate ones.

title: Pastor Goranson, the Son of God, and I: A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a personal story connected with belief in Jesus as Son of God.
searchSummary: Recounts how Ehrman's historical study of Scripture created doubts about Jesus' divinity during his transition away from evangelicalism. New Testament authors rarely identify Jesus as God, and explicit self-divine claims occur chiefly in John, prompting him to question whether Jesus actually spoke them. His former pastor Evan Goranson's emotional response to doubt about John 14:6 demonstrates how reassessing historical evidence challenged both foundational beliefs and cherished personal relationships.

title: Are Group Visions Possible?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores whether groups can have non-veridical visions.

title: Group Visions and Agnostic Jesus Scholars: Mailbag March 12, 2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about group visions and agnostic historical Jesus scholars.

title: What I’m Thinking about the Afterlife
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains preliminary thinking for a book on the afterlife.
searchSummary: Outlines the questions Ehrman hopes to investigate in a book on Judeo-Christian afterlife beliefs. He contrasts popular immortal-soul theology with biblical ideas of Sheol, bodily resurrection, and final judgment, then identifies topics including near-death experiences, consciousness, Revelation, ancient tours of heaven and hell, Greek influence, reincarnation, preexistent souls, universal salvation, and changing standards for damnation. The post presents a research agenda rather than one settled account, emphasizing how dramatically Christian expectations changed.

title: Does the Afterlife Matter for Other Things?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why afterlife beliefs matter for broader issues in religion and history.
searchSummary: Describes Ehrman's initial publisher pitch for a trade book tracing the origins of heaven and hell and the prospectus needed before full research begins. Because the subject interests readers beyond biblical studies, the editor asks him to identify its broader contemporary significance as well as its historical appeal. Ehrman considers whether afterlife beliefs correlate with political, environmental, or social attitudes, while leaving the question open and seeking evidence rather than building the book around an unsupported assumption.

title: Me and Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on personal identification with Jesus' ethical teachings.

title: Why Do Good People Suffer?  A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a discussion of why good people suffer.
searchSummary: Contrasts three biblical responses to why good people suffer. The prophetic view treats suffering as God's punishment for sin; the apocalyptic view blames evil cosmic powers and expects God soon to overthrow them; Ecclesiastes regards life, pleasure, pain, and achievement as fleeting and ultimately inexplicable. Ehrman rejects punishment theology and no longer expects apocalyptic deliverance. He favors Ecclesiastes' counsel to enjoy this life while helping others gain the same opportunity, rather than turning mortality into selfish hedonism.

title: Thinking about Hell
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on childhood and later thoughts about hell.
searchSummary: Uses two personal memories to show how belief in hell can shape conduct and religious doubt. As a child, Ehrman misunderstood a moral story about residents of heaven feeding one another with long forks as literal information about the afterlife. Later, while reconsidering fundamentalism at Princeton Seminary, a hot sauna made eternal torment feel terrifyingly real. The experience slowed his theological transition and illustrates why afterlife beliefs can carry agonizing emotional force beyond abstract doctrine.

title: Views of the Afterlife
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a research interest in different views of the afterlife.
searchSummary: Surveys competing evangelical understandings of heaven and hell to show that professed biblical authority does not produce one clear doctrine. Christians disagree over who reaches heaven and whether hell means endless conscious torment, temporary punishment, rehabilitative purgatory, or eventual universal salvation. Advocates defend each position from scripture, revealing both diverse biblical views and interpretive ambiguity. Ehrman argues that popular afterlife beliefs cannot simply be treated as an obvious, uniform teaching of the Bible.

title: Moving to My Next Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains plans to move from The Triumph of Christianity to a book on the afterlife.

title: The First Textual Variant in the Gospel of Mark
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses the first textual variant in Mark's opening verse.
searchSummary: Argues that "Son of God" was deliberately added to Mark 1:1 rather than accidentally omitted from diverse early manuscripts. A scribe had little reason to remove a title consistent with Mark, whereas proto-orthodox copyists could add it to prevent an adoptionist reading in which Jesus became God's Son only at baptism. Mark's baptism and crucifixion already frame divine sonship through corresponding scenes. The expanded opening instead establishes Jesus as God's Son before John appears or the baptism occurs.

title: Christians Who Thought Jesus Was Adopted by God: A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a discussion of Christians who believed Jesus was adopted by God.

title: Jesus’ Teaching in Aramaic and the Books of the Canon: Mailbag February 24, 2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about Jesus' Aramaic teaching and books outside the canon.
searchSummary: Answers questions about Jesus' Aramaic speech and the formation of the New Testament canon. Ehrman explains that no early Christian Aramaic writings survive, although preserved phrases and sayings that work better when retroverted from Greek can point toward early Palestinian tradition. He also identifies noncanonical works once treated as Scripture and canonical books once disputed, emphasizing that the present twenty-seven-book collection emerged through centuries of debate and consensus rather than one decisive church council.

title: An Interesting Scribal Change at the Beginning of Mark
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines a scribal alteration in Mark 1:2 that replaces "Isaiah the prophet" with "the prophets" to avoid an apparent discrepancy in the Gospel's opening quotation.
searchSummary: Explains why Mark's attribution of a composite quotation to "Isaiah the prophet" is original even though some words come from Exodus and Malachi. Early and strong witnesses preserve this harder reading, while scribes had an obvious motive to replace it with the accurate, less troublesome "in the prophets." Mark may have named the principal source rather than made a mistake, but interpretation follows textual reconstruction. The example demonstrates how textual criticism establishes the wording that other scholars then explain.

title: Is the Book of Revelation a Revised Version of a Non-Christian Apocalypse? Guest Post by James Tabor
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents James Tabor's argument that Revelation may revise an earlier non-Christian apocalypse.
searchSummary: Presents James Tabor's argument that Revelation contains a pre-Christian Jewish apocalypse later Christianized by editors. References to Jesus and Christ cluster at the book's edges and can often be removed without disrupting its grammar or narrative, while language about Israel's God and Messiah remains structurally integral. Tabor therefore proposes an underlying text from Judea in the 40s or 50s CE, originally directed against Jerusalem's authorities, followed by layers reflecting Nero, Rome, Pompeii's destruction, and later Christian interpretation.

title: How Variant Readings are Noted in the Greek New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Demonstrates how Greek New Testament editions mark variant readings.
searchSummary: Uses Mark 14:27-31 to illustrate how critical Greek New Testaments record manuscript variation. The translator-oriented UBS edition notes one consequential variant, whether the cock crows once or twice, while the scholarly Nestle-Aland edition lists eight differences involving additions, omissions, word order, and grammar. Ehrman explains why the harder twice reading is probably original and shows that manuscripts contain abundant variation, although most differences have little or no effect on meaning.

title: A Text That Doesn’t Exist!  What Do NT Translators Actually Translate?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains what text New Testament translators translate when no single original manuscript exists.
searchSummary: Explains that modern New Testament translations use an eclectic Greek text found in no single manuscript. Translators normally begin with the international committee's edition but may choose alternative readings where its apparatus records variation; editors likewise select the best-supported wording case by case because every witness contains errors. The resulting reconstruction is a modern scholarly combination, yet it better approximates the original at each point than printing one demonstrably imperfect manuscript.

title: How Do We Know When the Gospels Were Written:  A Mailbag Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts an explanation of how scholars date the Gospels.

title: The Gospel Truth: Sometimes A Little Hazy
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a Fresh Air interview on the Gospels and historical memory.
searchSummary: Introduces a Fresh Air interview about Jesus, Interrupted and its effort to bring established biblical scholarship to general readers. Familiar Gospel accounts differ over Jesus' birth, Judas's death, and Jesus' words from the cross, although pastors often do not explain such differences to congregations. Treating the four Gospels as one harmonized account therefore obscures each author's distinctive version rather than producing a more accurate historical memory.

title: The Standard Greek New Testament Today
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the standard Greek New Testament used by translators today.
searchSummary: Explains how the United Bible Societies created the standard Greek text underlying most modern New Testament translations. An international committee evaluated Greek manuscripts, ancient versions, and church-father quotations to reconstruct authorial wording, document important variants, rate confidence in disputed decisions, and note punctuation alternatives. First published in 1965 and repeatedly revised, its text is shared with the scholarly Nestle-Aland edition, whose much fuller apparatus serves specialists rather than translators.

title: What We Now Know about the Manuscripts of the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys what scholars know about New Testament manuscripts.

title: Free Memberships: Still Available!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces remaining free memberships for readers unable to pay.

title: My Work Habits the Letter allegedly by Jesus’ Own Brother: Mailbag 2/12/2017
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about work habits and the authorship of James.
searchSummary: Answers two unrelated reader questions about productivity and the authorship of James. Ehrman attributes rapid work to compartmentalizing responsibilities, focusing completely on one task, and writing quickly before shifting attention. He then argues that the epistle's author expected a broad Christian audience to identify him as Jesus' famous brother because he used the common name James without qualification, while linguistic and historical considerations make actual authorship by that Galilean figure unlikely.

title: A Major Controversy in New Testament Textual Criticism
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains John Mill's edition and the controversy over New Testament textual variants.
searchSummary: Recounts the controversy after John Mill cataloged 30,000 New Testament variants in 1707. Daniel Whitby feared the data would weaken Protestant scriptural authority and aid Catholic or deist critics, while Anthony Collins used it against revelation; Richard Bentley answered that Mill exposed rather than created existing differences. Bentley argued that additional manuscripts generate more variants but also more evidence for identifying errors and recovering earlier readings, helping spur modern textual criticism.

title: Better Editions of the Greek New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the development of better Greek New Testament editions after the Textus Receptus.
searchSummary: Traces the move from Erasmus's poorly supported Textus Receptus toward critical editions based on broader manuscript evidence. Early editors noted variants without replacing the customary printed text, but John Mill's 1707 edition documented about 30,000 differences drawn from Greek manuscripts, church-father quotations, and ancient translations. That evidence shattered confidence that the repeatedly printed Received Text simply reproduced the original New Testament and made textual criticism unavoidable for translators and theologians.

title: Major Scribal Corruptions in the New Revised Standard Version
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses major non-original passages included in the NRSV.
searchSummary: Examines how the NRSV presents three famous passages scholars consider scribal additions. It omits the Trinitarian wording in 1 John but retains the woman taken in adultery and two endings of Mark inside poorly explained double brackets. Ehrman argues that vague footnotes and unfamiliar notation leave ordinary readers unaware of the textual conclusions, partly because translators sought church acceptance and sometimes believed a nonoriginal story could still preserve authentic history.

title: Responses to Misquoting Jesus: Readers’ Mailbag
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to conservative critiques of Misquoting Jesus and scribal changes.
searchSummary: Responds to conservative criticism of Misquoting Jesus by separating agreed manuscript facts from disputes about emphasis and significance. Thousands of mostly late copies contain hundreds of thousands of differences, overwhelmingly trivial but occasionally important, and some original readings remain uncertain. Ehrman argues that variants matter for interpreting particular authors and passages even when theology can draw doctrines from other texts. He considers broad recovery of New Testament wording reasonable while rejecting claims of complete certainty without earlier evidence.

title: Drew Marshall Show – Jesus Before The Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a Drew Marshall interview about Jesus Before the Gospels.
searchSummary: Introduces an interview about Jesus Before the Gospels and the reliability of traditions transmitted before the Gospels were written. Research in psychology, anthropology, and sociology helps assess how Jesus' followers and later storytellers remembered, altered, and sometimes invented stories as they retold them for new audiences. These findings bear directly on the Gospels' historical accuracy, their interpretation, and broader understandings of how knowledge of the past is formed.

title: The Ending of Mark in the King James Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the long ending of Mark in the King James Bible was not original.
searchSummary: Explains why the final twelve verses of Mark are a later scribal addition. The passage is absent from the oldest witnesses, differs in style and vocabulary, and joins awkwardly to the women fleeing the tomb in silence. Some scholars propose a lost ending, but the abrupt conclusion fits Mark's recurring portrayal of disciples who never understand and people who disobey commands about speaking. The original ending may intentionally leave readers startled and informed while the disciples remain ignorant.

title: The Woman Taken in Adultery in the King James Version
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the woman taken in adultery was not original to John's Gospel.
searchSummary: Explains why the woman caught in adultery, although preserved in the King James Version and many modern Bibles, was not originally part of John or any Gospel. The passage is absent from the oldest manuscripts, differs from John's style, and appears in varying locations in later copies, suggesting that a scribe moved an oral story from a margin into the text. Its literary power does not overcome the manuscript evidence, leaving textual critics to exclude it from the New Testament.

title: The Trinity in the King James Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the Johannine Comma and the Trinity in the King James Bible.
searchSummary: Explains why the King James Version contains the explicit Trinitarian formula in 1 John 5:7-8 even though it was not original. Erasmus initially omitted the wording because his Greek manuscripts lacked it, but a later Greek witness apparently derived the passage from Latin, prompting its inclusion in subsequent editions used by King James translators. Later manuscript discoveries exposed the addition, yet modern translations that removed it faced resistance from readers attached to familiar wording.

title: Pressing Jeff Siker for Answers: An Intriguing Query and Response
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Jeff Siker's response to questions about faith, critical scholarship, and Christianity.
searchSummary: Clarifies Jeffrey Siker's Christian beliefs in light of his historical-critical understanding of the New Testament. He locates his orientation to God in Jesus while recognizing that Gospel portraits are ideological and shaped by resurrection faith. Siker rejects vicarious atonement, traditional co-eternal Christology, and certainty about bodily resurrection, emphasizing instead God's power to bring life from death. Jesus' solidarity with sufferers becomes a model for relieving suffering and confronting systems that cause it.

title: Jeff Siker Part 2: Why I am a Christian (and yet a New Testament scholar): A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts Jeff Siker's explanation of being both Christian and New Testament scholar.
searchSummary: Explains why New Testament scholar Jeffrey Siker remains Christian despite accepting historical-critical conclusions about Scripture. His moderate and liberal education allowed him to treat biblical differences as distinct perspectives rather than contradictions requiring reconciliation, integrating scholarship with faith instead of feeling betrayed by the church. Siker describes faith as an interpretive conversation across ancient and modern communities and grounds his continued belief especially in God's grace, resurrection hope, and response to human suffering.

title: Why He Is Still a Christian (And a Biblical Scholar): A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts Jeff Siker's account of remaining Christian while practicing critical scholarship.
searchSummary: Traces Jeffrey Siker's path from conservative Protestant youth to historically informed Christian faith. Unlike Ehrman's fundamentalist background, Siker encountered historical-critical study within a moderate tradition that did not require biblical inerrancy, so contradictions and the Bible's human character did not produce a crisis of betrayal. His education helped him move beyond literalism while integrating historical context, critical interpretation, and continued church commitment; the post sets up his fuller explanation of why he remains Christian.

title: Ehrman vs Craig: Evidence for Resurrection
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a debate with William Lane Craig on evidence for Jesus' resurrection.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's 2006 debate with conservative evangelical philosopher William Lane Craig on whether historical evidence supports Jesus' resurrection. Ehrman notes the exchange became lively and sometimes testy, that the participants had no later contact, and that Craig published a full transcript from his perspective. Because the original recording quality is limited, the posted video includes corrections but remains imperfect. The post offers the debate for evaluation without claiming who prevailed or restating the competing historical arguments.

title: Printing Errors in the King James Version
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains printing errors and minor revisions in the King James Version.

title: Does It Mean What It Says?  More Problems with the King James
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how obsolete language in the King James Version creates interpretive problems.
searchSummary: Shows how changes in English since 1611 can make the King James Version misleading even when its words still sound familiar. Terms such as admiration, conversation, strange, meat, prevent, quick, wealth, and careful once carried meanings different from their common modern senses. Through examples from both Testaments, Ehrman distinguishes the KJV's literary and historical value from its shortcomings as a study Bible for readers seeking an accurate understanding of the text.

title: Problems with the Language of the King James Version
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why King James English can mislead modern readers.
searchSummary: Explains why the King James Version's literary greatness does not make it a reliable modern study Bible. In addition to its weak manuscript base, its four-hundred-year-old vocabulary includes unfamiliar words, obsolete expressions, mythical animal renderings, and sentences that modern readers can scarcely understand. Ehrman contrasts the translation's enduring influence on memorable English phrases with the confusion its archaic language can create for readers trying to determine what biblical passages mean.

title: How Do We Know What “Most Scholars” Think?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how scholars gauge majority views in biblical studies.
searchSummary: Defines critical scholarship as weighing competing arguments and evidence without predetermining the result through theological commitments. Ehrman does not dismiss conservative scholars, but distinguishes open judgment from repeatedly reaching conclusions required by one's faith community. He identifies majority critical views through broad familiarity with scholars, curricula, and doctoral programs at non-evangelical universities, while acknowledging that claims about all scholars would require including conservative institutions and may yield different proportions.

title: Leading up to the King James Translation
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the historical background leading to the King James translation.
secondaryKeywords: History of the King James Bible

title: Where Did the King James Bible Come From?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains where the King James Bible came from and what its translators used.
searchSummary: Traces the King James New Testament to Erasmus's editions and the Textus Receptus, which depended on a few late manuscripts. Those sources included the woman taken in adultery and Mark's longer ending, while the Trinitarian addition in 1 John entered Erasmus's later edition through a Greek manuscript apparently made to satisfy his challenge. Repeated printing made this accidental textual form customary until modern critics reconstructed the text from older and stronger evidence.
secondaryKeywords: History of the King James Bible

title: The First Greek New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the first printed Greek New Testament and its importance for translation.
searchSummary: Recounts how Erasmus rushed the first published Greek New Testament into print in 1516 using only a few late medieval manuscripts. Missing and illegible portions of Revelation led him to translate Latin back into Greek, creating readings unknown in surviving Greek witnesses. Despite those defects, later publishers repeatedly reproduced his text for centuries; Stephanus added manuscript notes and the familiar verse divisions, but the editions underlying the King James Version still ultimately depended on Erasmus's limited evidence.

title: The Oldest Printed Versions of the Greek New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the oldest printed Greek New Testament editions and the rise of printed textual bases.
searchSummary: Explains how printing replaced variable handwritten copying with faster, cheaper, identical editions and transformed biblical transmission. Western publishers initially favored the Latin Vulgate because few scholars read Greek and many regarded it as the church's Bible. The first printed Greek New Testament appeared within the multilingual Complutensian Polyglot, completed under Cardinal Ximenes before Erasmus's edition but distributed later. The exact Greek manuscripts used remain uncertain, and a later account says some were sold as scrap parchment.

title: My Problem(s) With Fundamentalism: A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a critique of fundamentalism and biblical inerrancy.

title: Biblical Scholars Don’t Typically Call Themselves Biblical Historians
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why biblical scholars usually do not describe themselves as biblical historians.
searchSummary: Distinguishes biblical interpretation from historical research. Many biblical scholars specialize in exegesis, literary criticism, or theology, while historians use biblical texts alongside archaeology and external sources to reconstruct ancient Israel, Jesus, Pauline communities, and early Christianity. Ehrman identifies himself especially as a social historian whose work extends beyond the Bible into Christianity's first four centuries. He also explains why polished thematic books serve readers better than republishing large collections of informal blog posts.

title: What Text Are the Translators Translating?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains what textual base translators use when translating a New Testament book.
searchSummary: Explains that modern New Testament translators do not follow one manuscript but a critical Greek text reconstructed by textual specialists. Editors evaluate competing readings at every variation and choose the wording most likely written by each author, producing an eclectic text unlike any single surviving copy. Translators then use a published scholarly edition based on the most significant Greek manuscripts, ancient versions, and other evidence, with an apparatus documenting important alternatives and their witnesses.

title: What Do Translators Translate?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the books and textual forms Bible translators choose to translate.
searchSummary: Introduces the decisions Bible translators must make about both the canon and the wording they translate. The standard thirty-nine Old Testament and twenty-seven New Testament books are effectively fixed, while inclusion of the Apocrypha varies by tradition. Because New Testament writings originally circulated separately and survive only in copies whose scribes introduced differences, translators cannot consult an original or simply treat the present collection as one ancient manuscript; they need a reconstructed text.

title: What About the Apocrypha?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Old Testament Apocrypha and why its books are treated differently.

title: Did the Council of Nicaea Take Away Reincarnation and Give us the Bible?
author: BDEhrman
description: Corrects myths about Nicaea, reincarnation, and the biblical canon.
searchSummary: Corrects two myths about the Council of Nicaea: it neither selected the New Testament books nor removed teachings about reincarnation. Records show that canon debates continued after 325, with Athanasius first listing the familiar twenty-seven books in 367 and broader agreement emerging later without an early ecumenical vote. Pre-Nicene manuscripts also provide no evidence of deleted reincarnation passages. Nicaea instead debated how Christ was divine, not whether he was God's Son or merely human.

title: How We Got the New Testament (and not some other books!)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the long process by which the New Testament canon developed.
searchSummary: Explains the criteria and prolonged disputes that produced the New Testament canon. Church leaders favored books considered ancient, apostolic, widely used, and orthodox. Marcion's eleven-book collection may have prompted his opponents to define a broader authoritative corpus, but disagreement continued over Revelation, Hebrews, the Shepherd of Hermas, and other writings. Athanasius first named the familiar twenty-seven books in 367, and even his list did not end debate before wider agreement emerged centuries after the books were written.

title: Why Did We Get a New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Christians came to have a New Testament canon.
searchSummary: Explains why Christians developed a distinct New Testament alongside the Jewish Scriptures they inherited. Jesus' teachings and apostolic writings began to receive scriptural authority, while competing Christian groups produced numerous texts attributed to apostles in support of different beliefs about God, Christ, salvation, and creation. The struggle between emerging orthodoxy and rival forms of Christianity therefore drove canon formation, as the tradition that prevailed accepted writings supporting its views and rejected alternative apostolic claims.

title: How We Got the Hebrew Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes modern scholarship on the formation of the Hebrew Bible canon.
searchSummary: Summarizes modern scholarship on the gradual formation of the Hebrew Bible. The Torah was broadly authoritative by the fifth century BCE, the Prophets by the second, and the Writings remained less settled until around the first century CE. Dead Sea Scroll evidence reflects uncertainty over books such as Esther and Jubilees. Although the precise criteria are undocumented, Hebrew language, antiquity, and widespread communal use likely influenced which diverse Israelite writings became the twenty-four-book Jewish canon.

title: How We Got the Hebrew Bible: The Older View
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents an older view of how the Hebrew Bible canon was formed.
searchSummary: Describes and revises the older theory that the Hebrew Bible's three divisions were fixed successively: the Torah by 400 BCE, the Prophets by 200 BCE, and the Writings at a council in Jamnia around 90 CE. Modern scholarship retains the idea of gradual development in that general sequence but finds little evidence that Jamnia formally established or closed the canon. Jewish scriptural authority developed through a more complicated process than a single council's definitive ruling.

title: What is the Hebrew Bible?
author: BDEhrman
description: Defines the Hebrew Bible and its major divisions.
searchSummary: Explains the composition and organization of the Hebrew Bible and its relationship to Christian Old Testaments. The Jewish Tanakh contains Torah, Prophets, and Writings, arranging and counting the same core books differently from the thirty-nine-book Protestant Old Testament. Roman Catholic and Orthodox traditions include additional deuterocanonical works that Jews and Protestants exclude. These differences establish the terminology and collections needed to investigate how communities selected, ordered, and defined their respective biblical canons.

title: Looking Back on the Blog 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Reviews the blog's activity and results during 2016.

title: The Copying of the Hebrew Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how the Hebrew Bible was copied and transmitted.

title: Manuscripts of the Hebrew Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Hebrew Bible manuscripts and their importance for translation.
searchSummary: Introduces the manuscript history behind modern editions and translations of the Hebrew Bible. Its books circulated through handwritten copies for more than two millennia, allowing both intentional changes and accidental errors before printing standardized reproduction. The oldest complete surviving Hebrew Bible, Codex Leningradensis, dates around 1000 CE, long after the earliest writings. Ehrman explains why medieval scribal safeguards cannot establish that earlier transmission was equally stable and points toward evidence from the Dead Sea Scrolls.

title: Some Arduous Tasks for the New Revised Standard Version
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes difficult research tasks for the New Revised Standard Version translation committee.
searchSummary: Describes Ehrman's work checking the New Revised Standard Version for consistency across its separately assigned translation committees. He traced key Hebrew and Greek terms through the entire Bible, flagged inconsistent English renderings, and reviewed whether inclusive-language policies had been applied uniformly. He also checked fine stylistic rules, including the restrictive and nonrestrictive uses of that and which, using the slow computer tools available in 1986 under a demanding publication deadline.

title: Finishing the Work of a Translation
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the final stages of work on a Bible translation.
searchSummary: Describes the final stage of producing the New Revised Standard Version after its larger translation committee completed initial revisions. Because separate subcommittees differed in intervention, vocabulary, style, and implementation of evolving policies, a three-person group reviewed the entire Bible verse by verse to create a consistent translation. As its research assistant, Ehrman supported decisions that could override years of earlier committee work but were considered necessary to avoid uneven or contradictory results.

title: A Reflection on Christmas: Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on suffering, estrangement from Christian faith, and the ethical values still found meaningful in the Christmas story.
searchSummary: Reflects on how a Christmas Eve service changed Ehrman's emotional relationship to Christianity after suffering had contributed to his unbelief. He no longer expects a divine answer to starvation, violence, disease, and disaster, yet values Christianity's call to care for the poor, sick, homeless, lonely, and marginalized. Although he regards the incarnation as myth and death as final, he wishes secular communities more visibly cultivated the generosity, fellowship, and self-giving embodied by humble local churches.

title: Problems with Inclusive Language Bible Translation
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains inclusive-language problems in Bible translation.
searchSummary: Examines an unintended consequence of inclusive language in the NRSV's rendering of Psalm 8 when it is quoted in Hebrews. Translating the psalm's singular man and son of man as plural human beings and mortals appropriately expresses its original reference to humanity. In Hebrews, however, the same wording is interpreted specifically as a prophecy about Jesus. Ehrman argues that reproducing the inclusive plural there obscures the author's Christological argument and illustrates the difficulty of translating texts reused in new contexts.

title: The Marvels of our Universe
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on Psalm 8 and the marvels of the universe.
searchSummary: Uses Psalm 8 and estimates of two trillion galaxies to reflect on humanity's place within the universe. The biblical poet marveled that God cared for people beneath a small ancient firmament, while modern astronomy makes divine attention to one species on one planet incomparably harder to imagine. Believers may respond with gratitude that God notices humanity and unbelievers with skepticism that humans matter cosmically, but Ehrman sees both reactions as rooted in awe before reality's unimaginable scale.

title: Important Blog Issues
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces public lectures and other blog matters.

title: Problems with Inclusive Language Translations
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the NRSV policy on inclusive-language translation.
searchSummary: Explains the NRSV committee's three-part inclusive-language policy: general references to people became inclusive, passages explicitly about one sex remained so, and masculine language for God was retained. Applying those principles required difficult judgments in legal texts and passages where masculine grammar included women. Ehrman uses Jesus' call to become fishers of people to show the tension between accurate inclusion, familiar wording, and elegant English, even when the Greek itself clearly refers to humans of both sexes.

title: Inclusive Language in Bible Translations
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces inclusive language as a major issue for the NRSV committee.
searchSummary: Explores why inclusive Bible translation is both socially important and linguistically difficult. Ehrman argues that generic masculine language reflects and reinforces male dominance, yet replacing it can disrupt grammar, literary force, familiar phrasing, and the Bible's historically patriarchal perspective. Translators must decide how to refer to individuals, humanity, and God without obscuring meaning or pretending ancient authors were inclusive. The post frames these competing demands through familiar sayings and the male-directed Ten Commandments.

title: Lost in Translation
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the difference between literal and idiomatic translation.
searchSummary: Explains why no translation can reproduce every nuance of another language. Greek words for love carry distinct connotations, while translating slave can evoke a modern institution unlike ancient slavery even though softer alternatives are inaccurate. Literal translations preserve close verbal correspondence but can sound wooden; idiomatic versions convey sense and tone more freely but risk interpretation. Ehrman presents the NRSV committee's guiding compromise: remain as literal as possible and as free as necessary.

title: My Work for the New Revised Standard Version Committee
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes work as a graduate assistant for the NRSV committee.

title: Was Cephas Peter?  The Rest of the Argument
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues the argument over whether Cephas and Peter were the same person.

title: Cephas and Peter in the Writings of Paul (Who Knew Them)
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Cephas and Peter in Paul's letters.

title: Lecture at Fresno City College
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a Fresno City College discussion of How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Presents a public discussion of How Jesus Became God held at Fresno City College with philosophy professor Wendell Stephenson. The recorded event addresses the book's historical account of how Jesus came to be regarded as divine and then opens the conversation to audience questions. The post supplies the complete video and a contemporary news report about the well-attended program, without advancing an additional argument beyond the discussion itself.

title: Are Cephas and Peter Two Different People?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why an earlier theory separated Cephas from Peter.

title: A Different Interpretation of the Mischievous Boy, Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers a different reading of the mischievous child Jesus in the Infancy Gospel of Thomas.

title: Jesus the Superboy: A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a discussion of the child Jesus in the Infancy Gospel of Thomas.

title: Free Memberships for those Who Need Them!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces free memberships for readers unable to pay.

title: A Personal Transition
author: BDEhrman
description: Marks the completion of The Triumph of Christianity manuscript.

title: Finding Meaning in the Bible: More Responses to my Christmas Article
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares further responses to a Newsweek article on Christmas and biblical meaning.

title: Is the New Testament Authentic?  Readers’ Mailbag December 4, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to a question about New Testament authenticity and manuscript variation.

title: Response to my Newsweek Article on Christmas
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes responses to the Newsweek article on Christmas.

title: Gift Subscriptions, 2016!!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces holiday gift subscriptions for the blog.

title: Newsweek Article on Christmas: Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the second part of a Newsweek article on Christmas traditions.

title: Newsweek Article on Christmas: Part 1
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the first part of a Newsweek article on Christmas and birth narratives.

title: Looking Ahead to Christmas: A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a Christmas-season reflection on the Gospel birth stories.

title: Improving the Blog 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks readers for suggestions to improve the blog.

title: Personal Thoughts on Thanksgiving, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers personal Thanksgiving reflections.
searchSummary: Reflects on Ehrman's gratitude for a life produced through an unusual fundamentalist past that he sometimes resents but that enabled a career he loves. Losing belief made thanking God troubling because divine gifts to him would imply divine withholding from billions who suffer, yet gratitude remains an attitude worth cultivating without solving cosmic inequality. He argues that fortunate people should acknowledge their advantages and turn appreciation into generosity toward people whose circumstances provide far less.

title: Jesus’ Private Teachings about the King of the Jews
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Jesus' private messianic teaching may have led to the charge King of the Jews.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus privately taught his disciples that he would rule as messianic king in God's future kingdom. His saying that all twelve disciples would govern Israel is probably historical because it includes Judas, whom later Christians would not place on a throne. Jesus expected God and the heavenly Son of Man to defeat evil rather than leading a revolt himself, but Rome treated even this apocalyptic claim to kingship as treason.

title: Jesus’ Crucifixion as King of the Jews
author: admin
description: Argues that crucifixion as King of the Jews supports Jesus' messianic self-understanding.
searchSummary: Explains why Jesus' execution for calling himself King of the Jews strongly suggests that he claimed future kingship. All Gospel accounts connect the charge to his trial and cross, although neither Jesus' public preaching nor later Christian usage normally employs that title. The unexpected charge is therefore historically plausible and implies that an insider disclosed Jesus' private claim, allowing Roman authorities to prosecute him as a rival king.

title: The Apocalyptic Background to Jesus’ Messiahship
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the apocalyptic setting for Jesus' messianic self-understanding.
searchSummary: Provides the apocalyptic framework for understanding Jesus's claim to be the future messiah. Jewish apocalypticism combined cosmic dualism, pessimism about the present age, God's imminent vindication through resurrection and judgment, and expectation of an everlasting earthly kingdom. Bart places Jesus within this worldview: the Son of Man would soon defeat evil, Israel had to repent and love faithfully, and Jesus understood his own messianic role in relation to that approaching divine intervention.

title: Why Would Jesus’ Disciples Think He Was The Messiah?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores why Jesus' disciples may have thought of him as messiah before his death.
searchSummary: Asks why Jesus' disciples considered him the messiah when he did not fulfill common expectations of a priestly ruler, heavenly judge, or warrior king. Later Christian readings of passages about Bethlehem, virgin birth, suffering, and resurrection cannot explain the belief during Jesus' lifetime because those texts were not previously understood as messianic predictions. The post concludes that his followers probably accepted the title because Jesus privately told them he would become Israel's king.

title: Jesus the Messiah Before the Resurrection
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Jesus was understood as messiah before resurrection belief developed.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus' followers must have regarded him as messiah before his crucifixion. Neither death nor resurrection would independently suggest messiahship, since Jews did not expect the messiah to die and rise; resurrection could only cause followers to reconsider a title they already used. The post therefore establishes the starting point for explaining why Jesus' disciples adopted that belief during his life and how they later transformed its meaning.

title: The Invention of a Crucified Messiah
author: BDEhrman
description: Challenges mythicist explanations for inventing a crucified messiah.
searchSummary: Argues that first-century Jews would not invent a crucified Messiah because every known messianic expectation envisioned a powerful king, priest, or cosmic ruler who would defeat God's enemies. Claims about generic dying and rising gods are poorly supported, but the decisive issue is that earliest Christians specifically proclaimed “Christ,” meaning Messiah, as crucified. That combination contradicted Jewish expectations and hindered conversion, making it more plausible that followers reinterpreted messiahship after a real claimant's execution than fabricated the claimant.

title: Lost Gospels: The Greater Questions of Mary.  A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a discussion of the Greater Questions of Mary and its strange lost-Gospel tradition.
searchSummary: Discusses the supposed Greater Questions of Mary, a lost Gospel mentioned and quoted only by the unreliable heresy-hunter Epiphanius. He attributes it to the Phibionites and presents a scene in which Jesus performs a non-procreative sexual ritual before Mary Magdalene, allegedly reflecting a Gnostic desire to prevent divine sparks from entering new bodies. Because no independent witness confirms the text or its contents, its historical existence remains deeply uncertain.

title: Misquoting Jesus Interview C-SPAN
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a C-SPAN interview on Misquoting Jesus.
searchSummary: Introduces a C-SPAN2 Book TV interview recorded at the 2006 New York Times Great Read in Bryant Park. The conversation concerns Ehrman's Misquoting Jesus: The Story Behind Who Changed the Bible and Why, a book about changes made as scribes copied New Testament writings. The brief retrospective post identifies the event, date, setting, and book but does not summarize the interview's particular questions or Ehrman's explanations, leaving the archived video as the source for its substantive discussion.

title: Does Paul Know that Judas Betrayed Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Paul refers to Judas's betrayal in 1 Corinthians.
searchSummary: Argues that 1 Corinthians 11:23 should say Jesus was handed over, not betrayed, because Paul's Greek term elsewhere describes God's action rather than Judas's treachery. Paul never names Judas and reports an appearance to the Twelve, raising the possibility that the group name remained conventional after a member's loss or that Paul did not know the betrayal story. Ehrman therefore excludes Judas's betrayal from claims about Paul's knowledge of the historical Jesus.

title: Mythicists and the Crucified Messiah
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why a crucified messiah was not an expected Jewish invention.
searchSummary: Argues that the proclamation of a crucified Messiah is compelling evidence that Jesus was a real person. Jewish expectations pictured the Messiah as a victorious ruler, priest, or heavenly judge, not a criminal defeated and executed by Rome. Early Jewish followers nevertheless called Jesus Messiah and struggled to explain his crucifixion, which Paul identifies as a stumbling block. If they had invented a persuasive messianic figure, they would not have chosen the very fate most likely to discredit their claim.

title: Mythicists, Jesus, and the Messiah
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses messiahship to argue against mythicist claims about Jesus.
searchSummary: Explains the Jewish expectations that made a crucified Messiah seem contradictory. “Messiah” originally designated an anointed king and later referred to anticipated figures such as a restored Davidic ruler, authoritative priest, or heavenly judge, all characterized by power and victory over Israel's enemies. Jesus instead appeared as an obscure peasant whom Rome arrested, humiliated, and executed. This background prepares the argument that Jewish followers were unlikely to invent such a failed-looking claimant and then call him Messiah.

title: What Is Gnosticism?  A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Defines Gnosticism through a textbook-style overview.

title: What If the Mythicists Were Right:  Mailbag November 6, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to whether mythicism would undermine a scholarly career.
searchSummary: Explains why accepting mythicism would neither destroy Ehrman's career nor alter his personal beliefs. Early Christianity, its literature, institutions, conflicts, and historical influence would remain important subjects even if its founder were mythical, and Ehrman's agnosticism does not depend on Jesus' existence. He would simply teach a more radical account of Christian origins. Ehrman therefore rejects mythicism because he considers it poor history, not because his livelihood or identity requires a historical Jesus.

title: Carrier and James the Brother of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to Richard Carrier's interpretation of James the brother of Jesus.
searchSummary: Refutes Richard Carrier's claim that Paul calls James the Lord's brother because James was a baptized Christian who was not an apostle. No early Christian source defines “brother” that way, and apostles such as Paul could also be spiritual brothers. More decisively, Galatians 1:18-19 identifies James as another apostle whom Paul saw besides Cephas. Ehrman concludes that James is distinguished from Cephas because he was Jesus' biological brother, providing direct evidence that Jesus existed.

title: James the Brother of the Lord
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Paul's reference to James as the brother of the Lord.

title: Paul’s Acquaintances: Jesus’ Disciples and Brother
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Paul's acquaintances with Peter and James as evidence for the historical Jesus.
searchSummary: Argues that Paul's personal acquaintance with Peter, John, and James strongly supports Jesus' historical existence. Galatians mentions two Jerusalem meetings while Paul is defending the independent origin of his gospel, so the contacts are reluctant concessions rather than invented evidence. Paul identifies James as “the brother of the Lord,” consistent with several other ancient sources. Ehrman concludes that knowing Jesus' disciples and biological brother is exceptionally difficult to reconcile with claims that Jesus was only a celestial myth.

title: Paul and the Historical Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains what Paul can tell historians about Jesus as a real person.
searchSummary: Argues that Paul's authentic letters show both how early Christians proclaimed Jesus and how clearly Paul regarded him as historical. Paul's conversion around 32 CE places Christian claims within a few years of Jesus' death, well before the Gospels. His letters describe Jesus as a Jewish descendant of David with a mother, brothers, disciples, teachings, a final meal, crucifixion, and burial.
