Their failure to supply a complete biography reflects their occasional purpose, not belief in a celestial-only Christ.

title: What Can We Do About Presuppositions?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains presuppositions and their role in historical arguments about miracles.

title: Jesus, the Law, and a “New” Covenant Lecture
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a lecture on Jesus, Jewish law, and the new covenant.
searchSummary: Presents a recorded University of Michigan keynote lecture on Jesus, Jewish law, and the new covenant. The talk formed part of a symposium honoring Hebrew Bible scholar George Mendenhall and devoted to law and covenant in the ancient Near East, the Hebrew Bible, and Second Temple Judaism. Because the post supplies the lecture as a video without a transcript, it introduces the event and subject rather than reproducing the lecture's detailed argument.

title: Gospel Evidence that Jesus Existed
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Gospel evidence for Jesus' existence.
searchSummary: Presents the independent Gospel traditions and their Palestinian linguistic roots as evidence that Jesus was not invented. Multiple first-century authors relied on distinct written and oral sources, while Aramaic phrases and sayings that become clearer when translated back into Aramaic point to early circulation in Jesus' homeland. Together with numerous non-Gospel Christian witnesses and Paul's contact with Jesus' associates, this dispersed evidence is difficult to derive from one late fictional creation and instead indicates widespread traditions soon after Jesus' death.

title: The Gospels and the Existence of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Gospel traditions contribute to the case that Jesus existed.
searchSummary: Argues that the Gospels preserve multiple independent evidence streams rather than one story invented by Mark. Matthew and Luke used Mark, Q, and separate sources, while John drew on other traditions, producing at least eight probable written sources within decades of Jesus' life. Their shared basic claims across different authors, places, perspectives, and earlier oral traditions are difficult to explain if no underlying person existed, even though individual accounts contain errors and biases.

title: Mythicists and the Stories Told of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses stories about Jesus to respond to mythicist arguments.
searchSummary: Explains why stories modeled on scripture or familiar heroic patterns do not prove that their subject was invented. Legendary miracle accounts also accumulated around the historical Baal Shem Tov, showing that fabricated stories and a real person can coexist. Ehrman applies this distinction to Jesus' baptism, arguing that independent attestation, John the Baptist's historical activity, and the embarrassment of Jesus receiving baptism make an actual event more probable than Robert Price's proposed derivation from Zoroastrian mythology.

title: My Milwaukee Mythicist Debate
author: BDEhrman
description: Reports on a debate with Robert Price over mythicism.
searchSummary: Reports on Ehrman's Milwaukee debate with Robert Price over whether Jesus existed and reflects on the audience and arguments. Although many attendees were committed mythicists and some held strong opinions without adequate knowledge, the gathering was welcoming and the exchange remained constructive. Ehrman describes his effort to present accessible historical evidence, Price's more technical case, their questioning, and audience participation without declaring himself the winner, then introduces a series explaining his arguments and challenges to Price.

title: The Best Manuscripts and Social Justice: Readers’ Mailbag October 23, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how textual critics identify the best manuscripts and argues that social justice was central to Jesus' message.

title: Mythicists: Did Nazareth Exist?
author: BDEhrman
description: Addresses mythicist claims about whether Nazareth existed.
searchSummary: Refutes the mythicist claim that Nazareth did not exist in Jesus' time and therefore Jesus was invented. Archaeological remains, including a house, farm, and period coins, support a small first-century settlement at the traditional hillside location, while rival claims alternate inconsistently between denying the village and relocating it to an unexcavated site. Ehrman adds that even a mistaken birthplace tradition would not establish a person's nonexistence, so the Nazareth argument is both factually wrong and logically irrelevant.

title: Did Jesus Exist?  My Debate with Robert Price
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a debate with Robert Price on whether Jesus existed.
searchSummary: Explains why expert consensus matters when assessing the mythicist claim, even though consensus alone does not prove that Jesus existed. Ancient historians require languages, primary-source skills, critical methods, and extensive context, just as other fields depend on trained specialists; disagreement therefore needs substantial evidence rather than dismissal of expertise. Ehrman nevertheless plans to base his debate with Robert Price on the historical evidence itself, not an appeal to authority, because a debate should compare arguments rather than count scholars.

title: Marcion as Alive and Well Among Us
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Marcion-like views still appear in modern Christian attitudes toward the Old Testament.

title: The Arch-Heretic Marcion’s Theology
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Marcion's theology and rejection of the Jewish law and God.

title: The “Arch-Heretic” Marcion, Jesus, and the Jewish Law
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Marcion to approach Jesus' relation to Jewish law.
searchSummary: Explains Marcion's radical second-century claim that the Jewish law and Christian gospel came from different gods. He viewed the creator and lawgiver as just but wrathful, while Jesus revealed a previously unknown God of mercy and salvation. Consequently, Marcion rejected the Old Testament, treated Paul as the only apostle who understood Christ, and assembled a restricted canon consisting of an edited Luke and ten Pauline letters.

title: Why Don’t People See Discrepancies in the Bible?  Readers’ Mailbag October 15, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why biblical discrepancies can be hard to see from within an inerrantist framework.
searchSummary: Explains why readers often overlook biblical discrepancies and why the story of the woman caught in adultery is considered a scribal addition. Prior belief in divine inspiration makes problems seem like failures of interpretation, while ordinary readers rarely compare passages closely until alerted. Manuscript absence, non-Johannine style, and unusual vocabulary show John 7:59–8:12 was added later, probably from an oral tradition mistakenly incorporated from a margin.

title: Anti-Judaism in the Gospels: A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a discussion of anti-Judaism in the Gospels.
searchSummary: Distinguishes ancient anti-Judaism from modern racial anti-Semitism and traces an escalating transfer of blame for Jesus's death from Rome to Jews. Mark depicts Pilate and Jewish authorities cooperating, whereas Luke and Matthew emphasize Pilate's reluctance or innocence and John places execution increasingly in Jewish hands. Later apocryphal traditions further exonerate and even sanctify Pilate. This evolving narrative protected Christians from Roman suspicion while fostering hostility that later supported discriminatory laws and mob violence against Jews.

title: Jesus and the Ten Commandments
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Jesus' relationship to the Ten Commandments and Jewish law.
searchSummary: Uses common confusion about the Ten Commandments to introduce the historical problem of Jesus' relationship to Jewish law. Students recognize Jesus as Jewish yet struggle to explain whether he kept Torah, wanted followers to obey it, or exempted them from commands such as the Saturday Sabbath while retaining prohibitions on murder, theft, and adultery. The discussion shows that praising the commandments without knowing their content or place within Torah cannot resolve how Jesus and early Christians interpreted legal obligation.

title: (Later) Early Christian Understandings of Heaven and Hell
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains later Christian developments in heaven and hell after apocalyptic resurrection expectation.
searchSummary: Explains how delayed expectations of Jesus' return helped transform Christian afterlife belief. Jesus, Paul, and other apocalypticists expected bodily resurrection, judgment, and renewed life on earth at history's imminent end. When that end failed to arrive, Christians reinterpreted the temporal contrast between this age and the coming age as a spatial contrast between earth, heaven, and hell. The immortal soul's immediate reward or punishment thus replaced bodily resurrection as the dominant model, a development illustrated by the Apocalypse of Peter.

title: Jesus and Paul on Heaven and Hell
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Jesus' and Paul's apocalyptic views of heaven, hell, and resurrection.
searchSummary: Reconstructs the earliest Christian expectation of life after death as bodily resurrection rather than immortal souls departing for heaven or hell. Jewish apocalypticists used resurrection and judgment to answer why righteous people suffer while the wicked prosper: God would soon overthrow evil and establish justice on earth. Jesus shared this expectation, while Paul identified Jesus' resurrection as the beginning of the end and expected believers to receive transformed bodies. Revelation likewise places eternal life in a renewed earthly creation.

title: Why Don’t I Call Myself a Christian?  Mailbag: October 8, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers personal questions about not identifying as Christian and the origin of the blog.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman does not call himself Christian despite wanting to follow Christian ethics: he lacks belief in any divine being whom Jesus reveals, even though he imposes no doctrinal test on others. A second response recounts how a friend's suggestion became a membership blog devoted entirely to charity after years of planning, legal formation, technical design, and editorial decisions. The project exceeded its expected longevity and fundraising while continuing frequent public scholarship.

title: The Invention of the Afterlife: Request for Ideas!
author: BDEhrman
description: Requests reader input for a possible book on the invention of the afterlife.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's proposed book on how Christian beliefs about heaven, hell, and the afterlife developed. He contrasts the Hebrew Bible's Sheol and occasional denial of postmortem existence with New Testament images of Gehenna, outer darkness, bodily judgment, and Revelation's lake of fire. Because scripture does not straightforwardly teach souls departing for immediate reward or punishment, he asks how that familiar doctrine arose through Greek, Roman, Jewish, Christian, and popular traditions and invites readers to suggest questions the book should address.

title: How I Learned To Write for a General Audience
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains learning to write trade books for general audiences.
searchSummary: Explains how an unusually technical dissertation trained Ehrman to communicate with general audiences. Because research on Didymus the Blind's Gospel quotations sounded obscure and irrelevant outside textual criticism, he repeatedly learned to remove jargon, explain the project clearly, and show why it mattered. That practice shaped his university lectures, textbooks, and trade books, teaching him that successful public writing depends on understanding each audience's knowledge and interests rather than merely simplifying scholarly prose.

title: Gerd Luedemann on the Resurrection: A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a discussion of Gerd Luedemann's view of resurrection visions.

title: The Inerrancy of the Bible?  And Those Who Doubt.  Readers’ Mailbag October 2, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about biblical inerrancy and disciples doubting the resurrection.

title: The Process of Publishing a Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the editorial process after submitting a book manuscript.
searchSummary: Describes the long editorial process that follows submission of a completed book manuscript. Before submission, Ehrman researches, outlines, drafts, revises repeatedly, and incorporates comments from experts and general readers. The publisher's editor may then request structural or stylistic changes, a copyeditor corrects language and documentation, and a compositor creates proofs for final review; only after corrections and indexing does the work become a finished book, making submission an intermediate milestone rather than the end.

title: Writing Books that Are Interesting and Important
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on writing books that are both interesting and important.
searchSummary: Explains Ehrman's shift from writing only on his own technical interests to choosing consequential subjects that can engage wider audiences. Books such as Misquoting Jesus demonstrate how unfamiliar scholarship becomes compelling when its broader importance is clear. He presents The Triumph of Christianity as an especially significant example because it asks how a tiny Jewish movement grew into Rome's dominant religion and thereby transformed Western religion, politics, society, culture, art, law, and intellectual history.

title: Why Was the Emperor Worshiped?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Roman emperors were worshiped as gods.
searchSummary: Roman emperors could be worshiped because ancient people saw divinity as a spectrum and honored beings able to provide security, prosperity, and victory. Cult practices varied: living emperors received greater divine honors in the Greek East, while formal divinization after death depended on senatorial recognition. Local elites also promoted emperor worship to enhance their own status and connection with imperial power.

title: Faith and History: A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a reflection on the relationship between faith and historical study.
searchSummary: Argues that theological beliefs should not determine historical conclusions, although historical findings can legitimately reshape theology. Treating John's accounts as accurate because inspired Scripture must be true substitutes a predetermined doctrinal answer for historical investigation; historians must instead use evidence and methods applied to any ancient source. A believer may still regard a historically problematic text as theologically valuable, but honest interpretation requires allowing critical conclusions to challenge inerrancy rather than insulating doctrine from evidence.

title: Debate with a Mythicist! And the Book of Revelation.  Readers’ Mailbag September 25, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about a mythicist debate and interpreting Revelation.
searchSummary: Answers questions about preparing to debate mythicist Robert Price and about Revelation's place in early Christian apocalypticism. Ehrman's debate preparation builds on decades of historical Jesus research but will include rereading Price and newer mythicist works. Although successive Gospels increasingly soften or reject an imminent apocalypse after it failed to occur, not every Christian followed that trajectory. Revelation remained intensely apocalyptic around 95 CE, further demonstrating that its author differed from the non-apocalyptic author of the Gospel of John.

title: The God Julius Caesar
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the divinization of Julius Caesar in Roman religion.
searchSummary: Julius Caesar received divine titles and planned cult honors before his assassination, then was officially understood to have ascended among the gods after death. Octavian promoted this deification for political advantage and to identify himself as the son of a god, aided by the appearance of a comet. Caesar's cult established a precedent for emperors bearing titles later applied to Jesus, including God, Savior, Lord, and Son of God.

title: Rulers as Gods: The Context of Ancient Religion
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why ancient Greeks and Romans could regard rulers as divine.
searchSummary: Greek and Roman religion centered on practices such as prayer, sacrifice, and divination rather than required doctrines or creeds. Worship sought benefits from superhuman gods, while ethical conduct usually belonged to philosophy and social custom rather than religion itself. Because divinity was measured by power and benefaction, exceptional rulers who protected communities or provided prosperity could plausibly receive temples, sacrifices, and divine honors.

title: When Men Became Gods: My Lecture in Denmark
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a Denmark lecture on human rulers becoming gods and its relevance to Christology.
searchSummary: A lecture on Caesar and Christ places early Christian claims about Jesus within the broader tradition of ruler worship. Alexander the Great and Demetrius Poliorcetes received divine honors, temples, sacrifices, and titles such as Lord, Son of God, and bringer of peace. These precedents show that calling an extraordinary human divine was culturally intelligible before Christians applied comparable language to Jesus.

title: Bart Ehrman vs. Michael Brown on Suffering
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a debate with Michael Brown on suffering and the problem of evil.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's 2010 debate with Christian scholar Michael Brown over whether massive suffering can be reconciled with a God who controls the world. Ehrman stresses that the issue is not merely an intellectual puzzle but a human problem that must be confronted in order to live fully. The debate, prompted by the arguments of God's Problem, places Ehrman's agnostic assessment of biblical explanations against Brown's committed Christian response and invites viewers to evaluate their competing positions.

title: Fear of Dying etc.: Weekly Readers Mailbag, September 18, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about fear of death and Gospel traditions about Barabbas.

title: The Divine Realm in Antiquity
author: admin
description: Introduces the ancient divine realm as context for emperor worship and Christology.
searchSummary: Ancient people pictured the divine realm as a hierarchy ranging from a supreme deity through Olympian and local gods, daimones, and exceptional divine humans. Worship of many deities was compatible and generally tolerant because each could provide different forms of help. Within this continuum, emperors and other remarkable people could be considered divine without being equated with Zeus, providing context for both imperial cult and early Christology.

title: The Rise of the Roman Empire
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Roman imperial history as background for understanding divine rulers.

title: Arguments, Evidence, and Changing Your Mind
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how evidence and argument can change even deeply held beliefs.
searchSummary: Explores why logical arguments and evidence do not affect every reader alike. Students committed to an image of Jesus can overlook tensions such as Matthew's and Luke's incompatible genealogies because faith assumptions determine what they notice. Ehrman relates this to his gradual response to manuscript problems and warns that everyone interprets through presuppositions. Teaching should help people see alternative readings, but persuaders must recognize their own blind spots and remain willing to revise their conclusions rather than claiming complete objectivity.

title: Bruce Metzger Beliefs, My Loss of Faith: A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a discussion of Bruce Metzger's beliefs and loss of faith.
searchSummary: Explains that Ehrman never learned how Bruce Metzger viewed his transition from evangelical Christian to agnostic. Their teacher-student relationship focused on textual criticism, New Testament interpretation, and early Christian history, not personal faith, a pattern Ehrman also experienced with other believing scholarly collaborators. Metzger remained devout and said he liked Misquoting Jesus, but offered no known judgment about Ehrman's unbelief. The account illustrates how rigorous academic cooperation can proceed independently of participants' private theological commitments.

title: Why Textual Criticism is “Safe” for Conservative Christians
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why textual criticism can feel safer for conservative Christians than other biblical scholarship.
searchSummary: Explains why textual criticism has traditionally attracted conservative evangelical scholars. Historical-critical interpretation often requires acknowledging contradictions, disputed authorship, and the Bible's human limitations, creating conflict with inerrancy. Textual criticism instead reconstructs the wording of manuscripts without deciding whether the recovered words are inspired or true, allowing scholars with differing theological commitments to share its methods. Its technical neutrality made it a comparatively safe field for Ehrman and other evangelicals pursuing advanced biblical scholarship.

title: The Charities We Support
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the charities supported by the blog.
searchSummary: Explains the blog's charitable structure and identifies the organizations receiving its membership fees and donations. The Bart Ehrman Foundation had distributed $339,000 while Bart personally covered operating costs. The post describes Urban Ministries of Durham, the Food Bank of Central and Eastern North Carolina, CARE, and Doctors Without Borders, connecting each with homelessness, hunger, poverty relief, emergencies, or medical care. Bart also plans clearer philanthropy information and possible guest posts from charity representatives.
secondaryKeywords: Food Bank of Central and Eastern North Carolina

title: Do Most Manuscripts Have the Original Text?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the majority of manuscripts does not necessarily preserve the original text.
searchSummary: Explains why a majority manuscript reading is not necessarily original. More than 94 percent of Greek New Testament witnesses are medieval and form related textual families, while a small group of earlier manuscripts often agrees on different wording; counting descendants is unlike polling independent eyewitnesses. Historical attachment to the King James Version encouraged theological defenses of the majority text, but modern textual scholars generally prefer earlier evidence over unsupported claims of providential preservation.

title: My Original Interest in Textual Criticism
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the origins of an interest in New Testament textual criticism.
searchSummary: Traces Ehrman's interest in textual criticism to a Moody course on inspiration, canon, and altered manuscripts. Belief that God inspired the Bible's exact words made identifying those words urgent, while scribal additions such as the adulterous-woman story and Mark's longer ending turned reconstruction into an evidentiary detective problem. Only later did he conclude that failure to preserve inspired wording also challenged the purpose and plausibility of verbal inspiration itself.

title: Becoming a Textual Critic
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts becoming a textual critic and responding to conservative claims about that field.
searchSummary: Explains that Ehrman became a textual critic primarily through independent, extensive reading rather than formal coursework. Bruce Metzger directed his thesis and dissertation with a light touch, allowing him to master the field largely on his own while offering crucial guidance when necessary. Metzger's unusually severe critique of Ehrman's dissertation proposal, intended to help a technical project survive a theology-oriented committee, taught him that serious scholarship required more precise writing, stronger communication, and standards beyond merely competent work.

title: Does James Contradict Paul?
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares James and Paul on faith, works, and justification.
searchSummary: Examines whether James contradicts Paul's teaching that people are justified by faith apart from works. Their statements appear opposed, but Paul means trusting Christ rather than performing distinctively Jewish law, while James contrasts mere intellectual belief with good deeds that demonstrate genuine faith. Ehrman suggests James may be correcting a later distortion of Paul's slogan “faith, not works,” using Abraham and Genesis 15:6 to oppose conduct Paul himself would not have endorsed.

title: How You Can Help!
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks readers to help support the blog's charitable fundraising work.
searchSummary: Responds to slowing fundraising by asking readers to support the blog without increasing its basic membership price. Bart encourages those who can afford more to make one-time or recurring donations, while stressing that even small monthly gifts become significant collectively. He also asks members to recruit others or give subscriptions, and promises clearer information about the charities receiving the funds. These actions would expand both the educational audience and aid to people in need.

title: Where Did the Trinity Come From?  Video Lecture.
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a video lecture on the origin of the doctrine of the Trinity.
searchSummary: Introduces the third lecture in Ehrman's Coral Gables series on How Jesus Became God. The talk asks how Christians who regarded Christ as divine, continued to worship God, and affirmed monotheism eventually developed the doctrine of the Trinity. The post provides the complete recorded lecture as its substantive content, positioning the doctrine's emergence as a historical development that requires explanation rather than assuming its fully formed presence in the earliest Christian period.

title: How I Discovered Textual Criticism
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts the first serious encounter with New Testament textual criticism at Moody Bible Institute.
searchSummary: Defines textual criticism and recounts Ehrman's discovery of the field at Moody Bible Institute. Because believers considered every biblical word inspired yet possessed only differing copies, identifying the wording became more fundamental to him than it seemed to classmates who trusted divine preservation. Known additions such as the adulterous-woman story and Mark's longer ending showed that real uncertainty existed and motivated him to learn the original languages and investigate manuscript evidence.

title: Learning to Teach at Moody
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes early experiences learning to teach the Bible at Moody.
searchSummary: Recounts how youth ministry during Ehrman's student years taught him to communicate difficult biblical material to audiences who did not share his enthusiasm. Leading teenagers in Sunday school and weekday Bible studies forced him to make lessons true, organized, practical, interesting, and clear. That sustained early practice shaped his later teaching and public writing by training him to translate specialized knowledge into accessible presentations without sacrificing structure, substance, or intellectual seriousness.

title: Moody Bible Boot Camp
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues an autobiographical account of intensive Bible training at Moody Bible Institute.
searchSummary: Describes how Moody Bible Institute functioned as an intensive biblical boot camp that shaped Ehrman's career from age seventeen. A course on John inspired his decision to teach New Testament, and years of Bible, theology, ministry, memorization, and relentless study developed both expertise and intellectual discipline. He regrets missing a broad liberal-arts education, yet believes that his singular passion for Scripture built the mental capacity, factual knowledge, and later communication skills without which he would not have become a scholar.

title: Am I A Better Person as an Agnostic?  A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a reflection on whether becoming agnostic led to greater empathy or moral improvement.
searchSummary: Argues that agnosticism did not make Ehrman morally worse and may have intensified his commitment to reducing suffering. Without belief in an afterlife, he values family, friendship, meaningful work, ordinary pleasures, generosity, and the finite present rather than nihilistic indulgence. Compassion can arise from human evolution and shared humanity without divine command. Because no future world will repair present misery, helping people now becomes more urgent. Ehrman avoids claiming moral superiority but reports greater happiness, giving, and engagement with life.

title: Were Jesus and His Followers Armed?
author: BDEhrman
description: Considers whether Jesus and the disciples were armed around the time of Jesus' arrest.

title: Beginning My Study of the Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Traces the beginning of serious Bible study as part of an autobiographical account of becoming a public scholar.
searchSummary: Recounts how a charismatic Youth for Christ leader persuaded Ehrman to abandon plans for Kansas University and attend Moody Bible Institute as proof of serious Christian commitment. Arriving eager but biblically inexperienced, he encountered an entrance examination that exposed how much he did not know, including the identity of Israel's left-handed judge, Ehud. The humbling experience intensified his determination to master Scripture, beginning an educational path whose long-term scholarly consequences differed sharply from the evangelical future he then expected.

title: My Original Passion for the Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains an early passion for Bible study and its role in later scholarly development.
searchSummary: Explains how Ehrman's born-again conversion at fifteen transformed the Bible from a marginal part of Episcopal worship into the center of his faith. Embarrassed by his ignorance when friends asked questions, he read Scripture, joined Bible studies, changed his social circle, and began memorizing verses, starting with Philippians 1:21. His original interests were understanding the text and applying it to belief and life, forms of exegesis and theology that preceded his later specialization in other areas of biblical scholarship.

title: Different Ways of Describing the Theology of the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains different scholarly ways of describing the theology of the New Testament.
searchSummary: Surveys changing approaches to descriptive New Testament theology. Conservative synthesis seeks a single biblical teaching on subjects such as sin, salvation, or Christ, while critical scholarship recognizes substantial differences among authors. Earlier author-specific studies still imposed categories from modern systematic theology. A more historically sensitive approach begins with each writer's own emphases, allowing Paul's concerns about salvation, Jews, and Gentiles or John's focus on Christ's divine identity to emerge without forcing every text into the same framework.

title: How We’re Doing on the Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Reviews the state of the blog and asks readers for feedback.
searchSummary: Assesses the blog after four years and five months of continuous publication and asks members for candid feedback. Although it had raised $117,000 during the previous fiscal year, current fundraising was falling behind that pace. Bart invites readers to identify the two features they value most, two problems they see, and one improvement that could increase quality and charitable revenue. He frames the survey as a way to strengthen content, engagement, and future fundraising.

title: My Work as a Historian and Paul in Conflict with the Jerusalem Church: Readers’ Mailbag August 20, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about historical work and Paul's conflict with the Jerusalem church.
searchSummary: Answers why Ehrman's work qualifies as history and how Paul related to Jerusalem leaders. Textual criticism becomes historical when it reconstructs why scribes changed manuscripts within early Christian controversies, and most of Ehrman's scholarship directly studies Christian developments rather than textual variants alone. Paul indicates agreement with Peter and James about Christ's saving death and resurrection but serious conflict over Jewish-Gentile association and law observance. Because Jerusalem leaders left no authentic writings, fuller reconstruction remains necessarily speculative.

title: Video of How Jesus Became God: Part 2 (of 3)
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the second video lecture on How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Presents the second of three recorded lectures delivered at Coral Gables Congregational Church about How Jesus Became God. The series examines the historical process by which Jesus' followers came to regard him as divine, with this installment continuing the argument between the introductory and concluding talks. Because the post itself contains only event information and the embedded recording, its substantive treatment resides in the video rather than a separate written exposition.

title: Another Approach to New Testament Theology
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains another approach to New Testament theology and how scholars use the New Testament for theology.
searchSummary: Describes a historical approach to New Testament theology that reconstructs each author's views before comparing them. John, Luke, Paul, Revelation, and other writings address different communities, inherit different traditions, and disagree about God, Christ, salvation, human existence, and the afterlife. Combining verses into one supposedly uniform biblical theology obscures this diversity and often depends on treating God as the books' single author. Authorship questions matter because writings falsely attributed to Paul cannot simply be used to define Paul's theology.

title: Studying New Testament Theology
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses graduate training in New Testament theology and why scholars are often not trained for general audiences.
searchSummary: Distinguishes New Testament exegesis from theology in graduate biblical studies. Exegesis uses language, historical context, and related ancient evidence to reconstruct what a text meant to its author or earliest readers. Theology asks how those writings have addressed, and should address, later Christian communities, sometimes treating Scripture as a dialogue partner whose patriarchal or otherwise troubling claims may be challenged. The disciplines overlap, but one is primarily historical interpretation while the other concerns contemporary religious meaning and appropriation.

title: Being Trained To Interpret Texts
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes training in close textual interpretation as preparation for public writing.
searchSummary: Describes the specialized training required for responsible exegesis of ancient texts. Interpreters must work in original languages, analyze grammar, determine word meanings from varied contexts rather than dictionaries alone, and study each author's distinctive usage and historical setting. Graduate seminars can devote months to only part of a short biblical book because interpretation depends on this cumulative work. Ehrman valued such rigor but chose not to make book-by-book exegesis his primary scholarly specialty.

title: Speaking in Churches as an Agnostic; and Jewish Beliefs about Afterlife.  Readers Mailbag August 13, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about speaking in churches as an agnostic and Jewish views of the afterlife.

title: Video of How Jesus Became God, Part 1 (of 3)
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the first video lecture on How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Introduces the first of three recorded lectures delivered at Coral Gables Congregational Church about How Jesus Became God. The series presents Ehrman's historical account of how a Jewish apocalyptic preacher came to be understood as a divine being, beginning the sequence later continued in two additional talks. The post itself supplies event context and the complete video rather than a separate written explanation of the lecture's specific arguments.

title: Why Scholars Aren’t Trained To Write Trade Books
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why scholarly training often does not prepare academics to write trade books.
searchSummary: Explains why doctoral training prepares scholars to conduct specialized research and write for experts rather than general audiences. Bart describes technical seminars, comprehensive examinations, and narrowly focused dissertations, using his own textual-critical work on patristic evidence as an example. This training develops command of languages, sources, and prior scholarship, but it does not teach scholars how to translate complex findings into accessible trade books for nonspecialists.

title: What Do We Call It?  Coming Up with a Book Title.
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the process of choosing a title for a trade book on the triumph of Christianity.
searchSummary: Compares the descriptive precision expected of scholarly titles with the accuracy and immediate appeal required of trade-book titles. Publishers increasingly resist academic titles that promise accessibility the books do not deliver, while general-audience titles must be intriguing without becoming sensational. Ehrman's unsuccessful suggestions for his textual criticism book and initial opposition to Misquoting Jesus illustrate why experienced editors and marketers often judge public appeal better than authors, even when their preferred wording seems less technically exact.

title: Did Ancient Secretaries Actually Compose Writings?  A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how ancient secretaries could assist writers and whether they composed works for others.
searchSummary: Reviews whether ancient secretaries independently composed substantial works in another person's name. Secretaries took dictation, occasionally edited elite correspondence, and wrote brief formulaic documents for illiterate clients, but evidence for coauthoring or creating complex letters is virtually absent. The few examples associated with Cicero were exceptional and recognized as deceptive. Ehrman concludes that the secretary hypothesis lacks historical support as an explanation for disputed Pauline or Petrine letters, whereas pseudonymous writings are abundantly documented.

title: Does a Person Need the Holy Spirit to Interpret the Bible?  Is John’s Gospel Accurate?  Readers Mailbag August 7, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about the Holy Spirit in biblical interpretation and the historical accuracy of John's Gospel.
searchSummary: Answers whether the Holy Spirit is necessary for biblical interpretation and whether John accurately preserves Jesus' teaching. Contradictory readings among Spirit-led Christians and agreement between believers and nonbelievers show that ordinary linguistic and historical methods can interpret human language. Textual criticism can reconstruct much of what John wrote, but that does not establish that Jesus said it. Historical criticism separately evaluates Johannine dialogues and discourses, most of which probably reflect the Gospel's author or tradition rather than the historical Jesus.

title: How Did Ancient Writers Use Secretaries?  A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how ancient writers used secretaries and why that matters for authorship claims.
searchSummary: Examines evidence for secretaries taking dictation and stylistically editing ancient letters. Exact transcription is well documented, but meaningful editing is sparsely attested and confined to highly educated assistants serving wealthy Roman elites. Such examples do not resemble lengthy, intricately argued Christian treatises attributed to lower-class apostles. Nor can minor corrections account for wholesale differences in style and content between disputed and undisputed letters. Ehrman argues that commentators often invoke secretaries without producing evidence relevant to the works at issue.

title: Who Could Read and Write?  A Blast from the Past.
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains literacy levels in antiquity and their relevance for claims about New Testament authorship.
searchSummary: Assesses whether Peter or John could have written books attributed to them. Reading required years of training and was limited mainly to wealthy urban elites; composition in a second language was much rarer. Roman Palestine may have had literacy below three percent, with rural Galileans speaking chiefly Aramaic. Peter's background as a poor fisherman offered neither the resources nor education needed to compose an elegant Greek work, supporting the New Testament's description of him as illiterate.

title: The End of Time in Revelation and the Gospel of John
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares the end-time expectations in Revelation and the Gospel of John.
searchSummary: Contrasts Revelation's apocalyptic eschatology with the Gospel of John's present salvation to show that different authors wrote them. Revelation expects catastrophic divine intervention, judgment, and a future kingdom, preserving expectations associated with Jesus and the Synoptics. John largely replaces that temporal scheme with a spatial division between the world below and heaven: believers already possess eternal life through Jesus. Shared images such as Word and Lamb cannot outweigh these opposing accounts of when and how God's final salvation arrives.

title: Did John Write the Fourth Gospel?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether John the son of Zebedee wrote the Fourth Gospel.
searchSummary: Argues that the anonymous Fourth Gospel was not written by John son of Zebedee. John 21 distinguishes its authorial "we" from the Beloved Disciple whose testimony is invoked, so the writer does not claim that identity. More importantly, literary composition in Greek required years of elite education unavailable to a poor, Aramaic-speaking Galilean fisherman; Acts even calls John illiterate. Whatever tradition connected the Gospel with an eyewitness, the historical apostle could not have authored its fluent Greek narrative.

title: The Author of Revelation
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the author of Revelation is not usually identified with the author of the Fourth Gospel.
searchSummary: Explains why Revelation was written neither by the author of the Gospel of John nor by John, son of Zebedee. Revelation's error-filled Greek differs sharply from the Gospel's simple but fluent prose, a distinction already recognized by Dionysius of Alexandria. Its visionary author also appears separate from the twenty-four elders who likely include Jesus' twelve disciples. Revelation is therefore an orthonymous work by John but homonymous because later Christians confused him with the disciple, helping secure its canonical status.

title: Celibacy and Polygamy in the Bible: Weekly Readers’ Mailbag July 30, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about Jesus' possible marriage and polygamy in the Bible.

title: Who Wrote the Book of Revelation and the Fourth Gospel?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether the same author could have written both Revelation and the Gospel of John.
searchSummary: Explains how Revelation and the Fourth Gospel were attributed to John son of Zebedee while preparing to reject both claims. Revelation names its author John but never identifies him as an apostle; church leaders later needed apostolic authorship to secure its scriptural status. The anonymous Gospel was connected to the Beloved Disciple, then identified with John because Peter was distinct and James died early. These inferences do not demonstrate that either book came from the apostle or the same author.

title: Bart Ehrman discusses the Apocalypticist
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares an unusual video explaining apocalypticism, briefly touching on Jesus and modern end-time prediction.
searchSummary: Introduces an unusual video about ancient apocalypticism rather than a single figure called “the apocalypticist.” The clip moves from a Richard Harris film to Ehrman's explanation of apocalypse, briefly considers whether Jesus held an apocalyptic worldview, and ends with Harold Camping's failed prediction that the world would end in May 2011. Ehrman criticizes the video's confusing title but shares it as a compact, eclectic treatment of apocalyptic ideas and their appearance in ancient interpretation and modern prediction.

title: Constantine’s Vision(s): What Did He Really See and When?
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares the accounts of Constantine's visions and asks what Constantine may have seen.
searchSummary: The differing accounts of Constantine's visions may reflect multiple experiences or later memories reshaped by his subsequent Christian understanding. A possible reconstruction identifies the earlier public sign as a solar halo associated with Sol Invictus, followed by a dream before the Milvian Bridge that connected the supreme sun god with Christianity's God. Constantine's conversion was genuine but gradual, beginning with limited knowledge and exclusive commitment rather than mature theology.

title: Constantine’s Vision according to Eusebius
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Eusebius's account of Constantine's vision and conversion.
searchSummary: Eusebius's later biography says Constantine and his army saw a luminous cross over the sun bearing the message "By this conquer." Christ then appeared in a dream, instructed him to use the sign for protection, and Christian advisers explained its meaning and the incarnation. Constantine studied Christian writings, chose to worship this God alone, and adopted the Chi-Rho labarum as a military standard associated with divine victory.

title: Metzger and the Squirrel Part 2: Another Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues a humorous memory involving Bruce Metzger and an oral tradition about a squirrel.

title: Bruce Metzger and the Squirrel: A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a humorous autobiographical story about Bruce Metzger and an oral tradition.
searchSummary: Retells the Princeton Seminary legend in which Bruce Metzger responds to a squirrel's fatal fall by declaring that he knows the Greek word for squirrel. Ehrman traces variants that substitute Aramaic, identify him or another professor as Metzger's companion, and amplify the surrounding dialogue. A colleague notes that Metzger would simply state the Greek word rather than announce his knowledge, demonstrating that the famous version had changed in transmission and setting up a later account of the anecdote's likely origin.

title: Two Versions of Constantine’s Vision
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares two early accounts of Constantine's vision and their connection to Constantine's conversion.
searchSummary: Two early sources give substantially different accounts of Constantine's religious visions. A pagan panegyric from 310 describes Apollo promising long life and world rule, possibly marking devotion to Sol Invictus, while Lactantius says a dream before the Milvian Bridge directed Constantine to place a Chi-Rho-like sign on his soldiers' shields. The contrast raises unresolved questions about whether these were separate experiences, changing interpretations, or competing narratives of conversion.

title: Constantine Before His Conversion
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes Constantine's life and religious background before conversion to Christianity.
searchSummary: Constantine likely practiced local, civic, military, and imperial cults before becoming Christian, while evidence that his parents were already Christian is weak. His father Constantius may instead have favored Sol Invictus as a supreme god and avoided vigorous participation in Diocletian's persecution. Eusebius later reframed Constantius as devoted to Christianity and portrayed Constantine's military need for divine support as leading him from failed polytheism toward his father's one God.

title: Constantine and the Battle at the Milvian Bridge
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the Battle at the Milvian Bridge as background to Constantine's rise and conversion.
searchSummary: Diocletian's tetrarchic succession collapsed when Constantine and Maxentius claimed imperial authority through family connections and military acclamation. Their rivalry culminated in Constantine's 312 invasion of Italy and victory at the Milvian Bridge, where Maxentius drowned while retreating across a failed pontoon bridge. Constantine then controlled the western empire and eventually defeated Licinius to become sole ruler, with the battle also becoming the setting for his conversion to Christianity.

title: Knowing the “Original” Text — of the NT or of Isaiah.  Weekly Readers’ Mailbag July 17, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about knowing an original text for the New Testament or Isaiah.
searchSummary: Explains that knowing an ancient text historically means justified near-certainty rather than mathematical proof. Manuscript agreement makes most New Testament wording effectively secure, while competing readings, difficult sense, and balanced evidence produce varying degrees of doubt. The post also shows a different kind of textual fluidity in Isaiah, whose judgment, exilic consolation, and postexilic exhortation reflect three historical settings and authors later combined by an editor.

title: How Constantine Became Emperor
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Constantine came to power after the collapse of Diocletian's succession plan.
searchSummary: Diocletian's planned succession initially elevated new rulers by appointment, but Constantine's dynastic claim disrupted the second Tetrarchy. After his father Constantius died in Britain, the army proclaimed Constantine Augustus even though Severus was the designated successor. Galerius compromised by accepting Constantine as Caesar, but Maxentius then invoked the same hereditary logic in Rome, multiplying rival emperors and setting the stage for civil war.

title: Preface to Constantine: The Rule of the Four
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Diocletian's tetrarchy as background for Constantine's rise.
searchSummary: Diocletian created the Tetrarchy to solve the empire's military demands and chronic succession crises through two senior Augusti and two junior Caesars chosen by merit. The arrangement was intended to replace unreliable hereditary succession and competing army acclamations with orderly promotion. It collapsed almost immediately after Diocletian's retirement, however, as dynastic ambitions and military loyalties propelled Constantine and other claimants into conflict.

title: The Emperor Constantine: Some Background
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Constantine as a new topic in the study of Christianity's rise within the Roman world.
searchSummary: Constantine's conversion changed Christianity from a persecuted movement into a legally tolerated and imperially favored religion, but it neither made Christianity official nor alone caused its numerical triumph. The historical background begins with Diocletian's Tetrarchy, which divided imperial responsibilities among two senior and two junior rulers selected by merit. Constantine's father served within that system, whose failed succession opened Constantine's path to power.

title: Are the Hebrew Bible/Old Testament Manuscripts Reliable?  A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Hebrew Bible and Old Testament manuscripts matter for evaluating textual reliability.

title: Suggestions for Further Reading on the Pentateuch
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends further reading on the Pentateuch and its sources.

title: Did Matthew Write in Hebrew? Did Jesus Institute the Lord’s Supper?  Did Josephus Mention Jesus?  Weekly Readers’ Mailbag July 9, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about Matthew in Hebrew, the Lord's Supper, and Josephus on James.
searchSummary: Answers three historical questions about Matthew, the Last Supper, and Josephus. Matthew was written in Greek because it reproduces Greek Mark verbatim; Jesus probably shared a final meal but likely did not institute an atoning Eucharist; and Josephus's reference to James as brother of Jesus supports an earlier discussion of Jesus, although Christian scribes modified parts of it. The responses distinguish plausible historical cores from later interpretation and explain an accidentally omitted argument in Did Jesus Exist?

title: Another Creation Story
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares the Genesis creation story with ancient Near Eastern creation traditions.

title: Other Myths of the Flood from the Ancient Near East
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses ancient Near Eastern flood myths and their relation to the biblical flood story.

title: When Was the World Created?  A Blast From the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts a discussion of when Christians began dating the creation of the world.

title: Modern Views of the Authorship of the Pentateuch
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes modern scholarly views on the authorship and sources of the Pentateuch.

title: Did Moses Write the Pentateuch?  The JEDP Hypothesis.
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the JEDP hypothesis and why scholars question Mosaic authorship of the Pentateuch.

title: Other Literary Tensions in the Pentateuch
author: BDEhrman
description: Identifies literary tensions in the Pentateuch that suggest multiple sources.

title: Biblical Anachronisms: The Philistines and Beersheba
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Philistines and Beersheba as examples of biblical anachronisms in the Pentateuch.

title: Literary Tensions in the Creation Account of Genesis
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains literary tensions in Genesis's creation accounts as evidence for multiple sources.

title: Who Wrote the Pentateuch?  Early Questions of Authorship.
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces early questions about who wrote the Pentateuch.

title: The Name of Saul/Paul and the Sources of the Pentateuch: Weekly Mailbag June 26, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about Saul's name Paul and the sources behind the Pentateuch.

title: More on Numbers of Converts
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues a numerical discussion of early Christian conversion and growth.
searchSummary: Refines estimates of Christian growth from about twenty followers in 30 CE to roughly thirty million by 400. Ehrman proposes sharply declining rates: exceptional early expansion, about 30–35 percent per decade from 100 to 300, and slower proportional growth after Constantine as fewer pagans remained to convert. Household conversions made these rates plausible because one adult's decision could add an entire family. He stresses that the resulting figures are illustrative estimates, not precise population data.

title: Back to the Question of How Many People Converted
author: BDEhrman
description: Returns to early Christian growth and how many people converted.
searchSummary: Develops a model for Christianity's earliest growth while discounting births, health care, martyrdom, and other proposed demographic advantages as major causes. Beginning with approximately twenty followers in 30 CE and thirty million Christians by 400, Ehrman uses Paul's letters as evidence for rapid initial expansion across numerous sizable communities. He proposes that missionary enthusiasm produced about 1,280 Christians by 60 and roughly 8,381 by 100, while emphasizing that actual rates fluctuated and the calculations remain provisional.

title: Follow up on Knocking Opportunity….
author: BDEhrman
description: Provides a follow-up note about a blog fundraising opportunity.
searchSummary: Adds two practical details to an earlier offer allowing major donors to review Bart's forthcoming book manuscript. Contributions qualify as tax-deductible because the blog operates through an IRS-recognized nonprofit organization, and anyone wishing to participate should contact Bart directly by email. The brief follow-up corrects omissions in the original announcement and expresses hope that many readers will take advantage of the charitable opportunity.

title: Opportunity Comes Knocking!!
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers readers a chance to support the blog while discussing work on The Triumph of Christianity.
searchSummary: Offers readers who donate $1,000 an advance electronic draft of The Triumph of Christianity and an opportunity to comment before publication. Bart explains that the book examines Christianity's growth from a small movement to millions of adherents across the Roman Empire. Participants receive early access and acknowledgment in the finished book; he receives useful general-reader feedback; and the blog's supported charities receive the entire donation, making the arrangement both editorial review and fundraising.

title: Paul’s Converted Vision of Himself
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Paul's conversion changed Paul's self-understanding and mission.

title: What Paul’s Conversion Meant
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains what Paul's conversion meant for Pauline theology and life.

title: Reading Suggestions for the New Testament: A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends serious reading for lay readers interested in the New Testament.

title: The Conversion of Paul
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes Paul's conversion as part of the broader question of why people became Christian.

title: How Paul Persecuted the Christians
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Paul persecuted Christians before becoming a follower of Jesus.

title: Some Comments on the Gospel of John:  (Based on John Spong’s Book).  A Blast from the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates John Shelby Spong's claims about the authorship, sayings, signs, and historical characters of the Gospel of John.
searchSummary: Reviews John Shelby Spong's claims that the Fourth Gospel was not written by an apostle, does not preserve Jesus' historical words or miracles, and contains invented characters. The first and third conclusions broadly reflect critical scholarship, although saying Jesus spoke none of John's words is too absolute. Even if figures such as Nicodemus were not historical, nothing shows that the evangelist intended readers to treat them as fictional rather than real participants in Jesus' life.
topics: Signs in the Gospel of John

title: Jesus’ Death and Resurrection for Salvation; Paul’s Collection; and My Sunday Mornings: Readers’ Mailbag June 11, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about salvation through Jesus' death and resurrection, Paul's collection, and Sunday mornings.

title: Progressive Spirit Interview
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares an interview about Jesus Before the Gospels, memory, and the historical Jesus.
searchSummary: Introduces a Progressive Spirit podcast interview about Jesus Before the Gospels. The discussion draws on research into how memories form, are recalled, change as they pass from person to person, and are reshaped by later perspectives and events. Applying that research to early Christianity helps explain how traditions about Jesus circulated and developed for years before Gospel authors committed them to writing.

title: I Need Some Suggestions!
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks readers for suggestions about the blog's direction and future topics.

title: Paul, Jesus, and the Messiah
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores Paul's understanding of Jesus as Messiah in relation to resurrection belief.
searchSummary: Explains why calling the crucified Jesus messiah likely provoked Paul's persecution of Christians. First-century Jewish hopes varied, and many Jews expected no messiah, but a prominent expectation grew from God's promise of a lasting Davidic dynasty and envisioned a future anointed king. Jesus' humiliating execution made him the opposite of such a divinely favored ruler, turning the Christian claim into a scandal rather than merely an unusual messianic proposal.

title: Paul’s Own (and Only) Gospel
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Paul's claim that the gospel came through revelation rather than human instruction.
searchSummary: Clarifies what Paul meant by claiming that his gospel came through a revelation of Jesus rather than from human teachers. Paul inherited the belief that Jesus' death and resurrection brought salvation, but claimed revelation for his distinctive insight that salvation extended to gentiles without circumcision or Torah observance. Galatians therefore defends a law-free gentile mission, not the idea that Paul invented Christianity or first connected salvation with Jesus' death.

title: Were Jesus’ Followers Crazy?  Was He?  Mailbag June 4, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains early Christianity's persistence through cognitive dissonance and considers whether Jesus' apocalyptic outlook indicates mental illness.
searchSummary: Addresses why Christianity survived the failure of Jesus' imminent apocalyptic expectation and whether Jesus was mentally ill. Ehrman presents John Gager's application of cognitive dissonance: disappointed believers could reinterpret the delay, intensify evangelism, and gain social reinforcement from new converts rather than abandon the movement. He treats the theory as brilliant but not definitive. He also rejects diagnosing Jesus as insane, arguing that apocalyptic expectations and messianic confidence were intelligible within first-century Jewish culture.

title: The Core of Paul’s Gospel
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the core of Paul's gospel around Jesus' death, resurrection, and the kingdom of God.

title: Paul as a Persecutor of the Church
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes Paul as a persecutor of the church before conversion.

title: A Personal Note and a Bit of a Bummer
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers a personal update about illness and work on early Christianity.
searchSummary: Describes how a severe back injury forced Ehrman to cancel research travel to pagan and Christian sites in Athens, Alexandria, and Rome. He acknowledges genuine disappointment without treating a privileged lost trip as profound suffering and redirects the unexpected two weeks toward concentrated work on The Triumph of Christianity. The setback changes planned blog coverage but becomes a practical example of accepting limitation, remembering people facing real hardship, and finding a worthwhile alternative within disrupted circumstances.

title: Jesus’ Death; Good Scholars; and Writing the First Book: Readers’ Mailbag May 28, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about Jesus' death, good scholarship, and writing a first book.
searchSummary: Answers reader questions about atonement, influential scholars, and first scholarly publication. Ehrman distinguishes Marcus Borg's appealing modern theology from New Testament claims that Jesus' death brings salvation, recommends specialists across Jesus research, Pauline studies, Gnosticism, apocrypha, and textual criticism, and explains that serious academic publication normally follows doctoral training. A revised dissertation becomes most scholars' first book because supervised research, languages, seminars, examinations, and expert criticism cannot be replicated by independent reading alone.

title: The Resurrection and the Beginning of the Church
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how belief in Jesus' resurrection contributed to the beginning of the church.

title: How Did Christianity Start?
author: BDEhrman
description: Considers how Christianity began and what counts as Christianity at its earliest stage.

title: How Many Christians Could Read?
author: BDEhrman
description: Estimates literacy among early Christians near the end of the New Testament period.
searchSummary: Estimates that around 100 CE an average Christian congregation may have had only four adult male readers, yielding perhaps four hundred literate Christians worldwide. Yet Christianity relied unusually heavily on authoritative Jewish and Christian writings that were read, copied, and interpreted in worship. This imbalance gave literate leaders privileged access to sacred texts and considerable authority over doctrine. Ehrman considers whether preserving that interpretive power helped explain why churches did not attempt widespread adult literacy instruction.

title: The Accuracy of Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about Galatians, Paul's conversion, and the textual reliability of Paul's letter.

title: How Many Churches?  How Many Letters?
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses the number of early churches and letters implied by estimates of Christian growth.
searchSummary: Uses estimates of early churches and correspondence to emphasize how little evidence survives for Christianity's spread and diversity. Christians met in multiple house churches that may have differed in membership, doctrine, worship, and leadership. Even conservative assumptions imply that thousands of interchurch letters have disappeared, while many imperial towns may still have lacked any Christian presence around 180. Ehrman concludes that sparse records prevent confident claims about either the movement's geographical reach or uniformity among isolated communities.

title: How Significant Was Early Christianity?
author: BDEhrman
description: Considers how significant Christianity was within the Roman world before Constantine.
searchSummary: Explores the implications of estimates that Christians remained statistically insignificant through the first two centuries despite steady growth. Most imperial residents may never have encountered Christianity, Roman elites largely ignored it, and early persecutions were sporadic local responses rather than systematic campaigns. Only exponential expansion in the third century made Christians numerous enough to attract sustained imperial concern. Ehrman presents ordinary conversion through family and social relationships, not mass evangelism, as sufficient to explain that later visibility.

title: Whom Do We Consider a Christian?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on who should count as a Christian in historical discussions of early Christianity.

title: Playing with the Numbers (of Christians)
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines numerical models for the growth of Christianity.
searchSummary: Tests alternative growth calculations beginning with roughly twenty resurrection believers in 30 and several million Christians by Constantine's conversion. A constant rate produces implausibly few Christians during Paul's lifetime, so Ehrman proposes rapid early expansion followed by declining proportional rates. He also considers deaths, births, and household conversion: adopting the religion of a male household head could bring wives, children, slaves, and dependents into the church, allowing substantial numerical growth without extraordinary numbers of individual missionary successes.

title: How Many Christians Were There?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the problem of estimating how many Christians existed in the early centuries.
searchSummary: Critiques Rodney Stark's model of constant Christian growth by showing that its assumed starting population is unsupported and its unchanged rate would eventually exceed the Roman Empire's population. Ehrman argues that persecution and other conditions caused fluctuations, while different phases required different average rates. Christianity could still have reached about half the empire during the fourth century through modest continued conversion without Constantine being indispensable, suggesting that steady missionary growth was more consequential than a single imperial decision.

title: The Rate of Christian Growth
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses the rate of Christian growth and the assumptions behind conversion estimates.
searchSummary: Explains Rodney Stark's mathematical model for Christianity's rise from a small movement to roughly six million adherents by 300. An average increase near 40–43 percent per decade produces exponential expansion without miracles or mass conversion rallies, since growing numbers of Christians create more opportunities to recruit others. Ehrman finds the calculation illuminating and comparable to Mormon growth, while noting that Stark's historical explanations are more controversial and that all starting populations, imperial totals, and rates remain rough estimates.

title: Paul in a Nutshell and NT Views of Crucifixion: Readers Mailbag May 13, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about Paul in a nutshell and New Testament views of Jesus' crucifixion.
searchSummary: Answers two broad questions by summarizing Paul's life and gospel and comparing New Testament interpretations of Jesus's crucifixion and resurrection. Paul moved from persecuting believers to proclaiming salvation through Christ apart from Jewish law, founded gentile churches, wrote letters, faced opposition, and was reportedly martyred. Paul and Mark describe atonement, Paul also emphasizes victory over sin and death, John sees crucifixion as exaltation, while Luke presents an unjust death prompting repentance and divine forgiveness.

title: Christians and their Exaggerated Numbers
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses ancient Christian claims about numbers and the problem of exaggeration.
searchSummary: Shows why early Christian claims about their own numbers cannot be used as reliable population evidence. Acts depicts implausibly massive conversions in Jerusalem, Paul says the gospel reached the whole world, and Tertullian portrays Christians as nearly ubiquitous. Pagan writings and archaeology instead present Christians as a small, marginal group while traditional religion continued to flourish. Ehrman argues that such rhetorical exaggeration leaves historians without trustworthy contemporary statistics and requires indirect methods for estimating conversion and growth.

title: Trolling Advice!
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains blog policy on trolling and reader comments.

title: Help!!
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks for mathematical or statistical help with a research question.

title: Who Counts as a Christian?
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses who counts as Christian when estimating the rise of Christianity.
searchSummary: Examines the basic problem of deciding whom to count when estimating early Christianity's growth. Ancient believers included proto-orthodox Christians, Marcionites, Sethians, Valentinians, Ebionites, people with sharply different views of Jesus and God, and others who retained Jewish or pagan practices. Because surviving evidence represents only a tiny elite fraction of the population, historians cannot measure commitments or impose a reliable doctrinal test. Ehrman adopts the broad practical rule of counting anyone who considered themselves a worshiper of the Christian God.

title: My Progress on the Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes progress on planning and researching a book before drafting begins.
searchSummary: Explains Ehrman's two-stage research sequence while preparing The Triumph of Christianity. He first reads broadly across classic studies, specialized scholarship, and ancient sources, following bibliographies outward and recording detailed notes until additional reading produces few relevant discoveries. He then sketches the book, rereads every note to expand its outline, identifies weaknesses, and conducts narrowly directed research to strengthen the developing argument, turning a vast subject into the specific evidence needed for a coherent book.

title: My Trip to Athens
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers a personal travel narrative about a trip to Athens.

title: Life After Death in Rome, and other Questions.  Readers’ Mailbag May 6, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about Roman afterlife beliefs, Gospel temptations, and publishing.

title: The Conversion of Constantine and Beyond
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Constantine's conversion fits into the larger story of Christianity's rise.
searchSummary: Outlines a revised ending for The Triumph of Christianity that extends beyond Constantine's conversion through the fourth century. Constantine legalized, favored, funded, and built institutions for Christianity without making it Rome's official religion, encouraging further conversion. Ehrman plans to examine his successors, Julian's attempted pagan restoration, Theodosius's suppression of pagan sacrifice, and subsequent anti-pagan laws and violence. This broader account asks what Christianity's victory contributed to Western culture and what temples, art, practices, and freedoms it destroyed.

title: Final Exam for New Testament Class (2016)
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a New Testament final exam from an introductory course.
searchSummary: Presents a three-part final examination for an introductory New Testament course. Students identify people, texts, groups, methods, and historical concepts, then write essays on Gospel reliability or non-Gospel evidence for Jesus and on either a Pauline community or the emergence of early Christian orthodoxy. The examination tests concise factual knowledge alongside the ability to organize detailed arguments about historical sources, Pauline letters, competing Christian beliefs, and scholarly models of heresy and orthodoxy.

title: Why Christianity Succeeded
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains proposed reasons for Christianity's success in the Roman world.
searchSummary: Argues that Christianity succeeded because evangelism and exclusivity operated together in a religious world where most cults had neither feature. Christians sought converts by promising salvation and eternal life through Jesus while warning of judgment, then required converts to abandon all other gods. Pagan worship was additive, so adopting another deity cost paganism nothing; adopting Christianity removed a pagan adherent. Slow, steady conversion therefore expanded the church while progressively weakening competing traditions, eventually leaving Christianity dominant.

title: My Debate with Richard Bauckham – Round 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the second round of a debate with Richard Bauckham on eyewitness testimony.
searchSummary: Presents the second half of Ehrman's radio debate with New Testament scholar Richard Bauckham about Gospel memory and eyewitness testimony. The discussion asks whether the canonical Gospels substantially preserve dependable reports grounded in witnesses or contain traditions distorted as they were remembered and transmitted. Ehrman and Bauckham take opposing positions on that historical question, making the program a direct comparison of competing scholarly approaches to judging the reliability of the Gospel accounts.

title: The Death of Paul in Acts and Unrelated Topics:  Readers’ Mailbag April 29, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about Acts' silence on Paul and Peter's deaths and related topics.

title: The Early Growth of Christianity
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes the early growth of Christianity for a book on its triumph.
searchSummary: Outlines Ehrman's explanation for Christianity's growth from a few followers to millions by Constantine's reign. Mathematical models suggest that sustained increases around 40 percent per decade could produce this expansion without mass rallies. Conversion stories repeatedly attribute success to miracles performed through Jesus, reflecting widespread belief in Christian divine power even if historians reject the events themselves. Ehrman adds that miracle claims alone were insufficient; Christianity's distinctive combination of evangelism and exclusive worship enabled steady growth to displace competing religions.

title: From Jewish Sect to Gentile Church
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the movement from a Jewish sect centered on Jesus to a Gentile church.
searchSummary: Traces Christianity's transformation from a Jewish messianic sect into predominantly gentile communities within about fifty years. Jesus' followers reinterpreted the crucified Jesus as a suffering, risen messiah, but most Jews rejected that claim. Paul did not invent salvation through Jesus, yet made it accessible to gentiles without circumcision or Jewish law. Ehrman reconstructs Paul forming communities through workplace relationships and social networks while preaching that the risen Jesus revealed the only living God's superior power over pagan deities.

title: Roman Religion as the Context for Christianity
author: BDEhrman
description: Places Christianity's rise within the broader context of Roman religion.
searchSummary: Describes the Roman religious environment necessary for understanding Christianity's rise. Diverse polytheistic traditions centered on ritual prayer and sacrifice to secure divine help with present life, not creeds, exclusive allegiance, or salvation after death. Religion and government were inseparable, while adding a god never required abandoning others. Judaism shared ancient ritual concerns but differed by worshiping one creator God in a covenant with Israel. Christianity emerged from that Jewish setting before achieving its greatest expansion among pagans.

title: Bart Ehrman vs Richard Bauckham – Round 1
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the first round of a debate with Richard Bauckham on Jesus, memory, and eyewitness testimony.
searchSummary: Introduces a debate with Richard Bauckham over whether the Gospels rest on eyewitness testimony. Ehrman argues that the evangelists were not eyewitnesses, lacked direct access to them, and inherited stories that changed during decades of oral transmission. Bauckham contends that the Gospel writers did have access to testimony from Jesus' first followers and that this connection supports the narratives' historical reliability, establishing the debate's central disagreement.

title: The Fear of Hell, Good Debaters, and the Name of God: Mailbag April 22, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about fear of hell, public debates, and the name of God.
searchSummary: Answers three unrelated reader questions about fear of hell, effective debating, and God's Hebrew name. Ehrman argues eternal torture is incompatible with a good and proportionate God, advises aspiring debaters to master evidence, opposing arguments, evaluation, presentation, and repeated practice, and explains how Jehovah combines the consonants YHWH with vowels associated with Adonai. The responses connect personal deconversion, decades of debate experience, and textual-linguistic history while distinguishing thoughtful preparation from mere confidence.
