title: Older Explanations for Why Christianity Succeeded
author: BDEhrman
description: Reviews older explanations for why Christianity succeeded in the Roman Empire.
searchSummary: Rejects older explanations that Christianity filled a vacuum left by declining paganism or prevailed through obvious philosophical, moral, or social superiority. Pagan religions were flourishing, monotheism often appeared unreasonable to ancient observers, and Christians had a scandalous public reputation; outsiders could not freely inspect their closed worship communities. Ehrman instead proposes examining ancient conversion accounts and the religious assumptions Christians shared with pagans. Those sources repeatedly present converts as persuaded that the Christian God demonstrated greater divine power through miracles.

title: The Triumph of Christianity: The Ultimate Question
author: BDEhrman
description: Frames the central question behind a book on how Christianity triumphed in the Roman world.
searchSummary: Frames the central historical question behind The Triumph of Christianity: how a tiny movement of largely illiterate Jewish followers of an executed Galilean became Rome's dominant religion and reshaped Western civilization. Ehrman emphasizes the outcome's improbability given rival miracle workers, Judaism's similar monotheism and ethics, persecution, Christianity's lower-class membership, and Jesus' humiliating death. Without affirming or denying divine causation, he seeks the human mechanisms that made Christianity attractive and enabled its expansion over more than three centuries.

title: The New Book: The Triumph of Christianity
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a new book project on The Triumph of Christianity.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's plan for The Triumph of Christianity, a popular historical account of how Christianity spread through the Roman world and displaced traditional religions within four centuries. Drawing on years of teaching and research, he outlines the project's broad scope: Roman religion, Christian distinctiveness, Paul's mission, conversion and growth rates, persecution, apologetics, Constantine, anti-pagan policy, and consequences for Western history. The post explains why synthesizing so many specialist fields made the long-contemplated book unusually demanding but worthwhile.

title: Getting a Literary Agent
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how a literary agent became part of the move to a new trade publisher.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman eventually hired his former Harper editor as a literary agent despite previously negotiating successful contracts himself. Agents represent projects, negotiate complex terms, and often advise on manuscripts, though Ehrman wanted to preserve his independent research and outlining process. Roger Freet persuaded him that professional representation could improve contracts and handle tasks Ehrman did not recognize as burdens; the arrangement supported his move to Simon & Schuster and helped conceptualize his book on Christianity's Roman expansion.

title: New Archaeological Discoveries and the Bible! Readers Mailbag April 16, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about archaeological discoveries and historical claims in Jesus Before the Gospels.
searchSummary: Answers two questions about responsible historical scholarship. Newly studied seventh-century BCE ostraca show multiple literate writers at a Judean outpost, but their date is six centuries before Jesus and the inferred numbers remain compatible with an approximately three-percent literacy rate in Roman Palestine. Ehrman then defends using memory research in a book about Gospel traditions because he studied technical scholarship, consulted specialists, and had experts review his manuscript rather than presenting himself as a psychologist.

title: Getting a First Book Published
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers practical advice about getting a first trade book published.
searchSummary: Explains why publishing a first trade book is exceptionally difficult for an unknown author. Established scholars may receive invitations or secure contracts from a persuasive prospectus, with terms covering length, deadlines, rights, royalties, and advances, but publishers invest heavily and avoid unproven risks. New writers generally need an agent to present an outstanding proposal and manuscript, yet agents also depend on likely sales and favor established clients, creating a barrier that only rare projects overcome through conventional publishing.

title: Who Should Write Trade Books?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains who is qualified to write trade books for general audiences.
searchSummary: Argues that intellectually serious trade books should be written by established experts who can translate sound scholarship for general readers. Easy self-publication and poorly vetted bestsellers encourage uninformed authors to present idiosyncratic claims, while nonspecialists often assume any published book has survived expert scrutiny. Using popular but historically flawed books about Jesus as examples, Ehrman maintains that years of training and research are necessary to avoid factual errors and protect readers seeking reliable knowledge in unfamiliar fields.

title: Being Qualified to Write a Scholarly Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses qualifications for writing scholarly books and how scholarship differs from trade publishing.

title: Why I Have Moved to a New Publisher
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the move from HarperOne to Simon and Schuster for future trade books.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman moved his trade-book publishing from HarperOne to Simon & Schuster without dissatisfaction over Harper's performance. Harper produced seven books, including five bestsellers, but trusted editorial and publicity relationships had changed, and his former editor became his agent. At a later career stage, Ehrman wanted a new experience with a history-oriented publisher that had few religion authors, making him its principal New Testament and early Christianity writer rather than one among many specialists.

title: The New Edition of My Textbook: Reader’s Mailbag April 10, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers a question about a new edition of an introductory New Testament textbook.

title: Publishing with HarperOne
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on publishing with HarperOne and the books produced through that relationship.
searchSummary: Traces Ehrman's path from specialized textual scholarship through textbooks and Oxford trade books to a transformative twelve-year relationship with HarperOne. His attempt to explain Greek New Testament manuscripts to ordinary readers became Misquoting Jesus after Oxford hesitated and Harper accepted the project; its success led to six more Harper books. He credits the press with changing his career while announcing that future trade books will move to Simon & Schuster, leaving textbooks and most scholarly works with Oxford.

title: Evaluating My Debate on the Book of Acts
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates a classroom debate on the historical reliability of Acts.
searchSummary: Reflects on a classroom debate over whether Acts is historically reliable and explains why judging Luke by ancient historiographical standards does not resolve that question. A work may competently follow the conventions of its time yet still fail to report events as they happened. Ehrman distinguishes interpreting Acts within its ancient literary context from asking whether its narratives are factually trustworthy. The latter requires evidence about the events themselves, not merely comparisons with the practices of other ancient historians.

title: Is Acts Historically Reliable?  The Affirmative Rebuttal
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents the affirmative rebuttal in a classroom debate over Acts' historical reliability.
searchSummary: Presents the affirmative rebuttal in a classroom debate over Acts' historical reliability. The case argues that Luke followed ancient historiographic standards, intended accuracy, knew participants and first-century settings, and broadly agrees with Paul's itinerary and preaching despite minor differences. Apparent conflict between Acts 17 and Romans 1 is explained by different audiences, while archaeological confirmation of local titles and places supports Luke's knowledge. The post deliberately models the strongest affirmative argument rather than stating Ehrman's own conclusion.

title: Our Fourth Anniversary!
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the blog's fourth anniversary and its charitable work.
searchSummary: Celebrates the blog's fourth anniversary with more than 1,100 posts, 34,627 approved comments, and steadily rising charitable revenue. Annual fundraising grew from $37,000 in year one to $120,000 in year four, supporting organizations addressing hunger and homelessness. Bart discusses the time devoted to posts and questions, asks readers to suggest topics and improvements, recruit members, and donate, and thanks Steven Ray for managing the technical and membership work that keeps the site operating.

title: HNN News Story on Jesus Before the Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Jesus Before the Gospels to explain how memory affects historical claims about Jesus.
searchSummary: Examines whether Gospel memories of Jesus' final days are historically accurate as well as theologically meaningful. Because the educated Greek-speaking evangelists received stories transmitted orally for decades, research on eyewitness error, individual and collective memory, and oral cultures shows how traditions could be forgotten, reshaped, or invented. Such malleable memories may still inspire faith and action, but their power and meaning do not by themselves establish that the remembered events happened as narrated.

title: The Letters of Paul: Mailbag April 1, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about Paul's letters, Acts, and the Dead Sea Scrolls.

title: Is Acts Reliable?  The Negative Rebuttal
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents the negative rebuttal in a classroom debate over Acts' historical reliability.
searchSummary: Rebuts the claim that Acts is reliable because its author intended to write history, relied on eyewitness traditions, and accompanied Paul. Luke's preface does not say the author personally interviewed witnesses, while Acts' abrupt “we-passages” may derive from a travel source or a literary device that creates eyewitness authority. More decisively, Acts repeatedly conflicts with Paul's own accounts of his travels, companions, preaching, and theology, making firsthand companionship doubtful and showing that claimed proximity would not itself establish accuracy.

title: Is the Book of Acts Historically Reliable?  The Negative Case.
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents the negative case against the historical reliability of Acts.
searchSummary: Presents the negative case that Acts is not historically reliable in the modern sense of narrating events as they occurred. Internal versions of Jesus' ascension and Paul's conversion conflict, while comparisons with Paul's letters produce discrepancies over companions, Jerusalem travel, and the explanation of pagan idolatry. Accurate knowledge of first-century places and institutions cannot verify stories. The post argues that Luke's narrative and theological aims outweighed factual consistency, while explicitly framing the position as one side of a classroom debate.

title: Is the Book of Acts Historically Reliable?  Smoke and Mirrors.
author: BDEhrman
description: Prepares the negative side of a classroom debate on whether Acts is historically reliable.
searchSummary: Challenges the argument that archaeological confirmation of Acts' geography, titles, and customs proves its stories historically reliable. An author familiar with the Roman world could accurately locate an invented event and name real institutions without the event itself having occurred. Ehrman's analogy of a false modern report set accurately at UNC illustrates the distinction. Archaeology can demonstrate Luke's knowledge of places such as Athens, Thessalonica, and Lystra, but usually cannot verify the episodes he narrates there.

title: For Anyone Who Still Needs a Free Membership!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces remaining free memberships donated for readers unable to pay.

title: Bart Ehrman vs Tim McGrew – Round 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the second round of a radio debate with Tim McGrew.
searchSummary: Presents the second half of Ehrman's radio debate with philosopher and Christian apologist Timothy McGrew. Their discussion evaluates whether “undesigned coincidences” among Gospel narratives support their reliability, whether historical inquiry can validate miraculous conclusions, and how apparent correspondences in Acts should be assessed. Ehrman and McGrew disagree about the evidentiary force of these features and about historical method's limits. The post links McGrew's account of the argument and supplies the recorded exchange for evaluation.

title: My Book Sales and the “Relatives” of Paul:  Weekly Reader’s Mailbag March 25, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about book sales and the meaning of Paul's reference to relatives.
searchSummary: Discusses the disappointing early sales of Jesus Before the Gospels, attributing them to limited national media attention rather than the book's quality or its publisher's effort. Ehrman then interprets Romans 16:7, arguing that Junia was a woman recognized as a prominent apostle. He rejects the NRSV's translation of Andronicus and Junia as Paul's relatives because the same Greek term elsewhere identifies fellow Jews, not members of his personal family.

title: Is Acts Historically Reliable?  The Affirmative Argument
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents the affirmative argument for the historical reliability of Acts.
searchSummary: Constructs the affirmative side of a classroom debate over whether Acts is historically reliable without presenting it as Ehrman's own conclusion. The case appeals to Luke's stated historical purpose, the “we-passages” as evidence that the author traveled with Paul, agreements with Paul's letters, and archaeological confirmation of locations and civic terminology. Together these points argue that the author intended accuracy, possessed eyewitness access, and can be independently verified, establishing the strongest case that Acts reliably reports early Christian history.

title: Major Themes in the Book of Acts
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys major topics in Acts, including conversion, miracles, and apostolic mission.
searchSummary: Identifies the major literary and theological themes that govern Acts' selective account of early Christianity. God directs an unstoppable mission through the Spirit, miracles produce conversions, believers and apostles appear harmonious, and the message advances from Jerusalem across the Roman world. Gentiles join without adopting Jewish law, while Paul remains thoroughly Jewish and Christianity is portrayed as continuous with Judaism. Ehrman stresses that these themes describe Luke's presentation, not necessarily the historical character of the earliest church.

title: The Literary Artistry of the Book of Acts
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the literary artistry of Acts as an account of early Christian beginnings.
searchSummary: Examines how Luke's literary artistry supports the theological message of Acts. Parallels connect Jesus' Spirit-empowered preaching, miracles, opposition, and suffering in Luke with the apostles' experiences in Acts, presenting their mission as a continuation of his work. Further parallels make Peter and Paul preach, heal, endure persecution, receive divine deliverance, and embrace Gentile inclusion in corresponding ways. These carefully shaped patterns show that Acts is more than a neutral chronicle, even if it also preserves history.

title: The Book of Acts: An Overview
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Acts as the focus of a classroom debate on historical reliability.
searchSummary: Introduces Acts as the second volume of Luke's narrative, carrying the story from Jesus' resurrection and ascension through the birth and expansion of the church. The Spirit arrives at Pentecost, empowers miracles and preaching, and accompanies a mission that encounters Jewish opposition and moves beyond Jerusalem. Paul changes from persecutor to leading missionary, travels throughout the empire, faces arrest and trials, and reaches Rome. The overview establishes why Acts' historical reliability matters for understanding Christianity's earliest decades.

title: Bart Ehrman vs Tim McGrew – Round 1
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the first round of a radio debate with Tim McGrew on Gospel reliability.
searchSummary: Introduces the first half of a radio debate between Ehrman and conservative Christian philosopher Timothy McGrew on whether the Gospels can be trusted. Recorded for Justin Brierley's Unbelievable program, the exchange places historical-critical concerns about the Gospel narratives against an apologetic defense of their reliability. The post identifies McGrew's academic background and provides the recording rather than summarizing the individual claims, evidence, or rebuttals, leaving readers to assess the competing approaches in the two-part discussion.

title: Memory, Eyewitnesses, and the Relevance of Jesus: Readers Mailbag
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about memory, eyewitness testimony, and the continuing relevance of Jesus.
searchSummary: Answers three questions about memory, eyewitness authority, and Jesus' continuing relevance. Memory studies support viewing the Sermon on the Mount and Barabbas episode as altered or invented traditions, while modern appeals to eyewitness testimony resemble ancient efforts to guarantee truth through apostolic authority. Although Jesus' imminent apocalyptic expectation proved mistaken, his call to trust God's ultimate victory over suffering and serve others can be translated into a meaningful modern ethic.

title: Does the New Testament Condemn Modern Practices of Homosexuality?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a classroom debate on whether the New Testament condemns modern homosexuality.

title: Were Paul’s Views of Women Oppressive?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a classroom debate on Paul's views of women.

title: Do Paul and Jesus Represent Fundamentally Different Religions?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a classroom debate on whether Paul and Jesus represented fundamentally different religions.
searchSummary: Frames a classroom debate over whether Jesus and Paul advocated fundamentally different religions. Jesus announces God's imminent kingdom and calls people to repent, obey Torah as centered on love, and prepare for the Son of Man; Paul makes Jesus' death, resurrection, faith, and baptism the basis of salvation and identifies Jesus as the returning judge. Shared Jewish apocalypticism and moral expectations provide continuity, but conflicting accounts of law, faith, salvation, and the judge's identity leave “fundamentally” open to argument.

title: Weekly Readers’ Mailbag: March 12, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers personal questions about controversies with fundamentalists and accessible scholarly books.
searchSummary: Answers questions about Bart's unexpected controversy among fundamentalists and the accessibility of his publications. He explains that his trade books communicate mainstream or evidence-based scholarship rather than attack Christianity, though their conclusions challenge biblical inerrancy and other fundamentalist claims. He then classifies his work by intended readership, distinguishing highly technical monographs, more approachable scholarship, bilingual source editions, college textbooks and anthologies, and books written expressly for general audiences.

title: My Recitation Debates
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how recitation debates work in an introductory New Testament course.
searchSummary: Explains how weekly discussion sections and formal debates deepen a large introductory New Testament course. Position papers ensure that students arrive prepared to discuss Gospel differences, the Gospel of Thomas, and other disputed issues. Debate teams research opposing resolutions, deliver speeches and rebuttals, and write papers defending the side opposite the one they argue publicly. The design teaches evidence-based argument, public speaking, fair evaluation, and sympathy for positions students may not personally share.

title: The Value (or Not) of Debates
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the value and limits of public debates.
searchSummary: Reflects on the uncertain value of debates when speakers and audiences often enter with fixed commitments. Ehrman explains how complex but weak claims can impress listeners unable to evaluate them, then describes teaching debate by arguing both sides of whether Acts is historically accurate. Although he believes the negative case is much stronger, a majority of students selected the affirmative. He proposes examining both arguments to expose weaknesses, encourage intellectual flexibility, and ask whether persuasive performance genuinely advances understanding.

title: Buy New Book & Get Any Previous HarperOne Book for 50% OFF
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a promotion connected to Jesus Before the Gospels and earlier HarperOne books.

title: Irritating Amazon Reviews
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on Amazon reviews and public responses to Jesus Before the Gospels.

title: The Triumphal Entry as a Distorted Memory
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the triumphal entry to illustrate distorted memory in Gospel traditions.
searchSummary: Argues that the Gospel account of Jesus' triumphal entry is a distorted memory, although Jesus certainly entered Jerusalem. Roman troops guarding volatile Passover crowds would have arrested anyone publicly acclaimed as a Davidic king who would displace Roman rule. Later Christian storytellers shaped the scene to portray Jewish crowds as fickle: they welcome God's Messiah and then demand his death, reflecting subsequent Christian conflict with Jews more than the historical circumstances of Jesus' arrival.

title: The Memory of Jesus’ Triumphal Entry
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the triumphal entry as a remembered Gospel tradition in Jesus Before the Gospels.
searchSummary: Reconstructs the remembered triumphal entry against the politically charged setting of Passover under Roman occupation. Mark depicts crowds hailing Jesus as the coming Davidic king, while Matthew turns Hebrew poetic parallelism into two animals and presents Jesus riding both to fulfill Scripture literally. The variations show how Gospel authors shaped the tradition and prepare the historical question of whether such a public messianic demonstration could have occurred under Pilate's watch.

title: Weekly Readers’ Mailbag:  March 4, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about books, writing habits, and Jesus Before the Gospels.

title: My First Interview on Jesus Before the Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the first interview about Jesus Before the Gospels.
searchSummary: Introduces an American Freethought interview about Jesus Before the Gospels and the transmission of Jesus traditions. The discussion explains how memories form, are retrieved, change when passed between people, and are reshaped by later historical perspectives and current events. Research on these processes provides a framework for evaluating the oral stories that circulated about Jesus before the Gospel writers produced their written accounts.

title: Jesus Before the Gospels in Relation to My Other Books
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Jesus Before the Gospels relates to earlier books on the Gospels and the New Testament.

title: My New Book! (In Context of My Others)
author: BDEhrman
description: Celebrates the publication of Jesus Before the Gospels and places it among earlier books.

title: Did the Earliest Christians Believe Jesus *Became* God?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains a debate over whether early Christians thought Jesus became God at the resurrection.
searchSummary: Defends the view that the earliest Christians understood Jesus' resurrection as his elevation to divine status. Pre-Pauline material in Romans says he was appointed Son of God at resurrection, while an early tradition in Acts applies “today I have begotten you” to that event. Ehrman contrasts this exaltation Christology with later incarnation belief, in which a divine being descends to earth, and argues that resurrection naturally suggested deification within ancient Jewish and Greco-Roman frameworks.

title: Bart Ehrman on Problem of Suffering – UCB
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a video interview on the problem of suffering.
searchSummary: Traces how the problem of suffering contributed to Ehrman's movement from evangelical Christianity through a theology of God suffering alongside humanity to agnosticism. Free will could not explain natural disasters, disease, starvation, or unanswered prayer, and promised future justice came to seem like wishful thinking. His study of Scripture found multiple, sometimes contradictory explanations—punishment, testing, cosmic evil, mystery, and redemption. God's Problem presents these biblical responses to encourage reflection rather than conversion to unbelief.

title: Jesus’ Virgin Birth in Mark (Reader’s Mailbag February 26, 2016)
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers a question about whether Mark contains a reference to Jesus' virgin birth.
searchSummary: Argues that Mark probably did not know or believe a virgin-birth tradition rather than merely neglecting to mention it. Such a claim would strongly support divine sonship, yet Mark and most New Testament authors never use it. More decisively, Mark portrays Jesus' mother and brothers as trying to restrain him because they think he is out of his mind. Matthew and Luke omit that scene because their Mary already knows that Jesus was supernaturally conceived as God's Son.

title: Christ as the Adopted Son of God
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains adoptionist Christology and the claim that Jesus became Son of God.

title: What the Resurrection of Jesus MEANT
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains what Jesus' resurrection meant for early Christian views of Jesus' divine status.

title: A Less Weighty, Personal Matter
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers a personal update about weight loss and health.
searchSummary: Explains that Ehrman's noticeable weight loss resulted from a deliberate health improvement after a prediabetes diagnosis, not illness. A dietitian helped him adopt a sustainable Mediterranean, low-glycemic pattern centered on vegetables, fruit, fish, nuts, healthy fats, strategic snacks, fewer processed carbohydrates, and moderated alcohol, while he increased exercise despite frequent travel. Losing roughly one pound weekly for seven months brought him to a maintainable target weight, greater energy, and his best physical condition in decades.

title: Christ as Son of God in Mark’s Gospel
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Mark's portrayal of Jesus as Son of God in relation to suffering and messiahship.
searchSummary: Explains Mark's answer to the scandal of a crucified Messiah. Ancient Jewish expectations emphasized a powerful anointed ruler, not someone defeated by Rome, while texts later read as predictions of suffering were not previously messianic. Mark therefore presents Jesus as Messiah precisely because his suffering death atones for sin, although family, leaders, and disciples fail to understand. The Gospel does not address later Nicene questions about divine essence or clearly explain when and how Jesus became God's Son.

title: My Debate with Michael Bird Feb. 12 , 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Reports on a debate with Michael Bird about How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Presents the recorded Greer-Heard debate between Ehrman and evangelical New Testament scholar Michael Bird over How Jesus Became God. Bird edited the response volume How God Became Jesus, making the event a direct exchange between competing historical and theological interpretations of Jesus' divinity. The two-part program includes their formal presentations and responses followed by audience questions, with the video serving as the post's substantive content.

title: Weekly Readers’ Mailbag: February 18, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about Islam, Greek Gospel origins, and majority scholarly views.
searchSummary: Answers questions about Islam, the Gospels' original language, and critical scholarship. Ehrman distinguishes historical criticism from attacks on Christianity and stresses that Jesus' crucifixion conflicts with standard Islamic belief. He argues that the Gospels were composed in Greek because their phrasing resists Aramaic retroversion and the Synoptics share exact Greek wording impossible for independent translations. Critical scholars, he explains, follow historical evidence without allowing prior theology to dictate conclusions.

title: The Controversies about Christ: Arius and Alexander
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Arius-Alexander controversy over Christ's divine status.
searchSummary: Arius and Alexander agreed that Christ was the divine Son who created the universe but disagreed over his relation to the Father. Arius made the Son God's first creation, infinitely exalted over everything else yet subordinate and not eternal; Alexander argued that God's perfection required an eternally begotten Son equal in power and substance. Their dispute over similar versus identical divine essence led directly to the Council of Nicaea.

title: The Son of God, the Council of Nicea, and the Da Vinci Code
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses Nicaea, the Son of God, and popular misconceptions from The Da Vinci Code.
searchSummary: The Council of Nicaea did not determine the New Testament canon or decide whether Jesus was divine, contrary to claims popularized by The Da Vinci Code. Every participant regarded Christ as God's divine Son and creator; the disputed issue was his exact relationship to the Father. The controversy continued a much older Christian debate over the different senses in which Jesus could be called Son of God.

title: My Debate This Past Weekend
author: BDEhrman
description: Reports on a debate with Michael Bird about how Jesus came to be understood as God.
searchSummary: Describes the format and setting of Ehrman's Greer-Heard dialogue with Michael Bird about how Jesus became God. Ehrman's historical reconstruction traces an apocalyptic preacher's elevation into the eternal divine member of the Trinity, while Bird edited the evangelical response volume How God Became Jesus; invited scholars then expanded the discussion. The post emphasizes the unusually cordial exchange at a conservative Baptist seminary and prepares later explanations of the participants' specific arguments.

title: Drew Marshall Show – How Jesus Became God
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a radio interview about How Jesus Became God and a personal religious journey.
searchSummary: Introduces a Drew Marshall Show interview with Ehrman and University of Waterloo professor Natalie Evans. The conversation begins with Ehrman's religious journey and then turns to How Jesus Became God, his historical study of how followers came to regard Jesus as divine. Because the short post primarily supplies broadcast information and the recording, the interview itself contains the substantive discussion rather than an accompanying written analysis.

title: Weekly Readers Mailbag: February 13, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers a reader question about memory and Jesus Before the Gospels.
searchSummary: Explains that highly emotional memories can be vivid and frequently recalled without being accurate. Studies of “flashbulb memories,” including students' changing recollections of the Challenger explosion, found major errors despite strong confidence; many participants even preferred their later memories to records made immediately afterward. Dramatic experiences involving Jesus therefore would not automatically have been remembered reliably, and repeated retelling could make altered memories feel increasingly certain.

title: Upcoming Speaking Engagements 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Lists upcoming book readings and speaking engagements for 2016.
searchSummary: Lists public book events and lectures connected with Jesus Before the Gospels and related scholarship. The speaking program includes debates and talks on Jesus' divinity, memory, eyewitness testimony, early Christian recollection, and textual transmission, ranging from bookstore appearances to all-day seminars. Taken together, the schedule shows how Ehrman converts current research on memory and the historical Jesus into lectures for colleges, seminaries, community audiences, and public humanities programs.

title: On the Accuracy of Oral Traditions
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the accuracy of oral traditions as a central issue in Jesus Before the Gospels.
searchSummary: Argues that accurate geographical, cultural, or institutional details do not prove that an orally transmitted story's central event occurred. Archaeology confirms a temple of Zeus outside Lystra, but that fact cannot establish Acts' claim that residents mistook Paul and Barnabas for gods, just as finding a real classroom would not prove a story that its professor levitated. Background accuracy helps evaluate a source's knowledge, not the historical truth of every narrated action.

title: Are “Group Hallucinations” Possible?  The Case of Mary.
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses group hallucinations through the example of visions of Mary.

title: Upcoming Debate!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces an upcoming debate on how Jesus became God.
searchSummary: Previews Ehrman's debate with Michael Bird and summarizes the historical position he plans to defend. Jesus was not considered divine during his lifetime, but resurrection appearances led followers to believe God had raised and exalted him; subsequent Christians moved his divinity earlier until he became the preexistent, coeternal member of the Trinity. Bird is expected to argue instead that Jesus understood and proclaimed himself as divine, especially as portrayed in John.

title: Weekly Readers’ Mailbag: February 7, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about eyewitness testimony, visions, and media hopes for a new book.
searchSummary: Explains how people can sincerely remember witnessing an event that they never saw. Many educated respondents claimed to have watched nonexistent footage of an Amsterdam plane crash and supplied visual details, apparently combining inference, hearsay, and vivid imagination into false memories. The example challenges confidence in eyewitness testimony and collective claims, including arguments about resurrection appearances or Paul's conversion, because dramatic subject matter can intensify imagery without making recollection accurate.

title: Q & A about Jesus Before the Gospels, Part 1
author: BDEhrman
description: Reposts the first part of a Q and A about Jesus Before the Gospels.
searchSummary: Explains why memory research offers a new way to investigate traditions about Jesus that circulated orally for forty to sixty years before anonymous Gospel authors wrote them. Psychological studies of eyewitnesses and false memory, sociological research, and anthropology of oral cultures challenge assumptions that testimony and repeated stories remain accurate. These findings help explain Gospel contradictions and historical problems as products of remembering, misremembering, and repeated retelling rather than simply written mistakes.

title: Technical Problems on the Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Reports technical problems affecting the blog and lost posts.

title: Q & A about Jesus Before the Gospels, Part 3
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the final part of a Q and A about Jesus Before the Gospels.
searchSummary: Summarizes how psychological, sociological, and anthropological research changes the interpretation of Gospel traditions. Vivid memories of dramatic events may be false, communities shape recollections around their beliefs and experiences, and oral cultures alter stories without expecting verbatim preservation. The Gospels therefore are not transcripts but written products of decades of remembering and retelling; studying those processes illuminates both their historical limitations and the needs that led different Christian communities to remember Jesus differently.

title: Q & A about Jesus Before the Gospels: Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the second part of a Q and A about memory, eyewitnesses, and Jesus Before the Gospels.
searchSummary: Explains how oral cultures reshape stories for different audiences while still regarding changing performances as the same tradition. Jesus Before the Gospels uses memory research both to identify potentially distorted or invented Gospel accounts and to ask what those accounts reveal about the communities that preserved them. It also challenges alleged eyewitness guarantees and applies standard historical criteria to traditions including the Sermon on the Mount, miracles, Jewish responsibility for Jesus' death, and Barabbas.

title: Weekly Readers’ Mailbag:  January 30, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about Jesus' Jewishness and a difficult experience with editors.
searchSummary: Explains why earlier scholarship often obscured Jesus' Jewish identity and then answers a separate question about editorial misconduct. Christian anti-Judaism and Gospel polemic encouraged depictions of Jesus as opposing or transcending Judaism, while post-Holocaust scholarship recovered the historical consensus that he was thoroughly Jewish. Ehrman then recounts how a journal editor inserted an unauthorized attack on the New World Translation into his article, leaving him blamed for words he never wrote.

title: Do I Have the Expertise Needed for My Book?
author: BDEhrman
description: Defends the expertise behind Jesus Before the Gospels and its use of memory studies.
searchSummary: Explains how interdisciplinary expertise was incorporated into Jesus Before the Gospels. After extensive reading and consultation, Ehrman asked New Testament scholars Chris Keith and Zeba Crook to review its treatment of collective memory and Harvard psychologist Daniel Schacter to verify its discussion of false memory. Their review supports the book's use of psychology, sociology, and anthropology while leaving its judgments about which Gospel stories are distorted memories open to debate among specialists in early Christianity.

title: Buying David Lambert’s Book at Discount
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a discount for David Lambert's book on repentance.

title: Did Jesus Urge People to Repent?
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents David Lambert's argument about whether Jesus urged repentance.
searchSummary: A guest scholar questions the assumption that repentance stood at the center of Jesus' preaching. Mark's opening summary commands repentance, but the Gospel's healing, exorcism, and kingdom proclamation rarely mention it, while Luke explicitly adds repentance to earlier traditions. Because some Jewish apocalyptic movements expected God to transform humanity rather than people to reform themselves, the evidence may reflect later community discipline and diverse Gospel interests rather than a uniform historical message, leaving Jesus' own emphasis uncertain.

title: Press Release!  Jesus Before the Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a press release for Jesus Before the Gospels.

title: Weekly Readers’ Mailbag: January 24, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about Aramaic in Mark and English access to New Testament manuscripts.

title: What Is Repentance in the Bible?  Is there Repentance in the Bible?
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents David Lambert's response on repentance and biblical language.
searchSummary: Challenges the assumption that familiar biblical actions and terms already expressed the later concept of repentance. David Lambert distinguishes rituals of submission, appeals to God, familial reconciliation, and behavioral cessation of sin from an inward process of remorse that transforms future conduct. He argues that this recognizable idea emerged around the turn of the era in Greek thought, Philo, early Christianity, and rabbinic Judaism, then reshaped how readers interpreted older Hebrew texts.

title: Jesus and the Son of Man
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Jesus' Son of Man sayings within Jewish apocalyptic expectation.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus used “Son of Man” for a future heavenly judge distinct from himself. Independently attested sayings and the criterion of dissimilarity favor their authenticity because later Christians identified Jesus with that figure and were unlikely to invent ambiguous wording. Drawing on Daniel 7, 1 Enoch, and 4 Ezra, Bart explains that this humane cosmic ruler would overthrow oppressive powers, vindicate the suffering, establish God's kingdom, and reverse present social fortunes.

title: Am I Converting to Islam?
author: Diane
description: Responds to a Facebook exchange about Islam and religious proselytizing.

title: Is Repentance a Biblical Idea?  Interview with David Lambert
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces an interview with David Lambert about repentance as a biblical idea.
searchSummary: Presents David Lambert's argument that repentance was not an original, pervasive biblical concept but was read into Scripture through a later “penitential lens.” Practices such as fasting and confession originally changed a person's social or ritual status rather than expressing inward remorse, while prophetic calls to return addressed immediate circumstances. Lambert traces repentance's fuller development to the Hellenistic period, when Judaism and Christianity made inner transformation a powerful means of entering, remaining within, and governing religious communities.

title: The Rise of Apocalypticism
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the rise of apocalypticism from prophetic views under changing historical conditions.

title: Weekly Readers’ Mailbag:  January 16, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about Israel, Judaism, and Pauline forgery.
searchSummary: Answers how scholars distinguish Paul's authentic letters from writings falsely attributed to him. Seven New Testament letters cohere in vocabulary, style, theology, and a mid-first-century setting, forming a reliable core against which disputed works can be compared; Ephesians, Colossians, Second Thessalonians, and especially the Pastorals diverge significantly. The mailbag also explains Christian support for Israel through social environment and end-times theology, and clarifies how Trinitarian worship remains monotheistic.

title: Background to Apocalypticism: The Maccabean Revolt
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the Maccabean revolt as background for the emergence of Jewish apocalypticism.
searchSummary: Reconstructs the Maccabean revolt as the historical background for the rise of Jewish apocalypticism. Seleucid Hellenization and Antiochus IV's suppression of circumcision and traditional worship provoked armed resistance, Temple rededication, and eventual Hasmonean independence. The crisis, together with controversy over the Hasmoneans' non-Zadokite high priesthood and later Roman conquest, altered Jewish political and theological expectations and informed Daniel's response to persecution.

title: Are the Prophecies Being Fulfilled?
author: BDEhrman
description: Contrasts popular Christian prophecy interpretation with critical biblical scholarship.

title: Amos as a Representative Prophet
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Amos as a representative Hebrew prophet.

title: The Prophet Amos
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Amos as background for understanding Jewish apocalyptic thought.

title: The Prophetic Background of Jewish Apocalyptic Thought
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Hebrew prophetic thought forms background for Jewish apocalypticism.

title: Weekly Readers’ Mailbag:  January 8, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about chapters and verses, early atonement belief, and Muslim uses of his work.

title: Heaven and Hell, Part Two
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues an explanation of heaven, hell, resurrection, and eternal punishment.
searchSummary: Explains how the unfulfilled expectation of an imminent apocalypse contributed to a major change in Christian afterlife belief. Jesus, Paul, and Revelation anticipated bodily resurrection and eternal life on a renewed earth. As generations passed without the expected end, Christians reinterpreted the contrast between the present and future ages as a vertical division between earth, heaven, and hell. Later writings such as the Apocalypse of Peter depict disembodied souls receiving immediate reward or punishment, replacing resurrection with the soul's immortality.

title: Heaven and Hell, Part One
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the development of heaven and hell from Jewish resurrection expectation.
searchSummary: Traces bodily resurrection to Jewish apocalyptic attempts to explain why faithful people suffer while the wicked prosper. Rather than sending souls immediately to heaven or hell, apocalypticists expected God soon to defeat evil, raise the dead, judge everyone, and establish a just kingdom on earth. Jesus and Paul shared this expectation, with Paul viewing Jesus' resurrection as the first stage of the general resurrection. Revelation likewise anticipates resurrected saints living eternally in a renewed earthly Jerusalem.

title: The Resurrection in Paul
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Paul's understanding of resurrection within early Christian apocalyptic belief.

title: Readers’ Weekly Mailbag:  January 2, 2016
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about Sophia, non-apocalyptic Christianity, and John the Baptist.

title: Blog Year in Review 2015
author: BDEhrman
description: Reviews the blog's activity and charitable results during 2015.
searchSummary: Reviews the blog's strongest year to date, reporting 286 posts, 5,000 members, and $116,000 raised for charities addressing hunger, homelessness, and poverty. Bart discusses the weekly workload, occasional revisiting of older subjects, post ratings, and the new Readers' Mailbag feature. He invites ideas for improving the site, expanding membership, and increasing donations, asks readers to give subscriptions and promote the blog, and thanks Steven Ray and the community for sustaining its growth.

title: Jesus’ Resurrection as an Apocalyptic Event
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Jesus' resurrection as an apocalyptic event connected to suffering and vindication.
searchSummary: Explains resurrection as an apocalyptic solution to unjust suffering. Earlier Hebrew texts envision no meaningful afterlife, but Jewish apocalypticists attributed present misery to evil powers and expected God soon to intervene, raise the dead, punish oppressors, and vindicate faithful sufferers. Because Jesus and his followers expected this imminent reversal, the disciples' conviction that God had already raised Jesus meant the general resurrection had begun. They therefore concluded that history's end and God's final justice were immediately approaching.

title: Jesus’ Return to Life as a Resurrection
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why early Christians understood Jesus' return to life as resurrection.

title: The Death of the Messiah for Salvation
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Christians came to understand the Messiah's death as bringing salvation.
searchSummary: Explains how early Christians came to interpret Jesus' death as an atoning sacrifice that brought salvation. Once resurrection belief confirmed that the crucified Jesus was God's favored messiah, his undeserved death required a divine purpose and was understood through ancient sacrificial categories as occurring for others' sins. This reasoning transformed an apparent miscarriage of justice into God's planned means of reconciliation, even though earlier Jews did not expect the messiah to die.

title: Readers’ Mailbag:  December 27, 2015
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers a question about whether Jesus' messiahship during life explains later claims about Jesus.
searchSummary: Answers questions about why resurrection belief could establish Jesus' divinity without first creating belief in his messiahship, how scholarship recovered Jesus' Jewish context, and the disputed census in Luke. Ancient people could infer divinity from exaltation to heaven, whereas resurrection did not match existing messianic expectations. The post also criticizes older supersessionist portrayals of Jesus and presents an evangelical grammatical defense of Luke's chronology without endorsing it.

title: End of Year Giving
author: BDEhrman
description: Encourages year-end charitable giving through the Bart Ehrman Foundation.

title: A Christmas Reflection
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers a personal Christmas reflection beyond scholarly analysis.
searchSummary: Reflects on Ehrman's continuing love of Christmas after critical biblical study and the problem of suffering led from evangelical faith to agnosticism. He no longer regards Matthew's and Luke's conflicting infancy narratives as reliable history, yet their angels, dreams, miracles, danger, and rescue remain beautiful stories. Family memories, winter, music, illuminated trees, generosity, and the narratives' themes of divine and human giving preserve the season's emotional and moral meaning without requiring literal belief.

title: The Myth of the First Christmas
author: admin
description: Explains the Christmas stories as competing traditions about Jesus' birth.

title: Desmond Tutu, True Christians, and Christmas
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on Desmond Tutu, Christianity, and the meaning of Christmas.
searchSummary: Reflects on Ehrman's shared values with progressive Christians through meeting Desmond Tutu and his former chaplain in South Africa. Their faith prioritized truth, reconciliation, racial justice, peace, poverty, inclusion, and forgiveness over doctrinal policing, giving Ehrman more common ground with them than with socially disengaged secular friends. He argues that non-Christians should recognize the immense good such believers accomplish and join them in serving oppressed and vulnerable people rather than defining Christianity only by its harmful expressions.

title: Holiday Presents!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces remaining free blog memberships available as holiday gifts.

title: Christians, Muslims, and God:  Wheaton College in the News
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to questions about Wheaton College, Christianity, Islam, and whether Christians and Muslims worship the same God.

title: Does Revelation Contain an Eyewitness Account of the Eruption of Mount Vesuvius?  Guest Post by James Tabor
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents James Tabor's theory connecting Revelation with the eruption of Mount Vesuvius.
searchSummary: Presents James Tabor's proposal that Revelation 18 preserves an eyewitness-informed response to Vesuvius's destruction of Pompeii in 79 CE. Jews and Christians may have viewed the eruption as divine retribution against Rome nine years after Jerusalem's destruction. Revelation's Babylon burns suddenly while rulers, merchants, and sailors watch from a distance and mourn lost luxury and commerce, details Tabor connects with the prosperous port. The disaster was interpreted as an apocalyptic sign anticipating the Roman Empire's imminent fall.

title: Jesus the Suffering Messiah
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how belief in Jesus' resurrection led Christians to understand him as a suffering Messiah.
searchSummary: Explains how Jesus' followers created the idea of a suffering messiah after crucifixion and resurrection forced them to reconcile his death with their prior conviction that he was God's chosen king. They reread passages about righteous suffering, especially Isaiah 53, as messianic predictions. In their original contexts these texts do not mention a messiah, and Isaiah identifies the suffering servant as Israel, making the Christian interpretation a consequential theological innovation.

title: Readers’ Mailbag December 18, 2015
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about apocalyptic origins and a born-again Episcopalian background.

title: The Resurrection of the Son of God
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how belief in Jesus' resurrection reshaped claims about him as Son of God.

title: Did Some Disciples Not Believe in the Resurrection?
author: BDEhrman
description: Considers whether all of Jesus' disciples came to believe in the resurrection.
searchSummary: Uses widespread Gospel traditions of doubt and nonrecognition to question whether every disciple believed Jesus had risen. Ehrman proposes that Peter, Paul, Mary Magdalene, and perhaps a few others experienced visions they considered real, while some associates remained unconvinced; later stories expanded appearances to include all disciples. This limited-vision hypothesis explains why resurrection accounts repeatedly require proofs even though visionary experiences are normally accepted as genuine by those who have them.

title: Were the Disciples Martyred for Believing in the Resurrection?
author: BDEhrman
description: Questions the common claim that all the disciples were martyred for belief in Jesus' resurrection.

title: Ehrman-Bass Debate Did the Historical Jesus Claim to be Divine
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a debate with Justin Bass on whether the historical Jesus claimed to be divine.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's debate with pastor and apologist Justin Bass over whether the historical Jesus claimed to be God. Ehrman argues no and Bass argues yes before an audience drawn from Bass's church. Although skeptical that debates often change entrenched beliefs, Ehrman hopes a few listeners may think more deeply, recognize problems in their assumptions, or consider the opposing case. The post provides the recorded event and invites readers to judge both its substance and the broader value of such exchanges.

title: Readers’ Mailbag December 11, 2015
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers reader questions about Nazareth, inerrancy, and beginnings of life.
searchSummary: Answers three questions by separating Mark's literary rejection motif from the historical Jesus, recounting Ehrman's loss of biblical inerrancy, and explaining his agnostic atheism. In Mark, no one understands a Messiah destined to suffer, but that narrative device does not prove Jesus historically predicted his death. Critical study of contradictions made forced harmonization untenable and emotionally changed Ehrman's faith. He remains uncertain whether any higher power exists but believes natural processes produced life and finds meaning without a creator.

title: Does Paul Know about Judas Iscariot?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Paul knew the tradition that Judas Iscariot betrayed Jesus.

title: The Reversal of the Disciples’ Decisive Disconfirmation
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how resurrection belief reversed the apparent collapse of Jesus' messianic hopes.
searchSummary: Explains how crucifixion decisively disconfirmed the disciples' expectation that Jesus would become messianic ruler, while belief in his resurrection reversed that judgment and initiated a new understanding of Christ. The post distinguishes historical questions about when and why resurrection belief arose from theological claims that God performed a miracle. It also notes uncertainties about Judas and how many disciples believed, emphasizing that surviving traditions do not answer every historical question.

title: How the Crucifixion Destroyed Jesus’ Vision of the Future
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that crucifixion destroyed Jesus' expectation of the coming kingdom before resurrection belief developed.

title: Free Year-Long Memberships to Those Who Can’t Afford One!!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces free memberships for readers unable to afford the blog.

title: Many Thanks and One More Chance!
author: BDEhrman
description: Thanks donors for funding blog memberships and offers one more chance to give.

title: Readers’ Mailbag December 4, 2015
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about John the Baptist, textual criticism, suffering, and Jesus' apocalyptic message.
searchSummary: Answers three reader questions. Ehrman proposes that recurring end-time expectations function as theodicy: believers facing a suffering world expect an all-powerful, loving God to intervene soon and restore justice. He also explains that literary patterns can help textual critics identify original readings, citing Luke's bloody-sweat passage as disrupting a chiasm. Finally, he finds no evidence that John the Baptist was literate, knew Jesus during childhood, or taught him Scripture, though the possibility cannot be excluded.

title: Jesus Death as King of the Jews
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Jesus' execution as King of the Jews supports the view that Jesus saw himself as messiah.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus probably called himself the future messianic king because the Romans executed him specifically as King of the Jews. The charge appears independently, was not a title Christians ordinarily used, and therefore is unlikely to be a later invention. Jesus expected God rather than an army to overthrow evil, but Pilate would have treated any claimed kingship as a political threat and ordered the standard Roman punishment.

title: Judas and the Messianic Secret
author: BDEhrman
description: Connects Judas, secrecy, and Jesus' messianic claims before the crucifixion.
searchSummary: Explains Judas's betrayal as disclosure of Jesus' private messianic claim rather than merely revealing where authorities could arrest him. Jesus likely told the twelve that they would rule Israel under him in God's future kingdom while avoiding a public proclamation of kingship. Because the trial centers on a charge absent from his public teaching, the post argues that Judas supplied authorities with the politically dangerous secret needed to prosecute Jesus.

title: Jesus’ Claim to Be the Messiah
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Jesus probably understood himself as the future Jewish messiah.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus understood himself as the future messianic king within an apocalyptic expectation of God's earthly kingdom. His saying that the twelve would rule Israel is likely authentic because it includes Judas, and their subordinate thrones imply Jesus would rule above them. After resurrection belief, the disciples transformed this human royal expectation by identifying Jesus with the heavenly Son of Man who would return in judgment.

title: Gift Memberships to the Blog, 2015
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces holiday gift memberships for readers unable to afford the blog.

title: Readers’ Mailbag November 27, 2015
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about Jesus' singleness, Paul's visionary claims, and access to New Testament manuscripts.

title: Thanksgiving Reflections 2015
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers personal reflections for Thanksgiving.
searchSummary: Celebrates Thanksgiving as Ehrman's favorite holiday because family, shared food, physical existence, relationships, and gratitude provide meaning without requiring religious belief. His work, friends, travel, reading, and especially loved ones replace the purpose once rooted in God and afterlife, while the meal symbolizes life's sustaining pleasures. Awareness that refugees, victims, hungry people, and the lonely lack these goods turns thankfulness outward into remembrance and a commitment to help others gain reasons for gratitude.

title: The SBL and the Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the Society of Biblical Literature meeting and the blog's place in academic conversation.
searchSummary: Describes the Society of Biblical Literature meeting as a major professional gathering for intensive scholarship, publishing, organizational work, and academic relationships across religious studies. Ehrman's role has shifted from attending primarily for papers toward reconnecting with colleagues and former students, while a panel on scholarly blogging prompts reflection on his own public-facing, membership-funded model. He celebrates the blog's growth and charitable revenue but explains that its scale makes individualized interaction impossible despite the substantial time he already devotes to it.

title: The Teaching of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Jesus' teaching within first-century Jewish apocalyptic expectation.
searchSummary: Summarizes Jesus' preaching within a first-century Jewish apocalyptic framework. Ehrman describes an earthly Kingdom of God arriving soon through judgment by the Son of Man, reversing the fortunes of the powerful and the poor. Jesus therefore called people to prepare through devotion to God, love of neighbor, generosity, peace, and care for the needy, while his followers' conduct offered a present foretaste of the coming kingdom.

title: Fifty Ways to Forge a Gospel
author: FreedomBen
description: Discusses forgery and apocryphal Gospels in early Christian literature.
searchSummary: Reports on a conference about forgery in Christian apocrypha where Ehrman argued that ancient sources consistently treated false authorial claims as intentional deceit and condemned them as lying. Some participants resisted that conclusion without offering contrary evidence. The disagreement inspired New Testament scholar James McGrath to write and perform the parody song "Fifty Ways to Forge a Gospel." Ehrman connects the debate to his scholarly Forgery and Counterforgery and its shorter popular counterpart, Forged, both devoted to ancient literary deception.

title: Readers’ Mailbag November 20, 2015
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about unresolved historical Jesus problems and Mark's possible use of Paul's letters.
searchSummary: Identifies unresolved questions about Jesus' early occupation, literacy, following, reputation as healer, and treatment after crucifixion, emphasizing the limits of critical sources. It also reconsiders whether Mark knew Paul's letters or at least Pauline teaching. Mark's understanding of Jesus' death as an atoning sacrifice resembles Paul's theology, although ancient letters were not necessarily circulated widely. The evidence leaves direct literary dependence uncertain while making some relationship to Pauline ideas plausible.

title: The Beginning and End as Keys to the Middle
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Jesus' association with John the Baptist as evidence for an apocalyptic understanding of Jesus.
searchSummary: Uses the apocalyptic beginning and aftermath of Jesus's ministry to establish the orientation of the ministry itself. Jesus voluntarily joined John the Baptist's judgment movement, while Paul's earliest letters show that communities formed after Jesus's death expected his imminent return and the age's end. Together with apocalyptic sayings across Mark, Q, M, and L, this continuity makes a non-apocalyptic middle implausible and helps distinguish Jesus's historical proclamation from anti-apocalyptic sayings in Thomas.

title: The Baptism of Jesus as an Apocalyptic Event
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Jesus' baptism by John as part of the apocalyptic context for Jesus' ministry.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus's baptism by John the Baptist strongly supports an apocalyptic reconstruction of his ministry. Multiple independent sources attest the association, and Christians were unlikely to invent Jesus submitting to a supposedly superior baptizer offering forgiveness of sins. Since John warned that God's fiery judgment was imminent, Bart reasons that Jesus freely joined him because he shared that message. The apocalyptic movement at Jesus's beginning helps identify the framework of his later preaching.

title: Albert Schweitzer and the Apocalyptic Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Albert Schweitzer's interpretation of Jesus as an apocalyptic prophet.
searchSummary: Explains Albert Schweitzer's influential argument that Jesus expected God's imminent intervention, viewed himself as the coming kingdom's messiah, and was mistaken when the end failed to occur. Bart shows how later discoveries strengthened the case: the Dead Sea Scrolls document comparable Jewish expectations, while apocalyptic teachings appear throughout Mark, Q, M, and L. Their later fading in Luke, John, and Thomas suggests Christians modified Jesus's message after its timetable failed.

title: The Apocalyptic Context for Jesus’ View of the Messiah
author: BDEhrman
description: Places Jesus' messianic self-understanding within Jewish apocalyptic expectation.
searchSummary: Defines Jewish apocalypticism as the necessary context for evaluating whether Jesus considered himself the messiah. Its four themes are cosmic dualism, pessimism about improving the present age, God's universal vindication through judgment and resurrection, and the imminence of divine intervention. The earliest Jesus traditions share this worldview: the Son of Man would soon destroy evil and establish God's kingdom, while people had to repent, trust God, and love one another before judgment arrived.

title: Readers’ Mailbag November 13, 2015
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about Jewish Christian Gospels, atonement, and Peter in Rome.

title: How Do We Know What Jesus Said About Himself?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how historians evaluate what Jesus may have said about himself.
searchSummary: Explains the critical historical method needed to evaluate what Jesus said about himself rather than accepting every Gospel statement at face value. John's exalted claims and Synoptic passion predictions may embody later Christian convictions, especially when they align perfectly with post-resurrection theology. Historians compare independent testimony and account for authors' interests, so these sayings alone cannot establish whether the historical Jesus claimed messiahship or anticipated his death.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: Jesus, the Messiah, and the Resurrection
author: BDEhrman
description: Connects resurrection belief with early Christian claims that Jesus was the crucified Messiah.
searchSummary: Argues that resurrection belief confirmed rather than created the earliest identification of Jesus as messiah. Because no Jewish expectation held that a messiah would die and rise, a reported resurrection might imply divine exaltation but would not suggest the specific title Christ. The title's immediate and widespread use after Jesus' death therefore indicates that followers had already called him messiah during his lifetime, likely because he understood himself that way.

title: Another Problem with Calling Jesus the Messiah
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why many Jews rejected the claim that a crucified Jesus was the Messiah.
searchSummary: Uses Paul's argument in Galatians to explain why a crucified Jesus seemed incapable of being God's messiah. Deuteronomy declares one hanged on a tree cursed, so the pre-Christian Paul likely regarded Christian preaching as blasphemous. After believing Jesus was raised, Paul reversed his interpretation: the innocent Christ bore the law's curse on behalf of others, transforming the strongest objection to messiahship into an explanation of salvation.

title: Jesus and the Messianic Prophecies – Did the Old Testament Point to Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Old Testament messianic prophecies pointed to Jesus.
searchSummary: Argues that commonly cited Old Testament prophecies did not originally predict Jesus' virgin birth, suffering, resurrection, or other supposed messianic credentials. Gospel writers interpreted Scripture through their belief that Jesus was messiah and shaped narratives, including his Bethlehem birth, around those readings. Since a crucified victim contradicted Jewish expectations of a victorious deliverer, these retrospective interpretations did not persuade most Jews that Jesus fulfilled genuine messianic hopes.

title: Readers’ Mailbag on Revelation:  November 6, 2015
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers reader questions about Revelation and apocalyptic expectation.
searchSummary: Answers three reader questions about early Christianity. Revelation's intense expectation of an imminent end does not contradict later non-apocalyptic writings because communities developed different eschatologies simultaneously; this contrast also separates its author from the Gospel of John's. Matthew's four genealogical women foreshadow Mary's potentially scandalous pregnancy and may signal a mission beyond Israel. Paul's death is absent from the New Testament, but 1 Clement remembers his martyrdom and the later Acts of Paul supplies a legendary beheading under Nero.

title: The Crucified Messiah in 1 Corinthians
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses 1 Corinthians to discuss the scandal of a crucified Messiah.
searchSummary: Uses Paul's statement in 1 Corinthians that Christ crucified was a stumbling block to explain Jewish rejection of Christian preaching. Expected messianic power and divine signs contrasted sharply with a man humiliated and executed by Rome. Paul deliberately recasts apparent weakness and foolishness as God's wisdom, but his argument confirms that crucifixion itself made the claim that Jesus was messiah seem incoherent to many Jewish hearers.

title: The Jewish Messiah
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Jewish expectations of the Messiah as background for Mark's Gospel.
searchSummary: Traces Jewish messianic expectation from the anointed kings of Israel and God's promise of an enduring Davidic dynasty. After the monarchy ended, some Jews anticipated a restored king, while others imagined a priestly ruler or heavenly judge; all were figures of power who would establish God's rule. A crucified Galilean therefore appeared to be the opposite of a messiah, helping explain why most Jews rejected Christian claims about Jesus.

title: Jesus as the Messiah in Mark’s Gospel
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Mark's portrayal of Jesus as Messiah and Son of God.
searchSummary: Explains how Peter's confession in Mark both identifies and misunderstands Jesus as Messiah. Peter expects a powerful deliverer and rejects Jesus' prediction of suffering, prompting Jesus to call him Satan and define discipleship through the cross. "Messiah" means God's anointed one, while "Son of God" can designate angels, Israel, kings, or specially favored agents rather than automatically meaning God. The post introduces distinct historical questions about when Jesus received the title and how its meaning changed after resurrection.

title: I’m Openly Secular Documentary
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a documentary appearance connected to secularism and freedom from religion.
searchSummary: Introduces a Freedom From Religion Foundation documentary assembled from interviews recorded at its 2014 Raleigh conference, where Ehrman delivered a principal address. His comments appear alongside former clergy, secular activists, journalists, and advocates addressing atheism, freethought, religious departure, and church-state concerns in the Bible Belt and beyond. The post describes the participants and the Clergy Project's support for ministers becoming agnostic or atheist, but does not summarize Ehrman's individual contributions to the documentary.

title: Jesus as the Son of God in Mark
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Mark's portrayal of Jesus as Son of God.
searchSummary: Explains Mark's carefully structured presentation of Jesus as God's Son. The title appears at decisive points: God addresses Jesus privately at baptism, the heavenly voice speaks again at the Transfiguration, and a centurion recognizes him at crucifixion. Between these revelations, family, townspeople, leaders, and disciples fail to understand, while only God, Jesus, demons, narrator, and reader know. This literary pattern supplies background for comparing Mark's baptismal sonship with later interpretations of Luke's wording.

title: Reader’s Mailbag on Virgin Birth: 10/29/15
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers a reader question about the virgin birth and New Testament traditions.

title: An Irritating Criticism: My View of Paul’s View of Christ
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to criticism of the argument that Paul could portray Christ as an angelic being.
searchSummary: Responds to criticism that Ehrman makes Galatians 4:14 the sole basis of Paul's Christology while neglecting Philippians 2. He explains that Galatians grammatically identifies Christ as an angel and that his book treats the Philippians poem at length as the central narrative: the preexistent angel becomes human and is then exalted to equality with Yahweh. The criticism therefore faults him for omitting precisely the evidence and interpretation that his argument explicitly develops.

title: Really???  Stories of Jesus’ Virgin Birth
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how stories of Jesus' virgin birth could develop in oral tradition.
searchSummary: Argues that living relatives or eyewitnesses could not have prevented late first-century virgin-birth traditions from developing. Only Matthew and Luke preserve the claim, Jesus' immediate family was probably dead, and geographically and linguistically separated storytellers could circulate accounts without encountering anyone able to correct them. Even when knowledgeable witnesses exist, stories spread through non-witnesses, corrections do not reach every audience, and repeated retelling allows invented traditions to persist.

title: Taking the Pulse of the Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks readers for feedback on the state and direction of the blog.

title: Is Luke’s Christology Consistent?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Luke-Acts presents a consistent Christology.
searchSummary: Argues that Luke-Acts is not strictly consistent about when Jesus becomes Messiah, Lord, Savior, or Son of God. Those identities are associated with his birth, ancestry, baptism, ministry, and resurrection, showing that Luke does not assign them to only one event. This pattern makes the baptismal reading 'Today I have begotten you' plausible within Luke's theology and explains why scribes wary of adoptionism may have altered it.

title: Arguments that Luke Did Not Originally Have the Virgin Birth
author: BDEhrman
description: Gives arguments that Luke may not originally have included the virgin birth narrative.

title: Did Luke’s Gospel Originally Have the Virgin Birth?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Luke's Gospel originally contained the virgin birth story.

title: Scribes Who Changed the Voice at Jesus Baptism?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how scribes may have changed the heavenly voice at Jesus' baptism to resist adoptionist Christology.
searchSummary: Examines whether Luke's baptismal voice originally declared Jesus beloved or said, Today I have begotten you. Most Greek manuscripts match Mark's wording, but Codex Bezae, early Latin witnesses, and second-century church fathers preserve the Psalm 2 form. Because scribes commonly harmonized Gospels and the alternative could support adoptionist claims that Jesus became God's Son at baptism, Ehrman considers it likely that proto-orthodox copyists replaced Luke's distinctive wording with Mark's less theologically dangerous version.

title: Some Flak (Already!) Over My New Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to early criticism of Jesus Before the Gospels.

title: Other Christians Who Denied that Christ was Divine by Nature
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses early Christians who denied that Christ was divine by nature.
searchSummary: The Theodotians were gentile Roman Christians who taught that Jesus was born as an entirely human person and adopted by God because of his righteousness. Theodotus and his followers differed over whether Jesus became divine at baptism or resurrection, while claiming apostolic support for their view. Orthodox opponents excommunicated them, accused them of privileging secular learning, and alleged textual alteration, though direct evidence for Theodotian changes to scripture is scarce.

title: Was Christ God?  The View of Jewish-Christian Ebionites
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the Ebionite view that Christ was human rather than divine by nature.
searchSummary: Reconstructs the adoptionist Christology attributed to Jewish-Christian Ebionites while emphasizing the uncertainty of hostile sources. Church fathers describe one or more Torah-observant groups that claimed continuity with James, rejected Paul, favored Jewish-Christian Gospels or a version of Matthew, and viewed Jesus as Joseph and Mary's fully human son. Because of exceptional righteousness, Jesus was adopted as God's son at baptism rather than being divine by nature or born of a virgin. Surviving heresiological reports may conflate distinct communities and beliefs.

title: Adoptionistic Christologies
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces adoptionistic Christologies in the early church.

title: Are Their Any Completely Anti-Heretical Manuscripts?
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers a question about whether the same manuscripts preserve anti-heretical textual variants.
searchSummary: Explains why no surviving manuscript consistently contains every known anti-docetic or other proto-orthodox textual change. The shorter readings of Luke's Last Supper and bloody-sweat passages occur in different manuscripts because individual scribes knew and altered different passages, not because one editor systematically revised Luke. Ehrman argues that scattered, occasional changes responding to disputes over Jesus' humanity and divinity collectively demonstrate theological influence even though no manuscript exhibits a uniform doctrinal program.

title: Luke’s Last Supper and Orthodox Corruptions of Scripture
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Luke's Last Supper textual problem in relation to orthodox textual changes.
searchSummary: Concludes that the longer form of Luke's Last Supper account was added by proto-orthodox scribes during debates over whether Christ possessed real human flesh. Luke otherwise avoids describing Jesus' death as an atoning sacrifice, but the added words identify the bread and wine with a body and blood given for believers. Writers such as Tertullian and Irenaeus used precisely this language against docetists who denied Jesus' physical suffering and death.

title: The Striking Conclusion: Jesus’ Last Supper in Luke
author: BDEhrman
description: Draws a conclusion about Luke's Last Supper and the meaning of Jesus' death.
