searchSummary: Summarizes the textual case that Luke originally wrote the shorter Last Supper account, without the words declaring Jesus' body and blood given for others. An accidental omission is unlikely, and a deliberate deletion would not harmonize Luke with parallel accounts. A scribal addition, however, would both make Luke resemble 1 Corinthians and introduce an atonement theology absent elsewhere from Luke-Acts, setting up the question of its proto-orthodox motivation.

title: Luke’s Understanding of Jesus’ Death
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Luke does not portray Jesus' death as an atonement for sins.
searchSummary: Explains Luke's theological distinction between atonement and forgiveness. In the speeches of Acts, Jesus dies as God's innocent prophet whose rejection exposes human guilt and leads people to repentance; God then forgives them freely. Unlike Mark and Paul, Luke does not portray Jesus as paying humanity's debt through a sacrificial death, though the crucifixion remains essential as the event that awakens recognition of sin.

title: Anti-Judaism in the Gospel of Luke
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains anti-Jewish elements in Luke's portrayal of Jesus as a rejected prophet.
searchSummary: Examines anti-Jewish elements in Luke-Acts, where Jews who reject Jesus are portrayed as continuing Israel's rejection of God's prophets. The post argues that Luke's conflict with non-Christian Jews in his own time shaped his narration of events decades earlier. It situates this conclusion within historical criticism's broader insight that Gospel narratives reveal the beliefs and circumstances of their authors as well as traditions about Jesus.

title: Jesus’ Death as a Prophet in Luke
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Luke's portrayal of Jesus' death as the death of a prophet.
searchSummary: Explains why Jesus must die in Luke even though his death is not portrayed as an atoning sacrifice. Luke presents Jesus as a Jewish prophet like Samuel, Isaiah, Elijah, and Elisha, and assumes that God's prophets are rejected by their own people, especially in Jerusalem. Jesus' death as the final rejected prophet then allows the message of salvation to move beyond Israel, a development narrated throughout Acts.

title: My Big Day Appeal
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses a birthday appeal to ask readers to support the blog's charitable work.
searchSummary: Uses Bart's sixtieth birthday to request charitable donations instead of presents. He hopes to push annual blog fundraising beyond $100,000 after the previous year's $78,000, noting that membership had risen while donations had declined. The appeal describes Urban Ministries of Durham, the regional Food Bank, CARE, and Doctors Without Borders and their work against hunger, homelessness, poverty, and medical crises. Readers may contribute any amount through the site's donation link.

title: Ehrman Licona Debate – Prove Jesus Rose from Dead
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a debate with Mike Licona on whether historians can prove Jesus rose from the dead.
searchSummary: Presents a recorded 2008 debate between Ehrman and Christian apologist Mike Licona over whether historians can prove that Jesus rose from the dead. Held at a Baptist seminary before an audience sympathetic to Licona, the event contrasts their sharply different conclusions despite a friendly personal relationship. Ehrman notes Licona's later written discussion of the debate and his own treatment of the issue in How Jesus Became God. The post supplies the video rather than declaring a winner.

title: Luke’s View of Jesus’ Death
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Luke's view of Jesus' death in comparison with other Gospel accounts of the Last Supper.
searchSummary: Argues that the longer Last Supper reading in Luke conflicts with the author's treatment of Jesus' death. Paul and Mark describe the crucifixion as an atoning sacrifice, but Luke omits Mark's ransom saying and moves the tearing of the Temple curtain to before Jesus dies. Because Luke-Acts otherwise avoids atonement theology, the words about Jesus' body and blood being given for others are more plausibly a later scribal addition.

title: Why Would a Scribe Change Luke’s Account of the Last Supper?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why a scribe might have changed Luke's Last Supper account to make it sound more atoning.
searchSummary: Evaluates why a scribe might shorten or expand Luke's disputed Last Supper account. Removing the second cup would neither harmonize Luke's cup-bread sequence with other accounts nor explain deleting words about the bread. Adding the longer reading, however, would repair an apparently abrupt passage, align it with 1 Corinthians, and explicitly connect the bread and wine with Jesus' broken body and shed blood, making expansion more plausible.

title: The Last Supper in Luke: An Important Textual Problem
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a major textual problem in Luke's account of the Last Supper.
searchSummary: Introduces the textual dispute over Luke 22:19-20, where words identifying the bread and cup with Jesus' body and blood are absent from an early Greek manuscript and several Latin witnesses. Scholars must decide whether a scribe omitted or added the passage by comparing manuscript evidence, Luke's style and theology, and probable scribal motives. The shorter text reverses the familiar meal order and lacks an explicit connection between the meal and Jesus' death.

title: Early Christian Docetism
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces docetic Christology as background for textual variants in the New Testament manuscripts.

title: My Debate with Kyle Butt on the Problem of Suffering
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a debate with Kyle Butt on suffering and the problem of evil.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's 2014 debate with conservative Christian apologist Kyle Butt over whether suffering counts against the existence of the Christian God. Butt framed Ehrman's position as the claim that worldly pain and suffering make belief in that God impossible, while Butt defended the opposing view. The recorded event at the University of North Alabama, broadcast by Gospel Broadcasting Network, provides a direct confrontation between Ehrman's agnostic argument from suffering and a Christian apologetic response.

title: How Can You Know A Scribe’s Intentions?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how scholars can argue about scribal intentions in textual changes.

title: How Consistent are Orthodox Corruptions of Scripture?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores whether orthodox textual corruptions followed a consistent pattern.
searchSummary: Explains that early Christian scribes sometimes changed New Testament passages to prevent heretical interpretations or strengthen proto-orthodox Christology, but did so intermittently rather than through an organized revision campaign. Ehrman's survey found more than one hundred plausible cases, yet no manuscript or scribe consistently reworked the text and almost no convincing heretical counterexamples. Most scribes copied conservatively, while occasional departures reveal how their theological commitments could affect particular readings in historically significant ways.

title: On Falsification and Forgery
author: BDEhrman
description: Connects falsification, forgery, and the textual variant of Jesus' bloody sweat.
searchSummary: Treats intentional scribal alteration as a form of textual falsification and uses Luke's bloody-sweat passage as an example. The verses are absent from important early witnesses and probably entered later, placing a scribe's words under the Gospel author's authority even though the work is anonymous. Ancient writers strongly condemned such changes, while motive and truthfulness remain separate questions; variants themselves can reveal scribal literary activity rather than merely obstruct reconstruction.

title: How Do You Research Orthodox Corruptions?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how research on Didymus the Blind led into work on orthodox textual corruptions.
searchSummary: Reconstructs the research process behind The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture, beginning with Ehrman's interest in New Testament variants that affected claims about Christ. Rather than collating every manuscript, he examined the textual apparatuses of Metzger, Nestle-Aland, von Soden, and Tischendorf verse by verse across the entire New Testament. He sorted thousands of readings into strong, arguable, and remote Christological candidates, while also determining which reading was original and which represented a later alteration.

title: Do I Have a Grudge Against Dr. Bruce Metzger?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to a question about Bruce Metzger and alleged disagreement with Metzger's views.

title: Live Stream the Debate Tonight
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces livestream information for a debate on whether Jesus claimed to be divine.
searchSummary: Provides streaming information for Ehrman's debate with Justin Bass on whether Jesus claimed divinity and explains why Ehrman accepts such events. Speaking fees go to charities supported by the blog, and he hopes that even an audience favoring his opponent may include a few people willing to reconsider rigid religious assumptions. Ehrman does not expect to win over the crowd and acknowledges that most listeners retain prior views. Fundraising and encouraging open thought, rather than rhetorical victory, justify participating.

title: Magic and Manuscripts
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses magical uses of manuscripts in early Christian practice.

title: Debate in Dallas on Friday
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Dallas debate on whether the historical Jesus claimed to be divine.
searchSummary: Announces a free public debate in the Dallas area between Ehrman and pastor-apologist Justin Bass on whether the historical Jesus claimed to be divine. Bass argues yes, while Ehrman argues no. The brief post supplies the date, time, location, and event link and anticipates a substantive exchange between sharply opposed positions. It does not present historical evidence or summarize either case; its purpose is to notify nearby readers and invite them to attend.

title: Why Intentional Changes of the Text Might Matter
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why intentional scribal changes matter for understanding early Christian disputes.

title: Why Bother With Anything *Except* the “Original” Text??
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why textual critics should study more than the original form of the text.
searchSummary: Argues that textual criticism remains valuable even if new evidence is unlikely to transform the reconstructed Greek New Testament. Variants should not be discarded merely as errors hiding the original; intentional and accidental changes can reveal the beliefs, conflicts, interests, and practices of early Christian scribes. Because surviving literary sources mostly represent educated elites, manuscript alterations offer rare evidence about less elite Christians in the poorly documented second and third centuries.

title: My Focus on Christology in The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture focused especially on Christology.
searchSummary: Explains why The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture focuses on Christological changes made during the first three centuries. Later manuscripts usually preserve variants already present in earlier papyri, suggesting that most intentional alternatives arose when Christians fiercely debated whether Christ was human, divine, two beings, or one human-and-divine being. Ehrman investigates how scribes supporting the emerging orthodox position altered passages to strengthen their view or weaken rival Christologies.

title: The Unusual Thesis of The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes the thesis that early Christian scribes sometimes changed texts for theological reasons.
searchSummary: Describes the thesis that early Christian scribes participated in theological disputes by changing New Testament texts, joining manuscript studies with the history of doctrine. Against F. J. A. Hort's influential denial of dogmatic falsification, Ehrman's studies of Jesus' bloody sweat and another Christological variant suggested purposeful anti-docetic and anti-Gnostic alterations. Systematic research revealed enough cases to make The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture a substantial reassessment rather than the thin volume Bruce Metzger initially expected.

title: Back to the Question:  The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture
author: BDEhrman
description: Returns to the long-running discussion of The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture.

title: Back to the Forgery of the Gospel of Jesus’ Wife
author: BDEhrman
description: Reports new evidence that the Gospel of Jesus' Wife was a modern forgery.

title: Christ’s Self-Ignorance
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about Christ's knowledge and self-ignorance in relation to Philippians.
searchSummary: Explains how Christian theology can affirm Jesus' divinity even if the historical Jesus never claimed or knew he was God. Kenotic Christology interprets Philippians 2 as a preexistent divine Christ voluntarily relinquishing omniscience to become fully human, including accepting limits on self-knowledge. Ehrman does not accept this doctrine, but argues that historical silence about Jesus' divine identity cannot by itself disprove a theological model designed to preserve both complete humanity and complete divinity.

title: On “Knowing” the Original Words of the NT
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the original words of the New Testament cannot be known with certainty at every point.
searchSummary: Argues that scholars cannot know the original New Testament wording with absolute certainty if every surviving witness could descend from an altered early copy. Numerous manuscripts may preserve a common ancestor's additions or omissions while leaving no independent trace of the author's text. This limitation especially affects doctrines locating inspiration in exact Greek words; absent originals or several nearly contemporary independent copies, historical probability can support reconstruction but cannot satisfy a theological demand for certainty.

title: How Jesus Became God on Humanist Hour
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares an interview about How Jesus Became God on The Humanist Hour.
searchSummary: Introduces an hour-long Humanist Hour interview with Bo Bennett concerning Ehrman's background, historical approaches to the Bible, and How Jesus Became God. The conversation connects his former Christian belief with his scholarship on how Jesus' followers came to regard an apocalyptic Jewish preacher as divine. The post provides the complete recording as its principal content rather than restating the interview's arguments in a written essay.

title: Irrelevant Arguments and the So-called Tenacity of the Tradition
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques the argument that the tenacity of the manuscript tradition proves the original text is recoverable.
searchSummary: Challenges the claim that the manuscript tradition's tenacity assures that an original New Testament reading survives somewhere among known variants. Early papyri sharing readings with medieval manuscripts shows that later scribes preserved inherited alternatives, not that every variant created during the poorly documented first centuries survived. Because early, often untrained copyists changed texts more freely and their lost copies differed substantially, later manuscript stability cannot establish what readings disappeared before the earliest surviving evidence.

title: What Is the “Original” Text?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains what textual critics mean by the original text of the New Testament.
searchSummary: Uses the drafting and editing of Jesus Before the Gospels to show that an original text may have many plausible meanings. An outline, first draft, authorial revisions, editorial changes, copyediting, and publication are successive forms, while Romans adds dictation by Tertius, possible mishearing, correction, and a clean copy. Ehrman tentatively favors the first circulated form, but notes that it is not the earliest and may differ from inaccessible prior versions.

title: Arguments that We Have the Original Text
author: BDEhrman
description: Reviews arguments used to claim that scholars can recover the original New Testament text.
searchSummary: Assesses arguments that manuscript abundance and the tradition's tenacity preserve the original New Testament. Many late witnesses do not establish wording centuries earlier, and scholars likewise debate the exact texts of Homer, Plato, and other classics; religious copyists also had ideological motives for changes. Early papyri usually contain variants known from later manuscripts, showing persistence of readings, but that pattern alone cannot prove every original reading survived or identify it.

title: Contradictions and Silly Claims by Textual Critics
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to charges of contradiction in claims about textual criticism and the original text.
searchSummary: Explains why saying the reconstructed Greek New Testament is unlikely to change greatly does not mean scholars know its original wording. Modern editions resemble the 1881 text and probably approximate the authors in most places, yet precise confidence percentages are invented because the missing originals provide no statistical baseline. Mark's first complete witness appears about 300 years after composition, leaving early copying changes beyond direct observation even where later scholarly consensus is stable.

title: Textual Criticism Syllabus
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a PhD seminar syllabus on New Testament textual criticism.
searchSummary: Presents the syllabus for Ehrman's doctoral seminar in New Testament textual criticism, designed to ground students in the discipline's history and methods before they analyze a major variant. Coursework combines manuscript collation, critical apparatuses, textual criteria, scribal tendencies, early versions, patristic citations, classification, technology, and theological influences on transmission. Students repeatedly evaluate disputed readings, review major scholarship, present current developments, and produce an in-depth term paper establishing a passage's earliest recoverable form and interpretive significance.

title: Ruffling the Feathers of My Fellow Textual Critics
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why some textual critics objected to claims made in Misquoting Jesus.
searchSummary: Defends Misquoting Jesus by summarizing its undisputed claims: no New Testament originals survive, all copies differ, most variants are trivial, some affect interpretation, and certain original readings remain unresolved. Ehrman's further claim that editions are unlikely to move far beyond their current form reflects the stability of the Westcott-Hort reconstruction despite later discoveries and methods. Stable scholarly conclusions and complete certainty are compatible neither logically nor evidentially.

title: How God Could Become a Human
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses incarnation and Philippians to explain how God could become human.
searchSummary: Explains kenotic Christology, which interprets Philippians' statement that Christ “emptied himself” as a temporary surrender of divine powers in order to become genuinely human. On this view, the eternal Christ relinquished omniscience, omnipotence, omnipresence, and other prerogatives so he could experience limitation, suffering, and death. The theory aims to reconcile full divinity with authentic humanity, though incarnation would not literally let God experience every possible form of existence.

title: Did Scribes Add the Passage of the Bloody Sweat?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether scribes added Luke's bloody sweat passage.

title: The Bloody Sweat and the Scribes Who Changed It
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the bloody sweat textual variant and why scribes may have changed it.
searchSummary: Argues that Luke's bloody-sweat verses were probably added by scribes rather than removed. The passage disrupts Luke's literary structure and contradicts his otherwise composed Jesus, making it unlikely from the author's perspective. The post then introduces transcriptional probability: second-century scribes had theological reasons to prefer a vivid display of Jesus' human suffering, while manuscript evidence offers little support for docetic scribes systematically deleting such passages.

title: How Textual Criticism Became Relevant
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to criticism that recent claims about textual criticism were overstated.

title: Jesus’ Lack of Agony
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Gospel portrayals of Jesus' agony before death through the bloody sweat passage.
searchSummary: Compares Mark's anguished, abandoned Jesus with Luke's calm and confident Jesus to assess the bloody-sweat passage. Luke systematically removes Mark's signs of distress and portrays Jesus comforting others, forgiving his executioners, promising paradise, and entrusting himself to God. Because Luke 22:43-44 is the lone scene of severe agony and is absent from important early manuscripts, the post argues that it conflicts with Luke's editorial purpose and was likely added later.

title: When I First Realized the Importance of Textual Criticism: The Bloody Sweat
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts how the bloody sweat passage showed the importance of textual criticism.
searchSummary: Explains how the disputed bloody-sweat verses in Luke first demonstrated to Ehrman the interpretive importance of textual criticism. Luke systematically removes Mark's portrayal of Jesus' distress and structures the prayer scene around Jesus praying and calmly resisting temptation, unlike his sleeping disciples. Because the bloody-sweat episode interrupts that chiastic structure and contradicts Luke's passionless portrayal of Jesus, Ehrman concludes it was added by a later scribe rather than written by Luke.

title: An Amusing Anecdote about the State of Textual Criticism
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses an anecdote to illustrate the state of textual criticism in the early 1980s.

title: My Original Foray into Textual Criticism
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts an early entry into New Testament textual criticism.
searchSummary: Recounts why Ehrman pursued textual criticism when many New Testament scholars considered its major problems solved and remaining work technical and unrewarding. Moody's doctrine of verbal inspiration made recovering disputed Greek wording essential, while the field's evidentiary puzzle appealed to his temperament. Training with Bruce Metzger eventually let him combine textual reconstruction, exegesis, and early Christian history, disciplines usually practiced separately but necessary for understanding both a text and its transmission.

title: The Malaise in New Testament Textual Criticism
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why New Testament textual criticism seemed stagnant in the early 1980s.
searchSummary: Explains how Westcott and Hort's 1881 Greek New Testament displaced the long-dominant Textus Receptus. Erasmus had created that received text from only a few late manuscripts, even translating Revelation's missing ending back from Latin, yet publishers repeated it for centuries despite better discoveries. Westcott and Hort's sustained manuscript analysis removed famous later additions and established principles still shaping modern editions, whose stability later made scholars think textual criticism had largely finished its task.

title: Why New Testament Textual Criticism Had Grown Moribund
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why New Testament textual criticism had become moribund before renewed scholarly interest.
searchSummary: Explains why New Testament textual criticism seemed moribund when Ehrman entered graduate school in the late 1970s. Most scholars believed earlier editors had already reconstructed the original Greek text with great reliability, leaving only minor disputes reflected in critical apparatuses. Ehrman describes how successive Greek editions changed little and why this apparent completion of the discipline discouraged scholars from studying manuscripts and textual variants.

title: When I Started in Textual Criticism
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes entering the field of New Testament textual criticism as a graduate student.
searchSummary: Recalls Ehrman's entry into New Testament textual criticism when the field appeared technical, marginal, and nearly finished. Most scholars treated reconstructing manuscript texts as uninteresting, American doctoral training was essentially limited to Bruce Metzger at Princeton, and few students continued in the discipline. Ehrman nevertheless loved the work and pursued it intensely, eventually training later scholars and challenging standard assumptions that textual criticism concerned only recovering originals and that scribes almost never changed texts for theological reasons.

title: Gentle as a Nurse in 1 Thessalonians 2:7
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines the textual variant between gentle and infants in 1 Thessalonians 2:7.
searchSummary: Argues that Paul described himself and his companions as gentle, not infants, in 1 Thessalonians 2:7 despite stronger early manuscript support for infants. Later corrections show scribes preferred gentle, but those witnesses appear centuries after Paul and cannot settle the earliest reading. Paul's consistently negative use of infants, the coherent image of a gentle nurse, and a matching philosophical convention outweigh the external evidence and illustrate the multiple arguments textual critics must balance.

title: More Intriguing Problems with 1 Thessalonians 2:7
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues the textual problem of 1 Thessalonians 2:7 and why the evidence is difficult.
searchSummary: Examines the unresolved choice between infants and gentle in 1 Thessalonians 2:7 by testing Pauline vocabulary and literary context. Infants is common in Paul's letters but always negative, while gentle appears nowhere else yet fits the image of a nurse naturally. Although infants creates a confusing mixed metaphor that scribes might simplify, Paul demonstrably uses mixed metaphors elsewhere. These competing considerations leave the variant at a temporary standstill rather than deciding the original wording.

title: The Textual Problem of 1 Thessalonians 2:7
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the textual problem in 1 Thessalonians 2:7 after discussing the letter's purpose.
searchSummary: Introduces the one-letter textual problem in 1 Thessalonians 2:7: whether Paul said that he and his companions became infants or gentle among the Thessalonians. The preceding Greek word ends with the disputed letter, and both readings sound identical when read aloud, allowing either accidental omission or duplication during visual copying or dictation. Because scribes commonly made both kinds of error, the mechanics of transmission alone cannot determine which wording Paul originally used.

title: A Thief in the Night
author: BDEhrman
description: Recalls an evangelical film about the rapture and modern apocalyptic belief.

title: The Myth of the Rapture: Calling a Spade a Spade
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques the modern doctrine of the rapture as a mistaken reading of 1 Thessalonians.

title: The Return of Jesus (Rapture?) in 1 Thessalonians
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Paul's language about Jesus' return in 1 Thessalonians and its later connection to rapture belief.

title: Paul’s Letter to the Thessalonians
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces 1 Thessalonians as Paul's earliest surviving letter and as context for a textual variant.

title: Mark 1:1 as an Intentional Alteration of the Text
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that a variant in Mark 1:1 may be an intentional alteration of the text.
searchSummary: Argues that proto-orthodox scribes intentionally added "Son of God" to Mark 1:1. Diverse witnesses lacking the phrase make repeated accidental omission at the book's fresh beginning unlikely, while deliberate removal has no clear motive. Mark's baptismal Spirit and final cry could support Gnostic separation of the human Jesus from a divine Christ who enters and departs. The addition establishes Jesus' divine sonship before baptism and prevents readers from concluding that he acquired it only then.

title: A Variant in Mark 1:1 — Accidental or Intentional?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether the variant in Mark 1:1 was accidental or intentional.
searchSummary: Presents the competing accidental explanation for the disputed phrase "Son of God" in Mark 1:1. Sacred names were abbreviated, ancient manuscripts lacked spaces, and matching Greek letters stood beside one another. A copyist could return to the wrong matching letter after writing "Christ" and inadvertently skip the abbreviated words "Son of God." The post emphasizes that Mark calls Jesus God's Son elsewhere and leaves open whether this plausible copying accident is preferable to an intentional theological alteration.

title: An Intentional Change in Mark 15:34
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains an intentional scribal change in Mark 15:34.

title: Illustration of a Textual Change: Did Mark Make a Mistake?
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Mark's citation of Isaiah to illustrate intentional textual change.
searchSummary: Uses Mark's composite scriptural quotation to illustrate how textual critics identify scribal correction. The earliest and strongest manuscripts attribute words from Exodus, Malachi, and Isaiah to "Isaiah the prophet," while later copies read the more accurate "in the prophets." Because scribes are more likely to remove a perceived mistake than create one, the difficult attribution is original. Textual criticism establishes this wording and the correction's history before interpreters decide whether Mark actually erred by naming the most prominent source.

title: Intentional Changes of the Text
author: BDEhrman
description: Returns to the topic of intentional changes in New Testament manuscripts.

title: More Hard Issues on the Qur’an Fragments
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses difficult issues raised by early Qur'an fragments from Birmingham.
searchSummary: Explains why early Quran manuscripts provide the kind of evidence historians need to evaluate claims of exact transmission. Ehrman distinguishes Muslim traditions of memorizing the Quran from historically verifiable comparison: without written or recorded witnesses, later researchers cannot test whether recitations remained word-for-word identical across centuries. He neither denies accurate preservation nor claims expertise in Islam. Instead, he stresses that manuscripts, unlike inherited assurances about memory, make continuity and variation open to examination.

title: Fundamentalist Mistakes
author: BDEhrman
description: Warns against fundamentalist mistakes in interpreting the Birmingham Qur'an fragments.

title: More on the Discovery of Ancient Qur’an Fragments
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues discussion of the discovery and dating of early Qur'an fragments.
searchSummary: Responds to questions and cautions prompted by the Birmingham Quran fragments. Faithful copying would not establish the historical accuracy of the Quran's information about Jesus, and radiocarbon testing dates parchment rather than ink. Contributors raise issues involving script, recycled parchment, the Sanaa codex, sensational press coverage, and the need for specialist analysis. Ehrman treats the discovery as noteworthy but provisional, emphasizing probabilities and calling for paleography, codicology, peer review, and multispectral imaging.

title: Lunch Auction
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a lunch auction supporting charity.
searchSummary: Briefly promotes an auction for lunch with Bart in the Dallas area. Although the winning bid requires a substantial payment, he emphasizes that none of it will become personal income and that the entire amount will go directly to charity. The post supplies the external auction link rather than describing its terms, intended participants, scheduling, or bidding process in detail.

title: The Significance of an Astounding New Discovery
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the discovery of early Qur'an fragments at the University of Birmingham.
searchSummary: Explains why the radiocarbon dating of two Birmingham Quran pages to 568-645 CE is historically remarkable. Their possible proximity to Muhammad's lifetime may reveal early textual stability and raises questions about why Christian scribes produced so many New Testament variants. Ehrman then separates textual preservation from truth: knowing an author's wording does not establish that the writing's claims are reliable. The discovery may illuminate Quranic transmission without proving Islam, just as abundant New Testament manuscripts do not prove Christianity.

title: Accidental Scribal Changes
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains accidental scribal changes in New Testament manuscripts.

title: Patristic Evidence for the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains patristic evidence and its use in reconstructing the New Testament text.

title: The Versional Evidence for the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains versional evidence and how translations help textual critics reconstruct ancient texts.
searchSummary: Explains how ancient New Testament translations provide versional evidence for reconstructing the Greek text. Early Latin, Syriac, and Coptic forms may preserve readings older than most surviving Greek manuscripts, but grammatical differences can conceal articles, word order, or tense. Scholars must determine each version's date and source language, reconstruct its earliest wording from later copies, and retrovert it into Greek. The process is highly technical but can reveal both authorial readings and later scribal changes.

title: Google Cambridge Lecture on Forged
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a Google Cambridge lecture on Forged and ancient literary forgery.
searchSummary: Introduces a video of Ehrman's 2011 Google Cambridge lecture about his book Forged. The talk explains why ancient authors sometimes published writings while falsely claiming to be famous people, using prestigious identities to attract readers and lend authority to their works. Ehrman describes literary forgery as relatively common in antiquity but also widely condemned by ancient observers. His discussion concentrates on early Christian examples, including writings that eventually became part of the New Testament.

title: New Testament Manuscripts:  Good News and Bad News
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the good news and bad news about New Testament manuscript evidence.

title: The Manuscripts of the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys the manuscript evidence for the New Testament as background for textual criticism.

title: What Is Textual Criticism?
author: BDEhrman
description: Defines textual criticism and explains why it matters for the New Testament text.
searchSummary: Defines textual criticism as the specialized discipline that reconstructs an author's wording when originals are lost and surviving copies differ. Ehrman explains how accidental and intentional scribal changes complicate texts ranging from Shakespeare to ancient authors and the New Testament. He stresses that scholars use rigorous criteria, can often approximate original readings, and also investigate how, when, where, and why texts were changed.

title: Orthodoxy and Proto-Orthodoxy
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains orthodoxy and proto-orthodoxy in the context of early Christian diversity.
searchSummary: Explains why historians call second- and third-century Christians whose views later became dominant “proto-orthodox” rather than orthodox. Orthodoxy here denotes the theological position that eventually won, not a judgment that it was metaphysically correct or already dominant. Calling earlier advocates orthodox would therefore be anachronistic. Figures such as the Apostolic Fathers, Justin, Irenaeus, and Tertullian were proto-orthodox because they promoted beliefs that later defined orthodoxy, including positions that influenced how some Christian scribes transmitted Scripture.

title: Earliest Christian Diversity
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses earliest Christian diversity and a book about how Gospel traditions developed.
searchSummary: Presents Destro and Pesce's theory that Gospel geography preserves evidence of Christian diversity from the movement's beginnings. Mark, Matthew's special material, Luke's special material, and John emphasize different regions for Jesus' activity and resurrection appearances. Followers remaining in those locations could have preserved and developed distinct memories and interpretations before their traditions entered the Gospels. The model suggests scattered Palestinian groups, not one unified Jerusalem church, formed differing understandings of Jesus immediately after his death.

title: Orthodoxy and Heresy in the New Testament Itself
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether orthodoxy and heresy already appear within the New Testament.

title: A Milestone on the Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a blog milestone and reflects on the blog's charitable purpose.
searchSummary: Celebrates the blog passing $200,000 in lifetime charitable revenue and sets a goal of raising $100,000 annually. Bart explains that supporting charities addressing hunger, homelessness, and global crises makes the substantial weekly workload worthwhile. He profiles Urban Ministries of Durham, the regional Food Bank, CARE, and Doctors Without Borders, then asks readers to donate, give subscriptions, recruit members, and suggest improvements so the blog can expand both its audience and charitable impact.

title: NC Bookwatch: Lost Christianities
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a video interview on Lost Christianities and early Christian diversity.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's North Carolina Bookwatch interview about Lost Christianities and the diversity of early Christian movements. He discusses alternative forms of Christianity, the processes through which they were suppressed, reshaped, or forgotten, and the rival writings used to support their claims. Although these groups disagreed sharply, each asserted continuity with Jesus and the apostles and possessed texts attributed to authoritative followers, illustrating how later Christian orthodoxy emerged from competition among communities with different scriptures and beliefs.

title: Taming the Diversity of the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the New Testament itself does not show simple early Christian unity.
searchSummary: Explains how treating the New Testament as one divinely authored book conceals substantial differences among its twenty-seven writings. Later orthodox Christians preserved these books and excluded alternatives, then canonical collection encouraged readers to harmonize tensions such as James's insistence on justification by works and Paul's rejection of justification by works of law. Luther recognized the conflict strongly enough to relegate Hebrews, James, Jude, and Revelation to an appendix. Historical study likewise finds divergent Christologies, legal teachings, and Gospel accounts.

title: Doesn’t the New Testament Show that Christianity Was Originally Unified?
author: BDEhrman
description: Questions whether the New Testament proves Christianity began as a unified movement.

title: How Diverse Was Early Christianity?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the diversity of early Christianity as background for orthodox textual changes.
searchSummary: Defends Walter Bauer's broad claim that early Christianity comprised many competing forms rather than one dominant orthodoxy with marginal heresies. Newly found biblical manuscripts cannot identify their users because proto-orthodox, Marcionite, and Gnostic Christians shared many eventual New Testament books. By contrast, newly recovered noncanonical works are overwhelmingly associated with views later condemned, including the Nag Hammadi texts and the Gospels of Mary and Judas. Their Egyptian preservation does not confine their origins or circulation to Egypt.

title: Evaluating the Views of Walter Bauer
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates Walter Bauer's view of orthodoxy and heresy in early Christianity.

title: A Radically Different View of Orthodoxy and Heresy
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Walter Bauer's radically different account of orthodoxy and heresy.

title: What Are Orthodoxy and Heresy?
author: BDEhrman
description: Defines orthodoxy and heresy as historical categories for studying early Christianity.

title: What is An Orthodox Corruption of Scripture?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains what is meant by an orthodox corruption of Scripture.

title: Guest Post by Brice Jones on the Reliability of the Early Manuscripts
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares Brice Jones's guest post on the reliability of early New Testament manuscripts.
searchSummary: Guest contributor Brice Jones challenges Craig Evans's claim that New Testament autographs may have remained available for copying into the second or third centuries and thereby stabilized the text. Jones argues that Evans extrapolates improperly from limited evidence about the longevity of some ancient library books. Because the autographs are lost and early manuscript evidence is sparse and diverse, their continued use and stabilizing influence remain unsupported speculation.

title: Guest Post – Brent Nongbri on Manuscript Discoveries
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares Brent Nongbri's guest post on manuscript discoveries.
searchSummary: Explains why modern archaeology rarely repeats Grenfell and Hunt's rapid excavation of the Oxyrhynchus rubbish mounds. Their search recovered vast numbers of papyri but sacrificed contextual records and overlooked other artifacts, whereas contemporary excavation proceeds slowly because digging irreversibly destroys archaeological layers. Nongbri shows how missing context still complicates interpretation, including a Romans fragment later linked to a flax merchant's archive. Egyptian rubbish heaps nevertheless continue to yield Christian books when excavated with modern methods.

title: Kickstarting a Debate
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses requests for a debate with mythicists over whether Jesus existed.
searchSummary: Explains Ehrman's reluctance to debate whether Jesus existed because specialists do not regard mythicism as a live scholarly dispute, and public debates can lend fringe claims undeserved credibility. He also avoids interlocutors who substitute hostility and mockery for intellectual exchange. Robert Price is an exception because he has relevant scholarly training and engages respectfully. Ehrman therefore agrees in principle to a funded debate, with his speaking fee going entirely to the charities supported by the blog.

title: Questions on the Discovery of the Nag Hammadi Library
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about the discovery of the Nag Hammadi Library.

title: Contradictory Stories and Historical Method
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses conflicting discovery stories for Nag Hammadi to discuss historical method.
searchSummary: Explains how contradictions should and should not affect historical judgment. Conflicting accounts cannot both be correct in the disputed detail, but that fact alone does not eliminate the possibility that one version or their common core is historical. Gospel disagreements about meals or the empty tomb and changing stories of the Nag Hammadi discovery therefore require additional evidence about plausibility and context. Contradictions invite skepticism, but demonstrating that an entire event was invented demands an independent historical case.

title: The Dead Sea Scrolls
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Dead Sea Scrolls in comparison with Nag Hammadi.
searchSummary: Introduces the Dead Sea Scrolls as a Jewish collection associated with the Essenes rather than with the Christian writings found at Nag Hammadi. The scrolls preserve early biblical manuscripts, commentaries, hymns, prophecies, and community rules that reveal strict purity, shared property, and imminent apocalyptic expectations at Qumran. Their importance lies in illuminating Hebrew Bible transmission and Judaism around Jesus' time, not in containing information about Jesus or his followers.

title: My Response To Mark Goodacre on the Discovery of the Nag Hammadi Library
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to Mark Goodacre's doubts about the traditional Nag Hammadi discovery story.
searchSummary: Defends the basic Nag Hammadi discovery account against Mark Goodacre's five objections while accepting that many details may have changed in retelling. Ehrman argues that an expanding jar, shifting participant counts, later inconsistencies, and skeptical colleagues demonstrate ordinary memory distortion rather than proving the event was invented. He questions whether Jean Doresse's leaner account had stronger evidence. The popular story may require correction at the level of specifics, but Ehrman finds insufficient reason to reject its central outline.

title: Mark Goodacre: Questioning the Discovery of the Nag Hammadi Library
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Mark Goodacre's critique of the traditional Nag Hammadi discovery story.
searchSummary: Challenges the familiar dramatic story of the Nag Hammadi library's discovery. Goodacre points to the jar's increasing size, changing numbers and identities of discoverers, skeptical collaborators, contradictions in later testimony, and the absence of recordings or transcripts from James Robinson's investigation. He favors Jean Doresse's earlier, less sensational report that unidentified peasants found manuscripts in a jar. The embellished account may owe more to repeated storytelling and leading fieldwork than to securely documented history.

title: The Contents of the Nag Hammadi Library
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys the contents of the Nag Hammadi Library and its relation to canon and Athanasius.
searchSummary: Describes the Nag Hammadi library's forty-six distinct Coptic works, including previously lost Gospels, revelations, theological reflections, and critiques of proto-orthodox Christianity. The fourth-century codices preserve much earlier Greek compositions representing diverse ancient Christian thought. Because they may have belonged to a nearby Pachomian monastery, their concealment could relate to Athanasius's 367 directive identifying the twenty-seven New Testament books and opposing heretical texts, though whether monks hid them to preserve valued writings remains uncertain.

title: The Discovery of the Nag Hammadi Library
author: BDEhrman
description: Tells the traditional story of the discovery of the Nag Hammadi Library.

title: What I Saw at St. Catherine’s Monastery
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts a visit to St. Catherine's Monastery and its connection to Codex Sinaiticus.

title: St. Catherine’s Monastery
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces St. Catherine's Monastery and its connection to Codex Sinaiticus.

title: Tischendorf and the Discovery of Codex Sinaiticus
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts Tischendorf's discovery of Codex Sinaiticus at St. Catherine's Monastery.

title: How Are Manuscripts Discovered
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how ancient manuscripts are discovered and why discoveries are often accidental.
searchSummary: Explains the principal ways ancient manuscripts have been discovered. Earlier scholars searched uncatalogued libraries and monasteries, while Grenfell and Hunt deliberately excavated Oxyrhynchus's rubbish mounds and recovered thousands of literary and documentary papyri. Such repositories are now less productive or rarely pursued, although uncatalogued items still appear. Most celebrated discoveries, including Nag Hammadi and the Dead Sea Scrolls, instead resulted from chance finds by local people rather than planned archaeological expeditions.

title: The Discovery of Lost Documents
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses the discovery of lost early Christian documents.
searchSummary: Explains why spectacular discoveries of hypothesized Christian texts such as Q or a lost Pauline letter are extremely unlikely. Modern finds more often yield additional manuscripts of known works or texts no scholar knew existed, although ancient references occasionally help identify discoveries such as the Gospels of Peter and Judas. The Letter to Diognetus, found unexpectedly in a reused medieval manuscript and later destroyed by fire, shows both how chance preserves lost literature and why earlier copies still matter.

title: Papias and the Eyewitnesses
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Papias's claims about eyewitnesses and their value for Gospel history.
searchSummary: Challenges the use of Papias as a direct link to eyewitnesses of Jesus. Papias says he questioned visitors who knew elders who reportedly knew the apostles, making his information fourth-hand at best rather than testimony from witnesses or their immediate associates. Eusebius rejected Irenaeus's claim that Papias knew John the son of Zebedee and regarded some of Papias's material as legendary, demonstrating how later Christians elevated weak chains of transmission to enhance an author's authority.

title: Lecture:  Jesus and the Historian
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a lecture on the historical problems involved in studying Jesus from the Gospels.
searchSummary: Introduces a recorded lecture on Jesus and the historian delivered at Dickinson College. The lecture addresses the problems posed by the surviving Gospels when historians try to evaluate evidence for Jesus' life and teachings. The brief post supplies the event, subject, and video rather than reproducing the lecture's reasoning in text. Its central purpose is to direct readers to a sustained presentation of how historical inquiry handles limited and problematic Gospel sources.

title: Wine in the Kingdom
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses a fantastic saying attributed to Jesus in Papias about wine in the kingdom.

title: A Fantastic Saying of Jesus in Papias
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines a fantastic saying of Jesus preserved through Papias.
searchSummary: Examines a saying preserved by Papias that portrays the future Kingdom of God as a renewed earth producing fantastically abundant food. Papias claimed the tradition passed from Jesus through John and Christian elders, but the account survives only through later writers. Ehrman explains why ancient and modern readers generally doubt its authenticity, regarding it more plausibly as a later imaginative expansion of apocalyptic hopes attributed to Jesus.

title: Other Accounts of the Death of Judas
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares New Testament and later accounts of Judas Iscariot's death.

title: My Trip to Turkey
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers a travel update from the beginning of a trip to Turkey.

title: The Death of Judas in the NT
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares the New Testament accounts of Judas Iscariot's death.
searchSummary: Compares Matthew's and Acts' contradictory accounts of Judas's death as background for Papias's third version. Both connect betrayal money, a Jerusalem field, Judas's death, and the name Field of Blood, but disagree over who bought the field, whether Judas hanged himself or burst open, and why the place received its name. Rather than forcing a harmonized sequence, the post treats both as legendary developments possibly rooted in a tradition that Judas died near a potter's field known for red soil.

title: The Lost Writings of Papias
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the lost writings of Papias and why scholars wish they survived.

title: Losing Religion in America
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses polling data on the decline of Christian identification in America.
searchSummary: Examines Pew data showing a sharp decline in American Christian identification and growth among the religiously unaffiliated. Ehrman questions evangelical claims that only nominal Christians leave, citing correspondence from formerly committed believers whose doubts arose from biblical problems, church behavior, suffering, or broader knowledge. He rejects blame that critics lead people astray and instead favors informed personal judgment. Remaining Christian, adopting another religion, or becoming nonreligious is acceptable if people think carefully, avoid harming others, and aid those in need.

title: The Nature of John’s Signs Source
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the proposed Signs Source behind John's Gospel.
searchSummary: Reconstructs the proposed Signs Source as a missionary document containing seven miracles intended to bring nonbelievers to faith in Jesus as God's Son. John 20:30-31 appears displaced after chapters without signs and may have served as the source's original conclusion. A Greek tense variant in “believe” may preserve the source's call to begin believing, while the Gospel's editor changed it to encourage existing believers to continue in faith.
topics: Signs in the Gospel of John

title: Some Evidence for a Signs Source in John
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents evidence that the Gospel of John may have used a written Signs Source.
searchSummary: Presents literary evidence that John's seven signs came from an earlier written source. Internal seams place Jesus in locations he has supposedly just entered, and the Gospel calls one healing his second sign even after mentioning many intervening signs. The simplest explanation is that the evangelist inserted an enumerated sequence of miracle stories into a longer narrative without resolving every conflict, although the existence and precise contents of this proposed source remain debated.
topics: Signs in the Gospel of John

title: Why Jesus Does Miracles
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Jesus performs miracles in relation to Synoptic and Johannine traditions.
secondaryKeywords: Signs in the Gospel of John

title: The Temptation Narrative Missing from John
author: BDEhrman
description: Notes the missing temptation narrative in John while discussing the proposed Signs Source.
searchSummary: Explains why John's Gospel omits the Synoptic temptation narrative. In Matthew and Luke, Jesus rejects Satan's invitation to perform a spectacular miracle that would prove his identity, consistent with the Synoptic refusal to provide signs. John takes the opposite approach: Jesus' miracles are public signs specifically intended to reveal him as God's Son and produce belief. A story condemning such self-revelation through miracles would therefore conflict with John's central portrayal of Jesus.
topics: Signs in the Gospel of John

title: Signs in the Gospel of John
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the signs in John's Gospel and the possibility of written sources behind them.
searchSummary: Contrasts Jesus' miracles in John with those in the Synoptic Gospels while introducing the proposed Signs Source. The Synoptics do not present miracles as proofs of Jesus' identity, whereas John calls seven extraordinary deeds “signs” meant to demonstrate that Jesus is the Messiah and Son of God. John 20:30-31 states this purpose directly. Scholars therefore propose that the evangelist drew these distinctive accounts from an earlier written collection, although the theory remains disputed.
topics: Signs in the Gospel of John

title: Back To the Discovery of Lost Early Christian Writings
author: BDEhrman
description: Returns to the topic of lost early Christian writings.

title: My Resentment at Moody Bible Institute
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on resentment and appreciation connected to Moody Bible Institute.
searchSummary: Explains Ehrman's lasting resentment toward three aspects of Moody Bible Institute: restrictive social rules that denied students a normal young adulthood, a narrow curriculum that displaced the liberal arts and sciences, and indoctrination that supplied approved answers instead of teaching independent thought. Although he values the biblical knowledge and discipline he gained, he regrets spending formative years without broader education and finds the suppression of critical inquiry especially damaging because it tied intellectual conformity to happiness and eternal salvation.

title: Authors Who “Just Want to Sell Books”
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to the criticism that authors only want to sell books.

title: How I Moved into Trade Publishing
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how a scholarly career moved into trade publishing for general readers.
searchSummary: Explains how Ehrman reluctantly entered trade publishing after an editor repeatedly urged him to write about the historical Jesus. Scholars had not explained to general readers why the dominant academic view treated Jesus as an apocalyptic prophet, while popular books often promoted minority reconstructions. Recognizing a genuine public need, Ehrman presented the prevailing interpretation and its evidence in Jesus: Apocalyptic Prophet of the New Millennium, discovering that accessible scholarship could serve readers without replacing his academic work.

title: On Writing for A College Audience
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses writing textbooks for college students and criticism from former Moody classmates.

title: How the Bible Explains Suffering – Video
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a video lecture on how the Bible explains suffering.
searchSummary: Presents a recording of Ehrman's 2008 University of California, Berkeley lecture, "God's Problem and Human Solutions: How the Bible Explains Suffering." Delivered for the Foerster Lectures on the Immortality of the Soul, the talk addresses suffering rather than immortality directly and examines biblical efforts to explain why human beings experience pain. Late-antiquity historian Susanna Elm introduces Ehrman, whose lecture connects the theological problem to the broader concerns of the series.

title: Writing to Become Famous?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on writing, public recognition, and criticism from former classmates.
searchSummary: Rejects the claim that Ehrman began publishing to become famous and traces his unplanned move beyond technical textual criticism. His original ambition was recognition among New Testament manuscript specialists, and he repeatedly declined Oxford's invitation to write a historically oriented textbook. The chance to improve how undergraduates encountered the New Testament eventually persuaded him; translating scholarship for nineteen-year-olds then opened a career path he had neither anticipated nor pursued for personal celebrity.

title: The Threat of Judgment
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines evangelical claims about final judgment and eternal punishment in response to former Moody classmates.

title: Education at Moody
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the education received at Moody Bible Institute.
searchSummary: Evaluates Moody Bible Institute's educational emphasis on memorizing information and defending established evangelical truth rather than questioning assumptions or forming independent conclusions. Ehrman excelled at mastering biblical material and voluntarily memorized entire New Testament books, believing mental capacity expanded through exercise. He now sees that approach as seriously incomplete, yet credits its intense intellectual training and detailed scriptural knowledge with developing his mind and making his later career as a biblical scholar possible, leaving him ambivalent rather than wholly dismissive.

title: My Moody Experience
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues autobiographical reflections on Moody Bible Institute and fundamentalist formation.
searchSummary: Describes Ehrman's intense academic life at Moody Bible Institute, where Bible and theology replaced a liberal-arts curriculum and required ministry work included evangelism, hospital visits, radio counseling, and youth pastoring. A first-semester course on John inspired his decision at seventeen to become a New Testament professor. His eventual ambition was to earn respected credentials and serve as an evangelical scholar in a secular university, a missionary vision that directed his educational choices even though his beliefs later changed.

title: My Fundamentalist Beginning
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a fundamentalist beginning and ambivalence about Moody Bible Institute.
searchSummary: Traces Ehrman's fundamentalist beginning from an Episcopal childhood through a born-again conversion at fifteen and enrollment at Moody Bible Institute at seventeen. A charismatic Youth for Christ leader convinced him that church participation did not make him a real Christian, awakened his interest in Scripture, and urged a committed believer to reject secular college. Ehrman's tendency to pursue interests completely led him away from Kansas University, debate, and conventional young adulthood into an educational choice that permanently reshaped his life.

title: Year Three on the Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Updates readers on the blog's third year and charitable fundraising.
searchSummary: Reviews the blog after its third year, when it raised $78,000 for charity compared with $37,000 and $58,000 in its first two years. Bart hopes to approach $100,000 in year four and describes the membership's value: frequent scholarly posts, questions, comments, and broad coverage of early Christianity. He asks readers to promote the blog, recommend technical and editorial improvements, suggest topics, give subscriptions, and donate, while thanking members and assistant Steve Ray.

title: What Can We Know about the Life of Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers a question about what historians can know about Jesus' life.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: Truth and History
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on truth, history, and memory in relation to the historical Jesus.
searchSummary: Distinguishes historical accuracy from other kinds of truth conveyed by stories. The invented tale of George Washington and the cherry tree communicates ideals about honesty despite never happening, just as biblical narratives may express moral, religious, or literary meaning when their events are historically doubtful. Historians should still determine what occurred, but a Gospel story's value and power need not depend entirely on factual correspondence with the past.

title: Another Jewish Miracle Worker
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes a Jewish miracle worker known through eyewitness reports.
searchSummary: Compares Gospel traditions with stories about the Baal Shem Tov, an eighteenth-century Jewish teacher credited with healing, exorcism, heavenly journeys, and raising the dead. His disciples reshaped his teachings, while a collection written fifty-four years after his death claimed accurate eyewitness sources for hundreds of miraculous tales. Because such assurances do not make those stories credible, their parallel raises the same question for the Gospels: even traditions ultimately attributed to eyewitnesses need not preserve accurate memories or historical events.

title: Steps Toward Publishing the (a) Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes steps toward completing and publishing Jesus Before the Gospels.
searchSummary: Describes the final drafting and review stages for Jesus Before the Gospels. After extensive interdisciplinary research and outlining, Ehrman writes chapters rapidly, revises repeatedly on screen, performs a separate hard-copy edit, and circulates the manuscript to specialists and paying blog readers for substantive and stylistic feedback. He then incorporates comments, obtains further review from his literary agent and publisher's editor, and continues revising until the work cannot be improved before the year-long production process begins.

title: Misquoting Jesus Interview on WPSU
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares an interview about Misquoting Jesus and changes in the Bible.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's Pennsylvania Inside Out interview about Misquoting Jesus. He explains how accidental mistakes and intentional alterations by early scribes shaped the modern text of the Bible and how recognizing this manuscript history changed his own understanding of Scripture. The conversation also addresses Dan Brown's The Da Vinci Code, then a prominent public controversy, connecting the book's popular claims with broader questions about early Christianity, textual transmission, and what surviving copies can reveal about the New Testament.

title: York Symposium on Early Christian Apocrypha
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a symposium on early Christian apocrypha.
searchSummary: Announces a scholarly symposium on ancient and modern Christian apocrypha organized around fakes, forgeries, and fictional religious writings. Sessions address ancient Gospel fragments, apostolic pseudepigraphy, modern lost-gospel claims, cultural contexts, and the controversial Gospel of Jesus' Wife, with a keynote on apocryphal forgery. The event aims to broaden study beyond antiquity, connect specialists across related fields, and give students and the public more reliable information than popular films, novels, and fringe scholarship provide.

title: My Final Exam for NT
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a final exam for an Introduction to the New Testament course.
searchSummary: Reproduces a New Testament final examination requiring concise identifications and two substantial essays. The terms assess historical context, biblical interpretation, textual criticism, and early Christian literature. Essay choices ask students to evaluate a Gospel's historical accuracy, argue whether Jesus was an apocalyptic prophet, compare early Christian views of Judaism, or reconstruct the founding and problems of an undisputed Pauline community. The format rewards specific evidence, clear organization, and broad mastery of the course.

title: Help!  My Views of Memory
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks readers for feedback on a draft conclusion about memory.
searchSummary: Defends studying Gospel memories for their meaning and influence as well as their historical accuracy. Although the Gospels contain differing and distorted recollections shaped by early Christian communities, they remain powerful works of literature that reveal why those communities remembered Jesus as they did. The remembered Jesus, more than a historically reconstructed figure known to relatively few, transformed Christianity and Western history; memory therefore deserves analysis both as evidence and as a force in human life.

title: The Community Behind the Gospel of John:  Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues discussion of the community behind the Gospel of John.
searchSummary: Reconstructs a later stage in the Johannine community after its exclusion from the synagogue. Rejection encouraged an oppositional worldview of truth versus error, light versus darkness, and Jesus' followers versus “the Jews.” The community's understanding of Jesus also became more exalted: the human Messiah came to be viewed as the heavenly revealer, then as God's preexistent Word made flesh. These experiences shaped John's stories, discourses, and declarations of Jesus' unity with the Father.

title: The Community Behind the Gospel of John
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the community behind the Gospel of John as part of a memory-focused book project.
searchSummary: Reconstructs the first two stages of the community behind John to show how its circumstances shaped memories of Jesus. An early Aramaic-speaking Jewish group remained within the synagogue, proclaimed Jesus as the human Messiah, and used stories and signs to persuade other Jews. Continued missionary activity and rejection eventually led to expulsion. John 9's reference to believers being put out of the synagogue appears to project that later communal experience back into a story about Jesus.

title: More on Collective Memory
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains collective memory as a category for thinking about early recollections of Jesus.
searchSummary: Explains Maurice Halbwachs's theory that all individual recollection is reconstructed within social frameworks shaped by families, communities, nations, and present concerns. Religious groups likewise rebuild their past through surviving texts, rituals, and traditions to meet current beliefs and needs. Later scholars such as Barry Schwartz retain the insight while arguing that actual past events also constrain memory, making comparison between history and group recollection especially useful for studying figures such as Jesus.

title: My Memory Book, Chapter 6 on “Collective Memory”
author: BDEhrman
description: Outlines a chapter on collective memory in Jesus Before the Gospels.
searchSummary: Introduces collective memory as the way social groups construct and preserve a past that members may not have personally experienced. Contrasting Northern and Southern memories of the Civil War illustrates how families, communities, identities, and media shape competing versions of history. Rather than only labeling such memories accurate or false, memory-history examines what a group's recollection reveals about its present beliefs and allegiances, a method applied to early Christian communities' differing memories of Jesus.

title: My Memory Book:  False Memories and the Life of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains false memories in relation to Jesus traditions and the Gospel of John.
searchSummary: Uses Jesus' conversation with Nicodemus to illustrate a historically false memory preserved in John. The dialogue depends on the Greek word anothen meaning both “again” and “from above”: Nicodemus hears one meaning while Jesus intends the other. No Aramaic word supports the same misunderstanding, yet Jesus and Nicodemus would have spoken Aramaic. The exchange therefore could not have occurred as narrated and was likely created by John or an earlier Greek-speaking storyteller.

title: BBC Clip on “The Lost Gospels”
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a BBC clip on lost Gospels, Nag Hammadi, and the Gospel of Thomas.
searchSummary: Introduces a BBC documentary segment filmed near Nag Hammadi and in Cairo about lost Gospels, especially the Gospel of Thomas. Ehrman revises the categorical claim he made in the older clip that Thomas is Gnostic: its text lacks characteristic Gnostic mythology, although ancient readers could interpret it through a Gnostic framework and its manuscript appears with clearly Gnostic works. He therefore distinguishes how a text was read and transmitted from what its author may originally have intended.

title: On Being Controversial
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on why work on Jesus and early Christianity is often called controversial.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman does not seek controversy even though the public often treats his scholarship as provocative. Most positions in his popular books reflect widely held critical conclusions, and unchanged textbook language acquired a supposedly offensive tone only after his public reputation changed. He attributes the label to stating openly what scholars often reserve for colleagues and to presenting unfamiliar research vividly, refusing to make accurate scholarship dull merely because accessible, forceful explanation can unsettle readers.

title: “The Same” Traditions in Oral Cultures
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how oral cultures can treat varied performances as the same tradition.

title: Differences Between Oral and Written Cultures
author: BDEhrman
description: Contrasts oral and written cultures in relation to false memories and Jesus traditions.
searchSummary: Challenges the common claim that people in oral cultures possessed inherently better memories and preserved cherished traditions unchanged. Although oral societies must retain practical knowledge without written references, their brains are not fundamentally different, and information that is forgotten or altered in retelling cannot be recovered from an earlier record. This vulnerability makes it necessary to investigate rather than assume how oral cultures actually transmitted traditions about Jesus.

title: My Memory Book, Chapter 4 Again: The Death of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes a book chapter on memory, the death of Jesus, and Gospel traditions.
searchSummary: Distinguishes historically credible “gist” memories of Jesus' final week from questionable narrative details. Multiple accounts with changing patterns can expose storytellers' interests, as Pilate's increasing innocence shifts blame toward Jews amid later Christian-Jewish conflict; independently implausible episodes provide another test. These methods support a broad outline of Jesus entering Jerusalem, confronting authorities, facing Pilate, and being crucified while questioning the triumphal entry, temple cleansing, armed arrest, Barabbas, and torn curtain as narrated.

title: What Is A Memory?
author: BDEhrman
description: Defines memory and responds to objections about what counts as a memory.
searchSummary: Defines memory more broadly than personal recollection. Psychologists distinguish procedural memory for skills, episodic memory for experienced events, and semantic memory for learned facts; both episodic and semantic memories can be false. Sociologists additionally study collective memory, in which social groups construct differing accounts of a shared past. Traditions about what Jesus said and did can therefore be analyzed as true or false semantic and collective memories even when those remembering did not witness him.

title: Ramblings on Charity and Religion
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on charity, religion, and moral responsibility.

title: Can A Made-Up Story Be A False Memory?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how a made-up Gospel story can still function as a false memory.
searchSummary: Explains why an invented Gospel story can still become a false memory of Jesus. Whether Luke inherited or created the historically implausible census journey that places Jesus' birth in Bethlehem cannot be known, but once circulated it shaped how communities remembered the event. The distinction between invention and recollection does not change its later function as memory; broad “gist” traditions may preserve history more reliably than such narrative details.

title: My Memory Book, Ch. 4a
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a chapter on false memories and the psychology of memory.
searchSummary: Surveys psychological research showing that memory is reconstructive rather than a complete recording retrieved intact. Ebbinghaus charted rapid initial forgetting, while Bartlett demonstrated how successive reproductions shorten stories, lose details, and create clearer but less accurate connections as people fill gaps from other knowledge. Memory usually preserves the gist reasonably well, yet these mechanisms explain how oral retellings among early Christians could lose, alter, or invent details about Jesus' death.

title: My Memory Book, ch. 3
author: BDEhrman
description: Outlines a chapter on eyewitness testimony and memory in Jesus Before the Gospels.
searchSummary: Challenges the claim that eyewitness testimony guarantees Gospel reliability. Psychological studies show that imagination can implant vivid memories, and allegedly eyewitness-based stories about the Baal Shem Tov include spectacular miracles, while the canonical Gospels circulated anonymously before receiving apostolic names in the second century. Because the evangelists report stories heard or read from others rather than their own experiences, their narratives depend on transmitted memories whose historical accuracy still requires evaluation.

title: My Memory Book, chs. 1-2
author: BDEhrman
description: Outlines the first chapters of Jesus Before the Gospels on memory and oral tradition.
searchSummary: Outlines the first two chapters of Jesus Before the Gospels. Apocryphal stories and changing modern portraits show how communities can remember Jesus and related figures through vivid but historically false traditions, while critical scholars since Reimarus and the form critics have identified invention within canonical accounts as well. Against theories of verbatim rabbinic memorization or tightly controlled transmission, the book envisions stories changing as Christians retold them across diverse communities and religious settings for decades.

title: How I’m Writing This Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the process of writing Jesus Before the Gospels from a detailed outline.
searchSummary: Compares two fundamentally different writing processes through Ehrman and his wife, Sarah. Her nonlinear, synthetic thinking develops ideas during composition, whereas his analytical mind requires a complete argument and detailed chapter outlines before drafting. Ehrman rereads all research notes, embeds evidence and quotations into a forty-two-page plan for Jesus Before the Gospels, then writes each chapter during a protected day of concentrated work, allowing limited adjustments without abandoning the structure that makes rapid composition possible.

title: Sketch of My Memory Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Sketches the planned book on memory, oral tradition, and Jesus traditions.
searchSummary: Introduces Jesus Before the Gospels as a study of how early Christians remembered Jesus before written accounts existed. It first investigates how individual, eyewitness, oral, and collective memory could produce distorted or invented traditions without deliberate deceit. It then uses the contrasting memories preserved in Mark, John, and Thomas to examine what different communities believed about Jesus and why he mattered, drawing on psychology, legal research, anthropology, sociology, and historical study.

title: Different Kinds of Memory
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces different kinds of memory and their relevance for eyewitness claims about Jesus.
searchSummary: Explains that memory reconstructs experiences from scattered traces rather than replaying stored mental photographs, so missing material may be filled incorrectly or entire events falsely recalled. This applies not only to personal memories but also to collective memories through which groups preserve and interpret a past they did not experience. Comparing divergent group recollections can test accuracy and reveal present values, making psychological, sociological, and oral-culture research relevant to early Christian memories of Jesus.

title: My Original Interest in Memory
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how work on the Gospel of Peter led to an interest in memory.
searchSummary: Describes the personal and scholarly questions that led Ehrman to study memory directly.
