His own poor episodic recall prompted questions about how eyewitnesses, hearers, and successive storytellers could forget or alter traditions about Jesus before the Gospels were written. Rather than begin with New Testament scholarship, he first examined cognitive psychology, false and recovered memory, eyewitness research, and DNA exonerations showing that confident testimony often convicted innocent people, then planned to evaluate biblical scholars' use of that evidence.

title: Why I Shifted My Research Plans
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the shift from a Gospel of Peter commentary to research on memory and Jesus traditions.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman abandoned a contracted technical commentary on the Gospel of Peter and other Greek Gospel fragments. Detailed verse-by-verse source analysis would have required years of narrow work that no longer matched his broader scholarly interests. He instead chose to study memory and the oral traditions about Jesus, pursuing questions about how stories circulated before the Gospels that offered greater intellectual engagement than returning to the highly technical scholarship of his earlier career.

title: My New Project on Memory
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a new project on memory and the oral traditions about Jesus.
searchSummary: Introduces the research project that became Jesus Before the Gospels, a general-audience study of how early Christians remembered Jesus during the decades before written Gospels. The project emerged after Ehrman moved away from long-standing work in textual criticism and forgery and began, then abandoned, a scholarly commentary on surviving Greek Gospel fragments. Having completed extensive research on memory, he planned a book focused on the transmission and transformation of Jesus traditions rather than another technical textual study.

title: Jesus, Matthew, and the Law
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Matthew and Paul on whether followers of Jesus should observe the Jewish law.
searchSummary: Examines whether Matthew's command to observe Jewish law truly conflicts with Paul's rejection of imposing Torah on gentiles. Matthew may address Jewish followers and emphasizes ethical commandments rather than circumcision, food laws, or Sabbath observance, while also expecting gentiles to enter God's kingdom. Yet Jesus says all the law remains binding and presents his movement as proper Judaism rather than a separate religion. Matthew never resolves whether gentile converts must adopt specifically Jewish practices, leaving the comparison with Paul ambiguous.

title: Is Paul at Odds with Matthew?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Paul's view of the Law conflicts with Matthew's Gospel.
searchSummary: Argues that Matthew and Paul probably disagree about whether followers of Jesus must observe Jewish law. Both see Jesus' death and resurrection as salvific, but Paul insists that gentiles must not become Jewish or rely on Torah, whereas Matthew's Jesus says no command will pass away and followers must practice the Law more rigorously than scribes and Pharisees. Matthew presents these teachings as current guidance, not historical recollection, and gives no indication that complete observance is impossible or temporary.

title: Paul’s Christian Enemies:  Galatians
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Paul's Christian opponents in Galatia and their insistence on circumcision and the Law.
searchSummary: Reconstructs the position of Paul's opponents in Galatia, who taught pagan converts that following the Jewish messiah required becoming Jewish and observing Torah. They likely appealed to circumcision as God's eternal covenant and accused Paul of corrupting the apostles' original gospel. Paul answered that faith in Christ, not Jewish law, brought salvation, although he still expected believers to live morally; only his side of the dispute survives.

title: Lost Letters of Paul’s Opponents
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the lost letters of Paul's opponents would be valuable for understanding early Christianity.

title: Trip to Turkey?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a lecture trip to Turkey focused partly on Paul.

title: About the Blog: Charities and Improvements
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the blog's charitable commitments and recent improvements.
searchSummary: Identifies the four charities supported by the blog and announces usability improvements prompted by reader feedback. Membership fees and donations pass through the Bart Ehrman Foundation to Urban Ministries of Durham, the regional Food Bank, CARE, and Doctors Without Borders, while Bart pays operating costs. The site now provides a prominent search box, marks previously visited posts, and lets members rate posts, helping readers navigate the archive and helping Bart understand which subjects they value.

title: Q and the Passion Narrative
author: BDEhrman
description: Considers whether the lost Q source included a passion narrative.

title: Did Matthew Copy Luke or Luke Matthew?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why scholars ask whether Matthew copied Luke or Luke copied Matthew.
searchSummary: Explains why the order of shared Gospel material supports both Markan priority and the existence of Q. Matthew and Luke usually preserve the same sequence when following stories also found in Mark, but place their shared non-Markan sayings in different locations. This pattern is difficult to explain if either copied the other, but makes sense if both independently inserted material from a separate sayings source into Mark's narrative framework.

title: Q and The Gospel of Thomas
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Q with the Gospel of Thomas as collections of Jesus' sayings.

title: Evidence that the Synoptics Are Copying (one another? other sources?)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the evidence that Matthew, Mark, and Luke have a literary relationship.
searchSummary: Uses independent classroom eyewitness accounts to demonstrate why long verbatim agreements among Matthew, Mark, and Luke imply copying or common written sources. Their differences show that authors also altered what they borrowed. Mark was probably first because it is shorter overall yet usually tells shared episodes at greater length, making condensation from Matthew unlikely. The four-source explanation has Matthew and Luke use Mark, Q, and their separate special traditions M and L to produce their overlapping but distinct narratives.

title: The Lost Q Source
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the lost Q source as a desired discovery from early Christianity.

title: Quickly on the Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Thanks readers for feedback on the blog.

title: Taking the Temperature of the Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks readers for feedback on the blog's strengths and weaknesses.

title: Paul’s “Exceptional” Letter to the Romans
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Romans is only a partial exception to Paul's occasional letters.

title: Why I Wish We Had More of Paul’s Letters
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why additional lost letters of Paul would be valuable.

title: Lost Christian Writings: The Letters of Paul
author: BDEhrman
description: Begins a discussion of lost early Christian writings with Paul's letters.

title: Is “Jehovah” in the Bible?
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers whether Jehovah belongs in the Bible or the New Testament.
searchSummary: Explains why Jehovah is not the original biblical name of God. Ancient Hebrew wrote the sacred four consonants YHWH without vowels, probably pronounced Yahweh; later scribes supplied the vowel points of Adonai to remind readers to say Lord instead. Combining those consonants and substitute vowels through European spelling conventions produced Jehovah. Greek translations and the New Testament use kurios, meaning Lord, so Ehrman argues that inserting the manufactured English form Jehovah is unjustified in either Testament.

title: A Source for the Birth Narratives in Matthew and Luke?
author: BDEhrman
description: Considers whether Matthew and Luke used a common source for their birth narratives.
searchSummary: Argues that Matthew's and Luke's infancy narratives developed independently rather than through direct copying or a common written source. Their stories lack verbal overlap and disagree extensively, though both name Mary and Joseph and place a virginal birth in Bethlehem. The post treats the parents' names as historical traditions and the virgin birth and Bethlehem as widely circulating claims shaped by interpretations of Isaiah and Micah as prophecies about the Messiah.

title: My Debate with Dan Wallace: Is the Original NT Lost?
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a debate with Dan Wallace on whether the original New Testament text is lost.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's 2012 debate with New Testament scholar Dan Wallace over whether the original wording of the New Testament can be recovered. Ehrman emphasizes the scarcity of very early manuscripts and the resulting uncertainty in some passages, while Wallace stresses the abundance of manuscript evidence and confidence in the reconstructed text. The post also recalls Wallace's announcement of an unpublished purported first-century fragment of Mark.

title: Bethlehem and Nazareth in Luke: Where Was Jesus Really Born?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Luke's account of Bethlehem and Nazareth in the story of Jesus' birth.
searchSummary: Examines Luke's explanation for how Jesus, known from Nazareth, could be born in Bethlehem. The worldwide ancestral census is historically implausible and chronologically conflicts with the reigns of Herod and Quirinius, while Luke's prompt return to Nazareth contradicts Matthew's flight to Egypt. The post concludes that both Gospels created different Bethlehem stories to fulfill Micah 5:2 and that Jesus was most likely born in Nazareth.

title: Bethlehem and Nazareth in Matthew
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Matthew's account of Bethlehem and Nazareth in the story of Jesus' birth.
searchSummary: Argues that Matthew's Bethlehem birth story is historically implausible and was designed to reconcile Jesus' known Nazareth origin with messianic expectations. Matthew assumes that Joseph and Mary live in Bethlehem, where the Magi find Jesus in a house long after his birth; the family then flees to Egypt and later relocates to Nazareth because returning home is unsafe. The guiding star and unattested massacre create further problems, and Matthew's account conflicts with Luke's different explanation.

title: Was Jesus From Nazareth?
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers whether Jesus was from Nazareth or Bethlehem.

title: More on the Name “Nazareth”
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to questions about the name Nazareth and mythicist claims.
searchSummary: Refutes attempts to derive Nazareth from titles such as “branch,” “Nazarene,” or “Nazirite” and thereby deny the town's existence. Claims that Mark 1:9 was interpolated lack manuscript evidence, while linguistic proposals by Frank Zindler and G. A. Wells offer neither a plausible path nor evidence for inventing a nonexistent hometown. Multiple independent Gospel traditions locate Jesus in Nazareth, and archaeology confirms that a Jewish settlement occupied the site in his period, making speculative wordplay unnecessary.

title: Finally!  How To Understand the Symbols of Revelation
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how to interpret symbols in the book of Revelation.
searchSummary: Explains that Revelation's symbols convey mysterious heavenly realities rather than hiding criticism from Roman officials. Its imagery should not be converted into literal predictions about the modern world. Hal Lindsey's attack-helicopter reading of chapter 9 selects visual similarities but ignores that the locusts cannot harm plants or kill people and only torture victims for five months. Such omissions show the weakness of futuristic interpretation. Historical context instead reveals a metaphorical promise of God's ultimate sovereignty over first-century suffering and evil.

title: The Book of Revelation as an Apocalypse
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Revelation functions as an apocalypse.
searchSummary: Shows how Revelation exemplifies ancient apocalyptic literature through an angel-mediated heavenly vision, mysterious symbols, repeated catastrophes, and hope amid oppression. Its disasters intensify for literary effect rather than forming a linear chronology. The narrative moves from present suffering to God's triumph, promising a world without exploitation, violence, disease, or death. Because fulfillment is repeatedly said to be near, the book encourages persecuted Christians to remain faithful while warning defectors of judgment. Its central message is God's hidden but ultimate sovereignty.

title: The Book of Revelation in Historical Context
author: BDEhrman
description: Places Revelation within its historical context.
searchSummary: Places Revelation in its authorship, date, and social setting. Its prophet John was not Jesus' disciple or the Gospel's author: their theology and Greek differ, and Revelation does not present John as an apostle. Some material may come from the 60s CE under Nero, while the work likely dates around 95 under Domitian. Addressing churches in Asia Minor facing persecution, false teaching, hardship, and declining commitment, John promises that God will soon destroy oppressive Roman power and vindicate his people.

title: On Debating a Fundamentalist
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to criticism from Kyle Butt after a debate on suffering.
searchSummary: Responds to fundamentalist apologist Kyle Butt's accusation that Ehrman dishonestly seeks to destroy Christian faith. Ehrman rejects the claim that he wants to convert readers to agnosticism or is responsible for thousands abandoning belief. His goal is to encourage informed thought, not impose a religious or nonreligious conclusion. He contrasts that aim with apologetics focused on securing doctrinal agreement and argues that people of any worldview are welcome so long as they reject rigid fundamentalism and examine evidence thoughtfully.

title: The Book of Revelation and the Apocalypse Genre
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Revelation as part of the ancient apocalypse genre.
searchSummary: Defines recurring features of ancient Jewish and Christian apocalypses. Most use famous pseudonyms to authorize heavenly revelations and make accurate retrospective prophecies, as Daniel does. Their bizarre visions require angelic interpretation, while repeated catastrophes create a symbolic spiral rather than a literal timeline. Despite escalating suffering, these works move toward God's triumph over evil. Their primary purpose is motivational: they encourage distressed readers to remain faithful and hopeful because God controls history and will ultimately vindicate and reward them.

title: Apocalypticism and Apocalypses
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces apocalypticism and apocalypses as context for Revelation.

title: 666: The Number of the Beast
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains 666 through ancient numerology and the number of the beast.
searchSummary: Identifies Revelation's beast through gematria, the practice of calculating names from the numerical values of letters. The beast symbolizes the Roman Empire and its rulers rather than a modern dictator. Caesar Neron written in Hebrew totals 666; the spelling Nero omits a letter worth fifty and totals 616, explaining the variant in some manuscripts. The healed wound may evoke beliefs that the persecuting emperor Nero would return from death. Revelation promises God's defeat of Rome and reward for faithful Christians.

title: Symbolism in the Book of Revelation
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains symbolism in Revelation, especially the number of the beast.
searchSummary: Places Revelation within the ancient apocalypse genre and interprets its imagery from the first-century author's world. The book assures suffering Christians that God will soon defeat present evil and establish a world without misery. In chapter 17, the lavish prostitute Babylon sits on a Satanic beast with seven heads, identified as mountains and as the city ruling earthly kings. These clues point to seven-hilled Rome, whose wealth came through exploitation and whose authorities persecuted Christians, making it Revelation's principal enemy.

title: Creative Uses of Numbers in Scripture
author: BDEhrman
description: Shows how ancient writers used numbers creatively in scriptural interpretation.
searchSummary: Explores ancient numerology through the Epistle of Barnabas's interpretation of Abraham's 318 servants. Because Greek letters also represented numbers, Barnabas reads 318 as a tau shaped like a cross followed by the first two letters of Jesus' name. This calculation supports the work's anti-Jewish claim that biblical commands such as circumcision were always symbolic references to Christ, which Jews misunderstood while Christians alone recognized the Hebrew Bible's intended meaning.

title: Debates For A Price
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses a possible paid debate with Robert Price over mythicism.
searchSummary: Explains the circumstances under which Ehrman would debate mythicist Robert Price and why he charges a substantial speaking fee. Price is unusual among mythicists because he has relevant New Testament credentials, a substantial publication record, and a respectful demeanor, making serious engagement possible despite their disagreement about Jesus' existence. Ehrman's fees also limit travel demands and go entirely to charities addressing hunger and homelessness, so a successfully funded debate would serve a charitable purpose rather than personal profit.

title: Three Murders in Chapel Hill
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the murder of three Muslim students in Chapel Hill.
searchSummary: Responds to the murder of three Muslim students in Chapel Hill by connecting religious intolerance with Ehrman's teaching about early Christian diversity. Recognizing that Christianity has always contained competing beliefs can weaken claims that one's inherited position alone deserves authority and encourage empathy across religious and cultural differences. Rather than answer hatred, prejudice, and violence with retaliation, Ehrman urges truthful investigation, informed understanding, forgiveness, care, and peaceful resistance while acknowledging the community's immediate grief.

title: More on Greek Numerals
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Greek numerals and how letters could function as numbers.

title: How To Make Greek Numbers (!)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Greek letters were used as numerals.

title: My Non-Disclosure Agreement and the Gospel of Judas
author: BDEhrman
description: Resumes the story of a non-disclosure agreement connected to the Gospel of Judas.

title: False Rumors (or lies?) About My Teaching
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to false rumors about teaching and classroom practice.
searchSummary: Refutes a false report that Ehrman tells Christian students they are foolish or destined to fail. He explains that his historical and literary courses neither promote nor attack religious belief, and that students of every outlook receive equal treatment. His aim is to help students examine reasons and evidence, understand standard critical scholarship, and become more knowledgeable and thoughtful regardless of whether their personal beliefs change.

title: My UNC Seminar Tomorrow
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces an all-day UNC seminar on non-canonical Gospels.
searchSummary: Introduces an all-day UNC public humanities seminar in which Ehrman presents four lectures on noncanonical Gospels to an adult audience. The program combines faculty scholarship, accessible teaching, and extensive questions outside the regular university curriculum, using texts about Jesus' infancy, Thomas's sayings, Peter's resurrection narrative, and traditions that increasingly exonerate Pilate. Ehrman connects the seminar to his scholarly and popular editions, showing how public engagement translates specialized research for informed nonacademic learners.

title: The Gospel of Judas: Discovery, Restoration, and (Non-)Disclosure
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues the story of the Gospel of Judas discovery, restoration, and non-disclosure agreement.

title: How I First Learned that the Gospel of Judas Had Been Discovered
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how news of the Gospel of Judas discovery first arrived.

title: Finding Out about the Gospel of Judas
author: BDEhrman
description: Tells how involvement with the Gospel of Judas began.

title: Non-Disclosure Agreements and the Gospel of Judas Iscariot
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the Gospel of Judas to discuss non-disclosure agreements and scholarly access.

title: GUEST POST!  Dr. Brent Nongbri on How We Date Manuscripts
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares Brent Nongbri's explanation of how manuscripts are dated.
searchSummary: Presents Brent Nongbri's explanation of why ancient manuscripts cannot normally be dated to a precise decade. Paleographic comparison is limited by scarce dated examples, long scribal careers, inherited writing styles, and scribes' ability to use different hands, while radiocarbon testing produces broad probability ranges. Documents found in the same cartonnage supply only an earliest possible date. These limitations make claims that the alleged Mark fragment was definitely written before 90 CE methodologically implausible without exceptional evidence.

title: Another (Final!) Insight into that Mummy Mask and Papyrus
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses mummy masks, papyri, and claims about a first-century fragment of Mark.
searchSummary: Reposts Candida Moss and Joel Baden's analysis of the unpublished Mark fragment allegedly recovered from mummy cartonnage. They identify unanswered questions about its text, handwriting, material tests, ownership, provenance, and expert examination, emphasizing that claims cannot be assessed without publication. The article also challenges the destruction of Egyptian funerary artifacts, asks who decides which masks lack value, and notes that less destructive recovery methods exist. Until evidence appears, the principal story is cultural loss in pursuit of Christian texts.

title: Why I’d Be Thrilled If A First-Century Manuscript Appeared
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why a genuine first-century New Testament manuscript would be exciting but difficult to prove.
searchSummary: Clarifies why Ehrman would be thrilled by a genuine first-century fragment of Mark despite doubting that it would transform scholarship. Reports suggested that even prominent advocates had not examined the papyrus and that its precise dating rested on rumor. If an authentic copy from around 100 appeared, however, it would provide a rare, early physical piece of the manuscript record and encourage hope for further discoveries, even if it merely confirmed what textual scholars already infer about Mark's transmission.

title: Talks at the Smithsonian, March 21
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces Smithsonian talks on Jesus and early Christianity.
searchSummary: Announces an all-day Smithsonian seminar on major controversies surrounding Jesus' life and death. Four lectures examine Jesus as an apocalyptic prophet, whether he advocated violent revolution, the historical reliability of Gospel accounts of his final hours, and the claim that Jews were responsible for his death. The program uses historical sources and methods while also addressing the damaging legacy of Christian anti-Judaism.

title: Why Are Evangelical Scholars So Interested in Finding a First-Century Manuscript?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why evangelical scholars are interested in a first-century Gospel manuscript.
searchSummary: Questions why evangelical scholars urgently seek a first-century manuscript of Mark while claiming that the original New Testament text is already securely reconstructed. Ehrman argues that a small, ordinary fragment would add little unless it preserved unusually significant evidence, such as an early title attributing the Gospel to Mark or the Gospel's disputed ending. He suggests the search reflects an unacknowledged desire for evidence supporting existing confidence in textual stability.

title: How Accurate Are our Earliest NT Manuscripts?
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about the accuracy of the earliest New Testament manuscripts.
searchSummary: Evaluates whether early New Testament papyri justify confidence that surviving manuscripts preserve the original text. P75 is unusually careful and closely related to Codex Vaticanus, whereas other early papyri contain far more differences and less competent copying; Alexandrian evidence after 200 therefore cannot establish practices from 70 to 200. Ehrman considers radical alteration unlikely because copying is conservative, but stresses that confidence about the earliest period rests on probability and inference rather than direct manuscript evidence.

title: Would a First-Century Fragment of Mark Matter?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether a first-century fragment of Mark would matter for New Testament textual study.
searchSummary: Evaluates whether a first-century fragment of Mark would materially change New Testament textual criticism. Ehrman first questions how many mummy masks were being destroyed without knowing whether they contained useful texts. He then argues that a small early scrap, whether closely matching known Mark or containing variants, would mostly confirm existing expectations about first-century copying. Only a lengthy, unmistakable manuscript with radically unexpected wording could revise the field, making the fragment's apologetic hype disproportionate to its likely evidence.

title: An Expert Talks About Mummy Masks and Papyri
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares expert concerns about mummy masks, papyri, and manuscript claims.
searchSummary: Shares papyrologist Roberta Mazza's critique of the mummy-cartonnage project and the claims surrounding a first-century Mark. Published evidence indicates that recycled papyrus masks generally predate Christianity, while current conservation methods need not completely destroy artifacts. Mazza stresses the absence of provenance, protocols, documentation, qualified specialists, and public evidence. She also warns that sensational stories can raise market prices and even provide a way to disguise illicit papyri as finds from legally acquired cartonnage.

title: Defending the Destruction of Mummy Masks
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses arguments used to defend destroying mummy masks to recover papyri.
searchSummary: Presents Craig Evans's defense of recovering papyri from damaged or poorly made mummy cartonnage. Evans says specialists avoid museum-quality pieces, owners retain rights to recovered texts, and the value of written material can justify dismantling artifacts, much as archaeology sometimes removes later layers to reach earlier remains. He also defends the Green Scholars' expertise and independence while acknowledging continued secrecy and publication delays surrounding the alleged first-century Mark fragment.

title: New Manuscripts and the Destruction of Antiquities
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques the destruction of antiquities in the search for New Testament manuscripts.
searchSummary: Reports the controversy over researchers dismantling Egyptian mummy masks while searching for early Christian papyri, including the alleged first-century Mark fragment. Ehrman highlights unanswered questions about the manuscript's date, contents, provenance, and delayed publication, then reproduces concerns from archaeologists about destroying cultural artifacts and allowing private collectors or Christian apologists to control evidence. The post asks whether the pursuit of a sensational Gospel scrap can justify irreversible damage to antiquities and weak scholarly transparency.

title: Whom Do We Admit into our Graduate Program?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how doctoral admissions work in a graduate religious studies program.
searchSummary: Explains why admission to UNC's doctoral program in early Christianity is extraordinarily selective. Successful applicants usually bring a master's degree, excellent grades and writing, strong recommendations, advanced Greek plus other ancient and modern languages, focused research interests, and a close fit with faculty expertise and the program's secular Ancient Mediterranean Religions orientation. Because only one or two students may be admitted from dozens of qualified candidates, even outstanding undergraduates generally need substantial graduate preparation before they can compete.

title: Public Reactions to Muslim Extremists
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on public reactions to Muslim extremism without turning the blog into political commentary.

title: New Testament Programs and Ancient Med.
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how New Testament work fits within a secular program in ancient Mediterranean religions.
searchSummary: Explains how UNC's graduate program in Ancient Mediterranean Religions differs from a conventional New Testament program in a divinity school. Students study New Testament writings alongside noncanonical Christian texts, Judaism, and Greco-Roman religions rather than treating the canon as a theological boundary. Seminars on apocrypha, the Apostolic Fathers, forgery, and New Testament interpretation prepare them to analyze early Christianity within its wider historical and religious environment.

title: Ancient Mediterranean Religions?!?
author: BDEhrman
description: Contrasts seminary training with graduate study in ancient Mediterranean religions at a research university.
searchSummary: Ehrman contrasts New Testament training in a theological seminary with the historical study of ancient Mediterranean religions at a secular research university. UNC organized its program around Judaism, Christianity, Ancient Near Eastern religion, and Greco-Roman religion rather than around biblical canons. This approach treats the New Testament as part of early Christian literature embedded within the wider religious and cultural world of antiquity.

title: Departments of Religious Studies
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains religious studies departments as academic settings for studying religion historically.
searchSummary: Traces the development of UNC's religious-studies department and explains how secular study differs from confessional instruction. Rather than promoting or opposing belief, university courses treat religion as an academic subject, conveying knowledge and teaching students to evaluate evidence and arguments regardless of their own or their professor's commitments. Ehrman argues that this distinction allowed religious studies to become a legitimate public-university discipline and gradually replace the inherited seminary model that had shaped early departments and faculty training.

title: The Graduate Program in Religious Studies
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the graduate program in religious studies and what makes applicants stand out.
searchSummary: Explains why UNC created its doctoral program in religious studies as a secular academic enterprise rather than a version of seminary education. Ehrman chose the new program over an established Notre Dame opportunity so he could help shape its structure from the beginning. He situates that choice within the postwar recognition that religion can be studied historically and critically without preparing students for ministry, a change that enabled public universities to establish undergraduate departments and eventually research-focused graduate programs.

title: Defending Myself
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on public attacks and the difficulty of defending one's scholarship.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman rarely responds to personal attacks from fundamentalists, mythicists, or scholarly opponents. He usually avoids searching for criticism, considers character assaults irrelevant to substantive questions, and trusts fair-minded readers to compare his work with its critics rather than consume his limited time in self-defense. He welcomes respectful debate over important evidence and occasionally answers consequential misrepresentation, but refuses exchanges based on mockery, context-stripping, or attempts to make his reliability replace the actual historical issue.

title: My Forgery Seminar (Syllabus)
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a syllabus for a graduate seminar on literary forgery in early Christianity.
searchSummary: Presents the syllabus for Ehrman's doctoral seminar on literary forgery in early Christianity, organized around Forgery and Counterforgery. The course situates forged and falsely attributed Christian writings within pagan and Jewish practices and examines canonical and noncanonical examples by their polemical purposes. Weekly topics include disputed Pauline and Petrine letters, writings supporting or opposing Paul, anti-Jewish and apologetic works, church organization, bodily controversies, and later theology. Students evaluate primary texts, ancient criticism, modern scholarship, motives, deception, and authorship claims.

title: Matthew’s “Filling Full” of Scripture
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Matthew's idea of Scripture being fulfilled or filled full.
searchSummary: Explains Matthew's typological understanding of fulfillment, in which earlier biblical events receive their complete meaning in Jesus. The infancy narrative, baptism, temptation, and Sermon on the Mount parallel Moses' rescue from a tyrant, exodus through water, wilderness testing, and delivery of God's law. Matthew thereby presents Jesus as a new Moses who saves people from sin and authoritatively interprets Torah. Followers must embrace Moses through Jesus rather than abandon the Jewish law.

title: Matthew’s Fulfillment of Scripture Citations
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Matthew's fulfillment citations and their use of Scripture.
searchSummary: Examines Matthew's eleven distinctive fulfillment citations and two puzzling examples of his scriptural interpretation. “He shall be called a Nazorean” may use Hebrew wordplay connecting Nazareth with Isaiah's Davidic “branch,” despite no such biblical prophecy. Matthew also reads Zechariah's synonymous poetic lines as requiring two animals and depicts Jesus riding both into Jerusalem. These literalistic interpretations do not prove Matthew was gentile because comparable techniques also appear in Jewish texts.

title: Matthew’s Ancient Approach to Scripture
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Matthew's ancient approach to interpreting Hebrew Bible passages about Jesus.
searchSummary: Defends Matthew's application of Hosea's exodus verse to Jesus as consistent with ancient interpretive practices rather than modern contextual reading. Jewish and Christian readers often sought allegorical, numerical, prophetic, or hidden meanings unknown to a text's human author. The Dead Sea Scrolls' pesher commentaries likewise apply Habakkuk's references to Babylonians and ancient enemies to Romans, Jerusalem groups, and Qumran leaders. Matthew similarly assumes that Scripture's deeper divine meaning concerns Jesus even when its literal subject is Israel.

title: Did Jesus Exist? Interview by Guy Raz
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares an interview about Did Jesus Exist? and the historical argument for Jesus.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's NPR interview with Guy Raz about Did Jesus Exist? and the historical case against mythicism. Ehrman notes that claims Jesus never existed have exercised surprising influence in some political and cultural settings, despite their rejection by specialists. His book gathers the available evidence to argue that Jesus was a genuine first-century person, while the brief post supplies only that central conclusion and directs readers to the recording for the historical sources and responses to mythicist arguments.

title: The Virgin Birth and Jesus’ Brothers
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the virgin birth in relation to Jesus' brothers and Gospel traditions.

title: The Blog Year in Review: 2014
author: BDEhrman
description: Reviews the blog's activity and charitable results during 2014.
searchSummary: Reviews the blog's activity and growth during 2014. Bart published about 300 posts, managed thousands of comments, simplified member and public post handling, and introduced a moderated discussion forum. The blog raised $72,000 for charities addressing hunger and homelessness, roughly twenty percent more than the prior year. He asks readers to recruit members, give subscriptions, donate, and suggest improvements, while crediting Steven Ray and the community for making the demanding project worthwhile.

title: Miraculous (Not Virgin) Births in Ancient Pagan Texts
author: BDEhrman
description: Contrasts miraculous pagan births with the specific idea of virgin birth.
searchSummary: Distinguishes ancient pagan stories of miraculous divine births from the Christian virgin birth of Jesus. Greek and Roman figures such as Alexander and Hercules were considered sons of gods because a deity had sexual relations with a mortal woman, producing partly divine offspring; these women were not virgins. Christianity instead portrays the Jewish God creating Jesus through the Holy Spirit without intercourse, reflecting a monotheistic conception unlike the sexual behavior attributed to pagan gods.

title: Widespread Claims of Pagan Virgin Births
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates claims that pagan religions commonly included virgin birth stories.
searchSummary: Popular writers sometimes claim that Christianity borrowed Jesus' virgin birth from pagan stories about Osiris, Dionysus, Mithras, and other gods. Ehrman argues that these sweeping parallels lack support in ancient sources and depend on repeating modern assertions without evidence. Pagan traditions did describe sons born from gods and mortal women, but those conceptions involved sexual intercourse rather than a virgin birth comparable to Matthew or Luke.

title: The Virgin Birth and the Gospel of John
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how John's Gospel relates to the virgin birth tradition.
searchSummary: Argues that John neither narrates nor presupposes Jesus' virgin birth. Its Prologue instead describes the incarnation of God's preexistent Word, a concept that does not require virginal conception and could be imagined in other ways. Matthew and Luke present a miraculous conception without describing Jesus as a preexistent being, while John presents preexistence without a virgin birth. Later doctrine combines these distinct Gospel accounts into a view that none of their authors expresses independently.

title: Does Mark’s Gospel Implicitly Deny the Virgin Birth?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Mark's Gospel implicitly argues against the virgin birth.
searchSummary: Argues that Mark's Gospel implicitly works against the virgin birth. Greek grammar identifies Jesus' family, including his mother, as those who try to seize him because they think he is out of his mind, despite translations that insert unnamed "people." Mary therefore does not understand Jesus as a divinely born Son. Mark never mentions a virgin conception, Bethlehem, or Joseph, and Matthew and Luke omit this family scene because their birth narratives require a mother who knows Jesus' extraordinary origin.

title: Why Was Jesus Born of a Virgin in Matthew and Luke?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Matthew and Luke portray Jesus as born of a virgin.
searchSummary: Compares the different theological purposes of the virgin birth in Matthew and Luke. Matthew interprets Isaiah 7:14 through its Greek translation and presents Jesus' birth as one of many fulfillments of Scripture, although Isaiah originally concerned a young woman and a near-term political crisis. Luke instead says conception by the Holy Spirit makes Jesus literally God's Son. Later Christian interpretation combined these distinct emphases with John's Christology.

title: 2 Thessalonians as a Forgery: The Theological Argument
author: BDEhrman
description: Gives the theological argument that 2 Thessalonians was not written by Paul.
searchSummary: Develops the theological case that Second Thessalonians contradicts Paul's imminent eschatology. The letter counters expectations that the Day of the Lord is near by requiring rebellion and the man of lawlessness first, unlike First Thessalonians' sudden thief-like arrival without advance warning. Reversing the letters, assigning different audiences, or denying a plausible later setting does not resolve the tension, while ancient parallels show that a successful post-Pauline forgery could circulate readily.

title: The Writing Style of 2 Thessalonians
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines the writing style of 2 Thessalonians as evidence against Pauline authorship.
searchSummary: Uses detailed stylistic analysis to argue that Second Thessalonians differs from Paul's undisputed letters when not copying First Thessalonians. Its sentences contain far more embedded clauses, genitive strings, and subordination, patterns shared with other disputed Pauline works rather than Paul's normal prose. Style alone cannot determine authorship, but combined with extensive imitation of First Thessalonians and divergent theology, it supports identifying the letter as a later writer's attempt to sound Pauline.

title: Do You Have To  Believe in the Virgin Birth?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Christian faith requires belief in the virgin birth.

title: Is 2 Thessalonians Based on 1 Thessalonians?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the argument that 2 Thessalonians was based on 1 Thessalonians.
searchSummary: Argues that Second Thessalonians was constructed from First Thessalonians rather than independently written by Paul. The letters share nearly identical openings and endings, rare expressions, longer verbal sequences, parallel organization, double thanksgivings, eschatological teaching, and warnings against idleness, a degree of repetition absent from Paul's other related correspondence. Such copying is readily explained as a forger's strategy for establishing authenticity, especially because the new material departs from Paul's style and views.

title: 2 Thessalonians: The History of the Discussion
author: BDEhrman
description: Traces the history of scholarly discussion about 2 Thessalonians and Pauline authorship.
searchSummary: Surveys the history of scholarly doubts about Second Thessalonians. Schmidt first observed in 1801 that its delayed eschatological timetable conflicts with First Thessalonians and proposed that the problematic passage was interpolated; later scholars considered the entire letter forged. Wrede's analysis of its close imitation of First Thessalonians established a stronger foundation for non-Pauline authorship, while subsequent commentators refined the case and some critical and theologically conservative scholars continued defending authenticity.

title: The Inauthenticity of 2 Thessalonians: The Simple Reason
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the basic reason scholars question Pauline authorship of 2 Thessalonians.
searchSummary: Presents a concise case that Paul did not write Second Thessalonians. First Thessalonians expects Jesus to return suddenly and soon, while the second letter postpones the event until rebellion and the man of lawlessness appear, despite claiming Paul had previously taught this sequence. Its assertion that Paul authenticates every letter with his own handwritten greeting is demonstrably untrue of his undisputed correspondence and appears designed to make a forged letter look genuine.

title: Pauline Forgeries:  2 Thessalonians as a Test Case
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses 2 Thessalonians as a test case for Pauline forgery.
searchSummary: Introduces 2 Thessalonians as a test case for determining whether a New Testament letter falsely claims Pauline authorship. Ehrman distinguishes the seven widely accepted Pauline letters from the disputed Deutero-Pauline writings and the generally rejected Pastoral Epistles, explaining that scholars compare vocabulary, style, theology, and historical setting. Because 2 Thessalonians has a stronger case for authenticity than the other disputed letters, he begins a series contrasting accessible and scholarly arguments, first examining its view of Jesus' return against 1 Thessalonians.

title: Forgeries in the Name of Paul
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces forgeries written in the name of Paul.
searchSummary: Explains that letters forged in Paul's name certainly circulated during early Christianity, regardless of who wrote Second Thessalonians. If Paul wrote it, his warning about a letter falsely attributed to him proves another forgery existed; if he did not, Second Thessalonians itself supplies the example. Its warning against false apostolic writings also illustrates a known forger's tactic: condemning the very deception being practiced so readers will assume the present work is authentic.

title: Giving Ideas
author: BDEhrman
description: Suggests holiday giving ideas connected to blog memberships and charity.

title: Why Do I Devote Myself to Studying the Bible?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why studying the Bible remains worthwhile after losing faith.
searchSummary: Explains why an agnostic can remain professionally committed to biblical scholarship. In a secular research university, scholars study historically and culturally important subjects without needing to believe their religious, political, or philosophical claims. The Bible, Christianity, and Jesus have profoundly shaped Western history and remain intellectually compelling objects of historical and literary study. Ehrman's loss of faith changed the reasons for his work, but not its academic legitimacy, importance, or fascination.

title: The Best of Times and the Worst of Times
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers personal reflections on gratitude and difficult times.
searchSummary: Balances gratitude for Ehrman's family, work, health, friendship, and intellectual life against grief over suffering experienced by loved ones and strangers. Agnosticism initially made thankfulness feel strange without a divine recipient, but he learned that wonder and appreciation do not require belief in a governing God; indeed, widespread misery drives his disbelief. The blog turns gratitude into assistance through charitable fundraising and donated memberships, allowing fortunate readers to support people facing poverty, illness, bereavement, and other crises.

title: Is the Discovered Gospel the Gospel of Peter?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether the discovered Gospel of Peter is the same text known from ancient references.

title: The Discovery of the Gospel of Peter
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the discovery of the Gospel of Peter and what was known before it appeared.

title: Why Not the Gospel of Peter?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the Gospel of Peter was not included among the canonical Gospels.
searchSummary: Explains why the Gospel of Peter was not included among the four canonical Gospels. It lacked broad acceptance in proto-orthodox churches and became associated with docetic beliefs that Christ only appeared to suffer or was separate from the human Jesus. Bishop Serapion initially approved its use because it claimed Peter's authorship, then prohibited it after finding passages that could support heresy. Its rejection shows how theological acceptability and church usage influenced canonical judgments about apostolic texts.

title: Do You Need A Free Membership?
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces free blog memberships for readers unable to pay.

title: Gift Memberships on the Blog 2014
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces holiday gift memberships for the blog.

title: Why Was the Gospel of Mark Attributed to Mark?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the Gospel of Mark came to be attributed to Mark.
searchSummary: Proposes why the anonymous second Gospel received Mark's name. John Mark was not necessarily obscure to early Christians: Acts, letters attributed to Paul and Peter, and Papias connect him with apostolic leaders. A late second-century Roman editor may have avoided naming the Gospel for Peter because Peter was known as illiterate and another Gospel of Peter already circulated. Attributing it to Peter's companion Mark created a balanced collection authorized by disciples Matthew and John and apostolic associates Mark and Luke.

title: Why Was the Gospel of Luke Attributed to Luke?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the Gospel of Luke came to be attributed to Luke.
searchSummary: Explains how early Christians came to attribute the anonymous Gospel and Acts to Luke, a Gentile physician associated with Paul. The first-person 'we' passages in Acts appeared to identify the author as Paul's traveling companion; Demas and Epaphras seemed unsuitable, leaving Luke among the named Gentile associates in Colossians. The post distinguishes this traditional reasoning from the separate historical case that the real author was not actually Paul's companion.

title: Why Was the Gospel of John Attributed to John?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the Gospel of John came to be attributed to John.
searchSummary: Explains how the anonymous Fourth Gospel came to be attributed to John son of Zebedee despite the apostle's inability to compose sophisticated Greek prose. Christians wanted apostolic authority for the Gospel and identified its Beloved Disciple by eliminating Peter and the early-martyred James, leaving John. Later legends connected John with Polycarp and Papias, but surviving evidence does not support those relationships or Johannine authorship. The title appears only near the end of the second century.

title: Why Was The Gospel of Matthew Attributed to Matthew?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the Gospel of Matthew came to be attributed to Matthew.
searchSummary: Explains why a later editor may have attributed an anonymous Greek Gospel to Matthew the tax collector. The disciple would probably have been an illiterate Aramaic-speaking rural Palestinian, whereas the Gospel is sophisticated Greek and copies Greek Mark extensively rather than presenting eyewitness memories. A tradition reported by Papias claimed that Matthew compiled Jesus material in Hebrew. When four anonymous Gospels received authoritative names around 180 CE, that rumor offered a convenient apostolic identity for the work that names Matthew.

title: Do Textual Variants Really Matter for Anything?
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers whether textual variants matter for doctrine and interpretation.
searchSummary: Argues that textual variants matter even when they do not overturn a major Christian doctrine. Most manuscript differences are trivial, and theology can support doctrines from multiple interpreted passages, but significant variants alter individual verses, entire narratives, and an author's distinctive understanding of Jesus, atonement, or resurrection. Treating doctrinal survival as the only measure of importance obscures the interpreter's task of establishing what each New Testament writer actually said and how their views may differ.

title: Why Are the Gospels Anonymous?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the canonical Gospels circulated anonymously before receiving traditional names.

title: Papias on Matthew and Mark
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates Papias as evidence for the authorship of Matthew and Mark.
searchSummary: Argues that Papias cannot establish the traditional authorship of the canonical Matthew or Mark. His Matthew is a Hebrew collection of sayings, unlike the Greek narrative based on Mark and Q; his Mark supposedly records everything Peter preached, yet the canonical Gospel is brief and shows no distinctive Petrine perspective. Papias therefore either refers to other writings or reports inaccurate traditions. The first unambiguous attribution of the surviving four Gospels remains Irenaeus around 180 CE.

title: Believing Papias When It’s Convenient
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques selective reliance on Papias for claims about Gospel authorship.
searchSummary: Criticizes scholars who selectively trust Papias's claims about Matthew and Mark while rejecting his other traditions. Papias also attributes to Jesus a fantastic prophecy of extraordinarily abundant vines and grain and describes Judas becoming grotesquely swollen, emitting worms and pus, and leaving an unbearable stench. Since these testable traditions are recognized as legendary and his information came through several intermediaries, accepting his preferred Gospel-authorship reports merely because they support prior beliefs is credulous rather than critical scholarship.

title: Papias as an Earwitness?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Papias as an indirect witness to early traditions about the Gospels.
searchSummary: Explains why Papias's statements about Gospel authorship do not come from direct access to Jesus' disciples. Papias questioned companions of elders who had heard apostles, placing him several links down a chain from the original events: Jesus, apostles, elders, their companions, and Papias. Because eyewitnesses and earwitnesses can already misremember, each additional transmission creates further opportunity for change, weakening attempts to treat Papias's later claims about Matthew and Mark as reliably authorized apostolic information.

title: Why Don’t You Believe Like Your Teacher, Dr. Metzger?
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers why Bruce Metzger's faith and scholarship are often contrasted with later agnosticism.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman's disagreements with his mentor Bruce Metzger do not invalidate his views about faith or the New Testament text. Ehrman rejects appeals to a teacher's authority while expressing deep respect for Metzger. He contrasts Metzger's confidence that scholars can recover nearly all of the original text with his own concern about long gaps in early manuscript evidence, and clarifies that Metzger accepted biblical errors despite believing in inspiration.

title: Papias and the Gospels: Some Background
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Papias as background for traditions about Gospel authorship.

title: The Four Gospels in the Muratorian Fragment
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the Muratorian Fragment to discuss when the four Gospels received their names.
searchSummary: Examines the Muratorian Fragment, the earliest surviving Christian list of canonical books, probably composed in late-second-century Rome. It includes twenty-two eventual New Testament books plus the Wisdom of Solomon and Apocalypse of Peter, while excluding or rejecting other writings. Its named fourfold Gospel collection supports the hypothesis that a Roman edition first grouped Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John under apostolic names, helping those particular texts and attributions gain broad authority in the developing canon.

title: The Gospels are Finally Named!  Irenaeus of Lyons.
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Irenaeus as evidence for the naming of the four canonical Gospels.
searchSummary: Explains how Irenaeus became the first surviving writer to identify the authoritative Gospels explicitly as Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John around 185 CE. Earlier writers such as Justin quoted anonymous “Memoirs of the Apostles,” while competing Gnostic and other Christian groups used different accounts or privileged only one canonical Gospel. Irenaeus defended exactly four as a unified witness against heresy, suggesting apostolic names and a closed fourfold collection emerged between Justin and Irenaeus to strengthen proto-orthodox authority.

title: When Did the Gospels Get Their Names?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks when the Gospels became known as Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.

title: The Year’s Society of Biblical Literature Meeting
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the annual Society of Biblical Literature meeting as a major scholarly conference.
searchSummary: Describes the Society of Biblical Literature meeting as a vast professional ecosystem of research papers, publishers, colleagues, former students, and scholarly evaluation. Ehrman's schedule combines a public lecture on eyewitness testimony, a panel about presenting Christian apocrypha to general audiences, and an expert review of How Jesus Became God requiring an unrehearsed response to critics. The conference therefore supports research exchange, public communication, publishing relationships, professional networks, and direct scrutiny of a scholar's arguments.

title: Did the Beloved Disciple Write the Gospel of John?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether the Beloved Disciple wrote the Gospel of John.
searchSummary: Shows that the Fourth Gospel does not identify its author as the Beloved Disciple. At the crucifixion, the narrator reports that this disciple witnessed and testified but never speaks as that witness. John 21 similarly distinguishes the disciple who supplied testimony from the “we” who affirm it, placing the author among those relying on his account. The Gospel may claim access to the disciple's traditions, but it remains anonymous and does not name John or anyone else as author.

title: Our Anonymous Gospels, Starting with Luke
author: BDEhrman
description: Begins a discussion of anonymous Gospels with Luke and Acts.

title: A Newly Discovered Gospel?  Was Jesus Married with Children???
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to claims about a newly discovered Gospel involving Jesus and Mary Magdalene.

title: Some Other Gnostics
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes another group of early Christian Gnostics for a revised textbook section.

title: A Better Kind of Fundamentalist
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to a conservative critique of biblical errancy and fundamentalism.

title: My New Summary of Gnosticism
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a revised textbook summary of early Christian Gnosticism.

title: My New Discussion of Gnosticism: Introduction
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a rewritten textbook section on early Christian Gnosticism.

title: Discussion Forum (Please read to the end)
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces progress on the blog's discussion forum.

title: Why Would Christian Authors Write Forgeries?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Christian authors may have written works under false names.
searchSummary: Explains that Christian forgers adopted famous names to make readers accept their own teachings as authoritative. Ancient testimony about pseudo-Pythagorean works, writings attributed to Democritus, a magical letter in Christ's name, and Salvian's work as Timothy all connects prestigious identities with influence. Within Christianity, apostolic names carried the greatest authority and eventually supported scriptural status, prompting forged Gospels, letters, and apocalypses. Ehrman suggests that authors may have viewed their message as important enough to justify deception about who wrote it.

title: A New Box on Why A (Christian) Author Would Lie About Who He Was
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a textbook box on why Christian authors might falsely claim another identity.
searchSummary: Asks how authors who praised truth could justify writing as Peter, Paul, or another authority. Beginning with the irony of Ephesians urging truth while allegedly misrepresenting its author, Ehrman contrasts Augustine's ban on lying with pagan, Jewish, and Christian traditions that permitted deception for a greater good. Examples involving medicine, battle, Abraham, and Rahab show the ethical rationale available to writers. Christian forgers may therefore have considered false identities acceptable means of spreading teachings they believed were true and beneficial.

title: Who Changed the Bible and Why? Diane Rehm Show
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a Diane Rehm interview about Misquoting Jesus and textual changes in the Bible.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's Diane Rehm Show interview about Misquoting Jesus and the textual history of the New Testament. He explains that scribes made accidental errors and intentional changes while copying biblical manuscripts, sometimes altering passages related to Jesus' divinity, the Trinity, and beliefs about the Bible's divine origin. The conversation also ranges into how homosexuality was understood in Jesus' time and the Christmas holiday, connecting textual transmission with wider questions about Christian doctrine, interpretation, and practice.

title: Why I’m To Be Pitied for Having Been the Wrong Kind of Fundamentalist
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to criticism about being the wrong kind of fundamentalist.
searchSummary: Responds to Louis Markos's claim that Ehrman deserves pity because the wrong kind of fundamentalism left him unprepared for biblical difficulties. Ehrman corrects the biography, noting that he acquired inerrancy at Moody rather than being raised with it, and rejects the proposal that modern readers should suspend contemporary historical and scientific knowledge. Ancient interpretation remains essential for understanding biblical texts, but their authors' premodern assumptions do not require present-day readers to accept impossible events or abandon modern standards of evidence.

title: New Boxes Related to Literary Forgery and the NT
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents textbook boxes on literary forgery and the New Testament.
searchSummary: Clarifies two authorship questions in New Testament scholarship. First, Ehrman argues that ancient secretaries normally took dictation or occasionally corrected prose; evidence does not support their independently composing substantial theological works under another person's name, which would have counted as forgery. Second, he distinguishes anonymous writings and later false attributions from deliberate forgeries, homonymous works mistakenly linked to a famous namesake, and orthonymous books correctly identifying their authors. These categories separate the Gospels, Revelation, disputed letters, and authentic Pauline writings.

title: New Boxes on Problematic Social Values in the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces textbook boxes on problematic social values in the New Testament.

title: New Boxes on Jesus as God in the NT
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents textbook boxes on Jesus as God in the New Testament.
searchSummary: Condenses two arguments about Jesus' divinity for a New Testament textbook. Pagan and Jewish traditions treated mortals exalted to heaven as divine, explaining how belief in Jesus' resurrection could immediately imply that he became a god; Paul likewise describes Christ as preexistent and active in creation. Romans 9:5 may even call Christ “God over all,” although Greek punctuation permits another translation and prevents certainty.

title: New Boxes:  Oral traditions and the Dates of the Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces textbook boxes on oral traditions and the dating of the Gospels.

title: What Is Different in My Textbook?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains revisions in a new edition of the New Testament textbook.

title: Can My Students Believe in the Inerrancy of the Bible?
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers whether students can defend biblical inerrancy in a university course.

title: The Bloody Sweat and Historical Plausibility
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses the bloody sweat passage and historical plausibility.
searchSummary: Uses Luke's bloody-sweat episode to distinguish textual, literary, historical, canonical, and theological questions about a biblical passage. Historically, the sleeping disciples were absent from Jesus' private agony and had no later opportunity to report it before his arrest. Explanations involving a post-resurrection disclosure or divine inspiration require theological assumptions, so historical inquiry most plausibly concludes that Luke or an earlier storyteller created the episode, which can still carry literary or religious meaning.

title: Introduction to My Introduction (to the NT)
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a new introduction for the New Testament textbook.

title: The Life of Brian & The Apocalyptic Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Connects Life of Brian with the apocalyptic interpretation of Jesus.
searchSummary: Introduces Bart's conference presentation on The Life of Brian and the historical Jesus. He explains that as an evangelical seminarian he resisted the film's portrayal of numerous apocalyptic street preachers because it made Jesus's message appear ordinary and mistaken. Later study convinced him that the parody accurately captures the widespread end-time milieu of first-century Judaism and that Jesus's proclamation is best understood within that shared expectation of God's imminent intervention.

title: The New Discussion Forum!!!  Soon Up and Running.
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the launch of a discussion forum for the blog.

title: Jesus Sweating Blood: Transcriptional Probabilities
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the bloody sweat passage to explain transcriptional probabilities in textual criticism.
searchSummary: Explains transcriptional probability by asking which variant a scribe was more likely to create, often favoring a difficult reading that later copyists would want to clarify or correct. The bloody-sweat verses conflict with Luke's portrayal of Jesus but strongly served second-century proto-orthodox arguments against Docetists who denied Christ's real humanity. Their earliest citations use them for precisely that purpose, supporting the conclusion that scribes added the passage rather than removed it from Luke.

title: Jesus’ Sweating Blood and “intrinsic” evidence
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the bloody sweat passage to explain intrinsic evidence in textual criticism.
searchSummary: Explains intrinsic probability, which asks which competing manuscript reading best matches an author's vocabulary, style, and theology. Luke repeatedly removes Mark's indications that Jesus approached death in anguish, creating a passionless Passion, while the disputed bloody-sweat verses portray extreme agony and require angelic comfort. Their conflict with Luke's consistent editorial treatment supports the conclusion that scribes added them, demonstrating why textual critics must combine manuscript expertise with close literary interpretation.

title: External Evidence in Textual Criticism
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains external evidence used in New Testament textual criticism.

title: Textual Scholars as Technicians
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why textual critics are often viewed as technical specialists.

title: On Changing One’s Mind
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on changing one's mind through the example of the Martyrdom of Polycarp.
searchSummary: Reflects on changing a long-held scholarly judgment about the Martyrdom of Polycarp. Ehrman had accepted the work as a mid-second-century account based on eyewitness reporting despite its literary parallels between Polycarp and Jesus, but later concluded that it was written perhaps fifty years afterward by someone falsely claiming firsthand authority. He presents that reversal as a model of responsible scholarship: substantial changes should follow careful examination of evidence and counterarguments, while refusing ever to reconsider prevents intellectual growth.

title: A Text-Critical Dissertation
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes a text-critical dissertation on Didymus the Blind and Gospel quotations.
searchSummary: Explains how Ehrman's dissertation in textual criticism reconstructed New Testament quotations used by Didymus the Blind. Church fathers can locate textual forms in time and place, but their surviving writings, imprecise quotations, and later copying create methodological difficulties that Gordon Fee's work helped address. Ehrman stresses that this specialized project concerned manuscript transmission rather than most subjects studied by New Testament historians, while his graduate training in exegesis and early Christianity prevented the dissertation specialty from defining his entire competence.

title: My Graduate Training  (Textual Criticism??)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains graduate training in textual criticism under Bruce Metzger.

title: My Training as a Textual Critic
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes training as a textual critic and its relation to New Testament scholarship.
searchSummary: Describes Ehrman's broad graduate education and his initial specialization in New Testament textual criticism under Bruce Metzger. Although most of his seminary courses covered ministry, biblical interpretation, languages, and early Christianity, a course in manuscripts and textual criticism shaped his scholarly direction. His master's thesis on the Majority Text required studying manuscript traditions, the history of textual criticism, and debates over whether later medieval witnesses preserve the original text.

title: Where Does One Deal with Textual Criticism?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains where textual criticism belongs in an introduction to the New Testament.
searchSummary: Explains Ehrman's decision about where to place textual criticism in his New Testament textbook. He reviews why abundant but mostly late manuscript copies create both extensive evidence and numerous textual differences requiring scholarly reconstruction. Initially placing the chapter last to avoid defining the book by his specialty, he later moved it near the beginning so students would understand problems of canon and text before studying individual writings.

title: Getting the Facts of My Life Straight
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to inaccurate accounts of personal history by conservative apologists.
searchSummary: Corrects apologetic accounts claiming Ehrman's loss of biblical inerrancy caused him to abandon belief in Christ's divinity and resurrection. He held those doctrines before adopting inerrancy and retained them long after rejecting it, so chronological sequence does not establish causation. Critical study later led him to view divine Christology as a historical human development and to question resurrection on separate grounds; he asks critics to distinguish his intellectual journey from convenient personal narratives they could have checked with him directly.

title: Where Do You Start an Introduction to the NT?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the challenge of deciding where to begin an introduction to the New Testament.

title: Getting Started on My NT Introduction
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the initial approach to writing a historically oriented New Testament textbook.

title: On Boring Textbooks
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the effort to make a New Testament textbook interesting rather than boring.

title: The Importance of a Comparative Approach to the NT
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the importance of comparing New Testament writings with one another.

title: Gift Subscriptions!!!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the availability of gift subscriptions to the blog.

title: New Discussion Forum: Suggestions?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks readers for suggestions about a new discussion forum.

title: The (Ancient) Genre of the Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the ancient genre of the Gospels within Greco-Roman literary context.
searchSummary: Defines the canonical Gospels as a Christian subtype of Greco-Roman biography. Ancient biographies used chronology, sayings, speeches, anecdotes, conflicts, and miracles to display a subject's stable character for instruction, imitation, or propaganda, rather than documenting psychological development through modern archival research. Readers would therefore expect Jesus's identity to appear from each narrative's opening, his character to remain consistent, and divine teaching and deeds to reveal who he was; each Gospel nonetheless adapts the flexible genre distinctively.

title: Placing the New Testament in Its Own Historical Context
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why a historical introduction must place the New Testament in its ancient context.

title: A Historical Approach to the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the decision to write a historical introduction to the New Testament.
searchSummary: Explains the historical design of Ehrman's New Testament textbook. Rather than treating the canon chiefly as theology or isolated literature, the book situates each writing within Jewish and Greco-Roman history and among other early Christian Gospels, letters, and apocalypses. This approach treats the New Testament as part of a broader body of ancient religious literature, asking what texts meant in their original circumstances without opposing theological interpretation or granting canonical books exclusive historical importance.

title: Agreeing to Do the Textbook
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes agreeing to write a New Testament textbook despite initial reluctance.

title: My New Testament Textbook
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces work on a new edition of the New Testament textbook.

title: Yale Shaffer Lectures 3 of 3 – Christ Against the Jews
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a Shaffer lecture on anti-Judaism in textual variants and apocryphal texts.
searchSummary: Introduces the third of Ehrman's Shaffer Lectures, titled Christ Against the Jews. The recorded lecture examines textual variants and apocryphal writings that contain evidence of Christian anti-Judaism. Ehrman places that manuscript-focused subject within his broader interest in explaining the historical rise of Christian opposition to Jews and Judaism, a subject he hoped to address separately for general readers. The post primarily provides the lecture video rather than a written version of its argument.

title: Letter from Urban Ministries of Durham
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a letter from Urban Ministries of Durham about the blog's charitable support.
searchSummary: Explains why Urban Ministries of Durham receives more blog support than its three other charities and shares a thank-you letter from its director. Bart praises the secular organization's local work against hunger and homelessness, including food, clothing, shelter, employment, and permanent housing rather than emergency relief alone. He reminds readers that donations through the blog support UMD, the North Carolina Food Bank, CARE, and Doctors Without Borders and that every contribution goes to those organizations.

title: Why We Need Tenure
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why tenure matters for research and teaching at universities.
searchSummary: Argues that tenure is essential because research and teaching require freedom from political, religious, and institutional retaliation. Faculty remain accountable through post-tenure review and can face discipline for serious misconduct or failure, but cannot be dismissed merely because evidence-based conclusions offend powerful constituencies. Without that protection, scholars would avoid controversial findings, instructors would conform to approved views, and universities would lose their capacity to produce and teach knowledge independently across biblical studies, science, philosophy, politics, and other contested fields.

title: What Counts for Tenure?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains what counts toward tenure at a research university.
searchSummary: Explains why research universities count peer-reviewed articles and scholarly monographs, rather than textbooks or trade books, as the principal evidence for tenure. Popular and instructional writing demands expertise and communication skill but usually synthesizes established knowledge instead of producing new findings. Ehrman therefore advises junior faculty to establish themselves through multiple scholarly studies before addressing general audiences, arguing that public-facing books are strongest when written by mature experts who continue advancing their fields rather than abandoning research for packaging alone.

title: The Academic Tenure Situation
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the academic tenure system and why it matters for professors.
searchSummary: Outlines how academic tenure is awarded and what it guarantees. After a probationary period, faculty are evaluated in research, teaching, and service, with research universities expecting a strong scholarly book and peer-reviewed articles before departmental and administrative approval; tenure still permits dismissal for serious misconduct, institutional insolvency, or extreme nonperformance. Ehrman also traces the usual progression from assistant to associate to full professor and distinguished chair, distinguishing tenure-track careers from temporary adjunct appointments that offer no comparable employment security.

title: A Day In the Life of a Research Professor
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes a typical day in the life of a research professor.
searchSummary: Demonstrates that a research professor's work extends far beyond classroom hours. Ehrman's typical day combines professional email, Latin and Hebrew study, public writing, intensive seminar preparation and teaching, graduate mentoring, departmental fundraising, student assessment, and research reading, with other days devoted more fully to scholarship. The schedule illustrates how maintaining languages, producing knowledge, supervising advanced work, administering programs, and teaching together create a demanding but varied occupation despite a nominal load of only two courses per semester.

title: Manuscripts and Christian Magic
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses manuscripts used as Christian amulets and magical objects.

title: New Discovery of an Ancient Christian Amulet
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the discovery of an ancient Christian amulet containing biblical references.
searchSummary: Reports the discovery of a roughly 1,500-year-old Christian papyrus amulet in Manchester's collection. A reused grain-tax receipt bears remembered and imperfectly ordered passages about manna and the Last Supper, then was folded for placement in a locket or pendant. Spectral imaging helped reveal the recycled document. The artifact illustrates how Egyptian protective practices incorporated biblical language and suggests that Christian scripture and Eucharistic traditions had entered ordinary devotional or magical life.

title: How I Actually Write
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how trade books are written after research and outlining.
searchSummary: Explains Ehrman's intensely concentrated method for drafting a trade book in roughly two weeks. Complete research, notes, and detailed chapter outlines let him write twelve to fourteen thousand words during a focused day, revise the chapter the next day, and alternate those stages until the manuscript is complete.
