Because initial composition produces anxiety while revision does not, he writes quickly, then performs several stylistic edits and incorporates expert readers' comments before sending the polished book to its publisher.

title: How I  Begin to Write
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how a trade-book writing process begins after research.
searchSummary: Explains how detailed outlining bridges Ehrman's research and actual drafting. As reading clarifies a book's thesis and structure, he develops formal chapter plans, rereads every source note, inserts evidence and quotations at the appropriate points, tests the argument's sequence, identifies gaps, and conducts targeted additional research. The completed outlines state each chapter's claims and support in logical order, so writing becomes the comparatively direct task of expressing a fully developed argument in clear, compelling prose.

title: Communicating with Non-Scholars
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the challenge of communicating scholarship to non-specialists.
searchSummary: Explains why many scholars struggle to communicate with nonspecialists: traditional doctoral programs trained them in research and academic discourse but not teaching or public communication. Bart contrasts that training with newer attention to pedagogy and describes the distinct skill of simplifying complex scholarship without distorting it. He credits his early experience teaching Bible studies, youth groups, adult education, and sermons with preparing him to teach undergraduates and write successful trade books.

title: Choosing a Topic for A Trade Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how topics are chosen for trade books.
searchSummary: Explains how Bart chooses subjects for trade books amid a heavily researched field. He favors important scholarly topics that general readers know little about or topics whose existing popular treatments need improvement, while also seeking questions capable of sustaining broad interest. Lost Christianities and Misquoting Jesus illustrate the first approach by making early Christian diversity and New Testament manuscript variation accessible to readers largely unfamiliar with those longstanding areas of scholarship.

title: Yale Shaffer Lectures 2 of 3 – Christ The Divine Man
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a Shaffer lecture on Christ as a divine man in early Christian tradition.
searchSummary: Introduces the second of three 2004 Shaffer Lectures delivered at Yale under the series title Christ in Early Christian Tradition: Texts Disputed and Apocryphal. This installment, titled Christ the Divine Man, presents one part of Ehrman's treatment of disputed and noncanonical traditions about Christ. The post primarily supplies the lecture video, transferred from an older VHS recording, rather than summarizing or extending its argument in written form.

title: How Do You Know What To Write About?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how trade-book topics emerge from sustained reading and research.
searchSummary: Distinguishes choosing a scholarly research topic from selecting a general-audience book subject. Doctoral and later academic work must identify a specific, consequential question that prior scholarship has not adequately answered, requiring mastery of multilingual literature and an original contribution rather than a summary. Ehrman illustrates the challenge with current dissertations on Gospel texts, Paul, visions, magic, and demons, emphasizing that generating new knowledge demands both broad expertise and the ability to recognize a precise unresolved problem.

title: Where Do You Start Reading?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains where to begin reading when researching a trade book.
searchSummary: Explains how to begin reliable research in an unfamiliar field without trusting indiscriminate search results. Ehrman recommends asking an expert for a recent authoritative work or state-of-the-field study, mining its citations, following those sources' bibliographies, and identifying repeatedly cited classics. He used this method to enter cognitive psychology, collective memory, and oral tradition research, combining colleague recommendations with known foundational studies until expanding citation trails produced a strong, increasingly comprehensive bibliography.

title: Writing a Trade Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains planning and drafting a trade book for general readers.
searchSummary: Outlines the six stages Ehrman follows when producing a trade book: preliminary research, a publisher's prospectus, extensive reading, detailed outlining, drafting, and revision. Because he plans books years ahead and already knows the field, he can begin with substantial background. For Jesus Before the Gospels, however, he entered research on memory, oral cultures, and tradition outside New Testament studies to develop a genuinely new treatment rather than repeat his earlier work.

title: My Approach to Doing Research
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how research notes and reading shape a trade book project.
searchSummary: Describes Ehrman's method for mastering large amounts of scholarship and preserving what matters for later writing. He first determines whether a book requires complete reading or only its introduction, conclusion, and relevant chapters, then highlights material directly useful to his research. The following day he records quotations, summaries, and page references in computer files, spreading the work across two days to reinforce memory and creating notes that let him recover arguments or revisit sources efficiently.

title: Upcoming Speaking Schedule and … Cruises!
author: BDEhrman
description: Lists upcoming speaking engagements and travel events.

title: Yale Shaffer Lectures 1 of 3 – Christ Come in the Flesh
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a Shaffer lecture on Christ come in the flesh and disputed early Christian texts.
searchSummary: Introduces the first of three 2004 Shaffer Lectures delivered at Yale under the series title Christ in Early Christian Tradition: Texts Disputed and Apocryphal. Titled Christ Come in the Flesh, the lecture considers how early Christian groups restricted the acceptable interpretation of sacred texts to support their own purposes. The post chiefly provides the lecture video, preserved from an older VHS recording, with only brief written context for the series.

title: Titles for Trade Books, Like Misquoting Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how titles for trade books differ from titles for scholarly books.
searchSummary: Explains how titles for general-audience books are designed to attract readers without becoming misleading or sensational. Editors generate and test possibilities with colleagues and marketing departments, while overseas publishers may choose different titles. Ehrman recounts resisting Misquoting Jesus because it did not precisely describe the book, preferring Lost in Transmission, but ultimately acknowledges that his publisher's more memorable title proved effective and that professional editors often understand the trade market better than authors.

title: Titles of Scholarly Books
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how scholarly book titles are chosen and what they signal.
searchSummary: Explains why scholarly book titles generally identify a work's subject and argument rather than simply attracting a broad audience. Ehrman traces the revision of his dissertation title to specify Didymus the Blind and discusses his deliberate wordplay in The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture. He rejected Bruce Metzger's proposed word "Correction" because it implied approval of scribal alterations, while "Corruption" accurately invoked the technical textual-critical term and highlighted his argument about orthodox theological changes to manuscripts.

title: Scholarly vs. Trade Books
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares scholarly books and trade books on the same topic.
searchSummary: Begins comparing scholarly monographs with trade books by examining how their titles signal subject, audience, and difficulty. Bart contrasts Forgery and Counterforgery with Forged, explaining why academic titles must identify their precise field for specialist readers and library classification, while popular titles are designed to spark curiosity. His deliberately technical terms “counterforgery” and “polemics” warn prospective readers that the scholarly volume is not an easy general-audience treatment.

title: The Other Gospels: The Trade Book Version
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the trade-book version of a project on non-canonical Gospels.
searchSummary: Explains the creation of The Other Gospels as a general-audience counterpart to Bart and Zlatko Plese's scholarly edition of noncanonical Gospels. The academic volume places Greek, Latin, and Coptic texts beside English translations for specialists, whereas the trade edition supplies accessible translations and rewritten introductions without unnecessary technical material. Bart distinguishes both books from broader apocrypha collections and describes adding the Gospel of the Savior to the popular volume.

title: Apocryphal Gospels: The Scholarly Version
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the scholarly edition of apocryphal Gospels and its translation work.
searchSummary: Recounts how Ehrman and Zlatko Plese created a scholarly multilingual edition of approximately forty noncanonical Gospels. Moving the project from the Loeb Classical Library to Oxford allowed inclusion of Coptic works alongside Greek and Latin texts, with Plese providing needed Coptic expertise. Their facing-page translations were accompanied by introductions, manuscript and interpretive discussions, bibliographies, variant readings, and notes. The resulting Apocryphal Gospels later became the basis for a separate popular edition.

title: Suggested Donation for the Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks readers to consider donations beyond membership fees.
searchSummary: Asks blog members to consider an additional donation, suggesting $20 while welcoming smaller or larger gifts according to individual means. Bart argues that the low annual fee provides frequent, substantive posts across early Christian subjects and direct interaction through questions and comments. Because he personally covers operating expenses and sends every dollar of blog revenue to charities addressing hunger and homelessness, additional contributions would help the community reach its $100,000 annual fundraising goal.

title: How I Decided to Publish the Apocryphal Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the decision to publish the apocryphal Gospels.
searchSummary: Recounts the origins of a project to publish apocryphal Gospels in their original languages with facing English translations. A conversation with textual critic David Parker highlighted the lack of an accessible collection, especially for important works still dependent on nineteenth-century editions. Although Harvard declined the proposed Loeb volume, the need for a modern scholarly edition remained, leading Ehrman to pursue the demanding project elsewhere after recognizing its value for researchers and graduate students.

title: The Difficulties of Publishing a Translation
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the difficulty of publishing a translation project.
searchSummary: Explains why publishing a translation is harder than simply reading an ancient language. Private or classroom translation can explore several English renderings to capture a Greek word's nuances, but a published edition must commit to one choice for every phrase despite imperfect equivalents and predictable scholarly disagreement. Producing the Loeb Apostolic Fathers also required establishing Greek texts and researching each work, but the thousands of irreversible translation decisions made that part especially demanding.

title: My Third Scholarly and Trade Book Combination, Told Tangentally
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains a third pairing of scholarly and trade books on the same topic.
searchSummary: Recounts how complaints about Kirsopp Lake's aging Loeb edition of the Apostolic Fathers led Bart to undertake a completely new Greek-English edition. He describes proposing updated introductions, textual decisions, and translations to Harvard University Press after an accidental meeting with an editor. The demanding scholarly project later provided background for a separate pair of academic and popular books on the apocryphal Gospels, whose development he continues in subsequent posts.

title: My Scholarly and Trade Books on Forgery
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares scholarly and trade books on literary forgery.
searchSummary: Recounts how Bart's extensive research on ancient literary forgery produced both Forged for general readers and the scholarly monograph Forgery and Counterforgery. Dissatisfied with inherited claims that pseudonymous writing was accepted in antiquity, he studied pagan, Jewish, and Christian evidence alongside modern scholarship. Although he initially intended to publish the academic work first, his editor persuaded him to write the shorter trade treatment before completing the larger technical study.

title: Trade Books and Scholarly Books
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains planned future trade and scholarly books.
searchSummary: Explains the relationship between Bart's scholarly research and general-audience books, especially Misquoting Jesus. His technical work in New Testament textual criticism included monographs, articles, and editions intended for specialists; the trade book instead introduced nonspecialists to missing originals, differing manuscript copies, and scholars' efforts to reconstruct texts. Bart also considers whether research for Jesus Before the Gospels might eventually support both a popular book and a distinct scholarly study.

title: Freedom From Religion Foundation Lecture
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a lecture on being an agnostic who writes about religion.
searchSummary: Summarizes Ehrman's Freedom From Religion Foundation lecture about being an agnostic scholar of religion. He distinguishes freedom from state-imposed religion from hostility toward religious people, supporting the former while rejecting broad attacks on faith as mistaken and counterproductive. Although personally nonreligious and strongly opposed to fundamentalism across traditions, he does not regard religion itself as the enemy, using his own career studying beliefs he does not share to argue for a more careful relationship between secularism, scholarship, and religious freedom.

title: My Future Books
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses future book plans and ongoing research while in London.
searchSummary: Maps Ehrman's tentative ten-year writing agenda across trade books, scholarly monographs, textbooks, and revised editions. Planned projects included paired popular and academic studies of memory and oral tradition, a book on Christian appropriation of Jewish Scripture, a history textbook covering Christianity through Nicaea, and The Triumph of Christianity. He emphasizes that the sequence could change and that teaching, administration, graduate advising, and textbook revisions constrain how quickly even a carefully planned publishing program can be completed.

title: Clarification!
author: BDEhrman
description: Clarifies a point about Mark and the next book project.
searchSummary: Clarifies the scholarly range for dating Mark while defending the prevailing view. Critical scholars generally place the Gospel around the end of the Jewish War in approximately 70 CE, whereas fundamentalist and conservative evangelical scholars regularly favor an earlier date to bring it closer to Jesus. Nonconservative exceptions such as Maurice Casey, James Crossley, and John A. T. Robinson also argue for earlier dating. Their existence qualifies the generalization without changing where the broad critical consensus lies.

title: My Next Project
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a new project on memory and the oral traditions behind the Gospels.
searchSummary: Introduces a project on the oral traditions that circulated for forty to sixty-five years between Jesus' death and the anonymous Gospels. Rather than resembling a simple telephone game, transmission crossed languages, cultures, communities, and purposes, making the process considerably more complex and vulnerable to change. Research in cognitive psychology, neuroscience, collective memory, oral cultures, rumor, and legend challenges common New Testament assumptions about eyewitness reliability, accurate recall, and stable preservation in nonliterate societies.

title: My Apostolic Fathers Seminar/Syllabus
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a seminar syllabus on the Apostolic Fathers.
searchSummary: Presents the syllabus for a doctoral seminar on the Apostolic Fathers, covering ten proto-orthodox authors and writings after the New Testament period. Students translate Greek, evaluate authorship and date, report on scholarship, review Walter Bauer, and produce a research paper. The course uses texts such as 1 Clement, Ignatius, the Didache, Barnabas, and the Shepherd of Hermas to investigate persecution, church offices, canon, women, ritual, and anti-Judaism.

title: Suggestions for Improving the Blog (Its Content)
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks readers for suggestions about improving the blog's content.

title: National Cathedral Lecture – Misquoting Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a National Cathedral lecture on Misquoting Jesus.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's 2007 Washington National Cathedral lecture, Misquoting Jesus, about scribes who altered Scripture and readers who may never know the original wording. He identifies this recording as a particularly strong version of a lecture he has presented elsewhere, praising both his delivery and the setting. The short post does not restate its textual examples or conclusions, leaving the video to explain how copying changed New Testament manuscripts and why those variations matter for understanding the Bible.

title: ANT: Methods of Biblical Interpretation in the Early Church
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents material on early Christian methods of biblical interpretation.

title: Ideas for Raising More Money on the Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses ideas for raising more money through the blog.
searchSummary: Evaluates three reader proposals for increasing the blog's charitable revenue. Bart favors keeping membership affordable while encouraging a suggested annual donation, considers selling costly private conversations, dinners, or appearances for charity, and supports creating a simpler way to give annual memberships as gifts. He explains the benefits and constraints of each idea, distinguishes gift subscriptions from donated memberships for people in financial need, and invites members to assess or improve the proposals.

title: ANT:  More on Women in Early Christianity
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents material on women in early Christianity from After the New Testament.

title: After the New Testament: Women in Early Christianity
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces material on women in early Christianity from After the New Testament.

title: Follow-up Apologies for the Post on Dinesh D’Souza
author: BDEhrman
description: Apologizes for comments about Dinesh D'Souza that caused controversy.
searchSummary: Apologizes for comments introducing Ehrman's debate with Dinesh D'Souza after readers interpreted them as a personal attack. Ehrman explains that he meant to establish D'Souza's public prominence, not exploit his controversies, and revised the original remarks once he understood their effect. Recalling their cordial debates, his anxiety about facing a skilled opponent before a packed auditorium, and his wife's candid assessment afterward, he emphasizes respect despite their profound political differences.

title: My Debate with Dinesh D’Souza on the Problem of Suffering
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a debate with Dinesh D'Souza on suffering and the problem of evil.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's 2010 debate with conservative author and commentator Dinesh D'Souza at Gordon College. Their disagreement centers on whether suffering should affect belief in God: D'Souza argues that the world's suffering gives no reason to abandon faith, while Ehrman holds the opposite position. Ehrman describes D'Souza as an unusually intelligent and quick opponent and provides the recorded second of their three public debates, separating the theological arguments from D'Souza's unrelated political career and controversies.

title: The Skeletal Remains of Yehohanan and Their Significance
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses the skeletal remains of Yehohanan and their relevance for Roman crucifixion practices.

title: Josephus’s Clearest Claim about the Burial of Crucified Victims
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Josephus's clearest statement about the burial of crucified victims.
searchSummary: Examines Josephus's statement that Jews buried even crucified offenders before sunset, the strongest textual argument for Jesus's burial. Bart questions whether Josephus exaggerates Jewish piety, refers to Roman crucifixions, describes a longstanding or universal custom, or includes political enemies. Because mass crucifixions clearly went unburied and Jesus was executed as a rival king, he concludes that any occasional accommodation for ordinary criminals would not establish a decent same-day burial for Jesus.

title: More on Josephus and Jewish Burial Practices
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues evaluating Josephus and Jewish burial practices in relation to Jesus' burial.
searchSummary: Challenges an argument assembled from three Josephus passages to show Roman respect for Jewish burial practice. One concerns images rather than burial, another describes procurators after Jesus's time, and the third summarizes Moses's ideals rather than actual social behavior. Bart argues that Jewish legal obligations did not bind Roman executioners and that Josephus's apologetic praise of Jewish morality cannot demonstrate that Rome released crucified insurgents or enemies of the state for prompt burial.

title: Does Josephus Show that Jews Always Buried Their Dead?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Josephus shows that Jews always buried their dead.
searchSummary: Challenges the inference that Josephus's statement about Roman respect for Jewish laws includes same-day burial of Jesus. The cited passage specifically concerns exemptions from imperial images, while Jewish burial obligations applied to people Jews executed, not Roman victims. Because Rome killed Jesus for claiming kingship and used prolonged crucifixion to punish political threats, Bart argues that general accommodation of selected Jewish customs does not show that Roman authorities surrendered his body.

title: Hiatus: A New Teaching Company Course
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Teaching Company course while pausing a thread on Jesus' burial.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's twenty-four-lecture Great Courses series based on How Jesus Became God. The course moves from divine humans in paganism and Judaism through Jesus' life, death, resurrection traditions, visions, early exaltation and incarnation Christologies, later disputes, Constantine, Nicaea, and the Trinity. Ehrman explains that the audiovisual format sacrifices some detail but permits deeper emphasis on central points, making it a distinct presentation rather than merely a reproduction of the book.

title: Josephus and the Burial of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Josephus as evidence in debates about the burial of Jesus.
searchSummary: Introduces Josephus as the principal first-century Jewish source for evaluating claims about the burial of crucified people. Bart recounts Josephus's aristocratic background, military role in the Jewish revolt, surrender to Rome, relationship with Vespasian, and later historical writings. He emphasizes Josephus's political purposes while recognizing his exceptional value, then frames the question of whether passages about Jewish burial customs apply to Jesus, whom Rome executed as an enemy of the state.

title: Another Anecdote about Being Consistently Critical
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Josephus to illustrate the need for consistent critical judgment about sources.
searchSummary: Argues that historians must apply the same critical standards to every ancient source, including sources that appear to support their conclusions. The large number of New Testament manuscripts does not eliminate uncertainty about original wording because relatively few are early; classical scholars face even greater textual problems. Likewise, claims by Josephus, pagan historians, or biblical authors require examination for exaggeration, contradiction, authorship, and external confirmation rather than acceptance merely because an ancient writer reports them.

title: Being Consistently Critical (in the good sense)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why historical criticism must be applied consistently to all sources.
searchSummary: Argues that ancient sources must be examined critically and consistently rather than trusted selectively. A student willing to question Tacitus or the Talmud but not sayings in John illustrates how personal commitments can exempt favored evidence from scrutiny. Historians instead consider each source's bias, consistency, plausibility, and relationship to independently evaluated evidence. The same standards must govern the Gospels, Acts, disputed letters, Josephus, and every other document used to reconstruct past events.

title: Discovered Crucifixion Nails
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses alleged crucifixion nails and their relevance to Roman execution practices.

title: Pilate the Intransigent
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Pontius Pilate's character in the debate over Jesus' burial.
searchSummary: Rejects the claim that Pilate learned to respect Jewish customs and therefore would have permitted Jesus's burial. Josephus records that Pilate later funded an aqueduct from the Temple treasury and used disguised soldiers to beat protesting Jews, causing numerous deaths. Together with Philo's condemnation of Pilate's corruption, cruelty, and executions, the episode portrays a consistently brutal governor rather than one likely to depart from Roman crucifixion practice out of sensitivity to Jewish burial expectations.

title: Did Pilate “Learn His Lesson”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares different views of Pontius Pilate in arguments about Jesus' burial.
searchSummary: Rejects the claim that Pilate's early dispute over Roman standards taught him to respect Jewish customs and therefore permit Jesus's burial. Josephus says Pilate knowingly introduced imperial images at night, refused six days of protests, and threatened mass execution before demonstrators accepted death rather than submission. Bart argues that Pilate withdrew to avoid the political consequences of killing Judea's leaders, not from sensitivity, and continued acting brutally afterward.

title: Did Pontius Pilate Respect Jewish Sensitivities?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Pontius Pilate respected Jewish sensitivities in matters of execution and burial.
searchSummary: Evaluates whether Philo's account of golden shields shows that Pilate respected Jewish customs enough to permit crucified bodies to be buried. Bart emphasizes that Pilate stubbornly rejected Jewish appeals and removed the shields only after Emperor Tiberius intervened, while Philo portrays him as corrupt, cruel, and violently inhumane. The episode therefore undermines rather than supports a consistently accommodating Pilate, though Bart frames his burial conclusion as a probability judgment rather than certainty.

title: Discrepancies That Pay Rich Dividends
author: BDEhrman
description: Shows how Gospel discrepancies can produce historical and theological insight.
searchSummary: Shows how discrepancies between Mark's and Luke's passion narratives yield distinct theological interpretations of suffering. Mark's forsaken Jesus suggests that God can work redemptively even when suffering appears meaningless, while Luke's confident Jesus models awareness of God's presence, concern for others, and hope of paradise. Harmonizing the accounts removes these separate messages and demonstrates why historical-critical comparison can deepen rather than diminish the Gospels.

title: Why the Critical View of the Gospels Matters Theologically/Religiously
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why a critical view of the Gospels can matter religiously and theologically.
searchSummary: Argues that acknowledging Gospel discrepancies can deepen theological and literary interpretation rather than simply undermine faith. Mark depicts Jesus's death through silence, abandonment, and despair, while Luke presents a calm Jesus who forgives, consoles, promises paradise, and entrusts himself to God. Combining their words into one harmonized passion narrative creates a new Gospel and erases each author's message. Reading the accounts separately allows believers and nonbelievers alike to engage their distinct, powerful interpretations of suffering and faith.

title: Ancient Forerunners of Modern Gospel Critics
author: BDEhrman
description: Identifies ancient precedents for modern critical questions about Gospel reliability.
searchSummary: Argues that Matthew and Luke provide ancient precedents for critically revising Gospel accounts. If both used Mark, their additions, omissions, reordered events, and altered meanings show they valued his material without treating it as inviolably accurate. Luke's prologue says earlier narratives were inadequate enough to require his orderly account. Modern historical criticism continues this willingness to ask what happened, identify inaccuracies, and explain changes, while theological claims that canonical texts must be different remain a separate kind of judgment.

title: Why Are You Trashing the Gospels?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to concerns that critical scholarship is unfairly attacking the Gospels.

title: Did Roman Laws Require Decent Burials?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether Roman law required decent burial for crucified victims.
searchSummary: Examines a Roman legal ruling cited to show that executed criminals could be released for burial. Although the Digest preserves an earlier rule allowing relatives to request bodies, it explicitly notes that permission could be denied for high treason and does not specifically establish burial for crucified people. Because Rome executed Jesus as a rival king and political threat, Bart argues that the cited law supports nonburial as part of crucifixion's punishment and deterrent.

title: Did Roman Authorities Show Clemency?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Roman clemency as evidence in debates about Jesus' burial.
searchSummary: Challenges claims that Roman clemency makes Jesus's prompt burial historically probable. The cited examples concern prisoners or offenders in other places and periods, not people crucified for treason; even Albinus released petty offenders for bribes while executing those deemed worthy of death. Bart argues that isolated mercy toward lesser criminals cannot establish a practice of releasing crucified enemies of the state, whose prolonged exposure served Roman punishment, humiliation, and deterrence.

title: Did Romans Allow Decent Burials?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Romans allowed decent burial for crucified people.
searchSummary: Analyzes Philo's report that some Roman governors in Alexandria released crucified bodies before an emperor's birthday. Bart argues that this rare holiday clemency does not establish a general burial practice: the victims had already hung on crosses, their bodies went to relatives, and the occasion had no parallel in Jesus's Passover execution for treason. The passage therefore illustrates an exceptional circumstance rather than evidence that Pilate would permit Jesus's immediate burial.

title: Jesus Burial: My Personal Stake in the Question
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the personal and scholarly stakes in Jesus' burial.
searchSummary: Clarifies that Ehrman has no personal or theological stake in whether Jesus received a proper burial. A tomb burial would not prove resurrection, while delayed or dishonorable disposal would not prevent an omnipotent God from raising Jesus; the issue affects the empty-tomb tradition and timing, not whether a miracle occurred. He therefore frames his disagreement with Craig Evans as a historical judgment about evidence rather than an agnostic attempt to disprove Christian faith.

title: A Hiatus in the Thread: Editorial Duties!
author: BDEhrman
description: Pauses the burial thread because of editorial responsibilities.

title: Argument Against Jesus’ Burial in HJBG, Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues the argument that Jesus was probably not buried by Joseph of Arimathea.
searchSummary: Argues that Pontius Pilate's documented conduct makes an exceptional tomb burial for Jesus historically unlikely. Josephus and Philo portray Pilate as violent, contemptuous of Jewish sensitivities, willing to kill protestors, and inclined toward force rather than accommodation, unlike increasingly sympathetic Gospel portraits. Although certainty is impossible, normal Roman policy and Pilate's character give historians substantial reason to doubt that he released an executed political offender to Joseph of Arimathea for immediate honorable burial.

title: Argument Against Jesus’ Burial in HJBG, Part 1
author: BDEhrman
description: Begins the argument that Jesus was probably not buried by Joseph of Arimathea.
searchSummary: Argues that normal Roman crucifixion practice weighs against Jesus receiving an immediate honorable tomb burial. Literary and material evidence repeatedly associates crucified bodies with prolonged exposure, decomposition, and scavenging animals, while Philo's reported releases occurred as exceptional favors for connected families on imperial holidays, circumstances unlike Jesus' execution at Passover. Ehrman allows that an exception was possible but notes that later Christians needed a burial tradition before they could proclaim an identifiable tomb empty.

title: New Thread on the Burial of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a thread responding to arguments about the burial of Jesus.
searchSummary: Introduces a series evaluating Craig Evans's defense of Jesus' burial by Joseph of Arimathea in the response volume How God Became Jesus. Ehrman explains that research changed his longstanding acceptance of the Gospel burial account because Paul lacks the tradition, New Testament versions conflict, and Roman practices make it doubtful. He regards Evans's essay as the strongest informed counterargument but plans to test whether its literary and archaeological evidence actually establishes the traditional conclusion.

title: Violent Opposition to the Romans in the Days of Jesus (or Brian)?
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Life of Brian to discuss violent opposition to Rome in Jesus' day.
searchSummary: Challenges the common picture of Judea during Jesus' lifetime as filled with militant resistance to Rome. Martin Goodman points to Tacitus's description of calm, Rome's small local military presence, and Josephus's inability to identify more than a handful of disturbances before 66 CE. The revolutionary environment portrayed in Life of Brian fits the later Jewish revolt far better than the 20s and 30s, weakening claims that Jesus emerged among numerous contemporary zealots.

title: Brian and the Apocalyptic Jesus Part 3
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses parody as a way to think about historical method and Jesus traditions.
searchSummary: Uses Life of Brian's parody to challenge the historical plausibility of Jesus receiving an immediate honorable burial. Roman sources indicate that crucified bodies normally remained exposed for humiliation and scavenging; Philo's exceptional imperial-birthday clemency, Jewish burial rules, and Pilate's documented brutality do not support a special exemption. The film's comic indifference to local sensitivities captures Roman power more plausibly than apologetic harmonization. Ehrman concludes that thoughtful parody can reveal historical realities and generate serious analysis.

title: Brian and the Apocalyptic Jesus Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues a Life of Brian conference paper on memory and the apocalyptic Jesus.
searchSummary: Uses Life of Brian's “Blessed are the Cheesemakers” parody to expose the limits of eyewitness claims about Gospel traditions. Witnesses can misperceive, encode, store, and retrieve events inaccurately; experiments, false crash footage memories, and DNA exonerations show that confidence and emotional intensity do not guarantee accuracy. Since the Gospels were written decades later by non-witnesses, even a hypothetical eyewitness source could not ensure verbatim preservation of Jesus' sayings or deeds.

title: Brian and the Apocalyptic Jesus Part 1
author: BDEhrman
description: Begins a Life of Brian conference paper on Jesus as an apocalyptic figure.
searchSummary: Uses The Life of Brian's apocalyptic street preachers to reassess the historical setting of Jesus's message. Bart recounts initially rejecting the scene because it seemed to reduce Jesus's revelation to common visionary nonsense, then compares its parody with John the Baptist, Jesus son of Ananias, the Qumran War Scroll, and Jesus of Nazareth. All anticipate imminent disaster, divine intervention, and the need for repentance, showing that Jesus participated in a broader Jewish apocalyptic tradition.

title: Day Two of Jesus and Brian
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a report on the second day of the Jesus and Brian conference.

title: Day One of Jesus and Brian
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a report on the first day of the Jesus and Brian conference.

title: The Life of Brian Conference
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces posts on the Life of Brian conference and the historical Jesus.

title: Radio Debate with Pete Williams on Textual Variants
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a radio debate with Pete Williams on New Testament textual variants.
searchSummary: Presents a recorded radio debate between Ehrman and Peter J. Williams about New Testament textual variants and whether they matter. The discussion contrasts Ehrman's arguments in Misquoting Jesus, published in Britain as Whose Word Is It?, with Williams's evangelical confidence in the New Testament's reliability and his judgment that Ehrman's position is overly pessimistic. Hosted by Justin Brierley on Unbelievable, the exchange supplies an informed alternative perspective within Ehrman's series on manuscript differences.

title: Why Textual Variants Matter for the Rest of Us
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why textual variants matter beyond specialist debates about doctrine.
searchSummary: Argues that significant textual variants matter because each biblical author has a distinctive perspective that should not be harmonized into a single New Testament teaching. Disputed readings can change whether Mark narrates resurrection appearances, Luke presents Jesus' death as atonement or portrays anguish before it, and John calls Jesus the unique God. Although such consequential cases are few among hundreds of thousands of differences, they profoundly affect interpretation of particular books and their portrayals of Jesus.

title: Fundamentalists and the Variants in our Manuscripts
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why manuscript variants matter to fundamentalist claims about Scripture.
searchSummary: Explains why manuscript variants challenged Ehrman's former fundamentalist understanding of biblical inspiration. He initially viewed textual criticism as a sacred task of recovering God's inspired words from error-filled human copies. He later questioned why a God who miraculously inspired precise wording neither preserved the originals nor protected transmission, even though accurate copying was possible. The discrepancy led him toward a less literal view of Scripture, though not by itself toward agnosticism.

title: Who Cares???  Do the Variants in the Manuscripts Matter for Anything?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether New Testament manuscript variants matter for ordinary readers.
searchSummary: Argues that the significance of New Testament textual variants cannot be measured solely by whether they overturn a fundamental Christian doctrine. Most differences are trivial and none reverses a major traditional belief, but Christianity also depends on narratives, practices, worship, and the distinctive claims of individual biblical authors. Variants can therefore matter greatly when they change what a Gospel says about Jesus or reveal disagreements among New Testament writers, even without altering a creed.

title: Hypothetical Problems with Copies of Philippians
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Philippians to show hypothetical problems in identifying an original text.
searchSummary: Uses a hypothetical transmission history for Philippians to show why identifying its original wording remains difficult even if the original is defined as the letter Paul sent. Early copies could have contained different errors, while a relatively poor copy might have become the ancestor of most surviving manuscripts. The problem becomes still harder if Philippians combines two earlier letters, leaving scholars unable to prove that surviving witnesses reproduce Paul's wording exactly.

title: Dictation of Letters: More Complications for Knowing an “Original” Text
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how dictation complicates the idea of an original text of Philippians.
searchSummary: Explores further complications in defining the original text of Philippians when Paul dictated his letters to a scribe. Possible mishearing, misspeaking, authorial corrections, fresh copies, and Paul's changing intentions create competing candidates for what counts as original. Combined with the possibility that Philippians joins two letters and the absence of early copies, these uncertainties make it difficult to identify which surviving variants reproduce Paul's intended or earliest wording.

title: Complications with Finding an “Original” Text
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues the problem of defining and recovering an original text of Philippians.
searchSummary: Explains how Paul's practice of dictating letters complicates the meaning of an original text. A scribe could mishear or miswrite Paul's words, Paul could correct the draft, and the scribe could introduce new errors while producing the copy sent to recipients. Ehrman asks whether the original should mean Paul's intention, his spoken words, the scribe's first writing, the corrected draft, or the dispatched copy from which later manuscripts descended.

title: What Would Be the “Original” Text of Philippians?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks what would count as the original text of Philippians.
searchSummary: Examines what could count as the original text of Philippians given the possibility that an editor combined two separate Pauline letters. The edited form preserved by all surviving manuscripts may not have been created by Paul and could include additional alterations, while the two underlying letters no longer survive independently. Ehrman shows why neither the earliest surviving copies nor a perfectly accurate copy would itself be the physical original.

title: Are There Two Letters to the Philippians?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether Philippians may combine two separate Pauline letters.

title: Do We Have the Original Text of Philippians?
author: Diane
description: Answers questions about whether the original text of Philippians can be recovered.
searchSummary: Answers questions about whether surviving copies of Philippians can be called the original letter. Ehrman affirms Pauline authorship but distinguishes an original document from later copies, notes evidence that Philippians may combine two letters, and explains that the earliest surviving copy dates roughly 150 years later. Scholars can probably reconstruct much of its wording, but without the original they cannot directly measure how closely their reconstruction matches it.

title: My Debate on Suffering with Philosopher Richard Swinburne
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a debate with Richard Swinburne on suffering and the problem of evil.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's 2009 radio debate with Oxford philosopher Richard Swinburne about whether the world's pain and misery can be reconciled with theism. Ehrman recalls becoming genuinely angry because Swinburne's explanations seemed detached from the lived reality of severe suffering and deficient in empathy. Moderated by Justin Brierley for the Christian radio program "Unbelievable," the recording contrasts Swinburne's philosophical defense of Christian belief with Ehrman's moral and theological objections to such abstract solutions.

title: Christ as an Angel in Paul
author: admin
description: Explains the argument that Paul could think of Christ as an angelic being.
searchSummary: Defends the claim that Paul regarded the preexistent Christ as an angelic being. Galatians 4:14 uses a grammatical construction that elsewhere identifies two descriptions, supporting “an angel, namely Christ” rather than an ascending comparison. Ehrman acknowledges that Paul places Christ above angels after the resurrection, but argues that Philippians explains why: the chief angel became human and was subsequently exalted to divine equality. Later superiority does not erase Christ's earlier angelic status.

title: Why I (Actually) Discuss Hallucinations
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why hallucinations matter in discussing resurrection appearances and Christology.
searchSummary: Explains why How Jesus Became God discusses hallucinations without claiming that resurrection appearances were necessarily hallucinations. Historians can establish that some disciples experienced visions but cannot determine whether God caused real appearances; veridical visions require little explanatory discussion, whereas non-veridical experiences require psychological context. Ehrman therefore presents both possibilities and rejects Larry Hurtado's charge that the analysis covertly attacks Christianity, emphasizing that the book deliberately leaves the visions' external reality unresolved.

title: More Misreadings of How Jesus Became God
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to further misreadings of How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Corrects Larry Hurtado's claims that Ehrman misunderstands distinctions between Jesus and God the Father or lacks awareness of Jewish ideas about preexistence. Ehrman stresses that New Testament authors never identify Jesus as the Father, although later modalist Christians often did, and that omitted scholarship does not imply ignorance in a selective trade book. The exchange clarifies that asking whether Jesus is God requires specifying the particular kind of divinity an author attributes to him.

title: The Son of Man and Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the Son of Man in relation to Jesus and early Christology.

title: Jesus and the Life of Brian Conference
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the Jesus and Brian conference on Life of Brian and the historical Jesus.

title: Larry Hurtado’s Critique of How Jesus Became God
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Larry Hurtado's critique of How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Introduces Larry Hurtado's review of How Jesus Became God and distinguishes genuine scholarly disagreement from criticism based on misreading. Ehrman rejects Hurtado's suggestion that the book mainly reassures skeptics or lies outside his expertise, noting decades of Christological study and prior scholarly publications while acknowledging every scholar's dependence on others' research. He prepares to correct attributed positions Hurtado later retracted before addressing the smaller number of substantive disagreements that remain.

title: The Religion of a Sixteen-Year-Old
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on teenage religion, memory, and a fundamentalist past.
searchSummary: Reflects on returning to Ehrman's Kansas hometown and remembering the religious beliefs he held when he became born again as a teenager. He questions why some evangelical friends regard his sixteen-year-old faith as the truth he should never have outgrown, even though adults expect their understanding to mature in every other area. Distinguishing sophisticated theologians from intellectually static believers, he argues that religious thought should develop alongside one's knowledge, judgment, and experience.

title: Thomasine “Gnostics” and Others
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses Thomasine Christians and other groups sometimes connected with Gnosticism.

title: The Valentinian Gnostics
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a textbook discussion of Valentinian Gnostics.

title: The Sethian Gnostics
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a textbook discussion of Sethian Gnostics.

title: New Discussion of Gnosticism
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a revised discussion of Gnosticism in After the New Testament.

title: The Next Step: Redaction Criticism
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces redaction criticism as a stage in modern New Testament scholarship.
searchSummary: Introduces redaction criticism as the scholarly shift from reconstructing oral traditions and hypothetical communities to analyzing the surviving Gospel narratives and their authors. Beginning in the 1950s, scholars examined how evangelists edited sources by adding, deleting, rearranging, or changing material. Since Matthew and Luke used Mark, comparing their versions exposes their distinctive theological interests at both narrative and verse level; cautiously identifying characteristic framing and vocabulary can extend the method to Mark and John despite missing sources.

title: More on Jesus’ Wife!
author: BDEhrman
description: Reports new developments concerning the Gospel of Jesus' Wife.

title: Form Critics and Oral Tradition
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains form criticism and oral tradition in the study of the Gospels.
searchSummary: Explains form criticism as the study of Gospel stories during oral transmission before they were written. Scholars such as Schmidt, Dibelius, and Bultmann classified recurring forms—healings, controversies, pronouncement stories—and inferred the community situations that generated and shaped them. In this model, Christians adapted or created traditions to address worship, conflict, and teaching needs, while evangelists supplied narrative frameworks. The method challenged Gospel historicity but profoundly influenced twentieth-century scholarship before redaction criticism renewed attention to authors.

title: More Background on Oral Traditions
author: BDEhrman
description: Gives background on scholarly interest in oral traditions behind the Gospels.

title: Background to the Interest in Oral Traditions
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the scholarly study of oral traditions about Jesus before the written Gospels.

title: My Other Next Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses a possible future book on oral tradition and memory.
searchSummary: Proposes a new study of oral traditions about Jesus during the largely undocumented decades before the Gospels. The project joins three research areas: psychology of individual memory and eyewitness error, sociology of collective memory shaped by social groups, and anthropology of how oral cultures preserve and transform traditions. Together they promise a fuller model than older form criticism for explaining how stories about Jesus changed as people repeatedly transmitted them from approximately 30 to 70 CE.

title: My Next Books
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses possible future books, including Paul and Christian use of Jewish Scripture.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman did not plan to write a book on Paul and compares two projects competing to become his next trade book. He preferred subjects closer to his expertise and interest, especially how Christians came to claim Jewish Scripture as their own and how that process contributed to anti-Judaism. The post describes early Christian disagreements over the Jewish Bible and presents the project as a major, understudied historical story suitable for a general audience.

title: Interview for The Skeptic Fence Show
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a Skeptic Fence interview on faith, debates, and How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Introduces a Skeptic Fence Show interview about Ehrman's religious background, public debates, and How Jesus Became God. The conversation focuses especially on his historical explanation for how Jesus' followers came to understand him as divine after his death. The short post supplies the complete Skype interview and identifies its four hosts, leaving the recorded discussion rather than accompanying prose to present the detailed questions and answers.

title: Other Options for Paul and Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Considers possible reasons Paul says so little about the historical Jesus.

title: Why Doesn’t Paul Say More About Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks why Paul does not say more about Jesus' earthly life.

title: More on Jesus’ Teachings in Paul
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues discussion of Jesus' teachings known to Paul.
searchSummary: Considers additional places where Paul invokes a “word” or “command of the Lord,” including teaching about believers meeting Christ at his return and orderly Christian worship. Some statements may derive from otherwise lost traditions attributed to the historical Jesus, while others could have arisen through prophecy in Paul's churches. Ehrman argues that Paul's clearer parallels to recorded Gospel sayings show that he occasionally referred to teachings he believed Jesus had delivered.

title: Paul’s References to Jesus’ Teachings
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Paul's references to Jesus' teachings in the surviving letters.
searchSummary: Examines Paul's references to teachings of Jesus as evidence that Paul knew traditions about a historical teacher. Beyond the Last Supper, Paul attributes to the Lord instructions opposing divorce and allowing missionaries to receive material support, both of which closely parallel sayings preserved in the Gospels. Ehrman argues that these correspondences are better explained as Paul's use of traditions attributed to Jesus than as revelations newly delivered by Christian prophets.

title: An Interview about My Agnosticism
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares an interview about agnosticism and the Freedom From Religion Foundation.
searchSummary: Introduces a short interview recorded when Ehrman received the Freedom From Religion Foundation's Emperor Has No Clothes Award at its Raleigh convention. The accompanying lecture addressed what it is like to devote a professional career to the New Testament and early Christianity without personally being Christian. Unlike many videos he had shared, this interview speaks openly about his own agnosticism and beliefs and was prepared for an Openly Secular campaign promoting visibility for nonreligious people.

title: More on Paul’s Knowledge of Jesus’ Life
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues examining Paul's knowledge of Jesus' earthly life.

title: What Did Paul Know About the Historical Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks what Paul knew about the historical Jesus.

title: Jesus and Paul Compared and Contrasted
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Jesus and Paul on the kingdom of God, salvation, and resurrection.
searchSummary: Compares Jesus' proclamation with Paul's gospel, identifying both shared Jewish apocalyptic assumptions and fundamental differences. Both anticipated God's imminent victory, emphasized faith and love, and criticized reliance on meticulous legal observance. Jesus, however, taught preparation for judgment through his interpretation of Torah and expected the Son of Man to bring God's kingdom, whereas Paul identified Jesus as the returning judge and made faith in Jesus' death and resurrection the basis of salvation.

title: Paul and Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Paul's gospel with Jesus' teaching about God and the coming kingdom.
searchSummary: Contrasts Jesus' answer to the rich man's question about eternal life with Paul's understanding of salvation. Jesus directs the man to obey God's commandments, love his neighbor, give his wealth to the poor, and follow him; Paul instead requires faith in Jesus' death and resurrection and baptism. Ehrman considers attempts to reconcile the messages but concludes that Jesus and Paul offered significantly different accounts of how people would be saved at the coming judgment.

title: The Message of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Jesus' message in relation to Paul's views of salvation.
searchSummary: Outlines Jesus' message as an urgent Jewish apocalyptic proclamation that God's earthly kingdom would soon arrive through the heavenly Son of Man. Its judgment would reverse present fortunes, reward those devoted to God, and punish the forces of evil. Jesus called people to prepare by fulfilling Torah's intent through love, peace, justice, generosity, healing, and repentance, thereby anticipating in the present the transformed life of the coming kingdom.

title: Response to the Response: How God Became Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to How God Became Jesus, a response volume to How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Challenges the evangelical response volume How God Became Jesus for criticizing details without offering a coherent alternative historical account. Ehrman traces a development from a Jesus who did not claim divinity through resurrection belief to fourth-century Trinitarian doctrine, a transformation crucial to Christianity's growth and Western history. He argues that the responders' incarnation position rests on theological assumptions historical methods cannot demonstrate, explaining why they deconstruct his reconstruction rather than construct their own.

title: Other Models of Salvation in Paul
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains additional models of salvation in Paul's thought.

title: Comparison of Paul’s Two Principal Models of Salvation
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Paul's judicial and participationist models of salvation.

title: Paul’s “Participationist” Model of Salvation
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Paul's participationist model of salvation through union with Christ.

title: Paul’s “Judicial” Model of Salvation
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Paul's judicial model of salvation through Jesus' death and resurrection.

title: Video: Bart Ehrman vs. James White Debate
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a debate with James White on the New Testament text.
searchSummary: Introduces a video of Ehrman's debate with James White over whether scholars have access to the original New Testament text. Ehrman describes White as a capable but combative defender of biblical inerrancy and acknowledges that the encounter was unpleasant and did not show him at his best. He nevertheless posts both parts so viewers can evaluate the arguments and the debate for themselves.

title: Paul’s Gospel Message
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Paul's gospel message as centered on Jesus' resurrection and salvation.

title: Paul’s Importance in Early Christianity?
author: BDEhrman
description: Considers Paul's importance for early Christianity without making Paul the inventor of resurrection belief.

title: Did Paul Invent the Resurrection?
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Paul did not invent belief in Jesus' resurrection.

title: My Interview on Fresh Air
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses a Fresh Air interview and the role of media attention in book sales.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's Fresh Air interview with Terry Gross about How Jesus Became God and reflects on media's importance for reaching general readers. He praises Gross's preparation, insight, conversational direction, and willingness to let guests explain a book's significant ideas, qualities that support clear public scholarship and substantially affect readership. The embedded interview contains the substantive discussion of how early Christians came to regard Jesus as divine.

title: Attacks from the Other Side: An Ill-Tempered Richard Carrier
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to Richard Carrier's criticism of How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Defends Ehrman's claim that the absence of Roman literary references to Jesus is unsurprising by comparing him with Pontius Pilate. Richard Carrier accused him of overlooking Pilate's inscription and mentions by Philo and Josephus, although Did Jesus Exist discusses all three and distinguishes Jewish evidence and archaeology from Roman literature. Ehrman warns against attacking compressed statements without their fuller context and declines extended engagement with Carrier because he considers Carrier's ridicule incompatible with constructive scholarly exchange.

title: A Milestone for the Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a blog fundraising milestone of more than $100,000.
searchSummary: Celebrates the blog surpassing $100,000 raised in just over two years. Bart explains that he personally pays administrative costs, Steven Ray discounts technical services, and all membership fees and donations support four charities. He profiles Urban Ministries of Durham, the regional Food Bank, CARE, and Doctors Without Borders, with particular emphasis on local efforts against hunger and homelessness. The milestone and reader response reinforce his commitment to continued frequent educational posts despite the workload.

title: More on the Very Reverend Robert Barron
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to Robert Barron's critique of How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Rejects Robert Barron's claim that Synoptic details encode a Christology as high as John's. Fear among followers, Jesus' eastern approach to Jerusalem, and authority to announce forgiveness do not establish preexistence or identity with God; in Mark, forgiveness reflects authority God grants. Ehrman argues that Mark portrays a human adopted and exalted into divinity at baptism, while John portrays a preexistent divine being incarnated as human, distinctions erased by imposing later theology across texts.

title: Critique of the Very Reverend Robert Barron
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques Robert Barron's response to How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Responds to Robert Barron's review by identifying positions How Jesus Became God explicitly avoids. Ehrman does not declare resurrection visions hallucinations, claim a novel discovery, equate his reconstruction with the Passover Plot, or decide the theological truth of Jesus' divinity. He argues that Barron's rhetoric attacks a straw man rather than historical evidence and maintains that a careful account of developing Christology need not threaten informed Christian belief.

title: Interview on Trinities.org on How Jesus Became God Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the second part of a Trinities.org interview on How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Presents the second part of Dale Tuggy's Trinities.org interview with Ehrman about How Jesus Became God. Their discussion centers on the historical emergence of belief in Jesus' divinity while also ranging into related questions about Christian theology and its later formulations. The post contains introductory context and the complete telephone interview rather than a separate written argument, allowing listeners to evaluate the extended exchange directly.

title: Modern Appearances of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers why people continue to report visions of Jesus and Mary.
searchSummary: Uses documented modern visions of Jesus to show that reported appearances did not end with the New Testament. Cases include individual conversion visions and a Pentecostal congregation's alleged group appearances, one reportedly filmed but later lost, alongside surviving testimony and photographs of related phenomena. Ehrman neither verifies these claims nor dismisses them, noting that the decades separating event and report resemble the interval between Jesus' life and the earliest written Gospels.

title: Did Disciples Have Visions of Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers whether the disciples had visions of Jesus after the crucifixion.
searchSummary: Argues that the disciples' visions of Jesus are supported by evidence comparable to other historical claims about Jesus. Paul explicitly reports his own experience, personally knew Peter and James and says they had appearances, and independent traditions in multiple Gospels and Acts also attest visions. Ehrman concludes that visions best explain the rise of resurrection belief while distinguishing the historical claim that followers experienced them from the theological question of whether the risen Jesus objectively appeared.

title: Jesus as God in the Synoptics
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains divine status in the Synoptic Gospels and a changed view developed while writing How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Explains Ehrman's revised conclusion that every canonical Gospel portrays Jesus as divine, though in different senses. Miracles, forgiveness, and worship alone need not establish divinity, but combined with divine sonship they do: Mark presents adoption at baptism, Luke presents conception by God, and John presents a preexistent divine Word becoming human. The comparison demonstrates why historians must ask not merely whether Jesus is called God, but what kind and level of divinity each author means.

title: Interview with Trinities.org on How Jesus Became God
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares an interview with Trinities.org on How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Introduces Dale Tuggy's Trinities podcast interview with Ehrman about How Jesus Became God. Because Tuggy does not fully share Ehrman's conclusions, the conversation probes the book's historical account of developing belief in Jesus' divinity rather than offering only promotional questions. The short post supplies the recorded telephone interview as its substantive content and situates it within a range of public discussions approaching the book from different theological perspectives.

title: Christ as an Angel in Paul
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the argument that Paul could view Christ as an angelic figure.
searchSummary: Argues that Paul understood the preexistent Christ as God's chief angel who became human and was later exalted higher. The Greek construction in Galatians 4:14 identifies Jesus Christ as an angel rather than contrasting the two, a reading supported by Paul's parallel grammar and modern scholarship. This interpretation unifies Paul's statements about Christ's preexistence, divinity, earthly manifestation, and elevation toward equality with God after resurrection.

title: The Disciples who Doubted the Resurrection
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses disciples who doubted the resurrection in the Gospel traditions.
searchSummary: Explains Gospel traditions of doubt by proposing that only a limited number of followers initially experienced visions of Jesus. Peter, Paul, Mary Magdalene, and possibly others believed their own experiences, while some disciples remained unconvinced; later retelling expanded appearances to encompass the entire group. Repeated demands for physical proofs and scenes of nonrecognition therefore preserve traces of early disagreement rather than straightforward memories of everyone meeting an unmistakably resurrected Jesus.

title: Why I’m Obsessed with Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the fascination with Jesus behind work on How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Explains Ehrman's continuing scholarly focus on Jesus after leaving Christianity. The historical Jesus appears to have been an apocalyptic Jewish preacher who did not claim divinity, yet followers' belief that he was God enabled Christianity's growth beyond Judaism and its eventual transformation of the Roman Empire and Western civilization. The decisive historical question is therefore how the human Jesus became the divine Christ, not merely what the historical preacher originally taught.

title: Media: How Jesus became God – Ehrman vs Gathercole Pt 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the second part of a radio exchange with Simon Gathercole on How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Presents the second part of Ehrman's radio exchange with evangelical New Testament scholar Simon Gathercole about How Jesus Became God. This installment shifts emphasis from Gospel portrayals to Paul's understanding of Christ, where the scholars disagree about the origin and character of early belief in Jesus' divinity. The post provides the complete Unbelievable program recording and identifies the participants rather than reproducing their arguments in written form.

title: Fresh Air with Terry Gross and the Dish Book Club with Andrew Sullivan
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses media attention from Fresh Air and The Dish Book Club.
searchSummary: Explains how major media exposure can determine whether a trade book reaches a wide audience and announces two prominent opportunities for How Jesus Became God. Ehrman describes recording his sixth Fresh Air interview with Terry Gross and Andrew Sullivan choosing the book to relaunch the Dish Book Club. He emphasizes that publicists can seek coverage but cannot guarantee it, making these interviews unusually valuable chances to generate discussion and sales.

title: Women at the Tomb
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the women at the tomb matter for assessing the empty tomb tradition.
searchSummary: Challenges the apologetic claim that women at Jesus' tomb must be historical because Christians would not invent female witnesses. Women were prominent in early Christian communities, burial preparation was commonly women's work, the male disciples had fled, and Mark's literary portrayal favors women learning what the men do not. These plausible social and narrative reasons mean the women-at-the-tomb tradition cannot by itself prove that an empty tomb was discovered.

title: The God Augustus
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Augustus as an example of divine rulers in the Roman world.
searchSummary: Explains how an inscription calling Augustus God led Ehrman to place early Christian claims about Jesus within the wider Roman world. Emperor worship showed that calling a human divine was culturally intelligible and created an implicit competition over the true God-man. Because Jesus' earliest followers were Palestinian Jews rather than pagan devotees, the realization also prompted Ehrman to investigate Jewish traditions about divine humans before tracing later Gentile developments.

title: Jesus as the Adopted Son of God
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains adoptionist Christology and Jesus as Son of God.
searchSummary: Revises the assumption that adoption made Jesus a lesser or merely figurative Son of God. In elite Roman society, an adopted adult could be deliberately chosen as heir and receive the father's property, status, authority, and prestige, as Augustus did from Julius Caesar. Early Christians who said God adopted Jesus at his resurrection therefore claimed that he inherited divine power, could conquer death and judge the world, and functioned for practical purposes as God.

title: Why It Matters
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why early Christians calling Jesus God matters historically and religiously.
searchSummary: Argues that the declaration of Jesus as God matters historically because it helped transform a Jewish sect into a predominantly Gentile religion that reshaped Western civilization. Ehrman does not praise or condemn the resulting Middle Ages, Renaissance, Reformation, or modern world; he makes a counterfactual claim about how radically different history would have been. The post distinguishes the immense consequences of Jesus' divinization from any value judgment about those consequences.

title: Radio Debate on How Jesus became God: Part 1
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the first part of a radio debate with Simon Gathercole on How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Introduces the first half of a friendly radio debate about How Jesus Became God between Ehrman and Cambridge New Testament scholar Simon Gathercole. Gathercole contributed to the response volume How God Became Jesus and approaches early Christology from a conservative Christian perspective, creating substantive disagreement between respected scholars. The post supplies the Unbelievable program recording and identifies its participants and setting rather than presenting their detailed arguments in written form.

title: Article in the Huffington Post
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a Huffington Post article introducing How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Summarizes How Jesus Became God's account of how followers transformed a crucified apocalyptic preacher into an eternal divine creator. Ehrman argues that visions, not an empty-tomb discovery, convinced some disciples that Jesus had risen and been exalted to heaven, where ancient people could understand a human as divinized. Later Christians located Jesus' sonship progressively earlier, from resurrection to baptism, birth, preexistence, and finally eternal equality with God, with enormous consequences for Western history.

title: Scholars and Popular Audiences
author: BDEhrman
description: Defends writing serious scholarship for popular audiences.
searchSummary: Argues that biblical scholars should communicate important research to the public, but only when they possess both the skill and scholarly standing to do so responsibly. Writing for nonspecialists requires an accessible voice that neither assumes academic knowledge nor condescends or oversimplifies. Bart warns against premature popularization and maintains that public-facing authors should first establish sustained expertise through serious original scholarship, then continue contributing to that scholarship while addressing broader audiences.

title: Why Sell Books?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why scholars write and sell books for general readers as a way to disseminate knowledge.
searchSummary: Defends selling trade books as a means of educating far more people than a professor can reach in a classroom. Bart rejects colleagues' assumptions that popular publishing is chiefly about money or represents an abandonment of real scholarship. Because authors write to have their ideas read, broad sales can disseminate valuable historical knowledge, stimulate public discussion, and extend a scholar's teaching mission without requiring that scholar to give up university teaching or academic work.

title: My First Radio Interview on How Jesus Became God
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the first radio interview for How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's first radio interview for How Jesus Became God, recorded for Interfaith Voices with host Maureen Fiedler. The program frames the discussion as a debate over Jesus' divinity and uses perceptive questions to survey the book's principal historical claims about the exaltation of a Jewish preacher. The post's substantive content is the embedded interview, offered as an accessible overview before the book's release rather than a written account of its arguments.

title: How Books Are Sold
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how trade books are sold through timing, promotion, and media attention.
searchSummary: Explains why a trade book's quality, advertising, and traditional book tours do not by themselves produce strong sales. Ehrman identifies media coverage, especially influential radio and television appearances, as the principal driver of public attention and describes the publicist's role in securing it amid intense competition. Using the release of How Jesus Became God and his scheduled Fresh Air interview, he illustrates the excitement, uncertainty, and brief commercial window surrounding a new book's publication.

title: How Jesus Became God!!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the release of How Jesus Became God and introduces a new thread on the book.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman considers the question of how Jesus became God exceptionally important to Western history. Belief in Jesus' divinity enabled the movement to transcend its Jewish origins, attract Gentiles, grow throughout the Roman Empire, and eventually influence Constantine's conversion and Christianity's official status. Without that belief, Ehrman argues, the religious and cultural development of the Middle Ages, Renaissance, Reformation, Enlightenment, and modern West would have been incalculably different.

title: John from a Socio-Historical Perspective
author: BDEhrman
description: Applies a socio-historical method to the Gospel of John.
searchSummary: Applies the socio-historical method to John's differing portrayals of Jesus. An early Aramaic tradition calls Jesus rabbi, Messiah, and Lamb of God, titles suited to Jewish believers and a human agent of God. Other passages present him as a preexistent divine being from heaven. These layers may reflect successive stages in the Johannine community, whose changing social experiences affected its stories and gradually elevated its Christology from a chosen human Messiah to equality with God.

title: How Jesus Became God
author: BDEhrman
description: Provides a short promotional summary of How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Offers a brief introduction to How Jesus Became God and links readers to the book's information page. The post identifies the book's central historical movement: Jesus begins as a human prophet and is understood by followers as God's Son, exalted to divine status at the resurrection. It further indicates that visions of Jesus after his death were the decisive catalyst, but the locally archived text ends before developing that explanation.

title: The Socio-Historical Method
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the socio-historical method for studying the Gospel of John.
searchSummary: Introduces the socio-historical method as a way to infer how a community's experiences shaped the traditions it preserved. Because sermons and other texts address particular social circumstances, scholars can cautiously reason backward from their emphases to the communities that produced them. Applied to John, differing sources and perspectives may come from successive periods in the Johannine community. Analyzing those layers can therefore suggest how its social history influenced changing portrayals of Jesus.

title: Sources of the Fourth Gospel
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the sources thought to stand behind the Fourth Gospel.
searchSummary: Reconstructs several sources that may have been combined to form the Fourth Gospel: a seven-miracle Signs Source, collections of Jesus' discourses, a Passion account, and materials behind the Prologue and chapter 21.
