Literary seams and apparent endings support the proposal, although the sources no longer survive. John is therefore better understood as a layered work involving multiple authors and editors whose distinct social settings and views of Jesus remain visible in the final narrative.

title: More on John from a Redactional Perspective
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues the redactional argument that John used earlier sources.
searchSummary: Uses internal inconsistencies to argue that the Fourth Gospel combines multiple written sources. Problems include a “second” sign after other signs, abrupt geographical movements, repeated questions about Jesus' destination, and a command to leave followed by three more chapters of speech. The Farewell Discourse makes particular sense if chapters 13–14 and 18 once formed one account while chapters 15–17 came from another that an editor inserted between them, creating the surviving seams and repetitions.

title: John from a Redactional Perspective
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a redactional study of the Gospel of John.
searchSummary: Introduces redaction criticism of John by asking which sources the evangelist used and how they were edited. Limited overlap and little verbatim agreement make direct dependence on the Synoptic Gospels uncertain; shared stories may instead derive from related oral traditions. Differences in style, especially the poetic Prologue, and repeated versions of Jesus' farewell teaching point toward other written materials. Internal literary seams provide the strongest evidence, developed further in the following post.

title: Keep on Keepin’ On?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks readers whether to continue the series on methods and the Gospel of John.

title: More on John from a Comparative Perspective
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the comparative method to show how John's miracles differ from the Synoptic Gospels.
searchSummary: Compares John's portrayal of Jesus' deeds and teachings with the Synoptic Gospels. John's fewer but more spectacular miracles are public signs designed to reveal Jesus' divine identity, unlike Synoptic miracles performed without such self-demonstration; the raising of Lazarus illustrates this contrast. John's Jesus also speaks chiefly about his heavenly origin and unique relationship with God rather than announcing the coming kingdom through parables. These differences produce substantially different presentations of Jesus.
topics: Signs in the Gospel of John

title: The Gospel of John from a Comparative Perspective
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a comparative study of John and the Synoptic Gospels.
searchSummary: Compares the contents of John with Matthew, Mark, and Luke to demonstrate how distinctive the Fourth Gospel is. John omits major Synoptic episodes including the virgin birth, temptation, parables, exorcisms, Transfiguration, institution of the Lord's Supper, and Gethsemane prayer. In their place it offers unique signs and extended dialogues with Nicodemus, the Samaritan woman, opponents, and disciples. Even where the Gospels share characters or Passion events, John's overall selection of material is markedly different.

title: The Gospel of John from a Thematic Perspective
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses a thematic method to study the Gospel of John.
searchSummary: Demonstrates a thematic approach to John by tracing ideas introduced in the Prologue through the rest of the Gospel. Jesus' preexistence, unity with God, life, light, heavenly mission, rejection, and return recur in later declarations, signs, discourses, and prayer. Conversations with Nicodemus and other audiences develop related claims that access to God depends on Jesus. Some themes nevertheless appear in divergent forms, a feature later used to reconstruct the social history behind the Gospel.

title: More Literary-Historical Perspectives on John
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues a literary-historical reading of the Gospel of John.
searchSummary: Outlines John's plot as an ancient biography centered on a preexistent divine revealer. Chapters 1–12 cover Jesus' public ministry, where seven signs support declarations that he came from heaven, producing both belief and rejection. Chapters 13–17 compress his final meal, foot washing, Farewell Discourse, promise of the Spirit, and prayer into one evening. Chapters 18–21 narrate betrayal, trial, crucifixion, resurrection, and appearances that vindicate Jesus as alive and divine.

title: The Gospel of John from a Literary-Historical Perspective
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a literary-historical reading of the Gospel of John.
searchSummary: Introduces a literary-historical reading of John as a Greco-Roman biography rather than only a theological meditation. Like the Synoptics, it presents a religious leader's life, teaching, miraculous deeds, death, and divine vindication within a chronological narrative. Its Prologue initially resembles mystical poetry, describing God's eternal Word as divine creator, life, and light. Only at the Prologue's conclusion does the reader learn that this Word became the biography's human subject, Jesus Christ.

title: Did Jesus Exist?  Video Presentation
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a video presentation on the historical argument that Jesus existed.
searchSummary: Introduces a University of North Carolina bookshop presentation on Did Jesus Exist? and the evidence for Jesus' historicity. Ehrman rejects mythicist claims that Jesus was invented or is too poorly attested to count as a meaningful historical figure, while distinguishing the historical person from later biblical portrayals. He also reflects on hostile reactions from some atheists, arguing that ideological investment on either the right or left can obstruct the historian's attempt to determine what actually happened in the past.

title: Jesus’ Birth: Some Comparisons
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Jesus' birth narratives to illustrate comparison between Matthew and Luke.
searchSummary: Introduces the comparative method by placing Matthew's and Luke's birth narratives side by side without assuming a shared source. Both have Jesus born in Bethlehem and raised in Nazareth, but Matthew treats Bethlehem as the family's home before Egypt and a later move, whereas Luke begins in Nazareth and returns there soon after a census-driven birth. Their broad similarity highlights substantially different and difficult-to-reconcile narratives that popular Christmas retellings combine.

title: The Comparative Method and Luke
author: BDEhrman
description: Applies the comparative method to the Gospel of Luke.
searchSummary: Applies comparative analysis to Luke's identity, preface, audience, and historical claims. Luke-Acts is an anonymous two-volume work whose formal preface acknowledges earlier written and oral sources and presents the Gospel as orderly history. Although 'most excellent Theophilus' could suggest a Roman official, the post argues that Luke was more likely Christian literature for insiders, reassuring believers that their movement had been socially respectable and nonviolent from its beginning.

title: The Comparative Method
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the comparative method for studying the Gospels.
searchSummary: Defines the comparative method as interpreting a text through its similarities to and differences from related works, without requiring proof that one used another as a source. Unlike a narrow use of redaction criticism, it considers both what an author changes and what remains shared. The post grounds the method in the relational nature of meaning and proposes comparing Luke with Matthew and Mark to identify Luke's distinctive portrayal of Jesus and major themes.

title: More on the Response Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses a response book written against How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Distinguishes Ehrman's historical investigation of early belief in Jesus' divinity from the theological premises he expects in the response book How God Became Jesus. Historians can analyze when and why followers called Jesus God without affirming or denying God's existence, whereas claims about what God actually did require religious assumptions. Ehrman also notes his revised view that followers regarded Jesus as divine as soon as resurrection belief arose, even though Jesus had not publicly claimed divinity.

title: Books and Response Books
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains response books and reactions to How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Explains how media attention, controversy, and response books can draw readers to a trade book more effectively than advertising. Two rebuttals appeared around How Jesus Became God's release, including How God Became Jesus, written by evangelical scholars who received Ehrman's manuscript under a nondisclosure agreement. Ehrman welcomes informed disagreement but observes that the response volume's promotional summary appears to refute a claim he does not make: that Jesus' divinity was invented only centuries later.

title: Video: Does It Matter If Jesus Was Married?
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a video discussion about whether it would matter if Jesus were married.
searchSummary: Introduces a panel with Karen King and Mark Jordan asking what a married Jesus would mean for Christian theology, practice, and politics. Prompted by the Coptic fragment called the Gospel of Jesus' Wife, the discussion concentrates on the implications of the idea rather than deciding the fragment's authenticity, which many Coptic scholars doubted. Ehrman also addresses the prior historical question of whether Jesus was married, while the panel explores how such a possibility could affect changing Christian traditions.

title: The Literary-Historical Method and History
author: BDEhrman
description: Clarifies how the literary-historical method relates to historical claims.
searchSummary: Distinguishes literary-historical interpretation from investigation of factual history. Despite its name, the literary-historical method asks how a Gospel functions as a literary work and what distinctive portrait its author creates, not whether Jesus actually said or did what it narrates. Gospel discrepancies therefore have two separate implications: literarily, each account must be read independently; historically, incompatible details require critical criteria. Both inquiries are valuable, but they answer different questions and must not be confused.

title: Jesus’ Death and Resurrection in Mark
author: BDEhrman
description: Reads Jesus' death and resurrection in Mark through a literary-historical method.
searchSummary: Explains how Mark's crucifixion and empty-tomb ending reveal Jesus as the suffering Son of God. Jesus dies abandoned and anguished, but the torn Temple curtain signifies access to God through his sacrifice, and a gentile centurion recognizes the identity missed by his followers. The women then flee without reporting the resurrection, preserving the disciples' ignorance. Mark's readers nevertheless understand Jesus' vindication, the extension of salvation to gentiles, and the meaning of discipleship through suffering.

title: Mark’s Suffering Son of God
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Mark's portrayal of Jesus as the suffering Son of God.
searchSummary: Explains Mark's presentation of Jesus as the suffering Son of God through three passion predictions and the disciples' repeated failures. Peter rejects suffering, the disciples argue over greatness, and James and John seek prominence; Jesus instead defines following him through the cross, servanthood, and becoming slave of all. The narrative then advances from conflict in Jerusalem through arrest, denial, trial, and crucifixion. Mark makes suffering and death essential to Jesus' messianic identity rather than an accidental defeat.

title: Snake-Handling and the Gospel of Mark
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses snake-handling and the longer ending of Mark.
searchSummary: Connects modern Christian snake handling to a saying found only in the later ending added to Mark. The earliest recoverable Gospel ends at 16:8 with frightened women remaining silent, while scribes supplied resurrection appearances and promises about tongues, poison, healing, and snakes. Manuscript absence, distinctive vocabulary, changed style, and an awkward transition establish that these verses were not original. A pastor's death from snakebite illustrates the danger of building a practice on this secondary passage.

title: More on Mark
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues a literary-historical reading of Mark's portrayal of Jesus.
searchSummary: Explains Mark's theme of Jesus as the misunderstood Son of God through a literary-historical reading. Family, townspeople, leaders, and disciples remain blind despite his authority, while a two-stage healing symbolizes Peter's partial recognition. Peter calls Jesus Messiah but rejects the necessary suffering that defines Mark's Christ, earning a rebuke as Satan. The Gospel therefore contrasts conventional expectations of a powerful deliverer with its own claim that true perception recognizes Jesus specifically as the suffering Son.

title: More on the Beginning of Mark’s Gospel
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues reading the opening of Mark as an ancient biography of Jesus.
searchSummary: Presents Mark's Jesus as the authoritative yet opposed Son of God. Disciples immediately obey him, crowds marvel at his teaching, demons submit, and illnesses yield, but family, followers, and religious leaders still misunderstand him. Conflict grows over forgiveness, purity, association with sinners, Sabbath practice, and the Temple, although Mark portrays Jesus as faithful to Judaism rather than its enemy. Opposition culminates in execution because Israel's leaders cannot recognize God's representative or accept his interpretation of human need.

title: The Beginning of Mark’s Gospel/Biography
author: BDEhrman
description: Reads the beginning of Mark as ancient biography focused on Jesus' character.
searchSummary: Reads Mark's opening as an ancient biography that establishes Jesus' character through Jewish titles and early actions. "Messiah" evokes an anointed king or heavenly deliverer, while "Son of God" can identify a human specially chosen to mediate divine power. John the Baptist, scriptural fulfillment, baptism, the heavenly voice, temptation, and proclamation of God's kingdom present Jesus as God's authorized agent. The narrative must then explain how this powerful messianic Son could end as a Roman-executed criminal.

title: The Gospels as Biographies
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the Gospels can be studied as ancient biographies.
searchSummary: Explains why the Gospels are best read as ancient Greco-Roman biographies rather than modern documented lives. Ancient biographers used oral traditions, speeches, anecdotes, conflicts, and miracles to reveal a subject's stable character and encourage imitation, not to trace psychological development through comprehensive factual research. As biographies of a religious figure, the Gospels naturally emphasize Jesus's miraculous identity, teaching, deeds, death, and exaltation, with defining traits established early; each nevertheless offers its own portrait within the flexible genre.

title: How To Study the Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces methods for studying the Gospels and their distinctive messages.

title: Differences in the Gospels and Redaction Criticism
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Gospel differences lead into redaction criticism.
searchSummary: Shows how Gospel discrepancies can reveal an author's distinctive theology through redaction criticism. John's placement of Jesus's death before Passover portrays him as the Passover lamb, while Mark and Luke depict sharply different attitudes as Jesus dies; harmonizing them obscures both messages. Because Matthew and Luke used Mark, their additions and alterations identify interpretive priorities. Matthew's genealogy and infancy narratives, for example, establish Jesus's Jewish identity, Davidic descent, messianic timing, and unusual birth despite tracing Joseph's lineage.

title: Similarities and Differences: The Synoptic Problem
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Synoptic Problem through similarities and differences among Matthew, Mark, and Luke.

title: Discrepancies in the Resurrection Narratives
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses resurrection narratives to illustrate discrepancies among the Gospels.
searchSummary: Uses student comparisons of the resurrection narratives to show that Gospel differences include irreconcilable claims, not merely omitted details. Luke keeps the disciples in Jerusalem until Pentecost, whereas Matthew sends them immediately to Galilee to meet the risen Jesus. Ehrman treats recognizing this conflict as the beginning of interpretation: discrepancies reveal each Gospel writer's distinctive emphases and help readers understand what kind of writings the Gospels are.

title: Was Jesus Inserted Into Paul’s Letters?
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers whether Jesus could have been inserted into Paul's letters by later scribes.
searchSummary: Argues that references to the historical Jesus probably originated in Paul's letters rather than being inserted wholesale by later scribes. Although the earliest substantial Pauline manuscript dates around 200 and certainty about every word is impossible, separate letters circulated through multiple transmission lines before collection. Coordinated insertion across those independent textual histories is implausible, and a fabricator would likely have added far more biographical detail. The evidence supports probable authenticity without claiming absolute textual certainty.

title: Abraham and Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to a question about Abraham, Jesus, and historical claims in Genesis.

title: More on Camels and Genesis
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues discussion of camels, Genesis, and historical anachronism.

title: Camels and the Book of Genesis
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses camels in Genesis as a possible anachronism in the patriarchal narratives.

title: Jesus Kissing Mary Magdalene
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains references to Jesus kissing Mary Magdalene in the Gospel of Philip.

title: Video: Illuminated Manuscripts and Legends about Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a Getty Museum lecture on illuminated manuscripts and legends about Jesus.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's Getty Museum lecture on medieval illuminated Gospel manuscripts and legends about Jesus. Their images preserve cultural and historical evidence beyond the accompanying written text, sometimes depicting stories absent from the canonical Gospels. These visual narratives show that medieval artists knew noncanonical traditions and could treat apocryphal episodes as Gospel truth alongside Scripture, making manuscript illumination a source for tracing how stories about Jesus circulated, acquired authority, and shaped Christian imagination.

title: Mary Magdalene as a Prostitute?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Mary Magdalene came to be identified as a prostitute.

title: Mary Magdalene in Various Guises
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the complicated traditions that reshaped Mary Magdalene's image.

title: Jesus and Sexuality
author: BDEhrman
description: Considers what a married Jesus would mean for views of sexuality.

title: A Married Jesus and Celibate Priests
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses Jesus, marriage, and celibate priests.

title: Jesus and Marriage: An Actual Argument!
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates an argument that Jesus may have been married.
searchSummary: Argues from Jesus's apocalyptic ethics that he was not married. Jesus instructed followers to live now according to the coming kingdom's conditions, including peace, justice, healing, and relief of suffering. When challenged about resurrection, he taught that people in the kingdom would neither marry nor have sex but live like angels. Bart concludes that celibacy coheres with Jesus's own program and with other unmarried apocalyptic Jews, whereas claims of a prior marriage lack evidence.

title: Jesus and Mary Magdalene
author: BDEhrman

title: Was Jesus Married?

title: Video: The Lost Gospel of Judas Iscariot Part 1
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a lecture on the Gospel of Judas at the Ramtha School of Enlightenment.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's lecture on the Gospel of Judas at the Ramtha School of Enlightenment, a retreat community centered on teachings said to be channeled through its founder. The audience's belief that humans possess an inner divinity made Gnostic texts especially attractive, despite Ehrman's sharply different worldview. He describes the school, its practices, and the audience's receptive response, then presents the lecture as the first part of the event, with a later question-and-answer session to follow.

title: The New and Improved After the New Testament
author: BDEhrman

title: Final Bit of The Introduction to After the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Concludes the introduction to After the New Testament and explains added chapters.
searchSummary: The expanded introduction to After the New Testament surveys how second- and third-century Christians developed scripture, interpretation, preaching, church government, worship, gender roles, ethics, and theology. Competing groups claimed different apostolic books and beliefs, while proto-orthodox leaders increasingly defined canon, hierarchy, practice, and doctrine. The collection emphasizes learning this history through primary sources that reveal Christianity's diversity before the Council of Nicaea.

title: More on After the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues the introduction to After the New Testament and its chapters on early Christianity.

title: My New Edition of After the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the second edition of After the New Testament and its collection of early Christian texts.

title: Followup on the NT Quiz
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the purpose of a New Testament pop quiz and what the questions are meant to show.
searchSummary: Explains the teaching purpose behind the answers to a first-day New Testament quiz. Questions about the canon, Greek language, dates, Gospel discrepancies, Pauline authorship, ancient names, and the Jewish identity of Jesus and his earliest followers introduce foundational historical issues. Rather than merely testing recall, the quiz gives Ehrman opportunities to explain chronology, textual differences, pseudonymity, and the Jewish and Greco-Roman settings needed for studying early Christianity.

title: My New Testament Pop Quiz
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a New Testament pop quiz for an introductory course.
searchSummary: Reproduces an ungraded first-day quiz used with roughly 240 students in an introductory New Testament course. Its eleven questions cover the canon, original language, chronology, Gospel accounts of Jesus' baptism, crucifixion, and burial, Pauline authorship, ancient names, and the Jewish identity of major early Christian figures. The exercise serves as both an icebreaker and a diagnostic teaching tool, revealing how little many students know despite prior Bible study.

title: My New Testament Syllabus
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents the syllabus for an introductory New Testament course.
searchSummary: Outlines an introductory New Testament course for approximately 240 students taught from a nonconfessional historical and literary perspective. Students learn the writings' contents, messages, differences, and contexts while evaluating evidence and forming their own conclusions. Position papers, discussion sections, debates, and examinations address the Gospels, historical Jesus, Paul, anti-Judaism, disputed letters, early Christian diversity, Revelation, and textual criticism, emphasizing independent thought and evidence-based argument.

title: Final Loose Threads on the Zealot Hypothesis
author: BDEhrman
description: Wraps up remaining issues in the critique of the Zealot hypothesis.

title: Jesus’ Crucifixion as King of the Jews
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Jesus' crucifixion as King of the Jews in relation to political insurgency claims.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus was crucified as a claimed future king, not as an armed insurgent. Early traditions portray him as opposing violence, while a likely authentic saying promises the twelve disciples authority in God's coming kingdom and implies that Jesus would rule above them. Judas may have exposed this private messianic expectation, and Pilate treated the claim as treason without regard for Jesus' belief that God, rather than human force, would establish the kingdom.

title: Jesus and the Temple
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques the use of the temple incident in Reza Aslan's portrait of Jesus.

title: Looking Ahead to 2014 on the Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Looks ahead to blog goals and challenges for 2014.

title: End of the Year Blog Reflection
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the blog's year at the end of 2013.

title: More Evidence that Jesus was an Apocalypticist
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents additional evidence for understanding Jesus as a Jewish apocalypticist.
searchSummary: Presents the “beginning and end” argument that Jesus was an apocalypticist rather than a militant zealot. Jesus began by accepting baptism from John, an independently attested apocalyptic preacher of imminent judgment, and the earliest post-crucifixion churches expected Jesus's heavenly return and the end of the age. Because Jesus's ministry connects these movements, and early Gospel sources preserve matching teachings, Bart concludes that divine intervention rather than armed revolt defined Jesus's message.

title: The Later De-apocalypticizing of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that later traditions reduced the apocalyptic edge of Jesus' message.
searchSummary: Traces how later Christian sources muted Jesus' apocalyptic teaching as the expected end failed to arrive within his followers' lifetimes. Luke modifies Mark's predictions of an imminent kingdom and presents God's rule as already active in Jesus' ministry; John emphasizes present eternal life through faith in Jesus. The Gospel of Thomas goes further by rejecting a future earthly kingdom in favor of an inward reality, revealing a progressive de-apocalypticizing of earlier traditions.

title: Back to Aslan’s Thesis.   An Alternative View: Jesus the Apocalypticist
author: BDEhrman
description: Contrasts Reza Aslan's Zealot thesis with Jesus as an apocalypticist.
searchSummary: Offers an apocalyptic reconstruction of Jesus as a better-supported alternative to Reza Aslan's portrayal of him as a revolutionary zealot. Scattered details may suggest political resistance, but Mark, Q, M, and L independently and repeatedly present Jesus predicting God's supernatural overthrow of evil, the Son of Man's judgment, and an earthly kingdom within his generation. Bart argues that this pervasive early evidence outweighs isolated hints of armed nationalism and explains Jesus without making him an advocate of military revolt.

title: 2009 Debate With Mike Licona: Can Historians Prove the Resurrection of Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a debate with Mike Licona on whether historians can prove Jesus' resurrection.
searchSummary: Introduces a debate with Mike Licona over whether historians can prove Jesus' resurrection, carefully distinguishing that methodological question from whether the resurrection actually occurred. Licona argues that historical evidence establishes the event beyond reasonable doubt, while Ehrman denies that the discipline can demonstrate divine action. The post provides background on Licona's apologetic scholarship and the debate setting, then directs readers to the video. Its focus is the evidentiary limits of historical proof applied to a miracle claim.

title: About the Blog and Two Clarifications about Reza Aslan’s Zealot
author: BDEhrman
description: Clarifies points about the blog and about Reza Aslan's Zealot.

title: Aslan’s Zealot: To Start With…
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a series evaluating Reza Aslan's Zealot.

title: My New Teaching Company Course
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces work on a Teaching Company course based on How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Describes preparing a twenty-four-lecture Great Courses series on How Jesus Became God and the unusual discipline required to deliver each lecture alone on camera in exactly thirty minutes. Ehrman presents the course's larger historical premise: without belief in Jesus' divinity, Christianity would likely have remained a Jewish sect and the Roman Empire and Western civilization would have developed differently. He regards the course and book as his most important work in public scholarship.

title: Jesus Final Exam
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents the final exam for a course on Jesus in scholarship and film.
searchSummary: Presents the final examination for a first-year seminar on Jesus in scholarship and film. Students choose two essays addressing historical methods, differences among Gospel portrayals, criteria such as dissimilarity and independent attestation, the reliability of traditions, the apocalyptic Jesus, and comparisons between films and ancient sources. The questions require students to evaluate evidence, compare interpretations, and explain both literary portrayals of Jesus and historical reconstructions of his life.

title: Infancy Gospel of Thomas: The Technical vs. the Interesting
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how to present the Infancy Gospel of Thomas in a general-audience lecture.

title: Taking Jesus the Wunderkind Seriously
author: BDEhrman
description: Takes the Infancy Gospel of Thomas seriously as an early Christian portrayal of Jesus.

title: Jesus: L’enfant terrible?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a Smithsonian lecture on non-canonical Gospels and the child Jesus.

title: Video: Ehrman & Evans 2012 Debate – Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the second part of a debate with Craig Evans on the historical Jesus.
searchSummary: Introduces a second debate between Ehrman and evangelical New Testament scholar Craig Evans on whether the New Testament presents a historically reliable portrait of Jesus. Although they had debated the same question the previous evening, both change their presentations after hearing the other's arguments. Ehrman therefore offers the recording not as a duplicate but as an opportunity to compare revised cases for and against Gospel reliability, while the short post leaves the actual historical evidence and rebuttals to the video.

title: Jesus the Magician
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses Morton Smith's claim about Jesus as a magician.

title: The Giving Season
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on Christmas as a season for giving and charity.
searchSummary: Reflects on Christmas giving as a humane practice that need not depend on religious belief. Bart contrasts Christianity's history of harm and holiday materialism with traditions of self-giving, then explains why empathy, morality, and concern for suffering can arise from human nature rather than divine commands. He encourages readers of every belief to support a charity and notes that donations through the blog go entirely to organizations fighting hunger and homelessness.

title: A Third View of Jesus’ Body at the Resurrection
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a third early Christian view of Jesus' resurrected body.

title: A Gnostic View of Jesus’ Resurrection
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains a Gnostic view of Jesus' resurrection.

title: Paul and the Resurrection of a Spiritual Body
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Paul's view of resurrection as involving a spiritual body.
searchSummary: Explains Paul's belief that Jesus and his followers receive transformed “spiritual bodies” at resurrection. First Corinthians 15 opposes Christians who treated resurrection as an already realized inner experience; Paul insists bodily resurrection remains future because believers still inhabit mortal bodies. In ancient thought, spirit could be refined material rather than body's immaterial opposite. Jesus' corpse was therefore raised into an immortal body, establishing the pattern for believers while prompting later Christians to emphasize different aspects of Paul's formulation.

title: Is History Possible?
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses whether history is possible in light of social memory studies.
searchSummary: Considers and rejects the claim that pervasive memory distortion makes historical knowledge of Jesus impossible. Zeba Crook argues that because people cannot distinguish accurate from altered memories, later Gospel recollections and traditional historical criteria cannot recover Jesus' life. Ehrman responds that this reasoning would erase knowledge of every past event and undermine courts and scholarship; history cannot provide certainty about every detail, but comparative evidence can still establish many events with reasonable or overwhelming probability.

title: Papers at the SBL
author: BDEhrman
description: Reports on papers at the Society of Biblical Literature meeting.

title: SBL and ALL those Books
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the Society of Biblical Literature meeting and its large book exhibit.
searchSummary: Reflects on the Society of Biblical Literature book exhibit as both a center of professional connection and evidence of academic overproduction. Thousands of new volumes make it impossible for scholars to remain current beyond their active research areas, while publishing economics and tenure requirements encourage books that add little knowledge. Ehrman distinguishes necessary original contributions from repetitive commentary and argues that scholars should publish when they offer a genuinely new subject, method, or interpretation rather than merely satisfy institutional incentives.

title: The Gospel of Peter in a Papyrus Fragment?
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses a papyrus fragment that may relate to the Gospel of Peter.

title: My SBL Conference
author: BDEhrman
description: Reports from the Society of Biblical Literature meeting and mentions The Other Gospels.

title: Amusing Fund Raising and the Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Highlights fundraising for Urban Ministries of Durham and the blog's charitable work.
searchSummary: Highlights an unusual fundraising campaign by Urban Ministries of Durham, the charity receiving the largest share of blog support. Bart praises UMD for combining food and emergency housing with efforts to move people into permanent employment and homes. He links readers to its humorous Names for Change campaign and invites reactions. The post also reminds newer members that their fees and donations support the North Carolina Food Bank, CARE, and Doctors Without Borders.

title: Errant Texts and Historians
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers a question about original New Testament texts and historians' use of imperfect sources.
searchSummary: Explains why uncertainty about exact New Testament wording does not prevent historians from using passages such as Galatians 2. Ehrman distinguishes challenges to faith in an inerrant text from historical judgments based on probability. Manuscript agreement, literary context, vocabulary, and other evidence make Paul's meetings with Cephas and James highly probable, even though historians cannot claim absolute certainty about any lost original document.

title: Jesus and Brian!!!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a Life of Brian conference on the film and the historical Jesus.

title: Is The NT Portrayal of Jesus Accurate?  Debate With Craig Evans
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a debate with Craig Evans on whether the New Testament portrayal of Jesus is accurate.
searchSummary: Introduces a debate with New Testament scholar Craig Evans over whether the New Testament presents a reliable portrait of the historical Jesus. Evans defends the Gospels' reliability, while Ehrman challenges it; both concentrate on the four canonical accounts through opening arguments, rebuttals, and audience questions. The post primarily supplies Evans's scholarly background and the event video rather than rehearsing either case. It frames Gospel reliability as a historical question on which qualified scholars can reach sharply different conclusions.

title: Problem on the Site
author: BDEhrman
description: Reports a technical problem that prevented comments from posting on the site.

title: Why Historians Can Talk “About” the Resurrection
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why historians can discuss resurrection claims without proving a miracle occurred.
searchSummary: Explains that historians cannot confirm or disconfirm divine resurrection but can investigate associated human events and claims. Questions about Jesus' burial, an empty tomb, the first resurrection proclamation, and disciples' experiences remain historically discussable. Ehrman argues that visions most likely generated belief, and visions can be studied without deciding whether they were veridical encounters or hallucinations. Historical analysis thus addresses testimony, experience, and the development of belief while leaving supernatural causation outside its demonstrable conclusions.

title: Historians and the Problem of Miracle
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why miracles create special problems for historical method.
searchSummary: Explains why historical method cannot establish a miracle as the most probable account of a past event. Historians reconstruct unique, unrepeated events from surviving evidence and ordinarily prefer explanations consistent with repeatedly observed human and natural experience. Mistake, exaggeration, or deception remains more probable than an event that contradicts normal expectations, even with credible testimony. This limitation does not prove miracles impossible; it means historians who affirm one do so as believers rather than through the discipline's shared evidentiary standards.

title: History is Not the Past
author: BDEhrman
description: Distinguishes the past from historical reconstruction in discussing resurrection claims.
searchSummary: Distinguishes the entire past from history, the smaller portion historians can probably establish from surviving evidence and shared methods. Historical arguments cannot presuppose their conclusions, privilege favorable evidence, or rely on disputed assumptions about supernatural agents. Multiple attestation supports ordinary claims such as Jesus' existence, but cannot by itself demonstrate that God raised him, because that conclusion requires theological premises not shared across the discipline. Resurrection may belong to the past if true, yet remain historically unprovable.

title: Multiple Attestation for Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares multiple attestation for Jesus' existence with claims about the resurrection.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: Who Can Still Be A Christian?
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers whether Christians can accept an apocalyptic Jesus whose expected end did not arrive.
searchSummary: Explains how informed Christians can remain believers while accepting that Jesus wrongly predicted God's kingdom within his generation. Bart once treated Jesus as a genuinely human figure mistaken about timing but right that God would ultimately defeat suffering and evil. As an agnostic he no longer expects supernatural intervention, yet retains Jesus's ethical call to oppose human causes of suffering. He relocates hope from divine rescue to people creating meaning and helping others in this world.

title: Video:  Forgery in the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a lecture on forgery in the New Testament.
searchSummary: Introduces a video lecture based on Forged that explains why scholars identify some early Christian writings as works falsely composed in apostolic names. Ehrman distinguishes deliberate authorial claims in books such as Ephesians, 1 Timothy, 1 and 2 Peter, James, and Jude from anonymous Gospels that later received traditional names. Aimed at a general audience, the lecture outlines the evidence used to challenge alleged authorship, estimates how many New Testament writings may be forged, and includes an extended audience discussion.

title: Carrier, Bayes Theorem, and Jesus’ Existence
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to Richard Carrier's use of Bayes' theorem in arguments about Jesus' existence.
searchSummary: Questions Richard Carrier's use of Bayes' theorem to argue that Jesus never existed. Ehrman notes that other apologists have used the same framework to claim mathematical proof for God and Jesus' resurrection, suggesting that subjective inputs can produce incompatible conclusions rather than objective historical certainty. He points readers to R. Joseph Hoffmann's critique while explaining that mythicism lacks acceptance among specialists and that hostile, endlessly expanding exchanges make direct participation in the controversy unproductive.

title: New Hermeneia Manuscript
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a newly identified hermeneia manuscript of the Gospel of John.
searchSummary: Reports Brice Jones's identification of an unpublished Coptic parchment fragment of John 3 at Yale. Like five previously known Greek examples, it contains hermeneiai, short divinatory sayings associated with Gospel text; uniquely, both its biblical passage and hermeneiai are entirely Coptic. The fragment was registered as sa 972 and prepared for publication in New Testament Studies. Its discovery expands the small group of enigmatic Johannine manuscripts apparently used for interpreting future outcomes.

title: Fortune Telling with Manuscripts
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Gospel of John manuscripts used for fortune telling.
searchSummary: Explains unusual Gospel manuscripts containing the label hermeneia followed by brief promises or predictions unrelated to the adjacent biblical text. Comparisons with ancient Books of Fate suggest that users selected these sayings by chance to answer questions, effectively practicing Christian fortune-telling. Such use reflects belief that scriptural manuscripts possessed sacred power as physical objects, much as biblical texts were worn as amulets or placed nearby to repel evil, heal illness, or provide supernatural protection.

title: Video: Misquoting Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a video feature with a lecture on Misquoting Jesus.
searchSummary: Introduces an early Stanford lecture based on Misquoting Jesus, titled Scribes Who Altered Scripture and Readers Who May Never Know. Ehrman presents it as part of a new blog feature pairing recordings of his lectures and interviews with additional comments. The video also includes an extensive audience question-and-answer period covering subjects beyond the prepared lecture, making it useful both for his explanation of New Testament textual change and for his responses to a wider range of questions.

title: Writers Who Contradict Themselves
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how New Testament writers can contradict themselves.
searchSummary: Explains how New Testament authors could contradict themselves without recognizing their mistakes. Readers and writers naturally expect consistency and therefore overlook discrepancies, while ancient oral reading practices and lower literacy may have made such problems still harder to detect. Ehrman distinguishes these internal lapses from the more common conflicts between authors, including Acts versus Paul, differing Gospel portraits of Jesus, and contrasting theological positions in Paul, James, Luke, and Romans.

title: Discrepancies *Inside* the Fourth Gospel
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses discrepancies within the Gospel of John.
searchSummary: Identifies internal discrepancies in John as literary seams created when an editor combined different sources. Examples include a “second” sign after several signs, unexplained geographical movements, Jesus claiming no disciple asked where he was going after two had done so, and a command to leave followed by three chapters of teaching. Dividing the Farewell Discourse into two originally separate accounts explains its repetition and contradictions, showing how source combination can produce tensions within one finished book.

title: Was Paul Contemplating Suicide?
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers whether Paul may have contemplated suicide in Philippians.

title: A Rather Serious Mistake
author: BDEhrman
description: Corrects a mistake about Paul's view of resurrection.

title: Why Are There Contradictions in the New Testament?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why contradictions appear in the New Testament writings.
searchSummary: Distinguishes contradictions between New Testament authors from inconsistencies within a single writer. Different authors inherited or reshaped traditions, held different views, and never expected their books to be assembled into a perfectly consistent canon. Internal tensions may instead reflect retold stories, incorporated sources, carelessness, or changing beliefs; Ehrman begins with Paul's apparent shift from expecting to survive until Jesus' return to anticipating his own death.

title: Upcoming Lectures at the Smithsonian
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces upcoming Smithsonian lectures on non-canonical Gospels.
searchSummary: Outlines a Smithsonian lecture series on Gospels and related writings outside the New Testament. The sessions examine infancy stories in the Proto-Gospel of James and Infancy Gospel of Thomas, Jesus' sayings in the Gospel of Thomas, the alternative Passion and resurrection account in the Gospel of Peter, and later Pilate Gospels. Together these texts reveal how later Christians imaginatively expanded Jesus' life, expressed distinctive beliefs, and increasingly shifted responsibility for his death from Pilate to Jewish opponents.

title: Jesus’ Brother and the Mythicists (Part 2)
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses James the brother of Jesus as a problem for mythicist arguments.
searchSummary: Rejects Robert Price's proposal that James was called Jesus' brother because he uniquely reflected the heavenly Christ rather than shared a family relationship. The Acts of Thomas treats Thomas as Jesus' physical twin, not merely a spiritual counterpart, while texts about James assume an actual sibling relationship. Price's comparison with a nineteenth-century Chinese leader who called himself Jesus' little brother is historically remote. Ehrman concludes that these parallels do not explain away Paul's acquaintance with Jesus' brother.

title: Brothers of Jesus and the Mythicists
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Paul's references to James and Peter challenge mythicist claims.
searchSummary: Argues that Paul's identification of James as “the brother of the Lord” refers to Jesus' biological brother and creates a major problem for mythicism. Paul distinguishes Jesus' brothers from himself and Cephas, so “brother” cannot simply mean any believer, and independent sources likewise name James among Jesus' siblings. The proposal of an otherwise unattested Jerusalem missionary fraternity fails because no source records such a group and Cephas should belong to it. The straightforward reading is that Paul knew Jesus' brother.

title: Jesus’ Brothers?!?  And the Proto-Gospel of James
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses Jesus' brothers and the Proto-Gospel of James.

title: When Time Stood Still
author: BDEhrman
description: Highlights a striking scene in the Proto-Gospel of James where time stands still.

title: The Gospel according to Mel
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques Mel Gibson's Passion of the Christ as a portrayal of Jesus' death.

title: Jesus’ Passion in the Movies
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how films handle differences among Gospel passion narratives.

title: My Jesus Class and … Destroying Christianity?
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses passion narratives in a Jesus course to discuss Gospel discrepancies.
searchSummary: Uses classroom comparisons of the Gospel passion and resurrection narratives to identify conflicts in chronology, trial scenes, crucifixion details, witnesses, and post-resurrection locations. Ehrman argues that these discrepancies expose each author's distinctive literary message and prevent all four accounts from serving as one seamless history. Recognizing them neither attacks Christianity nor requires disbelief; it supports informed interpretation and the historical methods needed to determine what probably happened.

title: Podcast on My New Course
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a podcast about a Great Courses class on early Christian controversies.
searchSummary: Directs readers to a Great Courses podcast featuring Ehrman's course The Greatest Controversies of Early Christianity. The episode offers an accessible introduction to the course and places it alongside conversations with two other professors about their own lecture series. Rather than presenting the course material itself, the post recommends the podcast as an easy way to learn what the early Christianity course covers and how the participating instructors approach their subjects.

title: Jesus Books
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends accessible scholarly books on the historical Jesus.

title: Some Blog Self-Scrutiny
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the blog's finances, readership, and charitable goals.

title: Constantine and Christianity
author: BDEhrman
description: Corrects misconceptions about Constantine, Christianity, and the Council of Nicaea.
searchSummary: Constantine ended the Great Persecution and gave Christianity legal recognition, money, buildings, honor, and imperial favor, but he did not make it Rome's official religion. Earlier persecution had been sporadic rather than continuous, with the first empire-wide pressure arising only in the third century. Constantine's support greatly accelerated Christian growth and status, while Theodosius made Christianity effectively official decades later in 380.

title: More Conspiracy Nonsense
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to a conspiracy theory about Josephus, Romans, and the invention of Jesus.
searchSummary: Rejects Joseph Atwill's claim that Roman aristocrats fabricated Christianity as propaganda to pacify rebellious Jews. The theory conflicts with chronology because Paul's letters presuppose Jesus before the Jewish revolt, while its supposed Roman authors created a Messiah who predicted violent judgment, spoke of bringing a sword, and was executed for insurrection. Ehrman also challenges the premises of constant revolts, Jewish missionary activity, and ineffective Roman force, presenting the proposal as an untrained conspiracy theory rather than credible ancient history.

title: Widespread Misconceptions about the Council of Nicea
author: BDEhrman
description: Corrects widespread misconceptions about the Council of Nicaea.
searchSummary: Corrects two widespread misconceptions about Nicaea. The council neither selected the New Testament canon nor voted on whether Jesus was divine. Canon formation remained a prolonged, disputed process, and Athanasius first listed the familiar twenty-seven books only in 367. At Nicaea, bishops who already regarded Christ as divine debated whether he was subordinate and created or equal and coeternal with the Father. The overwhelming vote against Arius did not immediately end that theological controversy.

title: My New Course for the Great Courses
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a new Great Courses project on How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Announces a twenty-four-lecture Great Courses course based on How Jesus Became God and explains the educational reach of the series. Comparing audience reactions to his earlier courses, Ehrman suggests that critical study of the New Testament can challenge personal beliefs more directly than discussions of later Christian controversies, which may explain why Lost Christianities receives especially strong ratings. The post focuses on the teaching project and its audience rather than detailing the new course's Christological arguments.

title: Colbert on his Hero O’Reilly
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares Stephen Colbert's response to Bill O'Reilly's Killing Jesus.

title: Jesus as a First-Century Tea-Partier
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques Bill O'Reilly's portrayal of Jesus as politically aligned with modern conservatism.

title: Follow That Star!!
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the star of Bethlehem creates problems if read as a literal guide.

title: Riled by O’Reilly
author: BDEhrman
description: Expresses frustration with historical problems in Bill O'Reilly's Killing Jesus.

title: Killing Jesus is Killing Me….
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques the opening claims and method of Bill O'Reilly's Killing Jesus.

title: Bill O’Reilly’s Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces plans to review Bill O'Reilly's Killing Jesus.

title: Jesus Position Papers
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains position papers assigned in a course on Jesus in scholarship and film.
searchSummary: Explains the short position papers assigned in a seminar on Jesus in scholarship and film. These two-page exercises prepare students for discussion by requiring evidence-based arguments on Gospel portrayals, birth and passion narratives, miracle stories, noncanonical texts, historical criteria, Jesus' final days, and cinematic interpretations. Graded satisfactory or unsatisfactory, the papers have no predetermined correct answer; their purpose is to develop careful comparison, clear reasoning, and active participation.

title: You Won’t Find *This* in the New Testament!
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses unusual traditions in the Proto-Gospel of James.

title: Jesus at the Movies: Infancy Narratives
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses film portrayals of infancy narratives to compare Matthew and Luke.
searchSummary: Describes a classroom exercise comparing Matthew's and Luke's infancy narratives before examining how films depict Jesus' birth. Students identify shared claims alongside incompatible hometowns, chronology, Egypt journey, census, shepherds, and magi. Film directors must choose, combine, or supplement these accounts, so viewing adaptations after close textual comparison reveals how works from Ben-Hur to Jesus of Nazareth and Life of Brian construct their own versions of the story.

title: But Did It Really Happen?
author: BDEhrman
description: Clarifies the difference between interpreting Gospel stories and deciding whether events happened.
searchSummary: Separates two legitimate questions about Gospel narratives: what an author communicates as literature and what actually happened in Jesus' life. Mark's portrayal of Jesus healing a leper remains meaningful for literary interpretation even if the event is not historical, just as fiction or drama about historical figures can reward analysis. Historians may also use such texts cautiously to reconstruct events, but that requires different criteria. Confusing authorial meaning with historical factuality produces mistaken conclusions about both.

title: Early Gospels: A Messier Scenario
author: BDEhrman
description: Imagines a messier scenario for first- and second-century Gospel traditions.
searchSummary: Proposes that early Gospel transmission was far less stable than a model of fixed books simply copying one another. Written Gospels may have circulated in multiple editions while interacting with oral retellings, scribal changes, and other lost accounts; Luke itself may once have lacked its infancy narratives. If Matthew and Luke used different forms of Mark, and later works drew on similarly fluid traditions, apparent literary dependence and changes become much harder to reconstruct confidently.

title: The Messy World of Second Century Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the messy world of second-century Gospels through Papyrus Egerton.

title: Jesus’ Anger in Mark 1:41
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Jesus' anger in Mark 1:41 and its meaning in the healing of a leper.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus becomes angry in Mark 1:41 because the leper implicitly questions his willingness to heal. Explanations involving future disobedience, interrupted preaching, Jewish law, disease, Satan, or generalized suffering avoid the passage's direct wording. Elsewhere Mark links Jesus' anger to challenges against his authority, ability, or desire to heal, including Sabbath opposition, doubt about exorcism, and blocked access for children. Jesus therefore heals first and rebukes the man for doubting that he wants to help.

title: Jesus Getting Angry
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why a textual variant in Mark 1:41 may portray Jesus as angry.
searchSummary: Identifies a Markan pattern in which Jesus' anger occurs around healing or the transfer of divine power. He rebukes a father who doubts his ability to exorcise a boy, becomes indignant when disciples prevent children from receiving his touch, and condemns opponents who resist Sabbath healing. Mark does not explicitly attribute compassion in these scenes. The pattern supplies the literary context needed to explain why the original wording of Mark 1:41 may portray Jesus becoming angry before cleansing a leper.

title: Speaking of Lepers
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Mark's leper story as background for a textual problem.
searchSummary: Argues that Mark 1:41 originally portrayed Jesus becoming angry before healing a leper, although most manuscripts read "feeling compassion." Scribes had an obvious motive to soften the troubling emotion but little reason to introduce it. Matthew and Luke provide earlier indirect evidence because both omit Mark's emotion, just as they regularly remove Markan references to anger while preserving compassion. Their editorial pattern suggests that the copies of Mark available to them contained the difficult reading.

title: An Unknown Gospel
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a leper story from Papyrus Egerton as an unknown Gospel tradition.

title: The Lowdown on Why I Study the Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers a personal explanation for studying the Bible after losing faith.
searchSummary: Offers Ehrman's personal reasons for studying the Bible as a nonbeliever. He opposes its harmful misuse, not the Bible or Christianity, and argues that informed criticism requires understanding a subject deeply. The Bible is a culturally situated and internally diverse collection rather than a literal modern rulebook, so careful scholarship can challenge oppressive interpretations. Religious commitment is not required to study a tradition, and intellectual passion for early Christian history and literature is sufficient motivation.

title: Why Would Someone Like Me Study the Bible??
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers why someone without belief would devote a career to studying the Bible.
searchSummary: Explains why the Bible deserves historical and literary study regardless of a reader's beliefs. It stands at the center of Judaism and Christianity, has profoundly shaped Western institutions and culture, and continues to influence millions of people. Its teachings have inspired ethical service but have also been used to justify violence, slavery, racism, and oppression. Its enormous impact, frequent misunderstanding, and capacity for both constructive and harmful interpretation make informed study especially important.

title: My Bible Introduction!
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces publication of a historical and literary introduction to the Bible.

title: Apologies, Questions, and Excuses
author: BDEhrman
description: Apologizes for delayed answers to reader questions.

title: The Ebionites and their Gospel
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses the Gospel of the Ebionites through quotations preserved by Epiphanius.

title: Locusts or Pancakes?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains a Gospel of the Ebionites passage about John the Baptist's food.

title: Harmonizing the Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Gospel harmonization through a quotation from the Gospel of the Ebionites.
searchSummary: Criticizes harmonizing Gospel discrepancies by inventing additional events that no individual account reports. Proposals that Jesus cleansed the Temple twice or Peter denied him six times may preserve technical consistency, but they create a new composite Gospel and obscure each author's distinctive portrayal of Jesus. Ehrman argues that the Gospels should be read as separate works, just as stories by different writers are not combined to determine what either one meant.

title: Fun with the Jewish Christian Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Jewish Christian Gospels through fragmentary quotations in church fathers.

title: My PhD Seminar: Early Christian Apocrypha
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a PhD seminar syllabus on early Christian apocrypha.
searchSummary: Presents the syllabus for a doctoral seminar on early Christian apocrypha, including noncanonical Gospels, Acts, epistles, and apocalypses attributed to apostolic figures. Students read primary texts, translate Greek, lead substantial presentations, review scholarship on canon, and complete a revised research paper. The course examines textual, historical, and interpretive problems in works such as the Gospels of Thomas and Peter, apocryphal Acts, Pauline pseudepigrapha, and the Apocalypse of Peter.

title: Summing Up: Was Luke Luke?
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes the argument over whether Luke wrote Luke and Acts.
searchSummary: Summarizes the case against identifying the anonymous author of Luke-Acts as Luke, Paul's Gentile physician companion. The attribution appears only about a century after the Gospel was written, depends partly on Colossians, and conflicts with substantial differences between Acts' Paul and Paul's own letters concerning atonement, Jewish law, and pagan religion. The post accepts common authorship of Luke and Acts but concludes that Luke was anonymous and raises whether Acts uses the 'we' passages as a false authorial claim.

title: The Accuracy of Acts: Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues evaluating the historical accuracy of Acts.
searchSummary: Compares Paul's Areopagus speech in Acts with Romans to evaluate whether Acts accurately preserves his teaching. Acts says pagans were ignorant of the one God and that God overlooked their error, whereas Romans says they knew the creator, willfully embraced idols, and received divine punishment. The contrast is better explained if Luke composed Paul's speech, as ancient historians commonly did. Such discrepancies weaken both Acts' historical portrait of Paul and the claim that its author was his traveling companion.

title: The Historical Accuracy of Acts
author: BDEhrman
description: Begins evaluating Acts' historical accuracy in connection with Luke-Acts authorship.
searchSummary: Argues that Acts was probably not written by a companion who knew Paul personally because its account repeatedly conflicts with Paul's letters. Discrepancies concern Timothy's movements, Paul's first post-conversion visit to Jerusalem, his relationship with the original apostles, and his observance of Jewish law. Luke's portrayals serve a theological agenda of apostolic harmony and continuity with Judaism, whereas Paul describes greater independence and conflict. Acts therefore reveals Luke's understanding of Paul more reliably than Paul's actual biography or teaching.

title: Who Wrote Luke and Acts?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the traditional argument that Luke wrote Luke and Acts.
searchSummary: Examines the first-person 'we' passages in Acts, the principal evidence that its author traveled with Paul and therefore wrote the Gospel of Luke as an eyewitness companion. Their abrupt beginnings, endings, and shifts back to third person are difficult to explain as ordinary autobiography. The post argues that the author selectively inserted himself into travel scenes to give the narrative realistic detail and claim eyewitness authority for an account that otherwise conflicts with Paul's life and teaching.

title: Not for the Faint of Heart (Authorship of Colossians)
author: BDEhrman
description: Shows how scholarly arguments against Colossians differ in technical and popular forms.
searchSummary: Presents detailed stylistic and theological evidence that Colossians was written by someone other than Paul. Statistical comparisons show major differences in conjunctions, infinitives, relative clauses, and sentence construction, while its realized resurrection, understanding of forgiveness, exalted Christology, household ethics, and settled social outlook diverge from Paul's undisputed letters. These converging features indicate a later author adapted Pauline language and authority for a church expecting a long future rather than an imminent end.

title: Problems with Luke as the Author of Luke
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains problems with identifying Luke as the author of the Third Gospel.
searchSummary: Challenges the inference that Luke-Acts was written by Luke, Paul's Gentile physician companion. Only Colossians identifies Luke as both Gentile and physician, yet its vocabulary, style, and theology differ substantially from Paul's undisputed letters and lead many scholars to regard it as pseudonymous. Philemon names a coworker Luke but supplies neither trait, so the traditional identification loses a central piece of its evidence before larger authorship problems are considered.

title: Why Luke is Thought To Have Written Luke
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Luke has traditionally been identified as the author of Luke.
searchSummary: Reconstructs the traditional reasoning that assigned the anonymous Gospel and Acts to Luke. The 'we' passages suggested a traveling companion of Paul; Acts' concern for Gentiles suggested a Gentile author; Colossians named Luke as a Gentile physician; and apparent medical language seemed to confirm the choice. The post explains how this chain made Luke-Acts appear historically close to Paul while noting that nearly every link will be challenged.

title: The Final Part of My First-Day Quiz
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the final part of a first-day quiz used to teach Gospel traditions.
searchSummary: Explains the latter questions on a first-day quiz for a seminar about Jesus. Gospel differences concerning the crucifixion and burial lead to discussion of harmonization, while questions about Jesus' dates, Luke-Acts, traditional Gospel authorship, Jewish identity, and the shortest New Testament verse introduce historical and textual problems. Ehrman uses the answers not simply to correct facts but to show how critical study distinguishes ancient sources from later assumptions and English translations.

title: More on My Quiz
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how a classroom quiz helps teach students about Gospel knowledge.
searchSummary: Explains the first portion of a diagnostic quiz given in a seminar on Jesus. Questions about the New Testament canon, Greek language, chronology, anonymous Gospels, noncanonical accounts, and the meaning of the word gospel reveal students' starting knowledge. Ehrman turns each answer into a brief lesson on Hellenization, dating conventions, later authorial attributions, and the variety of early Christian writings, establishing basic historical tools for the course.

title: Reza Aslan’s View of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Reza Aslan's view of Jesus while discussing a class quiz.

title: My Pop Quiz For First-Year Students
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a first-day pop quiz for students in a Jesus seminar.
searchSummary: Presents an ungraded first-day quiz for a twenty-four-student seminar on Jesus. Twelve questions cover the New Testament canon, Greek language, chronology, canonical and noncanonical Gospels, the meaning of gospel, conflicting accounts of Jesus' baptism, crucifixion, and burial, traditional authorship, Jewish identity, and textual wording. Used as a diagnostic and icebreaker, the quiz introduces historical complexity and shows why close comparison of ancient sources matters.

title: Reza Aslan on Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers whether Reza Aslan is a recognized scholar of early Christianity.

title: Back To School!   My Jesus Syllabus
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares the syllabus for a course on Jesus in scholarship and film.
searchSummary: Outlines a first-year seminar examining Jesus in canonical and noncanonical Gospels, modern scholarship, and film. Taught nonconfessionally, the course asks students to assess evidence, compare portrayals, and form independent conclusions. Lectures, discussions, films, position papers, exams, a review of Reza Aslan's Zealot, and a student-written fictional Gospel address oral tradition, Gospel differences, Gnosticism, historical methods, Jesus' apocalyptic message, and modern cinematic interpretations.

title: Who Cares?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the broader significance of research on Didymus and patristic citations.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman's specialized research on Didymus the Blind mattered academically without directly changing his religious beliefs. By reconstructing the Gospel text used in late fourth-century Alexandria, the work contributed a small but important piece toward understanding the Alexandrian textual tradition and the New Testament's transmission. Ehrman distinguishes meaningful technical scholarship from trivial questions and argues that scholarship need not address faith directly to be valuable.

title: Conclusions Drawn from My Study of Didymus
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes conclusions from research on Didymus's quotations of the Gospels.

title: Problems with the Textual Evidence from Didymus
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains methodological problems with using Didymus as textual evidence.

title: Didymus the Blind and Patristic Evidence
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Didymus the Blind as patristic evidence for New Testament textual criticism.
searchSummary: Describes how quotations from the Gospels in Didymus the Blind's writings can illuminate New Testament textual history in fourth-century Alexandria. Because Alexandrian manuscripts were considered especially important for reconstructing early readings, comparing Didymus's citations word by word with surviving witnesses could identify the text circulating in his place and time. Ehrman explains how newly discovered commentaries attributed to Didymus supplied the evidence for his dissertation and first book.

title: Problems with Patristic Evidence
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains problems with patristic evidence in reconstructing the New Testament text.

title: Did Luke Originally Have Chapters 1-2?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Luke originally included chapters 1-2 and the birth narrative.
searchSummary: Argues that a first edition of Luke likely moved from its preface directly to chapter 3, with the infancy narrative added later. Chapter 3 reads like an opening, resembles Mark's beginning, and places Jesus' baptism and genealogy together coherently, while chapters 1-2 differ stylistically and introduce themes absent from later Luke-Acts. Marcion's Gospel may therefore preserve an early form without those chapters rather than reflect his deliberate deletion of them.

title: A Final Post (!) on Luke 3:22
author: BDEhrman
description: Concludes a detailed discussion of Luke 3:22 and its textual problem.
searchSummary: Concludes the textual argument that Luke's baptismal voice originally quoted Psalm 2:7: 'You are my son, today I have begotten you.' References in Acts describe God anointing and choosing Jesus at John's baptism, fitting an election formula better than a simple declaration of existing sonship. Because adoptionist Christians could use this reading, later proto-orthodox scribes likely harmonized Luke with Mark to remove its implication that Jesus became God's Son at baptism.

title: Luke 3:22 — More on What Luke Would Have Written
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues the intrinsic-probability argument about what Luke likely wrote at Jesus' baptism.

title: Luke 3:22 — What Luke Himself Would Have Written
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines internal evidence for the wording of the voice at Jesus' baptism in Luke.
searchSummary: Assesses which wording of Luke's baptismal voice best fits the author's own theology. Luke-Acts assigns the titles Messiah, Lord, Savior, and Son of God to several moments in Jesus' life, so 'Today I have begotten you' need not be excluded as inconsistent with the infancy narrative. References back to the baptism suggest that God conferred a new status there, supporting this election formula over the more common reading harmonized with Mark.

title: More Arguments over Luke 3:22
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Luke 3:22 to show why patristic evidence matters for textual criticism.
searchSummary: Argues on transcriptional grounds that Luke's baptismal voice originally said, You are my son, today I have begotten you, despite its survival in only one Greek manuscript. Patristic citations show the reading was widespread early, while the majority wording harmonizes Luke with Mark and avoids an adoptionist interpretation. Harmonization to a nearby Gospel parallel is more likely than a unique harmonization to Psalm 2, and scribes normally remove rather than create doctrinally troublesome readings.

title: Church Fathers and the Voice at Jesus’ Baptism
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how church fathers help establish the text of Jesus' baptism in Luke.

title: Patristic Evidence: Why Time and Place Matter
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why time and place matter when using patristic citations as textual evidence.

title: Doing a TV Interview
author: BDEhrman
description: Mentions a television interview for a documentary on Jesus.
searchSummary: Explains the demanding process of filming a long television interview for a documentary about Jesus. Scholars must produce complete, concise sound bites without the interviewer's questions, yet hours of answers may be reduced to minutes and edited to support a predetermined narrative with little nuance. Ehrman describes why he rarely watches the finished programs, illustrates how opposing scholarly views can be presented incoherently, and cautiously expects this documentary on myths about Jesus to be stronger because its producer is knowledgeable.

title: Church Fathers Who Quote the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers a question about church fathers who quote New Testament writings.

title: Early Doubts about the Pastorals
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses early doubts about Pauline authorship of the Pastoral Epistles.
searchSummary: Traces early and modern doubts about Paul's authorship of First Timothy, Second Timothy, and Titus. Nineteenth-century scholars developed historical and stylistic arguments that the Pastorals address later Gnostic opponents and post-Pauline church conditions, producing today's broad critical consensus. Doubts were not entirely modern: Marcion and perhaps Tatian lacked the letters, while some Christians around 200 rejected particular Pastorals because of their contents, even though these reactions do not by themselves settle authorship.

title: A Plea for My Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Appeals for readers to join the blog and support its work.
searchSummary: Urges readers of free excerpts to join the paid blog and current members to recruit others. Bart describes frequent substantive posts, reader questions, daily interaction, and coverage of the New Testament and early Christianity through the Council of Nicaea. The modest membership fee and tax-deductible donations go entirely to charities addressing hunger and homelessness. Expanding membership would therefore give readers access to the complete material while increasing the blog's humanitarian impact.

title: How Women Came to Be Silenced
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how women came to be silenced in early Christian tradition.
searchSummary: Women exercised authority in early Christian house churches because these communities met within domestic space where women had recognized responsibilities. As churches expanded, became public institutions, and developed hierarchy, Roman gender ideology and declining apocalyptic expectations displaced earlier movement toward equality. Women were increasingly barred from teaching, evangelizing, and leadership, while submission, marriage, and childbearing became defined as their proper Christian roles.

title: Male Domination in Antiquity
author: BDEhrman
description: Places the silencing of women within the broader male domination of antiquity.

title: The Non-Pauline Oppression of Women
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that 1 Timothy's restrictions on women should not be attributed to Paul.
searchSummary: Restrictions silencing women in 1 Timothy and 1 Corinthians 14 probably do not represent Paul's own position. The Corinthian passage resembles the Pastoral Epistles, interrupts its literary context, and conflicts with Paul's acknowledgment of women praying, prophesying, ministering, and serving as apostles. It likely originated as a later marginal note inserted by scribes who sought to align Paul with emerging church structures and patriarchal expectations.

title: Paul, the Pastorals, and Women
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Paul's views of women in the church.

title: Paul’s View of Women in the Church
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Paul's views of women's roles in the church.

title: Jesus’ Association with Women
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines Jesus' public association with women during ministry.

title: Women in the Ministry of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains women's prominence in Jesus' ministry.

title: Women in the Churches of Paul
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces women in Paul's churches and the broader topic of women in early Christianity.

title: Suffering and My Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Connects the problem of suffering with the purpose of the blog.
searchSummary: Summarizes Ehrman's conclusions about suffering and the purpose of his blog. Biblical authors offer conflicting explanations, but he attributes suffering to human cruelty and an indifferent natural world rather than God. More important than explaining pain is responding to it: everyone can help according to their means. He therefore created the paid blog primarily to raise money for hunger and homelessness charities, asks readers to recruit members or donate, and treats practical compassion as essential to being human.

title: Evaluation of Job’s View of Suffering
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates the prose story of Job and its explanation of suffering.
searchSummary: Evaluates Job's poetic dialogues as magnificent literature but rejects their portrayal of suffering and God.
