Innocent Job asks why he is tormented, yet God answers with overwhelming power rather than explanation and forces him to repent for questioning. Ehrman finds this deity wrathful, egocentric, and morally unacceptable, not loving. Human intelligence and moral judgment should expose innocent suffering as injustice, challenge conditions that cause it, and hold any responsible power accountable rather than passively accepting misery.

title: Suffering in the Poetic Section of Job
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the poetic section of Job and its treatment of suffering.
searchSummary: Reviews interpretations of God's climactic encounter with Job and argues that none explains his innocent suffering. Job neither presents his case, admits guilt, gains cosmic perspective, nor learns that God was too occupied to notice him. Instead, God refuses every explanation and uses overwhelming power to silence the very search for understanding. The poetic dialogue therefore suggests that mortals may not question God, leaving readers to ask whether divine power permits unaccountable torture and whether might can make right.

title: Key Passages in Job’s Back and Forth
author: BDEhrman
description: Highlights key passages in Job's poetic back-and-forth about suffering and divine justice.

title: The Poetic Section of Job
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the poetic section of Job and its different treatment of suffering.

title: Evaluation of Job’s Short Story
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates the prose story of Job and its explanation of suffering.
searchSummary: Evaluates Job's prose folktale as powerful fiction but a morally unacceptable theodicy. God authorizes the Adversary to destroy an innocent man's property, family, and health merely to test disinterested loyalty and win a wager. Job's eventual reward does not solve the problem, because replacement children cannot compensate for those murdered. Ehrman distinguishes condemning this author's portrayal from condemning God and rejects applying the story to real suffering as though tragedy were a divine test of faith.

title: The Prose Story of Job
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the prose story of Job as a separate account within the book.
searchSummary: Retells Job's prose framing story as an explanation of innocent suffering. God permits the Adversary, a member of the divine council rather than the later Devil, to destroy Job's wealth, servants, children, and health to test whether his devotion is disinterested. Job remains faithful and receives doubled possessions and a new family. The tale teaches that God may send suffering as a test and reward perseverance, a view Ehrman admires as fiction but finds disturbing as theology.

title: The Two Books of Job
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Job appears to contain two accounts with different views of suffering.

title: Personal Response to Suffering?
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers a question about personal views on suffering, God, and human responsibility.
searchSummary: Introduces God's Problem as a study of the Bible's diverse and sometimes contradictory explanations for suffering. Prophets portray calamity as divine punishment intended to produce repentance; wisdom texts generalize reward and punishment; Job challenges that scheme through testing and mystery; apocalyptic authors blame evil forces and expect their destruction. Ehrman finds many ancient answers unacceptable today and frames suffering as a central question for believers, sufferers, and anyone seeking to understand human existence and responsibility.

title: Jesus’ Literacy
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers whether Jesus was literate in the context of ancient literacy.
searchSummary: Evaluates Jesus' literacy against the low reading rates of Roman Palestine and the Gospel evidence. Ehrman sees no reliable reason to think Jesus could write; Mark portrays his hometown as surprised by his learning, while Luke alone explicitly depicts him reading Isaiah. Because teachers could acquire scriptural knowledge by hearing public readings, Jesus' authority does not prove formal schooling. Ehrman nevertheless slightly favors the possibility that a local synagogue leader taught him to read Hebrew Scripture.

title: Personal, Executive Privilege: My Daughter and Homeschooling!
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a personal note about a daughter's homeschooling business.
searchSummary: Promotes Ehrman's daughter Kelly's newly launched Lavender's Blue Homeschool business and its Waldorf-inspired kindergarten curriculum. He describes the venture as supporting families who want a thoughtful, holistic, and creative approach to homeschooling, with related writing on peaceful parenting, childhood, and learning at home. Departing deliberately from the blog's usual focus on ancient Christianity, he asks readers who know homeschooling families to visit the website, follow its social media presence, and spread awareness of the new curriculum.

title: Jesus and Sacrifices
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether early Christians turned Jesus into a symbol of sacrifice.
searchSummary: Asks whether Jesus rejected Jewish sacrifice before his followers interpreted his death as an atoning sacrifice. Ehrman argues that Jesus' Temple action probably symbolized coming judgment against corrupt leadership or improper worship, not opposition to sacrifice itself. Because Jesus otherwise accepted Torah, including its sacrificial laws when properly understood, early Christians were not necessarily embracing a system he had repudiated when they used Jewish sacrificial imagery to explain his death.

title: Paul’s Chronology
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why dating Paul's letters is more difficult than it may seem.

title: Early Christianity in Egypt
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether early Egyptian Christianity was initially orthodox or represented by Gnostic and other competing forms.
searchSummary: Assesses claims about the character of Christianity in Egypt before about 200 CE and concludes that the evidence is insufficient. Eusebius projects an early orthodox succession of Alexandrian bishops, while Walter Bauer argued that Gnostic forms preceded orthodoxy and were displaced around Origen's time. Noncanonical discoveries are heterodox, but canonical manuscripts cannot identify their communities because many groups used them. With no account of the church's founding, leaders, or dominant beliefs, neither original orthodoxy nor original Gnosticism can be established.

title: Would Matthew and Paul Have Seen Eye-to-Eye
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Matthew and Paul on the Jewish law and salvation.
searchSummary: Compares Matthew and Paul on whether obeying law and performing good deeds bring salvation. Matthew's Jesus tells the rich man that keeping the commandments leads to eternal life and giving wealth brings perfection; Paul says no one is justified by works of the law and that justification through law would render Christ's death pointless. Matthew also considers Jesus' death salvific, so the post presents the tension as an interpretive problem rather than declaring the two authors either reconcilable or contradictory.

title: Gentile Judaizers
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Gentile Judaizers in relation to Matthew's Jewish identity.
searchSummary: Argues that advocating Jewish law for Jesus' followers did not necessarily mean a Christian was born Jewish. Paul's opponents in Galatia were likely former pagans who nevertheless required gentile believers to adopt circumcision and Torah observance because Jesus fulfilled Israel's covenant promises. Their example shows that Matthew's strong commitment to the law cannot by itself establish the evangelist's Jewish background, since gentile converts could also become vigorous Judaizers.

title: So … Was Matthew a Jew?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether the author of Matthew was Jewish.
searchSummary: Asks whether the author of Matthew was born Jewish, converted to Judaism, or was a gentile Christian who adopted Jewish law, and concludes that the evidence cannot decide. The Gospel strongly values Torah but never clarifies whether followers must observe circumcision, dietary rules, and festivals or whether those practices are simply assumed. Even complete insistence on Jewish observance would not prove the author's birth identity because first-century gentile Christians could adopt Judaism and demand the same of other believers.

title: Was Matthew’s Community Gentile or Jewish?
author: BDEhrman
description: Considers whether Matthew's community was primarily Jewish or Gentile.
searchSummary: Examines whether Matthew's community was Jewish or gentile and whether gentile believers had to adopt Jewish practices. The Gospel expects people from all nations to enter God's kingdom through Jesus, baptism, ethical obedience, and care for those in need, but never states whether they must be circumcised or observe food and Sabbath laws. Matthew nevertheless treats Jesus' movement as Judaism properly interpreted rather than a separate religion, leaving its members' identities and cultic obligations unresolved.

title: The Jewish Emphases of Matthew: Part 5
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues Matthew's Jewish emphases, especially the importance of the Law.
searchSummary: Explains Matthew's view that Jewish ritual and ethical laws should be observed, but mercy and human need take priority. By adding Hosea's “I desire mercy, not sacrifice” to stories about eating with sinners and plucking grain on the Sabbath, Matthew criticizes Pharisees for elevating purity and ritual over helping people. Traditional practices such as Sabbath, tithing, and food observance remain valid, yet they are subordinate to love, the central command that governs faithful interpretation of the entire law.

title: The Jewish Emphases of Matthew: Part 4
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Matthew's radicalizing of the Jewish law.
searchSummary: Argues that Matthew's Jesus expects followers to retain traditional Jewish piety as well as ethical commandments. The Gospel affirms almsgiving, prayer, fasting, tithing, Temple offerings, tax payment, and Sabbath restrictions, while omitting Mark's statement that Jesus declared all foods clean. Matthew never directly discusses circumcision or commands gentiles to become Jewish, but these examples suggest that he assumes Torah observance rather than abolishing it. Other passages may complicate that conclusion, which the post leaves for later discussion.

title: The Jewish Emphases of Matthew’s Gospel: Part 3
author: BDEhrman
description: Shows how Matthew's Golden Rule and love commandments present love as the central purpose of Jewish law.
searchSummary: Explains Matthew's view that the Golden Rule and the commands to love God and neighbor express the central purpose of Jewish law. Jesus' followers must practice this love to enter God's kingdom rather than focus only on narrowly defined requirements. Because these ethical teachings were not uniquely Jewish, the post raises a further question: whether Matthew also expected believers, especially gentiles, to observe identity-defining practices such as circumcision, Sabbath, and dietary restrictions. That issue remains for subsequent discussion.

title: My New Course for The Teaching Company (The Great Courses)
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a new Great Courses project while pausing the Matthew thread.

title: The Jewish Emphases of Matthew: Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how Matthew's Sermon on the Mount intensifies Jewish law by applying its underlying intent to anger, lust, retaliation, and other conduct.
searchSummary: Argues that Matthew's Jesus does not abolish Jewish law but intensifies it by demanding obedience to its underlying purpose. The Sermon on the Mount extends prohibitions against murder, adultery, and excessive punishment to anger, lust, mercy, and nonretaliation. Matthew gives no indication that these standards are intentionally impossible or merely demonstrate humanity's need for grace. Followers must exceed scribes and Pharisees by fulfilling the law's spirit, though the post postpones identifying its ultimate purpose.

title: The Jewish Emphases of Matthew
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Matthew's Jewish emphases through genealogy, messiahship, and Scripture.
searchSummary: Surveys Matthew's Jewish emphases without assuming they prove that the author was Jewish. The genealogy ties Jesus to Abraham and David, eleven fulfillment citations connect his life with Jewish Scripture, and his early experiences parallel Moses' rescue, exodus, testing, and delivery of law. Matthew thus presents Jesus as Jewish Messiah and new Moses who saves from sin and interprets God's law. The author's own ethnic or religious identity, however, requires separate evidence.

title: Was the Author of Matthew Matthew?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the tax collector Matthew probably did not write the Gospel of Matthew.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus' disciple Matthew did not write the Gospel bearing his name. A rural Aramaic-speaking tax collector was illiterate and could not plausibly compose its educated Greek decades later. More decisively, the author copies most of Mark's Greek stories and Q material rather than recounting eyewitness memories, speaks anonymously, and describes Matthew in the third person. Later Christians attributed the work to a disciple to secure apostolic authority, possibly drawing on Papias's rumor about a different Aramaic sayings collection.

title: When Was Matthew Called Matthew?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains when the Gospel of Matthew came to be called Matthew.
searchSummary: Explains that the Gospel of Matthew circulated anonymously for decades and received its familiar attribution only around 180 CE. Justin calls such works “Memoirs of the Apostles” without authors, while Irenaeus names four authoritative Gospels amid competition from other Christian writings. Papias earlier mentions a Hebrew sayings collection by Matthew, but that description does not fit the Greek narrative based on Mark. A later editor likely applied the respected disciple's name to the most Jewish-seeming anonymous Gospel.

title: The Identity of “Matthew”
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Matthew's identity and whether the author was Jewish.
searchSummary: Explains why manuscript titles do not identify the anonymous author of Matthew. Surviving titled copies are centuries later, and “According to Matthew” is an editorial label distinguishing one Gospel version, not a title an author would give his book. The narrative never uses first person or claims eyewitness status, even when describing Matthew the tax collector's call in the third person. Later attribution to a disciple enhanced the account's authority, but the author's actual identity and Jewish background remain unknown.

title: On the Cutting Room Floor: Part 5 and Final!
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares final material cut from How Jesus Became God about faith, resurrection, and suffering.
searchSummary: Reconstructs Ehrman's movement from a liberal, demythologized Christianity to agnostic atheism and humanism. He could treat biblical narratives and doctrines about Jesus as myths conveying moral meaning, but realized while reciting the Nicene Creed that he believed literally only in Jesus' crucifixion, death, and burial. The problem of suffering ultimately made even a radically redefined God untenable, leading him to ground meaning and values in human existence rather than Christian doctrine.

title: On the Cutting Room Floor: Part 4
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares cut material from How Jesus Became God about suffering and loss of faith.
searchSummary: Corrects claims that manuscript variants, biblical contradictions, or intellectual rigidity caused Ehrman's deconversion. He remained a liberal Christian long after abandoning biblical inerrancy, understanding Jesus as a fully human teacher and resurrection and atonement as meaningful myths rather than literal events. The decisive challenge was suffering, while his former Christology illustrates why later Christian leaders' insistence on one saving set of beliefs sharpened conflicts between orthodoxy and heresy.

title: On the Cutting Room Floor: Part 3
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares additional cut material from How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Recounts how biblical discrepancies led Ehrman from inerrancy toward recognizing distinct New Testament Christologies. John portrays Jesus as a preexistent divine being equal with God, whereas Matthew, Mark, and Luke do not present Jesus making the same claims, raising questions about which account reflects the earliest belief. Ehrman concludes that the first Christians held exaltation Christologies, in which the human Jesus became God's Son, while John's later incarnation Christology presents a divine being becoming human.

title: Outta Here
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a short absence from the blog for a family trip.

title: Was Matthew a Jew?
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers whether the author of Matthew was Jewish.
searchSummary: Evaluates an argument that Matthew's misunderstanding of Hebrew poetic parallelism proves the author was gentile. Matthew treats Zechariah's synonymous lines as two animals and depicts Jesus riding a donkey and its colt into Jerusalem. John Meier argues that a Jew familiar with Hebrew poetry would not make that mistake, but Jewish interpreters sometimes divided parallel lines similarly. The episode creates an amusing image and may show literalism, yet it cannot determine Matthew's ethnic or religious identity.

title: On the Cutting Room Floor: Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares cut material from How Jesus Became God about resurrection and faith.
searchSummary: Uses Ehrman's teenage conversion to explain both evangelical resurrection faith and the historical limits of studying resurrection claims. Belief that the risen Jesus was a living savior made a personal relationship with him central and redirected Ehrman's life toward biblical study. Historically, however, scholars cannot establish that a miracle occurred, that Jesus received a proper burial, or that followers found an empty tomb, even though resurrection belief was indispensable to Christianity's emergence and survival.

title: On the Cutting Room Floor: Part 1
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces material cut from How Jesus Became God during final edits.
searchSummary: Introduces How Jesus Became God as a historical inquiry into how a crucified Jewish preacher came to be regarded as the divine creator. Research changed Ehrman's views about Jesus' burial and empty tomb, the Synoptic Gospels' understanding of Jesus' divinity, and the earliest Christians' exaltation beliefs. The governing issue is not simply whether they called Jesus God, but in what sense, reversing theology's question of how God became human into history's question of how a human became God.

title: More Criticisms of the Historical Criticisms of John (by John! Spong)
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues a critique of John Shelby Spong's treatment of the Gospel of John.
searchSummary: Challenges John Shelby Spong's claim that the Fourth Gospel deliberately resists literal reading and instead teaches mystical human divinization. Nicodemus misunderstands Jesus because a Greek word has two meanings, but John expects readers to grasp and accept the intended heavenly birth. The Gospel's exaggerated signs display Jesus' divine power rather than mock historical belief. Although salvation makes humans God's children, John grounds that result in the literal incarnation of a divine being, a Christology Spong's modern pastoral interpretation minimizes.

title: Spong’s New Book on John
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces John Shelby Spong's new book on the Gospel of John.
searchSummary: Reviews four claims from John Shelby Spong's book about the Fourth Gospel. John son of Zebedee almost certainly did not write it, its seven signs are not historical reports, and Johannine speeches do not preserve Jesus' words, although saying none do is too extreme. Spong also treats characters such as Nicodemus and the Samaritan woman as intentional literary creations, but their absence from other Gospels does not establish that John invented them or expected readers to regard them as fictional.
topics: Signs in the Gospel of John

title: Where Did Israel Come From?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks where Israel came from after discussing problems in the conquest narratives.
searchSummary: Surveys four historical explanations for Israel's emergence in Canaan: military conquest, outside immigration, peasant revolt, and gradual development from the indigenous population. Archaeological and literary problems have weakened the first three as comprehensive accounts. Many scholars instead favor gradual emergence, perhaps including a smaller group connected with Egypt and the spread of Yahweh worship. On this view, Joshua preserves amplified traditions and local memories rather than an accurate record of a unified conquest.

title: Historical Problems with the Hebrew Bible: The Conquest of Canaan
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses historical problems in the Hebrew Bible conquest narratives.

title: Historical Problems with the Hebrew Bible: The Exodus Narrative
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses historical problems in the Hebrew Bible exodus narrative.

title: Inconsistencies in the Hebrew Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains inconsistencies in the Hebrew Bible and their significance.
searchSummary: Surveys contradictions in the Pentateuch that led scholars to identify multiple written sources. Genesis 1 and 2 differ over creation order, divine names, God's character, and theological interests; the flood gives conflicting animal counts, Egyptian livestock die repeatedly, and Genesis and Exodus disagree about whether the patriarchs knew Yahweh's name. These tensions indicate that editors combined accounts written at different times rather than preserving one internally consistent work by a single author.

title: Problems with the Hebrew Bible Manuscripts
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains manuscript problems in the Hebrew Bible and Old Testament.

title: Jesus’ Inflammatory Words
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers whether Jesus' words could have provoked violence in Jerusalem.

title: Mark and the Resurrection
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses Mark's ending and the absence of a resurrection appearance by Jesus.
searchSummary: Clarifies that Mark includes a bodily resurrection even though it narrates no appearance of the risen Jesus. The empty tomb, announcement, and promised meeting in Galilee establish resurrection, while the women's silence preserves two literary themes: disciples never understand and people disobey commands about telling. The ending does not express Jewish grief after the Temple's destruction. Mark addresses gentile Christians and redefines the Jewish Messiah as one whose crucifixion itself brings redemption from sin.

title: More on Mark and Peter
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues explaining why Mark probably did not write Peter's recollections.
searchSummary: Argues that the Gospel of Mark neither records Peter's viewpoint nor was plausibly composed by Palestinian John Mark. The narrative is not first-person, its inaccurate generalization about Jewish handwashing suggests a gentile author and audience, and ancient literacy rates make Greek literary composition by an Aramaic-speaking Jerusalem Jew highly unlikely. Even Josephus required later Greek education and assistance. The traditional identification therefore reflects later legend, while the Gospel's actual author was probably an educated gentile Christian outside Palestine.

title: Mark as Peter’s Scribe
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why scholars doubt that Mark served as Peter's scribe.
searchSummary: Evaluates Papias's report that Mark wrote Peter's recollections and finds it too indirect and unreliable to establish authorship. Papias wrote decades after the anonymous Gospel, preserves third- or fourth-hand information, misdescribes Matthew, and claims Mark recorded everything from Peter despite the Gospel's brief scope. Other fantastical traditions attributed to Papias further weaken selective trust in his testimony. Dependable naming of the four canonical Gospels appears only near the late second century, roughly a century after their anonymous circulation began.

title: Future Books
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses possible future books and the alternation between scholarly and trade projects.
searchSummary: Explains Ehrman's practice of alternating scholarly monographs, general-audience trade books, and college textbooks rather than concentrating on a single publishing market. He argues that public-facing scholars should continue producing original scholarship instead of merely repackaging others' work. The post then surveys an eight-to-ten-year plan involving Gospel fragments, memory and oral tradition, Christian use of Jewish Scripture, Christianity's expansion, revised source collections, and a history of early Christianity through Nicaea.

title: Agnostic or Atheist?
author: BDEhrman
description: Clarifies the difference between identifying as agnostic and atheist.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman describes himself as both agnostic and atheist rather than treating those labels as stronger and weaker versions of the same position. Agnosticism concerns knowledge: he does not know whether some superior being or intelligence exists in the universe. Atheism concerns belief: he does not believe in the biblical creator who governs the world, answers prayer, and brings good from evil. Because uncertainty about knowledge can coexist with absence of belief, he considers either compound label accurate.

title: Historical Jesus Scholarship and Christians
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers whether Christians can accept an apocalyptic Jesus whose expected end did not arrive.
searchSummary: Explains why accepting Jesus as a mistaken apocalyptic prophet need not prevent informed scholars from remaining Christian. Most critical specialists view Jesus as expecting God's kingdom within his generation, but nonfundamentalist Christianity need not require a flawless Bible or an infallible Jesus. Bart notes that Christian colleagues regard Jesus as fully human, wrong about timing yet still uniquely revealing God and offering profound ethical teaching, while his own disagreement rests on not believing in God.

title: Exciting Discovery of a Hebrew Bible Scroll
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the discovery of an old Hebrew Bible scroll containing the Pentateuch.

title: More on Jews, Christians, and the Battle for Scripture
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a planned book on Jews, Christians, Scripture, and anti-Judaism.

title: The Next Trade Book: Jews and Christians
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains plans for a trade book on Jews, Christians, and anti-Judaism.
searchSummary: Introduces Bart's planned trade book on how Christians came to claim the Jewish Scriptures as their Old Testament and how competing claims to those writings shaped Jewish-Christian relations. The proposed book asks why Christians retained books whose laws they did not observe, why some early Christians rejected an Old Testament, and why opposing arguments prevailed. Bart situates this project alongside a separate scholarly commentary on early noncanonical Gospel fragments.

title: What Judas Betrayed
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains what Judas may have betrayed about Jesus.
searchSummary: Argues that Judas betrayed a private teaching rather than merely revealing where authorities could arrest Jesus. Jesus publicly preached the coming kingdom and promised that the Twelve would rule Israel, implying that he expected to become its king, yet the Gospels do not show him publicly claiming the title King of the Jews. Ehrman proposes that Judas disclosed this messianic expectation, enabling Roman authorities to treat Jesus as a political claimant and execute him.

title: More on Judas
author: BDEhrman
description: Clarifies the argument about Paul and the tradition of Judas's betrayal.

title: Paul on Judas
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Paul knew the tradition that Judas betrayed Jesus.

title: Jesus’ Appearance to the 500
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses Paul's reference to Jesus appearing to more than five hundred people.

title: Jesus’ Rejection in Nazareth
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Luke's story of Jesus' rejection at Nazareth is historically doubtful.
searchSummary: Argues that Luke expanded and relocated Mark's Nazareth story to introduce the central program of Luke-Acts. Jesus reads Isaiah, identifies himself with Elijah and Elisha, is rejected by his townspeople, and foreshadows a message rejected by Jews but carried to Gentiles. The scene establishes Jesus as God's final prophet, but its extensive reshaping around Luke's literary and theological purposes makes the attempted killing historically doubtful.

title: Persecutions for Calling Jesus God
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether calling Jesus God would have led to immediate persecution for blasphemy.

title: Geza Vermes
author: BDEhrman
description: Remembers Geza Vermes as a major scholar of the Dead Sea Scrolls and Jesus.

title: Jesus and the Dead Sea Scrolls
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how the Dead Sea Scrolls illuminate Jesus' Jewish world.
searchSummary: Compares Jesus with the Essenes represented by the Dead Sea Scrolls. Both opposed Jerusalem's leaders and expected God soon to defeat evil and establish a kingdom, but Jesus did not share Essene concerns about priestly lineage, ritual calendars, or withdrawal from impurity. His fellowship with sinners and outcasts sharply contradicted their separatist purity practices, making the scrolls evidence for Jesus' broader apocalyptic Jewish setting rather than for his membership at Qumran.

title: The Dead Sea Scrolls and Christianity
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the significance of the Dead Sea Scrolls for Christianity.

title: Back in the Saddle.  Sort of….
author: BDEhrman
description: Reports a slow return to blogging after travel.

title: Qumran and Masada
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes visits to Qumran, Masada, and the Dead Sea.

title: More in Jerusalem
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes parts of a Jerusalem trip focused on several historical periods.
searchSummary: Reflects on a Jerusalem tour that combines religious sites, archaeology, markets, neighborhoods, and modern political context. Contrasting an exceptionally informed and even-handed guide with a young guide who presents archaeology through a strongly pro-Israeli, Bible-confirming perspective, Ehrman emphasizes recognizing how interpreters' commitments shape historical claims. Disputed remains identified as David's palace illustrate why confidence about biblical figures and ancient kingdoms requires awareness of scholarly disagreement, even when a guide's conclusion might ultimately prove correct.

title: Touring Jerusalem
author: BDEhrman
description: Gives a travel update from a day touring Jerusalem.

title: On to Jerusalem
author: BDEhrman
description: Gives a quick travel update after arriving in Jerusalem.

title: Capernaum and the “Jesus Boat”
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes Capernaum, the Sea of Galilee, and the so-called Jesus Boat.

title: Caesarea Maritima
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes visiting Caesarea Maritima during an Israel trip.

title: Off to Israel
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces departure for a UNC alumni tour in Israel.

title: The God Christ and the Jews
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains anti-Jewish implications in later claims about Christ as God.
searchSummary: Explains how belief that Jesus was fully God intensified ancient Christian hostility toward Jews. If Jews were blamed for Jesus' death and Jesus was God, Christians could accuse them of deicide, as Melito of Sardis did in a second-century Passover sermon portraying Israel as murdering its creator and king. Ehrman warns that such rhetoric became still more dangerous after Christianity gained imperial power and a formerly persecuted minority could act against those labeled God's killers.

title: Sorry!
author: BDEhrman
description: Corrects mistakes in a previous post about astronomy and the age of the earth.

title: On Scholarly Consensus
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to a reader question about scholarly consensus.
searchSummary: Explains the proper role of scholarly consensus. Agreement among experts is not itself evidence, but it deserves serious attention because trained specialists know the relevant evidence and established methods for evaluating it. Authorities should be followed only when their conclusions are supported, and dissent remains possible when stronger evidence exists. Someone rejecting a broad expert consensus should therefore engage the underlying case and possess unusually compelling evidence rather than treating an uninformed contrary opinion as equally credible.

title: Back to School: Graduate Studies
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains graduate teaching and graduate study in religious studies.
searchSummary: Explains the demands of graduate study and teaching in early Christianity compared with undergraduate courses. Seminars require original languages, sustained engagement with scholarship, and specialized research that can also expand a professor's knowledge. Ehrman describes the usual doctoral path through coursework, modern and ancient language requirements, comprehensive examinations, a dissertation proposal, original research, and defense, arguing that scholarly expertise reflects years of disciplined training rather than mere academic status.

title: Growth Rate of Early Christianity
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers a question about estimating early Christian growth rates.
searchSummary: Estimates Christianity's expansion within a Roman Empire of roughly sixty million people. Ehrman suggests the movement grew from about twenty followers after Jesus' death to perhaps three million, or five percent of the empire, when Constantine converted in 312, then to around thirty million by the late fourth century. An average increase near 40 percent per decade could account for the pre-Constantinian rise through exponential growth, without requiring miraculous intervention or repeated mass conversions.

title: Different Kinds of Colleges and Universities
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains differences among colleges, universities, and teaching settings.
searchSummary: Compares teaching at small liberal arts colleges with teaching at a research university. Small colleges offer intimate classes, close mentoring, and heavier teaching loads, while research universities use large lectures and teaching assistants but give faculty more time and stronger expectations for scholarship. Ehrman values the wider reach and research opportunities of his setting while acknowledging its reduced personal contact, which he partly addresses through informal office hours with students.

title: My Start in Teaching
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts the beginning of a teaching career.
searchSummary: Recounts how an emergency midsemester appointment at Rutgers unexpectedly launched Ehrman's university teaching career. Although trained in Christian schools and expecting to teach in that setting, he discovered that he loved presenting religion historically rather than confessionally. The temporary position continued for four years and required him to prepare six handwritten ninety-minute lectures each week while finishing his dissertation, ultimately providing the experience that helped him secure his position at UNC.

title: Teaching Religion in the South
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on teaching religion and the New Testament in the South.
searchSummary: Reflects on teaching religion at a public university in the American South, where many students arrive with strong biblical commitments but limited historical knowledge. Ehrman emphasizes that his purpose is neither conversion nor deconversion, but careful reasoning from evidence. By presenting challenging scholarly views and encouraging civil disagreement, he seeks to help students develop coherent positions, appreciate alternative interpretations, and understand why informed people can reach different conclusions.

title: Teaching at Carolina
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on teaching at the University of North Carolina.
searchSummary: Describes teaching at UNC within a strong research department and graduate program connected with Duke. Large undergraduate lectures are paired with small, teaching-assistant-led discussion sections, combining broad reach with closer engagement. Ehrman's typical load includes one undergraduate course and one doctoral seminar; the latter centers on original-language texts and current scholarship. He presents this structure as a productive balance between teaching many students and maintaining an active research career.

title: Explaining myself….
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains ongoing work on How Jesus Became God and related Christology questions.
searchSummary: Describes Ehrman's work on How Jesus Became God's chapter about second- and third-century Christological controversies. Christians variously maintained that Jesus was human but not divine, divine but not human, a human temporarily inhabited by a heavenly being, or one entity both human and divine. Even the victorious final position generated new disputes over whether Son and Father were the same God and how Origen's influential explanation should be judged, showing doctrinal development continuing through conflict.

title: Humans Who Become Angels
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses traditions about humans becoming angels in ancient Judaism.
searchSummary: Explains Jewish precedents for understanding a human as transformed into an angelic or divine being. Texts describe the righteous becoming angels, Enoch receiving heavenly glory indistinguishable from angels, and Moses attaining status above angels who worship him. These traditions help explain how early Christians could place the resurrected Jesus beside God without abandoning monotheism: a human could become the chief angel, angels could be called gods, and divine agents could appear in human form.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: More on Divine and Human Angels
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues discussing divine and human angels in Jewish traditions.
searchSummary: Surveys Jewish traditions in which angels are called gods and heavenly beings take human form. Psalm 82 depicts members of God's divine council as gods made mortal for injustice, while the Prayer of Joseph identifies Jacob as a chief angel who descended to live as a man. The Apocalypse of Abraham likewise portrays the powerful angel Jaoel appearing in human likeness, establishing conceptual precedents for Christians to understand a divine or angelic Christ as human.

title: Angels as Divine
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how angels could be understood as divine in ancient Jewish texts.
searchSummary: Shows that biblical descriptions of the Angel of the Lord blur distinctions among angel, God, and human appearance. Hagar recognizes the angel as God, Abraham entertains the Lord and two angels as three men, and the burning-bush narrative shifts between the angel of the Lord and God speaking as one figure. Such Jewish traditions made it possible to regard a heavenly agent as both God's visible manifestation and a humanlike visitor, providing background for angelic Christology.

title: Why The Gospels Are Anonymous
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the canonical Gospels are anonymous.

title: Paul’s View of Jesus as an Angel
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents the argument that Paul understood Christ as an angelic being before incarnation.
searchSummary: Argues from Galatians 4:14 that Paul identifies Jesus Christ as an angel, probably God's chief angel. Paul's recurring Greek construction equates rather than contrasts the paired descriptions, so the Galatians received Paul as an angel such as Christ, not as either an angel or Christ. This reading helps explain Paul's portrayal of Christ as a preexistent divine being who became human and was glorified, especially in the early composition preserved in Philippians 2.

title: Paul’s Christology
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Paul's Christology in How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Explains Ehrman's revised understanding of Paul's Christology. Paul does not present a systematic account, and his apparently exalted view predates the seemingly lower portrayals in Matthew, Mark, and Luke, undermining a simple progression from low to high Christology. Ehrman instead distinguishes different models: the Synoptic Gospels present exaltation Christologies, while Paul presents an incarnation Christology in which a preexistent angelic Christ becomes human.

title: Moving from the Faith
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares an autobiographical account of moving away from faith.
searchSummary: Recounts how rigorous graduate study exposed biblical discrepancies that gradually dismantled Ehrman's inerrancy and raised deeper questions about competing New Testament portrayals of Jesus. Fear of error, lost salvation, and hell made the transition emotionally painful, but his conviction that all truth belongs to God kept him investigating rather than defending comforting assumptions. He ultimately concluded that John's preexistent divine Christ represents a later incarnation Christology, unlike the earlier exaltation views in which the human Jesus became God's Son.

title: A Third Forgery in the Name of Peter
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Apocalypse of Peter as a forgery in Peter's name.

title: Another Forgery in the Name of Peter
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses another noncanonical forgery written in Peter's name.

title: Forgery and the Gospel of Peter
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the Gospel of Peter to introduce forgery outside the New Testament.

title: Making Things Interesting
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on making lectures and scholarship interesting for public audiences.

title: Our One-Year Anniversary!
author: BDEhrman
description: Celebrates the blog's one-year anniversary and charitable purpose.
searchSummary: Celebrates the blog's first anniversary with more than 1,300 members, nearly 300 posts, active reader interaction, and over $37,000 raised for charities addressing hunger and homelessness. Bart identifies the four supported organizations and explains the foundation's direct distribution of funds. He proposes topic-based categories, guest contributors, and video commentary, discusses sustaining publication after returning to teaching, invites suggestions and donations, and thanks Steven Ray and members for establishing the project.

title: Fuller Account of Resurrection Discrepancies
author: BDEhrman
description: Expands on Gospel discrepancies in the resurrection narratives.
searchSummary: Examines irreconcilable differences among Gospel resurrection accounts and the problems created by harmonizing them. The women encounter different figures, Mark says they tell no one while other Gospels say they report immediately, and Matthew sends the disciples to Galilee while Luke keeps them in Jerusalem. Ehrman argues that these later, non-eyewitness sources cannot all describe what happened and that their conflicts matter when reconstructing where the disciples first claimed to see Jesus alive.

title: Resurrection Narratives in the Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the Gospels are problematic witnesses to the resurrection.
searchSummary: Explains why Gospel resurrection narratives are difficult historical sources apart from the philosophical problem of proving miracles. They were written decades later by non-eyewitnesses using oral and written traditions that changed over time, and side-by-side comparison reveals disagreement about the women, stone, tomb visitors, messages, reports, appearances, and locations. Because the accounts conflict on nearly every detail, harmonizing them requires imaginative reconstruction rather than ordinary historical analysis, limiting what they independently establish about events after Jesus's death.

title: More on Recent Manuscript Discoveries
author: BDEhrman
description: Updates readers on recent manuscript discoveries, including Mark and the Gospel of Jesus' Wife.
searchSummary: Reviews the stalled claims surrounding the Gospel of Jesus' Wife and an alleged first-century fragment of Mark. Ehrman summarizes the linguistic and textual evidence suggesting that the former was forged, while noting that the latter remained unpublished and unverifiable. Even if a tiny early Mark scrap proved authentic, it would likely confirm that the Gospel circulated in the first century rather than revolutionize textual criticism. He rejects claims that its importance could exceed that of the Dead Sea Scrolls.

title: Progress on My Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Reports progress on writing How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Outlines the planned structure and writing process for How Jesus Became God. Its chapters move from divine humans in pagan and Jewish contexts through Jesus' self-understanding, what history can and cannot say about resurrection, early exaltation and incarnation Christologies, later controversies, and the road to Nicaea. Ehrman also explains drafting intensive chapters from detailed outlines, allowing time before revision, seeking criticism from fellow scholars, and revising again with his editor before publication.

title: Modern Visions of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses modern visions of Jesus as background for resurrection appearances.
searchSummary: Uses documented modern visions of Jesus to illuminate how claims of postmortem appearances are evaluated. Cases include an individual conversion vision and alleged group appearances in a Pentecostal church, one reportedly filmed but later lost, with surviving witnesses and photographs of related phenomena. Ehrman neither verifies nor dismisses the events; he highlights that the decades between event and written report resemble the interval between Jesus' life and the earliest Gospels, supporting opposite conclusions for believers and skeptics.

title: Visions of Mary
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses visions of Mary while writing about visions of Jesus.
searchSummary: Places the disciples' visions of Jesus alongside well-documented modern claims that people saw the Virgin Mary. Reports from Venezuela and Egypt involved large groups, educated witnesses, clergy, interviews, and photographs, while Fatima attracted tens of thousands of observers. Ehrman does not conclude that Mary appeared; he argues that eyewitness evidence can be abundant across religious traditions, and believers often accept miracles supporting their own faith while discounting comparable testimony for another tradition.

title: Divine Wisdom
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces divine Wisdom as part of Jewish divine-being traditions.
searchSummary: Explains the Jewish concept of divine Wisdom as a hypostasis: an attribute of God understood as a distinct being who nevertheless expresses God's own essence. Proverbs 8 portrays Wisdom as created before the world and working beside God in creation, while the Wisdom of Solomon depicts her as God's image, throne companion, and saving agent. Such traditions show how a divine being could exist alongside God and perform God's works without simply constituting a second independent deity.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: Jesus as the Messiah
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a draft discussion of Jesus as the Messiah.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus' followers probably regarded him as messiah before his death. No Jewish expectation held that the messiah would be defeated, crucified, and resurrected; the anticipated figure would conquer enemies and rule Israel, so those events could not independently have generated the title. Resurrection belief instead restored hopes that crucifixion had shattered, causing followers to reinterpret how Jesus would fulfill a messianic role they had already attributed to him.

title: The Son of Man as Divine
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents a draft discussion of the Son of Man as a divine figure.
searchSummary: Traces the Son of Man from Daniel 7's humanlike representative of God's people to a preexistent divine judge in later Jewish tradition. The Similitudes of Enoch portray this figure as eternally chosen, enthroned beside God, worshiped, and empowered to save the righteous and overthrow kings. A later layer identifies him with the human Enoch, demonstrating how Jewish texts could exalt a mortal to divine status and functions without identifying him as God Almighty.

title: The Divine Realm in Antiquity
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the divine realm in antiquity for How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Explains the ancient conception of humanity and divinity as overlapping continua rather than realms separated by an unbridgeable gulf. Polytheists recognized many graded levels of gods, so an emperor already honored as divine could be further deified through additional benefactions without becoming Zeus. This hierarchy allowed gods to appear as humans and exceptional humans to rise into lower divine ranks, providing the cultural framework within which claims about Jesus' divinity could be understood.

title: The Jewish King as God
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses the Jewish king as God within ancient Jewish traditions.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: Who Is Really God?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a chapter of How Jesus Became God on identifying God and divine beings.
searchSummary: Recounts how an inscription calling Augustus God caused Ehrman to reframe early Christology within Roman imperial culture. Christian claims about Jesus developed alongside emperor worship and could become a competition over the true divine ruler, rather than an isolated internal evolution. Because the first believers were Palestinian Jews committed to one God, the discovery also created a central research problem: how Jewish followers could call Jesus divine without understanding themselves to worship two gods.

title: Gods Who (Apparently) Become Human
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Greco-Roman traditions about gods appearing as humans.
searchSummary: Uses the story of Jupiter and Mercury visiting Phrygia in human form to show how ancient people understood movement between human and divine status. Their hospitable hosts, Philemon and Baucis, are transformed and worshiped as lower-level gods, while the greater gods temporarily appear as mortals. The account illustrates a graded divine realm in which gods had different ranks, humans could be divinized, and incarnation-like appearances were culturally intelligible before Christianity.

title: Seriously off topic….
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares an off-topic anecdote connected to a neighbor with an unusual name.

title: Jesus and My First Girlfriend
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers an anecdote about a first serious girlfriend and Jewish identity.
searchSummary: Recounts how Ehrman's first girlfriend exposed the limitations of his early born-again theology. After converting at sixteen, he attempted to persuade his Jewish former girlfriend that she needed Jesus for salvation, but her question about why someone who already had God also needed Jesus left him without an answer. The embarrassing exchange helped motivate him to study Christianity intensively, and within two years he was at Moody Bible Institute memorizing Scripture and acquiring the confident theological explanations he previously lacked.

title: Pastor Goranson, the Son of God, and I
author: BDEhrman
description: Drafts an anecdote about Pastor Goranson and the Son of God for How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Recounts how Ehrman's study of the Bible led him to question Jesus' divinity after years of evangelical certainty. He noticed that explicit claims equating Jesus with God are rare, that some New Testament authors distinguish them, and that Jesus' strongest self-identifications occur only in John, the latest and most theological Gospel. A painful exchange with his former pastor captures the implication: a cherished saying cannot establish belief if the historical Jesus may never have spoken it.

title: Anecdotes in Trade Books
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how anecdotes can help trade books introduce scholarly topics.
searchSummary: Explains how personal narrative helped Bart make the technical subject of New Testament textual criticism compelling in Misquoting Jesus. After identifying accessible questions about missing originals, scribal mistakes, manuscript differences, and uncertain readings, he connected the scholarship with changes in his own theology and beliefs. Despite concerns that such disclosure could invite criticism, he concluded that anecdotes showed readers why the subject mattered and helped him find an effective general-audience voice.

title: A New Phase for My Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes a new and enjoyable phase in writing How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Explains Ehrman's research method for How Jesus Became God as four overlapping stages: reading, thinking, organizing, and writing. Extensive notes and reflections reshape the project, but the decisive step is building detailed chapter outlines that select relevant evidence, establish logical flow, and connect the book's argument. Because this organizational work determines almost everything he will say, Ehrman can draft trade-book chapters rapidly, then revise them and seek scholarly and editorial criticism.

title: A Privileged View of Suffering
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to criticism about discussing suffering from a position of privilege.
searchSummary: Responds to criticism that Ehrman's privileged circumstances disqualify him from discussing suffering. He argues that everyone may examine what others' pain implies about the world and a caring, powerful God, while sufferers' beliefs need not dictate another person's conclusions. Personal comfort should prompt attention rather than silence. Ehrman refuses to impose his views on those enduring hardship and maintains that compassionate action matters more than a ready explanation: reflection should shape how one helps people in need.

title: Maintaining Your Moral Compass – Morally Agnostic
author: BDEhrman
description: Connects agnosticism, morality, and the problem of suffering.
searchSummary: Explains how an agnostic moral outlook can grow from Ecclesiastes' recognition that life is brief, unjust, and probably not followed by compensating reward. Ehrman distinguishes agnosticism, concerning knowledge, from atheism, concerning belief, and describes himself as combining both. Losing belief in God did not remove his moral compass or produce hedonism. He finds compelling secular reasons to live ethically, share life's goods, love neighbors, and help others, because concern for their well-being deepens human happiness.

title: Biblical Views of Suffering
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes biblical views of suffering from a lecture at NYU.
searchSummary: Contrasts three biblical explanations of suffering presented in Ehrman's NYU lecture. Prophets attribute calamity to God's punishment for sin; apocalyptic thinkers blame cosmic evil and expect imminent divine intervention; Ecclesiastes treats life and achievement as fleeting, without promising eventual justice. Ehrman rejects punitive theology and no longer accepts apocalyptic hope, favoring Ecclesiastes' counsel to enjoy this short life. He adds that genuine enjoyment requires helping others in need rather than pursuing selfish pleasure.

title: “Human” Appearances of God in the Old Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses Old Testament texts where God appears in human form.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: The Divine Pyramid
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the ancient divine realm as a hierarchy rather than a simple divine-human divide.
searchSummary: Ancient people often understood divinity as a pyramid rather than a sharp boundary between one God and humanity. A supreme deity stood above Olympian gods, local deities, daimones, demigods, rulers, and exceptional humans, each possessing a different degree of power and divine status. This hierarchy helps explain how gentile Christians could call Jesus God while still distinguishing him from the highest divine being.

title: Jesus as Divine in the Synoptics
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how the Synoptic Gospels portray Jesus as divine in some sense.
searchSummary: Explains how the Synoptic Gospels portray Jesus as divine without John's claim that a preexistent Word became flesh. Mark and an early form of Luke present exaltation or adoption at baptism, while later infancy traditions connect divine sonship with conception; miracles, forgiveness, and worship support this elevated status. Ancient divinity existed on a spectrum, so Jesus could be a Jewish divine man above ordinary humanity without being identical or equal with God, as John's incarnational Christology later presents him.

title: Early Christology: How I Have Changed My Mind
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains a change of mind about early Christology and incarnation.
searchSummary: Replaces a simple low-to-high model of Christological development with multiple early trajectories. Exaltation views made the human Jesus God's Son at resurrection or baptism; incarnation views made a preexistent divine being human; Paul combines incarnation with further exaltation, while virgin-birth traditions begin Jesus' sonship at conception. Ehrman's central correction is that ancient divinity existed on a spectrum, so asking whether a New Testament author considered Jesus God must always be followed by asking in what sense.

title: The Greatest Controversies
author: BDEhrman
description: Reports on recording Great Courses lectures about early Christian controversies.
searchSummary: Reflects on recording a twenty-four-lecture Great Courses series about major controversies in early Christianity. Designed for nonspecialists, the course addresses Jesus' birth, teachings, death, and resurrection; disputed Gospels and apostles; Paul; persecution; Revelation; textual transmission; the Old Testament; the Trinity; and the formation of the canon. Ehrman explains that each lecture presents accessible historical analysis and concise scholarly conclusions about debates that continue to shape modern understandings of Christianity.

title: Futuristic Interpretations of the Book of Revelation
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses futuristic interpretations of the book of Revelation.
searchSummary: Challenges interpretations that turn Revelation's symbols into literal predictions of events in the reader's lifetime. The proposal that chapter 9's locusts are attack helicopters links crowns, faces, armor, wings, and stingers with modern machinery. Yet it ignores details: the creatures cannot damage vegetation or kill anyone and torture people for five months. Such futuristic readings fail to account for the text itself. Historical interpretation instead reads the vision as a metaphor for God's rule over a world afflicted by evil.

title: A Hiatus
author: BDEhrman
description: Pauses the Christology thread because of lecture recording work.
searchSummary: Announces a temporary blogging hiatus while Ehrman records a twenty-four-lecture Great Courses series titled The Greatest Controversies in Early Christianity. He describes the substantial preparation and recording schedule and previews topics including Jesus' birth and marital status, the Dead Sea Scrolls, Paul, Gospel authorship, Revelation, the Trinity, the Old Testament, and canon formation. The audio course is intended to make major historical disputes about Jesus, the New Testament, and the early church accessible to general audiences.

title: What Kind of a Text is the King James Bible?
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses the King James Bible as a textual and historical artifact.

title: John’s Logos and Jewish Wisdom
author: BDEhrman
description: Connects John's Logos with Jewish traditions about Wisdom.
searchSummary: Connects John's divine Logos with Jewish traditions about God's personified Wisdom rather than treating the Prologue as simply Greek philosophy. Proverbs 8 describes Wisdom as present with God before creation, participating in his work and giving life, themes closely paralleling John 1. Other Jewish writings equate word and wisdom, while Philo presents the Logos as a divine intermediary. “Logos” may also fit Genesis creation by speech and the incarnation of a male Christ more naturally than feminine Sophia.

title: The Christ-Poem in John
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Christ-poem in the prologue of John's Gospel.
searchSummary: Analyzes John 1:1–18 as a poetic Christ hymn that may have been added to an earlier version of the Gospel. Its staircase parallelism celebrates the Logos as a distinct divine being who was with God, was God, created everything, brought life and light, and became human as Jesus Christ. Unlike Christologies in which Jesus is exalted after resurrection, this Prologue presents him as the incarnation of a preexistent being equal with God before creation, without invoking a virgin birth.

title: Final Thoughts on the Philippians Christ-Poem
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers final thoughts on the Philippians Christ-poem and incarnation Christology.
searchSummary: Rejects an interpretation of Philippians 2 that makes Jesus a purely human second Adam. Although the proposal sees Christ refusing the equality Adam sought and reversing Adam's disobedience, the poem uses different vocabulary from Genesis, attributes the original aspiration to Eve, and states that Christ became human. Other Pauline passages independently establish preexistence. Ehrman concludes that an angelic divine being entered human life and was exalted after obedient death to equality with God.

title: An Ancient Accusation of Textual Tampering
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses an ancient accusation that Christians tampered with Gospel texts.

title: More on the Philippians Christ-Poem
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues discussion of the structure and interpretation of the Philippians Christ-poem.

title: The Pre-pauline “Poem” in Philippians 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the pre-Pauline poem in Philippians 2 and incarnation Christology.
searchSummary: Explains why Philippians 2:6-11 is probably a pre-Pauline poem rather than prose composed for the letter. Its balanced stanzas, distinctive vocabulary, and complete exaltation half do not perfectly serve Paul's immediate appeal for selfless behavior. The poem narrates Christ's descent from divine form into human life and death, followed by elevation to universal lordship. Its existence before Philippians means incarnation Christology circulated very early, before the oldest surviving Christian writings were completed.

title: Dead Sea Scrolls Scandal
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses a scandal connected with the Dead Sea Scrolls.

title: A Brief Break from Christology
author: BDEhrman
description: Pauses the Christology thread to assess how the blog discussion is going.

title: Incarnation Christology, Angels, and Paul
author: BDEhrman
description: Connects incarnation Christology, angels, and Paul's understanding of Christ.
searchSummary: Defines incarnation Christology as the belief that a preexistent divine being became human, contrasting it with exaltation views in which a human gains divine status. Ehrman argues that Paul regarded Christ as God's chief angel based on Galatians 4:14 and Philippians 2. Christ relinquished divine form, entered human life, and died obediently; God then exalted him higher, bestowed the title Lord, and made him equal with God while keeping him personally distinct from the Father.

title: An Important and Relevant Textual Variant in Luke 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses a textual variant in Luke 2 to discuss early Christology.
searchSummary: Explains why Luke's baptismal voice probably originally said, 'You are my son, today I have begotten you,' rather than repeating Mark's affirmation of the beloved Son. Early church fathers across several regions attest the alternative reading before the oldest surviving manuscripts, and scribes had motives both to harmonize Luke with Mark and to suppress adoptionist implications. The post then raises Luke's differing associations of divine sonship with Jesus' birth, baptism, and resurrection.

title: Pushing Back the Exaltation
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how exaltation Christology was pushed earlier in Jesus' life in Christian tradition.

title: Exaltation Christology in the Speeches in Acts
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains exaltation Christology in the speeches in Acts.
searchSummary: Explains how speeches in Acts preserve early exaltation Christology even though Luke probably composed the speeches according to ancient historical practice. Peter and Paul sound alike because Luke gives them their words, yet portions of their sermons appear to incorporate older traditions. Acts 2 and 13 say God made Jesus Lord, Messiah, and Son through the resurrection. Because this view differs from Luke's own belief that Jesus held these identities earlier, the passages provide access to pre-Lukan Christian claims.

title: Gospel of the Savior
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Gospel of the Savior from a translation project on non-canonical Gospels.
searchSummary: Introduces the fragmentary Coptic Gospel of the Savior, preserved in Berlin and Strasbourg manuscripts but probably composed in Greek during the second or third century. Its surviving scenes include Jesus' Last Supper discourse, a heavenly vision of his anguished prayer before God, sayings to the disciples, a striking address to the cross, and a possible resurrection appearance. Scholars debate whether these fragments came from a full Gospel, a Passion narrative, an apocalypse, a homily, or another literary form.

title: Exaltation Christology in an Early Creed
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains exaltation Christology in an early creed about Jesus.

title: Exaltation Christology: Some Background
author: BDEhrman
description: Provides background for understanding exaltation Christology.

title: The Earliest Christology
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the earliest Christology and the move beyond a simple low-to-high model.

title: How Jesus Became God: More Questions
author: BDEhrman
description: Raises further questions about the direction of How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Argues that early Christology developed through external cultural pressures as well as internal Christian experiences. An inscription calling Augustus God alerted Ehrman that Christians and Romans applied overlapping titles such as Lord, Savior, God, and Son of God to Jesus and the emperor. As pagan converts entered the movement, claims about Jesus functioned within this imperial environment, so the book must examine competition with emperor worship alongside community-specific developments such as John's high Christology.

title: How Jesus Became God: My Change of Direction
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains a change of direction in planning How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman abandoned a title-by-title and linear account of how Jesus became God. The familiar progression from Mark's human Jesus to John's divine Jesus cannot explain why Paul, the earliest surviving Christian author, already preserves an incarnation Christology in Philippians 2. That pre-Pauline composition portrays Christ existing in God's form, becoming human, dying, and then being exalted to universal worship, demonstrating that different Christological trajectories coexisted earlier than a straight chronological model permits.

title: How Jesus Became God: The “Original” Idea, Part 3
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues the original prospectus for How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Outlines five competing paths through which second- and third-century Christians tried to reconcile Jesus' humanity and divinity. Ebionites denied divinity, docetists denied genuine humanity, gnostics separated the human Jesus from a divine Christ, and other once-respected solutions were later condemned. Emerging orthodoxy combined the polemical requirements that Christ be fully human, fully divine, and one person, producing the paradoxical fourth-century confession of one divine substance and ultimately appealing to mystery where ordinary logic strained.

title: How Jesus Became God: The “Original” Idea, Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues the original idea for How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Presents Ehrman's original plan to trace five titles from Jesus' ministry into claims of divinity: Son of Man, Son of God, Messiah, Lord, and Prophet or Word. Resurrection belief transformed expectations about Jesus as future ruler, divine son, heavenly lord, and embodiment of God's self-expression, while Jewish scripture and pagan understandings shaped each trajectory. The proposal treats these as converging conceptual paths rather than a single doctrinal declaration that immediately made Jesus identical with God.

title: How Jesus Became God: The *Original* Idea
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the original idea for How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Introduces Ehrman's original proposal to explain how an apocalyptic Jewish prophet became worshiped as God. Jesus proclaimed God's imminent kingdom, but his crucifixion shattered followers' messianic hopes until resurrection belief redirected attention from Jesus' message to claims about Jesus himself. The project begins with the historical Jesus and traces the development from resurrected messiah to divine creator and eventually the Nicene confession, making early belief in resurrection the crucial turning point.

title: During my Leave…
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains plans for research leave and continued blogging.
searchSummary: Surveys the major writing and teaching projects Ehrman pursued during academic leave while continuing the blog. He was revising introductions for an English-only collection of apocryphal Gospels, editing a full-Bible textbook, preparing a Great Courses lecture series, and moving toward concentrated work on How Jesus Became God. The post shows how these overlapping publication stages compete for time and explains why the blog's charitable purpose motivated him to sustain its demanding posting schedule after returning to teaching.

title: Being on Leave
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains what academic leave means at a research university.
searchSummary: Explains what academic leave means at a research university and why research, rather than classroom hours alone, dominates a professor's professional evaluation. Ehrman originally hoped to teach in a Christian seminary or college but unexpectedly found secular university teaching more rewarding because students bring diverse religious backgrounds and encounter the material without doctrinal assumptions. His leave supports the publication work required at UNC, where strong teaching matters but hiring, tenure, promotion, and disciplinary leadership depend heavily on sustained scholarly research.

title: Posts by Outsiders
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains plans for occasional guest posts on the blog.

title: From Jeff Siker: A Response to Comments
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares Jeff Siker's response to comments on earlier guest posts.
searchSummary: Presents Jeff Siker's explanation of why historical criticism and innocent suffering did not destroy his Christian faith as they did Ehrman's. Siker seeks mutual understanding rather than persuasion and shares Ehrman's commitment to alleviate suffering, but grounds that humanitarian response in a God revealed through Jesus who enters, embraces, and ultimately redeems suffering. Personal experience of Christ motivates participation in that redemptive work, while friendship and respectful dialogue remain possible across their contrasting theological conclusions.

title: Jeff Siker Part 2: Why I am a Christian (and yet a New Testament scholar)
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues Jeff Siker's explanation of being both Christian and a New Testament scholar.
searchSummary: Explains why New Testament scholar Jeffrey Siker remains Christian despite accepting historical-critical conclusions about Scripture. His moderate and liberal education allowed him to treat biblical differences as distinct perspectives rather than contradictions requiring reconciliation, integrating scholarship with faith instead of feeling betrayed by the church. Siker describes faith as an interpretive conversation across ancient and modern communities and grounds his continued belief especially in God's grace, resurrection hope, and response to human suffering.

title: Guest Post: Jeff Siker — Why I Am Still a Christian (and a NT Scholar)
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Jeff Siker's guest post on remaining Christian as a New Testament scholar.
searchSummary: Traces Jeffrey Siker's path from conservative Protestant youth to historically informed Christian faith. Unlike Ehrman's fundamentalist background, Siker encountered historical-critical study within a moderate tradition that did not require biblical inerrancy, so contradictions and the Bible's human character did not produce a crisis of betrayal. His education helped him move beyond literalism while integrating historical context, critical interpretation, and continued church commitment; the post sets up his fuller explanation of why he remains Christian.

title: Something New on the Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces guest contributions as a new feature for the blog.

title: Why Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Jesus remains important after rejecting Jesus' apocalyptic worldview.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman still draws ethical inspiration from Jesus despite rejecting Jesus' apocalyptic worldview and denying that he must be history's greatest moral teacher. Christianity formed Ehrman's culture and identity, while New Testament scholarship remains his deepest expertise, making Jesus a natural but not exclusive source alongside literature and other thinkers. Translated into modern terms, Jesus' vision motivates work against poverty, oppression, illness, isolation, injustice, war, and environmental harm without requiring belief that God will establish a supernatural kingdom.

title: Answer to My Objections on Demythologizing
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to objections about demythologizing Jesus' ethics.

title: More Problems with Demythologizing
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains further problems with moving Jesus' words into a different modern context.

title: Against Demythologizing the Ethics of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues against demythologizing Jesus' ethics too easily.
searchSummary: Questions whether Jesus' ethical teaching can retain its meaning after being removed from his apocalyptic worldview. Ehrman considers the linguistic argument that words and teachings acquire meaning entirely from their historical context, leaving no timeless ethical “kernel” that can simply be separated from its mythological “husk.” If Jesus' ethics were thoroughly shaped by expectation of an imminent kingdom, translating them into a modern framework may alter rather than preserve their original significance.

title: In Favor of Demythologizing the Ethics of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Makes the case for translating Jesus' ethics beyond their apocalyptic framework.
searchSummary: Explores whether Jesus' ethics can be adapted for people who no longer share his Jewish apocalyptic worldview. Drawing on Rudolf Bultmann's concept of demythologizing, Ehrman asks whether teachings rooted in expectation of an imminent divine kingdom can be stripped of that framework and applied today. Jesus' blessing of the poor, for example, might become a modern obligation to aid them, but the post leaves open whether such reinterpretation is appropriate or plausible.

title: Liar Lunatic or Lord…..Is Jesus a Moral Teacher?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates Jesus as a moral teacher in response to C. S. Lewis's argument.
searchSummary: Challenges C. S. Lewis's claim that Jesus' divine self-identification leaves only the choices of liar, lunatic, or Lord. Jesus claims equality with God only in John, whereas the earlier Synoptic Gospels and their sources never place such teachings on his lips. Ehrman argues that John's divine claims reflect a later development within the Johannine community rather than the historical Jesus, adding “legend” as the missing explanation without denying that Jesus existed.

title: Was Jesus a Great Moral Teacher?
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks whether Jesus was a great moral teacher.
searchSummary: Explains why Jesus can be considered a great moral teacher while placing his ethics within a worldview unlike modern moral reasoning. Jesus urged love, peace, generosity, healing, and justice not to improve society indefinitely, but to fulfill Torah and prepare for God's imminent kingdom. His followers were to embody that kingdom before the Son of Man's judgment; later Christians shifted the basis of salvation from such conduct to belief in Jesus' death and resurrection.

title: My Problem with Fundamentalism
author: BDEhrman
description: Defines fundamentalism in practical terms and explains why it can be harmful.

title: Textual Problems with the King James: The Trinity
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses the Johannine Comma to explain textual problems in the King James Version.
searchSummary: Explains why the King James Version includes a Trinitarian statement in 1 John 5:7-8 that was not written by the letter's author. Erasmus's Greek edition relied on a few late manuscripts and initially omitted the passage, but he later included it after opponents produced a Greek manuscript apparently translated from the Latin Vulgate for that purpose. Subsequent editions transmitted the addition to King James translators, while older manuscript evidence led modern versions to remove it.

title: Heaven and Hell: When was Heaven and Hell Invented?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how ideas of heaven and hell developed in relation to apocalyptic expectation.
searchSummary: Explains the historical shift from Jesus' apocalyptic expectation of God's imminent earthly kingdom to the later Christian doctrine that souls go to heaven or hell at death. Jewish apocalypticism contrasted the present evil age with a future age of justice and eternal life on earth. When the expected end did not arrive, Christians reconfigured this temporal dualism into a spatial one: God and the saved above, the Devil and the condemned below.
