This reinterpretation produced the familiar popular afterlife model.

title: More King James Curiosities
author: BDEhrman
description: Lists curiosities and obsolete language in the King James Version.

title: Misleading Translations in the King James
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains misleading translations in the King James Version.
searchSummary: Outlines three limitations of the King James Version as a study Bible: its reliance on inferior Greek manuscripts, occasional theological bias, and four centuries of English-language change. Ehrman emphasizes the last problem through terms that still look understandable but no longer mean what they did in 1611. Conversation in Philippians refers to citizenship rather than speech, while admiration in Revelation means astonishment, demonstrating how familiar words can produce confident but mistaken interpretations.

title: An Agnostic Teaching the Bible
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers how an agnostic can teach and study the Bible.
searchSummary: Explains why an agnostic scholar finds teaching the Bible intellectually rewarding. A public research university differs from a seminary because its purpose is critical inquiry rather than strengthening faith, and academic freedom permits assumptions to be questioned. Ehrman aims to challenge students without dictating their beliefs, make difficult scholarship understandable, encourage informed debate, and counter harmful fundamentalism by teaching people to evaluate evidence and arguments for themselves.

title: When Will The End Come?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to end-times expectations and uncertainty about when the end will come.

title: New Reference Tool
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the publication of a major reference work on ancient history.

title: Paul’s “Gospel” and Marcion
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers a question about Paul's Gospel and Marcion's use of Luke.
searchSummary: Clarifies that Paul's 'gospel' meant his preached message, not a written Gospel, because Luke and the other narratives were composed after his death. Marcion mistakenly treated the Gospel used in his second-century church as Paul's book and edited it to recover what he considered its original form. The post favors the view that Marcion chose Luke simply because it was his congregation's familiar Gospel, not because he identified its author as Paul's companion.

title: The Mayan Calendar, Y2K, and the Letter of Barnabas
author: BDEhrman
description: Connects failed end-time expectations with the Letter of Barnabas.

title: How to Date Documents, including Barnabas
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how scholars date ancient documents, including the Letter of Barnabas.

title: Why Was Barnabas Attributed to Barnabas: Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues explaining why the Letter of Barnabas was attributed to Barnabas.

title: End of the Year Reflections on the Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the blog at the end of 2012.

title: Why Was The Letter of Barnabas Attributed to Barnabas?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the anonymous Letter of Barnabas came to be attributed to Barnabas.

title: Introductions to The Lost Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses introductions to The Lost Gospels and translation of apocryphal Gospel texts.

title: Responses to Reactions (on “Christmas Longings”)
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to reader reactions to a post on Christmas longings.
searchSummary: Responds to sharply divided reactions to Ehrman's reflections on missing aspects of Christianity without intending to return to church or faith. He argues that secular humanism should offer more than opposition to religion by celebrating human life, practicing empathy, and actively helping people in need. Rejecting both moral indifference and the claim that concern for others requires God, he maintains that compassion and charitable action are essential expressions of being fully human.

title: Christmas Longings
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on Christmas, incarnation, and suffering after the holiday season.

title: Reflections on the Season
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers seasonal reflections before a short Christmas break from blogging.
searchSummary: Reflects on Ehrman's enduring affection for Christmas after losing the religious beliefs and worship practices that once gave the season meaning. Although he feels some sorrow over that absence, he rejects dwelling on loss and finds purpose in family, friendship, literature, music, food, and other ordinary pleasures. Most importantly, he renews his commitment to helping people in need, combining appreciation for Christmas memories and traditions with a nonreligious understanding of a meaningful life.

title: Luke’s First Edition
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that Luke may have first circulated without the opening birth chapters.
searchSummary: Explores whether Luke first circulated without its birth narrative. Marcion's second-century Gospel lacked chapters 1-2, and it is possible that he inherited rather than removed that form. Beginning with Jesus' baptism and the probable words 'Today I have begotten you' would make the text especially compatible with adoptionist Christianity, where God elevates a human Jesus as Son, though the post stops short of claiming that Luke himself necessarily held that view.

title: Luke’s Genealogy
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Luke's genealogy and how it differs from Matthew's.
searchSummary: Examines Luke's genealogy and argues that its unusual placement after Jesus' baptism supports a first edition without chapters 1-2. Chapter 3 reads like an opening, infancy themes disappear from later Luke-Acts, and Acts summarizes Jesus' story from John's baptism. If baptism originally introduced Jesus as God's Son, tracing Joseph's ancestry backward through Adam to God immediately afterward would make literary sense, despite the genealogy not being Jesus' biological line.

title: The Women in Matthew’s Genealogy
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the women named in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus.
searchSummary: Examines why Matthew unusually includes Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba, and Mary in Jesus' genealogy. The first four may show that gentiles have always participated in God's saving plan, although Mary was Jewish. Each was also associated with a sexual circumstance outsiders considered scandalous but that advanced divine purposes. Their inclusion may therefore prepare readers for Mary's premarital pregnancy, which Joseph initially suspects yet Matthew interprets as another surprising means by which God accomplishes salvation.

title: Another Instance of Gematria
author: BDEhrman
description: Shows another instance of gematria in the Letter of Barnabas.

title: Matthew’s Genealogy: The Number “Fourteen”
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the symbolic number fourteen in Matthew's genealogy.
searchSummary: Explains possible significance of Matthew's three groups of fourteen generations in Jesus' genealogy. Fourteen is twice seven, a number associated with perfection and divinity, and it also equals the numerical value of David's Hebrew consonants through gematria. Matthew may therefore use the pattern to portray Jesus' ancestry as divinely ordered and emphasize him as Davidic Messiah. Achieving that symbolism requires omitting generations and counting only thirteen names in the final group.

title: Matthew’s Genealogy
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Matthew's genealogy and its significance for messiahship.
searchSummary: Explains Matthew's genealogy as a theological construction connecting Jesus with Abraham, David, Israel's exile, and messianic salvation. Its repeated fourteen-generation pattern portrays national history as divinely ordered toward Jesus, even though Joseph is not his biological father, known ancestors are omitted, and the final section has only thirteen names. The genealogy is therefore historically inaccurate but programmatically important: it introduces Jesus as Jewish and Davidic Messiah who fulfills Israel's hopes, upholds its law, and faces rejection from its leaders.

title: Genealogies of Matthew and Luke
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares the genealogies of Jesus in Matthew and Luke.
searchSummary: Compares Matthew's and Luke's genealogies of Jesus. Both actually trace Joseph despite the virgin birth, but Matthew moves from Abraham through Solomon to Joseph, while Luke works backward through Nathan and Adam to God. Their different scopes reflect Matthew's emphasis on Jesus' Jewish identity and Luke's universal mission, yet the incompatible names and Davidic lines cannot be reconciled by claiming that Luke supplies Mary's ancestry.

title: More Responses to My Newsweek Article
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to reactions to a Newsweek article on the birth of Jesus.

title: Responses to my Newsweek Article
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses public responses to a Newsweek article on Jesus' birth.

title: The Infancy Narratives Compared
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Matthew's and Luke's infancy narratives and their differences.
searchSummary: Argues that discrepancies between Matthew's and Luke's infancy narratives are keys to interpretation, not merely reasons to distrust the Bible. Their genealogies conflict, their accounts assign the family different hometowns, and Luke's immediate return to Nazareth leaves no room for Matthew's later flight to Egypt. Because harmonization erases each author's distinct claims, the narratives should be read separately as theologically motivated efforts to place a Jesus known from Nazareth in Bethlehem.

title: Cover Stories on Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Mentions cover stories on Jesus while preparing a Great Courses lecture series.

title: Matthew’s Version of the Birth of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Matthew's version of Jesus' birth.
searchSummary: Reconstructs Matthew's birth story independently of Luke and argues that Bethlehem is the family's original home within this account. Joseph and Mary live in a house there, receive the Magi months or years after Jesus' birth, flee Herod to Egypt, and plan to return to Judea before Archelaus forces relocation to Nazareth. Matthew omits Luke's census, shepherds, and Temple presentation, while using dreams and fulfillment citations to portray Jesus as the Messiah who saves people from sin.

title: Luke’s Version of Jesus’ Birth
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes Luke's version of Jesus' birth.
searchSummary: Reconstructs Luke's account of Jesus' birth, from the announcements concerning John and Jesus through the census, Bethlehem journey, manger, shepherds, circumcision, Temple rites, and return to Nazareth. Its central purpose is to explain how Jesus of Nazareth could be born in David's city. The post argues that an otherwise unattested empire-wide ancestral census and the incompatible dates of Herod and Quirinius make the narrative historically implausible.

title: The Christmas Story: Some Basic Background
author: BDEhrman
description: Gives basic background on the Christmas story in canonical and later Gospels.

title: The Myth of the First Christmas
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the first Christmas story and competing understandings of the season.

title: An Agnostic Reflects on Christmas
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces an agnostic reflection on Christmas and ancient Gospel birth stories.
searchSummary: Introduces a series on Jesus' birth narratives while reflecting on why Christmas remains meaningful to Ehrman as an agnostic. He explains that Matthew and Luke offer differing stories whose historical claims he no longer accepts, yet he still values their beauty, drama, and cultural power. The angelic visitors, miraculous conception, wise men, danger, and rescue continue to communicate themes of giving, light, music, and hope even when read as stories rather than factual history.

title: Feedback on Excursus
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains a literary and historical approach to reading the Bible.
searchSummary: Proposes a sensitive textbook framework for studying the Bible through literary and historical rather than confessional methods. Literary analysis attends to genre, structure, themes, sources, and each author's distinctive message instead of harmonizing contradictions. Historical analysis situates writings in their original contexts and tests their accounts against external evidence and archaeology. Because historians reconstruct publicly accessible probabilities rather than divine action, the approach neither validates nor rejects faith claims, allowing believing and nonbelieving students to engage the same evidence.

title: Melito and arly Christian Anti-Judaism
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses Melito and the rise of early Christian anti-Judaism.

title: Apostles as Guarantors of the Truth
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to claims that apostles guaranteed reliable oral tradition about resurrection.

title: Rene Salm at the SBL (2)
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues explaining why Rene Salm's claim about Nazareth is rejected by experts.
searchSummary: Presents archaeological responses to René Salm's claim that Nazareth was uninhabited during Jesus' lifetime. Specialists criticize Salm's handling of pottery, coins, hydrology, and topography, while a hillside house with pottery dating roughly from 100 BCE to 100 CE confirms habitation in the relevant period. The modest dwelling and nearby evidence suggest a poor hamlet of about fifty houses, explaining its absence from major literary sources and making it an unlikely hometown for Christians to invent for their Messiah.

title: Rene Salm at the Society of Biblical Literature Meeting
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses Rene Salm's appearance at the Society of Biblical Literature meeting.
searchSummary: Critiques René Salm's archaeological argument that Nazareth disappeared before Jesus' lifetime and was resettled only after 70 CE. Later rock-cut tombs cannot establish earlier nonoccupation, especially because such tombs were costly and poor residents used graves unlikely to survive. Salm also relocates the village to an unexcavated valley while treating the absence of evidence there as proof. Excavated farms and coins from Hellenistic, Hasmonean, and early Roman periods instead support occupation on the traditional hillside site.

title: The Pope’s New Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Reviews Pope Benedict's book on Jesus' infancy narratives.

title: The Other Gospels and the Birth of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces birth stories in non-canonical Gospels.
searchSummary: Uses Christmas traditions to distinguish popular legends, historical uncertainty, and the divergent infancy accounts in Matthew and Luke. The date and year of Jesus' birth remain unknown, familiar details such as animals at the manger are absent from the canonical Gospels, and several narrative elements are difficult to reconcile historically. Later works such as the Proto-Gospel of James and Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew added influential stories, showing that legendary development occurred both inside and outside the New Testament.

title: Thanksgiving
author: BDEhrman
description: Offers a Thanksgiving reflection amid a busy season.
searchSummary: Reflects on Thanksgiving as Ehrman's favorite holiday and on the strange experience of gratitude after becoming an agnostic. He remains deeply thankful for family, health, work, friendship, and material security but no longer believes there is a divine giver to thank. The unequal distribution of these blessings, amid hunger, homelessness, disasters, and war, helped undermine his faith in a God who rewards some while withholding necessities from others, leaving him grateful for extraordinary good fortune without attributing it to providence.

title: The SBL Meeting
author: BDEhrman
description: Reports on the annual Society of Biblical Literature meeting.
searchSummary: Describes Ehrman's professional work at the Society of Biblical Literature meeting. He presents a public lecture on ancient divine men and Jesus, introduces a substantially revised reference volume surveying current New Testament textual criticism, hears colleagues' research, meets former students and friends, and evaluates new publications. The conference joins scholarly communication, public outreach, editorial work, professional relationships, and awareness of disciplinary developments, while also exposing the exhausting pace and overwhelming volume of modern academic production.

title: How Do I Read Books?
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers a question about reading habits and research methods.
searchSummary: Explains how Ehrman varies his reading method according to a book's importance, subject, and relevance to his research. Foundational works in unfamiliar fields receive complete reading, highlighting, and detailed notes; familiar or narrower studies may require only introductions, conclusions, selected chapters, reviews, or a research assistant's synopsis. The governing principle is to identify what information or argument he needs, then read closely enough to master that material without treating every scholarly book identically.

title: Modern Interest in the Apostolic Fathers
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains modern scholarly interest in the Apostolic Fathers.
searchSummary: Traces the rise of modern scholarly interest in the Apostolic Fathers. Renaissance humanists preferred later, more polished church fathers, while Reformation debates gradually made the earliest noncanonical Christian writers valuable evidence for competing claims about ancient church practice. Seventeenth-century manuscript discoveries and editions of 1 Clement and Ignatius then intensified disputes over apostolic succession, episcopal authority, and authenticity, establishing these texts as important sources for reconstructing Christianity immediately after the New Testament era.

title: The Collection: Apostolic Fathers
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Apostolic Fathers as a collection of early Christian writings.
searchSummary: Explains how the modern collection called the Apostolic Fathers developed rather than existing as a fixed ancient corpus. Individual works circulated separately, though some appeared together in manuscripts and several, including Barnabas and the Shepherd of Hermas, were copied as Scripture. Early modern editors eventually assembled the category from writings associated with the generations after the apostles, while discoveries and textual criticism separated authentic early works from later forgeries attributed to figures such as Clement, Ignatius, and Dionysius.

title: Thomas and the Other Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses the Gospel of Thomas in relation to other Gospels.

title: Lost Gospels That Are Still Lost 4: Q
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Q counts as a lost Gospel that remains lost.

title: Lost Gospels That Are Still Lost 3: The Greater Questions of Mary
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the lost Gospel called the Greater Questions of Mary.
searchSummary: Examines the alleged Greater Questions of Mary, known solely through Epiphanius's attack on a Gnostic group he calls the Phibionites. His quotation depicts Jesus demonstrating a non-procreative sexual ritual to Mary Magdalene, supposedly expressing the belief that procreation traps divine sparks in material bodies. Since Epiphanius was an unreliable polemicist and no other source preserves the work or episode, scholars cannot determine whether the Gospel actually existed or whether he invented it.

title: Forgery and Counterforgery
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Forgery and Counterforgery as a comprehensive study of early Christian pseudepigrapha.

title: It Has Arrived!  Forgery and Counterforgery in Early Christian Polemics.
author: BDEhrman
description: Celebrates the arrival of author copies of Forgery and Counterforgery and describes the book as a major scholarly project.
searchSummary: Celebrates the publication of Forgery and Counterforgery and outlines the problem it addresses. Ehrman notes that very few surviving Christian writings correctly identify their authors, while forged and falsely attributed apostolic and patristic works proliferated afterward. Despite the evidence, scholarship had rarely studied early Christian forgery as a broad historical phenomenon. The book therefore examines forgeries from the first four centuries within Greco-Roman and Jewish literary practices, concentrating on their role in disputes over authority, theology, leadership, and communal identity.

title: Lost Gospels That Are Still Lost 2: The Gospel of Basilides
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines the Gospel of Basilides as a lost Gnostic Gospel known only through hostile ancient reports.
searchSummary: Explains a lost tradition associated with the second-century Gnostic teacher Basilides, possibly preserved in a Gospel that no longer survives. In Irenaeus's report, Jesus transforms Simon of Cyrene to look like him and assumes Simon's appearance, so the Romans crucify Simon while Christ watches and laughs. The story reflects the conviction that a divine Christ could not suffer, but it is uncertain whether Basilides possessed a written Gospel or transmitted the account orally.

title: Lost Gospels That Are Still Lost 1
author: BDEhrman
description: Begins a series on lost Gospels by using the Gospel of Judas as a once-lost example.

title: The Apocryphal Gospels: Texts and Translations
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the purpose and scope of a bilingual edition of the Apocryphal Gospels.
searchSummary: Describes Ehrman and Zlatko Plese's Apocryphal Gospels, a scholarly facing-page collection of nearly forty Greek, Latin, and Coptic texts. They divided and reviewed the translations, supplied introductions, and included works ranging from infancy and ministry narratives to sayings, passion accounts, fragments, and otherwise unattested sayings of Jesus. The collection generally excludes Nag Hammadi works available in other bilingual editions but retains Thomas and Mary, with a separate English-only edition planned for general readers.

title: Serendipity 3: The Apocryphal Gospels Volume
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the chance circumstances that led to producing a volume on the Apocryphal Gospels.
searchSummary: Recounts how a chance publishing conversation led to The Apocryphal Gospels: Texts and Translations, a collection of roughly forty non-canonical Gospels in Greek, Latin, or Coptic with facing English translations. After the Loeb Classical Library declined the project, Oxford accepted an expanded quadrilingual edition. The volume addressed a major scholarly need because many original texts were scattered across inaccessible or outdated publications, even as discoveries such as Nag Hammadi had increased interest in Christian writings outside the canon.

title: A Stranger Problem with Lake’s Translation
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques Kirsopp Lake's translation of Barnabas by pointing to cultural assumptions behind the wording.
searchSummary: Uses Kirsopp Lake's rendering of Barnabas 10 to show how a translator's era and publishing rules can distort an ancient text. Because early Loeb contracts required potentially offensive material to be altered or omitted, Lake rendered the passage's sexual claim about rabbits in Latin rather than English. A later English replacement still obscured the anatomical reference with misleading euphemisms. Ehrman argues that such dated censorship, together with other errors, made a new Apostolic Fathers edition necessary.

title: Problems with Lake’s Translation of the Apostolic Fathers
author: BDEhrman
description: Gives examples of dated language and translation problems in Lake's Apostolic Fathers.
searchSummary: Identifies problems in Kirsopp Lake's otherwise valuable Apostolic Fathers translation. Its deliberately archaic diction and complex syntax became dated, while some English phrases now suggest meanings different from the Greek. Ehrman also points to specific mistranslations involving residence, grammar, agency, and comparison. He emphasizes that every large translation inevitably contains errors, including his own, but argues that Lake's accumulated linguistic and technical problems justified a modern replacement.

title: A Common Criticism (of me!)
author: BDEhrman
description: Addresses a criticism about ancient secretaries, dictation, and arguments over pseudonymous writings.

title: Lake’s Apostolic Fathers
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Kirsopp Lake's Loeb edition of the Apostolic Fathers and Lake's scholarly background.
searchSummary: Profiles Kirsopp Lake, the distinguished textual critic and translator whose 1912 Loeb edition of the Apostolic Fathers Bart Ehrman later replaced. Lake's career ranged across New Testament manuscripts, palaeography, Eusebius, and early Christian literature, paralleling several of Ehrman's own scholarly interests. Bruce Metzger recalled that Lake could dictate an English translation directly from the Greek while reclining on a sofa, illustrating the extraordinary linguistic facility behind his influential edition.

title: The Art of Translation
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the difficulty of producing publication-ready translations of ancient texts.
searchSummary: Reflects on the artistic and theoretical choices involved in translating the Apostolic Fathers for publication. Ehrman had to balance his preference for a fairly literal facing-page translation against his editor's desire for idiomatic readability. He also confronted whether English should preserve an ancient author's grammatical errors, unfinished thoughts, repetition, and awkward style or silently improve them. The project taught him that every fixed rendering sacrifices alternatives and makes translation far more demanding than simply understanding Greek.

title: The Sense of an Ending
author: BDEhrman
description: Takes a break from academic topics to discuss a recently finished novel.

title: Textual Problems in the Apostolic Fathers 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines a significant textual variant in the Martyrdom of Polycarp.
searchSummary: Defends the dove emerging at Polycarp's martyrdom as potentially original despite its absence from Eusebius's quotation. Every surviving manuscript includes it, and the narrative already contains comparable miracles, weakening claims that a later scribe added the bird merely to magnify Polycarp. A scribe may instead have removed it because the account parallels Jesus' passion and could evoke Gnostic separationist beliefs. The case shows that translators must first determine which textual form to translate.

title: Textual Problems in the Apostolic Fathers 1
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces textual problems in the Apostolic Fathers caused by lost originals and differing copies.
searchSummary: Explains why editing the Apostolic Fathers requires deciding among divergent copies before translation can begin. In Ignatius's Letter to the Magnesians, Greek and Latin manuscripts say Christ did not come from Silence, while the Armenian version says he did. Context and Ignatius's theology support the Armenian wording, and its Gnostic associations explain why scribes would negate it. The opposing readings demonstrate how a single textual decision can substantially change an ancient author's claim.

title: The Loeb Apostolic Fathers: The Challenges
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the challenges of preparing a new Loeb edition of the Apostolic Fathers.
searchSummary: Describes the work required to create Ehrman's two-volume Loeb edition of the Apostolic Fathers. Beyond translating each passage, he had to reconstruct the original-language text from differing manuscripts, choose variants for a concise apparatus, balance literal correspondence with readability, and write introductions addressing authorship, date, themes, interpretation, transmission, and surviving witnesses. The project offered a different form of scholarship from writing monographs but proved so painstaking that he initially vowed never to undertake another translation.

title: The Apostolic Fathers: Serendipity Strikes
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts the chance circumstances that led to a Loeb translation of the Apostolic Fathers.
searchSummary: Recounts how a doctoral seminar and a chance taxi conversation led Bart Ehrman to produce a new Loeb edition of the Apostolic Fathers. His students found Kirsopp Lake's 1912 edition dated in its introductions, manuscript evidence, and English, prompting Ehrman to mention the need for a replacement to a Harvard University Press editor. The resulting commission supported a major translation project and deeper study of early Christian authority, worship, canon, diversity, and church organization.

title: Translating the Apostolic Fathers
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the difference between reading ancient languages and producing translations for publication.
searchSummary: Introduces the Loeb Classical Library and Ehrman's commission to replace Kirsopp Lake's 1912 Apostolic Fathers. Loeb volumes place Greek or Latin beside an English translation and include a concise apparatus of manuscript differences. Ehrman identifies the works commonly grouped as Apostolic Fathers and explains that historians call them proto-orthodox because their beliefs later became dominant, not because historical study can determine correct theology. Lake's once-essential edition had become outdated and needed replacement.

title: My Translation of the NT?
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers whether Ehrman plans to publish an English translation of the New Testament.

title: Lincoln’s Watch and Eyewitnesses
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Lincoln's watch to reflect on eyewitness testimony and memory.
searchSummary: Uses Abraham Lincoln's pocket watch to demonstrate the unreliability of long-term eyewitness memory. Forty-five years after secretly inscribing the watch, its repairer quoted a patriotic message about slavery and the president, but opening the watch revealed substantially different wording with neither reference. If a direct participant could transform his own action over the same interval separating Jesus from the Gospels, decades of indirect oral transmission offer still less assurance of verbatim preservation.

title: Secret Followers of Jesus?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether secret followers of Jesus in the Sanhedrin are historically plausible.

title: Pilate and Barabbas
author: BDEhrman
description: Assesses the Barabbas episode as evidence for Pilate's willingness to placate Jewish crowds.

title: Decent Burials for Crucified Victims
author: BDEhrman
description: Considers whether crucified victims in Judea could receive decent burial.
searchSummary: Reviews four arguments that Romans may have allowed Jesus a decent burial: Jewish law, Yehohanan's buried remains, Josephus's rescue of crucified associates, and Philo's account of holiday clemency. Bart finds none closely analogous because Romans controlled Jesus's body, Yehohanan's circumstances are unknown, Josephus stopped executions rather than arranged burials, and Philo describes an exceptional imperial birthday concession to relatives. He concludes that prompt burial was conceivable but historically improbable.

title: Crucified Bodies and Scavengers
author: BDEhrman
description: Reviews ancient evidence for crucified bodies being exposed to scavengers and applies it to Jesus' burial.
searchSummary: Surveys ancient literary evidence that crucified victims were commonly left exposed to birds and other scavengers. Bart cites Horace, Juvenal, Petronius, an inscription, and Artemidorus to show that postmortem exposure formed part of crucifixion's humiliation and deterrent effect. Although he once dismissed John Dominic Crossan's suggestion that scavengers consumed Jesus's body, this evidence leads him to reconsider whether Joseph of Arimathea instead provided Jesus a prompt and honorable burial.

title: Women Who Did Not Doubt the Resurrection
author: BDEhrman
description: Notes that women at the empty tomb are not portrayed as doubting the resurrection.

title: Disciples Who Doubt the Resurrection
author: BDEhrman
description: Surveys Gospel traditions in which disciples doubt resurrection appearances.

title: Why Was Jesus Killed?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Roman authorities would have executed Jesus despite limited evidence of anti-Roman activity.

title: Anti-Judaism in the Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses anti-Jewish tendencies in Gospel passion narratives and the shift of blame away from Rome.
searchSummary: Distinguishes ancient religious anti-Judaism from modern racial anti-Semitism while tracing increasing Jewish responsibility in Gospel passion narratives. Mark portrays Pilate and Jewish leaders acting together; Luke and Matthew increasingly declare Pilate reluctant or innocent; John appears to hand Jesus to Jewish authorities for crucifixion. Later apocryphal traditions go further, sometimes converting or canonizing Pilate. Exonerating Rome while blaming Jews helped Christian storytelling develop into hostility that produced discriminatory law and violence after imperial conversion.

title: Books and Icebergs
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why strong books require extensive background research, using resurrection research and a planned textbook as examples.
searchSummary: Explains why a concise popular book requires far more research than readers ever see. Resurrection belief is central to How Jesus Became God because it initiated the process by which followers reinterpreted a failed messianic claimant as divine, even though resurrection alone did not immediately make Jesus God. Ehrman compares a book to an iceberg: visible arguments must rest on extensive hidden reading, and scholarly judgment includes knowing which well-researched material to omit rather than displaying everything learned.

title: The Gospel of Jesus’ Wife: Another New Development
author: BDEhrman
description: Reports new scholarly arguments that the Gospel of Jesus' Wife fragment may derive from the Gospel of Thomas.

title: Were the Disciples Martyred for Believing the Resurrection?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates evidence for claims that apostles were martyred because of belief in the resurrection.

title: Was Jesus Given a Decent Burial (By Joseph of Arimathea)
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines historical doubts about Joseph of Arimathea and the burial of Jesus.
searchSummary: Questions whether Joseph of Arimathea historically gave Jesus a known tomb burial. Bart notes that Roman crucifixion normally included prolonged exposure or disposal in a common grave, while Jewish burial requirements did not bind Pilate or Roman executioners. He argues that Christians had a strong narrative reason to develop a named burial place as evidence for an empty tomb, and therefore considers improper disposal more probable despite the Gospel accounts and scholarly disagreement.

title: Paul and the Resurrection of the “Flesh”?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to questions about Paul's idea of bodily resurrection and the spiritual body.
searchSummary: Clarifies why Paul's rejection of resurrected “flesh” does not mean he denied bodily resurrection. For Paul, flesh is humanity's corrupted dimension, whereas the body is God's creation awaiting redemption. Ancient thinkers could understand soul and spirit as highly refined material, making a spiritual body both physical and immortal. Later theologians lost Paul's technical distinction and defended resurrection of the flesh against Gnostic opponents, even producing works such as 3 Corinthians that attributed to Paul a position different from his own.

title: The Women and the Empty Tomb
author: BDEhrman
description: Considers why Gospel writers give women a prominent role in empty tomb stories.
searchSummary: Reconsiders the argument that women discovering Jesus's empty tomb must be historical because ancient audiences distrusted female testimony. The stories addressed Christian insiders rather than courts or skeptical converts, and women's credibility has likely been overstated as a problem. Early belief arose from visions of Jesus, while an empty tomb was a later narrative implication of bodily resurrection. Women became discoverers because burial care belonged to them and the male disciples were remembered as having fled Jerusalem.

title: Christians Charged as Perverts and Criminals
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents second-century accusations that Christians were immoral and criminal.

title: Paul’s View of Resurrection
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores Paul's view of resurrection, the empty tomb, and visionary experiences.
searchSummary: Answers objections to reading Paul as a believer in physical resurrection. Paul does not mention women discovering an empty tomb because he probably did not know that tradition, and his letters never describe the appearance as a blinding light; Acts does. First Corinthians 15 assumes Jesus' transformed bodily resurrection to argue that believers' bodies will likewise be redeemed, not replaced. “Flesh” signifies corruption vulnerable to sin, while the resurrected body remains materially continuous with the mortal body but becomes immortal.

title: Gerd Lüdemann on the Resurrection of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses Gerd Ludemann's historical argument about resurrection belief and visions.

title: The Resurrection as a Key to Early Understandings of Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Argues that belief in the resurrection was crucial to early claims about Jesus and Christianity's origins.
searchSummary: Argues that Christianity began not with Jesus' teaching or death alone, but when followers came to believe God had raised him. Jesus proclaimed God's imminent kingdom and Torah obedience, whereas Christianity centered salvation on Jesus' death and resurrection; belief in resurrection transformed a humiliating execution into an atoning death and revived messianic expectations in a new form. Whatever happened physically, the followers' sincere resurrection belief is historically decisive because it initiated increasingly exalted claims about Jesus.

title: The Next Project: How Jesus Became God
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces the beginning of work on How Jesus Became God.
searchSummary: Announces Ehrman's return to How Jesus Became God after years of postponement for other timely projects and explains the book's revised popular orientation. Moving the trade-book contract from Oxford to Harper requires renewed research and a less technical presentation for a wider audience. Ehrman identifies resurrection belief as a central mechanism in changing understandings of Jesus and begins comparing conservative, skeptical, and critical scholarly accounts before writing and discussing the research on the blog.

title: More on the Criterion of Independent Attestation
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the criterion of independent attestation and the independence of Gospel sources.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: Blog Preferences
author: BDEhrman
description: Asks blog readers about posting frequency and blog preferences.

title: Jesus and the Historical Criteria
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains historical criteria used in Jesus research and debates about their value.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: Faith, History, and Isaiah 7
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Isaiah 7 and the virgin birth to distinguish historical interpretation from faith claims.
searchSummary: Interprets Isaiah 7 within its eighth-century BCE setting rather than as a direct prediction of Jesus' virgin birth. Isaiah addresses Ahaz during the Syro-Ephraimite crisis and points to an already pregnant young woman whose child's early years will mark the enemies' defeat. Later Christians may legitimately adopt a theological or Christological rereading, but that is distinct from Isaiah's historical meaning. Ehrman argues that interpretation can employ many lenses while refusing to identify a later faith application with original authorial intent.

title: More on Faith and History
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to reader comments about separating faith and history in biblical interpretation.
searchSummary: Clarifies Ehrman's view of how historical research and theological belief should interact. Individuals may allow historically grounded conclusions to reshape their theology, but they should not use prior theological commitments to decide what the historical evidence must show. Using the Gospel of John as an example, he distinguishes historically evaluating an ancient account from declaring it accurate because it is inspired, while stressing that a historically problematic text may still possess theological value and that historical inquiry is never objective.

title: The Bible as History and Theology
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the difference between studying the Bible historically and theologically.
searchSummary: Explains the difference between historical and theological approaches to scripture. Historians reconstruct publicly observable events from evidence available to people of any faith, so they can describe what biblical writers claimed and what probably occurred but cannot identify God's actions, true doctrine, or salvation's meaning. Believers may integrate historical findings with theology, yet those conclusions arise outside historical method. Ehrman's textbook therefore investigates biblical origins and interpretations without attempting either to confirm or disprove its religious claims.

title: Does Luke Combat a Docetic Christology?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates claims that Luke's resurrection story combats docetic Christology.
searchSummary: Evaluates whether Luke's risen Jesus, who displays flesh and bones and eats fish, was written to refute docetism. The post finds that possible but unlikely because docetism denied Jesus' humanity during life, whereas Luke emphasizes bodily existence specifically after resurrection. Luke is more directly opposing Christians who accepted Jesus as a real human but believed only his spirit survived death, affirming instead a physical resurrection for Jesus and future believers.

title: Peter, The Smoked Tuna, and the Flying Heretic
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces an apocryphal Acts of Peter story about Peter, a revived tuna, and Simon Magus.

title: Is the New Gospel Fragment a Modern Forgery?
author: BDEhrman
description: Reviews early arguments that the Gospel of Jesus' Wife fragment may be a modern forgery.

title: A Problem with My Textbook
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses the challenges of writing an introductory Bible textbook for students.

title: The Gospel of Jesus’s Wife
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Gospel of Jesus' Wife fragment and questions about authenticity.

title: BREAKING NEWS!  A Significant New Non-Canonical Gospel Fragment
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces Karen King's release of a newly public Coptic fragment in which Jesus mentions a wife.

title: How My Loss of Faith Affected My Scholarship
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores whether loss of faith affected New Testament scholarship and academic conclusions.
searchSummary: Argues that losing Christian faith had almost no effect on Ehrman's scholarship. Before becoming agnostic, he already accepted manuscript variation, biblical contradictions, disputed authorship, Jesus' apocalyptic message, diverse New Testament theologies, and competing early Christian groups. His scholarly shift occurred earlier as he moved from fundamentalism into critical study while remaining a liberal believer. Because Christian scholars share these conclusions, students can accept critical evidence without abandoning faith; Ehrman's teaching aims at knowledge and thought, not conversion or deconversion.

title: On the Blog Itself
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the first five months of the blog and its charity-focused purpose.

title: Possibilities for the Afterlife
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces ancient afterlife options to explain Paul's expectation of bodily resurrection.
searchSummary: Compares three ancient possibilities for what follows death: annihilation, disembodied survival, and bodily resurrection. Greco-Roman epitaphs often imply extinction, while Platonic traditions imagine a refined soul liberated from the body's prison. Jewish apocalyptic thought instead treats the body as God's good creation, temporarily subject to evil and death but destined for transformation into an immortal spiritual body. Paul adopts this third model, whereas his Corinthian opponents may have retained the second, helping explain their dispute over resurrection.

title: The Need for Context
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents textbook material stressing the need for historical and cultural context before studying the New Testament.
searchSummary: Argues that biblical texts must be interpreted within the cultures, assumptions, and genres of their ancient authors rather than as modern statements. A deliberately Jesus-like summary of Apollonius of Tyana shows that divine births, miracles, disciples, trials, ascensions, and postmortem appearances were recognizable Greco-Roman narrative patterns, not uniquely Christian categories. Understanding stories about Jesus therefore requires comparison with the first-century Mediterranean world. Removing them from that context changes their meaning and encourages anachronistic readings.

title: Autobiographical.  Metzger and My Loss of Faith
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers how Bruce Metzger responded to Ehrman's loss of faith.
searchSummary: Answers how Bruce Metzger reacted to Ehrman's loss of faith: Ehrman does not know because they never discussed either man's beliefs. Their relationship centered on manuscripts, New Testament studies, and early Christian history, as do his collaborations with other believing scholars, since faith is irrelevant to their shared academic work. Metzger likely knew of the change and remained Christian, but his respect for mystery and scholarly boundaries may have led him to leave students' convictions in their own hands.

title: Autobiographical: Back to Metzger and Me
author: BDEhrman
description: Recalls Bruce Metzger's personality and the mentor-student relationship at Princeton.
searchSummary: Describes Bruce Metzger as a shy, formal, courteous Christian gentleman who became Ehrman's mentor and father figure without becoming emotionally intimate. Anecdotes about mowing in a three-piece suit, awkward conversation, and initial skepticism toward The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture show his old-fashioned reserve, while encouragement, sermon attendance, hospitality, and willingness to serve a small church reveal generosity and humility. Ehrman remained close to him for years and struggled even after graduation to address the revered scholar by his first name.

title: Why Did Scribes Add the Bloody Sweat?
author: BDEhrman
description: Interprets why later scribes may have added the bloody sweat passage to Luke.
searchSummary: Argues that scribes added Luke's bloody-sweat verses by the mid-second century to oppose Docetists who denied Jesus' genuine humanity and suffering. The passage conflicts with Luke's otherwise calm portrayal of Jesus and is absent from important manuscripts, yet Justin, Irenaeus, and Hippolytus cite it early specifically against nonhuman interpretations of Christ. In a period of competing adoptionist, docetic, separationist, and proto-orthodox Christologies, the addition supplied vivid flesh-and-blood evidence for the emerging orthodox position.

title: Jesus’ Death in Mark and Luke
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Mark and Luke on the meaning of Jesus' death.
searchSummary: Compares how Mark and Luke use Jesus' death to address suffering communities. Mark's anguished Jesus cannot perceive God's purpose, yet his death opens access to God and teaches that divine redemption can operate unseen. Luke removes atonement imagery and presents a composed Jesus who knows God is present and paradise awaits, modeling confidence under persecution. Combining the narratives obscures these different explanations of suffering and rewrites both Gospels.

title: Jesus Going to His Death in Luke
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Luke's calm portrayal of Jesus going to death and the later bloody sweat addition.
searchSummary: Contrasts Mark's silent and despairing Jesus with Luke's composed portrayal of Jesus approaching death. In Luke, Jesus comforts grieving women, asks forgiveness for his executioners, promises paradise to a criminal, and entrusts his spirit to God. These deliberate changes show that Luke understood Jesus' suffering differently from Mark, while harmonized lists such as the seven last words conceal the individual narratives rather than explain them.

title: An Interlude: My Other CIA
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the UNC Christianity in Antiquity reading group as another academic community.
searchSummary: Describes Ehrman's informal Christianity in Antiquity reading group for UNC and Duke faculty and graduate students. Participants circulate substantial research papers before meeting to critique arguments, defend interpretations, encounter subjects outside their specialties, and practice scholarly discussion without grades. A session on Michael Penn's Syriac evidence for early Christian-Muslim relations illustrates the group's value: neglected texts complicate modern assumptions about inevitable conflict by revealing interactions ranging from hostility to mutual understanding and cooperation during the early Islamic centuries.

title: More on The Bloody Sweat
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses the structure of Jesus' prayer in Luke and the textual problem of the bloody sweat.
searchSummary: Shows that Jesus' prayer before arrest in Luke forms a chiasmus centered on prayer and preparation for trial. Jesus prays and calmly accepts arrest, while the disciples sleep and flee; the literary structure makes prayer the explanation for their contrasting responses. The disputed angel and bloody-sweat verses break this structure and reintroduce precisely the agony Luke removes from Mark, supporting the conclusion that scribes added them later.

title: Problems with the NRSV (Part 5)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the bloody sweat passage in Luke is likely not original.
searchSummary: Argues that Luke's bloody-sweat passage was not original despite its inclusion in the NRSV. Comparing Luke with Mark shows that Luke consistently removes Jesus' distress, repeated pleas, and collapse in Gethsemane to create a calm, controlled passion narrative. The disputed verses, absent from important early manuscripts, abruptly make Jesus agonize and require angelic strength, undermining Luke's editorial pattern and pointing to a later insertion.

title: Problems with the NRSV (Part 4)
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents an NRSV textual disagreement involving Luke's bloody sweat passage.
searchSummary: Argues that the NRSV should omit Luke 22:43-44 from the main text rather than retaining it in unexplained double brackets. The verses describe an angel strengthening Jesus and sweat like blood, but the oldest and strongest manuscripts lack them. Ehrman also says they conflict with Luke's otherwise composed portrayal of Jesus' death and disrupt the passage's literary structure. Familiarity, he suggests, led translators to print a scribal addition they themselves considered nonoriginal.

title: Problems with the NRSV (Part 3)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how a disputed Last Supper passage affects whether Luke presents Jesus' death as an atoning sacrifice.
searchSummary: Explains how a textual decision in the NRSV changes Luke's theology of Jesus' death. The translation includes disputed Last Supper words declaring Jesus' body and blood given for others, although an early manuscript tradition lacks them. Because Luke-Acts nowhere else treats the crucifixion as an atoning sacrifice, the post argues that scribes expanded the passage to resemble 1 Corinthians and that the NRSV should have translated the shorter text.

title: Problems with the NRSV Bible (Part 2)
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques an NRSV gender-inclusive translation that changes the meaning of a passage.
searchSummary: Criticizes the NRSV's inclusive rendering of Psalm 8 when Hebrews quotes it as a prophecy about Christ. In the psalm, plural language about human beings accurately conveys a statement about humanity in general. Hebrews, however, interprets the singular man and son of man specifically as Jesus and uses the passage to establish Christ's superiority. By repeating the inclusive plural, the translation removes that Christological meaning and leaves English readers unable to follow the argument.

title: Problems with the NRSV (Part I)
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces problems with the NRSV while recalling work with Bruce Metzger.
searchSummary: Argues that the NRSV mistranslates John 3:22 by saying Jesus went into the Judean countryside rather than the land of Judea. The Greek creates a geographical difficulty because Jesus is already in Jerusalem, which lies within Judea. Ehrman believes the altered wording removes a discrepancy instead of translating it, obscuring a literary seam produced when the Gospel's author combined sources. He contrasts this with a similar geographical transition between John 5 and 6 that translation cannot conceal.

title: Carlo Martini, in memoriam
author: BDEhrman
description: Memorializes Carlo Martini as a textual scholar and Roman Catholic leader.

title: Another Take on Jesus’ Existence
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to mythicist objections while distinguishing scholarly consensus from evidence.
searchSummary: Explains the distinction between expert consensus and historical evidence in debates over whether Jesus existed. Agreement among New Testament specialists does not prove the conclusion, but readers should understand qualified judgments while examining their supporting evidence. Ehrman cites Larry Hurtado's view that earlier scholarship already answered modern mythicist arguments and that specialists can more productively advance research than repeatedly revisit claims they regard as ill-informed and logically defective.

title: Problems with Other Translations
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares problems in popular Bible translations such as the KJV and NIV.

title: My Preferred Bible Translation
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why the NRSV is preferred by many biblical scholars.

title: Am I a Better Person as an Agnostic?
author: BDEhrman
description: Addresses whether agnosticism changes moral character and ethical motivation.
searchSummary: Considers whether becoming agnostic made Ehrman morally worse and rejects his fear that ethics requires belief in God. Because he regards this life as the only one, he values relationships, meaningful work, pleasures, and compassion rather than pursuing empty self-indulgence. He gives more, feels urgency about suffering that no afterlife will repair, and grounds moral concern in evolved empathy, concluding that he may not be better but is no worse, and is happier and more engaged with life.

title: Autobiographical.  Metzger and Me: More on the NRSV
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares humorous stories from work with the NRSV revision committee.
searchSummary: Recalls two stories from Ehrman's work on the committee revising the Revised Standard Version. He preferred the playful title RSVP before the committee settled on New Revised Standard Version, and his office held ashes from an RSV burned by a fundamentalist pastor angered by translation changes such as Isaiah's young woman rather than virgin. Metzger used the relic to observe that modern opponents burn a translation instead of its translator, illustrating both resistance to biblical revision and his understated humor.

title: Did Jesus Speak Greek?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether Jesus likely spoke Greek, especially during the trial before Pilate.

title: The NRSV Bible Translation Committee (Part 2)
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes experiences as a secretary for the NRSV translation committee.
searchSummary: Describes Ehrman's responsibilities as Bruce Metzger's full-time research assistant during the New Revised Standard Version's final production. He computerized years of committee decisions, checked terminology and repeated phrases for consistency across independently translated books, verified application of inclusive-language policy, and flagged problems in English style or translational accuracy for committee review. After two years of detailed work, he prepared the completed translation for its eight authorized publishers before its 1989 release.

title: Autobiographical.  Metzger and Me.  The NRSV Bible Translation Committee
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts the invitation to serve as secretary for the NRSV Bible translation committee.
searchSummary: Recounts Ehrman's graduate-student work as a secretary for the committee revising the Revised Standard Version into the NRSV. Diverse specialists reviewed proposed changes verse by verse using Hebrew, Greek, related ancient languages, early translations, manuscript evidence, and modern scholarship. Subcommittees decided contested renderings by majority vote, allowing consensus to restrain individual preferences. Ehrman recorded those decisions and supported the meetings before later taking responsibility for coordinating the committees' accumulated work.

title: My First Teaching Position
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on the difficulty of obtaining a first teaching job and the move to Rutgers.
searchSummary: Recounts how Ehrman's first teaching position arose unexpectedly after repeated failure on the academic job market. His seminary education and highly technical specialization made both secular and confessional institutions reluctant to interview him, despite his broader teaching range. An emergency Rutgers vacancy allowed him to take over New Testament courses midsemester, leading to four years of temporary appointments and the secular teaching experience that eventually enabled his UNC career, though the opportunity originated in another family's profound misfortune.

title: Sad News: The Passing of Marvin Meyer
author: BDEhrman
description: Memorializes Marvin Meyer and scholarly work on Coptic and Gnostic texts.

title: Questions on Jesus’ Language and on the Crucifixion
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about Jesus' language before Roman authorities and the public nature of crucifixion.

title: Autobiographical.  Metzger and Me.  The Dissertation Defense
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the dissertation defense process and Metzger's role in it.
searchSummary: Recounts Ehrman's 1985 dissertation defense after writing a technical textual study while teaching three new Rutgers courses and supporting a young family. He packed the defense with friends and prepared for rigorous methodological challenges, but Metzger unexpectedly asked only which ancient people were named Didymus and which were blind. Because the other faculty lacked specialized knowledge to probe deeply, the anticipated ordeal became easy, ending with a successful doctorate and a celebration rather than the demanding examination he had expected.

title: Bible Intro: Nearing the finish line
author: BDEhrman
description: Reports nearing completion of a Bible introduction textbook and revisiting Hebrew Bible scholarship.

title: Autobiographical.  Metzger and Me: Finishing the Dissertation
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Metzger's approach to supervising dissertation work.
searchSummary: Describes how Bruce Metzger's light-touch supervision suited Ehrman's independent approach to completing his dissertation. Metzger read chapters, corrected language, and answered questions without controlling the research; after retirement, David Adams became adviser while Metzger remained central. Ehrman published the methodological chapter as an article and the rest as Didymus the Blind and the Text of the Gospels, then persuaded Gordon Fee to launch a church-fathers textual series that began with this volume and later continued under Ehrman and his students.

title: Autobiographical.  Me and Metzger: More on the Dissertation
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues reflections on the dissertation project and the challenge of describing it briefly.
searchSummary: Explains the technical dissertation that established Ehrman's expertise in New Testament textual criticism. He extracted every Gospel quotation from Didymus the Blind, distinguished citations from adaptations and allusions, compared their wording with numerous Greek and Latin manuscripts, catalogued differences, applied statistics, and reconstructed the text's Alexandrian transmission. The project also developed a new method for classifying manuscripts from earlier suggestions Metzger had not pursued, illustrating why doctoral research demands years of specialized work that few readers may ever directly use.

title: A Forger Who Was Caught.  The Case of Salvian, Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues the case of Salvian as a Christian forger caught in the act.
searchSummary: Evaluates Salvian's defense after his treatise written as Timothy was exposed as a forgery. Salvian claimed that Timothy was a symbolic pen name expressing honor for God and that anonymity reflected humility, yet he admitted adopting another identity because an obscure author lacked authority. Ehrman rejects these explanations: Salvian could have remained anonymous, and the apostolic name uniquely attracted attention. Salonius's objection confirms that contemporaries recognized the deception, while the case reveals authority as a motive for pseudepigraphy.

title: A Christian Forger Caught in the Acts
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces Salvian as a rare known case of a Christian forger being caught.
searchSummary: Describes the unusual case of Salvian of Marseille, a Christian forger identified by his former student and bishop Salonius. Salvian published a call for radical almsgiving under the apostolic name Timothy, then defended the false identity by claiming that a book's content mattered more than its author while admitting his own obscurity would limit its influence. Ehrman argues that the contradictory appeal to Timothy as a symbolic pen name cannot conceal the real purpose: borrowing apostolic authority to gain readers.

title: Autobiographical.  Metzger and Me: The Dissertation
author: BDEhrman
description: Recounts a dissertation project on Didymus, Metzger, and the Greek manuscript tradition.
searchSummary: Recounts how Gordon Fee's rigorous work on church fathers' New Testament quotations inspired Ehrman's dissertation under Bruce Metzger. Such citations can locate particular textual readings in a known time and place, though quotations from memory, paraphrases, and inconsistent wording make reconstruction difficult. Metzger recommended analyzing Didymus the Blind's newly published Old Testament commentaries, giving Ehrman access to previously unstudied evidence, including an unpublished handwritten edition loaned by Ludwig Koenen.

title: Peter as Literate?  Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Assesses whether Peter's social background makes authorship of 1 Peter plausible.
searchSummary: Uses Peter's social setting and the language of 1 Peter to reject Petrine authorship. Archaeology portrays first-century Capernaum as a poor, isolated, predominantly illiterate village with no elite institutions or Greek inscriptions. Peter was an Aramaic-speaking fisherman, whereas 1 Peter exhibits polished Greek rhetoric and detailed reliance on the Septuagint. Missionary travel could provide conversational Greek but not years of advanced composition training, and no evidence shows adults receiving such education in antiquity.

title: Peter as Literate?
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces ancient literacy evidence relevant to whether Peter could have written 1 Peter.
searchSummary: Explains why ancient literacy cannot be equated with modern reading and writing. Perhaps ten percent could read in favorable societies and less than three percent in Roman Palestine, while composition required further education available chiefly to urban elites. Greek literary ability was rarer still among rural Aramaic speakers. These findings make Peter an implausible author of sophisticated Greek works: a poor Galilean fisherman lacked the time, resources, and schooling to become part of the tiny educated minority.

title: Ancient Secretaries (Part 2)
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines whether ancient secretarial practices could explain pseudepigraphic New Testament writings.
searchSummary: Evaluates whether ancient secretaries could explain New Testament letters whose style and content differ from their alleged authors' known writings. Evidence supports dictation and occasional light editing among elites, but not routine coauthorship or the composition of complex letter-essays under another person's name. The few examples associated with Cicero involve short communications and acknowledged deception. Ehrman concludes that the secretary hypothesis for Petrine and disputed Pauline letters rests on nearly nonexistent evidence, whereas ancient pseudonymous writing is abundantly documented.

title: Ancient Secretaries (Part 1)
author: BDEhrman
description: Summarizes ancient secretarial practices in relation to 1 Peter and Pauline pseudepigraphy.
searchSummary: Examines ancient evidence for secretaries as dictation takers and stylistic editors. Word-for-word dictation is well attested, but occasional editing appears only among wealthy, educated elites and concerns ordinary correspondence, not long theological treatises. Such limited corrections cannot explain wholesale differences in language, argument, and content among disputed Pauline or Petrine letters. Ehrman argues that commentators frequently invoke secretaries without evidence, overlooking that the writings themselves claim apostolic authorship rather than identifying another person as their composer.

title: Always Looking for MORE!!
author: BDEhrman
description: Encourages readers to promote the blog to raise more money for charity.
searchSummary: Asks satisfied members to promote the young blog so it can attract more subscribers and raise additional money for hunger and homelessness charities. Bart reports steady growth of about two members per day, notes that he personally absorbs all operating costs, and welcomes direct donations. He reproduces a member's endorsement praising the quantity and range of posts, Bart's responses to reader questions, and the thoughtful interaction among participants as reasons others should join.

title: Forgery.  Another Deceived Deceiver (Part 2)
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues analysis of the Apostolic Constitutions as a pseudepigraphic work that condemns forgery.
searchSummary: Analyzes the ironies of the forged Apostolic Constitutions, whose author speaks as Jesus' apostles, includes the work itself among scriptural books, and condemns rival pseudepigrapha. Although the compiler rejected only writings considered heretical and viewed his own teachings as true, his warnings reveal awareness that authors falsely used apostolic names. The work also accepted other forged writings as authentic. Its later reception, including partial approval by the Trullan Council, demonstrates how successfully a forger could condemn forgery while deceiving readers.

title: Forgery.  Another Deceived Deceiver (Part 1)
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the Apostolic Constitutions as a pseudepigraphic church order.
searchSummary: Shows how the fourth-century Apostolic Constitutions transformed earlier church orders into a work falsely presented as the apostles' teaching. The compiler inserted first-person claims by Peter, Paul, James, Philip, and others, with Clement serving as the imagined bearer rather than author. By linking obedience to the book with hearing Christ and God, the forgery claimed authority even while condemning lies. Ehrman identifies the resulting irony: a writer using deceptive apostolic identities to denounce deception was himself misled by other forgeries.

title: Forgery and Deceived Deceivers
author: BDEhrman
description: Opens Forgery and Counterforgery with an anecdote about deceivers deceived by forgeries.
searchSummary: Recounts the ancient story of Heraclides Ponticus, a learned philosopher associated with hoaxes, plagiarism, and forged tragedies who was himself fooled by forgery. His former student Dionysius composed a play under Sophocles' name and exposed Heraclides' mistaken attribution through increasingly pointed acrostics. Ehrman considers scholarly doubts about whether the anecdote itself was fabricated and compares a similar trick attributed to Lucian. The episode opens Forgery and Counterforgery by illustrating the recurring irony of deceivers becoming victims of literary deceit.

title: So Much For THAT Idea….
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes publication tasks that interrupted planned writing on a Bible textbook.
searchSummary: Describes how simultaneous arrival of page proofs for two technical books disrupted Ehrman's plan to draft chapters of a Bible introduction. Page proofs reproduce the final typeset pages and require authors to inspect every word, punctuation mark, omission, hyphenation, and formatting choice before publication. The task becomes especially demanding when books contain French, German, Greek, and Latin, making meticulous proofreading an unavoidable and time-sensitive stage of scholarly publishing despite its interruption of new writing.

title: Silvanus as Peter’s Secretary?
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates whether Silvanus could explain 1 Peter as Peter's letter through a secretary.
searchSummary: Explains why 1 Peter's reference to writing “through Silvanus” does not identify Silvanus as Peter's secretary. Ancient usage shows that this expression names the letter carrier, and Silvanus was likely another Aramaic-speaking Palestinian without the literary Greek needed to compose the work. Secretaries commonly recorded dictation but only rarely edited elite correspondence, with no evidence that they routinely created substantial works in another person's name. Ehrman therefore finds pseudonymous authorship more plausible than a secretarial explanation.

title: Autobiographical.  Metzger and Me: My PhD Exams
author: BDEhrman
description: Recalls PhD comprehensive exams under Bruce Metzger at Princeton.
searchSummary: Recounts Ehrman's compressed preparation for Princeton's grueling PhD examinations while taking seminars, supporting a family, and pastoring a church. Expecting Metzger to repeat familiar history questions, he was shocked when Metzger tried to help by tailoring the exam to Ehrman's bibliography. Ehrman then discovered that his first essay had assigned the wrong position on the canon to Harnack and feared failure, but Metzger missed the error; he passed the written and oral examinations and advanced to his dissertation.

title: Resurrection and Resuscitation
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains resurrection as distinct from resuscitation and other biblical afterlife ideas.
searchSummary: Distinguishes resurrection from both older Hebrew Bible afterlife beliefs and temporary resuscitation. Many biblical writers envision either no afterlife or a shadowy existence in Sheol, while Jewish apocalyptic thinkers later proposed that God would bodily raise the righteous and wicked for reward or punishment. People restored by Elijah and Elisha eventually die again, but resurrection produces an immortal body. Early Christians therefore interpreted Jesus' return to life as the first event of the expected end-time resurrection, not ordinary revival.

title: Paul in Acts: Part 3
author: BDEhrman
description: Contrasts Acts' portrayal of harmony between Paul and the Jerusalem apostles with Paul's account of conflict involving Peter and James's associates.

title: Accessing the Squirrel
author: BDEhrman
description: Corrects an access problem with the previous squirrel story post.

title: Autobiographical.  Metzger and Me: The Squirrel Story, Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues the story about verifying the anecdote involving Metzger and the Greek word for squirrel.
searchSummary: Reconstructs the origin of the legendary story about Bruce Metzger identifying the Greek word for squirrel after one falls dead. Seeing a real squirrel survive such a fall and witnessing Metzger's compassion showed Ehrman that the narrative was fictional, while hearing Metzger spontaneously explain the word skiouros suggested a real remembered saying. He proposes that a colleague placed the philological remark into an invented comic scene, paralleling Gospel apophthegms in which memorable sayings acquire narrative settings during oral transmission.

title: Paul in Acts: Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues the discussion of Paul in Acts by considering Luke's sources and discrepancies with Paul's letters.

title: Autobiographical.  Metzger and Me: The Squirrel Story
author: BDEhrman
description: Begins a Princeton anecdote about Bruce Metzger and the Greek word for squirrel.
searchSummary: Recounts the Princeton Seminary legend in which Bruce Metzger responds to a squirrel's fatal fall by announcing that he knows the Greek word for squirrel. Ehrman follows variants that change the language, substitute different companions, and expand the exchange, showing how oral tradition altered the anecdote as it circulated. A colleague's observation that Metzger would simply provide the word rather than boast about knowing it suggests that the familiar form was invented or reshaped, leaving its origin for the sequel.

title: Paul the Persecutor and the Historical Jesus
author: BDEhrman
description: Addresses why Paul likely lacked firsthand knowledge of Jesus' crucifixion despite persecuting Christians.

title: Autobiographical.  Metzger and Me:  Metzger’s Faith
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes Bruce Metzger's old-school piety and theological outlook.
searchSummary: Describes Bruce Metzger's traditional but nonfundamentalist Christianity and its relationship to his exceptional scholarship. Metzger accepted biblical myths, discrepancies, and at least one pseudonymous writing while treating Scripture as inspired, praying regularly, preaching, and remaining deeply pious throughout life. Ehrman contrasts their divergent beliefs but rejects the assumption that religious commitment indicates intellectual weakness: Metzger's faith did not compromise his philological brilliance, vast historical knowledge, or critical scholarship, and personal belief does not determine scholarly ability.

title: Some Questions on the Greek
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers questions about paleography, Greek writing styles, and manuscript dating.

title: Reflections on Books
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on books, travel to London, and progress on a Bible introduction textbook.
searchSummary: Reviews Ehrman's scholarly and textbook work over the preceding year while explaining how he evaluates progress and plans future writing. He discusses completing Forgery and Counterforgery, updating a major collection on New Testament textual criticism, and revising A Brief Introduction to the New Testament. The post distinguishes original monographs from collaborative reference works and recurring textbook editions, emphasizing the research, editing, translation, and bibliographic updates required to keep each kind of publication useful.

title: Autobiographical.  Metzger and Me: Serving as his Teaching Assistant
author: BDEhrman
description: Recalls serving as Bruce Metzger's teaching assistant at Princeton.
searchSummary: Recalls serving as Bruce Metzger's teaching assistant and learning both efficiency and scholarly discipline. While Ehrman graded large numbers of exegesis papers, Metzger urged complete fairness without unnecessary labor, expressing practical principles about recognizing weak work, completing chores promptly, and using waiting time productively. Ehrman especially admired how Metzger combined exceptional philological talent with humility and relentless work, a model that encouraged him to maximize his own more limited gifts in research and teaching rather than rely on ability alone.

title: Wisdom as God’s Consort in the Beginning
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents Woman Wisdom in Proverbs as a possible figure connected with God's divine household.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: Possibly of Some Interest
author: BDEhrman
description: Points readers to a defense of critical biblical scholarship against biblical inerrancy.
searchSummary: Highlights Ron Hendel's defense of methodological doubt in critical biblical scholarship. Rather than beginning with certainty about scriptural inerrancy or relying on spiritual illumination alone, critical inquiry questions inherited authority and tests interpretations against evidence. Conclusions that survive scrutiny become more reliable while remaining open to future revision. Hendel also notes that inspiration was not always equated with complete inerrancy, since Reformers such as Calvin and Luther acknowledged errors or limited human perspectives in biblical passages.

title: Autobiographical.  Metzger and Me:  My Dissertation Proposal
author: BDEhrman
description: Recalls a dissertation proposal and Bruce Metzger's mentoring style.
searchSummary: Recounts the unusually severe critique Bruce Metzger gave Ehrman's dissertation proposal on Didymus the Blind. Because Princeton's committee resisted historical textual projects without a theological agenda, Metzger knew the proposal had to be exceptionally clear and persuasive, so he dissected its style and substance line by line instead of offering his usual brief praise and punctuation corrections. Though devastated, Ehrman recognized the effort as support and resolved to learn the disciplined writing needed to communicate original scholarship effectively.

title: A Virgin Birth?  The Importance of Context
author: BDEhrman
description: Uses Isaiah and the virgin birth to show why historical context matters for interpretation.
searchSummary: Uses Isaiah 7:14 to demonstrate why biblical passages must be interpreted in their own historical contexts. Isaiah addresses King Ahaz during a military crisis and predicts that a pregnant young woman will bear a child before Judah's enemies withdraw; the Hebrew does not mention a virgin or future Messiah. Matthew, using a Greek translation whose wording could mean virgin, reapplies the verse to Jesus. Understanding Isaiah's original message and Matthew's later fulfillment claim requires keeping their different contexts distinct.

title: Autobiographical: Metzger and Me.  The Seminar on the Canon
author: BDEhrman
description: Recalls Metzger's seminar on canon lists and its role in later work on Didymus.
