searchSummary: Recounts how a graduate seminar with Bruce Metzger led to research challenging the idea that Athanasius finalized the New Testament canon in 367. Translating ancient canon lists and studying Didymus the Blind revealed that this contemporary Alexandrian teacher treated 1 Clement, the Shepherd of Hermas, and Barnabas as Scripture. The evidence demonstrated continuing disagreement even in Athanasius's city and became Ehrman's first scholarly publication, while also broadening his work beyond New Testament textual criticism.

title: The Suffering Servant of Isaiah
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the Suffering Servant in Second Isaiah and its later importance for Christian interpretation.

title: Autobiographical.  Metzger and Me: Beginning the PhD Program
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes beginning the PhD program at Princeton and focusing on textual criticism with Metzger.
searchSummary: Describes Ehrman's entry into Princeton's New Testament PhD program as Bruce Metzger's only advisee amid faculty focused mainly on exegesis and theology. While Ehrman's faith was becoming more liberal, intensive Greek seminars demanded close textual interpretation and international scholarship. Metzger's canon seminar began with the difficult Latin Muratorian Fragment and questions about how authoritative Christian books were selected, immediately establishing the program's linguistic demands and giving Ehrman concentrated access to the mentor whose historical interests matched his own.

title: Autobiographical: Metzger and Me.  My First Work on the Text
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the relationship with Bruce Metzger and early work on the New Testament text.
searchSummary: Recounts the beginning of Ehrman's close academic relationship with Bruce Metzger at Princeton Seminary. Guided by a Wheaton professor, Ehrman sought the leading textual critic, wrote an award-winning master's thesis evaluating Majority Text arguments, and entered the PhD program as Metzger's final doctoral student. Metzger's extraordinary command of ancient languages, manuscripts, and early Christian history, along with his support in research, publishing, and professional service, made him a father figure and established the scholarly path Ehrman continued to pursue.

title: The Sons of God and the Daughters of Men
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the Genesis story of the sons of God, the daughters of men, and the Nephilim.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

title: Introduction to the Bible: Part 1
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a Bible textbook by explaining why the Bible matters historically and culturally.

title: Creation in 4004 BCE?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains James Ussher's calculation of creation in 4004 BCE from biblical genealogies.

title: Income from Books
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers a question about income from scholarly books, textbooks, and trade books.
searchSummary: Compares the economics of scholarly books, college textbooks, and trade books while noting that authors do not set retail prices. Scholarly monographs usually earn little and may require publication subsidies; textbooks can provide steady income only when widely and repeatedly adopted; and trade books can earn substantially when they sell well but usually have short commercial lives. Ehrman stresses that most books in all three markets do not produce significant income despite their different prices and audiences.

title: My Colleague’s Archaeological Find!
author: BDEhrman
description: Reports a colleague's archaeological discovery as an example of careful professional archaeology.
searchSummary: Highlights Jodi Magness's discovery of an ancient synagogue floor mosaic in Israel as an example of careful archaeological work. The find challenges the widespread assumption that ancient Jews rejected pictorial art, including human images, in places of worship. Ehrman contrasts such methodical discoveries by established archaeologists with sensational claims that reach the news despite being doubtful or rejected by specialists.

title: My Bible Introduction
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes work on a fifteen-chapter Bible textbook and the challenge of writing for students.

title: My Next Book
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the next major writing project and the different audiences for different kinds of books.
searchSummary: Describes Ehrman's three publishing audiences and his concentrated method for drafting a new college textbook on the entire Bible. He distinguishes technical scholarship, general-audience trade books, and classroom textbooks, then explains how complete preparation lets him write for six or seven focused hours and produce thousands of words in a day. His immediate goal was eight Hebrew Bible chapters in two weeks, driven by strict isolation, daily routines, and eagerness to reach the next research project.

title: Q & A with Ben Witherington: Part 10 (and last!)
author: BDEhrman
description: Distinguishes Jewish resurrection belief from pagan fertility and death-and-return motifs.
searchSummary: Begins distinguishing Jewish resurrection belief from pagan stories about fertility gods who disappear, die, and return with recurring seasonal cycles. Ehrman locates Jesus and his earliest followers within first-century Jewish apocalyptic thought rather than pagan mythology. The complete locally preserved post is a brief question-and-answer fragment that introduces this contrast but ends before developing the Jewish understanding of resurrection or applying it fully to early Christian claims about Jesus.

title: Q & A with Ben Witherington: Part 10 (the last!)
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the final Witherington Q&A section on resurrection in Jewish apocalyptic context.
searchSummary: Distinguishes early Christian belief in Jesus' resurrection from pagan myths about fertility gods who cyclically descend and return with the seasons. Jesus and his followers were Jewish apocalypticists who expected God soon to defeat evil, raise the dead for judgment, and establish an earthly kingdom. Jesus' resurrection signaled that this final sequence had begun, making him the “first fruits” before everyone else. The belief therefore arose from Jewish apocalyptic expectation, not from stories of annually dying and rising gods.

title: Helping Charity and Improving My Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Connects blog fundraising, charitable giving, and debate claims about the problem of suffering.
searchSummary: Reflects on claims that conservative Christians give more to charity than liberal nonbelievers and argues that humanists should respond through greater generosity. Bart explains that charitable impact, rather than self-promotion, motivates the time he devotes to the blog, which had raised more than $8,000 in its first months. He asks readers to donate, suggest low-effort improvements, and identify ways to attract more members so the project can provide scholarship while helping hungry and homeless people.

title: Q & A with Ben Witherington: Part 9
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues the Witherington Q&A on Did Jesus Exist and mythicist criticism.
searchSummary: Critiques G. A. Wells's theory that an obscure Jesus lived a century earlier while first-century Christians independently invented a divine Christ from Jewish personifications of Wisdom. Paul's references do not fit a remote figure, and the earliest traditions identify Jesus primarily as the recently crucified Messiah rather than as Wisdom. Because Jewish Wisdom texts never call Wisdom the Messiah, they cannot plausibly generate the entire Christ story. Ehrman concludes that Christians knew a recent Jesus had lived and been executed.

title: Would We Recognize an Original Manuscript?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why an original New Testament manuscript would probably not be recognizable as original.

title: Outta here (for a couple of days)
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a brief absence from the blog and delayed responses to comments.

title: The Hebrew Bible and Its Sources
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends resources on Hebrew Bible composition and the Documentary Hypothesis.
secondaryKeywords: Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman

title: Q & A with Ben Witherington: Part 8
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues the Witherington Q&A on mythicism and the aims of Did Jesus Exist.
searchSummary: Explains why alleged pagan precedents for Jesus' resurrection do not support mythicism. Jonathan Z. Smith's close examination of ancient sources showed that supposed dying-and-rising gods either disappear and return without dying or die without returning; the category rested on late, ambiguous, or reconstructed evidence. No new discoveries produced this correction, only more careful analysis. Ehrman argues that mythicists continue using a dated comparison even though scholarship no longer recognizes an unambiguous pre-Christian pattern from which Jesus' resurrection was simply copied.

title: Why Did “Orthodox” Christianity Win: Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares Eusebius, Walter Bauer, and later scholarly views on orthodoxy and heresy.
searchSummary: Explains how proto-orthodox Christianity gained dominance amid a diversity even greater than Walter Bauer described. Later discoveries and regional studies reveal Jewish-Christian, Marcionite, Gnostic, and other movements alongside a widespread but not universal proto-orthodoxy. The victorious movement developed three institutional advantages: clergy who enforced doctrine through hierarchy, creeds that defined required beliefs, and a canon attributed to apostles that authorized those beliefs and excluded alternatives. By the late third century these mechanisms had marginalized many rivals before Constantine's conversion.

title: Why Did “Orthodox” Christianity Win?
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses why one form of Christianity won out amid early Christian diversity.
searchSummary: Contrasts Eusebius's traditional account of original Christian orthodoxy with Walter Bauer's historical model of competing early Christianities. Eusebius portrayed apostolic truth as always dominant and heresies as later demonic corruptions; Bauer argued that forms later condemned were sometimes the earliest known Christianity in particular regions. Roman Christianity's wealth, organization, and eventual imperial association helped its theology prevail. The winners then preserved their books, destroyed rivals' works, and rewrote the conflict as an unbroken transmission of apostolic truth.

title: Q & A with Ben Witherington: Part 7
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues the Witherington Q&A on mythicism, Old Testament parallels, and evidence for Jesus.
searchSummary: Distinguishes literary shaping from historical invention in claims that Gospel stories imitate the Old Testament or pagan divine men. Matthew can present Jesus as a new Moses, and miracle traditions can use familiar heroic patterns, without implying that Jesus never lived; patterned stories also surround known historical figures. Genuine ancient parallels exist, but virginal conception and bodily resurrection are not standard pagan motifs. Historical existence must therefore be tested with independent evidence rather than inferred from a narrative's recognizable form.

title: The Growth of Early Christianity: A Clarification
author: BDEhrman
description: Clarifies Constantine's importance while focusing on Christian growth before the fourth century.
searchSummary: Clarifies that Ehrman's question concerns Christianity's growth before Constantine rather than the emperor's transformative fourth-century support. Beginning with perhaps twenty resurrection believers around 30, the movement reached an estimated three million adherents, about five percent of the Roman Empire, in under three centuries. He asks what early Christians said or did that proved sufficiently compelling to generate such exponential expansion and notes that existing historical explanations, though substantial, do not fully resolve the problem.

title: Why Did Christianity Succeed?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains questions about Christianity's success and the rise of orthodox Christianity.
searchSummary: Explains two central factors in Christianity's victory over Roman religions. Christians appealed to the familiar ancient expectation that gods demonstrate power through healing, protection, prosperity, and miracles, while claiming their God possessed greater power than all rivals. Unlike additive pagan worship, Christianity also demanded exclusive allegiance and threatened punishment for worshiping other gods. Consequently, every Christian conversion removed an adherent from pagan practice, allowing a missionary movement to expand while steadily shrinking competing traditions that remained inclusive.

title: Q & A with Ben Witherington: Part 6
author: BDEhrman
description: Addresses interpolation arguments used by mythicists and critical scholars.
searchSummary: Distinguishes plausible textual interpolations from convenient attempts to dismiss New Testament passages that contradict a preferred theory. Because an interpolation appears in every surviving manuscript, accepting one requires unusually compelling, case-specific evidence; Ehrman finds that standard met for 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 but not for mythicist removals of Paul's references to Jesus. He also rejects claims that Nazareth's alleged nonexistence disproves Jesus, noting both the logical non sequitur and archaeological evidence for the village.

title: Some Reading Suggestions on the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends balanced scholarly books on the New Testament and early Christianity.
searchSummary: Recommends resources that expose readers to balanced and competing perspectives on the New Testament. Ehrman urges students to examine arguments he disagrees with, weigh evidence, and form their own conclusions. Suggested starting points include historical introductions by Dale Martin and Raymond Brown, one-volume Bible commentaries for passage-level interpretation, and scholarly Bible dictionaries for topical background and bibliography. The recommendations emphasize reputable academic expertise rather than a single ideological or theological viewpoint.

title: Q & A with Ben Witherington: Part 5
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers Witherington's questions about Paul, Gospel sources, and evidence for the historical Jesus.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: My Apocrypha Seminar at the National Humanities Center: Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes a National Humanities Center seminar on non-canonical Gospels, Acts, epistles, and apocalypses.

title: Q & A with Ben Witherington: Part 4
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues the Witherington Q&A on oral tradition, multiple attestation, and evidence for Jesus.
searchSummary: Presents three arguments for Jesus' existence: multiple independent sources, Paul's contact with Peter and James, and the proclamation of a crucified Messiah. Early traditions trace claims about Jesus close to Palestinian origins, while Paul knew Jesus' disciple and brother. Jewish expectations envisioned victorious messianic figures, not someone executed by enemies, so followers seeking converts would not invent a crucified Messiah. Ehrman concludes that they called Jesus Messiah despite crucifixion because both the man and his execution were historical.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

title: Personal Reflections: My Apocrypha Seminar at the National Humanities Center
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on summer academic work while leading an apocrypha seminar.
searchSummary: Describes a three-week National Humanities Center seminar for college professors on what early Christian apocrypha reveal about Christianity. Participants from varied disciplines read noncanonical Gospels, Acts, letters, and apocalypses alongside scholarship on topics such as Gnosticism. Ehrman explains the seminar's intensive schedule, institutional setting, and unusually engaged discussions, while also using the experience to illustrate the substantial preparation and summer work that can accompany a university scholar's teaching responsibilities.

title: Which Charities Does The Blog Support?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains which charities the blog supports and addresses concerns about administrative costs.
searchSummary: Answers questions about how blog revenue is administered and which organizations receive it. Bart states that he takes no income, personally pays all operating expenses, and sends every donated dollar to charity. He identifies Urban Ministries of Durham, the Food Bank of Central and Eastern North Carolina, CARE, and Doctors Without Borders, describing their local and international work against poverty, hunger, and homelessness. Readers may raise concerns and make additional tax-deductible donations through the site.

title: Q & A with Ben Witherington: Part 3
author: BDEhrman
description: Addresses Josephus, Celsus, and non-Christian evidence related to Jesus.

title: Should We Change the Canon of Scripture?
author: BDEhrman
description: Considers whether the New Testament canon should change in light of authorship questions.
searchSummary: Explains why books accepted under mistaken apostolic attributions remain in the New Testament. Ancient leaders favored writings considered early, widely used, orthodox, and apostolic, but often inferred authorship from acceptable theology rather than close literary analysis. Modern scholars dispute traditional authorship for Hebrews, Revelation, and several attributed letters, yet the canon rests on durable religious claims about inspiration and authority. Historical scholarship can reassess authorship, but it cannot practically revise the established collection.

title: Q & A with Ben Witherington: Part 2
author: BDEhrman
description: Continues the Witherington Q&A on evidence for Jesus' existence in Paul and other sources.
searchSummary: Explains why the absence of contemporary public records does not count against a non-miraculous historical Jesus, since most ordinary ancient people went unmentioned. Whether Jesus performed spectacular miracles is a separate question that should not be assumed before testing his existence. Later pagan and Jewish references offer limited corroboration, but the strongest evidence comes from numerous Christian sources, especially Paul's early letters and personal acquaintance with Peter and James. Bias requires critical evaluation, not automatic rejection of useful evidence.

title: Was Jesus an Essene?
author: BDEhrman
description: Assesses whether Jesus or John the Baptist were influenced by the Essenes.
searchSummary: Asks whether Jesus or John the Baptist learned their apocalyptic message from the Essene community at Qumran. The Dead Sea Scrolls show shared expectations that evil powers would soon be destroyed and God's kingdom established, but no source connects either figure to the sect. Essene withdrawal and rigorous purity directly conflict with Jesus' and John's outreach to sinners, showing parallel Jewish apocalyptic beliefs rather than institutional dependence.

title: Q&A With Ben Witherington: Part 1
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a Witherington Q&A series about Did Jesus Exist and mythicist criticism.
searchSummary: Explains why Ehrman wrote Did Jesus Exist before a planned book on how Jesus became regarded as God. Internet mythicism was gaining an audience despite the absence of a book-length response by a specialist, and examining deification logically presupposed deciding whether Jesus lived. Ehrman frames existence as a historical question distinct from theology, exegesis, textual criticism, and miracle claims. He also suggests that some atheist mythicism is driven by opposition to Christianity, allowing an ideological goal to shape historical conclusions.

title: Which Bible Translation Do I Prefer?
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends Bible translations and comments on reliability, bias, and readability.

title: The Work of the Professional Scholar 10:  Editorial Work (Books)
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes editorial work for scholarly book series as part of professional scholarship.

title: My Views on Suffering Are Not Held by Those Who Suffer
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to the debate objection that views on suffering differ from the views of those who suffer.
searchSummary: Responds to the objection that people who suffer often retain faith and therefore undermine Ehrman's argument from suffering. He notes that some lose faith through tragedy, while any belief's emotional comfort or popularity among sufferers does not establish its truth. Those enduring deprivation need not share either his theological analysis or a conservative economist's account of poverty. Ehrman presents agnosticism as his personal conclusion, not a demand on others, and urges humility and compassionate action toward those in need.

title: Am I an Agnostic or an Atheist?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains why Ehrman identifies as an agnostic rather than an atheist.
searchSummary: Clarifies Ehrman's preference for the label agnostic while acknowledging that atheist also describes him. He treats atheism as a statement of belief: he does not believe in traditional gods or the Judeo-Christian God. Agnosticism concerns knowledge: he does not know whether some spiritual power or intelligence exists and doubts anyone else knows either. Because the categories address different questions, they can coexist, but he emphasizes agnosticism as a scholar interested in knowledge and in humility before an incompletely understood universe.

title: Religion in the News: Dating Jesus’ Death by the Earthquake
author: BDEhrman
description: Evaluates a geological claim that an earthquake can date Jesus' death to April 3, 33 CE.
searchSummary: Rejects a geological claim that Matthew's crucifixion earthquake dates Jesus' death to April 3, 33 CE. Matthew alone reports the quake alongside darkness, a torn Temple curtain, opened graves, resurrected corpses, and a gentile centurion's confession. These details convey theological meanings about cosmic upheaval, access to God, resurrection, and recognition of the suffering Messiah rather than eyewitness events. Matching seismic evidence to this symbolic narrative therefore cannot establish a historical date and instead misuses the text.

title: The Life of a Professional Scholar 9:  Editorial Work, Journals (2)
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the work of editing academic journals and managing peer review.

title: At the Beach (3): Thinking Yet More of Books
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on books, reading, writing, and scholarly friendships during a beach trip.
searchSummary: Reflects on Ehrman's lifelong immersion in books, from nineteenth-century novels to biblical texts, and how reading helps him consider character, values, modernity, and the meaning of human life. Although he is an agnostic who does not regard the Bible as God's word, he studies it for its literary power, historical influence, and capacity to provoke deep thought. Contradictory voices across literature and history together shape the intellectual and ethical framework through which he understands himself.

title: Question: Would I Be Personally Devastated if the Mythicists Were Right?
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to whether proving mythicism true would be personally devastating.
searchSummary: Explains that Ehrman would not be devastated if evidence proved Jesus never existed and might find the discovery energizing. He contrasts historical inquiry with Christian attempts to prove resurrection and atheist efforts to discredit Christianity through mythicism, both of which can confirm prior commitments. His studies instead changed his preferred portrait of Jesus into an apocalyptic prophet he considers mistaken. Historians must identify their stakes, follow evidence, and revise conclusions rather than reshape the past to serve belief or unbelief.

title: At the Beach (2): Reflecting on Books
author: BDEhrman
description: Reflects on reading and writing books during a beach stay.
searchSummary: Reflects on a productive publishing year and the different kinds of work completed or moving through production. Ehrman discusses Did Jesus Exist, a multilingual edition of apocryphal Gospels, a revised New Testament textbook, an updated collaborative reference work on textual criticism, and his major monograph Forgery and Counterforgery. He explains the purpose and audience of each project while emphasizing the satisfaction of finishing years of intensive research and preparing to move toward new books.

title: Personal Reflections: At the Beach
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces personal reflections from the beach and their connection to academic life.
searchSummary: Begins a series of personal posts by describing Ehrman's annual beach retreat with his wife, Sarah, and New Testament scholar Dale Martin. Their days combine reading, long walks, lively conversations, food, and friendship, while Ehrman works through the copyedited manuscript of Forgery and Counterforgery. The post connects restorative time with loved ones to the practical routines of scholarly life, including languages, novels, blogging, and the demanding final stages of preparing a major academic book for publication.

title: Personal Reflections Page
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a new blog category for personal reflections.

title: The Life of a Professional Scholar 8:  Editorial Work, Journals (1)
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces editorial board work for academic journals as professional service.

title: Question on How We Got the Canon of the New Testament
author: BDEhrman
description: Recommends resources on how the New Testament canon developed.
searchSummary: Recommends major studies of New Testament canon formation and summarizes the historical process they address. Different early Christian communities recognized competing Gospels, letters, and other works as Scripture, while the tradition that became orthodox ultimately shaped the prevailing collection. Athanasius first listed the familiar twenty-seven books in 367, centuries after their composition, but disagreement continued. Proto-orthodox leaders generally judged candidate writings by antiquity, apostolic connection, widespread use, and theological conformity.

title: Undergraduate Courses (2): Introduction to the New Testament (Part 2)
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how an Introduction to the New Testament course moves from Gospel content to historical criteria.
searchSummary: Explains the historical Jesus portion of Ehrman's introductory New Testament course after students have studied the Gospels as distinct literary works. The class examines non-Gospel references to Jesus, the limitations of sources written decades later, and scholarly criteria such as multiple attestation, dissimilarity, and contextual credibility. Applying these methods supports basic conclusions about Jesus' Jewish setting, baptism, Galilean ministry, crucifixion, and especially his proclamation of God's approaching apocalyptic kingdom.

title: Did the Gospels Originally Contain Miracle Stories?
author: BDEhrman
description: Answers whether the earliest Gospel manuscripts preserve miracle stories.
searchSummary: Explains why surviving Gospel manuscripts from around 200 do not imply that miracle stories were added only then. Independent Greek manuscripts, early translations, later witnesses descended from earlier copies, and second-century church-father quotations all preserve the same miracle traditions without evidence of non-miraculous versions. Ehrman concludes that the Gospels originally contained miracle stories, while distinguishing that textual conclusion from the separate historical question of whether the miracles occurred.

title: Undergraduate Courses (1): Introduction to the New Testament (Part 1)
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes an undergraduate Introduction to the New Testament course and teaching at a research university.
searchSummary: Describes the first portion of Ehrman's introductory New Testament course and its rigorously historical textbook and method. After surveying Greco-Roman and Jewish contexts, students study each Gospel separately, compare discrepancies in birth, crucifixion, and resurrection accounts, and identify each author's distinctive message. These literary comparisons also expose historical problems, preparing the class to evaluate what the Gospels and selected noncanonical writings can reliably reveal about the historical Jesus.

title: Why Did Jesus Go To Jerusalem?
author: BDEhrman
description: Examines why the historical Jesus went to Jerusalem before the crucifixion.
searchSummary: Argues that Jesus traveled to Jerusalem to proclaim his urgent apocalyptic message, not to arrange his own sacrificial death or enact a resurrection plot. During Passover he warned crowds that God would soon judge Romans as well as Jerusalem's priestly aristocracy and destroy the temple. Local authorities viewed his growing audience as a threat to public order, delivered him to Pilate, and secured his crucifixion. Bart concludes that Jesus's message unexpectedly caused his death.

title: The Work of a Professional Scholar 7: Publishing in Academic Journals
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains academic journal publishing and its role in scholarly research.

title: Question on Mistakes in Ancient Sources
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how modern historians evaluate mistakes in ancient sources.
searchSummary: Explains how modern scholars can know ancient events better than people who lived near them. Contemporaries regularly lacked accurate maps, records, communication, and specialized knowledge, while today's historians can compare multiple surviving sources and test their disagreements. Living through an era does not make someone expert on distant events within it, just as an eyewitness to wartime society may know less than a later specialist. Ancient Gospel discrepancies show why contemporary testimony still requires critical evaluation rather than automatic deference.

title: Question about Eyewitnesses and the Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Addresses whether Gospel traditions could stem from eyewitness testimony within living memory.
searchSummary: Explains that eyewitnesses may have remained alive when Mark was written, but their existence does not establish that Gospel authors consulted them. Surviving followers were largely Aramaic-speaking rural Galileans, while the evangelists were educated Greek-speaking Christians writing elsewhere and never claimed direct interviews. Matthew, Luke, and John inherited stories that had circulated for decades across languages and countries, where repeated retelling could alter existing accounts and generate new ones.

title: The Work of a Professional Scholar 6: Getting the PhD
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes the training required for professional New Testament and early Christian scholarship.
searchSummary: Explains the extensive preparation required for professional scholarship in New Testament and early Christianity. Ehrman's path included an MDiv, Greek exegesis, Hebrew, German, French, Latin, and Coptic, doctoral seminars and examinations, and original dissertation research reconstructing Didymus the Blind's Gospel text. He argues that expertise rests on languages, disciplinary literature, historical knowledge, and scholarship that advances the field, making doctoral study worthwhile only for people whose passion for intellectual work can sustain years of rigorous training.

title: Did Jesus Exist?  The Birth of a Divine Man
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains mythicist claims about Jesus as an invented divine man.
searchSummary: Refutes claims that pagan divine men closely parallel Jesus from virgin conception through crucifixion and ascension. Kersey Graves's comparisons combine unrelated figures and misdescribe ancient traditions. Pagan heroes such as Alexander, Helen, and Heracles have supernatural births, but their mortal mothers conceive through sexual encounters with gods in human or animal form. Ehrman finds no genuine pagan example of a mother remaining physically untouched, so divine paternity is not equivalent to the Christian claim of virginal conception.

title: The Work of a Professional Scholar 5: Graduate Seminars
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes graduate seminars in ancient Mediterranean religions and early Christianity at UNC.
searchSummary: Describes UNC's doctoral seminars in New Testament and early Christianity as intensive training in languages, primary sources, scholarship, discussion, and original research. Ehrman highlights a textual criticism seminar and surveys courses on forgery, the Apostolic Fathers, apocrypha, anti-Judaism, orthodoxy and heresy, and foundational New Testament studies. Small classes, collaboration with Duke, extensive reading, and publishable research papers prepare students to become the next generation of scholar-teachers.

title: Dates of the Gospels
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains how scholars date the Gospels using internal evidence and source relationships.

title: Did Jesus Exist as Part One
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains Did Jesus Exist as part of a larger project on how Jesus came to be seen as divine.

title: The Work of a Professional Scholar 4: Undergraduate Courses
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes undergraduate teaching expectations at a research university and their relation to research.
searchSummary: Explains how Ehrman's undergraduate teaching fits the expectations of a research university. His large introductory New Testament course combines historical lectures with small teaching-assistant-led discussions, while other courses address Jesus in scholarship and film, Paul, early Christian diversity, Christianity's expansion, apocalypticism, and biblical suffering. He contrasts this teaching with faculty research demands and emphasizes the personal satisfaction of making scholarship accessible, challenging students' assumptions, and encouraging deeper thought about important historical questions.

title: The Work of a Professional Scholar 3: Undergraduate Theses
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes directing undergraduate independent studies and honors theses.
searchSummary: Explains how senior honors theses give undergraduates their first sustained experience of original research. Ehrman illustrates the process through projects on atoning interpretations of the Passover lamb and apologetic themes in Luke-Acts, both requiring narrow but complex questions, substantial scholarly reading, yearlong writing, and oral defense. Because undergraduates usually lack graduate-level languages and experience, the work tests their aptitude and motivation; unfinished theses can become independent studies while still clarifying whether research belongs in their future.

title: The Work of a Professional Scholar 2: Supervising PhD Dissertations
author: BDEhrman
description: Describes supervising PhD dissertations as part of professional scholarly work.
searchSummary: Describes doctoral dissertation supervision as demanding work that also broadens a professor's intellectual life. Advanced students produce expert, book-length studies using specialized evidence and methods, while advisers and committee members must understand enough to evaluate their originality and defensibility. Projects on inscriptions, manuscripts, martyrdom, Josephus, Paul's mission, resurrection visions, and Syriac traditions show the field's range, explaining why graduate mentorship consumes substantial time yet continually leads faculty into questions they would not otherwise investigate.

title: The Work of the Professional Scholar 1: Introduction
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces a series explaining what professional scholars do.
searchSummary: Introduces a series explaining the varied work performed by senior faculty at research universities. Using his own career as a representative case, Ehrman plans to examine dissertation supervision, writing, editing, teaching, undergraduate research, languages, professional reading, doctoral preparation, conferences, and seminars. The purpose is not to settle whether experts possess special authority, but to show readers outside academia the activities, training, and obligations that underlie a professional scholar's judgments and daily use of time.

title: A Recent Interview
author: BDEhrman
description: Shares a restored interview about Did Jesus Exist and historical Jesus questions.
searchSummary: Presents a restored interview about Did Jesus Exist? and the historical Jesus. Ehrman explains why scholars had rarely defended Jesus' existence systematically, rejects modern efforts to remake Jesus as a middle-class American rather than a Jewish apocalyptic prophet, and urges cooperation between religious and humanist communities in helping suffering people. He argues that belief in Jesus' resurrection distinguished his followers from other messianic movements and transformed concepts of messiah, God, Jewish law, salvation, and the identity of God's people.

title: The Irony of our Earliest Manuscripts
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains the irony that the earliest New Testament manuscripts are fragmentary and still removed from the originals.
searchSummary: Explains the irony that the earliest New Testament manuscripts are both closest to the originals and often copied by less skilled scribes. Most surviving manuscripts are medieval, while early papyri are sparse, fragmentary, and frequently differ from one another. Because copying errors accumulated and many textual changes arose before 300, these early witnesses offer indispensable evidence about transmission while also making reconstruction of original wording especially difficult.

title: For the “Original” Text: What Kinds of Manuscripts Would We Need?
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains what manuscript evidence would be needed to know the original New Testament text with certainty.
searchSummary: Describes the manuscript evidence Ehrman would need to reconstruct the original New Testament with greater certainty. Thousands of surviving copies are mostly late, while the few early manuscripts are fragmentary and often contain more scribal errors despite being closer to the originals. He would want multiple extensive or complete first- and second-century copies whose agreements and differences could expose individual mistakes and provide firmer evidence for authorial wording.

title: The Text of the New Testament:  Are the Textual Traditions of Other Ancient Works Relevant?
author: BDEhrman
description: Compares the New Testament textual tradition with other ancient works and the limits of knowing originals.
searchSummary: Challenges the argument that the New Testament's far greater number of manuscripts guarantees knowledge of its original wording. Classical texts also generate substantial textual disputes, and being better attested than other works does not make the evidence sufficient. Because most New Testament manuscripts are many centuries late and early extensive copies are missing, Ehrman believes scholars can often approximate authorial texts but cannot verify their reconstructions with certainty.

title: A Final (for now) Post on the Resurrection
author: BDEhrman
description: Explains resurrection as a Jewish apocalyptic idea behind early belief in Jesus' resurrection.
searchSummary: Explains Jesus' resurrection as an event interpreted through first-century Jewish apocalypticism. Earlier Jewish texts generally anticipated extinction or existence in Sheol, but apocalyptic thinkers expected God soon to overthrow evil, raise everyone bodily, punish opponents, and reward the faithful in an earthly kingdom. Jesus' followers concluded that his resurrection inaugurated this final process, with the general resurrection imminent. When the end did not arrive, Christians revised the meanings of resurrection, God's kingdom, and their expectation of an immediate climax.

title: More on the Resurrection
author: BDEhrman
description: Discusses uncertainty about the empty tomb, resurrection belief, and the timing of that belief.

title: Another Question on the Resurrection
author: BDEhrman
description: Explores how belief in Jesus' resurrection may have begun after the crucifixion.

title: Response to Carrier
author: BDEhrman
description: Announces a fuller response to Richard Carrier's criticisms of Did Jesus Exist.
searchSummary: Announces that Ehrman is preparing a fuller public response to Richard Carrier's accusations of factual error in Did Jesus Exist. Although other obligations delay the reply, he says he takes charges of scholarly incompetence seriously and intends to address them at length rather than answer each inquiry separately. In the meantime, he recommends a critical and humorous post by established early Christianity scholar R. Joseph Hoffmann, offering readers another informed perspective on Carrier, mythicism, and the controversy surrounding the book.

title: What Do Tectonic Plates Have To Do With Suffering?
author: BDEhrman
description: Challenges free-will explanations for natural suffering such as earthquakes.
searchSummary: Rejects free will as a complete explanation for suffering because it addresses human-caused moral evil but not disasters, disease, drought, or starvation. Dinesh D'Souza argues that tectonic activity and its dangers were necessary for life to evolve. Ehrman replies that this limits an all-powerful creator to existing physical laws and makes victims' misery instrumental to humanity's existence. Rather than treating suffering as necessary for fortunate observers, believers should admit uncertainty, share victims' pain, and work to reduce it.

title: Acharya S, Richard Carrier, and a Cocky Peter (Or: “A Cock and Bull Story”)
author: BDEhrman
description: Responds to Richard Carrier and Acharya S in the debate over mythicism.
searchSummary: Responds to Richard Carrier's charge that Ehrman falsely denied the existence of a penis-nosed rooster statue allegedly representing Peter. Ehrman's claim was that no such statue of Peter exists: the artifact may be real, but its inscription and iconography identify Priapus, not Jesus' disciple. Carrier isolated wording from context, mistook acknowledgment of an object for validation of Acharya S's interpretation, and used a peripheral complaint to allege incompetence without affecting the book's historical case.

title: Concerns for the Blog
author: BDEhrman
description: Addresses concerns about membership fees, blog access, and the charity purpose of the site.

title: Richard Carrier on The Huffington Post Article (1)
author: BDEhrman
description: Replies to Richard Carrier's criticism of a Huffington Post summary of Did Jesus Exist.
searchSummary: Defends the claim that no scholar trained in New Testament or early Christianity and teaching in an accredited institution endorses mythicism. Richard Carrier cites Hebrew Bible scholar Thomas Thompson, but expertise in Israelite history does not confer authority in a different period and field. Ehrman stresses that consensus is not evidence; broad agreement instead reflects specialists' assessment of evidence presented in Did Jesus Exist. Thompson's contrary view receives treatment but does not invalidate the narrower disciplinary claim.

title: Do My Research Assistants Do All My Work For Me?
author: BDEhrman
description: Defends scholarly integrity against claims about research assistants and Did Jesus Exist.
searchSummary: Rejects accusations that research assistants performed Ehrman's mythicist research for Did Jesus Exist. He normally asks graduate assistants to summarize scholarship only to prioritize his own reading, never as a substitute for examining cited sources. For this book, assistants worked on references for Forgery and Counterforgery while Ehrman personally read and annotated the mythicist literature. He distinguishes disagreement over evidence from unsupported allegations of dishonesty and explains that assistantships provide paid research experience without transferring scholarly responsibility.

title: What Charities Does The Blog Support?
author: BDEhrman
description: Identifies the charities supported by the blog and states that proceeds go to charity.
searchSummary: Explains the blog's charitable purpose shortly after its launch and assures prospective members that Bart personally covers administration while all revenue supports humanitarian work. He identifies Urban Ministries of Durham, the regional Food Bank, CARE, and Doctors Without Borders as the two local and two international beneficiaries. Bart describes the blog as a way to volunteer his scholarly expertise for people facing poverty, hunger, and homelessness and invites questions about the organizations or mission.

title: First-Century Copy of Mark? – Part 1
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces the debate over a claimed first-century fragment of the Gospel of Mark.
searchSummary: Recounts Dan Wallace's surprise announcement during a 2012 debate that a first-century copy of Mark had been discovered. Wallace would not reveal the fragment's size, provenance, dating method, expert, or independent verification, leading Ehrman to object to unverifiable evidence used as a debating point. Ehrman explains that even an authentic tiny scrap would be exciting but unlikely to alter textual criticism, unlike the Dead Sea Scrolls' extensive new writings and thousand-year advance in biblical manuscript evidence.

title: Q & A – Historical Events in Jesus Tradition
author: BDEhrman
description: Revisits claims about Joseph of Arimathea, the burial of Jesus, and the empty tomb.
searchSummary: Explains why Bart changed from treating Joseph of Arimathea's burial and the empty tomb as historical facts to doubting both traditions. Roman authorities rarely granted honorable burial to crucified victims, Joseph is unattested outside the Gospels, and Isaiah's reference to a rich man's tomb may have shaped the story. Bart still regards Jesus's crucifixion and some disciples' later claims of appearances as historical, but considers disposal in a common grave more plausible.

title: Latest HarperOne Book: Did Jesus Exist?
author: BDEhrman
description: Presents HarperOne's description of Did Jesus Exist and its argument for a historical Jesus.

title: Is Suffering All About Us?
author: BDEhrman
description: Critiques the argument that suffering can be justified by benefits to others.
searchSummary: Rejects the claim that extreme suffering is justified because it improves those who observe it. Mild personal hardship can produce growth, as hepatitis redirected Ehrman toward scholarship, but another person's agony is not a tool for one's development. He condemns Richard Swinburne's suggestion that the Holocaust helped ennoble humanity: genocide has no redeeming benefit for comfortable survivors. Accounts of victims should provoke horror and determined resistance to evil, not gratitude for lessons supposedly gained through their destruction.

title: Ben Witherington Critique
author: BDEhrman
description: Introduces evangelical critiques of Misquoting Jesus and debates over textual variants.
searchSummary: Responds to Ben Witherington's criticism that no New Testament textual variant threatens a central Christian doctrine. Ehrman distinguishes claiming that variants affect theologically important passages from claiming they destroy entire doctrines, which normally draw on many texts. He argues that doctrinal impact is an inadequate measure of significance because variants can still alter verses, narratives, an author's theology, or the interpretation of an entire book even when established creeds remain intact.
